Launchway platform plan

The story

Launchway launches applications into the future. A change is a flight: it is planned, checked, cleared, launched, watched while it flies, brought back to base if anything is wrong, and every moment of it is on the record.

  • One story holds for every module and every place software runs: a Kubernetes cluster, a virtual machine, a physical server, an image-based host or a serverless platform.
  • The promise is complete without being complicated: one model, one way to do each thing, a built-in default for everything, and every safeguard on from the start.
  • All 17 principles of the public roadmap stay as they are. This plan adds six, from what you said most recently.
  • Nothing you asked for is removed or narrowed. Status is honest: Available, In progress or Planned, tied to the exact titles on the roadmap.

A change is a flight

Every change you make goes through the same six moments. You plan it as a pipeline. Launchway checks it before take-off with Preflight (checks). The people who must agree give it Clearance (approval) with a Go. It is launched to an Airfield (environment). Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) judges it against live traffic and metrics. If things get worse, it comes back with Return to base (rollback), which is always possible and never blocked.

Each moment writes what it decided, and why, to one record. The Logbook (audit trail), the Debrief (test report), the metrics and the evidence for an auditor are all read from that same record. Nothing is true that is not on it.

One release of storefront, from a commit to prod and back

The plan uses one example everywhere, so the chapters read as one story. The Harbor Lights team is a small company. Its web shop is a Flight (codebase: one repository and its pipelines) named storefront: a Go service, a web front end and a PostgreSQL database. It runs on a Kubernetes cluster and flies through three Airfields: dev, staging and prod. The map introduces the whole example.

You are a Pilot (developer) on the storefront Flight. You change the checkout so it shows the delivery date, and you open a pull request.

  1. Plan. Your pipeline is one file in the repository, next to the code. When you start a Sortie by hand, you fill in a run form: you pick the branch from a list and the Airfield from the ones you may use. You type nothing a list could offer. Available Pipelines as code. Planned Flight plans as job templates, with a form.
  2. Build. A Station (runner) on a Ramp (runner pool) takes the steps. Tests run, and the Debrief shows which passed, which failed and which are flaky. The image is stored as Cargo (artifact) in the Depot (registry), named by its digest. Available Warm builds with caches; A built-in OCI registry; Polished test reports as HTML and PDF.
  3. Preflight. Inspection (security scan) looks for secrets and vulnerable dependencies. Standing orders (policies and repository standards) give a verdict that blocks only what your change introduced. Your pull request shows one plain sentence about what still stops it from merging. Available Vulnerability, secret, dependency and license checks; Standing orders for every repository.
  4. Clearance. You merge. The release flies to dev and staging by itself. For prod, a Controller (approver) must say Go, and the person who started the Sortie cannot clear their own production Launch. Available Approvals and protected environments (on the list of things available today).
  5. Launch. The release goes to prod as a Pathfinder (canary): one small share of real traffic first, then more in steps you can see. Available Rollout control inside a run. Planned Weighted canaries and traffic control; Every rollout strategy.
  6. Overwatch. Launchway compares the new version with the old one on error rate and latency. Ten minutes in, checkout errors double. Available A health proof built into verification. Planned The watch.
  7. Return to base. Launchway sends all traffic back to the last good version by itself and tells you why, with the graph that showed it. You did not have to be awake for it. Available Roll back after a successful deployment. Planned Automatic return to stable.
  8. On the record. The next morning you open the release and read its story: who cleared it, which checks passed, what Overwatch measured and why it came back. You fix the bug, and the next flight completes its mission. Available An event log that explains every decision. Planned Tamper-evident audit trail.
What works today

Every step above exists in a first form, except three: the run form that offers values instead of free text, traffic shifted in weighted steps by Launchway itself, and an automatic Return to base after a watch. Those three are planned. The same story for the team's virtual machines, image-based hosts and serverless function is mostly planned; One way to launch, anywhere says exactly what exists.

Who Launchway is for

The public roadmap names four people first. After them, the aim is a product that larger companies would also choose. The wants and the status lines below are the roadmap's own words.

Self-hosting

One small machine runs everything, stable and low cost, with nothing leaving the house. Delivery, backup and restore you can trust.

A good fit now; the guided installer is on the main branch.

The small team

Zero setup, free to start, real deployments later, and no need to move code that already lives on a hosted code host.

Not yet: working alongside a hosted code host and sign-up are planned.

The freelancer

A laptop and many clients: demos fast, sites that look and rank well, cheap hosting, and a clean hand-over to each client.

Weak today: previews, a space per client and site starters are planned.

Mobile and games

Apple and Windows build machines, signing and store upload, very large files and long builds.

Not yet: the build machines come first.

The larger company New in this plan

Hundreds of pipelines running at once, many Squadrons (teams), products already paid for, auditors, and production that must not go down. It needs every safeguard, separation of duties, evidence, high availability, real resource numbers for capacity planning, and connections to what it already runs, each as good as the built-in choice.

Partly today: high availability, policy gates and Clearances exist; directory groups, the tamper-evident trail, change records and connections for every capability are planned.

Complete without being complicated

Launchway has to have an answer for everything teams rely on, and still be a product a beginner can use on the first day. The plan keeps both halves of that promise with four rules.

One model

Every module uses the same levels, the same permissions, the same record and the same policy points. Nothing brings its own users, roles, settings or log. The seven layers and the module contract hold every chapter to this.

One way to do each thing

One pipeline file, one expression language, one launch model, one kind of form. A second way is added only when you decide one is needed.

Everything optional, with a built-in default

Each capability is built in and works on day one with nothing else installed. A connection to what a team already has is an equal choice, and one provider is in charge at a time. Modules are off until wanted, and nothing switched off appears in the menus.

Every safeguard on

Scans, Standing orders, the watch after a Launch and automatic Return to base start on. Your team may tune them or turn them off; only a level above you can require one.

The big picture

The public roadmap draws Launchway as one change traveling from an idea to insight and back. This plan keeps that picture. The flight above is what happens between Pipelines and Runtime.

Each station has chapters in this plan: Code in Code and review, Pipelines in the flight plan chapters, Packages in the Depot, Launch in One way to launch, anywhere, Runtime in Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch and Switches, and Insight in Radar, insight and keeping it healthy and the software graph and Maintenance.

The principles

These are the standard every item is held to, throughout and not as a milestone. The first 17 are the public roadmap's principles, word for word. The last six are new in this plan; each one records what you said most recently.

The 17 principles of the roadmap

Everything, without the mess.
Every feature uses the same objects, permissions, audit trail and policy point, and nothing switched off appears in the menus.
One way in, every way in.
A wizard for each task, with the same operation in the HTTP API, the agent endpoint, the command line and Terraform.
Only a database and Git.
Everything else is built in; outside integrations stay optional.
Boring upgrades.
One binary and a database, additive migrations, an older binary running on a newer schema, and Return to base by image.
High availability and security are part of done.
A feature says what happens when a server, the database or a Station dies, and who may do what, before it merges.
Honest status.
An item is available only when it is merged, tested and documented. Order is by value and is not a schedule.
Security first.
Everything Launchway holds is encrypted at rest, every part runs with least privilege, and the secure choice is the default.
Help, never enforce or overwrite.
Launchway explains, proposes and previews. It never rewrites your application or infrastructure silently; you accept, edit or decline.
Safeguards on, the team in charge.
Every protection starts on and your team may tune or turn it off. Only a level above you, such as the Wing for production, can require one.
Never a button that does not work.
An action that cannot work here is absent or shown unavailable with the reason. A risky action that is allowed asks first, in plain words.
Everything optional, with built-in defaults.
Each capability has a built-in default and a popular backend you can use instead, so an installation needs the fewest tools.
The hosted service holds nothing sensitive.
Your network and your secrets stay with you, seen only through a small program that runs on your side.
Accessible to everyone.
Automated checks hold every screen, and the API, agent endpoint and command line, to a top-tier standard for keyboard, screen reader and contrast.
Simple to install, nothing assumed.
A handful of values, no secrets manager or identity provider required, and a guided first sign-in that is the same for everyone.
Every customer’s Base is walled off, and proven.
Isolation between customers is not a promise: tests try every route from one Base into another and gate every release.
A cache only makes a build faster.
It may never change a build’s result: what can change is looked up again, and a Sortie says when it cannot be sure.
The system works out the order; a person can always override.
Build order, release order and branching patterns are worked out from your code, shown with their reasons, and open to correction.

Six principles added by this plan

One expression language, written one way. New in this plan
Decisions and values in a pipeline use one existing, documented open-source expression language, always written inside ${{ }} and never inside script text. A field that is only an expression keeps the expression's type, and every expression is type-checked before a Sortie starts. Today's structured references and closed when: tests keep working.
Logic is tested code; YAML holds only glue. New in this plan
A pipeline file says what runs, in what order, with what. Anything that thinks is a real program with a manifest and tests, which can be mocked and unit tested like any other production code. A pipeline may hold up to 10 lines of inline script (a lint warns beyond that); anything shared may hold 3 (an error beyond that). A Standing order can tighten these limits, never loosen them.
One launch model for every place software runs. New in this plan
Kubernetes, virtual machines, physical servers, image-based hosts and serverless platforms are launched the same way: a release identified by its digest flies a route through Airfields, with a chosen strategy. Traffic is watched during and after every Launch, deployments have zero downtime, and Return to base is never blocked.
Pick, do not type. New in this plan
Inputs are as good as a modern web application: values are looked up, fetched, narrowed by earlier choices and validated as you go. Free text is the last resort, and when it is needed its validation is easy to set up.
Built in by default; a connection is an equal choice. New in this plan
Every capability is built in and excellent by default. Connecting what a team already has is an equal, first-class choice, never a second-rate adapter. One provider is in charge of each capability, every capability screen says what it is served by, and pipelines name the capability, never the product.
Original answers, no other product named. New in this plan
Launchway has an answer for everything teams rely on elsewhere, and each answer comes from its own model, with its own shape, words and screens. No other product is named in the product, the documentation or this plan, except an open standard or a system you choose as a connection.
For the editor

The new principle "Built in by default; a connection is an equal choice" sharpens the kept principle "Everything optional, with built-in defaults", which still says "a popular backend you can use instead". Both are shown as they stand. Whether the old wording should later be changed to match is your call.

The chips

Available
Merged, tested and documented, and on the roadmap's available list or marked available in a milestone. The exact roadmap title is always beside the chip.
In progress
Partly built. The roadmap says what is missing.
Planned
On the roadmap, not built yet.
New in this plan
Proposed by this plan: a principle, an item or a change to an item. It is not on the roadmap until you accept it.
Open question
A choice only you can make. The plan shows the options and does not decide.
Now Next Later
The roadmap's milestone timing. Order is by value, not a schedule, and there are no dates.

Syntax and screens that do not exist yet are labeled as designs. Each chapter ends with its proposed roadmap changes and its open questions; coverage checks that every request you made has a home, and the hand-over lists what to build first.

What this plan changes

The plan extends and reconciles the existing roadmap; it does not replace it. No item is dropped. In one list:

  1. A story and a map. The roadmap gains one story (a change is a flight) and one model of seven layers on one record, and every chapter places itself on it. New in this plan
  2. Six principles. The six above join the 17, which stay word for word. New in this plan
  3. One expression language, chosen. The planned item "Expressions for conditions" gains a named language (an existing open-source one, written inside ${{ }}) and grows from conditions to values. An earlier ruling chose a different language; your latest word replaces it. New in this plan
  4. Limits on inline script. Ten lines in a pipeline and three in anything shared, enforced by lint and by error. This is new; the existing item "Custom steps in your own language" carries the rest. New in this plan
  5. One launch model. Launch items spread over Milestones 3, 8 and 11 are read as one model: a release by digest, a route through Airfields, a strategy, Overwatch and Return to base. Serverless, which today has five planned items and no home, gets its own chapter. Items keep their milestones unless a chapter proposes a move.
  6. Run forms as a first-class group. Inputs are thin on the roadmap today (no group of their own). The plan gives them a chapter and proposes items so every input is picked, fetched and validated. New in this plan
  7. A slot for every capability. Every capability gets one named slot with a built-in default, an equal connection, one provider in charge and a "served by" screen. The capability table lists them all.
  8. Two new words, proposed. Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it) and Route (the Airfields a release flies through). Both need your yes. Open question
  9. A fifth reader. "Who Launchway is for" gains the larger company as a named line after the four, with an honest status. New in this plan
  10. Overlaps named, not merged by stealth. Where the roadmap lists the same idea twice (for example GitOps depth in Milestones 3 and 8, or Switch items in Milestones 3 and 8), the chapter names both and proposes which one owns it. Renaming an item changes its address, so title changes are proposed, never assumed.
  11. Words brought into line. Item titles that still say "toggle" or "project" (for example "Stale-toggle hygiene" and "Per-project packages and permissions") are proposed for Switch and Flight by the chapters that own them. A new title changes the item's address, so each rename is listed for you rather than made. New in this plan
Open question

Four questions stay with you across the whole plan: one pod per step or per Sortie on Kubernetes; whether the switchable plain word set stays; the policy language beyond the typed catalog; and which new words are accepted. They are listed with their options under open questions.

Launchway platform plan

The map

Launchway is seven layers on one record, and every module fills a named slot under one contract. This page shows where everything sits, so each chapter can say which layers it uses and what it builds on.

  • Seven layers: the foundation, the record, flight plans, flight operations, Launch, Command and mission support, with every way in and Hardpoints (extension points) around them.
  • A module belongs in Launchway only if it meets all ten points of the module contract.
  • Every capability has one slot: a built-in default, a connection as an equal choice, and one provider in charge, shown as "served by".
  • One running example, the Harbor Lights team, is used in every chapter.

Seven layers, one record

Read the layers from the bottom up. Each one uses the layers below it and writes every decision to the record. Nothing is true that is not on the record, so the screens, the Logbook (audit trail), the Debrief (test report), the metrics and the evidence never disagree.

LayerWhat lives thereChapters
1. The foundationOne program and a database, plus Git. One binary with roles that scale separately, run as a hosted service, on Kubernetes (recommended) or on a single server. Levels Base (installation), Wing (organization), Squadron (team) and Flight (codebase) carry permissions, variables, Standing orders and capability choices downward, with locks. Secrets are sealed and resolved on the Station (runner), never seen by the server. On a hosted installation every Base is walled off, and tests prove it.The system; Levels, people and secrets
2. The recordOne append-only event record: the source of truth for the interface, the Logbook, the Debrief, metrics and evidence. A trigger that did or did not start a Sortie (run), a Standing order verdict, a Clearance (approval), a Launch (deployment) verdict: each is an event with its reasons.The record, The Logbook and evidence
3. Flight plans (authoring)A pipeline is one file with one graph of steps. Steps have typed inputs and typed outputs. One expression language decides and selects. Logic lives in tested code; the file holds glue. Reuse comes from custom steps, Maneuvers (step templates), Flight plans (whole ready-made pipelines) and libraries, pinned and locked. People start Sorties through run forms built from typed inputs. Triggers live with the pipeline and filter in the same expression language.Pipelines, values and expressions; Code you can test; Reuse that keeps growing; Inputs and run forms; What starts a Sortie
4. Flight operations (execution)Stations take steps from Ramps (runner pools), waiting in a Holding pattern (queue) when there is no room. The workspace travels with the Sortie. Caches only make things faster. Cargo (artifacts) and the Depot (registry) hold what was built, by digest. The Debrief shows what the tests said.Stations and where work runs, The Depot
5. Launch (delivery)One model for every target. A release is an artifact identified by its digest. It flies a route through Airfields (environments). Each Launch uses a strategy: all at once, rolling, Pathfinder (canary) or a two-fleet swap. Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) judges it against live traffic and metrics. Return to base (rollback) is always possible and never blocked.One way to launch, anywhere; Launching to Kubernetes; Launching to virtual machines and physical servers; Launching to image-based hosts; Launching to serverless; Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch
6. Command (governance)Standing orders (policies and repository standards) are judged at fixed points on the path to production, with no side doors. Clearances record who said Go. A Hold (freeze) stops Launches. The Logbook and evidence packs prove what happened.Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; Security and the supply chain; The Logbook and evidence

Each is optional, has a built-in default and can be served by a connection instead.Code and review; The Depot; Switches; The software graph and Maintenance; Work, from idea to running software; The Wingman and agents; Radar, insight and keeping it healthy

The module contract

A module belongs in Launchway only if it meets all ten points. Each module chapter shows how it meets them. The reason for each point is what it protects you from.

PointThe ruleWhy it exists
1. One set of peopleIt uses the same levels and permissions. No private user or role model.You grant and remove access in one place. A person who leaves loses everything at once, and no module has a hidden administrator.
2. One recordIt writes its decisions to the one record and reads its history from it.Screens never disagree, an auditor reads one trail, and any decision can be explained later with its reasons.
3. One set of gatesIts gates are Standing orders judged at the common points. No private policy.A rule written once applies everywhere. There is no side door around it, and you check one place to know what is enforced.
4. One kind of formAnything a person supplies comes through the same typed input forms.Values are picked and validated the same way in every module and every way in, and free text stays the last resort.
5. One way to runAnything it runs is a step under the one step contract, on a Station.Secrets stay on the Station, the hosted service holds nothing sensitive, and every module gets sandboxing, sizing, logs and retries without building them again.
6. One slotIt fills one named capability slot, with a built-in default and a connection as an equal choice, and shows "served by".You always know which provider is in charge. A single developer gets the built-in on day one; a company keeps the product it already pays for.
7. Off until wantedIt is off until wanted, and nothing switched off appears in the menus. Safeguards, scanning and standards are the exception: they start on.A new installation shows a small product that grows as you switch things on, so a beginner is never faced with everything at once.
8. Every way inWeb, API, command line, agent endpoint and Terraform can all do what it does.Nothing is reachable only by clicking, or only by editing text. A build fails when one way in falls behind.
9. Failure and rights statedIt says what happens when a server, the database or a Station is lost, and who may do what.High availability and security are part of done, decided before the module merges and not found out in production.
10. The way back stays openIt never blocks Return to base.Moving toward the safe state is always immediate and recorded. No module, outage or rule can trap a bad release in production.

The capability slots

Every capability Launchway offers or plans has one slot. The slot has a built-in default that works with nothing else installed, and a connection to what a team already has as an equal choice: same screens, same API, same permissions, same record. One provider is in charge of a slot at a time for each Squadron, and the capability's screen says what it is "served by". A connected product's extra features appear in place. Pipelines name the capability, never the product, so changing the provider never means rewriting pipelines.

Two providers serve one slot only in a named role: one in front of the other, one alongside for a single stated purpose, or a migration with a visible end.

How modules build on each other

Modules are optional, but they are not independent. Read an arrow as "is needed by". A module can be switched on only when what it needs is on, and the switch says so in plain words.

The words

Launchway's own concepts have aviation names, shown with the plain industry word in parentheses on first use in each chapter. Words everyone already knows stay plain: pipeline, step, variable, secret, branch, commit, pull request, cache, trigger, retry, lane, target, library and custom step. Machine names, such as API paths, command-line commands, pipeline keys and environment variables, stay plain and never change. The theme is flying and ground operations, never combat. These are ordinary words used descriptively; Launchway is not affiliated with or endorsed by any military service.

Launchway platform plan

What only Launchway does

Matching what teams rely on elsewhere is the floor. The fifteen advantages on this page are Launchway's own: each one follows from the way the product is built, so it is not a feature that can be bolted on somewhere else.

  • Five properties of the model make the advantages possible: one record for everything, every piece of work a typed step, one launch model for every place software runs, the software graph, and one way in for people and agents alike.
  • From them come releases that are proven before they fly and watched until they are safe, pipelines that do only what a change can affect, continuous deployment for the way a team already branches, and audits answered from evidence that already exists.
  • Status is honest. Some of each advantage works today; much of it is designed in a chapter of this plan and not built. Every claim names the exact roadmap item or the proposed item behind it.
  • Every advantage has a measure read from the record, so the claims can be checked, and published only when they hold.

Where the advantages come from

Most delivery tools grew by adding parts: a build server, then a deployment tool, then a scanner, then a dashboard, each with its own users, its own settings and its own log. Every part can be good on its own. What none of them can do is answer a question that crosses the seams: why did this release reach production, what did it cost in waiting, and would the safeguard we added last year have stopped it? Launchway starts from five properties that answer those questions by construction. They have to be there from the first line of code; a product cannot add them afterwards without rebuilding itself.

One record for everything

Every decision (a trigger that did or did not start a Sortie (run), a Standing orders (policies and repository standards) verdict, a Clearance (approval), a Launch (deployment) verdict) is written once, in order, with its reasons, to one append-only record. Pages, the Logbook (audit trail), the Debrief (test report), metrics and evidence are all readings of it. The record.

Makes possible: audits as a by-product, reports worth opening, honest metrics, speed budgets, explanations for every decision, and the evidence that a safeguard can go.

Everything is a typed step

Builds, tests, scans, Clearances, Launches and Drills (chaos tests) are all steps with typed inputs and typed outputs, under one contract, run on a Station (runner). Pipelines, values and expressions.

Makes possible: a pipeline tested without flying it, steps that say what they read so only affected work runs, results reused safely, the same sandbox for every step, and import into a model rich enough to hold what other systems express.

One launch model for every place software runs

A release named by its digest flies a Route (proposed word: the ordered Airfields it flies through) through Airfields (environments), with a strategy, judged by Overwatch (the watch after a Launch), and Return to base (rollback) is always possible. The same for Kubernetes, virtual machines, physical servers, image-based hosts and serverless. One way to launch, anywhere.

Makes possible: stable releases by proof on every kind of target, continuous deployment as a Route setting, and branching patterns that map onto Routes.

The software graph

One graph from code to what runs where: which folder builds which image, which package uses which library, which digest runs in which Airfield, each link with its source. The software graph and Maintenance.

Makes possible: building and testing only what a change can affect, a vulnerability traced to every place it runs and patched by an ordinary Launch, and a branching pattern recognized from history.

Every way in is the same way in

The web interface with a wizard for each task, the HTTP API, the command line, the agent endpoint and the infrastructure-as-code provider reach the same operation with the same rights, the same checks and the same record, and a parity test fails the build when one falls behind. Every way in.

Makes possible: inputs checked the same way whoever sends them, agents that prove their changes with the same checker people use, and nothing a team can do only by clicking.

The running example is the one every chapter uses: the Harbor Lights team, its Wing (organization) of three Squadrons (teams), and its Flight (codebase) storefront flying through the Airfields dev, staging and prod. Dana writes changes, Ana reviews them and gives Go for storefront in prod, Sam is the Commander of the Wing, and Priya is on call. The map introduces the whole example.

1. Proven before it flies

As teams live it
You change a pipeline, push it, and wait for a real run to find out that the deploy step was skipped because a condition read the wrong value. You fix it, push again and wait again. Pipeline files are the one kind of production code that most teams cannot test.
What is common today
A schema check in the editor, a lint, and sometimes a local runner that executes the steps for real. These catch typing mistakes. None of them tells you which steps a given event will run, with which values, or what a change to the file would have done to last week's runs.
What Launchway does instead
Three things, all using the real checker and planner. Before take-off, every step is labeled "will run", "will not run" or "depends on" a named value, and after landing each skipped step says why with the values filled in. The Simulator (proposed word: testing a pipeline without flying it) takes an event, inputs and a stand-in result for each step, and says which steps run, in what order, with which values, which Clearances would be asked for and which Launches would happen, while executing nothing. Replay plans a changed pipeline against the last Sorties on the record, using what each step really wrote, and lists every step that would now run or be skipped and every Launch that would go somewhere else.
Why it is not bolted on
It needs typed steps (so a stand-in output can be checked against its type), values known before take-off kept apart from values known in flight, and every past Sortie's resolved values on one record. A tool whose steps exchange untyped text, or whose history lives in separate logs, can run a file but cannot simulate it.
What it gives you
A pipeline change that has passed its Simulator tests flies the same graph for real, because the same planner made both. The measure is simple: Sorties that fail after a merge because of the pipeline definition itself, which should fall toward zero, and pipeline changes whose replay found a difference before review.

You move the storefront smoke tests behind a new condition. The Simulator test "a pull request from a fork never deploys" still passes, but replay over the last 50 Sorties shows that 12 pushes to main would no longer have reached staging, because the condition reads run.branch, which a pull-request Sortie does not have. You fix the condition before anyone reviews the change, and nothing reached a Station.

Status today
Available Validate pipelines offline (Milestone 1); Test like the pipeline (Milestone 1); An event log that explains every decision (Milestone 2, for triggers). In progress Typed outputs between steps (Milestone 2). Planned Expressions for conditions; Run it locally, the same way (Milestone 2). 2. Stable releases by proof, not hope

As teams live it
A release goes out on Friday afternoon. Someone watches a dashboard for twenty minutes, decides it looks fine, and goes home. At night the error rate creeps up, a person on call is woken, works out which change did it, and rolls it back by hand. "Stable" meant that nobody happened to see a problem.
What is common today
Fixed thresholds written by hand ("error rate under 1 percent"), checked during a canary and then forgotten; or a statistical comparison during the rollout that stops when the last traffic step completes. Reliability targets live in a separate tool, so the delivery tool cannot read how much budget a release is spending. Few teams can say when they last proved that a release really goes back by itself.
What Launchway does instead
Every service gets an Envelope (proposed word: the measured limits of error rate, latency and load inside which the service is healthy). Two sources set it. The service's own good Launches teach it: the last passed verifications in the same Airfield form the baseline, and a pass a person forced by hand is never added. The reliability target sets the outer edge: the share of good requests over a window, and the error budget left. Overwatch judges every Launch against the Envelope from the first new copy until a set time after the last step. A Launch that leaves the Envelope returns to base by itself, with the evidence on the record. Thin data is never a pass: it waits one more window, then pauses and asks. A Drill (chaos test) on a Patrol (schedule) proves the claim: a seeded bad release must be caught and returned within the time the plan states.
Why it is not bolted on
The Envelope is made of things only one record holds together: earlier Launches and their verdicts, the target and its budget, the Switches (feature toggles) changed during the Launch, and the Drills that tested the service. Overwatch is the same step on every kind of target, so the same Envelope guards a cluster, a fleet of machines or a serverless function.
What it gives you
Fewer bad releases reach all of your users, and the ones that do come back without a person. The measures: Launches that left the Envelope and the median minutes until they were back; failed requests during Launches against the hour before; and Drills passed. Each Launch carries one sentence of proof, such as "fewest healthy copies 6 (floor 4); failed requests 0.03 percent against 0.03 percent the hour before", and says "not measured" when a source is missing, never "zero".

Ten minutes into a Launch of storefront in prod, the Pathfinder (canary) carries 5 percent of traffic and its checkout error rate is 0.042 against the stable version's 0.003, six standard deviations above. Overwatch fails the interval twice in a row and returns to base. Nobody was paged to decide. In the morning Dana opens the release and reads the verdict, the chart with its bands, and the new log pattern that appeared with the release.

Status today
Available Verification after a deploy (Available today list), with comparison against the stable version, baselines from earlier good Launches, log patterns and automatic abort or Return to base during the Launch; A health proof built into verification (Milestone 3); Roll back after a successful deployment (Milestone 8). In progress Guarded queries for monitoring data; Kill switches and automatic toggle-back (Milestone 8). Planned The watch; Automatic return to stable; Proofs; Chaos experiments as plans (Milestone 8); Service reliability targets; Signal sources (Milestone 3). Monitoring, without another monitoring stack

You asked for monitoring. Launchway's answer is Radar (monitoring) that reads the metric, log and trace stores a team already runs, through guarded queries, and shows them per version during a Launch, in the same view as the Launch's steps. It does not ship its own dashboard server. What is new is not another graph; it is that the graph is joined to the change that caused it, judged against the Envelope, and acted on. Radar, insight and keeping it healthy designs it.

3. The fastest safe path

As teams live it
You change two files in the web front end and wait twenty minutes while the back end is built and tested again, exactly as it was an hour ago. The pipeline grew slower by a minute a month and nobody noticed until it took half an hour. Path filters were written once by hand and no longer match the code.
What is common today
Caches keyed by a lockfile, hand-written path filters, test splitting by timing in a few tools, and reuse of unchanged results in a few others. Each is a separate feature with its own settings, and each trusts its configuration without checking it. Speed is a dashboard someone may look at, not a check that fails.
What Launchway does instead
Speed is managed like correctness. Steps declare what they read; with the software graph, Launchway works out the affected set before the Sortie starts and shows it in the same "will run, will not run" form as the checker. A step whose inputs have not changed reuses its recorded result, keyed on its digest-pinned image, its declared paths, its upstream outputs and the versions of its secret references. Reuse follows the same trust scopes as caches (a pull request never feeds the default branch), and one reused step in twenty is built again in the background and compared, so a wrong declaration is found rather than trusted. Tests are split across Stations by how long they take. Images and Stations are warm before the Sortie needs them. Every pipeline has a speed budget; going over it is a speed check reported like a failing test, naming the steps that grew and the change that made them grow.
Why it is not bolted on
The affected set needs the graph and typed steps that declare their reads. Safe reuse needs every step's inputs and outputs on the record. The budget needs every Sortie's time split into six parts (waiting for a Station, starting, fetching, building, testing, waiting on people), which only a system that records all six can do. A step that declares nothing runs every time, as today, so nothing becomes faster by accident.
What it gives you
Minutes back on every pull request, and a slowdown caught the day it is introduced. The measures: median time to first signal on pull requests; Sortie time against budget; step time saved by reuse and skipping, at each step's typical time; selection misses (a test left out that later failed), which tighten the map.

Dana's pull request #482 changes web/src/cart.tsx and web/src/price.ts. Before the Sortie starts, the page says: api-build and api-test reused from Sortie 1203 (nothing they read changed); web-e2e will run 2 of 6 groups (the graph links price.ts to the checkout and cart pages only); migrate-check will not run (no migration changed); the Inspection (security scan) always runs. The first result arrives inside the two-minute budget.

In progress Pipeline history and flaky tests; Why is my run waiting (Milestone 2). 4. Continuous deployment for the way you already branch

As teams live it
Every guide to continuous deployment assumes trunk-based development. Your team has a long-lived integration branch, release branches for three versions in the field, or a regulator who wants production changes reviewed as pull requests. So you copy pipelines per branch, hard-code branch names into conditions, and promotion between environments is a script someone wrote years ago.
What is common today
Branch filters on triggers, a template per pattern if you are lucky, and promotion as a chain of jobs or a separate tool. Moving from one pattern to another means rewriting the pipelines and hoping. Continuous deployment is either on for everything or off.
What Launchway does instead
Branches have roles (trunk, change, integration, release, hotfix, environment, contribution), and pipelines, Routes, branch rules and version schemes read the role, never the branch name. Launchway reads a repository's history and says which of ten common patterns it uses, how sure it is and why, and offers the Flight plan (ready-made whole pipeline), Route and branch rules that fit, as one reviewed change. A move to another pattern is a plan of small steps, each replayed in the Simulator against the team's own recent pushes before it is taken, and the pipeline file does not change because it reads roles. Continuous deployment is then not a feature but a Route whose stops advance by themselves, with the safety every Launch already has: Standing orders judged before each Launch, a Pathfinder, Overwatch against the Envelope, and automatic Return to base. A person is asked only where a rule says so.
Why it is not bolted on
Recognition reads branch history, pull-request targets, tags and the record of which branch launched to which Airfield; the move plan is replayed by the Simulator; and a Route is the launch model's own object for promotion. Without one record and one launch model, each of these would be a separate tool with its own idea of what a release is.
What it gives you
Continuous deployment a team can adopt without changing how it works first. The measures: lead time from merge to production per Flight; the share of production Launches that needed no person; and moves between patterns completed with no pipeline file edited.

Harbor Lights' billing Flight has an integration branch that receives 94 percent of pull requests. Launchway recognizes the pattern and offers a move to feature branches into main in four steps. Before the step that changes the roles, replay over six weeks shows the same 41 pull requests, the same 41 Sorties, and 23 releases to staging instead of 3. Before the step that turns on the Route, replay shows the median time from merge to staging falling from 9 days to 40 minutes. prod keeps its Clearance.

Status today

5. Audit-ready as a by-product

As teams live it
Audit season. Someone spends two weeks taking screenshots of approvals, exporting logs from four tools, matching commit hashes to deployment times in a spreadsheet, and writing a story that the auditor then has to take on trust.
What is common today
An audit log per tool, each with its own format and retention; compliance reports that list which scans ran; and evidence assembled by hand across the seams between the code host, the build tool, the deployment tool and the ticket system.
What Launchway does instead
The evidence already exists, because everything that happened is on one record. For any release, an evidence pack is produced on request: the signed commit, the review and merge verdict, the Sortie and its build record, the tests, the Inspection findings and any accepted risks with their owners and end dates, every Standing orders verdict, who gave Clearance and what they were shown, every Launch, Overwatch's measurements, any Return to base, and the Logbook checkpoint that covers it, signed by the Base (installation). The pack maps those facts to the control areas of published frameworks, labeled as evidence support and not a certification. An auditor gets a read-only view for a scope and a stated time, and every page they open is itself recorded. The Logbook becomes tamper-evident: each entry carries a hash of the one before, the Base signs checkpoints, and a verify command walks the chain offline.
Why it is not bolted on
A pack can only be complete if review, build, tests, scans, Clearances, Launches and verification write to the same record with the same identifiers. Assembling the same story from separate tools is the two weeks of screenshots.
What it gives you
An audit question answered in minutes from evidence nobody had to collect, and a separation-of-duties report that shows, per release, that nobody cleared their own change. The measures: time to produce a pack; the share of production releases whose pack has no missing section; and auditor questions answered from the pack alone.

Weeks after the fact, Sam is asked why a release of storefront returned to base. Sam opens its evidence pack: Dana's signed commit; Ana's review and Clearance with change ticket CHG-88 and risk "low"; 412 tests passed; no new findings and one accepted with its end date; every Standing orders verdict; the Pathfinder at 10 percent; Overwatch's error-rate measurement against the baseline; the automatic Return to base with its reason; and the signed checkpoint. Sam sends the file. The auditor checks the signature offline.

Status today
Available Audit lines for every sensitive action; Releases with notes and evidence (Milestone 1); An event log that explains every decision (Milestone 2); Releases that are promoted (Milestone 13). In progress Retention, legal hold and encryption at rest (Milestone 7). Planned Separation of duties; Automatic change records (Milestone 3); Tamper-evident audit trail; Evidence for auditors (Milestone 12). New in this plan An evidence pack for every release; The Logbook at every level; Reads recorded where they matter; Read-only access for auditors, granted for a time; A separation-of-duties report (proposed in The Logbook and evidence).

6. Reports worth opening

As teams live it
Test results in one tab, coverage in another tool, scan findings in a third, and a performance run in a spreadsheet. The release manager asks "is this one good?" and nobody can send a single thing that answers. Reports are made for the people who were there.
What is common today
Each tool writes its own HTML report; a run page shows a summary; trends live in a separate dashboard. A report is a file anyone can edit, so nobody outside the team can trust it.
What Launchway does instead
One Debrief for everything known about a change: tests, coverage of the changed lines, code quality (complexity, duplication, style), Inspection findings, accessibility, performance and the pipeline's own code, each judged by the same Standing orders. Every Sortie and every release gets one self-contained report made from the record: the verdict first, then what changed, what was tested, what passed and failed, the comparison with what it replaces, who cleared it, where it launched and how it behaved in production, with trends. It loads nothing and runs no script, so it works offline; it reads as one column on a phone; it is accessible in light and dark; and it carries the record events it was made from and the Base's signature, so anyone can check offline that it was not edited.
Why it is not bolted on
A report that follows a release from commit to behavior in production can only be written by a system that saw the commit, the tests, the Clearance, the Launch and Overwatch, and recorded them together. The signature works because the facts are on a record with a chain, not in a file.
What it gives you
One link answers "is this release good?" for an engineer, a manager or an auditor. Quality gates (tests, changed-line coverage, findings by kind, quarantine debt, performance) are set once at a level and judged at merge and before each Launch. The measures: reports opened and from where (a pull request, a phone, an auditor's view); the time from a Sortie's end to its report; and reports verified as unedited.

Your manager asks whether storefront 2.4.0 is good. You send its release report. On a phone it opens on one line: runs in prod since 14:08, Overwatch passed, no new test failures, no new severe findings. Below: 14 pull requests; 1,284 tests with 412 reused and linked to the Sortie that ran them; coverage 82.4 percent (+0.6) and changed lines at 91 percent; checkout latency inside the Envelope; Ana cleared it, and Dana, who wrote it, could not.

Status today
Available Test, coverage and HTML reports; The Debrief; Security findings and SBOMs (Available today list); Polished test reports as HTML and PDF (Milestone 2); Language profiles (Milestone 12). In progress Pipeline history and flaky tests (Milestone 2). Planned Findings and failures on the diff; Light, dark and phone widths (Milestone 1); Performance gates in preflight (Milestone 8); Delivery metrics and executive dashboards (Milestone 3). New in this plan One Debrief for everything known about a change; Code quality measures in the Debrief; Coverage of changed lines on the diff; A report for every Sortie, in one file; A release report from commit to behavior in production; Reports that prove they are unedited; Quality trends per Flight, Squadron and Airfield; Tagged PDF reports; Quality gates as Standing orders (proposed in Quality, reports and the Debrief).

7. Secure without being asked

As teams live it
Security is a project someone starts after an incident: add a scanner here, rotate a key there, pin an action someone else wrote. Until then, the build server can read every secret, a shared template can change under you overnight, and a pull request from a stranger runs with the same rights as your own.
What is common today
Scanners that are available but off by default, secrets stored on the server and injected into jobs, shared steps referenced by a movable tag, and plug-ins that run inside the server with its full rights.
What Launchway does instead
Every protection starts on. The Inspection runs on every repository from the first Sortie, and blocks only what a change introduces, so it is never turned off for being noisy. Values reach scripts only as variables, never pasted into script text. Secrets are resolved on the Station; the server never sees a value. Pull requests from forks run without secrets, deploys or cache writes. Everything a pipeline borrows is pinned in one lockfile. Third-party code never runs inside the server: it runs as a step in a sandbox, or outside at a Hardpoint (extension point). Every Launch is designed to verify the image's signature, its build record and its list of contents before anything runs.
Why it is not bolted on
Secrets the server never sees is a property of where steps run, not a setting. One sandbox for every step is possible only because every kind of work is a step on one contract. Scans that block only what is new need the record of what was there before.
What it gives you
A new team is secure on its first day without a security project. The measures: the share of Sorties that ran the Inspection; borrowed pieces not pinned to an immutable reference (should be zero); Launches whose signature and contents were verified; and secret values that reached the server (zero by design, proved by tests).

A contributor outside Harbor Lights opens a pull request against platform-library from a fork. Its Sortie runs the tests and the Inspection, but has no secrets, cannot write to the cache, and cannot launch. The Inspection finds a new high-severity dependency; the pull request shows one plain sentence about what stops it from merging. Nobody had to configure any of it.

Status today
Available Secure by default in the chart; Restricted runs for untrusted pull requests (Milestone 1); Standing orders for every repository; Share and pin steps and templates (Milestone 2); Vulnerability, secret, dependency and license checks; Encrypt stored secrets and tokens (Milestone 12); Secrets that stay with runners (Available today list). In progress Steps run in a sandbox (Milestone 2); Signing and verification (Milestone 4). Planned Cloud sign-in per step (Milestone 1); Extensions without fragility (Milestone 2); Workload identity and dynamic credentials; Build provenance, level two now and three next (Milestone 12). New in this plan Provenance and contents verified before every Launch; One sandbox profile on every executor; Builds reach what they need, and every refused connection shows (proposed in Security and the supply chain); A lockfile for everything a pipeline borrows (proposed in Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints).

8. One launch model for every kind of place software runs

As teams live it
Your containers deploy with careful canaries and automatic rollback. Your two legacy virtual machines deploy with a shell script over SSH. Your edge devices update themselves whenever they reboot. Your serverless function deploys straight from a laptop. Four ways, four kinds of history, and zero downtime only on one of them.
What is common today
One tool per kind of target, or one tool that is deep on containers and shallow everywhere else. The safety a team builds for one kind of target does not carry to the others.
What Launchway does instead
One model for all of them. A release is named by its digest and built once. It flies a Route through Airfields. Each Launch uses a strategy (all at once, rolling, Pathfinder, or a two-fleet swap). Four zero-downtime rules are checked before, during and after every Launch: ready before traffic, drained before stopped, never below a floor of healthy copies, and back by itself. Overwatch judges it the same way, and Return to base is never blocked by a Hold (freeze), a Standing order or a lock. Where a kind of target does not fit the model (a host that is switched off, a function platform with cold starts), the plan says so and says what Launchway does about it.
Why it is not bolted on
The model is the product. Every chapter on a target fills in the same nouns, so the Envelope, Standing orders, Clearances, the evidence pack and the report work on a fleet of image-based hosts exactly as they work on a cluster.
What it gives you
Your oldest service gets the same safety as your newest. The measures: for each kind of target, the share of Launches with a zero-downtime proof and an Overwatch verdict, and the median time a Return to base took.

Harbor Lights launches the same week to four places: storefront to a Kubernetes cluster behind a Pathfinder; billing to two virtual machines, one at a time behind the load balancer; kiosk-os to a rack of image-based hosts that reboot into the new image in batches; and image-resize as a new serverless version that takes traffic by weight. All four appear on one page, each with its Route, its verdict and its way back.

Status today
Available Launches to Kubernetes through a GitOps controller (Available today list); Rollout control inside a run (Milestone 3); VM deploys; Delivery to machines over SSH; Image-based hosts (Milestone 3), as a fleet run by a Station and not yet scheduled by the server. In progress What is deployed where (Milestone 5). Planned Delivery by choice (Milestone 3); Every rollout strategy; Hosts and pools; Serverless and managed container services; Safeguards on by default (Milestone 8). New in this plan One Launch lifecycle for every target; Return to base that nothing can block; Digests on every Launch record (proposed in One way to launch, anywhere); Fleets held in the product; Fleet Launches scheduled by the server (proposed in Launching to virtual machines and physical servers). The serverless column is designed in Launching to serverless and the image hosts in Launching to image-based hosts.

9. Inputs that are picked, not typed

As teams live it
A manual run asks for a version, an environment and a region in three empty text boxes. You type stagging, the run starts, and twenty minutes later it fails at the deploy step.
What is common today
Typed inputs with a few choice lists written into the file. Options that depend on other answers, or that come from a live source, need a plug-in or a script.
What Launchway does instead
One typed input definition becomes a form that fetches real values (branches, tags, image digests, Airfields you may launch to), narrows later fields by earlier answers, checks every value as you type, shows what will run before you start, and is checked again on the server whoever sends it: the web form, the command line, the API or an agent. Free text is the last resort.
Why it is not bolted on
The form is generated from the same typed inputs the checker uses, and every way in goes through the same input check. A form drawn separately from the pipeline would drift from it.
What it gives you
Fewer runs that fail on a typo, and a run form a newcomer can use. The measures: the share of fields filled by picking rather than typing, and runs refused by the server after the form accepted them (zero, because it is one check).

You start a release of storefront by hand. The Airfield field lists only staging and prod, the two you may launch to. You pick prod, and the version field narrows to the digests that passed staging. The summary says: "Will launch 2.4.0 to prod behind a Pathfinder; Ana must give Clearance."

Status today
Available Pipelines as code, with typed inputs and a branch and tag picker; Guided setup wizards (Available today list). In progress A do bar for every task (Milestone 1). Planned Flight plans as job templates, with a form (Milestone 3). New in this plan A run form that offers real values; Fields that follow earlier answers; Pickers in place of typed fields; One input check for every way in; What will run, shown before you start (proposed in Inputs and run forms).

10. Bring everything with you

As teams live it
Moving to a new delivery tool means months of rewriting pipelines by hand, discovering halfway that something the old system did silently has no equivalent, and running both systems for longer than planned.
What is common today
A converter for one or two formats that handles the easy cases and drops the rest, sometimes without saying so.
What Launchway does instead
Launchway imports pipelines, templates, shared libraries, triggers, variables, delivery settings and policies from every major kind of build and delivery system. It generates as much as it can even when the result is incomplete, never drops anything silently, and marks what a person must finish. Inline logic is lifted into tested custom steps. Old and new run side by side and results are compared by commit, one pipeline at a time. Import quality is a public number that may only rise: today 73 of 205 known constructs convert exactly and 132 exactly or with a stated difference.
Why it is not bolted on
Import works because the target model is richer than the sources: fan-out, typed outputs, conditions in one expression language, Routes and Standing orders give each imported construct a better home than "now always runs".
What it gives you
A move measured in pipelines converted per day, not in months. The measures: the share of constructs converted exactly, weighted by how often teams use them; pipelines cut over; and constructs dropped silently (zero by rule).

Designed in Bringing work in. Status: Planned A converter and a move-over guide (Milestone 1; five formats are on the main branch and the chapter proposes marking it Available); Run old and new side by side (Milestone 1); Import of existing jobs (Milestone 2); Importers for other delivery platforms (Milestone 3). New in this plan Scan a Wing before converting anything; Compare old and new results by commit; Cut over one pipeline at a time; No Launch from an unfinished import; A public measure of import quality.

11. Built in or connected, never both by accident

As teams live it
Your company already pays for a scanner, a secret store and a metrics service. A new delivery tool either ignores them, or bolts them on so loosely that nobody can tell which one a pipeline is really using. Some features are kept back for a more expensive edition.
What is common today
Built-in features with plug-ins for outside tools, where the plug-in is second class; or no built-in at all, so a small team must install five things first.
What Launchway does instead
Every capability has one slot with a built-in default that works on day one and a connection to what a team already has as an equal choice. One provider is in charge per capability, every capability screen says what it is "served by", and pipelines name the capability, never the product, so changing provider changes a setting and not a pipeline file. Running both at once is allowed only in a named role (in front, alongside for one purpose, or migrating, with a visible end). Outside systems plug in at Hardpoints and never run code inside the server. Every feature is open: plans change limits, never features.
Why it is not bolted on
The slot is part of the module contract every module must meet, and the step contract is the same for built-in and connected steps. A product that grew one integration at a time has no slot to put a provider in.
What it gives you
The fewest tools to install, and no rewrite when a team brings what it already pays for. The measures: capabilities whose "served by" is shown; provider moves completed with no pipeline file changed.

Designed in Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints. Status: Available pipelines already name a slot, not a product, for the Depot (registry), secret stores and health sources; Open source (Available today list). Planned Bring your own backend (Milestone 3); Every feature on, the spend limit at zero (Milestone 7); Built in by default, a backend by choice; Adapters for the tools teams already pay for (Milestone 12); Published extension points (Milestone 14). New in this plan One provider in charge for each capability; A guided move between providers; Built-in steps on the one step contract.

12. Every way in is the same way in, for people and for agents

As teams live it
The button you need exists only in the web interface, so the automation has to click. The API can do something the interface cannot, so the interface is wrong about what is possible. An AI agent gets a special token with broad rights because its integration was added last.
What is common today
An API that covers most of the product, a command line that covers less, and an agent integration that covers a slice, each kept up by hand.
What Launchway does instead
The web interface, the HTTP API, the command line, the agent endpoint and the infrastructure-as-code provider reach the same operation. A table in the build holds one row per operation; the build fails if a way in is missing, and the number of gaps may only go down. Agents are users: the same permissions, limits and Logbook as anyone. An agent proves its change with the same checker and Simulator a person uses before anyone reads it.
Why it is not bolted on
Parity is enforced by a test that reads the server's own route list, the agent endpoint's own tool list and the command's own help. A product cannot add that without first making every operation the same operation.
What it gives you
Anything a person can do, a script or an agent can do, with the same safety. The measure: the parity gap count, published and falling; and agent changes that passed the checker and Simulator before review.

Designed in Every way in and The Wingman and agents. Status: Available One capability, every interface; An endpoint for agents (Available today list); Agents as users (Milestone 6). Planned the infrastructure-as-code provider (Milestone 1). New in this plan The web interface in the parity test; Every wizard shows its other ways in; The checker and the Simulator as agent tools; Per-tool rules for the agent endpoint.

13. Every decision explains itself Added by this chapter

As teams live it
"Why didn't my pipeline start?" "Why was this step skipped?" "Why is production still on the old version?" Each question is a search through logs in several places, and often the answer is that nobody can tell.
What is common today
Logs of what happened, rarely of what was decided and why; a skipped step shown as gray with no reason; a trigger that did not fire leaves no trace at all.
What Launchway does instead
Every decision is an event with its reasons: a trigger that did not start a Sortie says which filter refused it; a skipped step says which condition was false and with which values; a waiting step says why it waits, with a stable code; a Standing orders verdict lists its facts; an Overwatch verdict says what it measured against what. The plan makes it a rule the build enforces: a decision written without reasons fails the build. The Wingman (helper and AI helper) answers "why" questions from the same record.
Why it is not bolted on
Reasons have to be written at the moment of decision, by the code that decides. Adding them later means reconstructing them from logs, which is exactly the search teams do today.
What it gives you
Monitoring of the delivery system itself: you see not only what happened but why. The measures: decisions on the record without reasons (zero, enforced); and "why" questions answered from the record by the Wingman without a person.

Designed in The record and Pipelines, values and expressions. Status: Available An event log that explains every decision (Milestone 2); A failed step says why (Available today list). In progress Why is my run waiting (Milestone 2). New in this plan One record behind every view; A decision without reasons fails the build (proposed in The record); Every condition explained before and after a Sortie (proposed in Pipelines, values and expressions).

14. From advisory to verified Launch Added by this chapter

As teams live it
A new advisory lands. Someone opens a spreadsheet: which services use the package, which versions are deployed where, who owns them. Weeks later the spreadsheet says "patched", but nobody can show that the patched version is the one running.
What is common today
Dependency scanning per repository, update pull requests per repository, and a separate inventory of what is deployed. The link between "fixed in the code" and "fixed in production" is made by hand.
What Launchway does instead
The software graph answers "where does this run?" with the path it checked. Maintenance (dependency updates) opens ordinary pull requests that fly the same path as any change: Inspection, Clearance, a Launch by digest, Overwatch. The finding closes in each Airfield when the fixed digest is live there, with the time it was open.
Why it is not bolted on
Only a graph that links packages to images to digests to Airfields, and a record that knows which digest runs where, can close a finding in production rather than in a repository.
What it gives you
Patch deadlines answered by a query, not a spreadsheet. The measure: time from advisory to the fixed digest running in prod, per finding.

An advisory names an image-transform package below 3.2.2. The graph answers: the storefront web front end in prod and the image-resize function, both owned by the same group; the billing machines do not use it, and the graph shows the path it checked. Maintenance opens two pull requests at once. They merge, launch by digest, and the findings close in prod when the new versions are live.

Designed in The software graph and Maintenance. Status: Available One graph from code to hardware; Findings and SBOMs per run; Built-in dependency updates (Milestone 5). Planned Blast radius of a vulnerability; Automated patching; Patch deadlines and evidence (Milestone 5); Patch everything affected by an advisory (Milestone 12). New in this plan Updates merged by themselves where a level allows (proposed in The software graph and Maintenance).

15. Safeguards that earn their place Added by this chapter

As teams live it
A manual approval was added after an incident three years ago. It has been clicked "approve" 118 times in a row. Everyone suspects it catches nothing and costs a day per release, but nobody can prove it is safe to remove, so it stays. New rules are switched on blind and block the wrong things on day one.
What is common today
Approvals and policies that are either on or off, with no record of what they ever caught; a dry-run mode at best.
What Launchway does instead
For every Clearance on a Route, a card shows the facts over a chosen period: how often it said No-go, the time it added, the Launches it cleared that later went wrong and whether Overwatch caught them, the quality of the signals that would replace it, and what the Simulator says would have happened without it. A new Standing order can be tried against the record to see what it would have blocked, and starts in report mode. The card never removes anything by itself: it offers the change as a pull request, and a safeguard required by a level above can only be changed by that level.
Why it is not bolted on
It needs every Clearance, every verdict and every Launch outcome on one record, and a Simulator that can replay a Route without the step. That is the whole model at work.
What it gives you
Continuous deployment earned with evidence, not assumed; and new rules that do not surprise anyone. The measures: Clearances retired with a card, and what happened to failure rate afterwards; rules tried against the record before they were enforced.

The card for the Clearance before storefront in prod, last 90 days: 118 Go, 0 No-go; a median 3 hours 10 minutes added per release, 61 releases waiting overnight; 2 cleared Launches later returned to base, both caught by Overwatch in 3 and 4 minutes. Readiness: ready to replace with Overwatch alone, by the Squadron's own criteria. Sam opens the pull request the card offers.

Designed in Fast pipelines and continuous deployment and Standing orders, Clearance and Hold. Status: Available Policy gates (Available today list), with report or enforce modes and expiring waivers. New in this plan Evidence that a manual step can go; Speed suggestions proved in the Simulator (proposed in Fast pipelines and continuous deployment); Try a rule against the record (proposed in Standing orders, Clearance and Hold).

How it will be measured

An advantage is a claim, and a claim needs a measure. Each measure below is read from the one record, worked out the same way on every installation, and shown to the Base it belongs to. It is never a guess, a period with no data says "none", and nothing ranks people. Where a measure has no data yet, it says "not enough data", never a flattering number.

Proposal

Two roadmap changes make the measures real. A Wing's own page reads them from its record ("What each advantage did for you, measured"), and the existing item "Published proof points" publishes them for Launchway's own delivery, with the method, describing the usual approach generically and naming no other product. Both are listed under proposed roadmap changes.

The floor: nothing lost

The advantages above sit on a floor. For every capability teams rely on in the major build and delivery tools, this plan has an answer that matches it and aims to better it, derived from Launchway's own model rather than copied. The Coverage proves it capability by capability: what the capability is, what the best of today looks like, what would be clearly better, where Launchway stands, and the chapter that answers it. Where the honest answer is "connect", it says so, and the connection is an equal choice with its own slot.

A team does not have to start again to get there. Bringing work in covers importing pipelines, templates, shared libraries, triggers, variables, delivery settings and policies from every major kind of system, with nothing dropped silently, a finding for everything a person must finish, and old and new run side by side until the results agree.

What Launchway will not do

Some things are better left to the systems that do them well. Launchway connects to them, reads from them and acts on what they say, and it is a stronger product for not trying to replace them.

  • It will not be a metrics, log or trace store, or a dashboard server. Radar reads what a team already runs, through guarded queries, and joins it to the change that caused it. That joining is the advantage; another storage engine would not be.
  • It will not be an incident or on-call system, or an error tracker. It sends alerts in with the change, the evidence and an explanation, and updates the incident from the record. Radar, insight and keeping it healthy leaves open whether a small built-in incident record is wanted.
  • It will not certify anyone. It provides controls and evidence and says on every pack that it is evidence support, not a certification. The assessor examines the customer's system.
  • It will not make an unsafe change safe. A change that is not backward compatible cannot launch with zero downtime; Preflight (checks) says so. Return to base restores the release, never the data.
  • It will not rewrite your application or infrastructure silently. Recognition, Maintenance, the Clearance card and the Wingman propose changes as pull requests; a person accepts, edits or declines.
  • It will not run anyone else's code inside the server, or rank people. Extensions run as sandboxed steps or at Hardpoints; measures are for teams.

Proposed roadmap changes

Every advantage is already carried by items the chapters propose. This chapter proposes only what no other chapter does: a home for the Envelope, and a way to show and publish the measures. The JSON is in the plan's proposals file for this chapter.
