Simulator Open question
The proposed word for testing a pipeline without flying it (advantages 1, 4 and 15 lean on it). Without it, the plain words are "pipeline tests". Its design does not change either way.
Route Open question
The proposed word for the ordered Airfields a release flies through, with what must be true at each stop. Advantages 4 and 8 rest on promotion being an object of its own, whatever it is called.
Envelope Open question
The proposed word for a service's measured limits of healthy behavior. One clash to settle: The record and What starts a Sortie already use "envelope" in its plain technical sense, for the common wrapper around every event and the open standard events go out in. Either accept Envelope with a capital for the service's limits and keep the lower-case word for event wrappers, or choose another word for one of them ("event wrapper" is the plain alternative).
Continuous deployment by default? Open question
Advantages 4 and 15 depend on the default Route for a new Flight. Fast pipelines and continuous deployment recommends that dev and staging advance by themselves and prod waits for a Clearance until its card says it is ready, so continuous deployment is earned, not assumed.
How long Overwatch watches Open question
Advantage 2 needs a default. Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch recommends 30 minutes for production-class Airfields and 10 elsewhere, with automatic return on.
May a release reuse test results? Open question
Advantage 3 saves the most when it can; some auditors expect every release to test fresh (advantage 5). The recommendation is reuse allowed by default, with a "fresh tests for releases" Standing order offered in the compliance packs.
May a level require a branching pattern? Open question
Advantage 4 offers patterns and moves; whether a level above may require one, with a lock, is open in Every way of branching.
One pod per step or per Sortie Open question
One of the four plan-wide questions. It changes how warm Stations and short chains of steps are made fast (advantage 3), not whether they are.
Publishing comparisons Open question
The existing item "Published proof points" promises comparisons anyone can reproduce. Under the rule that no other product is named, the proposal is to publish Launchway's own measures with the method and describe the usual approach generically. Confirm, or say what a comparison may show.

The system

Launchway is one program, a database and Git: you can run it on one server, on Kubernetes or as a hosted service, and it behaves the same way in all three.

  • One program with roles you can scale apart: the web interface and API, the engine that moves Sorties (runs) forward, the Git host, the Depot (registry) and the schedulers. Today every server runs every role.
  • A database holds everything that matters: SQLite for one server, PostgreSQL for several. Servers keep nothing on their own disks that cannot be rebuilt.
  • Stations (runners), Launch Stations (deploy runners) and the Detachment (the small program on a customer's side) only ever connect outward.
  • Kubernetes is the recommended way to run it. Upgrades are boring: additive migrations, an older program on a newer schema, Return to base (rollback) by image.
  • Backups with point-in-time recovery, a second site and the offline bundle each count only when a regular test has proved them: a restore drill into a throwaway installation, a rehearsed promotion, an install with the network cut.
  • The hosted service comes shared (your Base walled off from every other) or dedicated (an installation of its own, run for you). Either way your data stays in the region you chose, your company's domain can claim its people, and a plan changes limits, never features.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 1 of the map, the foundation, together with Levels, people and secrets. Everything else runs on it. It relies on the record for its own history: every server reads and writes the same append-only record, which is why any server can carry on where another stopped. Stations are described in depth in Stations and where work runs, and the outside systems that plug in are in Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints.

Layers used
1 (foundation) and 2 (the record)
Builds on
A database and Git, and nothing else required
Built on by
Every other chapter

What you will be able to do

You try Launchway on one server. One command installs it with its own database file, you open the address, sign in with the one-time setup code, and you are guided from there. Months later you move it to several servers with one guided step, without losing a Sortie.

You run Launchway on your Kubernetes cluster for a company. Two servers serve by default, more start when request load rises, and a node drain never takes the last one away. Steps run in their own namespace at a lower priority, so a busy build day slows builds, not Launchway.

A server dies while three Sorties are airborne. The load balancer stops sending it traffic, the other servers carry on from the record, and nobody notices except the server count on the System page.

You upgrade by changing the version and nothing else. Halfway through, you change your mind and go back to the old image. It starts against the newer schema and keeps working.

Every night a Patrol (schedule) restores last night's backup into a throwaway copy of Launchway that can run nothing and send nothing, checks that every secret opens, every stored file is there and the record is complete, and throws the copy away. The System page says "Backups proven: restored to 03:12 in 6 minutes; at most 40 seconds would be lost." New in this plan, on Planned Backups and point-in-time recovery.

Your company moves to the hosted service. You pick the region where its data will live, prove your company's domain with one DNS record, and every colleague who signs up with a company address is asked to sign in through your company's provider. A customer of yours later asks for a database of your own: you move to a dedicated installation with the same features and the same Flights. New in this plan, on Planned Data residency.

You sign up for the hosted service with a friend. Your Base (on the hosted service, your own private installation) is walled off from every other customer, your Stations on your own machines connect out, and neither of you opens a port.

How it works

The system in context

The servers hold no secret values and no credentials for your clusters. Stations look up secrets in their own network. Launch Stations hold the identity that reaches an Airfield (environment). On the hosted service, the Detachment holds both, so the hosted side never does. The blob store is the database itself by default, so several servers need nothing else; a shared folder or S3-compatible storage is optional.

Built today

One program, launchway server, serves the web interface and HTTP API, runs the Sortie engine, polls and hosts Git, fires schedules, judges policy and, unless turned off, runs a built-in Station (docs/start/architecture.md). The database is PostgreSQL for several servers and an embedded SQLite file for one. The Helm chart turns the built-in Station off and runs Stations as their own pods (deploy/helm/launchway/values.yaml).

One program, several roles

The program is divided into roles. A role is a part of the program with one job, its own load and its own way of failing. Today every server runs every role. The plan is that each server can be told which roles to run, so the roles can be scaled apart while they stay one program, one version and one release.

RoleWhat it doesWhat it keepsStatus
Web and APIThe web interface, the HTTP API, the agent endpoint, the live stream, sign-in, incoming webhooks and event sources.Nothing. Sessions and tokens are in the database as hashes, so a browser can reach any server.Available as part of every server
EngineMoves Sorties forward: plans steps, grants leases to Stations, judges Standing orders (policies and standards) at their fixed points, opens and watches Launches (deployments).Nothing. A Sortie's state is rebuilt from its events whenever it is needed.Available as part of every server
Git hostServes hosted repositories over HTTPS and SSH, keeps mirrors, polls outside hosts.A cache of each repository, rebuilt when a server starts. Refs are in the database; packs are in the blob store.Available as part of every server
DepotStores and serves images, charts, packages and other Cargo (artifacts), by digest.Nothing. Blobs are in the blob store.Available as part of every server
SchedulersPatrols (schedules), timers, retention clean-up, outgoing deliveries and other background work.Nothing. Each job is claimed in a database transaction, so exactly one server does it.Available as part of every server
Choosing roles per serverA setting that tells a server which roles to run. The default is all of them.Not applicable.New in this plan Planned
Proposal

Roles are a setting of the same program, never separate programs. A server that runs only some roles still checks the same schema, reads the same record and answers /readyz for the roles it runs. Splitting never introduces a second database, a message bus or a cache that holds the truth. The role names above are plain words for a design sketch; their machine names are for the build to choose.

Stations, Launch Stations and the Detachment connect outward

A Station takes steps from a server and runs them in containers, Kubernetes pods or on its own machine. A Launch Station is a Station with a delivery section, placed in or near an Airfield; it carries out Launches and never runs a script. Both connect outward over HTTPS and wait for work in requests of up to 25 seconds, so they work behind a firewall, a NAT or a proxy that inspects TLS. A Station enrolled with a join token holds its own key, which never leaves it, and is given only the work of the Flights (codebases) its Ramp (Station pool) serves (docs/guide/runner-identity.md).

The Detachment is the small program on a customer's side when Launchway is hosted. It starts the customer's Stations, looks things up in the customer's secret store and reads the customer's clusters, metrics, logs and DNS. It only calls out. The same Detachment serves a self-hosted installation, so moving between the two is a change of address, not a new design (roadmap item Self-hosted is the same shape).

Proposal

The Detachment is built from the same source as the server and released with the same version and signature, as its own small program. One release means one upgrade story and one set of tests for the wire format between them.

Three ways to run it

For a trial, a laptop, a small team or a machine without Kubernetes. One process runs every role and a built-in Station. With no database setting it keeps everything in an embedded SQLite file. A brand-new installation on SQLite generates its own root key file at first start, so encryption at rest is on with nothing to set up (docs/guide/encryption-at-rest.md). A server without sign-in refuses to listen beyond the loopback address.

What it cannot do: survive the loss of its machine. There is one copy of everything. Back up the database file and the root key, separately.

The way up is a guided move to PostgreSQL and then to several servers. That move is a proposal in this plan; today it is a backup and restore.

The recommended way, for anything a team depends on. The Helm chart starts a secure installation from one required value, the address. Two servers run by default. Each has readiness and liveness checks, a rolling update that never removes a server before its replacement is ready, a soft spread across nodes, and a disruption budget that lets at most one server be evicted at a time. Autoscaling of servers and of Stations is one setting each (off by default). Stations run steps as pods in a step namespace of their own (deploy/helm/launchway/values.yaml).

The chart's bundled PostgreSQL is one pod on one volume: fine for a trial, not highly available. For production, point the chart at a managed or operator-run PostgreSQL. A highly available database mode with one primary and two copies is planned (Milestone 10).

A laptop can run Kubernetes too. A small bundled Kubernetes for a server with none is planned, so the recommended shape is reachable from a bare machine.

Launchway without running it. The operator runs the hosted service on Kubernetes, as its production installation, with at least two servers, encryption at rest and tested backups. Every customer has its own Base, walled off from every other Base and from the operator's own; see the wall.

A customer then chooses one of three ways to use it: fully hosted (nothing to install), hosted with their own Detachment (builds, secrets and files on their side), or self-hosted (the same product on their own machines). Moving between them is previewed, verified and reversible, one Flight or one Base at a time.

Until the tests that prove the wall pass, the production installation serves only the operator's own Base.

The hosted service itself comes in two shapes, shared and dedicated, and in every shape you choose the region where your data lives, can claim your company's people by its domain, and get every feature on every plan. Each is designed below, from shared or dedicated to plans.

QuestionA single serverKubernetesThe hosted service, sharedThe hosted service, dedicated
DatabaseSQLite by default; PostgreSQL allowedPostgreSQLPostgreSQL, with row-level security as a second lock between BasesA PostgreSQL database of its own, in the region you chose
ServersOneTwo or more, autoscaled on request loadTwo or more, autoscaledTwo or more, autoscaled, serving only you
StationsThe built-in one, plus any you enrollPods, autoscaled on steps waitingYours, outbound; sandboxed hosted ones laterYours, outbound, or the installation's own
Survives losing a machineNoYes for servers and Stations; the database depends on how you run itYesYes, and a site, when you choose a second site
Who upgrades itYou, by replacing the programYou, by changing the version in the chart or in GitThe operator; your Detachment updates only when you allow itThe operator, inside an upgrade window you set
Recommended forTrying it, one person, a machine without a clusterAny team that depends on itSmall teams that want nothing to runCompanies that need a database of their own, a region of their own or their own upgrade window

The hosted service: shared or dedicated

The hosted service is the same program and the same release in two shapes. Which one you use is a hosting choice, never an edition: every feature is the same in both, and the same as self-hosted (ruling: no feature is gated by plan).

Shared

Your Base (installation, on the hosted service your own private one) is one of many on an installation the operator runs. It is walled off from every other Base by rows tagged with their Base, row-level security as a second lock, its own data key, and an isolation test suite that is a release gate. Nothing to run, and the default for small teams.

Dedicated

An installation of its own that the operator runs for one customer, from the same chart and the same signed release, in the region you choose. It has its own database, blob store, root key and servers; nothing is shared with another customer but the release itself. Your Base is still walled off from the operator's own, as on every installation.

QuestionSharedDedicated
FeaturesAllAll, the same
What keeps you apart from othersThe wall: tagged rows, row-level security, a data key per Base, the isolation suiteA separate installation and database, and the same wall inside it
UpgradesThe operator, on the service's rhythmThe operator, inside an upgrade window you set; you may hold one release back for a bounded time, security fixes excepted (a proposal)
What you see of the installationYour Base, and the service's statusAlso the System page: servers, versions, backups and their last restore drill, the standby and its last rehearsal
The operator's accessThe same in both: nothing inside a Base without a break-glass you approve, for a limited time, and every action the operator takes is written to your Logbook (audit trail)
LeavingExport the whole Base and import it anywhere (Nothing held hostage)The same, or take the whole installation in-house: because it is the same chart, its backup restores into your own cluster with your own root key, and the restore drill proves it first
Proposal

A dedicated installation run for you is a new roadmap item in Milestone 7. It needs no new code path: it is the self-hosted shape, operated by the vendor, which is why "Self-hosted is the same shape" is its foundation. Which cloud it first runs on is open (see Open question).

Where your data lives

Two questions decide where your data is, and the hosted service asks both in plain words when a Base is created.

  1. In which region is the hosted side? A Base is pinned to a region when it is created. Its database rows, stored files, logs, backups and the copies a standby holds all stay in that region. Each region is a whole installation of its own (a cell, in the words of Decompose only when it makes sense), so no shared database spans regions. The region is shown on the Base's settings page and written into every evidence pack and every export. Moving to another region is a guided move (export, import, verify, switch), recorded and reversible until the old copy is deleted; it never happens as a silent copy.
  2. What stays on your side? With your own Detachment (the small program on your side), builds, secrets, logs, Cargo (artifacts) and reports never reach the hosted side at all. The recorded recommendation for the default is the standard mode, with "Cargo and logs at home" one switch away.
Kind of dataFully hostedHosted with your Detachment
Settings, the record, work itemsThe region you choseThe region you chose
RepositoriesThe region you chose, or your own code hostThe region you chose, or your own code host
SecretsSealed in the region you chose, opened only on StationsYour own secret store; never on the hosted side
Logs, Cargo, reportsThe region you choseYour side, with the hosted side holding names, states, counts and timings
BackupsThe same region as the data they copyHosted part in the region; your part where you keep it
What the vendor console seesPer region: how many Bases, their resource use and the health of the hosted side. Never anything inside a Base.

Your company's domain claims its people

On the hosted service a person has one account and can belong to several Bases: their company's, a friend's side project, their own. A company Base can prove that it owns a domain and then claim the accounts that use it. Self-hosted installations do not need this: the installation already belongs to one company and signs in through its provider.

  1. Prove it. A Commander (owner) of the Base adds the domain (the one value typed, checked as a domain name as you type). Launchway shows one DNS record to publish and finds it. The record is looked up again on a Patrol; if it disappears, the claim pauses at once (no new claims; claimed people keep their state), the Commander is told, and after a notice period the claim ends. Nothing is deleted, and a claim never ends silently.
  2. Claim. An account whose verified e-mail address is at the domain is claimed: it must sign in through the Base's sign-in provider, its tokens can be listed and revoked by the Base's Commanders, and when the provider removes the person, the account is signed out everywhere on the hosted service. An account that existed before the claim is told first and given a grace period.
  3. Keep the wall. The claiming Base sees the claimed accounts and what they did inside its own Base, never another Base's name, members or contents. A person's own Bases stay theirs. If the company chooses "claimed accounts may not join other Bases", the refusal is shown to the person only, so no Base learns that another exists.
  4. One proof, two uses. The same proved domain can serve the Base's own address beside its name on the operator's domain, at no charge.

Verified domains are on every plan, the free one included, because no feature is gated by plan.

Proposal

Verified domains for a Base is proposed once, with the completeness fixes for the access and governance chapters, in Milestone 7; this chapter designs it on the hosted side and references that item. It assumes one account can belong to several Bases, which is still open there.

Plans change limits, never features

  • Every feature is on in every plan, the free plan included (ruling ; roadmap item Every feature on, the spend limit at zero).
  • Plans differ only in limits: the people in a Base, private repositories and their size, other storage, hosted Station minutes, the Base's size ceiling, and how the hosted side is run (shared or dedicated, one site or two). Price follows availability, people and hosting.
  • The spend limit starts at zero, so nothing is charged until a Commander raises it.
  • At a limit, only the growing kind of thing stops. Reading, cloning, exporting, moving and builds on your own Stations keep working, and nothing is deleted for being over (Size ceilings on hosted Bases).
  • Every Base is walled off on every plan. The free plan is not a weaker wall, a shared Station pool or a public space; it is a smaller ceiling.

The numbers themselves, whether your own Stations ever count against a plan, and whether public repositories are offered on the free plan are not decided and are not published in this plan (see Open question).

Harbor Lights tries the hosted service before moving. Sam creates the Base in the region nearest the shop's customers, proves harbor-lights.example, and Dana, Ana and Priya are claimed after their notice. Priya's own Base for a hobby project stays hers, and the company never sees it. A year later a payments partner asks for a database not shared with anyone: Sam picks the dedicated shape, the Flights move by export and import, and the restore drill on the new installation passes before the switch.

What scales, and on what signal

Each part grows on the signal that says it is short of room, inside a ceiling you set, and the ceilings come from measured numbers rather than guesses. Builds live apart from the platform: it is better to have slower builds than an unstable platform.

PartGrows onNever onToday
Servers (web and API)Requests in flight and time to answerThe number of Sorties airborne, which costs a server littleThe chart's autoscaler uses processor and memory, with room for other metrics
EngineLease requests and events written per secondLog volume, which is the Stations' and the blob store'sRuns in every server
Git hostConcurrent clones, fetches and pushesRepository countRuns in every server
DepotBytes movedNumber of stored imagesRuns in every server
SchedulersDoes not scale out; two copies for availabilityAnything: each job runs onceRuns in every server
StationsSteps waiting in the Holding pattern (queue), per RampProcessor use: a Station waiting for work is idle while its steps run in pods of their ownThe metric launchway_queue_depth exists and the chart documents it as the better signal; processor use is the chart's default
DatabaseGrows up, not out: one writer, with copies for failoverMore writers; multi-writer databases are not offeredOne PostgreSQL, yours or the bundled one

A step that cannot start waits with a plain reason instead of failing (Steps wait for room instead of failing). Today the chart can put step pods in a namespace of their own and give them a low scheduling priority, and neither is on by default. Making both the default, so that when a node is short of room a build is the one that waits, is proposed in Stations and where work runs as Builds never take room from the platform, together with Stations added and removed by the steps waiting. This chapter proposes the servers' half: Servers grow on request load.

When something is lost

Every module states what happens when a server, the database or a Station is lost (module contract, rule 9). For the foundation itself:

What is lostWhat happensWhat you seeStatus
A serverThere is no leader. Every decision that must happen once (a start, a lease, a Patrol firing, a Clearance (approval), a policy verdict) is made in a database transaction, so exactly one server wins. The load balancer stops sending traffic when /readyz fails. Stations reconnect to any server.One fewer server on the System page. Sorties carry on.Available
The database, brieflyServers retry errors that pass by themselves for up to two minutes (resilience.stall_budget), then answer 503 with Retry-After, never 500. Stations keep running their steps and keep logs and results on their own disk, then deliver them in order.The step log says "The server could not be reached from 14:02:10 to 14:03:40; nothing was lost."In progress (the first parts exist)
The database, for longerNothing is decided while it is away, and nothing happens that is not on the record. A highly available mode keeps the gap under about two minutes: one primary, two copies, a write reported done only when a copy has it, automatic promotion.launchway doctor database says whether the installation would survive losing its database.Planned (Milestone 10)
A StationA Station sends a heartbeat every 15 seconds. A step whose Station is silent for its lease (90 seconds by default) is marked lost and queued again; a step is never recorded as finished twice. If the Station that holds a Sortie's workspace is gone for three lease periods, another Station takes the Sortie over in a fresh checkout.The step shows a second attempt with the reason.Available
A Launch StationA Launch Station takes a rollout command only until a stated time (deploy.command_taken carries it), and each command records what it expects, so a stale command does nothing. A Launch step that waits for observations has a deadline, so a lost observer ends in a recorded failure, not a wait without end.The Launch page says what it is waiting for.Available (described from the event model, not drilled)
A server's diskIt holds only caches, such as repository mirrors, rebuilt when the server starts. An acknowledged push is committed in the database before Git is told it succeeded.A slower first fetch after a restart.Available; the failover test is Planned
The root keyServers refuse to start rather than run without it, and say which key and why. Without a copy, the sealed secrets cannot be recovered. The first-run wizard asks you to back the key up.A refusal at start, recorded as encryption.unseal.Available
The database's data, by mistake or damageA restore to a point in time from the backups, through a wizard that lists what will be lost by name. Only backups a restore drill has proved are offered.The System page shows the last proven point and how much would be lost.Planned (Milestone 10); a drill on any installation is New in this plan
A whole siteA person promotes the standby in the other site; the old primary is fenced by the record's generation number. See A second site.Both System pages show the lag; the wizard shows what the gap would lose.Planned (Milestone 10)
The hosted service, seen from your sideYour Detachment keeps working for what it can, then catches up.A notice on your side, not a stopped Sortie.Planned (Milestone 7)
Honest limit

While the database is unreachable, no decision is made, a Return to base included. The record cannot accept the decision, and a decision that is not on the record did not happen. Until the highly available database mode exists, the manual path for a GitOps Launch is to revert its commit in Git, which the Airfield's controller then applies.

Backups and point-in-time recovery, proven by a restore drill

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. The roadmap already says it: a restore that has not been tested is not counted. This plan turns that sentence into a mechanism you can see.

PartHow it is keptPoints you can return to
The database, PostgreSQLA full copy on a Patrol, and the database's own change log archived continuously to storage you nameAny moment inside the window you keep
The database, SQLite on one serverThe consistent online copy the guide describes today, taken on a Patrol instead of by handThe moment of each copy
Stored files: Git packs, Cargo, reportsEach file is named by its digest and never changes, so a copy only adds. Clean-up of a file nothing refers to waits until no backup inside the window could still refer to it.Whatever the database at that moment refers to, always present
The root keyNever in the same place as the backups. The wizard asks where it is kept, and the drill proves the backup opens with it.Not applicable

The restore drill runs on a Patrol (daily by default) and does five things:

  1. Picks a point. The newest point every day, and once a week a random point inside the window, so the whole window is proved and not only its end.
  2. Restores into a throwaway installation. On Kubernetes, a namespace of its own with no route to your Stations or Airfields; on one server, a separate data folder that listens on the loopback address only. Patrols, Station leases and outgoing deliveries are off in it, so a restored copy can never run a step or send a webhook.
  3. Checks what matters. The schema matches. Every sealed secret opens with the root key (launchway doctor encryption --restore-drill does this part today). The record's chain verifies up to the point, and its head equals the head recorded at that moment. Every stored file the record refers to is there with the right digest. Every Git ref resolves. A sample of Sorties rebuilt from their events gives the state that was recorded.
  4. Measures two numbers. How much would be lost (the gap between the point and the newest archived change) and how long the restore took.
  5. Records a verdict. An event with the numbers and the reasons, shown on the System page: "Backups proven: restored to 03:12 today in 6 minutes; at most 40 seconds would be lost." A failed or missing drill turns the card to "Not proven" and sends a Comms (notifications) notice. Then the copy is thrown away.

Restoring for real is a wizard. You pick the point on the timeline of the record, with Launches and pushes around it shown, so you choose the moment before the bad change rather than typing a time. The wizard lists by name what will be lost: Sorties started, pushes acknowledged and settings changed after the point, each with its author, because no backup can bring back what came after it. It restores into a throwaway installation first so you can look, then switches. Going forward again is possible until the old database is deleted.

One Sunday the Harbor Lights drill fails: a test report that the record of Sortie 417 points to is missing from the restored copy. The clean-up had removed it a day early. Nobody needed that backup yet; the drill found the fault first, the notice named the file and the rule that removed it, and the fix shipped before the next drill passed.

On the hosted service the operator backs up the whole installation, and the same drill runs on it. A dedicated installation shows you its own drill results. A shared Base that wants a copy of its own uses Backup and recovery on your own machines and the whole-Base export; Leave completely destroys a Base's key, which makes every backup unreadable for that Base.

A second site, with a rehearsed promotion

A standby is a second installation of the same version in another site, kept a few seconds behind. Promotion is always a person's decision: automatic promotion across sites is avoided, because two sites that both believe they lead would make two records.

  • While it waits. The standby streams the database and copies stored files by digest. Its servers accept no Station, fire no Patrol and send nothing; its address shows one page: "This is the standby of launchway.harbor-lights.example, 3 seconds behind." The lag is shown in seconds and in events on both System pages, with a notice when it passes a limit you set.
  • Promotion. The wizard shows the lag and lists, by name, what the gap would lose (pushes acknowledged in the last seconds, with their authors). It raises the record's generation number, so everything from the old primary is refused from then on. Stations, Launch Stations (deploy runners) and Detachments reconnect by address and keep their own keys, because their enrollment is in the copied database. Results they kept on their own disk are delivered; a step whose start was lost in the gap is queued again under the lease rule and is never recorded twice.
  • Rehearsal. On a Patrol (weekly by default) a copy of the standby is promoted in isolation, fenced from everything real, and checked like a restore drill; the System page shows "Promotion rehearsed: 4 minutes, at most 2 seconds lost." A full switch-over and switch-back, in a window you set and under a Clearance (approval), proves the address move and the Stations' reconnection as well.
  • Afterwards. The old primary is seeded again as the new standby. Going back is the same wizard.
Honest limit

During the minutes of a promotion no decision is made, a Return to base included, for the same reason as in When something is lost. The manual path for a GitOps Launch, reverting its commit in Git, still works.

Running with no internet: the offline bundle and the relay

Some networks have no way out. Launchway runs there with everything it needs brought in on purpose, checked at the door, and kept fresh without a connection.

In the offline bundleWhy
The program and Station images for each processor architecture, by digest, signedInstall and run
The chart and the installerThe same walk-through, ending in the browser
The small bundled Kubernetes, when you choose itA bare machine
Step images of the built-in steps and the Hangar's (built-in library's) starters, by digestA first pipeline runs with no outside registry
The scanners and their advisory data, with the date it was takenInspection (security scan) works from the first Sortie
Flight school (learning) and the referenceLearning with no connection
A manifest, checksums, a software bill of materials and the bundle's signatureProof of exactly what came in

The installer carries the release's public key and refuses a bundle whose signature or any digest does not match, before anything is installed. Images go into the built-in Depot (registry) at install, so every Station pulls from inside. The next bundle is the next upgrade, and the upgrade preview works offline.

  • Advisory data stays fresh. A small signed advisory update is published daily. You bring it in by upload, by command or through the relay. Every Inspection finding and the System page show its age ("advisory data is 9 days old"), and a Standing order (policy) can warn or hold Launches when it is older than a limit you set. It is never stale without saying so.
  • The relay. The same program, started in a relay role on a machine at the edge of your network. It fetches signed releases, advisory updates, Maintenance (dependency update) data and the images you allow, verifies each, and either serves them to the inside on one address or writes a transfer file for a network where only a carried disk crosses. Every import is an event naming what came in and its signatures.

TestHow oftenWhat it provesWhere you see it

Boring upgrades, and the upgrade gate

An upgrade should be "change the version, nothing else", by helm upgrade, by a GitOps controller, image first or chart first, and a Return to base should always work. Five rules make that true:

  1. One program and a database. There is nothing else to upgrade in step with it.
  2. Additive migrations. Every migration declares whether it is additive (code that knows only the earlier ones keeps working) or breaking. The database records the newest migration and the minimum code schema, the number of the newest breaking one.
  3. An older program on a newer schema. A server that knows at least the minimum code schema starts against a newer database and says so once. A server that knows less refuses to start and names the schema it needs.
  4. Return to base by image. Going back is running the previous image. Nothing is undone in the database, so nothing can half-undo.
  5. An upgrade never changes what an existing pipeline does. New behavior arrives off, or as a default only for new things.

The upgrade gate is the set of checks that make an upgrade impossible to half-apply. Built so far: migrations taken in turn under a database lock, a check that the recorded schema matches the real tables, a root key that is never generated for a shared database, secrets sealed only after every older server has gone, and a release that is not cut unless make test-upgrade upgrades the previous release by each method on a throwaway cluster and returns to base. Still being finished: the server learns which chart revision rendered it and warns when it is older than the program expects, and parent applications sync before their children. Known gaps today: the upgrade matrix runs against a simulated GitOps controller and one network plugin (docs/roadmap/installing.md).

Proposal

An upgrade preview before every upgrade, in the interface and the command line: the version you have, the version you will get (picked from the signed releases), whether any migration is breaking and what that means for a Return to base, whether a recent backup exists, how many older servers and Stations are connected, and the network checks. The preview changes nothing. It turns the upgrade gate into something you can read before you start.

Decompose only when it makes sense

The rule is yours: scale the components, keep it simple, do not decompose until there is a need. Splitting a role onto servers of its own is a configuration change, not a new program, and it is justified only by one of these:

Its load is different

Measured numbers show that scaling the role with the others wastes resources, for example the Depot moving large images while the web role is quiet.

Its failure must not spread

A fault in the role must not take the others down, for example a flood of clones starving the API.

Its reach must be different

The role needs a different network path or exposure, for example Git over SSH on its own address, or a secret store that only Stations may reach.

A different release rhythm is never a reason: there is one version. A part becomes a separate program only when its trust is different (a Station, a Launch Station, the Detachment) or when its license requires it to run apart. The database is never split into several databases for convenience; very large installations become cells, each a whole installation owning a set of Wings (organizations), with a small directory above them (Cells for very large installations, not scheduled until a customer needs it).

Worked example: Harbor Lights

Harbor Lights is a small company. Its Flights are storefront (a Go service, a web front end and a PostgreSQL database), payments, and the shared library platform-library. It has three Airfields, dev, staging and prod, and four kinds of places its software runs: a Kubernetes cluster for storefront, two virtual machines behind a load balancer for the legacy billing service, a rack of image-based hosts for edge kiosks, and one serverless function that resizes images.

Harbor Lights runs Launchway on its own Kubernetes cluster, the recommended shape. You run launchway install, choose Kubernetes, and confirm the cluster by name. You point the chart at the company's managed PostgreSQL and turn autoscaling on for both servers and Stations. These keys exist in the chart today:

externalURL: https://launchway.harbor-lights.example
database:
  existingSecret: launchway-database
server:
  autoscaling: { enabled: true, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 6 }
runner:
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 2
    maxReplicas: 10
    extraMetrics:
      - type: External
        external:
          metric: { name: launchway_queue_depth, selector: { matchLabels: { pool: default } } }
          target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "2" }

Stations for the storefront builds run as pods in the cluster. A Launch Station in the same cluster carries out storefront Launches. A second Launch Station runs on a small machine next to the two billing virtual machines, and a third sits in the kiosk network. Each one connects out to the servers; none of the three networks accepts a connection from Launchway.

  1. On release day the Holding pattern for the default Ramp reaches 14 waiting steps. The Station autoscaler adds Stations until there are about two waiting steps for each.
  2. During the storefront Launch to prod, the cluster's operator drains a node. The disruption budget lets one server go; the other keeps serving, and the Launch carries on.
  3. That evening Harbor Lights upgrades Launchway. The upgrade preview says every migration is additive, so a Return to base by image is safe. A new server starts, applies the migrations, becomes ready, and the old ones stop one at a time.

The foundation it relies on

  • A database. SQLite or PostgreSQL. It holds the record, every setting, sessions and tokens as hashes, refs of hosted repositories and, by default, the blobs.
  • Git. The real git program, for hosted repositories and for reading pipelines from their own commit.
  • The record. Every server works out the same state from the same events (The record).
  • Levels, people and secrets. Who may do what, and where secrets are resolved (Levels, people and secrets).

Safety

On failure

See When something is lost. The invariant behind every row: a decision is written in the same transaction as what it allows, so whatever fails, there is either one decision on the record or none.

Who may do what

ActionWhoRecorded as
Install, upgrade, Return to base of Launchway itselfWhoever operates the installation: the cluster or the machine, not a Launchway roleEach server records the configuration revision it applied (config.server_state)
Change autoscaling ceilings and role placementThe operator, in the chart or in GitThe chart revision the server sees
See the System pageA Commander (owner) of the BaseNot applicable

On by default

  • Sign-in from the first moment, with a one-time setup code; a server without sign-in refuses to listen beyond loopback.
  • Encryption at rest of stored secrets; the chart makes the root key once and keeps it.
  • Default-deny network policies and restricted pods; nothing exposed publicly.
  • Two servers and a disruption budget on Kubernetes.
  • Rolling updates that keep every old server until its replacement is ready.
  • Restore drills, once a backup place is set; until then the System page says "No backups" as a problem, never as a calm state.
  • A restored copy that can run nothing and send nothing; a standby that accepts no Station until a person promotes it.
  • Bundles, advisory updates and relay imports checked against their signatures before use.

Open question

Decision needed

Where hosted customers' files may live. Whether strangers' file content is stored on the operator's own server at all is still open. The recorded recommendation is never on the home server for public sign-up. This chapter assumes nothing either way.

Decision needed

SQLite and several Bases. Hosted needs PostgreSQL with row-level security. For a self-hosted single server, the open choice is rows tagged with their Base now and a file per Base evaluated later, or a file per Base from the start (wall plan, decision 4).

Decision needed

Turning several Bases on is one-way. The wall plan proposes that switching it on can be undone only from a backup. Accept, or ask for a different point of no return (wall plan, decision 2).

Decision needed

One pod per step or per Sortie on Kubernetes is listed as open in the plan's spine. It changes how Stations ask for room, not the system shape in this chapter; it is discussed in Stations and where work runs.

Decision needed

The dedicated installation. Whether and when it is offered, on which cloud it first runs, and whether a customer may hold one release back (this plan proposes one release, security fixes excepted). The business plan's revenue order lists dedicated installations; the choice of host for them is still open.

Decision needed

The first regions and which region is the default at sign-up. The cloud for the first region is still open.

Decision needed

The free plan's numbers, whether your own Stations never count against any plan (the recorded recommendation), and whether public repositories are on the free plan (recorded recommendation: not at first). The rule that every feature is on is decided; the numbers are not, and they stay out of public documents.

Decision needed

Claimed accounts and other Bases. Whether a company may refuse its claimed people joining other Bases at all, or only require that they sign in through its provider everywhere. This plan offers both as a choice of the claiming Base and shows a refusal only to the person.

Decision needed

How often drills and rehearsals run by default (this plan: a restore drill daily, an isolated promotion rehearsal weekly) and whether a standby may serve reads while it waits (this plan: no, one page only).

Decision needed

The roles' plain names (web and API, engine, Git host, Depot, schedulers) and whether the Detachment ships as its own small program from the same source are proposals here. Confirm or rename.

The record

Everything that happens in Launchway is written once, in order, to one append-only record, and every page, report, number and piece of evidence is read from it.

  • The record is the source of truth: a Sortie's (run's) state, the Logbook (audit trail), the Debrief (test report), metrics and evidence packs are all views of it.
  • Every decision is an event with its reasons: a trigger that did or did not start a Sortie, a Standing order (policy or standard) verdict, a Clearance (approval), a Launch and Overwatch verdict, a change to a setting.
  • Nothing is true that is not on the record. A decision is written in the same transaction as the thing it allows.
  • Today there are four separate streams. This chapter shows the path to one, in stages that never break an older server.

Where it sits

This is layer 2 of the map. It sits directly on the system (one database shared by every server) and on levels, people and secrets (every event belongs to a Base, a Wing, a Squadron and a Flight, the installation, organization, team and codebase, and is read only by people who may see it). Stations (runners) and Launch Stations (deploy runners) report to it through the servers. Every layer above writes to it: triggers write their decisions, Launches and Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) write their verdicts, Standing orders write their judgments, and evidence is a period of the record, exported. The module contract asks every module to write its decisions here and read its history from here (rule 2).

Layers used
2 (the record), on 1 (the foundation)
Written by
Every layer and every module
Read by
The interface, the Logbook, the Debrief, Radar (monitoring) and metrics, evidence packs, Comms (notifications) and events sent out

What you will be able to do

A push did not start a build. You open the push in the record and read one sentence for each trigger: paths: only docs/** changed. You fix the filter and replay the push; the new Sortie points back to the push that should have started it.

An auditor asks who released storefront 2.4.0 to prod, on what evidence. You export one week of the record for the Flight (codebase), and the export shows the Standing order verdicts with the facts they judged, who said Go, the Overwatch verdict with its measurements, and a chain head that proves nothing was taken out.

Your incident tool wants to know about every failed Launch. You add a subscription at the Wing, pick the kind "Launch finished" and the condition "verdict is not deployed" from lists, and choose the tool's connection. Each event arrives in an open standard event format, signed, with a delivery log and retries.

Your Squadron writes a new module that tracks database change sets. It registers three event kinds in the catalog; from that moment its events appear on the Flight's timeline, in the Logbook, in exports and in subscriptions, with no code in any of those readers.

Checkout errors rise in prod. You open the timeline for storefront and see, on one line, the Launch of 2.4.0, a Switch flip, a variable change and the first alert, because all of them are events in the same record. New in this plan

A delivery dashboard says lead time rose this month. You open the number and see the Sorties and Launches behind it, because the number is counted from the same events.

How it works

Today: four streams

The idea is not new to Launchway. The engine is already event-sourced: a Sortie's state is never kept in memory, it is rebuilt from the Sortie's events whenever it is needed, and every server works it out the same way (docs/start/architecture.md). But there are four separate streams, each with its own shape, its own retention and its own way of being read (docs/reference/events.md, docs/guide/events.md).

StreamWhat it holdsHow it is keptHow it is read
The Sortie event logrun.*, step.*, approval, deploy.*, policy.evaluated and verify.* events, each with a schema numberAppend-only; nothing changes or deletes an event; one number (seq) across the whole databaseThe Sortie page, GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/events, the live stream
The trigger event logEvery received push, pull request, Patrol (schedule), webhook, event-source call, manual start and result, with a decision for each trigger and a sentence saying whyThe newest 5000 per Flight, and only the newest 200 that were not verified; payloads scrubbed of credentials and cut at 16 KiBThe Events page, launchway events, the agent tool list_events; replay
The LogbookEvery call that changes something, allowed or refused, every refused token, every webhook call, every sign-in and sign-out, every key operationOnly ever added to; kept until an administrator removes old rows; also written as JSON lines on standard outputThe Logbook page, GET /api/v1/audit, any log collector
Hosted-repository eventspush, pull_request, review, work_item and other repository eventsKept for outgoing repository webhooks, with a delivery logSigned webhooks to other tools

Notification rules, the live stream and the delivery metrics are each built from one or two of these. A change to a variable is in the Logbook and in the variable's own history, but not in the Sortie log. A trigger decision and the Sortie it started are written in the same transaction, but in different tables with different identifiers. The record this chapter describes keeps every one of these guarantees and removes the seams between them.

From a source to its readers

A writer is the code that makes a decision or a change: the trigger judge, the engine, the Standing order judge, the Launch observer, the settings store. It appends the event in the same database transaction as the change itself, so the record and the state can never disagree. A reader is anything that shows or sends what happened. Readers may keep their own indexes and summaries for speed, but each one can be thrown away and rebuilt from the record.

Step output, the Flight recorder (run log), is the one large thing that stays beside the record rather than in it, as today: an event names the step and attempt, and the lines are stored and streamed on their own. Test reports, Cargo (artifacts) and attachments are stored the same way and referenced by digest.

What is recorded

Kind of eventExamplesThe reasons it carriesToday
Trigger decisionsstarted, held, waiting, filtered, superseded, skipped, duplicate, refused, errorOne sentence per trigger, such as the signature did not matchAvailable in the trigger log
Sortie and step eventsrun.created with everything it started with, step.leased with every input but secret values, step.finished with outcome, cause and report summariesCause (exit, timeout, infrastructure), the last lines of output, why a step was skippedAvailable in the Sortie log
Standing order verdictsA verdict at Sortie start, before a Launch, before an image pushEach policy and rule as judged, what was found and wanted, the evidence, the waivers considered, the facts judgedAvailable as policy.evaluated
ClearancesWaiting, one of several approvals recorded, Go, No-go, nobody decided in timeWho, their comment, the deadline, why the server rejected itAvailable as approval events
Launch verdictsA Launch opened, each action done, each observed phase, closed as deployed, failed, returned to base or abandonedThe commit, what changed, the phase reached, the command and what it expectedAvailable as deploy.*
Overwatch verdictsThe watch started, each interval's measurements, the verdict, a person's overrideEach check's reason, the baseline, and a model's explanation marked as untrusted textAvailable as verify.*
Changes to settingsA variable set or locked, a role granted, a policy changed, a Station revoked, a key rotatedWho, from which address, through which token, old and new value (a secret only as its reference)Available in the Logbook
Module eventsA Switch (feature toggle) flipped, an Inspection (security scan) finding, a work item movedAs the module's catalog entry declaresPartly: some go to the Logbook (toggle.*, registry.*, work.*), work items also to repository webhooks

One common event format

Every event in the record is written in one common event format, whatever wrote it. The format answers the questions every reader asks: what happened, to what, where in the levels, who did it, and why. (This plan keeps the word Envelope only for a service's measured healthy limits; the wrapper around an event is always called the common event format.)

FieldMeaning
id and positionA unique identifier and a number that only increases, as seq does today
atWhen it was written, on the database's clock
whereThe Base, and the Wing, Squadron and Flight when it belongs to one, and the Airfield (environment) when it has one
kind and schemaThe kind from the catalog, the schema it came with, and the oldest schema that understands it (as requires today)
subjectWhat it is about: a Sortie, a step attempt, a Launch, a release, a setting, a repository
actorA person, a token, an agent, a Station, the system; with the address and the request it came in on
decisionFor a decision: the verdict and its reasons, each reason a sentence and the facts behind it
causeThe event that led to this one, so a chain can be followed: a push to its trigger decision to its Sortie to its Launch
dataThe rest, as the catalog entry for the kind declares it
Proposal

The common event format is the design for every stream to adopt. Field names above are descriptions, not the final machine names. The cause link is new: today a Sortie names its trigger and a replay points back to its event, but there is no single thread from a push to a Launch.

Every decision carries its reasons

A decision without a reason is a defect. The rule for every writer: a verdict names the rule or condition that decided it, what was found, what was wanted, and where the evidence is. A test walks the catalog and fails on a decision kind with no reasons field, the same way the documentation tests today fail on an event type that the reference page does not list. Readers show the reasons in plain words: the Events page shows the sentence, the Sortie page shows "What went wrong", the Launch page shows what was measured against what.

Readers built from the record

The interface

Pages show the current state rebuilt from events, and the live stream sends each new event to the pages that show its subject. Every view agrees with every other because they read the same thing.

The Logbook

The Logbook is the record seen as "who did what": every event whose actor is a person, a token or an agent, and every refusal. It is no longer a separate table.

The Debrief

Test results, flaky tests and coverage come from the summaries each step reports in its finished event, with the full reports stored beside it.

Metrics

Delivery frequency, lead time, failure rate and time to restore are counted from Launch and Sortie events, so every number opens onto the events behind it.

Evidence

An evidence pack is a period of the record for a scope, with the Standing orders that were on, their verdicts, the Clearances and the exceptions, and the chain head that proves it is complete.

Comms and events out

Notifications and outgoing events are subscriptions to kinds of events, filtered in the same expression language pipelines use.

The timeline

The timeline of changes and symptoms is one reader: Launches, Switch flips, setting and secret changes, Clearances and the alerts that came in through a Hardpoint, in order, for a level, an Airfield or a service. It is drawn once and shown in three places: the record page, the Launch page and Radar.

Proposal

One timeline, one owner. The roadmap has two timeline items: A timeline of changes and symptoms (Milestone 3) and One timeline of what changed (Milestone 8). Both are this one reader. This plan makes the Milestone 3 item the owner of the component and has the Milestone 8 item add the kinds that land with it (Switches, settings, secrets), so it is built once. The change is proposed in Radar, insight and keeping it healthy.

Replay

Replay means three different things, and the record supports all three.

  1. Rebuilding state. The engine already rebuilds a Sortie from its events after a crash or on another server. The same holds for every reader: drop its index and rebuild it from the record.
  2. Starting again what an event should have started. An operator of a Flight replays a verified trigger event after fixing the cause; the new Sortie is a new event that points back to the first, and the Logbook records event.replay. Available today.
  3. Trying a changed pipeline against past events. Given a recorded event and stand-in results for each step, show which steps would run and why the others would be skipped, without flying. This is the proposed Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it), a new word that needs your yes; see What starts a Sortie.

Retention, holds and export

The record keeps events by class, not by table:

ClassExamplesKept
Decisions and actionsVerdicts, Clearances, Launch verdicts, setting changes, sign-insThe longest; never removed while the thing they allowed is still running in an Airfield
ProgressSteps queued, leased and started, Overwatch intervalsAs long as the Sortie they belong to
Unverified inputCalls whose sender could not prove itselfThe shortest, and capped in number, as today

A retention setting is made at a level and flows down like any other setting: a level above can set a minimum that a level below may only raise. A hold (a legal hold, for example) stops clean-up for its scope until it is lifted, and the hold itself is on the record. The planned item Retention, legal hold and encryption at rest carries this; the numbers are yours to decide (see Open question).

Export writes a scope and a period of the record in an open, documented format with a verifier: the same format a whole-Base export uses when a customer leaves or moves (Leave completely, Nothing held hostage). Today the Logbook can be paged through the API and is written as JSON lines on standard output for any log collector.

Tamper evidence. Each Base's record forms a chain: every entry carries a hash of the one before, so a deletion or an edit shows. The chain head can be exported and kept elsewhere. This is the planned Tamper-evident audit trail and Tamper-evident audit and SIEM export, which this plan reads as one design.

Events sent out in an open standard event format

Outside systems receive events in the CloudEvents format, an open standard event format, so any tool that reads that standard can take Launchway's events without an adapter. The record's common event format maps onto it: the identifier, the source (the installation and Base), the kind as the type, the subject, the time, and Launchway's own fields as extensions. Delivery is at least once, each event keeps its identifier so a receiver can drop a repeat, every request is signed, and every delivery is logged with its answer and retried with growing pauses. A subscription that keeps failing is paused with a notice to its owner, never dropped silently.

Subscriptions are set at a level (Base, Wing, Squadron or Flight), choose kinds from the catalog, and filter with a condition in the same expression language as pipelines, written inside ${{ }} and type-checked when it is saved. Destinations are connections: a web address, a queue or an event bus. This is the same door through which Hardpoints receive events (Cards and events in, notifications out).

Built today

Notification rules send run and delivery events to signed webhooks and chat channels with a delivery log and retries, and hosted repositories send signed webhooks. No event is sent in an open standard event format yet, and Switch changes and Depot events have no outgoing webhook (docs/guide/notifications.md, docs/guide/webhooks.md; a search of the product's code and documents finds no use of the standard).

How a module adds its events

  1. Declare each kind in the catalog: its name, the schema it arrives with, its fields with types, which fields are its reasons, which fields are sensitive and must be removed before it leaves the server, its retention class, and who may read it (by default, whoever may see its Flight).
  2. Write it in the same transaction as the change it describes, through the one writer the record offers. A test fails on module code that writes its own log table.
  3. Get every reader for free. The timeline, the Logbook, search, exports, the chain, subscriptions and the agent endpoint read the catalog, not the module.
  4. Keep older servers safe. A server leaves alone a subject with an event kind it does not know, as it does today with a Sortie; new kinds arrive with a new schema number and are additive.

The path from four streams to one

Each stage is additive, keeps every older server working on a newer schema, and can be returned to base by image (see boring upgrades).

StageWhat changesWhat keeps working
1. One common event format and one catalogA catalog lists every kind in all four streams. One read interface returns any of them in the common event format, with the level, the actor and the reasons filled in.All four tables, unchanged. Older servers notice nothing.
2. One table, written alongsideNew events are written to the one record as well as to their old table, in the same transaction. Each Base's chain starts here.Every old reader still reads its old table.
3. Readers moveThe Logbook page, the Events page, the Debrief, metrics and notifications read the record. Old tables become views of it.The API answers in its old shapes; the documented fields do not change.
4. Writers moveOnce no server older than stage 3 is seen, writers write only to the record. Events go out in the open standard event format.A Return to base to a stage-3 server still reads the record.

The life of one Sortie, as events

Worked example: storefront 2.4.0, from a commit to prod and back

Dana merges pull request #482 ("Show the delivery date at checkout", work item STORE-41) into main of storefront. Release 2.4.0 is built as digest sha256:4f9c…a17 and is to replace 2.3.2 in prod. You want to know, a week later, exactly what happened to it.

You open the release in the record and follow the cause thread. These are the events you see, shortened. The shape is a design; the kinds and reasons in the middle column exist today in the Sortie log.

KindWhat it saysReasons
Trigger decisionThe push to main started Sortie 417; the documentation trigger was filteredpaths: only src/** and web/** changed
Standing order verdictPass at Sortie startImages pinned by digest; platform-library at a tagged commit
Step finishedtest succeeded, 412 tests, 2 flaky in quarantineSummary used by the Debrief
Standing order verdictPass before the Launch to prodNo new critical finding; the image is signed
ClearanceGo for prodGiven by Ana, the Controller (approver) for prod; not Dana, whose change it is
Overwatch verdictFailed after 6 minutesError rate 3.1% against a baseline of 0.4%
Launch closedReturned to base (rolled back) to 2.3.2Automatic, because Overwatch failed

As it would leave Launchway in the open standard event format (Design: not built; names are not final):

The foundation it relies on

  • One database shared by every server, so an event and the change it describes are one transaction (The system).
  • Additive migrations, so a new event kind never confuses an older server (Boring upgrades).
  • Levels and permissions, so every event has a place in the levels and is read only by those who may see that place (Levels, people and secrets).
  • The key hierarchy, so the record's sensitive fields are encrypted at rest once files and logs are (Encryption at rest).

Safety

On failure

  • The database is away. Nothing is recorded, so nothing is decided; servers answer 503 with a time to retry, and Stations keep their logs and results until it returns. Nothing happens off the record.
  • A server dies mid-write. The transaction either committed the change and its event, or neither.
  • A subscriber is down. Deliveries are retried with growing pauses and logged; after a limit the subscription pauses and its owner is told. The record is not affected.
  • A reader falls behind. The live stream cuts a slow client off rather than slow the server, and the client reconnects and reads the current state, as today.

Who may do what

ActionWho
Read events of a FlightAnyone who may see the Flight: an Observer (viewer) and up. The live stream and lists contain only what you may see.
Read the Logbook across a Wing or BaseA Commander (owner) of that level. Today: an admin from a binding without Flight patterns.
Replay a trigger eventA Pilot (developer) of the Flight, for verified events only.
Add a subscriptionA Commander of the level it is set at; the destination must be a connection that level may use.
Export a period, set retention, place or lift a holdA Commander of the level. Lifting a hold is itself an event.
Edit or delete an eventNobody. Clean-up by retention is the only removal, it is recorded, and the chain shows it.

On by default

  • Every decision and every change is recorded, with sign-in on or off.
  • Credential-looking values are removed from payloads; secrets are recorded only as references; pipeline text is recorded as a hash.
  • The Logbook is also written to standard output.
  • Events sent out are signed.

Open question

Decision needed

How long each class is kept by default, on a self-hosted installation and on the hosted service. Today the Logbook is kept until an administrator removes rows, and trigger events are capped per Flight. The plan proposes classes, not numbers.

Decision needed

Where a hosted customer's record lives. The roadmap says logs, Debriefs, Cargo and an audit trail stay on the customer's side by default, and the hosted service keeps a separate record of what it did. This chapter follows that. Whether the decisions themselves (trigger decisions, verdicts) are also kept only on the customer's side, with the hosted side holding names, states, counts and timings, is for you to confirm with the published boundary table.

Decision needed

The word Simulator for testing a pipeline against recorded events is one of the new words this plan proposes, and it needs your yes.

Decision needed

Whether events are sent out by default. This plan proposes none until a Commander adds a subscription, because every destination is an outside system.

Levels, people and secrets

Four levels carry permissions, variables, Standing orders (policies and standards) and capability choices down to every Flight, people get exactly the rights their role gives them there, and secrets reach a step without the server ever seeing them.

  • Base (installation), Wing (organization), Squadron (team) and Flight (codebase). What is set higher flows down; a nearer level overrides; a lock from above wins.
  • Four roles: Commander (owner), Controller (approver), Pilot (developer), Observer (viewer). Signing in grants nothing by itself.
  • Secrets are references. A Station (runner) looks the value up in its own network and masks it; the server and the record hold only the reference. A short-lived identity per Sortie (run) and step replaces stored cloud keys.
  • On the hosted service every Base is walled off, and tests that try every route from one Base into another gate each release.
  • Custom roles are named sets of the server's own actions, on every plan; every trigger acts as a named identity with its own grants; and a store releases a secret only to the branches and kinds of Sortie its rule names.

Where it sits

This is the second half of layer 1 of the map, beside the system. Every other chapter uses it: Flight plans read variables from it (Inputs and run forms), Launches (deployments) check who may say Go (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold), Stations resolve secrets under its rules (Stations and where work runs), and every module uses its levels and roles rather than its own (module contract, rule 1). Everything it changes is written to the record. Security across the product is in Security and the supply chain.

Layers used
1 (foundation), writing to 2 (the record)
Builds on
The database, the key hierarchy, the Stations' outward connection
Built on by
Every chapter and every module

What you will be able to do

You lock the variable registry at the Wing to the company's Depot (registry), with the reason "Everything ships through the audited Depot". A Pilot who writes another value in a pipeline file is told, before any Station starts, who locked it and why.

You give a colleague the Controller role on the prod Airfield (environment) only. She can say Go or No-go for production Launches and do nothing else there.

Your payment key stays in your own secret store. The pipeline names it; the Station in your network reads it when the step starts, gives it to the step and replaces it with *** in the log. A copy of Launchway's database has no trace of it.

Your pipeline publishes an image resizer to a cloud's serverless platform with no cloud key stored anywhere. The step proves who it is with a token that names the Flight, the branch and the Airfield and expires when the step ends; the cloud trusts it because you set that up once.

On the hosted service, someone in another Base guesses the name of your Flight. Launchway answers exactly as it would for a Flight that does not exist.

How it works

The four levels

The levels are Base, Wing, Squadron and Flight. The plain words are Installation, Organization, Team and Codebase, and every word can be renamed in Settings, Words. Machine names never change with the words: the stored kinds are installation, organization (org in the code), unit and project.

LevelPlain wordStored asWhat it isToday
BaseInstallationinstallationThe top: on a self-hosted installation, the whole installation; on the hosted service, one customer's complete, private space. Words, limits and retention are set here.Every installation has one Base, the default one
WingOrganizationorganizationThe one that owns the Flights. A company, or a client of a freelancer.Exactly one Wing; the tables already carry it in their keys
SquadronTeamunitA named folder of Flights with its own people and shared settings. Never nested. Made with a name only.Any number
FlightCodebaseprojectOne repository and its pipelines.Each Flight has one pipeline today

What flows down, and how

One rule for every kind of setting, with three verbs: set (the nearest level wins), lock (nothing below may change it; the topmost lock wins) and floor (a level below may make it stricter, never looser). Settings below a lock are kept and shown as ignored, so removing the lock brings them back.

KindHow it flowsLock or floorToday
Role bindingsA role granted at a level applies to everything below it. Where several match, the highest role wins.Not needed: grants only addAvailable; bindings are settings in the database and can be made at a Squadron
VariablesNearest wins; for one Airfield beats general at the same levelLockAvailable
Standing orders: policiesA policy applies to every Flight below; pipelines cannot opt outAlways a floorAvailable
Standing orders: repository standardsEach check off, advice or block; nearest level winsFloor and lockAvailable
Flight plans and templatesBound at a level, used by every Flight below; a Flight overrides what the level allowsLockAvailable
Ramps (Station pools), Airfields, libraries, secret stores, health sources, AI modelsDefined at a level, used below itNot yetAvailable
Capability choicesOne provider in charge of each capability per Squadron, chosen at a level and inheritedLockPlanned
Words, limits, retentionSet at the BaseRetention takes a floorAvailable for words and limits

Nothing crosses a Wing: variables and locks set in one Wing never reach another (docs/guide/variables.md). Levels nobody uses stay out of sight: with no Squadron there is no Squadron column, picker or page.

Roles

Four roles, each named for what a person does. A role is granted to a person, a group from the sign-in provider or a service account, at a level, and optionally only for some Airfields. The "May" column is this plan's design for the four roles; the last column is what the server stores today (docs/guide/words.md).

RolePlain wordMayStored today as
CommanderOwnerEverything, including who may do what; read the Logbook (audit trail); waive a policy rule; manage Stationsadmin; there is no owner role
ControllerApproverDecide whether a change may go on: Go and No-go on a Clearance (approval), a Hold (freeze), Promote or Abort on a Launchoperator; there is no approver role yet
PilotDeveloperWrite code and pipelines, start, cancel, resume and re-run Sorties, replay an event, Return to base (rollback)operator; there is no developer role
ObserverViewerSee everything about the Flights they may see; change nothingviewer

Rules that hold today (docs/reference/roles.md): rights are worked out on every request on the server, whatever the interface shows. A Flight you may not see answers 404, exactly as if it did not exist; one you may see but not change answers 403. Someone who signs in but matches no binding sees nothing. The person who started a Sortie cannot approve its production Launch. A token or an agent never has more than the person or account that made it.

Proposal

Store the four roles as four roles: owner, approver, developer, viewer. On upgrade, admin becomes owner and operator becomes both developer and approver, so nobody gains or loses a right. From then on a team can give someone the right to start Sorties without the right to approve them, or the reverse. Return to base is a Pilot's right on every Airfield they may Launch to, because retreat is never gated. Custom roles and directory groups follow on the same model (Directory groups and custom roles).

Custom roles: named sets of the server's own actions

The server already has a complete list of what can be done: every route of the HTTP API has an access class and a named action, and the same names are the agent endpoint's tools and the command line's commands, kept equal by the parity test (docs/reference/interface-parity.md). A custom role is a name and a set of those actions. Nothing else is invented: no second permission model, no free-form rights.

  • Built from the list. The role wizard shows the actions grouped by area (code, pipelines, Launches, Standing orders, Stations, people, evidence), each with one sentence; you tick what the role may do. The four built-in roles are shown as ready-made sets to start from.
  • Granted like any role. At any level, optionally for some Airfields only, to a person, a directory group, a service account or a trigger identity. Where several bindings match, rights add up.
  • Never above the granter. Nobody can make or grant a role holding an action they do not hold at that level.
  • Safe across upgrades. When a release adds an action, the built-in roles get it as the release notes say; a custom role never gains one silently: its page lists "new actions not in this role" for you to decide.
  • Explained. "Who can do what, and why" names the role and the binding that allowed or refused each action, and every change to a role is recorded as a difference.
  • On every plan, without a cap. Custom roles are part of the product for everyone, as every feature is on the free plan.
# Design: not built. Two custom roles for Harbor Lights.
roles:
  - name: release-manager
    from: controller                  # start from a built-in set
    add: [start_release_run, promote_release, begin_hold, lift_hold]
    remove: [abort_launch]
  - name: security-reviewer
    from: observer
    add: [accept_finding_risk, read_logbook_security, read_posture]
bindings:
  - { group: shop-release, role: release-manager, level: squadron/shop, airfields: [staging, prod] }

Action names in the example are illustrative; the real names are those of the route table.

Every trigger acts as a named identity

A Sortie started by a push records the person who pushed. A Sortie started by a Patrol, an outside event or another pipeline's result runs today under a named identity on the record (patrol:nightly, source:payments-webhook, result:storefront#417), not under a system account. The plan makes each of these a principal of its own: the Commanders of the Flight bind roles to it, at the Flight or for some Airfields only, like any service account. A trigger can then never start more than its grants allow, whoever wrote the pipeline; a Patrol granted only staging cannot reach prod, and the Logbook names the trigger identity on every action it takes. With no binding, a trigger identity may start Sorties of its own Flight and nothing else.

Signing in

Way to sign inWhat it isStatus
Built-in accountsPasswords stored as Argon2id hashes, a password policy with an offline list of leaked passwords, lockout that doubles and then ends by itself, an authenticator app (TOTP) with ten recovery codes, required for administrators by default. The first administrator is made with a one-time setup code. Works with no identity provider.Available
Single sign-on with OpenID ConnectAny provider, through discovery, with groups mapped to roles. Built-in accounts can stay on beside it, so switching providers never locks everyone out.Available
PasskeysThe preferred second factor and, later, a way to sign in with no password.Planned
Directory groups over LDAP, and SAMLGroups from the company directory mapped to roles at each level; leavers removed automatically; SAML sign-in and automatic provisioning.Planned
