Text-message codes are not offered, on purpose. On the hosted service, staff will not be able to reset a second factor or let anyone in (Recovery that is not a back door, planned). Behind a proxy, lockout and rate limits count the address of the person, believed only from proxies you name.

Addresses allowed to reach a Base

Tokens can already be limited to source addresses. The plan adds the same limit for a whole Base: a list of address ranges from which anyone may sign in, call the API or use the agent endpoint. It is set at the Base by a Commander, tested before it is saved ("your own address is inside the list"), and every refusal is a Logbook entry with the address and the route. Stations, which only call out, and signed webhooks keep their own checks and are not affected.

  • Break-glass. The installation's internal address (the machine itself, or the cluster's own network) is always allowed, so a wrong list can never lock the operators out; the hosted service offers the same through the customer-approved support session.
  • One shape with privileged changes. It joins the proposal that changes to clusters, secrets, access and DNS come only from a trusted path or behind a fresh second factor: the allow-list says who may reach the Base at all; the trusted path says who may make the most dangerous changes.

Verified company domains (hosted service)

On the hosted service a company wants every account with its email domain to belong to its Base. A Base proves it owns a domain by publishing a record in the domain's DNS that Launchway gives it. From then on:

  1. Accounts with an address at that domain are claimed by the Base: they sign in through the Base's own sign-in provider and its second-factor rule.
  2. Existing accounts at that domain are told before the claim takes effect, and what they keep.
  3. Nobody else can claim the domain, and losing the DNS record ends the claim after a notice, without deleting anything.
  4. Every claim, notice and release is in the Base's Logbook.

On a self-hosted installation the installation is the company's own, so the same need is met by its sign-in provider. How claiming works across Bases depends on the open decision on one account per Base or one account across Bases (below).

Tokens and automation accounts

Automation holds the least credential that does its job. Every credential expires, is stored only as a hash, and names itself in the Logbook on every request (docs/guide/credentials-for-machines.md, docs/guide/runner-identity.md).

CredentialWho holds itLimits
A person's API tokenA script acting as that personExpiry (90 days by default, at most 365 unless raised); optionally a role, Flights, repositories and source addresses. Made only from a signed-in browser.
A service account's tokenAutomation that must outlive any one personThe same, never more than the account's role
A Sortie credentialOne Sortie, for GitRead-only, one repository, 30 minutes; nobody makes or sees it
A Station's keyAn enrolled StationAn Ed25519 key that never leaves the Station; each request carries a 15-minute token signed with it; rotated every 30 days; revocable at once on every server
A join tokenSomeone enrolling a StationShown once, an hour by default, one Station unless it says more
An agentAn agent on the agent endpointExactly the rights of the token it holds; browser sessions are not accepted there
Check before publishing

The roadmap lists Tokens and scoped access and Access tokens for one repository as Planned, while docs/guide/credentials-for-machines.md and docs/guide/access.md describe service accounts, tokens limited to repositories and limits by source address as working. One of the two is out of date. The plan proposes moving Tokens and scoped access to Available once a check of the code confirms the guides.

Nothing by default. The Sortie credential is the model for every credential a pipeline holds: minted per Sortie, read-only, for one repository, for 30 minutes, and never seen by a person. It is built today and described in the detail of Git over SSH (Milestone 1, Available). A step gets nothing else unless it declares it.

Lifetime as a Standing order. Today the longest life of any token is one number for the whole server (auth.tokens.max_days, 365 by default). The plan makes it a token_lifetime rule of the Standing orders, judged when a token is made: a Base, Wing or Squadron sets the longest life for each kind of token and whether a source-address limit is required, and a level below may only shorten it. A token that asks for longer is refused with the rule's name; tokens made before the rule are listed with their end dates, never cut off silently.

Variables and precedence

A variable is a named setting with a type and a value, set once at a level. One sentence decides which value a step gets, the same on every page and in every message (docs/guide/variables.md):

  1. What is given when the Sortie starts.
  2. The pipeline file's own with:.
  3. The Flight.
  4. The Squadron.
  5. The Wing.
  6. The Base.
  7. The template's own default.

At the same level, a variable set for the Airfield being launched to beats the general one. A lock set at a level beats everything below it, the pipeline file and the Sortie included. Lists replace, never merge. A name keeps one type everywhere. Types are text, number, true or false, list, map, secret (a reference, never a value) and connection. A step receives only the variables its pipeline names with from:; a variable that happens to share a name reaches nothing. Every Sortie records the variables it used, with the whole chain at that moment, so a re-run repeats exactly.

If you write code, the analogy is exact: a template's inputs are the interface, a variable at a wider level is an abstract class that supplies a value, a nearer level is the class that overrides it, and a lock is final.

Not built yet

Variables bound inside env: and with:, templates that a level requires, connections as objects of their own, more than one Wing, and the Terraform resource (docs/guide/variables.md).

How a secret reaches a step

Each Station has only the stores you configure for it: environment variables, files in a directory (such as a mounted Kubernetes secret), or a key-value engine of Vault or OpenBao. Any pipeline can ask for any key, so every store takes allow-lists of Flights and keys, checked on the Station. A secret that does not exist or may not be read fails the step, naming the store and the key. A store that cannot be reached is asked again for 30 seconds, then the step is handed back to run later. Values shorter than four characters are not masked, and the log says so (docs/guide/secrets.md).

A Station's own accept: section is its limit on what the server may ask of it: which Flights, repositories, images and Airfields, whether pull requests may run. The server cannot change it, because it lives only on the Station. Keep each Station's stores and reach as narrow as its Ramp's work, and give production its own Ramp.

Proposal: the built-in secret store

Launchway's own secret store (A built-in secret store, planned) keeps the rule that the server never sees a value. A value entered in the interface is sealed at once and can never be read back through the interface, the API, the command line or the agent endpoint: they can set, replace, rotate and delete it, and see its name, version and history. Only a Station holding a live lease for a step that names the secret can open it. On the hosted service with a Detachment (the small program on the customer's side), the store runs on the customer's side, so the hosted side never holds it. Fully hosted, the honest trade is stated at sign-up: the service stores the secrets, sealed under the Base's own keys.

Release rules: which Sorties may have a secret

Today a store releases a key to the Flights its allow-list names. That is not enough for a production key: a pull request's Sortie, a re-run of an old commit or a debug session of the same Flight should not have it. The plan adds a release rule to every store, and to any key or key pattern within it: a condition in the one expression language over the facts of the Sortie and the step, judged on the Station before the store is asked. The fact names below that pipelines do not already use are proposed names.

FactValues
run.branch, run.protectedThe branch or tag, and whether a branch rule protects it
run.kindnormal, restricted (a fork or automation account), rerun, draft, debug (a session to reproduce a failed step), patrol
run.triggerThe trigger identity that started it
environmentThe Airfield of the step, if it launches
run.flight, run.squadronWhere the Sortie belongs, as today's allow-list
# Design: not built. On the Station, in its store configuration.
stores:
  vault-prod:
    kind: vault
    projects: [payments]
    keys: ["payments/*"]
    release_if: ${{ run.protected && run.branch == "main" && run.kind == "normal" && environment == "prod" }}

A refused release fails the step before it starts, naming the store, the key and the condition that was false, and is recorded. The facts come signed in the step's lease from the server, so the Station checks the signature; and because a taken-over server could sign false facts, the Station's own accept: section stays the hard limit it cannot change. A secret_release Standing order can require that every store at a level has a rule at least this strict.

One store interface, many backends, one published matrix

Each store on a Station answers the same small interface, so every backend behaves the same for a pipeline: resolve a reference (store, key, field, optional version) to a value; list key names, never values, for the reference picker; report versions and health; and, for stores that issue credentials, lease and revoke them. Masking, allow-lists, release rules, retries and refusals are done by the Station around the interface, the same for every backend.

BackendStatus
Environment variables and files on the StationAvailable
Key-value engines of Vault and OpenBaoAvailable
The secret services of the three largest public clouds, reached with the step's short-lived identityPlanned (Secrets with an external store)
A script-backed store: a tested custom step program on the Station that returns a value, for anything elseNew in this plan
Launchway's own storePlanned (A built-in secret store)

Every backend must pass one conformance suite: resolve and version, missing and refused keys, masking in logs and outputs, release rules, unreachable store and retry, rotation picked up by the next step, and no value ever sent to the server. The published parity matrix (Popular backends instead) is generated from the suite's results at each release, so it can never claim what the code does not do.

A short-lived identity for each Sortie and step

Stored cloud keys are the secrets most often leaked. In their place, Launchway issues each step a short-lived signed token that says who the step is, and the cloud, the Depot or any other system that trusts Launchway's issuer gives the step what it needs for as long as it needs it.

PartDesign
What the token saysThe Base, Wing, Squadron and Flight; the pipeline; the branch or tag and the commit; the Airfield for a Launch step; the Sortie, the step and the attempt; whether the Sortie is restricted (a pull request from a fork, for example)
Who it is forOne audience per token, chosen by the step: a named cloud connection, the Depot, a Git host
How long it livesNo longer than the step's lease; never stored; recorded as "issued to this step for this audience", never as the token
How it is signedWith a key under the installation's key hierarchy, published as a key set at a well-known address, following OpenID Connect so any system that trusts that standard can trust it
How trust is set upOnce per cloud account, by a wizard that writes the trust rule with conditions picked from lists (this Flight, these branches, this Airfield)

The Sortie credential for Git already works this way for one repository and 30 minutes. The same issuer serves Cloud sign-in per step (Milestone 1) and Workload identity and dynamic credentials (Milestone 12), and the short-lived credential minted for a Sortie to publish to the Depot. One issuer, one audit line per token, one place to revoke.

Encryption at rest

Everything Launchway stores that is secret is sealed under a root key held outside the database, so a copy of the database, a backup or a snapshot alone reveals no secret (docs/guide/encryption-at-rest.md).

root key            held outside the database: a key file, an environment variable,
                    a passphrase, or the transit service of Vault or OpenBao
  wraps
key-encryption keys versioned, stored wrapped
  wrap
data keys           per purpose, and per Wing where a row belongs to one
  seal
values              AES-256-GCM, bound to the installation, purpose, Wing, table, column and row

Sealed today: the keys every server shares, the shared Station token, Git host keys, webhook secrets and addresses. Stored only as one-way hashes: sessions, API tokens, join and access tokens. Not yet sealed by Launchway: Cargo (artifacts), logs, caches, hosted Git packs, Depot blobs, and the authenticator secrets of built-in accounts; until then, encrypt the volume. A new single-server installation makes its key at first start; a shared PostgreSQL database never gets a key made by itself. launchway doctor encryption and Settings, Security say plainly what is and is not protected.

Proposal

Data keys per Base as well as per purpose and Wing, so that on the hosted service each Base's data is sealed under keys of its own. Deleting a Base then ends with destroying its keys, which makes every copy, backups included, unreadable (Leave completely, Customer-held keys and deletion by key destruction).

The wall between Bases

On the hosted service every customer has its own complete Base, the highest thing that customer can see or name. The operator's own Base is a separate Base that no customer or visitor can see, list, search or guess, and nothing flows down from it. The wall is built in the code so that keeping it is cheap and forgetting it is impossible (docs/development/the-wall.md).

  1. Every table has an owner. It is the installation's own, or a Base table whose every key begins with the Base, or pending with a named stage. A test fails on a table that is not on the list.
  2. Every query has a scope. A statement on a Base table that does not name the Base fails a test.
  3. No new database code outside the store. Older files are on a baseline that may only shrink.
  4. A scope comes from somewhere trustworthy. It cannot be written as a literal; it comes from the address of the request or a background job that names its Base.
  5. The database is the second lock. On PostgreSQL, row-level security on every Base table; the application connects as a role that owns no tables.
  6. "Not found" looks the same as "not allowed", so a guess learns nothing.
  7. Proof, not promise. A suite tries every list, search, lookup, count, error, export and agent tool from one Base against another's data. No outside customer is admitted until it passes, and it gates every release.

The vendor console sees how many Bases exist, plans, usage and the health of the hosted side, and never repositories, Flight recorders (run logs), secrets, findings or traffic. Every vendor action that touches a Base appears in that Base's own Logbook. When something is wrong, the customer sends a ticket and a support bundle they chose and previewed; if that is not enough, the customer can grant a time-limited, read-only-by-default session for one problem and end it at any moment.

Built today

Stage 1 of the wall: Bases, accounts and memberships exist, the identity area is walled, every table is registered with its owner, and the rest is registered as pending its stage. A second Base cannot be turned on yet: the server refuses to start with several Bases until requests know their Base (docs/development/the-wall.md).

Worked example: Harbor Lights

Harbor Lights runs Launchway on its own cluster, so its Base is the whole installation. Its Wing is harbor-lights. The Squadron "shop" holds storefront, payments, image-resize and the shared library platform-library; the Squadron "back office" holds billing; the Squadron "kiosks" holds kiosk-os.

PersonRoleWhereWhat that means
SamCommanderThe WingSets the Wing's variables and locks, reads the Logbook, manages Stations
DanaPilotFlight storefrontWrites and runs storefront's pipeline; cannot see payments
AnaControllerThe Wing, Airfield prod onlySays Go or No-go for every production Launch; cannot approve a Sortie she started
The release botPilotSquadron shop, as a service accountStarts release Sorties with a token limited to storefront and to the office's addresses
An auditorObserverThe WingReads everything, changes nothing

Sam sets and locks the Depot for the whole Wing, and sets the number of copies for production on storefront only. These commands exist today:

launchway variables set registry --organization --type connection --of registry --value depot
launchway variables lock registry --organization --reason "Everything ships through the audited Depot"
launchway variables set replicas --project storefront --environment prod --type number --value 4
launchway variables effective storefront --environment prod

The payments pipeline names its gateway key as a reference. The Stations of the payments Ramp have a Vault store whose allow-list names only payments, so a storefront step that asked for the key would be refused on the Station, before anything ran.

steps:
  charge-test:
    secrets:
      GATEWAY_KEY: { store: vault, key: payments/gateway, field: api_key }

The image resizer's Launch step asks for a token for the cloud connection harbor-cloud. The token names Flight image-resize, branch main, Airfield prod and this step, and lasts until the step ends. No cloud key is stored in Launchway or on the Station. (A design: this is the planned Cloud sign-in per step.)

The foundation it relies on

  • The system: one database for bindings, variables, sessions and tokens as hashes; Stations that connect outward (The system).
  • The record: every grant, lock, sign-in and refusal is an event with its actor and reasons (The record).
  • The key hierarchy: a root key outside the database.
  • Stations under your control: their accept: section and secret stores live only on them (Stations and where work runs).

Safety

On failure

  • The sign-in provider is down. Built-in accounts can stay on beside it, and the first administrator is the break-glass account. A server cannot be locked out by its own provider.
  • A secret store is down. The step is asked again for 30 seconds, then handed back to run later; it never runs without its secret.
  • A token leaks. It expires, it can be revoked at once by its owner or by a Commander, it was limited to what its job needed, and every use is in the Logbook.
  • A Station is taken over. It reaches only what its Ramp's Flights and its own stores allow; revoke it and its steps are queued again elsewhere.
  • The server is taken over. It still cannot read a secret value it was never given, and a Station still refuses work its accept: section does not allow.
  • A query forgets its Base. Row-level security returns nothing instead of everything.

Who may do what

ActionWho
Grant a role at a levelA Commander of that level, never above their own role
Set a variableAn administrator of the level: of every Flight for the Base and the Wing, of the Squadron's Flights for a Squadron, a Pilot for a Flight
Lock a variableThe level's administrator, with a reason that is shown wherever it stops someone
Make a tokenAnyone signed in, from a browser, never with another token and never above their own rights
Make a service account and its tokensA Commander
Enroll, revoke, rotate a StationThe role set by runner_admin on every Flight (admin by default)
Rotate keys, set the key sourceWhoever operates the installation, on the machine that has the root key
See inside a BaseIts own members only; the vendor never, except in a session the customer grants and can end

On by default

  • Sign-in required; a second factor required for administrators; built-in accounts when nothing else is set.
  • Every token expires; only hashes are stored.
  • Stored secrets sealed under the root key; the server never holds a secret value for a step.
  • Pull requests from forks and automation accounts run without secrets until a maintainer approves.
  • "Not found" for anything you may not see.

Open question

Decision needed

Permanent machine names for the levels. The API, files and tokens use unit and project today and must keep working; what they become, if anything, is not recorded as decided.

Decision needed

Approving what you started. The recorded design response, not yet confirmed: a one-person Base may allow the starter to approve by policy, with a plain note in the record; larger teams keep separation of duties.

Decision needed

Privileged changes. The shape agreed with the security reviewer and awaiting you: changes to clusters, secrets, access and DNS only from the internal or private-mesh address, or behind a fresh second factor, with the path and the factor's age in the Logbook.

Decision needed

Whether a Pilot keeps the right to approve by default once roles are stored apart. The proposal keeps every right people have today; a team then narrows it if it wants separation.

Decision needed

Credentials across Bases. One account per Base until a late stage of the wall (chosen in the wall plan) or one account across Bases earlier (wall plan, decision 5). Also the words Installation and Base for the two meanings (wall plan, decision 1).

Decision needed

Several Wings on the hosted service: the recommendation is a library registered in each Wing, revisited after the first request. The order of levels and Airfields in precedence was recorded as level first, with locks, by default; you may reopen it.

Decision needed

Verified domains and accounts. Whether a claimed account belongs only to the claiming Base follows the decision on one account per Base or one across Bases; the claim's notice period is also yours to set.

Decision needed

The Base-wide address allow-list: off by default (recommended, so a new installation is reachable) or on with the installation's own network only.

Decision needed

A standard identity format for Launchway's own components (servers, Stations, the Detachment), now or only on request. The recorded recommendation is on request.

Stations and where work runs

Every step runs on a Station (runner) that you own or choose, that only ever calls out, that can say no, and that gives the same result on a laptop, a cluster or a machine made for one job.

  • A Station connects outward only, enrolls once with a one-time token, keeps its own key, and refuses work its owner does not want. This is built today on Linux, in containers and on Kubernetes.
  • Stations are grouped into Ramps (runner pools). Launch Stations (deploy runners) are a separate kind that runs no one's scripts.
  • The workspace travels with the Sortie (run), so the repository is cloned once per Sortie. Caches make builds faster and never change what they produce.
  • Planned: Windows and macOS Stations, on-demand Stations, scaling by waiting steps, step groups, warmed images, and attaching to a failed step. One choice stays open for you: one pod per step or one pod per Sortie on Kubernetes.
  • Designed in this chapter: the same Station on Windows and macOS with a sandbox on each, hosted Stations on all three systems in named sizes up to graphics-processor machines, and mobile and games builds with signing material resolved as secrets on the Station and store upload as a step.
  • Also designed: services beside a step with readiness, start order and their own log tab; hooks before, after and on exit of every step; fan-outs of thousands of members; a hosted build cache shared by every Station of a Base; and Stations that update themselves under a Standing order, with a pin and a way back.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 4 of the seven layers, flight operations. It builds on three others:

  • The foundation (the system; Levels, people and secrets). Levels decide which Ramps a Flight (codebase) may use. Secrets are sealed and resolved on the Station, never seen by the server.
  • The record (the record). Every lease, refusal, enrollment, rotation and revocation is an event with its reason.
  • The step contract (Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints). A step declares what it needs from a Station. This chapter describes how a Station provides it.

Several things build on this chapter. Every Launch (deployment) runs on a Launch Station (One way to launch, anywhere; Launching to Kubernetes; Launching to virtual machines and physical servers). Inspection (security scan) steps and agents run as steps (Security and the supply chain, the Wingman and agents). The hosted service's Detachment (site agent) starts Stations on the customer's side.

What you will be able to do

You add a Station on a spare Linux server in your office. You make a join token on the Stations page and paste one command. The Station creates its own key, enrolls, and starts taking your Flight's steps. Nobody opened a port into your network. Available

A burst of pull requests arrives at nine in the morning. Your Kubernetes Ramp grows from two Stations to six while steps wait. By lunch it is back to two, and the Stations it removed finished their steps first. Planned

Your kiosk image must be built for arm64 once a week. You mark a Ramp as on-demand. When the step waits, a cloud machine is made for it, enrolls with a token that lasts minutes, builds the image, hands back the workspace, and is gone. The Logbook (audit trail) shows when it was made, what it did and when it was removed. Planned

Formatting, vet and lint are three quick steps that run one after another. You put them in one step group. They share one pod and one workspace, each in its own tool container, and the chain pays for one pod start instead of three. Planned

An integration test fails only on the Station. You choose Attach on the failed step. A fresh pod opens with the same image, the workspace as the step left it and the same inputs. You look around for fifteen minutes. The session is recorded and has no production secrets. Planned

A colleague lends a workstation to the team. While she compiles her own work, her Station stops taking steps. It never runs pull requests from forks, because her accept: list says so. Available for accept:, Planned for holding back when busy.

How it works

Station (runner)
A program that takes steps from the server and runs them. One binary, the same command everywhere.
Ramp (runner pool)
A named group of Stations. A Ramp says whose Flights' work its Stations may take. Its configuration kind is runner-pools.
Launch Station (deploy runner)
A Station with a deploy: section on a deploy-kind Ramp. It runs Launch, Return to base (rollback), rollout and verification work for named targets, and runs nothing else.
Executor
How a Station runs a step: container (Podman or Docker), kubernetes or host. auto picks a container engine if it finds one.
Lease
A Station's hold on one attempt of one step. It lasts 90 seconds and is renewed at least every 15.

How a Station takes work

Today, in order:

  1. Enroll. Someone with the Station role makes a join token for a Ramp. They use the Stations page, launchway runners join-token --pool web or POST /api/v1/runner-join-tokens. The token is shown once and stored as a hash. It lasts an hour by default and at most 7 days. It enrolls one Station unless it says more.
  2. Hold an identity. launchway runner --server URL --join lwj_… makes an Ed25519 key that never leaves the machine. The Station registers the public half. From then on it starts without the token. Each request carries a 15-minute access token, obtained by signing a 60-second assertion that any server accepts once. Keys rotate every 30 days. Revoke refuses a Station at once on every server, and its steps are queued again.
  3. Ask for work. The Station long-polls for up to 25 seconds. The server caps a wait at 50. Candidate steps are matched by Ramp, labels and schema, oldest first. The server checks the Ramp when it looks for work and again when it grants it, whatever the Station claims.
  4. Keep the Sortie. All of a Sortie's steps go to the Station that took its first step, because that Station holds the workspace. A Station silent for 90 seconds loses its lease. Another Station then takes over with a fresh checkout, and the log says so.
  5. Ride through outages. If the server cannot be reached, the Station keeps running the step. It keeps up to 256 MiB of log lines per step on its disk, and the result is never dropped. It delivers them in order when the server answers.

Sources: docs/guide/runner-identity.md, docs/reference/runner-config.md. A shared Station token from before identities still works. Such Stations are marked on the Stations page, and require_identity: true on a Ramp refuses them.

A Station's owner can refuse work

Whoever controls the server decides what is asked of a Station. The Station's accept: section is its owner's own limit on that request. It lives only in the Station's file, so the server cannot change it. The Station checks it before anything happens: no clone, no secret looked up, no container started. A refused step fails without retries, says why, and is recorded as runner.refused.

SettingWhat the Station's owner limits
accept.projectsThe Flights whose work it takes
accept.repositoriesThe repositories it clones, the Sortie's own and every library's
accept.images, images_by_digestThe images steps may use, and whether they must be pinned by digest
accept.executorsIts own executor for ordinary steps, the image builder for image steps, deploy for Launch work
accept.environmentsThe Airfields (environments) a Launch Station deploys to
accept.pull_requests, accept.draftsWhether it runs code from pull requests, and pipeline text that is not in Git
accept.max_timeout, accept.env_denyThe longest step it runs, and variables a step may not set
Honest limit

accept: narrows what reaches a Station's network and secrets. It cannot make accepted work safe. A server that has been taken over can still send any script for a Flight, repository and image the Station accepts. The product's advice stands: keep each Station's accept:, secret stores and network as narrow as its Ramp's work, and give production its own Ramp.

Ramps and Launch Stations

A Ramp is a database object (runner_pools[]) with a name, a kind (build or deploy), the Flights or targets it serves, the events it serves, and require_identity. A pipeline picks a Ramp, and labels a Station must have, with runner: { pool, labels } for the whole pipeline or for one step. If no Station may take a Sortie, its page says why. Either no Ramp serves the Flight, the Ramp it asks for does not, or no Station seen lately has the labels or accepts the work.

A Launch Station is kept apart on purpose. It holds the right to change a target, and it sits next to the monitoring systems that verification reads. It runs no one's script. Its targets, the GitOps repositories it may write and the health sources it may query are listed in its own file. Each one is narrowed to the Flights that may use it.

Where Stations run

You ruled that Stations run anywhere (, standing rule 2, and your latest answer). The same binary and the same identity model are used everywhere. Only the executor and the way the Station is installed change.

PlaceHow it runsStatusRoadmap item
A Linux machine, virtual or physical, on premises or in a cloudThe binary as a service, with the container or host executor. An install script and packages are part of the release work.Available In progress for signed packagesRunner identity and pools (Available list); Signed releases and installers (m1)
A container on any machineThe Station in a container, enrolled with LAUNCHWAY_JOIN; steps in sibling containersAvailableSecure step execution (Available list)
A Kubernetes clusterThe Station chart. Each pod enrolls with an ephemeral join token held in a Secret, and steps run as pods in a step namespace.AvailableRunner identity and pools; Secure step execution
A personal machine lent to the teamThe same Station, holding back while its owner is busy and within limits its owner setsPlannedRunners on personal machines hold back when busy (m2)

Built today

Stations run on Linux only. The roadmap lists Windows and macOS Stations as a gap, honestly. Android and iOS builds, and the cross-platform mobile frameworks, depend on them (Android builds, iOS and macOS builds, Cross-platform mobile frameworks, all m2).

Stations on Windows and macOS: a design

The rule is one Station, not three. The Windows and macOS Stations are the same program built for those systems. They enroll with the same one-time token, keep the same per-Station key, take work by the same outward-only long poll, check the same accept: list, resolve secrets on the machine in the same way, and spool logs through an outage in the same way. A pipeline does not learn a second model to build on another system. What differs is how the Station is installed, how it isolates a step, and where it keeps its files.

QuestionLinux (today)Windows (design)macOS (design)
Installed asA system service, a container, or the Kubernetes chartA Windows service, from a signed installer or one command in an administrator shell; it runs under its own low-privilege service account, never an administratorA launch daemon from a signed package or one command; it runs as its own user with no administrator rights
Executorscontainer, kubernetes, hosthost; container with Windows containers, process-isolated or, where the machine allows, each in its own small virtual machine; vm: a throwaway virtual machine per step, made from a template imagehost; vm: a throwaway macOS virtual machine per step, cloned from a template image with the system's own virtualization, at most two at a time on one machine as the system's license allows
A fresh, separate place per stepA container or pod per stepYes with container or vm. With host: a fresh working folder and a fresh, empty user profile for the step's process, removed after itYes with vm. With host: a fresh working folder and a temporary user home, removed after the step
Network for a custom stepAs todayThrough an egress point the Station runs on the machine, which allows only the hosts the step's manifest lists and records every refusal on the Sortie. A machine-wide firewall rule makes the egress point the only way out for the step's user.
Custom steps on hostRefused unless allow_unsandboxed_stepsThe same rule: refused unless the machine's owner sets allow_unsandboxed_steps, because a host process cannot be sandboxed as tightly as a container or a virtual machine
Where files liveThe Station's data directoryA data folder on a local drive the installer picks, with long paths turned on, kept out of virus scanning by the installer's suggestion (with the reason), and a short root so deep trees fitA data folder in the Station user's home, on the internal disk
CachesKeyed by image digest, system and architectureThe same rule. The key's "image" part is the template image's digest for vm, or the Station's reported tool versions for host, so a cache from one toolchain never lands on another.
Shellssh, bashpwsh by default, cmd, bash where installedzsh by default, bash, sh
Labels it reports by itselfos:linux, architectureos:windows, architecture, system version, the toolchains it finds (each with its version)os:macos, architecture, system version, the platform developer tools it finds (each with its version)

One matrix across the three systems. A step repeated over systems names the system in its for_each, and each member asks for a Station with that label. Members land on three Ramps (runner pools) and come back as one grid in the Debrief (test report).

Design: not built

for_each and runner: { labels } exist today; shell, the os: labels reported by the Station and the expression in labels are designs. Key names are not final.

steps:
  test:
    for_each: { os: [linux, windows, macos] }
    runner: { labels: ["os:${{ each.os }}"] }
    shell: "${{ each.os == 'windows' ? 'pwsh' : 'bash' }}"
    run: go test ./...

A member that no Station can take waits with the reason no_runner and the label it asked for, as any step does today. The Stations page shows each Station's system and version, so a missing macOS Station is one look away.

Hosted Stations on all three systems: a design

Hosted Stations are run by the hosted service for teams that do not want to run their own. They are the same Station program as yours, so a pipeline moves between a hosted Ramp and your own by changing one Ramp name, and nothing else in the file. Every hosted step runs in its own fresh machine with the sandbox your requires: a hardware-virtualized boundary, an internet-only network, firm quotas, and nothing shared between Bases (installations).

SizeLinuxWindowsmacOSFor
small2 processors, 8 GiB2 processors, 8 GiB-Lint, unit tests, small builds
standard (the default)4 processors, 16 GiB4 processors, 16 GiB4 processors, 14 GiBMost builds
large8 processors, 32 GiB8 processors, 32 GiB8 processors, 24 GiBLarge compiles, app builds
xlarge16 processors, 64 GiB16 processors, 64 GiB-Monorepos, game builds
gpu8 processors, 32 GiB, one graphics processor8 processors, 32 GiB, one graphics processor-Model training checks, rendering, shader builds

The figures are a proposal; the sizes are names, so a pipeline writes runner: { pool: hosted, size: large, labels: ["os:windows"] } and never a machine type. Disk is at least 100 GiB on every size, more on request per Ramp.

  • Images you can read. Each system has one hosted image, rebuilt weekly, published with its full list of contents and versions, signed, and pinned by digest on every step that used it. A pipeline can pin an image digest for a while; an image is retired with a notice on every Flight (codebase) that still pins it, never silently.
  • Warm and quick. The service keeps a small pool of started machines per size and system, so a step does not wait for a machine to boot. The step's page shows the wait, the boot and the work apart.
  • Quotas that are firm and visible. Each Base has a ceiling per size: machines at once, minutes per period, graphics-processor minutes apart. A step over the ceiling waits with quota_full and the figure; it never fails for that reason alone. A spend cap set by a Commander (the Base's owner role) stops new hosted steps, never a Return to base (rollback).
  • Your own Stations are never metered. The pricing rule this plan recommends: steps on Stations you run, including those behind the Detachment (site agent), are never counted as minutes. Only the service's own machines are. This is a recommendation for you to confirm (see Open question).
  • Graphics processors only when asked. A gpu step must name the size; it is never given one by default. Its time is shown before the Sortie starts as an estimate from earlier Sorties, so nobody is surprised.

Where hosted machines run, and from which stage of opening, are your earlier decisions on the hosted service: they are not changed here.

Mobile and games builds: a design

Phone apps and games ask more of a build machine than a web service does: a particular operating system, a platform toolchain of an exact version, signing material that must never leak, a store upload at the end, files of many gigabytes and steps that run for hours. Each of these is answered by a piece of the model that already exists.

NeedHow Launchway answers itFrom the model
The right machineToolchain images for Linux (the Android toolchain, game engines' command-line builds) live in the Hangar (the built-in library) as images with a published list of contents. Machine images for macOS and Windows are template images for the vm executor. A Station reports the toolchain versions it has as labels; a step asks for one: labels: ["android-sdk:35"].Labels, Ramps, images by digest
The right toolchain versionA step names the platform toolchain version it needs (toolchain: { platform-tools: "16.2" }). On a macOS Station that has several installed, the Station selects that one for the step's process only. A version the Station lacks is a placement reason, not a failure halfway through.Typed step needs, checked before the Sortie
Cross-platform frameworksA Hangar recipe for each framework declares its parts and the labels each part needs: the shared code on Linux, the Android part on Linux with the Android toolchain, the iOS part on macOS. Each part lands on the right Ramp; one Debrief joins them.Flight plans (ready-made pipelines) and Maneuvers (step templates)
SigningCertificates, private keys, provisioning profiles and keystores are secrets, named on the step and resolved on the Station. They go into a temporary keychain or keystore made for the step, with a random password, unlocked only for the step's process, and deleted when the step ends, however it ends. They never touch the workspace, the cache or Cargo (artifacts).Secrets resolved on the Station; the server never sees them
Store uploadA Hangar step, launchway/store-upload, sends a signed build to the phone makers' app stores or a game distribution service. Its credential is a secret reference. Its inputs are typed (track, release notes from the release, rollout share) and its result is recorded with the build's digest.Custom steps on the one contract
Large filesLarge files in the repository are fetched by the Station's own tooling (Large files, m1) and kept in a per-Station store, so each Sortie fetches only what changed. A Ramp that opts in raises its workspace limit (for example 200 GiB) and its Cargo limit. Cargo over 1 GiB is uploaded in verified chunks that resume after a dropped connection.The workspace rule, Cargo by digest
Long buildsA Ramp opts in to long steps (up to 24 hours) and the Station's accept.max_timeout must allow them too. The lease and heartbeat are unchanged, so a long step on a lost Station is noticed in 90 seconds, not hours later. A step may write checkpoints to a declared cache so a retry starts from the last one.Leases, caches that only make things faster
Design: not built

signing, toolchain and launchway/store-upload are designs. secrets, runner and needs exist today. Key names are not final. The example is an illustration: Harbor Lights' running example has no phone app, so imagine the Squadron (team) "shop" adds one beside storefront.

steps:
  ios:
    runner: { pool: macos, labels: ["os:macos"] }
    toolchain: { platform-tools: "16.2" }
    signing:
      kind: keychain
      certificate: shop-ios-distribution-cert     # secret references, never values
      key: shop-ios-distribution-key
      profile: shop-ios-app-store-profile
    run: ./scripts/build-ios.sh
    artifacts: [build/shop.ipa]
  store:
    needs: ios
    uses: launchway/store-upload
    with:
      platform: ios
      build: "${{ steps.ios.outputs.artifacts.shop_ipa }}"
      track: beta
    secrets: [shop-store-api-key]

On-demand Stations: a design

An on-demand Station exists only while there is work for it. Two things must change for that to be safe and fast: enrollment and workspace travel.

What changes in enrollment. Today a join token lasts up to 7 days and may enroll several Stations. The chart already uses tokens marked ephemeral, so each Station is revoked when it leaves. For on-demand Stations the launcher asks for one token per machine. That token enrolls once, lasts minutes and carries the Ramp and labels. The new Station keeps its key in memory and never writes it to disk. When the Station has drained, the server revokes it. A token that was not used expires by itself.

Who makes the machine. The automatic-resources design keeps a rule: the server never creates machines itself. On Kubernetes the built-in launcher needs only a narrow right on the Stations' own workload. For virtual machines and clouds the launcher is a provider Hardpoint that the team runs with its own cloud credential (Hardpoints). Launchway publishes the "Stations wanted" figure and the one-use token. It holds no cloud key. Whether the hosted service may ever hold one is open for you.

What changes in workspace travel. A new Station has no checkout. It receives the Sortie's workspace from the hand-off store and returns only what it changed, as described in the workspace travels with the Sortie. Without the hand-off, every on-demand Station would clone the repository again.

How a step gets its tools

Today a script step has exactly one image or one container. A custom step has one image or one toolchain (go, python, node or sh, with an optional version). Services such as a test database run as extra containers beside the step, and a step cannot use a service as its own container. To combine tools today, you build an image that holds them, or you split the work over steps and pass files through the workspace. This plan keeps the first shape and adds two more.

ShapeWhat it isWhen to use itStatus
One tool image per stepThe step runs in one image. On Kubernetes that image is in a pod of its own, sized for that step alone.The default, and the right choice for most stepsAvailable
A step groupSteps that run one after another share one pod and one workspace. Each step runs in its own tool container, and each keeps its own log, result, outputs and retry.Chains of short steps, where a pod start would cost more than the workNew in this plan
A step with several tool containersOne step names a main image and helper tool images. They share the step's workspace. The script runs in the main one and calls a helper with one built-in command.One piece of work that needs two toolchains, such as a front-end build inside a back-end buildNew in this plan

The rules that keep these honest:

  • Steps of one group never run at the same time. Two steps that share a memory limit were killed together, and that failure is not brought back (see the pod models below).
  • A group holds its reservation for as long as it runs. That is its stated cost, and the reason it is opt-in.
  • Every container of a group, or of a multi-container step, has its own memory limit. Its image digest is listed on the step. The Station's accept.images applies to each one.
Design sketch, keys not final

The shape follows the plan's model sheet. Nothing below exists yet.

groups:
  checks: { containers: { go: golang:1.27, lint: registry.example.com/tools/lint:2 } }
steps:
  fmt:  { group: checks, container: go,   run: gofmt -l . }
  vet:  { group: checks, container: go,   run: go vet ./..., needs: fmt }
  lint: { group: checks, container: lint, run: lint ./..., needs: vet }
  web:
    image: node:22
    tools: { go: golang:1.27 }            # a helper tool container
    run: |
      npm ci && npm run build
      launchway tool go -- go generate ./web/...

Services beside a step: readiness, order and their own logs

A test step often needs a database or a message broker beside it. Today a pipeline declares such a container with service: true under containers, a step says which services it needs with services: [db], and a ready check (a command, a TCP port or an HTTP path, with every and within) holds the step until the service answers. On Kubernetes the check is the container's readiness probe; with the container executor it is the container's health check, on the container engine that supports it. A service that is not ready in time fails the step as an infrastructure problem, with the check and the last lines of the service's output. The host executor, and the container engine that has no health checks, do not run services and say so.

This plan adds three things, so a service is as visible as the step it serves.

AdditionHow it worksStatus
Readiness checksready: { run | tcp | http, every, within }, as aboveAvailable on Kubernetes and with the container executor
Start orderafter: [db] on a service starts it only once the named services are ready, so a cache that needs the database waits for it. A cycle is refused when the pipeline is checked.New in this plan
A time limit for the servicetimeout on a service bounds its whole life. When the last step that needs it ends, the service is stopped and its exit is recorded; it never outlives its steps.New in this plan
Its log as a tab on the stepEach service's output, from its start to its stop, is kept as its own log, masked like the step's, and shown as a tab beside the step's log: Log, db, cache. The readiness checks appear in it with their times. On failure the step's summary names the service and links to the line.New in this plan
Facts on the record"Service db ready after 6 s", "service cache stopped, exit 0" are events, so the Debrief and the step's "where it ran" panel show them, and a slow service is a measured part of the step's timeNew in this plan
Design: not built

containers, service, ready and services exist today. after and timeout on a service are designs.

containers:
  db:    { image: postgres:17, service: true, ready: { tcp: 5432, within: 60s } }
  cache: { image: registry.example.com/test/cache:2, service: true, after: [db], ready: { tcp: 6379 }, timeout: 30m }
steps:
  test: { image: golang:1.27, services: [db, cache], run: go test ./... }

Hooks around every step: a design

Some work belongs around every step rather than in any one pipeline: checking that the machine is clean before a step, collecting the tool versions a step used, scrubbing a shared cache folder, sending a step's resource figures to the team's own monitoring. Today a team copies that work into every pipeline, or bakes it into images. This plan makes it a hook: a pinned custom step that runs before a step, after it, or on_exit, whatever the step's result.

  • Who declares it. A level (Base, Wing (organization), Squadron or Flight), in the product's settings for that level, by someone with the Commander role there; or a Station's owner, in the Station's own file beside accept:, for work that belongs to that machine. A level's hook can be locked so levels below cannot remove it. A pipeline cannot remove a hook; it can only see it.
  • What a hook is. A custom step from a library, pinned to a commit and a manifest digest, under the one step contract. It has its own image, its own permissions and its own secrets by name; it never receives the step's secrets. It reads the step's name, kind, inputs, result and timings as typed inputs.
  • Which steps it wraps. A hook names the steps it applies to by kind, by label of the Station, or by Ramp: for example "every build step on Ramp macos". Launch steps and Return to base are never wrapped by a hook that can fail them.
  • What it may do to the step. A before hook that fails stops the step with "refused by hook clean-check", and the step can be retried. An after or on_exit hook never changes the step's result or outputs; it may only add notes, files to Cargo and its own result. Each hook has a time limit (one minute by default).
  • Seen everywhere. Hooks appear on every step that ran them, as small rows before and after the step with their own logs, times and results, and in the Simulator's plan before a Sortie starts. Nothing runs that the Sortie page does not show.
Design: not built

A Squadron's hook, as it would be set in its settings (and in Terraform). Keys are not final.

hooks:
  - name: tool-versions
    when: after
    uses: platform-library/report-tool-versions@v1.3.0   # pinned; the lockfile records its digest
    applies_to: { kinds: [script, image], pools: [harbor-build, macos] }
    timeout: 1m
    locked: true

Hooks follow the one step contract (Hardpoints), so a hook is written, tested and reviewed like any custom step, and a Standing order (policies and repository standards) can require that a level's hooks come only from approved libraries.

Pod models on Kubernetes: an open choice

On Kubernetes, one question decides how much of a Sortie a pod holds. You have not answered it yet, so this plan does not decide it. Production runs one pod per Sortie today, while the code's default is one pod per step. The setting is kubernetes.pod (chart: runner.kubernetes.pod). The product's documentation says per-run "exists for one release ... and will be removed". That removal belongs to the same open decision.

The facts on both sides, as measured by the product team. Sources: docs/reference/runner-config.md ("One pod for each step") and docs/development/automatic-resources.md.

QuestionOne pod per stepOne pod per Sortie
Start costOne pod start per step. About 3 seconds on a node that already has the image. A whole step that does nothing took 3.4 to 4.2 seconds, including handing a 20 MB workspace in and out. Steps of a minute or more do not notice it. Many tiny steps do.One start for the whole Sortie
MemoryEach step has its own limit. Two steps on one image cannot kill each other.Steps on the same image share one container and one limit. Two such steps, compiling at once, went past 8 GiB together and were both killed.
ReservationHeld only while a step runsHeld for the whole Sortie. One pod reserved 8448 MiB while using about 1.1 GiB. One Sortie reserved 16.9 GiB while using 1 GiB.
WorkspaceCopied in from the Station's copy and only changed files copied back. For a synthetic 3 GB workspace of 150,000 files over nine steps, executor time fell from 319 s to 147 s with caches kept out, and to 71 s with dependency folders excluded too.Shared live inside the pod, with no copy
Parallel stepsEach starts from the workspace as it was and hands back its changes, which are merged. No step sees another's files while they are being written.Share one filesystem live
ServicesA fresh service with each step's pod. Its state does not carry to the next step.One per Sortie, so its state carries
Tool caches in the home folderCold in each step unless declared as a cache:Warm across steps
Size of one podAt most the step, the workspace helper and the servicesFourteen containers in one pod were seen
A lost lease or a restarted StationThe abandoned pod is removed at once, so a retry never waits for room its own pod holdsThe pod is removed. A resume makes a new pod from the Station's checkout, and files earlier steps wrote inside the pod are gone.
Open question

One pod per step, or one pod per Sortie, on Kubernetes. The product's own open question reads: "Is a pod per step acceptable for start-up time on the home cluster, given that images are already on the node after the first pull?" This chapter's proposals work under either answer. Step groups, warmed images and pull times reduce the per-step cost. The workspace hand-off and on-demand Stations do not depend on the model.

The workspace travels with the Sortie

The rule: a Sortie clones its repository once, every later step sees what earlier steps left, and caches travel on their own path. Today that holds within one Station. This plan extends it across Stations.

Today.

  • The Station clones the Sortie's commit when the first step lands. It makes a full clone, so tags are there, using a read-only credential made for that Sortie. Libraries are mirrored per Station and exported at their recorded commit into .launchway/lib/<name>.
  • With container or host executors, steps share one directory on the Station. On Kubernetes with one pod per step, the Station keeps a copy of the workspace and fills each pod from it. It takes back only files changed after the pod's clock reading, plus new directories and removed names. Nothing is hashed, and links stay links. Names are checked so they cannot escape the copy.
  • Limits: 4 GiB per Sortie's workspace and 12 GiB for everything a Station holds, with a message naming the setting when either is passed. workspace: { exclude: [...] } keeps a tree out. Declared cache paths never travel with the workspace.
  • A step with its own runner:, or a Sortie taken over after its Station was lost, starts from a fresh checkout. A re-run of a Sortie also starts fresh and reuses outputs, not files.

Proposed: the workspace handed between Stations. When a Sortie's next step lands on a different Station, the Station that holds the workspace uploads what changed since the last hand-off. It uses the same chunked, verified upload that Cargo (artifacts) use. The other Station downloads the base and the changes. The hand-off:

  • is encrypted from the first version, because a workspace can hold what a step wrote, and is readable only by that Sortie's Stations;
  • is bounded by the same workspace limits and deleted when the Sortie ends;
  • needs nothing beyond the database and Git, because it uses the store Launchway already has;
  • is what lets Per-step runner and workspace (m1), A build’s parallel steps spread across machines (m2), on-demand Stations and a takeover after a lost Station work without a second clone.

Fan-outs of thousands of members: a design

Today a for_each step runs at most 500 members at once (max_parallel, 1 to 500), and each member is a step of its own on the record. That is right for a matrix of versions. It is wrong for a test suite split into three thousand shards, a scan of every image in the Depot (registry), or a render of every frame of a game cinematic. This design lets one step fan out to thousands of members without the record, the database or the Sortie page growing with them. It is the execution half; the record half is designed here too, so that chapter's model stays one record.

  • One node, with counts. On the record a fan-out is one step with member counts (queued, running, passed, failed, skipped, retried) and a compact member table: index, values, Station, time, result and a link to its log. Every member's log and results are kept, but the Sortie's own event stream carries one event per batch of changes, not one per member.
  • Back-pressure, not a flood. The server holds a cursor over the members rather than queueing thousands of rows. It hands out the next wave when Stations of the Ramp free up, never more than the Ramp can start, so other Flights' work keeps its fair share. max_parallel still caps a fan-out, and its default becomes "what the Ramp can take".
  • A limit far above 500. A fan-out may have up to 10,000 members by default; a Base may raise its own limit to 100,000. max_parallel may go up to 2,000. Beyond a limit the pipeline is refused when it is checked, with the number, never part-way through.
  • Failures that stay readable. The page and the Debrief show counts first, then failed members grouped by failure shape ("212 failed: timeout connecting to the test database"), then a searchable member list. fail_fast and continue_for keep their meaning; a new tolerate lets a fan-out pass with a stated share of failures (for example tolerate: 0.5%), and the Debrief says how many it tolerated.
  • Re-run only what failed. Re-running a fan-out re-runs only its failed members by default, reusing the passed ones, which already works for one matrix member today.

Gathering members' outputs into typed lists, and conditions over them, are designed in Pipelines, values and expressions.

Design: not built

for_each over a list a step produced, tolerate and the higher limits are designs; for_each, max_parallel, fail_fast and continue_for exist today.

steps:
  shards:
    run: ./e2e/list-shards.sh > "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS/shards.json"
  e2e:
    needs: shards
    for_each: { shard: "${{ steps.shards.outputs.shards }}" }   # 3,000 values
    tolerate: 0.5%
    run: ./e2e/run.sh --shard "${{ each.shard }}"

Speed that never changes the result

Each of these makes a Sortie faster. None of them may change what it produces. In the words of the product's own rule: "A cache makes a build faster. It never changes what the build produces."

Caches

Available A cache key always includes the step's image resolved to its digest, the operating system and architecture, the cache name and the format. To that it adds the lock files, text and tool versions you name. Entries are never changed once saved; a changed result is the next generation. Entries expire after 7 days by default. Who reads and writes is decided by the server, by how the Sortie started, so a pull request never writes what the default branch reads. A cache holding a file that looks like a credential is not saved, and nothing turns that refusal off.

Not yet: entries are not encrypted or signed by Launchway (Encrypt stored files, logs and caches, m12).

Warmed images

New in this plan When a Sortie is created, the server knows the digest each step's image resolved to. It asks the Ramp's Stations, or the Kubernetes launcher, to fetch those digests ahead. Today an image is pulled when its step starts and reused if the machine has it. Warming is a head start only. It fetches digests, never moving tags, and uses the step's own pull credentials and accepted-images list.

Pull time on every step

New in this plan Each step shows three times: fetching its image, starting its pod or container, and its own work. A slow step then says which part was slow. Today only the 10-minute start timeout bounds a slow pull.

Sizes from measurement

In progress Each attempt's peak memory and processor use is already measured from the step's own container and shown. Next, reservations come from those figures plus headroom. A written size becomes a floor. A step killed for memory runs once more with more, then fails plainly, never in a loop (Size hints for steps, m2, as changed below).

Scaling on steps waiting

New in this plan A Station's processor use says little. The number of steps waiting, and what they need, says a lot. The server publishes "Stations wanted". A built-in scaler with a narrow right acts on it by default, or the cluster's own autoscaler reads it. A Ramp grows after steps have waited about 30 seconds and shrinks one Station at a time after about 10 minutes idle. It never removes a Station that is running a step. Today the Station chart has an optional autoscaler on processor use, off by default.

Waiting, never failing

Available A step with no room waits with a plain reason and a stable code (quota_full, cluster_full, no_runner, runners_busy, retry_pause). It waits up to 60 minutes by default. A step that can never fit fails at once with both numbers. Runs over a limit are held in a fair order, and pushes to the default branch are never held (docs/guide/queues.md).

The hosted build cache: a design

Today's caches save and restore folders. Some build tools can do better: they ask a remote cache, one action at a time, "has anyone already built this exact thing?", and container builds can reuse image layers by their digest. The roadmap item Shared build caches Launchway hosts asks Launchway to serve that cache itself. Here is how.

  • The open protocols tools already speak. The cache answers the open remote-cache protocols that the common build tools use (a content-addressed store and an action cache, over HTTP and the common remote-procedure transport those protocols define), and the open container registry protocol for image layers, through the Depot. A build tool is pointed at localhost by the Station; no token is ever put into the step.
  • Content-addressed and checked. Every entry is stored by the hash of its contents and checked on write and on read, by the server and again by the Station. An entry that does not match its hash is dropped and reported.
  • The same trust scopes as caches today. A pull request reads what the default branch wrote and writes only to its own scope; the default branch never reads a pull request's entries; a fork reads nothing and writes nothing. Action results, which say "this input gives that output", may be written only by trusted scopes, so an untrusted change cannot plant a result that a release later trusts.
  • One cache for a Base. Every Station of a Base shares it, whether it runs on Kubernetes, on Windows, on macOS or behind the Detachment, so the first build of the morning warms the rest. Nothing is shared between Bases.
  • Encrypted, bounded, measured. Entries are encrypted at rest with the Base's key, kept within a size the Base sets, and evicted least-recently-used. Each step shows its hits, misses and bytes saved; the Ramp page shows the hit rate over time. A sample of hits is rebuilt and compared (the roadmap's Build twice and compare), so a wrong entry is caught.
  • Off the platform's path. The cache is its own server role, scaled on its own, using the object store Launchway already has; a cache that is down makes builds slower, never wrong, and never stops a Sortie.

Isolation: what is enforced today, and what is owed

The principle is least privilege. A step gets only the secrets it names, only the network its owner allows, no token for the cluster, and no root. Here is what each executor enforces today. Sources: docs/reference/step-manifest.md ("What a step may do"), docs/reference/runner-config.md and the Station chart's values.

ProtectionPodman or DockerKubernetesHost
A fresh, separate place per stepA fresh container per stepA pod per step attempt, or per Sortie with per-runNo. A process on the machine, only for pipelines its owner trusts.
Not root, no capabilitiesCustom steps: all capabilities dropped and no new privileges. Script steps run as the image's user.On by default (restricted: true): user 1000, no capabilities, the default seccomp profile, a private home folder. Pipelines cannot change it.The Station's own user
Read-only root filesystemCustom stepsCustom stepsNo
Network for a custom stepNone unless the manifest lists hosts. The list itself is not enforced by name.The pod is labeled for the chart's network policies, which give no egress or the operator's host rules. The chart's policies are off by default.Not enforced. Custom steps are refused unless allow_unsandboxed_steps is set.
Writable paths for a custom stepThe workspace is read-only except the listed pathsRecorded, not enforcedNot enforced
SecretsResolved on the Station just before the step, only those the step names. A secret the manifest does not name is refused. Values are masked in logs. The server never sees them.
Cluster rightsNoneNo service account token is mounted unless an operator names one. The Station's own role covers pods in the step namespace only.None
Image buildsSent to a rootless image builder that the operator runs apart from step pods, because it cannot run under the strict pod profile

Hardening still owed, each tied to a roadmap item:

  1. Enforce a custom step's hosts by name, through an egress point the Station controls, and its writable paths on Kubernetes. Missing parts of Steps run in a sandbox (m2, in progress).
  2. Turn the step network policy on by default where the cluster enforces policies. Show every refused connection on the Sortie. Build network that allows what builds need and shows what it refused (proposed, m2).
  3. Put step pods in their own namespace at the lowest priority. Both exist as chart settings and are off by default. Builds never take room from the platform (proposed, m2).
  4. A hardware-virtualized boundary per step, an internet-only network, firm quotas and nothing shared between Bases, before any outside customer's step runs. Sandboxed hosted runners (m7), required by. The ruling also makes the same profile a product feature for any self-hosted installation.
  5. Keep unchecked images away from sandboxed builds. Image guard for sandboxed builds (m4).
  6. Encrypt and sign cache entries. Encrypt stored files, logs and caches (m12).

Stations that update themselves: a design

A fleet of Stations drifts: one machine runs last spring's version, another refuses a key the server now sends. Your rule settles the defaults: updates on by themselves for hosted Ramps, a notice for Stations you run, and never for Stations on Kubernetes, which follow the chart. This design makes the update safe enough that a team chooses to turn it on.

  • Signed releases only. A Station fetches a version manifest from the server (or from the hosted service's release channel), checks its signature against the key built into the Station, and checks the download's digest. A Station never runs a binary whose signature does not verify, whoever offered it.
  • Under a Standing order. Each level can set how its Stations update: automatic, notify (the default for your own Stations) or pinned to a version line such as 2.14, with a window ("Sundays 02:00 to 05:00, America/Chicago") and waves (one Station first, then a tenth of the Ramp, then the rest). A level above can lock it. The Station's own file may only narrow it, for example to refuse updates outside office hours.
  • Drain, then swap. A Station that may update stops taking steps, finishes what it holds, downloads, checks, and swaps, keeping the previous version beside the new one.
  • Prove it, or go back. The new version must enroll, renew its token and pass a small self-test step within ten minutes. If it does not, it returns to the previous version by itself, takes work again, and the failure is an event with the reason; that version is not offered to that Ramp again until someone clears it.
  • A published support window. Every server release states which Station versions it supports: the current minor version and the two before it are supported; the one before those is accepted with a warning and a date-free notice "update before the next server release"; older ones are refused when they ask for work, with the version they need. The window is in the release notes, on the Stations page and in launchway runners versions.
  • Seen as a fleet. The Stations page shows each Station's version, the waves in progress, and Stations outside the window.
Design: not built

The Standing order rule as it might be written. Keys are not final.

standing_orders:
  - name: station-updates
    rules:
      station_updates:
        mode: automatic          # automatic | notify | pinned
        line: "2.14"             # with pinned: stay on this version line
        window: { days: [sun], from: "02:00", to: "05:00", timezone: America/Chicago }
        waves: [1, 10%, 100%]
    lock: true

Debugging: attach to a failed step

Today a failed step says why with the evidence, and you can re-run from it. The roadmap adds one command to reproduce it (Reproduce a failed step, m2). This plan names attach as part of that item.

What opens
A shell in a fresh pod or container made from the failed attempt: the same image digest, the workspace as the step left it, and the same inputs and variables.
What does not
Production secrets, ever. A Controller (approver) may allow the non-production secrets the step named.
Who may
A person who may re-run that step on that Flight. The action is offered only where it can work, and says why when it cannot.
Limits
A time limit set by the level. The Station keeps the failed attempt's workspace only for that window. The session counts against the same quota as steps.
Record
Opening, every command typed and closing are in the Logbook.
Ways in
A button on the failed step, the command line (sketch: launchway sortie attach 42 test), the API and the agent endpoint.

Worked example: storefront on Harbor Lights' Stations

Harbor Lights runs its builds on its Kubernetes cluster and keeps production apart.

RampKindServesStations
harbor-buildbuildFlights storefront, paymentsTwo Station pods from the chart, require_identity: true. Planned: grows on steps waiting.
harbor-launch-proddeployTarget prod-clusterOne Launch Station in the cluster, with accept.environments: [prod]
billing-vmsdeployThe two billing virtual machinesA Launch Station that can reach them (see Launching to virtual machines and physical servers)
arm-on-demandbuildFlight storefront, label arm64None standing. A cloud machine is made per waiting step (proposed).
  1. A commit to storefront creates Sortie 42. A Station of harbor-build takes the first step and clones once.
  2. fmt, vet and lint take seconds each. Today each gets its own pod. As a step group they would share one pod. That is two pod starts saved, about 6 seconds on a warm node by the measured figure.
  3. test runs with a PostgreSQL service in its own pod, sized from what it used in earlier Sorties. Its readiness check holds the tests until the database answers, and with this plan the database's own log is a tab beside the test log. web builds the front end in a node image. Both restore their caches, keyed by lock file and image digest; with the hosted build cache, the Go compiler's results built by this morning's first Sortie are hits for every later one.
  4. image is sent to the rootless image builder. A second image step for the kiosks asks for arm64. With the proposals, a machine is made on arm-on-demand, takes the workspace from the hand-off store, builds, and is removed.
  5. The Launch to dev is taken by a Launch Station. Later the Launch to prod is taken by the harbor-launch-prod Station, which runs no script. Its Return to base would be taken first, ahead of any other Launch (proposed).

The foundation it relies on

  • Levels and roles. Ramps serve Flights. The Station role is named on every Flight and is held by admins by default. A Ramp may be shared from a Wing (organization) or Squadron (team) down, like any other object.
  • The record. Leases, refusals, enrollments, rotations, revocations and every Station a step ran on are events. A Sortie's page is rebuilt from them.
  • Secrets on the Station. Stores are configured on the Station, narrowed by Flight and key, and read just before a step runs.
  • The step contract. What a step needs from a Station (executor, labels, network, secrets, images) is declared once and checked before the Sortie starts (one step contract).
  • The wall between Bases. On a hosted installation, Stations, caches, workspaces and hand-offs are never shared between Bases (each customer's walled-off installation).

Safety

What failsWhat happens
A serverAny other server answers, because leases and sessions are in the database. The Station spools logs and the result to its disk and delivers them when a server answers. Today.
The databaseStations keep running their steps and spool their logs. No new step is handed out until it returns. The database failover item covers the rest (Database failover and no lost push, m1).
A StationIts lease lapses after 90 seconds. The step runs again once on another Station, and finished steps are kept. Its abandoned pods are removed. Today the new Station starts from a fresh checkout. With the hand-off, it continues from the last handed-off workspace.
A step's podRemoved however the step ends. A reaper runs at start, after each result and every 30 seconds, and no pod lives past 24 hours unless a step in it is running.
An on-demand launcherThe step waits with the reason "no Station" and the launcher's error. It fails after the longest wait. A token that was never used expires by itself.
RoomSteps wait, never fail, until the longest wait. A step that can never fit fails at once with both numbers.
A hook (proposed)A before hook that fails or times out refuses the step with the hook's name and log; the step can be retried. An after or on-exit hook that fails is shown on the step and never changes its result. Hooks never wrap Launch or Return to base steps in a way that can fail them.
A Station update (proposed)A download whose signature or digest is wrong is discarded and nothing changes. A new version that does not pass its self-test within ten minutes returns to the previous one by itself and reports why.
The hosted build cache (proposed)Builds run without it, slower. An entry that fails its hash check is dropped and reported. No step fails because the cache is away.
A fan-out of thousands (proposed)Members on a lost Station are handed out again; finished members are kept. A server that takes over reads the member cursor from the database and carries on.
Signing material (proposed)The temporary keychain or keystore is deleted when the step ends, however it ends; if the Station itself dies, it is deleted when the Station starts again, before it takes any work.

Who may do what. Only the Station role makes join tokens, revokes Stations or rotates their keys, and each of those is in the Logbook. A Station's owner sets accept:, which no one on the server can widen. Attaching to a step needs the right to re-run it.

On by default. Outward-only connections, identity per Station, restricted step pods, no cluster token in steps, secrets only by name, refusal of custom steps on the host executor, refusal to cache credentials, and pull requests from forks without secrets.

Return to base is never blocked. Launch Stations are on their own Ramps and take no build work. Today a Launch step, and its Return to base, waits up to 15 minutes for a Station like any other Launch step. This plan proposes that a Return to base goes ahead of every other Launch on its Ramp, with room kept for it at all times.

Stations

Station versions and updates

The fleet by version, the support window, waves in progress, and the update rule in force with where it comes from.

Build cache

Hit rate over time per Ramp and per step, bytes saved, size used against the limit, and entries dropped for a bad hash.
