Shortened here. The complete set, with every detail, need and note, including the changed items, is in plan-notes/proposals/arch-stations.json; the second pass's items are in plan-notes/proposals/fixes-flightplan-b.json.

Open question

Open: your own Stations never metered

This plan recommends that steps on Stations you run, including behind the Detachment, are never counted as minutes on the hosted service; only its own machines are. Your rule that price follows availability, people and hosting, not features, points this way, but the hosted prices are still open. Confirm the rule.

Open: hosted sizes and graphics processors

The size names and figures in hosted Stations are a proposal. Whether graphics-processor machines are offered from the first hosted stage, or later, depends on where hosted machines run, which you have decided separately; this plan does not change it.

Open: fan-out limits

The proposal is 10,000 members per fan-out by default, up to 100,000 if a Base raises it, and up to 2,000 at once. Confirm the numbers, or set others.

Open: the support window

The proposal supports the current Station minor version and the two before it, accepts the next older with a warning, and refuses older ones. Confirm, or choose a longer window for customers who update slowly.

Open: pod model

One pod per step or one pod per Sortie on Kubernetes, and with it whether per-run is removed as the product's documentation says. The facts on both sides are in the table above. Production runs per Sortie while the code's default is per step.

Open: who makes on-demand machines

This plan keeps the existing design rule that the server never creates machines itself. Outside Kubernetes, the launcher is a provider the team runs with its own cloud credential. Should the hosted service ever hold a cloud credential to make Stations for a customer? says the hosted side holds no credential to a customer's systems, so this plan assumes no.

Open: two items for Windows and macOS

Windows and macOS runners and Builds on macOS and Windows machines (both m2) overlap. This plan keeps both, because merging them could narrow one. The design above serves both: the first gets the Station and its sandbox on each system, the second the signing, store upload, large files and long builds. You or the editor may merge them.

Not verified

That production runs per-run comes from the brief for this chapter. It was not read from the deployment. The measured figures are the product team's, from a one-node test cluster with images present, and from a synthetic workspace. A real network adds transfer time.

Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints

Launchway keeps growing without becoming a mess. Every capability has one slot with one provider in charge. Every kind of step speaks one contract. Outside systems plug in at Hardpoints (extension points) and never inside the server.

  • Each capability has a built-in default and a connection as an equal choice. Exactly one provider is in charge per Squadron (team), and every screen says which one: "served by".
  • Pipelines name the capability, never the product. A second provider is allowed only in a named role: in front, alongside for one stated purpose, or migrating with a visible end.
  • Five Hardpoints: events out, the API and agent endpoint in, workers that claim work, providers Launchway calls, and panels in pages. Nothing third-party runs inside the server.
  • One step contract for every kind of step, so a new capability is one module. Custom steps use it today. Built-in kinds are still hard-coded, and this chapter lists where.

Where it sits

This chapter is the frame around all seven layers. It gives layer 7, mission support, its rules: each module fills one named capability slot. It sets the step contract that layer 3, authoring, and layer 4, execution, both use. Hardpoints are the only way an outside system reaches the record, the levels or the work.

It builds on the record: every provider change, connection and Hardpoint call is an event. It also builds on Levels, people and secrets: every connection and Hardpoint has its own scoped credential. What builds on it: every module chapter (the Depot; Switches; the software graph and Maintenance; Work, from idea to running software; the Wingman and agents; Radar, insight and keeping it healthy), every Launch target in One way to launch, anywhere, and Reuse that keeps growing, which describes the authoring side of libraries.

What you will be able to do

Harbor Lights already pays for an outside container registry. On the Depot (registry) page of the web Squadron you set it as the provider in charge. The page now reads "served by: the team's registry". No pipeline file changes, because the pipelines say registry: default, not a product. Planned

A year later you move to the built-in Depot. A guided task imports the images, runs both providers in the migrating role with an end date shown on the page, and switches the old one off when nothing reads it any more. Planned

Your security team has its own alerting system. You give it an events-out Hardpoint with a token that can only receive Launch (deployment) and Clearance (approval) events. It gets every one, and the Logbook (audit trail) shows each delivery. No code was added to Launchway. Available for signed webhooks, Planned for the general Hardpoint.

A shared step in platform-library gets a new tag that asks to reach one more host. Your lockfile does not move by itself. An update notice opens a pull request that says "permission: the step may now reach registry.example.org", and a Controller (approver) must say Go before it merges. In progress for the notice, Planned for the lockfile.

The Launchway team adds performance testing. It arrives with a release as one module. It has a built-in load generator, a slot your existing load-testing service can serve instead, a step in the Hangar (template library), a page, a command and a Terraform resource. You turn it on for storefront and nothing else changes. Planned

How it works

Capability slots

Your principle: "I want an enterprise CI/CD platform for enterprise applications with a world-class built-in stack for everything, but we also equally support connecting to whatever the client environment has, and allow those products to add additional features our built-in solution doesn't have, and the user just turns off our version. Both are valid and equally supported decisions."

And your concern, which answers: "I just don't want to confuse the platform when things are connected vs our own."

The rules, from :

  1. One slot per capability, one provider in charge. "For each Squadron and capability exactly one provider (built-in or a connection) is the default: where things go when a pipeline does not say. 'Which one am I using?' always has one answer."
  2. One screen per capability, "the same whichever provider serves it, labeled 'served by'. A switched-off built-in leaves no second menu and no empty page."
  3. Pipelines name the capability, never the product. "Changing provider changes a setting, not pipeline files."
  4. Both at once only in a named role: "in front (our cache or proxy before theirs), alongside for one stated purpose, or migrating (with a visible end). Never both with no stated role."
  5. A connected product's extra features appear in place, "marked as coming from that product."
  6. A cost-saving path for each built-in that replaces a paid product: "connect theirs, import, run both in the migrating role, switch theirs off: a guided step."

adds that a connection is "an equal, first-class choice, never a second-rate adapter". It gets the same conformance suite, screens, API, command line, Logbook entries and permissions. Each built-in can be switched off per installation and, where it makes sense, per Squadron.

Built today

Pipelines already name a configured slot, not a product, in three places. An image step pushes to a Depot by the name an operator gave it, and the name launchway is the built-in Depot. A secret reference names a store. A verification step names a health source. Git hosts have a connection model, and a common contract for every host is planned (A common provider model, m1). There is no general slot object, no default per Squadron and no "served by" screen yet.

The table shows the rule cuts both ways. For delivery, the connection exists today and the built-in default is still planned. The slot model treats both the same.

Design sketch, keys not final

A pipeline names the capability, and the slot chooses the provider.

steps:
  image:
    kind: image
    tags: [{ registry: default, repository: storefront/api }]   # the Squadron's Depot slot
  perf:
    uses: launchway/performance-test                            # the capability, not a product
    with: { target: staging, profile: checkout }

When Launchway builds it in

, in your words: "We build in house our bread and butter, AI first class, and the dependency graph core, and we strongly consider how it helps our competitive advantage; strive to have a solution built in for each area but also connect."

The working test from the same ruling: build it in when "at least two of (on every pipeline's path; needed by a solo developer on day one; the commercial product is costly and the commonly used 80% is tractable)" hold. "Deep specialties (application monitoring, security event systems, meshes, cloud providers, ticketing) are connected well, not replaced."

adds the limits on reuse: "our own simple built-in version, plus connections to the leading systems; build it ourselves where that is better; pull in an outside project only where it clearly beats building, and never at the cost of a simple install." The core starts with a database and Git and nothing else. Code under a license that would stop Launchway being sold or offered as a hosted service is never embedded. Such a project may only run as a separate program.

What is never handed to an outside system

Design, section 5, gives the test: "does the capability decide, record or prove something that the product is sold on, using data that must stay in one place and one wall? If yes, it is built in." The catalog in that document is a proposal, and its rules come from your rulings. Its list:

  1. "The run: pipeline model, queue, lanes, leases, approvals."
  2. "The decision record: events with reasons, policy evaluation, waivers, approvals, audit."
  3. "The wall itself: tenant keys, per-Base blob prefixes, per-Base data keys, the isolation suite."
  4. "Secrets resolution on the runner and masking."
  5. "The delivery evidence chain: build, scan, sign, deploy, verify, return."
  6. "The verdict on a deployment."
  7. "Test and run reports."
  8. "The Git provider contract and write-back."
  9. "Credential brokering for connections."

"Everything else (a data plane, a broker, a vulnerability database, a database server, a mesh, a dashboard server) is a commodity that is cheaper to reuse than to maintain." adds two more that are never outsourced: AI is first class in every area, and the software graph is core.

So an outside engine may run a step, store an image or serve a Switch. It may never own a Sortie (run), a verdict, a secret's value or the record of what happened.

Hardpoints

Your rule: the product contains nothing only its author can use. "We don't want to tie Launchway into my customized security and AI systems; that isn't usable by others." Site-specific systems connect from outside, through five Hardpoints.

HardpointDirection and shapeTodayExact roadmap titles
Events outSigned events with a delivery log, retries and test deliveries, filtered by kind and levelAvailable Notifications and repository webhooksNotifications (Available list); Cards and events in, notifications out (m14)
API and agent endpoint inHTTP API, command line, agent endpoint and signed event sources, each exactly as powerful as its token. A parity test keeps them equal.AvailableOne capability, every interface; An endpoint for agents; The event log and event sources (Available list); Terraform provider (m1)
Workers that claim workAn outside program takes typed work with its own identity and a lease, and must report a resultAvailable for Stations. Agents and Detachments (site agents) are planned.Runner identity and pools (Available list); The Detachment (m7); Workers that claim work (proposed, m14)
Providers Launchway callsAn outside program serves a capability slot over a small published protocol, with the same conformance tests as the built-inAvailable as fixed kinds only: Git hosts, secret stores, Depots, health sourcesA common provider model (m1); Providers Launchway calls for a capability (proposed, m14)
Panels in pagesAn outside system supplies typed data, such as a title, rows, links and a status. Launchway draws it with its own components. No outside script runs in the page.PlannedCards and events in, notifications out (m14): "richer cards come later because they widen the attack surface"

Every Hardpoint is documented and versioned. Each has its own scoped credential, a Logbook entry for every use, a rate limit and an off switch. Two supporting pieces come from the design draft: an extension manifest that declares the scopes an extension asks for, so a person sees them before saying yes, and data out, the same exports every person already has. A build check keeps company-specific names out of the product (Published extension points, m14).

Built today

There is no plug-in mechanism in the server: no plug-in loader and no embedded script runtime. Extension today means custom steps, libraries and templates, event sources, webhooks and notifications, the HTTP API, the command line and the agent endpoint. The roadmap item Extensions without fragility (m2) states the direction: "A step catalog and typed custom steps instead of plug-ins that run inside the server. Nothing a team adds can crash or compromise the server, and every extension has a version and an owner."

One step contract for every kind of step

The rule: "A step is a program." Every kind of step, built-in or custom, declares its inputs, its outputs, its permissions and what it needs from the Station (runner). Then adding a capability is one module.

Today, for custom steps (docs/reference/step-contract.md, docs/reference/step-manifest.md). A step is a directory in Git with a manifest, code in any language, and tests. Contract version 1 is small and the same in every language:

WhatHow
InputsA JSON file named by LAUNCHWAY_STEP_INPUTS, typed string, number, boolean, list, record or secret, and checked against the manifest before the Sortie starts
OutputsOne JSON object written to LAUNCHWAY_STEP_OUTPUTS, checked against the declared types. A step that passes without writing them "broke the contract".
ResultsOne JSON line each for a summary, annotation, finding, test, mask, or a question for a person. At most 5,000 lines and 4 MiB.
Cargo and reportsFiles in LAUNCHWAY_STEP_ARTIFACTS, and SARIF or JUnit files in LAUNCHWAY_STEP_REPORTS
Exit codes0 passed, 1 to 63 failed, 64 failed but allowed, 65 needs a person, above 65 a crash
Permissionsnetwork hosts and write paths, none by default. Fixed at the pinned commit when the Sortie is created, so a step cannot widen its own.
Trust boundaryNothing is read from what a step prints. Results come only from files the Station made for this attempt.
Kits and testsKits for Go, Python, TypeScript and shell. launchway step new, launchway step test, launchway step validate --against.

Today, for built-in kinds. The kinds image, deploy, rollback, rollout, verify, ai and approval are not built on the contract. Each is hard-coded, and a new built-in kind touches all of these places:

  1. The pipeline parser: a kind constant, its own parse function, a case in the special-step switch, and the key lists from which the published pipeline schema is generated.
  2. The reference documentation's key tables, which a documentation test compares with the parser.
  3. The engine: the list of known step kinds, the queueing, advance and persistence hooks, and kind-specific fields on the job sent to a Station.
  4. Schema markers and upgrade tests, so older servers and Stations leave the new kind alone.
  5. The Station: the branch in its step dispatch. Launch kinds have a separate Launch Station path.
  6. An executor, if the kind needs a new way to run.
  7. The API routes, the agent endpoint tool, the command, and a row in the interface parity table.
  8. The architecture test's allowed imports, if a new package is added.
Proposed: the contract reaches further

Two designs in other chapters stand on this contract. Every step, not only a custom one, gets the results file, so a plain script can write a summary and notes on lines (summaries and notes from any step). And hooks that run before, after and on exit of every step are custom steps under this contract, declared by a level or a Station's owner (hooks around every step).

A custom step, by contrast, is a layer on a plain script step and needs no engine change. That is why the Hangar's own custom steps (license checks for Go and Python, a secret scan) could ship without one.

Proposed: built-in kinds on the one contract. Each kind becomes a module with the same manifest a custom step has, plus two fields:

Manifest fieldMeaningToday
inputs, outputsTyped, checked before the SortieCustom steps
permissionsNetwork, writable paths, secrets by nameCustom steps
requires New in this planWhat it needs from a Station: executor, labels, a capability slot such as the image builder or a Launch target, and the contract versionImplied by hard-coded routing
settles New in this planWhere it runs: on a Station, or on the server for kinds that run no program, such as a ClearanceHard-coded
 
# Design sketch: the image kind described by the one contract. Keys are not final.
step: image
contract: 2
settles: station
requires: { executor: image-builder, capability: depot }
inputs:
  context:   { type: string, default: "." }
  platforms: { type: list, default: [linux/amd64] }
  tags:      { type: list }
outputs:
  digest: { type: string }
  sbom:   { type: string }
permissions:
  network: [depot]            # the slot, resolved to the provider in charge

The pipeline keys people write today stay as they are (kind: image, tags:). Kinds move one at a time. Each move ships with a test that the old and new forms produce the same Sortie. Once a kind is a module, its page, its command, its agent endpoint tool and its Terraform resource are generated from the manifest, so the parity table cannot fall behind.

How new templates, steps and modules arrive

Two kinds of author add to Launchway over time, on the same foundation.

The Launchway team

The Hangar ships inside each release: Flight plans (pipeline templates), Maneuvers (step templates) and custom steps. A Station compares a hash of the Hangar's files with the server's and refuses a Sortie when they differ: "update the runner, rather than run other scripts than the server planned." New capability modules follow the module contract below.

Developers

A library is a Git repository of templates and custom steps. A pipeline pins it by tag, branch or commit. The pin is resolved when the Sortie is created and recorded with the manifest's digest. A library that needs other libraries pins a tag or full commit, never a branch, and nesting stops at four levels.

PieceStatusExact roadmap title
Pins by tag, branch or commit, recorded on each SortieAvailableShare and pin steps and templates (m2); Shared libraries (Available list)
A page per step: inputs, outputs, permissions, versions, usersAvailableStep pages (m2)
Update notices showing what changed in inputs, outputs and permissionsIn progress: built for custom steps, not for templates, not yet a reviewable changeUpdate notices for shared libraries (m2)
A catalog to find, compare and updatePlannedA browsable catalog of templates and steps (m2)
Templates that read like codePlannedTemplates that read like code (m2)
A lockfileNew in this planA lockfile for everything a pipeline borrows (proposed, m2)
Checks a contribution must passNew in this planChecks a shared step or template must pass (proposed, m2)

The lockfile. Today a pin by branch or tag is resolved again for each Sortie. Two Sorties of the same commit can therefore use different library commits if the tag or branch moved. says templates are "pinned like dependencies", and a lockfile makes that exact. The pin is resolved once and written down, and changes only through a reviewed update.

# Design sketch: .launchway/hangar.lock (the file name is not final)
platform-library:
  pinned: v3                     # what the pipeline asked for
  commit: 9f2c41e0d7…            # what it resolved to
  steps:
    notes: { manifest: sha256:5be1…, permissions: { network: [], write: [dist] } }
launchway:
  pinned: builtin
  commit: 3a77c0…                # the Hangar of this release

The checks a contribution must pass.

CheckApplies toToday
The manifest is valid and names a contract version the Stations speakEvery step and kindAvailable launchway step validate
The step keeps to the contract: declared outputs and types, results on the right channel, no reserved exit codesEvery step and kindAvailable launchway step test
Its own unit tests pass, in its own pipelineEvery step and modulePossible, not required
No more than 3 lines of inline code in anything sharedTemplates, Flight plans, ManeuversDecided, not built
Permissions declared, and any widening called out against the last versionEvery stepAvailable --against
Inspection (security scan): secrets, vulnerabilities, licensesEvery library repositoryAvailable through Standing orders (policies)
No company-specific namesThe Hangar and product modulesPlanned with Published extension points
An interface parity row, the architecture test, an upgrade test, documentation tests, and a reviewer who is not the authorModules of the Launchway teamAvailable as the product's quality gates

Worked example: adding performance testing, from idea to available

You asked for performance testing as a first-class part of delivery . The roadmap item is Performance tests as proofs (m8, planned). Here it is taken through the one contract and the module contract. Harbor Lights' storefront is the first user. Its Launch to staging is followed by a load test, and the Launch to prod needs the test's result.

Module contract ruleHow performance testing meets it
1. Same levels and permissionsWho may start a test, and against which Airfield (environment), are ordinary roles on the Flight (codebase) and Airfield. No new role is added.
2. Writes to the one recordEvery test is an event with its profile, its target, the provider that served it and its verdict. Baselines are read back from earlier events.
3. Gates are Standing orders"A passing performance result before production" is a Standing order judged at the common point before a Launch (Performance gates in preflight, m8). It is advisory until a level makes it required.
4. Typed input formsThe target is picked from the Flight's Airfields, the profile from the repository's profiles, and the duration from a list. There is no free-text address.
5. Runs as a step on a Stationuses: launchway/performance-test, a module on the one contract. It requires a Station that can reach the Airfield and declares the target's host as its only network permission.
6. One slot, served byThe slot performance-test. The built-in default is a load generator in the Hangar. The connection is the team's existing load-testing service, through a provider Hardpoint. The page says "served by".
7. Off until wantedNothing appears in the menus until a Squadron turns the slot on
8. Every way inThe step page, a command, an API call, an agent endpoint tool and a Terraform resource are generated from the manifest. The parity row is part of the checks.
9. Loss and rights statedIf a server is lost, the step goes on and its result is spooled. If the Station is lost, the test runs again once, from the start. If the provider is lost, the step fails with "the provider did not answer" and the page shows it. Raising capacity for the test uses Temporary capacity for tests, which always restores what was there.
10. Never blocks Return to baseA Return to base never waits for a performance test, and a running test is stopped when a Return to base starts on the same Airfield
  1. Idea. A slot is named (performance-test) and the test for building it in is applied. It is on many delivery paths, a solo developer needs a simple load test, and the commonly used part is tractable, so it is built in and a connection is offered too.
  2. Module. A manifest, the load generator's code with unit tests, and a provider protocol for the connection, all in Git.
  3. Checks. Contract conformance, parity, architecture, upgrade and Inspection checks pass. A reviewer who is not the author reads it.
  4. Release. It ships in the Hangar of a release. The roadmap item moves to Available only when it is merged, tested and documented.
  5. Use. Harbor Lights turns the slot on for its Squadron, adds one step after the staging Launch, and pins the Hangar in its lockfile.

The module contract, and the foundation it relies on

This chapter is where the module contract is enforced. A module belongs in Launchway only if it meets all ten rules of the module contract. The worked example shows each one applied. The mechanisms that make the rules checkable rather than hoped for:

  • Rules 1 and 2 rest on Levels, people and secrets and the record. A module has no tables of its own for people or roles.
  • Rule 3 rests on Standing orders, Clearance and Hold judged at the common points.
  • Rule 4 rests on Inputs and run forms.
  • Rule 5 rests on the one step contract in this chapter and on Stations and where work runs.
  • Rule 6 rests on capability slots in this chapter.
  • Rule 8 rests on the interface parity test, which already fails the build when one way in falls behind (Every way in).

Safety

What failsWhat happens
A connected providerIts capability page says so at once with the provider's error. Steps that need it fail with that reason. Nothing falls back silently to another provider, because only a named role may put two providers in play.
A Hardpoint receiverEvents are retried with a delivery log. A receiver that stays down is shown on the Hardpoint's page. It never slows a Sortie.
A worker that claims workIts lease lapses and the work is offered again, as with a Station
A server or the databaseSlots, connections and Hardpoints are database objects with history. Any server reads them, and the usual high-availability rules apply.
A library tag that movesWith a lockfile, nothing changes until a reviewed update. Without one, the Sortie records the commit it used, as today.

Who may do what. Choosing the provider in charge of a slot is an administrative change at a level. A level above may lock it, as with variables. Registering a Hardpoint creates a credential with only the scopes it declares, and a person must accept them. Switching any Hardpoint off is immediate and recorded. A permission that widens in an update can be made to need a Controller's Go by a Standing order.

On by default. Built-in providers, so the core needs only a database and Git. No Hardpoint registered. Credentials narrow and audited. Update notices on, and widening permissions called out.

Return to base. No slot, connection or Hardpoint is ever on the path that blocks a Return to base. If the provider in charge of the delivery engine is down, the Launch page says so and offers the ways back that do not need it.

Screens

Full descriptions are in the screens notes for this chapter. In short:

Capabilities

One row per capability for a level: served by, role of any second provider, state, and who set it.

Capability page

The same page whichever provider serves it: "served by", the provider's health, its extra features marked, and its use.

Connect a provider

A wizard: pick the capability and provider from lists, give the credential by reference, test it, choose a role.

Move between providers

A guided task: connect, import, run both with an end date, switch off.

Hardpoints

Every registered extension with its kind, scopes, last use, rate and an off switch.

Catalog and update review

Find and compare libraries, steps and modules. Review an update as a difference in inputs, outputs and permissions.

Open question

Open: out of process only

Design asks you to confirm "out of process only, never in-process plug-ins". This chapter follows the roadmap items that already say it (Extensions without fragility, Published extension points) and your do-not-remove list. The formal answer is still recorded as open.

Open: the policy language

Whether Standing orders gain a language beyond the typed catalog is yours to decide. The performance gate in the worked example uses only the typed catalog.

Open: design 's questions

Six questions on the build-or-connect catalog are unanswered. Among them: whether any dashboard stack is bundled, and how strictly to apply the rule that embedded code must keep a commercial license possible. The slot model works whatever they decide.

For the editor: where the slot item lives

This chapter puts One provider in charge for each capability in Milestone 2, next to Shared connections. It could instead sit in Milestone 1's foundations, because the Git host and Depot connections already need it. Moving it into Milestone 1 would widen a milestone you want closed first.

Pipelines, values and expressions

One file, one graph of steps, typed values passed by name, and one checked expression language, so a pipeline says exactly what it will do before it flies.

  • A pipeline is one file with one graph. Every kind of work is a step with typed inputs and typed outputs.
  • Values pass by name, such as steps.version.outputs.tag, never by pasting text into a script.
  • Expressions are written in one existing language inside ${{ }}, and every one is type-checked before the Sortie (run) starts.
  • Before a Sortie each step shows as will run, will not run, or depends on a named value; afterwards a skipped step says why, with the values filled in.
  • Each typed kind of failure gets a declared response: retry with back-off (by default only when the machinery failed), wait for a person without holding a Station, allow, stop, abort, or run recovery steps.
  • A fan-out's results come back as typed lists, with an overall result and tests over its members; clean-up steps always run, read run.status, and still run when their Station (runner) is lost.
  • A step can wait on the server for a signed outside answer, holding no machine; unsaved text can fly as a draft that never launches.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer (authoring). It builds on the foundation (levels, variables and sealed secrets, layer 1) and on the record (layer 2): every value a step produces and every decision a condition makes is an event there. Layer 4, flight operations, runs what this layer plans.

What builds on it: Code you can test (where logic lives and how it is tested), Reuse that keeps growing (custom steps, Maneuvers, Flight plans and libraries), Inputs and run forms, What starts a Sortie (filtered in the same language), and every Launch (deployment) chapter, because a deploy step is a step like any other.

What you will be able to do

You are on the Harbor Lights team. You write when: ${{ run.branch == "main" || steps.check.outputs.is_release }} on the deploy step of storefront. You misspell is_relase. The editor underlines it as you type: "steps.check has no output is_relase; it has is_release (boolean) and channels (list)". Nothing has run.

You open a pull request from feat/cart. Before the Sortie starts, its page lists every step: eight will run, deploy depends on steps.check.outputs.is_release, and smoke depends on deploy. After it lands, deploy reads "Skipped: the condition was false. run.branch is feat/cart, steps.check.outputs.is_release is false."

Your release check prints the list of sales channels a version must be smoke-tested on. The smoke step fans out over that list while the Sortie flies, one step per channel, each with its own log and Debrief (test report).

A ticket system calls an event source when a release is approved. You replace its old filter with ${{ event.body.action == "released" }}, written in the same language as your conditions. Launchway shows that the old and new filters gave the same answer on the last 500 calls before you switch.

You try to put a fork's pull request title into the image of a step. The checker refuses it before take-off: the title is untrusted input, and an image name is a privileged field.

You bring a pipeline across from another system. The report lists 41 constructs: 33 converted exactly, 6 converted with a stated difference, 2 need a person. 33 + 6 + 2 = 41: nothing was dropped silently.

How it works

One file, one graph, every kind of work a step

A pipeline is one YAML file in Git, read at the commit the Sortie is for. Its keys are the ones Launchway already has and keeps: pipeline, on, inputs, libraries, containers, defaults, runner, workspace, lane and steps, and on a step needs, when, uses, with, for_each, kind and outputs. There is no second notion of job, stage or workflow: a flat set of steps joined by needs is the graph, and the graph is what the Sortie page draws.

A script, a custom step, a Clearance (approval), an image build, a Launch, a verification and a Return to base (rollback) are all steps. Each takes typed inputs and gives typed outputs, so any step can feed any other the same way. The types are the ones the step contract already uses: string, number, boolean, list, record and secret.

Built today

Steps, needs, conditions, retries, lanes, loops, caches, run inputs, templates from pinned libraries, and custom steps with typed inputs and outputs in a manifest. Values pass by writing key=value to $LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS and are read as LAUNCHWAY_NEEDS_<STEP>_<KEY>. The reference says plainly: "There is no expression language". Values are written in place or taken from a closed set of value forms: { output: step.key }, { run: sha }, { input: name }, { each: key } and, in templates, { param: name }. A top-level outputs key is refused today with a hint that it is not built.

The life of a pipeline file

Text becomes a checked plan before anything runs, and the same checker runs in the editor, in launchway validate on a laptop, and on the server.

  1. Read. Unknown keys, wrong shapes and missing names are errors with a line number, as today.
  2. Expand. Every uses is replaced by the Maneuver (step template) or Flight plan (pipeline template) it names, from the library commit recorded in the lockfile (see Reuse that keeps growing). Expanded steps are ordinary steps from here on.
  3. Type-check. Every ${{ }} is checked against the declared types of inputs, outputs, variables and event payloads. A misspelled name or a wrong type stops here.
  4. Sort by moment. Each value is marked as known before take-off or known only in flight, and the checker refuses a flight-time value in a field that must be known before take-off.
  5. Judge. Standing orders (policies and repository standards) see the expanded graph at run start, with no side door.
  6. Plan. Every step is labeled will run, will not run, or depends on a named value. The plan is an event on the record.
  7. Fly. As steps finish, their outputs are recorded and the remaining decisions are made from recorded values, each one an event with its reasons.

Values pass by name

A step refers to anything it uses by a name the checker knows: steps.version.outputs.tag, inputs.environment, run.short_sha. A step receives only what it names: that is the whole of dependency injection in Launchway. Values reach a step's code in exactly two ways: as environment variables bound in env, or as typed inputs of a custom step read through its kit. An expression never appears inside script text, so no value can turn into a command.

Any step can declare typed outputs, not only custom steps, and can capture one from a command's standard output, a file or a JSON document, so the common "run a command and keep what it printed" case is one line.

Today's mechanism keeps working: $LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS lines still become outputs, and LAUNCHWAY_NEEDS_<STEP>_<KEY> variables are still set for steps that need the writer. Named references are how new pipelines are taught.

Expressions: one existing language inside ${{ }}

Launchway adopts an existing, documented language rather than inventing one: the open-source expr language. It is small, has no side effects, always finishes, and can check an expression against declared types before running it. Launchway embeds the same checker in the server, the command line and the browser editor (as a WebAssembly build of the one implementation), so the three can never disagree.

RuleWhat it meansExample
Only inside ${{ }}Anything outside the wrapper is plain text.tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}"
Never inside script textA run block containing ${{ is an error. Bind the value in env and read the variable.env: { TAG: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" } then echo "$TAG"
A whole-value expression keeps its typeA field that is entirely ${{ … }}, quoted or not, takes the expression's type: a boolean stays a boolean, a list stays a list.for_each: { channel: "${{ steps.check.outputs.channels }}" } is a list
Mixed text only in text fieldsText around ${{ }} is allowed in a text field and refused in a true-or-false or number field, so ${{ run.branch }} == "main" can never be read as a non-empty string.description: "Deploy ${{ run.short_sha }}" is allowed; the same in when is refused
Checked before the Sortie startsNames, types and moments are checked in the editor, in launchway validate and when the Sortie is created.A typo is an error on its line, not a failure at step 7
Today's forms keep workingThe structured references and the closed when: tests stay valid and mean what they mean today. No existing pipeline changes.when: { branch: main } and version: { output: build.digest }

The structure of a pipeline is written, never computed: step names, needs, uses, libraries and trigger kinds take no expressions. A pipeline whose shape must be computed uses a step that generates steps, which is checked the same way (below).

The names inside an expression

NameWhat it holdsTypeKnown
runFacts about the Sortie: branch, tag, sha, short_sha, event, number, actor, commit_time, pull_requestA record. branch, tag and pull_request are optional: a pull-request Sortie has no branch, as todayBefore take-off
inputsThe run inputs the pipeline declaresEach as declared: a choice is a string, a list a listBefore take-off
varsVariables from the levels (Base, Wing, Squadron, Flight) and the Airfield (environment), with locksText as string, number as number, a connection as its name. A secret reference cannot be readBefore take-off
environmentThe Airfield the step lands on: name, protectedA record; only in a step that names an AirfieldBefore take-off
eventThe payload that started the SortieTyped by its trigger: a push or a pull request has a fixed shape; an event source with a schema is typed by it; anything else is an untrusted recordBefore take-off
steps.<name>.outputs.<key>An output of a step this step needs, directly or through othersAs the step declares itIn flight, after that step ends
steps.<name>.resultHow that step endedOne of succeeded, failed, failed (allowed), skipped, canceledIn flight, after that step ends
eachThe values of this member of a for_eachEach key as its list's item typeBefore take-off for a written list; in flight for a list a step produced
steps.<fan-out>.result New in this planThe overall result of a fan-out step, worked out from its members (see gathering)One of succeeded, failed, skipped, canceledIn flight, after every member ends
steps.<fan-out>.members New in this planEvery member in order, each with its each values, result, attempts and outputsA list of recordsIn flight, after every member ends
steps.<fan-out>.outputs.<key> New in this planOne output gathered from every member that wrote it, in member orderA list of the output's declared typeIn flight, after every member ends
run.status New in this planHow the Sortie stands so far, from the steps that have ended (see steps that always run)One of succeeded, failed, canceledIn flight, read when the step is ready
failure New in this planOnly inside retry and on_failure: the failure being answered: kind, exit_code, attemptA record; kind is one of the failure kinds belowIn flight, when the step fails

Secrets are not in this table on purpose: a secret is never readable in an expression. It is bound to a step by reference, and the Station resolves it, as today.

Two moments: before take-off and in flight

Some fields must be settled before a Sortie leaves the Holding pattern (queue): where it may run, which Airfields it may land on, how long it may take. Others can wait for an earlier step. The checker knows which is which and refuses a value used too early.

FieldMust be knownWhy
runnerBefore take-offThe Holding pattern places and explains waiting steps before they start
The Airfield of a LaunchBefore take-offA Sortie says before it leaves which Airfields it may land on, so locks, Clearances and Standing orders can be judged and shown
timeout, retry, laneBefore take-offLimits are checked against what a level allows
whenEitherA condition that names a flight-time value shows as "depends on" in the plan
env, with, a Launch's version, image tagsEitherResolved when the step is ready
imageEitherA plan-time image can be fetched early; a flight-time one (testing the image just built) is fetched when the step starts
for_each listsEitherA list a step produced fans out when that step ends
.launchway/pipeline.yaml:38: steps.deploy.environment: must be known before take-off,
  but steps.check.outputs.target is known only in flight (after step check ends).
  Use a run input (inputs.environment), or write one deploy step per Airfield with a when.

Secrets and untrusted input are kinds of value

Two kinds of value carry rules the checker enforces, the way a type does. In the expression language they are wrapper types with only the operations Launchway declares for them, because a plain renamed string type would not keep the mark through an operation.

Secret

  • Never readable in an expression: no comparison, no text joining, no condition.
  • Bound to a step by reference in secrets, or passed only to an input of type secret.
  • A secret output can flow only into a secret input, and is masked everywhere it is recorded.
  • Never a pipeline output, never in a run form, never in the Logbook (audit trail).

Untrusted

  • Anything an outside party controls: a fork's branch name and pull request title, a body with no schema, a header.
  • May be tested: ==, in, startsWith, matches. The answer is an ordinary boolean.
  • May reach a script only as an environment variable, never as text the script runs.
  • Refused in privileged fields: image, runner, the Airfield of a Launch, a Launch's version, image tags, a Depot (registry) path.
  • Becomes trusted only by passing a check: mapped into a run input with a pattern or options, it is validated like a person's entry and is then an ordinary typed value.
.launchway/pipeline.yaml:22: steps.preview.image: event.pull_request.title is untrusted
  (it comes from the pull request's author) and cannot choose an image.
  Map it into a run input with a pattern if it must, or choose the image from inputs or vars.

What expressions cannot do, and where that work goes

An expression decides and selects. It cannot loop without end, read a file, call a service, define a function, remember anything between steps or read the clock. The built-in list functions visit each item of a finite list once, so every expression finishes; expressions are also limited in size and in the memory they may use, and the clock function is switched off so the same values always give the same answer. Anything more is a step, whose typed outputs feed the next expression.

You want toWhere it goes
Retry until something is readyretry on the step, or a custom step that polls and reports
Read a file, call a service, compare Git historyA step that writes a typed output; changed paths keep the closed when: { changed } test
Walk nested data of unknown depthA custom step with a unit test
Reuse a calculationA custom step or a Maneuver, from a pinned library
Count or collect across stepsStep outputs are the state; a later step combines them
Use the timerun.commit_time, recorded at creation and kept for re-runs, or a step
Shape the graph from dataA for_each over a produced list, or a step that generates steps

The checked function list

Authors should not have to guess what an expression can call. Launchway publishes one list: every operator and function the checker accepts, with its types. Most come from the language itself; two are added by Launchway because pipelines need them. Anything not on the list is an error on its line, and the editor's completion offers only what is on it. Every function keeps the untrusted mark: lower(event.pull_request.title) is still untrusted.

Design: not built

The list is a proposal for the reference page. Which of the language's own functions are switched on is the decision recorded here; the clock functions are switched off, as above.

Operator or functionTakes and givesFromExample
startsWith, endsWith, contains, matchestext and text, gives a boolean; matches takes a regular expression with a size limitThe language (operators)run.tag startsWith "v2."
in, not ina value and a list, or a key and a record; gives a booleanThe languageinputs.environment in ["staging", "prod"]
lower, upper, trimtext, gives textThe languagelower(inputs.component)
split, jointext and a separator, gives a list; a list and a separator, gives textThe languagejoin(steps.check.outputs.channels, ",")
lentext, a list or a record; gives a numberThe languagelen(steps.check.outputs.channels) > 0
all, any, none, counta list and a test on each item; gives a boolean, or a number for countThe languageany(steps.smoke.members, .result == "failed")
filter, map, first, lasta list and a test or a value per item; gives a list or one itemThe languagemap(steps.smoke.members, .each.channel)
max, min, suma list of numbers, gives a number; an empty list fails the step with the expression shown, unless guarded with lenThe languagemax(steps.smoke.outputs.p95_ms)
toJSON, fromJSONany value, gives JSON text; JSON text, gives a record or a list (untrusted when the text was)The languagefromJSON(steps.plan.outputs.summary).changes
string, int, floatconvert, or fail the step with the value shownThe languageint(steps.check.outputs.build_number)
??, ?.a default for an optional value; a step into a value that may be absentThe languagerun.branch ?? "none"
globtext and a path pattern with * and **, gives a boolean; the same matcher as path filtersLaunchwayglob(run.branch ?? "", "release/**")
formata pattern with {} places and values, gives textLaunchwayformat("storefront-{}", inputs.component)

A name from another system that is not on the list is not an alias: the checker answers with the one Launchway name ("no function startswith; did you mean the operator startsWith?"). So the list stays one name per thing, and familiarity is a hint, not a second spelling.

Explained before and after

Because plan-time names have values before the Sortie starts, the checker can fold them in and show what remains. Every step gets one of three labels before take-off, and one plain sentence after landing.

Step of storefrontBefore take-off (pull request from feat/cart)After landing
test, web, version, check, imageWill runMission complete (succeeded)
deployDepends on steps.check.outputs.is_release: run.branch == "main" is false for this SortieSkipped: the condition was false. run.branch is absent (a pull-request Sortie), steps.check.outputs.is_release is false
smokeDepends on deploy and on the list steps.check.outputs.channelsSkipped: the step it needs, deploy, was skipped
notifyWill not run: when: { event: schedule } and this Sortie came from a pull requestSkipped: the event was pull_request

The "why" with its values is stored on the record when the decision is made, so the answer is the same tomorrow and in the Logbook. The same explanation is available from the command line and the agent endpoint.

Fan-out over a list an earlier step produced

Today for_each takes written lists, run inputs of type list and template parameters. The design adds a list from an earlier step. The producer must be in needs and must declare the output as a list. When the producer ends, its output is recorded in its finish event and a new event adds the members, so every server rebuilds the same steps from the record. Before take-off the plan shows the step as "fans out over steps.check.outputs.channels: members known in flight". The limits stay: 64 members by default, at most 500 by the server's setting, member values of 1 to 40 safe characters (other text goes through format), and a list that breaks a rule fails the fan-out node with the reason, never the server. What the members produce comes back to later steps as typed lists (next section). Fan-outs of thousands of members are a matter for Stations and where work runs and the record; this chapter keeps today's limits.

Gathering what a fan-out produced

A fan-out is not finished when its members are: later steps need their answers. Launchway gathers them on the server, from the members' finish events, into three typed names that any step needing the fan-out can read in conditions and in with, env and other values.

A typed list per output

steps.smoke.outputs.p95_ms is a list of numbers, because the custom step declares p95_ms as a number. Items are in member order (the order of the list the fan-out ran over), from every member that wrote the output. The type is known before take-off, so a wrong use is an error on its line.

Every member, aligned

steps.smoke.members is a list of records, one per member, in the same order: each (its values, such as channel), result, attempts and outputs. A member that was skipped or failed is still in it, so nothing is lost by gathering.

One overall result

steps.smoke.result is succeeded when every member succeeded or failed (allowed); failed when any member failed for good and was not allowed; skipped when every member was skipped, or the list was empty (the reason says which); canceled when the Sortie was canceled before every member ended.

Conditions over members use the language's own list tests, so there is nothing new to learn: all, any, none and count. A step whose condition reads a fan-out's members or result waits until every member has ended, however it ended, so a report step can run after failures without a special key.

Design: not built

The three names, the overall result rule and continue_for inside a fan-out over a produced list are sketches. Today a step that needs a loop needs every member, continue_for tolerates chosen members, and Cargo can be fetched from every member; outputs are not gathered.

  smoke:
    needs: deploy
    for_each: { channel: "${{ steps.check.outputs.channels }}" }
    continue_for: [{ channel: kiosk }]          # the kiosk channel may fail without failing the Sortie
    uses: platform/smoke                         # outputs: p95_ms (number), errors (number)
    with: { channel: "${{ each.channel }}" }
  smoke-report:
    needs: smoke
    when: ${{ any(steps.smoke.members, .result != "succeeded") || max(steps.smoke.outputs.p95_ms) > 300 }}
    uses: platform/post-summary
    with:
      failed_channels: "${{ map(filter(steps.smoke.members, .result == 'failed'), .each.channel) }}"
      slowest_ms: "${{ max(steps.smoke.outputs.p95_ms) }}"
  promote:
    kind: deploy
    needs: smoke
    when: ${{ count(steps.smoke.members, .result == "failed") == 0 }}   # stricter than the overall result
    environment: prod
    version: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}

For Sortie 417 of storefront (release 2.4.0, digest sha256:4f9c…a17), the kiosk member failed and was allowed. The overall result is succeeded, so a step that only needs smoke runs; smoke-report runs because one member did not succeed; promote is skipped, and its sentence says: "Skipped: the condition was false. count of members with result failed is 1 (smoke, channel kiosk)."

Decision needed: short names for result tests

The list tests above need no new names. A proposal for three shorthands, built from Launchway's own result words rather than borrowed ones: all_succeeded(x), any_failed(x) and ended(x), where x is a step, a list of steps, or a fan-out's members. Each is defined as one of the list tests, so it is checked and explained the same way. The question stays open for you (see the end of this chapter): take the shorthands, or teach only steps.<name>.result with the list tests.

Steps that generate more steps

For shapes that a list cannot describe, a step can print more steps. Launchway reads them with the same parser, expands any uses from libraries already locked for this Sortie (a generated step cannot fetch a new library mid-flight), type-checks their expressions, applies the inline code limits, judges them with the same Standing orders, and only then adds them to the graph, drawn under the step that made them. A generated step cannot reach an Airfield the Flight (codebase) may not use. The generator is itself a step: it runs in the sandbox, its printed steps are recorded, and a re-run reuses them unless the generator itself runs again.

Pipeline outputs for a later pipeline

A pipeline can declare outputs at the top, built from its steps' outputs. A later pipeline started by this one's result (see What starts a Sortie) reads them as typed values under event. The storefront release pipeline publishes image (the digest) and version; the payments integration-test pipeline starts on that result and tests against exactly that digest.

Files handed between steps

Values travel by name; files travel as Cargo (artifacts). Today a step keeps named sets of files with artifacts, a later step that needs it puts them in its workspace with fetch, every file is checked by SHA-256 end to end, and the Cargo tab lists each file with its digest. The design makes Cargo a typed value like any other, so a file is handed over by name and its identity is on the record.

  • By name, checked before take-off. steps.build.cargo.binary names a Cargo of a step this one needs. A misspelled name, or a Cargo kept only on success fetched by a step that runs after a failure, is an error on its line, as today's launchway validate already says for loops.
  • Its digest is a value. steps.build.cargo.binary.digest is the digest of the whole set, readable in expressions and in with, so a later step, a Launch or a pipeline output can say exactly which files it means.
  • Verified on fetch, recorded on the fetching step. The Station checks every file against the digest the producer recorded before the step starts; a mismatch fails the step with the kind infrastructure and names the file. The fetching step's record lists the Cargo and digests it received, so "which binary did the smoke test run?" has one answer.
  • Kept while a release needs it. Cargo that a release, an Airfield's current version or an evidence pack points to is never removed by retention, whatever retain says; retention removes it only once nothing points to it. How the Depot and its retention honor that is in The Depot.
Design: not built

artifacts, fetch, SHA-256 checks and per-file digests exist today. The cargo name inside ${{ }}, the set digest as a value, the fetch record on the receiving step and the release hold on retention are sketches.

  build:
    image: golang:1.27
    run: make dist
    artifacts: [{ name: binary, paths: [bin/storefront] }]
  package:
    needs: build
    fetch: [{ from: build, name: binary, into: out }]       # verified against the recorded digest first
    uses: platform/package-tarball
    with: { expect: "${{ steps.build.cargo.binary.digest }}" }
outputs:
  binary: ${{ steps.build.cargo.binary.digest }}

Local runs and re-runs

launchway validate and launchway run use the same checker and evaluator as the server, because they are the same library in the same binary. A design flag, launchway run --explain, prints the before-take-off labels for a local run; the Simulator goes further and tests a pipeline with stand-in results. Re-running from a failed step keeps the inputs and reuses the recorded outputs of the steps it does not run again; conditions of the steps it runs are decided again from recorded values, so the same values give the same decisions.

What happens when a step fails

A failure is not one thing. A test that found a bug, a machine that vanished and an image that could not be pulled need different answers, and retrying a real test failure only hides it. So every failure is given a typed kind when it happens, recorded on the step, and the pipeline declares a response per kind. Today's pieces stay and become the base: retry with times, wait, backoff and the causes exit, timeout and infrastructure; on_failure: stop or continue; and the rule that a lost Station's step is run again a bounded number of times.

Failure kindWhat happenedWho decides the kindRetried when on is not written
exitThe step's own code ended non-zero: a test failed, a build brokeThe Station, from the exitNo
timeoutThe attempt ran past its timeoutThe Station, confirmed by the serverNo
infrastructureThe machinery failed: an image could not be pulled, the workspace or fetched Cargo could not be prepared or verified, a secret store did not answerThe Station states it, as todayYes
station_lostThe Station stopped answering or its pod disappeared mid-stepThe server, when the step's lease runs outYes, at most the server's max_lost times, as today
contractThe step broke the step contract: a declared output missing or of the wrong type, a results file that does not readThe server, when the step endsNo
refusedA Standing order refused it, a Clearance said No-go, a coverage floor was missedThe serverNever, and no response can change it: a refusal is not a fault to work around

The responses are the same everywhere, chosen per kind under on_failure (today's single word still works and means the same for every kind):

ResponseWhat it doesHolds a Station?
retryAnother attempt after the retry pause, counted against times. Back-off is fixed (backoff: 1) or grows by a factor, with a cap: max_wait (new; today the cap is a fixed hour)No: the step waits in the Holding pattern (queue) until the pause is over, as today
holdThe step waits for a person. Its state is "Waiting for a person"; its logs, Cargo and the failure are kept; the Station is released at once. A person chooses Retry, Allow, Stop or Run recovery from the decision card. for limits the wait and then says what happens if nobody answersNo: the wait is settled on the server, like a Clearance
allowToday's continue: the step ends failed (allowed), the Sortie goes on, and the Sortie's summary counts itNo
stopToday's default: the Sortie fails, no new step starts except steps that always run, and running steps finishNo
abortThe Sortie fails now: running steps are canceled, then steps that always run still runNo
recoverRuns the named recovery steps, which are ordinary steps in the list, then does what then says: retry (a new attempt of the failed step), allow or stopOnly while the recovery steps run, like any step

Retries default to the machinery. Under the next schema version, a retry that does not write on retries infrastructure and station_lost only, so a real test failure is never retried blindly. A file on today's schema keeps today's meaning (every cause), and launchway validate offers to write on: [exit, timeout, infrastructure] into it, so nothing changes until a person accepts the change. An exit that passes on a retry is recorded as a flaky result, which Fast pipelines and continuous deployment counts. A finer rule may read the failure: retry.if: ${{ failure.exit_code == 75 }}.

Launch steps keep their own safety. A deploy, rollout or verify step that fails returns to base first, as today, and nothing declared can delay or replace that: Return to base (rollback) never waits. A response on a Launch step may only add what happens after it, such as hold for a person to look, or recovery steps.

Design: not built

The on_failure mapping, the kinds station_lost, contract and refused as names a pipeline can write, hold, abort, recover, max_wait, retry.if and the new default are sketches; key names are not final (the name on_failure is among the pipeline words waiting for your confirmation).

  migrate:
    needs: migrate-plan
    image: golang:1.27
    run: ./bin/migrate --to "$TO"
    retry: { times: 2, wait: 15s, backoff: 2, max_wait: 2m }   # no "on": machinery failures only
    on_failure:
      exit: { hold: { for: 2h, notify: shop, then: stop } }   # a person looks before anything else happens
      timeout: { recover: [restore-snapshot], then: retry }
      contract: stop
  restore-snapshot:
    needs: migrate                                           # an ordinary step; it runs only through a response
    uses: platform/restore-db-snapshot
    with: { database: storefront }

Dana's change in pull request #482 adds a column for the delivery date. In Sortie 417, migrate ends with exit code 1: the kind is exit, so it is not retried. The step shows "Waiting for a person: exit code 1, the migration found 3 rows with no delivery date." The Station that ran it is free again. Priya, on call, reads the log on her phone, fixes the three rows by hand, and chooses Retry; attempt 2 succeeds. The Logbook (audit trail) shows the failure, its kind, who chose Retry and when.

Steps that always run, and clean-up that survives a lost Station

Today a step with when: { upstream: always } runs once the steps it needs have ended, whatever happened, and when: { upstream: failed } runs only after a failure. Both stay. The design adds three things.

  • A status to read. run.status says how the Sortie stands so far, from the steps that have ended: succeeded, failed or canceled. A clean-up or notification step reads it in a condition or as the environment variable LAUNCHWAY_RUN_STATUS (proposed), and can read each needed step's result as well.
  • A step that ends the Sortie. needs: "*" (a sketch) means every other step that is not itself an ending step, so a final report or a tear-down does not have to list twenty names and cannot miss the one added next month.
  • A guarantee. A step that always runs is marked as clean-up on the record, and Launchway owes it a run.
  1. Station lost. When a clean-up step's Station stops answering, the step is offered again to another Station of the same Ramp (runner pool), whatever retry says and on top of max_lost, until it ends or a person stops it. The step starts from the Sortie's workspace, which travels with the Sortie, not from the lost machine's disk.
  2. Nobody to take it. If no Station takes it within the Ramp's wait limit, the Sortie does not say Mission complete or Failed: it says "clean-up pending", and Comms (notifications) tells the Flight's on-call person. A Sortie with clean-up pending holds its lane, so the next Sortie does not start on top of half-torn-down resources.
  3. Canceled. Cancel stops the running steps, then runs the clean-up steps. Skipping clean-up is a second, separate choice, needs the right to operate the Flight, and is a Logbook entry with the reason.
  4. Server lost. Another server rebuilds the Sortie from the record and carries on, as for every step.
  tear-down-preview:
    needs: "*"                                  # sketch: after every other step
    when: { upstream: always }                  # today's form, unchanged
    uses: platform/delete-preview
    with: { airfield: "pr-${{ run.pull_request.number }}" }
  tell-the-team:
    needs: "*"
    when: ${{ run.status != "succeeded" }}
    uses: platform/post-summary
    with: { status: "${{ run.status }}" }

In the storefront Sortie for pull request #482, the preview Airfield pr-482 must go when the pull request closes. The Station running tear-down-preview is restarted halfway. The step is offered again to another Station of the "shop" Ramp, which finishes it; the Sortie page shows "Clean-up re-run after its Station was lost", and the record holds both attempts.

Design: not built

when: { upstream: always } and failed exist today. run.status, LAUNCHWAY_RUN_STATUS, needs: "*", the clean-up mark, re-offering beyond max_lost, "clean-up pending" and the two-step cancel are sketches.

A step that waits for an outside answer

Some steps are not work at all: they wait for another system to say something. A change board approves a ticket, a partner's test lab finishes a run, a manual hardware check is signed off. Holding a machine for that is waste, and polling from a script holds it longer. A step of kind: wait runs nothing. It is settled on the server, like a Clearance (approval), and ends when a signed call that matches it arrives, or when its timeout runs out.

  • Through an event source. The answer arrives at an event source the Flight already has (see What starts a Sortie), so it is signed, checked within five minutes, accepted once, and stored before anything else happens. A wait step cannot open a new door into Launchway.
  • Matched by an expression. match is one condition in the one language, over event and the outputs of steps this one needs. A call that matches no waiting step is kept on the source's page as "matched nothing", never dropped silently; a call that arrives before the wait step starts is held for it until the Sortie ends.
  • Typed outputs. outputs map the payload to typed values. A body without a schema is untrusted, so its values are untrusted outputs and cannot choose an image, a Station or an Airfield.
  • A timeout and the usual responses. Without a matching call by timeout, the step fails with the kind timeout and follows its on_failure, so a missing answer can wait for a person or stop the Sortie.
Design: not built

kind: wait and its keys are a sketch; names are not final. Event sources with signed calls exist today.

  ticket:
    needs: image
    uses: platform/open-change-ticket          # writes the output ticket
    with: { version: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}", work_item: STORE-41 }
  board:
    kind: wait
    needs: ticket
    source: change-board                        # an event source of the Flight
    match: ${{ event.body.ticket == steps.ticket.outputs.ticket }}
    timeout: 3d
    outputs:
      decision: { type: string, from: "${{ event.body.decision }}", options: [approved, rejected] }
      reviewer: { type: string, from: "${{ event.body.reviewer }}" }
    on_failure: { timeout: { hold: { for: 1d, notify: shop, then: stop } } }
  deploy-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: board
    when: ${{ steps.board.outputs.decision == "approved" }}
    environment: prod
    version: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}

Whether a step that waits for an outside answer is also a Clearance in the sense of Standing orders is decided by the Standing orders chapter; here it is only a step whose answer comes from outside. A wait step is different from a step that starts another pipeline and waits for its result (pipeline to pipeline): that one waits on Launchway, this one on the world.

Draft Sorties from unsaved text

Trying a change to a pipeline should not need a commit. Today the editor already has Run this draft: it runs the edited text against the branch's current commit, marks the Sortie Draft everywhere, keeps the text and its SHA-256, makes draft its own event so a step guarded by when does not run, and refuses secrets unless the Flight allows them. The design makes the promise stronger and the difference visible.

  • Never launches. A draft's plan refuses every deploy, rollout, Return to base and Launch-guarding Clearance before take-off, whatever its when says, and image steps build without pushing to the Depot. This is a rule of the planner, not of the conditions the author wrote.
  • No secrets by default, set by level. Whether drafts may read secrets, and who may start one, become level settings with locks (today they are server settings per Flight). A Standing order can forbid secrets in drafts for a whole Wing.
  • The difference is recorded. The Sortie records the commit it started from and the line difference between that commit's pipeline file and the draft text. The Sortie page has a Changes tab showing it, and the Logbook entry carries it.
  • Shown before it flies. Starting a draft shows its plan first (will run, will not run, refused because it is a draft), with the same explanation as any Sortie. The Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it) can run the same text with no Station at all.
  • Kept apart. A draft never supersedes another Sortie, never counts as a required check, and never feeds a result trigger. Its Cargo is kept for the draft's short retention only.
Built today

Run this draft, the draft event, no secrets by default, who may start one, the kept text and its SHA-256, and the draft API (POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/draft-runs). Not built: the planner-level refusal of Launch steps, the recorded line difference and its tab, the plan shown before starting, and the settings by level.

The visual designer edits the same file

The roadmap already promises a visual pipeline designer that edits the same file as the text editor. The design says how that stays true:

  1. One parser, both ways. The designer reads the file with the same parser as the text editor and writes back only the lines that change. Comments, key order, blank lines and quoting are kept. A round-trip test reads and writes every pipeline in Launchway's own examples and the Hangar (the built-in library) and fails the build if one byte changes that the person did not change.
  2. Checked on every change. Each drag, connection or form edit runs the WebAssembly build of the checker in the browser, so the drawing shows the same problems, on the same lines, as launchway validate.
  3. Picked, not typed. Connecting two steps adds needs; a value is chosen from the reference picker's typed tree; a failure response is chosen per kind from the list above; a fan-out list is picked from the outputs of steps already needed.
  4. Saved as a commit. Before saving, the designer shows the line difference it will commit, and saving is a commit as you, or a new branch for a pull request, as text editing is today.

Worked example: storefront

Design: not built

The ${{ }} wrapper and its rules are decided; the step-level outputs key with from, the top-level outputs, and a for_each list from a step are sketches. Key names under them are not final.

pipeline: storefront
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"] }
  pull_request: { into: [main] }
inputs:
  environment: { type: choice, options: [dev, staging, prod], default: dev }
libraries:
  platform: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.2.0 }
steps:
  test:
    uses: platform/go-test                    # a Maneuver from the shared library
  web:
    image: node:22
    run: npm ci && npm test
  version:
    image: golang:1.27
    run: git describe --tags --always
    outputs:
      tag: { type: string, from: stdout }     # capture what the command printed
  check:
    uses: ./steps/check-release               # a custom step: is_release (boolean), channels (list)
    needs: version                            # a referenced step must be needed, directly or through others
    with: { tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }
  image:
    kind: image
    needs: [test, web, check]
    tags: [{ registry: depot, repository: harbor-lights/storefront, tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }]
  deploy:
    kind: deploy
    needs: image
    when: ${{ run.branch == "main" || steps.check.outputs.is_release }}
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}    # known before take-off
    version: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}
  smoke:
    needs: deploy
    for_each: { channel: "${{ steps.check.outputs.channels }}" }
    uses: platform/smoke                      # a custom step from the library
    with: { channel: "${{ each.channel }}" }
outputs:
  image: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}
  version: ${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}
Built today

This version runs on Launchway as it is, using the structured forms. It cannot fan out over the channel list, cannot combine the branch test with an output in one condition, and cannot publish pipeline outputs.

pipeline: storefront
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"] }
  pull_request: {}
inputs:
  environment: { type: choice, options: [dev, staging, prod], default: dev }
libraries:
  platform: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.2.0 }
steps:
  test: { uses: platform/go-test }
  web: { image: node:22, run: npm ci && npm test }
  version:
    image: golang:1.27
    run: echo "tag=$(git describe --tags --always)" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS"
  check:
    image: golang:1.27
    needs: version
    run: ./scripts/check-release.sh           # reads $LAUNCHWAY_NEEDS_VERSION_TAG, writes is_release=...
  image:
    kind: image
    needs: [test, web, check]
    tags: [{ registry: depot, repository: harbor-lights/storefront, tag: { output: version.tag } }]
  deploy:
    kind: deploy
    needs: image
    when: { output: check.is_release, equals: true }
    environment: { input: environment }
    version: { output: image.digest }

Note check: today a custom step's with takes written values, run inputs and loop values, not another step's output, so the release check has to be a script that reads $LAUNCHWAY_NEEDS_VERSION_TAG instead of the tested custom step. Typed references close that gap.

One language for every filter: replacing the event-filter language

Launchway has a second, hand-written expression language today. Event sources use it for filters, input mappings and deduplication keys, and result triggers use it for filters. It reads paths such as body.release.version, compares, tests with in, contains, startsWith, endsWith and glob, and has a few functions such as default(x, y). It is safe and limited, but it is a second syntax with looser rules: a missing path is null, and values that are not numbers compare as text.

The design replaces it with the same expression language (and triggers declared in the pipeline file get a when in it too), so a pipeline condition, a trigger filter, a run form's show-if rule and, later, extra policy rules are all written one way. The names change to the pipeline's: body becomes event.body, headers becomes event.headers, and a result trigger's run, launch and outputs become event.run, event.launch and event.outputs.

  1. Collect. Every saved filter, mapping and deduplication key on the Base is gathered with the events it judged, as a corpus with known answers.
  2. Translate. Most forms are the same in both languages. The differences are mechanical: a glob "v1.*" becomes the Launchway function glob(a, "v1.*"); default(x, y) becomes x ?? y; a path into a body without a schema uses optional steps (event.body?.release?.version) so a missing field still does not match; a comparison that relied on text conversion gets an explicit string.
  3. Shadow. For a release, both evaluators judge every event. A difference is noted on the event's decision; behavior does not change.
  4. Switch, one source at a time. A person accepts the translation on the source's page or with one command. The change is a Logbook entry with the old and new text.
  5. Retire. In the next major release the old syntax is refused with the translation offered. Nothing switches silently. Until a source is switched, its old filter keeps deciding exactly as it does today.

Bringing pipelines in from other systems

The importer reads another system's pipeline files and proposes a Launchway pipeline. It does not run them, fetch what they include or evaluate their expressions. Each construct lands in exactly one of three classes: converts exactly, converts with a stated difference, or needs a person, and a test checks that the three counts add up to the number of constructs read, so nothing is dropped silently. A step that could not be converted becomes a line that prints NEEDS A PERSON and fails, so a half-converted pipeline can never pass by accident.

With the expression language, two things improve. Conditions from other formats are translated into ${{ }} where the meaning is exact, and reported as "converts with a difference" where the old language converted types loosely. And where an old file pasted a value into script text, the proposal moves it into an env binding and says so: the converted pipeline is safer than the original.

Status to reconcile

The product's own guide describes an importer for five file formats with this three-way report and a side-by-side mode, while the roadmap item "A converter and a move-over guide" is still Planned. The editor should confirm whether the item has met the bar for Available (merged, tested, documented) before this chapter's table changes.
