The foundation it relies on

Git
The pipeline is read at the Sortie's own commit; editing in the browser is a commit. Nothing about a pipeline is kept only in the database.
Levels
vars come from Base, Wing, Squadron and Flight with locks; the hierarchy view shows where each value comes from.
The record
Plans, decisions, outputs and fan-out members are events. Re-runs and explanations read them back; nothing is recomputed from a changed world.
Stations
Stations receive resolved values and resolve secrets themselves. They never evaluate expressions and never see another step's secrets.
The checker
One library, used by the server, launchway validate, launchway run, the editor and the agent endpoint. Every interface reports the same problem with the same words.

Safety

  • On failure. An expression that cannot be checked stops the Sortie before it starts, with the file and line. A flight-time evaluation that fails (a list with a bad member, an optional value used without ??) fails that step with the expression and the values, and the Sortie follows its normal failure rules. A server lost mid-Sortie is replaced by another that rebuilds the same state from the record.
  • Who may do what. A Pilot (developer) writes pipelines in Git like any code, under the branch rules of the repository. Commanders (owners) and levels above set Standing orders and locks that a pipeline cannot loosen. Starting a Sortie needs the right to operate the Flight; a library override is recorded.
  • On by default. The type and moment checks, secret and untrusted rules, the ban on expressions in script text, size and memory limits on expressions, and a disabled clock. None can be switched off by a pipeline.
  • What it will not do. It will not run a general program on the server. It will not paste a value into a script. It will not guess a missing value: an optional one must be given a default with ??.

Screens

Full descriptions for the mock-up builders are in the screens notes; each is listed on the screens chapter.

  • Pipeline editor with live checking and plan preview. Text on the left; on the right the graph with each step labeled will run, will not run or depends; problems on their lines; an event picker (push to a branch, pull request, tag, schedule, a recorded event) chooses what the preview assumes.
  • Reference picker. Inserting a value opens a typed tree (run, inputs, vars, steps of the steps this one needs, each) with each name's type and moment; only names valid at that field can be picked.
  • Why was this skipped. On a step of a Sortie: the condition as written, each name with its recorded value, and the result, with a link to the decision event.
  • Where did this value come from. On any input or variable a step received: the chain from the producing step or level to this step.
  • Event filter translation. On an event source: the old filter, the new expression, and the shadow results over recent events, with Accept.
  • Import an existing pipeline. Today's wizard, with the three-way counts and their sum shown at the top.
  • Re-run plan. Which steps run again, which are reused, and which decisions will be made again from recorded values.
  • Failure responses on a step. In the editor and the designer: one row per failure kind, each with a response picked from a list (retry, hold, allow, stop, abort, recover), the retry numbers picked from bounded lists, and recovery steps picked from the steps in the file.
  • Waiting for a person. On a failed step that holds: the failure kind, the last log lines, Cargo kept, the time left, and four buttons (Retry, Allow, Stop, Run recovery); the same card on a phone.
  • Fan-out members. On a fan-out step: the overall result with its reason, a table of members with their values, result, attempts and outputs, and the gathered lists as later steps will see them.
  • Clean-up pending. On a Sortie: which clean-up step is owed, which Station was lost, each re-offer, and who was told.
  • Waiting for an outside answer. On a wait step: the event source, the match condition with its values, the time left, and calls that arrived and matched nothing.
  • Draft Sortie. The Draft mark, the plan with steps refused because it is a draft, and the Changes tab with the line difference from the starting commit.
  • Visual designer. The graph and the text side by side, the same problems on both, and the line difference shown before Save.

Open question

  • Open question Familiar function names. Whether to add a few host functions under names people know from hosted CI services (for example, tests of how earlier steps ended), or to teach only steps.<name>.result. Recorded as still open in the agreed model. This chapter now proposes a middle way (see gathering and the function list): no borrowed names and no aliases; the language's own all, any, none and count over results; three optional shorthands from Launchway's own result words (all_succeeded, any_failed, ended); and a "did you mean" answer when a familiar name is typed. Take it, or take a part of it.
  • Open question Retries by default. Under the next schema, a retry without on retries only machinery failures. Today it retries every cause. Files on today's schema keep today's meaning; confirm that new files should get the narrower default.
  • Open question The new pipeline words. hold, recover, abort, max_wait, kind: wait, match, needs: "*" and the on_failure mapping join the list of pipeline words waiting for your confirmation. They reuse today's keys where one exists.
  • Open question "No loops" in Milestone 2's done text. This chapter reads it as "no loop that can run without end": the built-in list functions visit a finite list once and always finish. Confirm, or ask for them to be switched off.
  • Open question Fields that hold only an expression. In an event source's filter field, which can hold nothing but an expression, is the wrapper required, or implied? This chapter requires it everywhere so there is one way.
  • Open question The policy language beyond the typed catalog (on the spine's open list). If extra policy rules are written in this same language, "Policy rules in an open language" (Milestone 3) changes meaning.
  • Open question How a secret output travels. A secret output is masked and kept only as *** today, so a secret cannot pass from one step to another through the server. Sealing it for the receiving Station is a design for Security and the supply chain; until then a secret output can only be bound inside the step that made it.
  • Open question Sandbox for generators. An older ruling says the generate step has no script sandbox; a later one requires sandboxed custom steps. This chapter runs the generator in the sandbox.

Code you can test

Every piece of logic a pipeline runs is ordinary code with unit tests, and the pipeline itself can be tested without flying it.

  • Logic is tested code; YAML holds only glue: up to 10 lines inline in a pipeline, up to 3 in anything shared.
  • A custom step is a real program in Go, Python, TypeScript or shell, with a manifest, declared permissions and a passing test from the first command.
  • The Simulator (proposed new word: testing a pipeline without flying it) runs a pipeline against stand-in results and checks which steps run, in what order, with which values.
  • Test results and coverage for pipeline code appear in the Debrief (test report), and a Standing order can refuse shared code that has no passing tests.
  • Teams that prefer it can write a pipeline in TypeScript, Python or Go with builder libraries generated from the published pipeline schema; what flies is still the one checked pipeline file.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer (authoring), and reaches into layer 4 for test results and layer 6 for the Standing order (policy and repository standard) that enforces it. It builds on Pipelines, values and expressions, which defines steps, typed values and the checker, and on the record, which keeps every past Sortie (run) for replay. Reuse that keeps growing builds on it: nothing is shared through a library unless it is tested the way this chapter says.

Your rule

In your words: "any code in the pipelines, or used in the pipelines must be unit tested… Everything should be able to be mocked and unit tested just like any other normal production application."

And in the requirements ledger: "Code is code, not inline text. Custom steps and pipeline logic are real programs in the repository: runnable on their own and unit-testable like any application. … A template is an interface; code is what runs."

What you will be able to do

You are on the Harbor Lights team. You write a 14-line shell block in storefront that decides whether database migrations must run. The editor marks it: "14 lines of inline code; the limit here is 10. Inline code should be glue." You choose Move into a custom step. Launchway writes steps/migration-plan with a manifest, your code, the kit and a test that passes, and replaces the block with a three-line uses.

You run launchway step new --lang go --name check-release, write the function, and test it with go test on your laptop, giving it stand-in inputs and reading back its outputs, with no server and no network.

You change the deploy condition of storefront. Before you push, the Simulator replays your change against the last 100 Sorties of main and says: "The changed pipeline would have deployed 3 more times: Sorties 812, 815 and 830." You look at those three before you merge.

You keep a test file beside the pipeline: "a pull request from a fork never deploys and never asks for a secret". It runs on every change to the pipeline, like any unit test, and its result is in the Debrief.

You are a Commander (owner) of the Harbor Lights Wing. You set a Standing order: no library step may be used unless its tests passed at the pinned commit. A Sortie that would use an untested step from platform-library is refused before take-off, with the step and the commit named.

How it works

Logic is tested code; YAML holds only glue

Glue calls a tool, moves a file, sets a value or binds one name to another. Logic decides: it branches, loops, parses, compares versions, chooses what happens next. Glue can stay in the pipeline. Logic lives in a custom step or a script with unit tests, where it can be read, tested and reused.

Lines are the line between them. The count is a stand-in for "no real logic", it is easy to see, and it cannot be argued with in review. The numbers are a starting point and easy to change.

Where the code isLimitBeyond the limitCan be tightened by
A run block in a pipeline file10 linesA lint warning, with an offer to move the code into a custom step with a test. The Sortie still runs.A Standing order at any level, down to 0
A run block in anything shared: a Maneuver (step template), a Flight plan (pipeline template), any library3 linesAn error when the library is validated. Shared pieces hold no logic; they call tested custom steps.A Standing order at any level, down to 0
A custom step or a script file in the repository or a libraryNoneIt is code: unit tests are expected, and a Standing order can require themThe Standing order for untested shared code
  • Lines are counted without blank lines and comments.
  • A Standing order can only tighten a limit. One that tries to loosen it is refused when it is saved, with the limit it would exceed.
  • Inline glue may be written in shell or in any interpreter the step's image has, such as Python, so a team can use the language it knows without a test for three lines of glue. How the interpreter is named is not decided; shell: python below is a sketch.
  • Inline glue is still exercised: by launchway run on a laptop, and by the Simulator's tests of the pipeline it sits in.

Worked example: glue and logic in storefront

This step decides whether the database needs migrating. It parses file names, compares versions and branches. It is logic, and nothing tests it.

  migrate-plan:
    image: golang:1.27
    run: |
      current=$(cat db/CURRENT_VERSION)
      latest=0
      for f in db/migrations/*.sql; do
        n=$(basename "$f" | cut -d_ -f1)
        if [ "$n" -gt "$latest" ]; then latest=$n; fi
      done
      if [ "$latest" -gt "$current" ]; then
        echo "needed=true" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS"
        echo "from=$current" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS"
        echo "to=$latest" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS"
      else
        echo "needed=false" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS"
      fi
      grep -l "DROP TABLE" db/migrations/*.sql && echo "destructive=true" >> "$LAUNCHWAY_OUTPUTS" || true
.launchway/pipeline.yaml:41: steps.migrate-plan.run: 14 lines of inline code (the limit here is 10).
  Inline code should be glue: calling tools, moving files, setting a value.
  Move it into a custom step with a test:  launchway step extract migrate-plan
Design: not built

The ${{ }} wrapper and the limits are decided; shell:, step-level outputs and launchway step extract are sketches with names not final.

  migrate-plan:
    uses: ./steps/migration-plan              # logic: a Go custom step with unit tests
    with: { migrations: db/migrations, current_file: db/CURRENT_VERSION }
  migrate:
    kind: step
    needs: migrate-plan
    when: ${{ steps.migrate-plan.outputs.needed && !steps.migrate-plan.outputs.destructive }}
    image: golang:1.27
    env: { FROM: "${{ steps.migrate-plan.outputs.from }}", TO: "${{ steps.migrate-plan.outputs.to }}" }
    run: ./bin/migrate --from "$FROM" --to "$TO"       # glue: one line calling a tool
  stamp:
    image: python:3.13
    shell: python                             # glue in another interpreter, under 10 lines
    env: { TAG: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }
    run: |
      import json, os
      json.dump({"tag": os.environ["TAG"]}, open("build-info.json", "w"))

The pipeline now only connects things. The one decision left in YAML, the when, is an expression with typed inputs, and the Simulator tests it (below).

steps/migration-plan/step.yaml is today's manifest format:

step: migration-plan
contract: 1
description: Decide whether the database must be migrated, and whether the change is destructive
toolchain: go@1.27
command: go run .
inputs:
  migrations:   { type: string, description: The directory of numbered migration files }
  current_file: { type: string, description: The file holding the version now deployed }
outputs:
  needed:      { type: boolean }
  from:        { type: number }
  to:          { type: number }
  destructive: { type: boolean }
permissions:
  network: []          # none: it only reads the workspace
  write: []

Its test uses a stand-in for the step context, so the function runs with chosen inputs and its outputs are read back, with no Station:

Design: not built

The test helper package and its function names are a sketch. Today the scaffold writes a test that calls the step's own function directly.

func TestDestructiveMigrationIsFlagged(t *testing.T) {
    dir := t.TempDir
    write(t, dir, "CURRENT_VERSION", "41")
    write(t, dir, "migrations/042_drop_legacy_carts.sql", "DROP TABLE legacy_carts;")

    s := lwsteptest.New(t, lwsteptest.Inputs{
        "migrations": dir + "/migrations", "current_file": dir + "/CURRENT_VERSION",
    })
    run(s)                                    // the step's own function

    s.WantOutput("needed", true)
    s.WantOutput("from", 41)
    s.WantOutput("to", 42)
    s.WantOutput("destructive", true)
}

Where each kind of logic lives, and how it is tested

KindLives inTested byWith stand-ins for
GlueA run block in the pipelineA local run; the Simulator's pipeline testsOther steps' results
LogicA custom step, or a script file in a libraryIts language's own test tools; launchway step test in the sandboxThe step context: inputs, secrets, outputs; anything the code calls, by the team's usual injection
InterfaceA Maneuver or a Flight planSimulator tests in the library; a real run against a sample repositoryThe custom steps it calls
Decisionswhen and other expressionsCondition tests; condition coverageThe names the expression reads
ShapeA step that generates stepsAs a custom step; the generated set through the SimulatorThe generator's printed steps

Custom steps: programs with a manifest

A custom step is a directory in Git: a manifest (step.yaml), the code, a small kit for its language and its tests. The manifest declares typed inputs and outputs (string, number, boolean, list, record, secret) and what the step may do: network hosts, writable paths and the secrets it names. Nothing else is allowed in the sandbox.

  1. Scaffold. launchway step new --lang go|python|ts|sh --name NAME writes the manifest, the code, the kit, a test that passes and a README.
  2. Test with the language's own tools. go test, the Python test runner, the Node test runner or a shell test script. The code under test is the same function the step runs.
  3. Test as a Station would. launchway step test steps/NAME --with key=value runs it in its image with no network, a read-only workspace and only the secrets it names, then checks it kept to the step contract: declared outputs of declared types, results on the right channel, sensible exit codes.
  4. Use it. uses: ./steps/NAME in the same repository, or uses: platform/NAME from a library pinned by tag or commit. A wrong with is an error on its line before anything runs.
  5. Change it safely. launchway step validate --against v1 lists what changed in inputs, outputs and permissions since a tag, and marks anything that widens what the step may do.
Built today

All five commands and behaviors above exist on the main branch, in four languages. Results reach Launchway only through files the Station gives the step, so a line a build tool prints cannot forge a test result or an output. Still missing, per the roadmap: parts of the sandbox on Kubernetes (the list of hosts and of writable paths is recorded, not enforced by name), and the remaining pieces of "Custom steps in your own language".

Everything can be stood in for

A unit test should not need a Station, a network or a secret store. Three things make that true:

  • A stand-in step context in every kit. A test gives it inputs and secret values, runs the step's function, and reads back outputs, results, notes and the failure reason. Each kit (Go, Python, TypeScript, shell) has one, built from the same contract, so the stand-in cannot drift from the real thing.
  • Nothing reaches out by accident. In the sandbox a step has no network unless its manifest lists hosts, so a test that forgot to stand in for a service fails the same way locally and on a Station.
  • Ordinary injection for the rest. A step that talks to the Depot (registry), a ticket system or a database takes the client as an argument, as any production code does, and the test passes a fake. The scaffold's example shows the pattern.

The Simulator: testing a pipeline without flying it

The Simulator is the pipeline's unit test. Given an event, inputs and a stand-in result for each step, it runs the real checker, the real planner and the real Standing orders, and executes nothing. It answers three questions: which steps run, in what order, and with which values. It also says why every other step was skipped, which Clearances (approvals) would be asked for, and which Launches (deployments) would happen, without doing any of them.

Tests live beside what they test: .launchway/tests/ next to the pipeline, and a library's tests/ next to its templates. A step with no stand-in succeeds and writes nothing; if a later step reads one of its outputs, the Simulator stops and names the missing stand-in rather than guessing. With exploring switched on, it tries every value of each boolean and choice that a condition reads, and lists the paths through the pipeline.

Design: not built

The test file and the command are sketches; file names, key names and the command name are not final. Values in the file are typed against the pipeline: a stand-in output of the wrong type is an error on its line.

# .launchway/tests/release-from-main.yaml
test: a push to main deploys and smoke-tests every channel
pipeline: storefront
event: { push: { branch: main } }
inputs: { environment: staging }
stand_ins:
  version: { outputs: { tag: v2.4.0 } }
  check:   { outputs: { is_release: true, channels: [web, kiosk] } }
  image:   { outputs: { digest: "sha256:0f3a9c" } }
  migrate-plan: { outputs: { needed: true, from: 41, to: 42, destructive: false } }
expect:
  runs: [test, web, version, check, image, migrate-plan, migrate, deploy,
         "smoke[channel=web]", "smoke[channel=kiosk]"]
  skips: { notify: "the event was push" }
  before: [[check, image], [migrate, deploy], [deploy, "smoke[channel=web]"]]
  values:
    deploy.environment: staging
    deploy.version: "sha256:0f3a9c"
    migrate.env.TO: "42"
# .launchway/tests/fork-pull-request.yaml
test: a pull request from a fork runs checks, never deploys, never asks for a secret
pipeline: storefront
event: { pull_request: { into: main, from_fork: true, title: "Fix cart total" } }
stand_ins:
  check: { outputs: { is_release: false, channels: [web] } }
expect:
  runs: [test, web, version, check, image]
  skips: { deploy: "the condition was false", smoke: "the step it needs, deploy, was skipped" }
  no_secrets: true
  launches: []
  clearances: []

A condition test names the step whose condition it tests, so it always tests the real expression, never a copy of it.

# .launchway/tests/conditions.yaml
conditions:
  migrate:
    - given: { steps: { migrate-plan: { outputs: { needed: true,  destructive: false } } } }
      gives: true
    - given: { steps: { migrate-plan: { outputs: { needed: true,  destructive: true } } } }
      gives: false
    - given: { steps: { migrate-plan: { outputs: { needed: false, destructive: false } } } }
      gives: false
  deploy:
    - given: { run: { branch: feat/cart }, steps: { check: { outputs: { is_release: true } } } }
      gives: true

Condition coverage counts, for every when, whether some test made it true and some test made it false. "migrate: true in 1 test, false in 2" is covered; a condition only ever true is listed as half covered.

launchway simulate                          # every test in .launchway/tests
launchway simulate --event push:main --explore
launchway simulate --replay 100 --branch main
release-from-main      passed   10 steps run, 1 skipped as expected
fork-pull-request      passed   no secrets, no Launches, no Clearances
conditions             passed   6 cases; condition coverage 5 of 6 (deploy: never false)
replay main, 100 Sorties: the changed pipeline would have run deploy 3 more times
  Sortie 812: steps.check.outputs.is_release was true on a pull request
  Sortie 815: the same
  Sortie 830: the same

Replaying a changed pipeline against past Sorties

Every Sortie is on the record with its event, its inputs, the values it resolved and every step's outputs and result. Replay plans the changed pipeline against each of the last N Sorties, using what each step really wrote as its stand-in, and compares the plan with what happened: steps that would now run, steps that would now be skipped, values that would differ, and Launches that would go to a different Airfield (environment). A new step has no history; the report names it and asks for a stand-in. Replay reads only the record: it never re-runs a step, never reads a secret and never touches an Airfield.

Pipeline code in the Debrief

The Debrief already reads thirteen test formats and coverage with thresholds, finds flaky tests and keeps history. It gains a Pipeline code section, so the code a pipeline runs is reported like the product it builds:

  • Unit test results and coverage of each custom step, from its language's tools, by step.
  • The step contract check from launchway step test, by step.
  • Simulator tests, one suite per file, and condition coverage, by condition.
  • Inline blocks over the limit, with their line counts and the offer to move them.

A library's own pipeline produces the same section for every tag, and the step's page in the catalog shows the result for each version.

A Standing order that refuses untested shared code

Standing orders are judged at fixed points with no side doors. A new typed rule adds two checks:

  • At run start: every custom step a Sortie takes from a library has a passing test record at the exact commit it is pinned to: the library's own pipeline ran that step's unit tests at that commit, at least one test ran, and all passed. A coverage floor is optional. Every Maneuver and Flight plan it uses has at least one passing Simulator test at that commit.
  • For steps in the same repository: the Sortie itself ran the step's tests in an earlier step, and they passed. The Flight plans in the Hangar (the built-in library) add that stage on their own when a repository has a steps/ directory.
Design: not built

A Standing order at the Wing. Key names are not final.

standing_orders:
  inline_code: { pipeline_lines: 5, shared_lines: 0 }       # tighter than 10 and 3; looser is refused
  shared_code_tested: { mode: enforce, coverage_minimum: 70 }
Refused before take-off: storefront Sortie 931.
  Standing order "shared code is tested" (Wing: Harbor Lights, enforce):
  platform-library/smoke at v4.2.0 (commit 7c1e2d) has no passing test record.
  The library's pipeline at that commit failed in steps/smoke/tests. Pin v4.1.3, or fix and tag v4.2.1.

It is on by default in report mode, which records and shows the finding without stopping anything. A level can switch it to enforce. Like every Standing order, a level above can lock it, and a waiver is recorded and expires.

Pipelines built from typed code

Some teams would rather write a pipeline in the language they write everything else in: with types, completion, functions and their own unit tests. Launchway lets them, without a second pipeline format. Builder libraries in TypeScript, Python and Go are generated from the same published pipeline schema the server validates against. Your code calls the builder; the builder writes the ordinary pipeline file; the one checker judges that file. What flies is always the checked file, never the code.

  • Generated, never hand-kept. Each builder is generated from the schema for every schema version, so a key the server accepts exists in the builder the same day, and a key it refuses does not. Each builder release says the schema version it writes; a server refuses a file newer than it knows, as it does today.
  • Typed down to the references. A step's outputs are typed handles. Using version.outputs.tag where a string is expected writes ${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }} and adds version to needs in the file it writes, so a missing dependency cannot happen; using it where a boolean is expected does not compile. A custom step's manifest becomes a typed function with its inputs as named arguments.
  • Two ways to use it. Write the file and commit it (Launchway adds a check that the committed file equals what the code writes now, so they cannot drift); or run the code in a generator step, where it is steps a step generates, checked and judged like written steps and run in the sandbox.
  • The same rules. Inline run text written through a builder counts against the same 10 and 3 line limits. Logic in the builder code is ordinary code, tested with the language's own tools; the builder ships a helper that runs the Simulator on the result, so one test file can say "a pull request from a fork never deploys".
  • Order of languages. TypeScript first, then Python, then Go, following the order already agreed for the product's other client libraries. A builder for another language is generated from the same schema and joins when someone keeps it.
Design: not built

Package names, function names and the drift check are sketches. Today the published editor schema for pipeline files exists and the server, launchway validate and the editor share one checker.

// .launchway/pipeline.ts
import { pipeline, step, deploy, input, run } from "@launchway/pipeline";
import { checkRelease } from "./steps/check-release/step";   // typed from its manifest

const environment = input.choice("environment", ["dev", "staging", "prod"], { default: "dev" });

export default pipeline("storefront", {
  on: { push: { branches: ["main"], tags: ["v*"] }, pullRequest: { into: ["main"] } },
  inputs: [environment],
}, (p) => {
  const version = p.add(step("version", {
    image: "golang:1.27",
    run: "git describe --tags --always",
    outputs: { tag: { type: "string", from: "stdout" } },
  }));
  const check = p.add(checkRelease("check", { tag: version.outputs.tag }));     // needs: version, added for you
  const image = p.add(step.image("image", { tag: version.outputs.tag }));
  p.add(deploy("deploy", {
    when: run.branch.eq("main").or(check.outputs.isRelease),
    environment,
    version: image.outputs.digest,                                             // a string where a string is wanted
  }));
});
# .launchway/pipeline.yaml   (written by launchway build .launchway/pipeline.ts; do not edit by hand)
pipeline: storefront
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"] }
  pull_request: { into: [main] }
inputs:
  environment: { type: choice, options: [dev, staging, prod], default: dev }
steps:
  version:
    image: golang:1.27
    run: git describe --tags --always
    outputs: { tag: { type: string, from: stdout } }
  check:
    uses: ./steps/check-release
    needs: version
    with: { tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }
  image:
    kind: image
    needs: version
    tags: [{ registry: depot, repository: harbor-lights/storefront, tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }]
  deploy:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [image, check]
    when: ${{ run.branch == "main" || steps.check.outputs.is_release }}
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
    version: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}
// .launchway/pipeline.test.ts
import { simulate } from "@launchway/pipeline/testing";
import storefront from "./pipeline";

test("a pull request from a fork never deploys", async  => {
  const result = await simulate(storefront, {
    event: { pullRequest: { into: "main", fromFork: true } },
    standIns: { check: { outputs: { is_release: false } } },
  });
  expect(result.skipped("deploy")).toBe("the condition was false");
  expect(result.launches).toEqual([]);
});

Dana keeps storefront in TypeScript. When she adds the delivery-date check for pull request #482, her editor completes the custom step's inputs, refuses a number where the step wants text, and her test runs the Simulator. The pull request contains both files; review reads the YAML difference, which is what will fly.

The foundation it relies on

The step contract
Versioned, small and the same in every language: a JSON inputs file, a JSON outputs file and a results file. Kits and their stand-ins are built from it.
The sandbox
No network, a read-only workspace and only named secrets, the same on a laptop and on a Station.
The record
Every Sortie's event, inputs, resolved values and outputs, so replay is a read, not a re-run.
The checker and planner
One library; the Simulator uses it unchanged, so a passing test describes what would really fly.
Standing orders
Judged at fixed points, set by level, tightened from above, with recorded and expiring waivers.

Safety

  • On failure. A lint warning never stops a Sortie; a shared-code error stops the library version from being used, with its file and line. A Simulator test that fails is a failed test in the Debrief, like any other. If the record is unavailable, replay says so and runs nothing.
  • Who may do what. A Pilot (developer) writes steps, tests and pipelines. A Commander sets the limits and the tested-code rule for a level; a lower level may tighten, never loosen. Running the Simulator needs only read access to the Flight (codebase); replay reads past Sorties the person may already see, and never shows a secret.
  • On by default. The line limits, the shared-code error, the sandbox for launchway step test, and the tested-code rule in report mode.
  • What it will not do. It will not judge what code means: a ten-line block of logic passes the count, and review is still review. It will not run a step to make a test pass. It will not let a Standing order loosen a limit.

Screens

  • Inline code warning and "Move into a custom step". In the editor, a mark on the block with its line count and the limit; the action opens a short wizard that proposes the step's name, inputs (from the block's env), outputs (from what it writes) and permissions, and shows the files it will write.
  • New custom step. Language, name, inputs and outputs with types, permissions picked from lists; writes the scaffold as a commit on a new branch.
  • Custom step page. Today's step page, with the test result and coverage of each version and the contract check.
  • The Simulator. Pick an event, set inputs, fill stand-ins by form, run; see the graph with run, skipped and why; save as a test file.
  • Replay report. The Sorties where a change would differ, step by step.
  • Debrief: Pipeline code. Step tests, contract checks, Simulator suites and condition coverage.
  • Standing order: inline code and tested shared code. Numbers chosen from a list no higher than the level above allows; mode picked from report or enforce.
  • Write this pipeline in code. A short wizard: pick the language from three, pick committed file or generator step, see the files it will write (the code, its test and the unchanged YAML), and save them as a pull request.
  • Generated file notice. In the editor, a file written by a builder opens read-only with a banner naming the code file it comes from and whether the two still match, with Open the code.

Open question

  • Open question The word Simulator. Proposed on the spine; it needs your yes. Without it the plain words are "pipeline tests".
  • Open question The numbers. 10 and 3 lines are the proposed numbers; confirm or change them.
  • Open question Default for the tested-code rule. This chapter starts it in report mode. Your rulings put safeguards on by default; enforce from day one would block every library that has no tests yet.
  • Open question How an inline interpreter is named. shell: python is a sketch; the key is not decided.
  • Open question Coverage floors for step code. Whether a coverage minimum for shared steps should have a default, or stay a choice per level.
  • Open question Builders: committed file or generator step by default. This chapter offers both and recommends the committed file, because review then reads exactly what will fly. Confirm, and confirm the language order (TypeScript, Python, Go), which follows the order agreed for the other client libraries.

Reuse that keeps growing

Write a piece once, pin it, and let the Launchway team and every developer keep adding steps and templates without ever changing a pipeline that did not ask for the change.

  • One ladder: a custom step (code), a Maneuver (step template), a Flight plan (pipeline template), a library (a Git repository of all three), and the Hangar (the built-in library).
  • Everything taken from a library is pinned by tag or commit and written into a lockfile, so a moved tag can never change what flies.
  • An update arrives as a notice that shows what changed in inputs, outputs and permissions, and is accepted as a reviewable change.
  • A template authorizes nothing: what it expands into is checked and judged exactly like steps written by hand.
  • A pipeline may ask for a range (v4.*) or a channel; it is resolved once into the lockfile and moves only when you accept an update, and every update shows how the expanded pipeline would change.
  • A pull request to a library replays the pipelines that use it in the Simulator and fails when their behavior would change unexpectedly.
  • A community index, seeded from the Hangar, is searchable from the editor and shows what each library may do before you add it.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer (authoring). It builds on Pipelines, values and expressions (typed steps and the checker) and Code you can test (custom steps, the Simulator and the tested-code Standing order). It uses the levels of the foundation (Base, Wing, Squadron, Flight) to share and to lock, and the record to know who uses what. The Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints (extension points) chapter covers what plugs in outside pipelines; this chapter covers what pipelines reuse.

What you will be able to do

You are on the Harbor Lights platform Squadron (team). You tag v4.3.0 of platform-library. Its pipeline runs the contribution checks, finds that the smoke step now reaches a new host, and still allows a minor version because no input or output changed. Every Flight (codebase) that uses smoke gets a notice: "v4.3.0 is available. Permissions: it may now reach status.example.test."

You own payments. You open the notice, read the change in one screen, and choose Review update. Launchway opens a pull request that changes the version and the lockfile, with the Simulator's replay of the last 50 Sorties (runs) attached: "no step would run differently". You merge it.

Someone moves the tag v4.2.0 to another commit. The next Sortie of storefront is refused before take-off: "platform v4.2.0 now points to 9d0e11, but the lockfile says 7c1e2d. Review the change before using it."

You are a Commander (owner) of the Wing. You require the security-scan Maneuver from platform-library at v4.* in every Flight. A Sortie without it is refused, naming the Maneuver and the range.

You upgrade Launchway. The release adds two Flight plans and a new check to go-service. Your pipelines expand to exactly the same steps as before; the new check appears as advice in the Debrief, and an update notice offers the next major version of go-service, where the check can block.

You browse the catalog in the product, filter by "Go" and "deploys", compare two Maneuvers by their inputs and permissions, and add one to a pipeline through a form, without typing a version or an input name.

How it works

The ladder

Each rung is built from the one below. Code lives only at the bottom; everything above it is an interface.

RungWhat it isHolds logicWritten as todayIn the coding analogy
Custom stepA program in Go, Python, TypeScript or shell with a manifest of typed inputs, outputs and permissionsYes, with unit testssteps/<name>/step.yaml, used as uses: ./steps/name or uses: library/nameA function
Maneuver (step template)One or more steps behind typed parameters and outputsNo: up to 3 lines of gluetemplates/<name>.yaml with template, params, steps, outputsAn interface
Flight plan (pipeline template)A whole pipeline for a kind of repository, with named stagesNo: up to 3 lines of glueA template used at the top of a file: uses, with, skip, extend, replace, stagesAn abstract class
LibraryA Git repository holding all three, released by tagsIn its steps onlyNamed in libraries; may require other libraries in library.yamlA package
Hangar (built-in library)The library inside each Launchway release, used as launchway/<name>In its steps and tested scripts onlyNo listing needed; the name launchway is reservedThe standard library

Your pipeline is the class that fills the interfaces in. A value set at a nearer level overrides the one above, and a lock from above is final: a Flight fills or overrides only what is left open.

A Maneuver in platform-library

The Harbor Lights platform Squadron keeps platform-library. Its go-test Maneuver is an interface over a tested custom step: typed parameters in, a typed output out, and no logic of its own. It is written in today's template format, with one detail to confirm: a template calling a custom step of its own library by its bare name, with parameter values in its with, is how this plan expects it to work, and the reference documents bare names only for templates.

# platform-library/templates/go-test.yaml
template: go-test
description: Test a Go module with a report and a coverage floor
params:
  go:               { type: string, default: "1.27", options: ["1.26", "1.27"] }
  coverage_minimum: { type: number, default: 70 }
  race:             { type: boolean, default: true }
steps:
  test:
    uses: go-coverage                      # a custom step of this library, with unit tests
    with: { go: { param: go }, minimum: { param: coverage_minimum }, race: { param: race } }
outputs:
  coverage: { from: test.coverage }
# storefront/.launchway/pipeline.yaml (part)
libraries:
  platform: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.2.0 }
steps:
  test: { uses: platform/go-test, with: { coverage_minimum: 80 } }

A Maneuver whose shape follows its parameters

A good template is one interface for many cases: one channel or five, with migrations or without. Today a template step can be left out by if on a parameter, and a step can repeat with for_each over a list parameter. The design keeps those keys and adds two promises. First, every expansion is type-checked as if it were written by hand: the checker expands the Maneuver (step template) for each set of parameters it is given and reports problems in the template's own file and line. Second, the library tests the shapes it promises, with the Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it), one case per parameter set.

# platform-library/templates/release-checks.yaml
template: release-checks
params:
  channels:        { type: list, default: [web] }
  with_migrations: { type: boolean, default: false }
  environment:     { type: environment }
steps:
  migrate:
    if: { param: with_migrations }                 # left out unless the parameter is true
    uses: migrate                                  # a tested custom step of this library
    with: { environment: { param: environment } }
  smoke:
    needs: migrate                                 # when migrate is left out, smoke needs what migrate needed
    for_each: { channel: { param: channels } }     # one member per channel
    uses: smoke
    with: { channel: { each: channel } }
outputs:
  p95_ms: { from: smoke.p95_ms }                   # gathered from every member, in order
Design: not built

if, for_each over a list parameter and lists of records exist today. The per-case Simulator test file, exploring every boolean and choice parameter, and a template output gathered from a fan-out are sketches.

# platform-library/tests/release-checks.yaml
template: release-checks
cases:
  - name: one channel, no migrations
    with: { channels: [web], with_migrations: false, environment: staging }
    expect:
      steps: ["smoke[channel=web]"]
      left_out: { migrate: "with_migrations is false" }
  - name: three channels with migrations
    with: { channels: [web, kiosk, app], with_migrations: true, environment: prod }
    expect:
      steps: [migrate, "smoke[channel=web]", "smoke[channel=kiosk]", "smoke[channel=app]"]
      before: [[migrate, "smoke[channel=web]"]]

With exploring switched on, the library's checks also expand the Maneuver for every value of each boolean and choice parameter and for an empty and a full list, and fail the tag if any expansion does not check. A Flight that uses release-checks sees, in the add-to-pipeline form, the exact steps its own parameter values produce before it saves anything.

Pins and the lockfile

Today a pipeline names a library and a version: a tag, a branch or a full commit. When a Sortie is created the server resolves it to a commit and records the library, the version as written and the commit, so a resume and every Station (runner) use the same files. A library's own requirements must be a tag or a commit, never a branch, and are resolved the same way up to four levels down. Standing orders can already require that every library is pinned to a tag or a commit.

What is missing is a record in the repository of what the team agreed to run. Tags can be moved; the Sortie records what a tag pointed to on the day, but nothing notices that it changed. The lockfile closes that gap.

Design: not built

File name, keys and layout are not final. The agreed model sketch calls it .launchway/hangar.lock; see the open question on the name below.

# .launchway/hangar.lock   (written by Launchway, reviewed like code)
lock: 1
libraries:
  platform:
    repo: platform-library               # the server's name for it, never an address
    version: v4.2.0                      # as written in the pipeline
    commit: 7c1e2d4f90ab31c6e2d8a7b5f0c4e9d1a2b3c4d5
    content: sha256:91ab0c...            # digest of the files a Sortie fetches
    steps:
      go-coverage: { manifest: sha256:4d2e11..., network: [], write: [reports] }
      smoke:       { manifest: sha256:a01f77..., network: [storefront.staging.example.test], write: [] }
    templates: [go-test, security-scan]
  tools:
    repo: shared-tools
    version: v2.1.0
    commit: 3b9d02c7aa1e5f6b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b
    content: sha256:5e7c40...
    required_by: platform
hangar:
  go-service: { major: 3, content: sha256:0b44de... }
  • The lockfile is written by Launchway (the editor, launchway validate --lock (a design flag), an accepted update notice), never by hand, and changes only through a commit like any code.
  • It holds every library a Sortie fetches, including the ones other libraries require, each with the library that asked for it.
  • For each custom step it keeps the manifest's digest and its permissions, so a widened permission shows in review as a changed line.
  • A pipeline that names a branch is still accepted, as today; the lockfile then records the commit, and the update notice offers each new commit as an update.
  • A repository with no lockfile works as today. A Standing order can require one.

Ranges and channels, resolved once

Writing an exact version everywhere is tedious, and writing a moving one makes Sorties unrepeatable. A pipeline may ask for a range or a channel; Launchway resolves it once, writes the exact commit into the lockfile, and keeps using that commit until a person accepts an update.

Written in the pipelineMeansResolved to
version: v4.2.0Exactly this tag, as todayIts commit
version: "v4.2.*"The newest patch of 4.2The newest matching tag that passed the contribution checks, when the lockfile is written
version: "v4.*"The newest 4.x: compatible changes only, by the version ruleThe same
version: { channel: stable }The version the library's owners call stableThe tag the channel names in library.yaml on the library's default branch, so moving a channel is itself a reviewed commit
  • A range or a channel needs a lockfile: the first launchway validate --lock (a design flag), or the editor, writes it. Without one, the Sortie is refused with the command to run.
  • A newer tag inside the range, or a moved channel, is never picked up by itself. It arrives as an update notice, and the lockfile changes only through the pull request that accepts it. Every Sortie is still repeatable from the lockfile alone.
  • A level that locks a range (below) also bounds what a pipeline's own range can resolve to.
# platform-library/library.yaml (part)
channels:
  stable: v4.2.0
  next: v4.3.0
Design: not built

Range and channel syntax are sketches; names are not final. Today a version is a tag, a branch or a commit.

Update notices

When a library gets a new tag, Launchway reads it, compares its interface with the version each Flight has locked, and tells the Flights that use it what would change for them.

Kind of changeExamplesVersion ruleHow the notice shows it
CompatibleA new input with a default; a new output; a fix behind the same interfaceMinor or patchA plain list of what was added
BreakingAn input removed, renamed or made required; a type changed; an output removed; a Flight plan stage removed or renamedMajor onlyEach line that would no longer check, in this Flight's own files
Widens permissionsA new network host, writable path or secretAny version, always called outAt the top, in one sentence; a level can require a Clearance (approval) to accept it
Newly blockingA check that can now fail a Sortie where it could not beforeMajor, or in report mode firstWhich step could now fail, and on what

The expanded pipeline, and how an update would change it

A pipeline full of uses is short to read, but a reviewer must be able to see what will really run. Today launchway validate --resolved prints every step of every template as the server would expand it, given a directory for each library, and POST /api/v1/validate?expand=1 does the same on a server. The design makes the expanded view something you never have to ask for:

  • From the lockfile. launchway validate --resolved reads the locked commits through the server or a local mirror, so no library directory is needed, and the output is exactly the graph a Sortie would plan.
  • An Expanded tab. The editor and the pipeline page show the final graph beside the text, each expanded step marked with the library, version and Maneuver or Flight plan it came from.
  • The difference on every update notice. Each notice carries the expansion difference between this Flight's locked version and the offered one, computed on this Flight's own file: steps added, steps removed, and keys that changed, line by line.
Update notice: platform-library v4.2.0 to v4.3.0, for storefront
  Compatible. Permissions: smoke may now reach status.example.test.
  Expanded pipeline, this Flight only:
    + test/vet            new step from go-test (runs go vet before the tests)
    ~ smoke[channel=web]  timeout 10m becomes 15m
    ~ smoke[channel=app]  timeout 10m becomes 15m
    no step removed; no Airfield, Clearance or secret changed
  Replay of the last 50 Sorties: no step would be skipped or added except test/vet.
Built today

For custom steps, a step's page and launchway steps get already show, for every Flight that uses a version, the newer tag and what it changes in inputs, outputs and permissions, with a call-out when it asks for more. launchway step validate --against v1 gives the same list to the author. Missing: the same for Maneuvers and Flight plans, and opening the update as a reviewable change.

The catalog

The catalog is one place in the product to find, compare and add every reusable piece a Flight may use: the Hangar's starters, the libraries the Base allows, and their steps, Maneuvers and Flight plans. Each entry shows its interface (inputs and outputs with types), what it may do, its versions with what changed in each, its test results, who uses which version, its owner, and whether it is deprecated and what replaces it. Adding an entry to a pipeline is a form: pick the version from a list, fill the inputs by their types, and see the lines it will change before saving.

Publishing as a team. An administrator allows a repository as a library and says which level it serves (a Squadron, the Wing or the whole Base) and which Squadron owns it. From then on, every tag that passes the contribution checks appears as a version; a tag that fails is listed for the owners only, with the reason. A pipeline still names a library by the server's name, never by an address, so a pipeline can never make the server fetch from anywhere.

Publishing to the community. A proposal: a public index of libraries that others publish. A Base can take one only by mirroring it into a library its administrator allows, at a tag, after the same contribution checks run on the Base's own Stations. Nothing in a pipeline ever fetches from the internet directly. The design follows.

The community index

A library ecosystem grows when people can find what already exists without leaving their editor. The community index is a public list of libraries: each entry is a whole library of typed, sandboxed, tested pieces, never a loose script. It is seeded on the first day, so it is useful before anyone else publishes.

  1. Seeded. Every Hangar entry is listed, and so is every packaged step of other systems that the importer's catalog maps to a Launchway step (see Bringing work in), with the Launchway step that replaces it.
  2. Listed with proof. An entry is shown only for a tag that passed the contribution checks below, on the index's own Stations. Each entry shows its interface, its declared permissions, its test results, its version history with the change classes, its owner and how many Bases mirror it.
  3. Searched from where you write. In the editor and through the language server, typing uses: offers matching entries, first from the libraries your Base already allows, then from the index. Before anything is inserted, a card shows what the piece may do: hosts it reaches, paths it writes, secrets it names.
  4. Brought in by mirroring. Choosing an index entry that the Base does not yet have asks an administrator to mirror it. The mirror is taken at a tag, the contribution checks run again on the Base's own Stations, and only then may a Flight lock it. A Base that does not allow the index never contacts it; an offline Base can load a signed copy of the listing.
Decision needed: bring the index forward

The index is proposed for Milestone 14. This chapter proposes moving it to Milestone 2, beside "Publish a library to the catalog", because a library model without a searchable catalog of ready pieces is the one place Launchway is clearly behind on reuse, and seeding from the Hangar and the importer's catalog needs no outside publishers. The cost is a public service to run and moderate earlier. Whether Launchway runs a public index at all, and who may list in it, stay open (below).

Required templates and locks from a level above

  • Bound at a level. A Flight plan or a template set at the Wing or a Squadron is used by every Flight beneath it, and a Flight overrides only what the level leaves open. Available today.
  • Required. A Standing order can require that every Sortie uses a template of a library at a version matching a range, and that every library is pinned to a tag or a commit. Available today, judged at run start.
  • Locked versions. A design addition: a level can lock a library to a range (platform-library at v4.*). A Flight cannot pin outside it, and update notices offer only versions inside it.
  • Visible. The hierarchy view, already built for variables, shows for each library and template which level set it, what it overrides and who locked it.

A template authorizes nothing

When a Sortie is created, a Maneuver's or Flight plan's steps become ordinary steps and are checked as if the pipeline had written them. The Airfield (environment) must exist and list the Flight; Standing orders see every expanded step; Clearances are not skipped; secrets are looked up for the using Flight, so a secret store's allow-list applies to template steps as to any step; and expansion cannot change whose work a step is. A library cannot be used to reach an Airfield the Flight may not use. The same holds for steps a step generates, and for every rung of the ladder: what a piece may do is the sum of what its steps declare, shown before anyone adds it.

How the library keeps growing without breaking anything

The Launchway team adds steps, Maneuvers and Flight plans to the Hangar in every release, and teams add them to their own libraries every week. Four rules keep that safe for the pipelines already using them.

Versions say what changed

Library tags are semantic versions. The contribution check computes the interface change against the previous tag and refuses a minor or patch tag for a breaking change. A published version is never removed while a lockfile on the Base names it; it can be hidden from the catalog.

Deprecation names a replacement

An input, an output or a whole entry can be marked deprecated with a message and what to use instead. launchway validate, the editor and the Debrief show it as a warning. It is removed only in a later major version, and the update notice for that version lists every line it affects.

The Hangar never changes under a pipeline

Each Hangar entry has a major version, recorded in the lockfile. Within a major, a release may only add: new optional inputs, new outputs, new advice. Launchway's own build expands a set of sample pipelines with every entry and fails if any expanded graph changes other than by addition. A check that can newly fail a Sortie arrives in report mode first and blocks only in the next major, which a Flight takes through an update notice.

New capabilities are one module

Built-in step kinds (image, deploy, verify, approval, Return to base, rollout, AI) move onto the same step contract as custom steps, one at a time. Adding a capability then means implementing the contract and registering it, not changing seven parts of the product; and nothing a developer adds runs inside the server.

The checks every contribution passes

The same checks run for a tag of any library before the catalog offers it, and for every change to the Hangar in Launchway's own build:

  1. Every manifest and template reads cleanly, and every example in it passes launchway validate.
  2. No run block in a Maneuver or Flight plan is longer than 3 lines.
  3. Every custom step's unit tests pass, and launchway step test passes in the sandbox.
  4. Every Maneuver and Flight plan has Simulator tests that pass; every Flight plan also runs for real against a small sample repository of its language (the Hangar does this today).
  5. The interface change against the previous tag matches the version rule; any widened permission is listed.
  6. Every entry has a description, a description for each input and output, and an example.
  7. An Inspection (security scan) of the step code and its dependencies finds nothing that blocks, and no secret is in the files.
  8. For the Hangar only: the vocabulary and originality checks, and the unchanged-expansion check above.

A library change tested against the pipelines that use it

A library's own tests say the library works. They cannot say that the Flights using it still behave the same. So every pull request to a library is also checked against its users: Launchway knows from the lockfiles on the Base which Flights lock which version, and replays their pipelines with the changed library in the Simulator. Nothing runs on a Station, no secret is read and no Airfield is touched.

  • What is compared. For each using Flight: the expansion difference (steps added, removed, keys changed), and the behavior difference over its recent Sorties (steps that would now run or be skipped, values that would differ, Launches that would go elsewhere), plus that Flight's own Simulator tests.
  • What counts as unexpected. A change the version rule does not allow for the version the pull request is heading to: in a patch or minor, any step that would be skipped or would run differently, any value that would differ, any Launch that would change; in a major, nothing is unexpected but everything is listed. An owner of the library may accept a listed difference with a reason; the acceptance is recorded and copied into the update notice the using Flights will see.
  • Privacy. The author sees the details for Flights they may read. For the others they see counts only ("2 Flights you cannot see: 1 with no difference, 1 with a difference; its Pilots were told"), and the owners of those Flights get the details on their own pages.
  • A branch on purpose. A Flight may also point one draft Sortie at the pull request's branch to try it by hand; the replay above runs for every push anyway.
platform-library pull request: "smoke: wait for the kiosk cache before checking"
  Heading to v4.2.1 (patch): behavior must not change.
  storefront     replayed 50 Sorties: no difference; Simulator tests 4 passed
  payments       replayed 50 Sorties: no difference; Simulator tests 2 passed
  image-resize   replayed 18 Sorties: smoke[channel=kiosk] timeout 10m becomes 12m in 18 of 18
  Result: failed. 1 unexpected difference. Accept it with a reason, or tag v4.3.0 instead.
Design: not built

The check, its output and the acceptance are sketches. A pipeline may name a library branch today, which is the manual half.

Starters for each language

"Starter" means two things, both kept:

  • Starter kits for writing a custom step, in Go, Python, TypeScript and shell, scaffolded by launchway step new with a passing test. Available today; a new language joins by implementing the small step contract and its stand-in context.
  • Language starters: Flight plans in the Hangar for Go, Python, Node and TypeScript, Java with Maven or Gradle, container images, static sites and Helm charts, used by detection, launchway init and a gallery. In progress. Still to come: Groovy, which you named among the first languages, and the files a starter can write into a repository: assistant instruction files, formatter and linter settings, a test layout and naming standards.

Keeping what detection ran. A repository with no pipeline file can run the Flight plan that detection picks, and today the Sortie page offers Add this file to the repository, which saves the text on a new branch for a pull request. The design makes that button, renamed Keep this pipeline, open a pull request with exactly what the Sortie ran: the pipeline file naming the same Flight plan and the same Hangar major, the lockfile with the content digest that Sortie used, and a first Simulator test that expects the steps that Sortie ran. Merging it changes nothing about what runs; it only makes the pipeline the repository's own, readable and reviewable. A choice in the same dialog writes the Flight plan out in full instead, as ordinary steps, for a team that wants to change everything.

The foundation it relies on

Git
Libraries, templates and step code live in Git and are pinned like dependencies. Nothing is imported into Launchway or registered as a copy.
Server configuration
Which repositories may be libraries, by name; one connection to a Git host covers every library it may read.
Levels
Bindings, requirements and locks flow down from Base to Flight; a nearer level overrides only what is open.
The record
Every Sortie records each library, the version as written, the commit and the content digest, and every use of a custom step with its manifest digest, for audit and for the software graph.
Standing orders
Required templates, pinned versions and the tested-code rule are judged at run start.

Safety

  • On failure. A library that cannot be fetched, a version that does not exist or a tag that moved refuses the Sortie before take-off, at the line that names it. A Station of another release refuses a Sortie planned with a different Hangar, rather than run files the server did not plan with, as today.
  • Who may do what. Whoever can push to a library or move its tags changes what pipelines would run; the lockfile and the refusal of moved tags make that a reviewed change for every Flight. Administrators allow libraries; a library's owning Squadron publishes tags; a Flight's Pilots (developers) accept updates through pull requests; Commanders set requirements and locks for a level.
  • On by default. Pinning by tag or commit for library requirements, the contribution checks, permission call-outs, the moved-tag check whenever a lockfile exists, and "a template authorizes nothing".
  • What it will not do. It will not update a pipeline by itself. It will not run code a developer adds inside the server. It will not fetch a library from an address a pipeline wrote.

Screens

  • The catalog. Filters by kind, language, what it does, owner and level; cards with interface, permissions and test status; compare two entries side by side.
  • A catalog entry. Interface, permissions, versions with changes, tests, users by version, deprecation, an example, and Add to a pipeline.
  • Add to a pipeline. Pick the Flight and the step's place in the graph, the version from a list, inputs by type; preview the changed lines and the lockfile change; save as a pull request.
  • Update notice. What changed for this Flight, classified, with the replay result; Review update, Later, Skip this version.
  • Libraries of a Flight. Each library with the version written, the locked commit, who required it, and any notice.
  • Publish a library. Choose the repository, the owning Squadron and the level it serves; see the contribution checks of its latest tag.
  • Required templates and locks. At a level: required templates with version ranges, locked library ranges, and the Flights that do not meet them yet.
  • Expanded tab. Beside the pipeline text: the final graph, each expanded step marked with its library, version and template; a toggle shows the expansion at the offered version of any pending update, with the difference marked.
  • Library pull request check. On a library's pull request: the version it is heading to, one row per using Flight (or a count for Flights you cannot see) with its expansion and behavior differences and its Simulator tests, and Accept difference with a reason picked from a short list plus a sentence.
  • Search the index from the editor. The completion list after uses:, grouped into "allowed on this Base" and "community index", each with a permissions card; choosing an index entry opens the mirror request.
  • Mirror request. For an administrator: the entry, the tag picked from a list, the permissions, the checks to run on the Base's Stations, and Approve or Decline.
  • Keep this pipeline. On a Sortie that used detection: keep the Flight plan by reference or write it out in full (a choice of two), the files that will be written, and Open pull request.
  • Version picker. In Add to a pipeline: exact tag, a range (patch or minor, picked) or a channel (picked from the library's channels), with what it resolves to today.

Open question

  • Open question The lockfile's name. The agreed model sketch says .launchway/hangar.lock, but the Hangar is the built-in library only, and the file covers every library. .launchway/libraries.lock would say what it holds.
  • Open question Hangar versions. This chapter gives each Hangar entry a major version kept in the lockfile, so a pipeline file never changes and an upgrade never changes what it runs. The other choice, every Hangar entry tied to the Launchway release, is simpler but means an upgrade can change a pipeline.
  • Open question A community index. Whether Launchway should run a public index at all, and who may list in it.
  • Open question When the index comes. This chapter proposes moving it from Milestone 14 to Milestone 2 (see the community index). Keep it in Milestone 14, move it to Milestone 2, or to Milestone 3.
  • Open question Ranges and channels. Allowing v4.* and channels makes pipelines shorter; the lockfile keeps Sorties repeatable. Confirm that ranges are wanted at all, since exact tags are the simpler rule.
  • Open question Library pull requests that fail. A patch or minor change that alters a using Flight's behavior fails the library's check until an owner accepts it. Confirm that it should fail rather than warn.
  • Open question Branches as versions. Pipelines may name a branch today. Should a Standing order requiring tags or commits be on by default for new Flights?
  • Open question The word "Maneuver". The product's own guide already uses it for step templates; the roadmap titles still say "Shared step templates". Confirm the roadmap should adopt it in prose.

Inputs and run forms

A person should almost never type what Launchway can offer: one typed input definition becomes a form that fetches real values, reacts to earlier answers, checks every value as you go, and is checked again on the server whoever sends it.

  • Free text is the last resort. When it is used, it has a pattern, a plain message and a live check.
  • One definition in the pipeline file drives every way to start a Sortie (run): the web form, the command line, the HTTP API, the agent endpoint, Patrols (schedules) and triggers.
  • Options come from four places: a fixed list, Launchway's own objects, a lookup an operator defines, or the outputs of an earlier Sortie.
  • Fields appear, narrow, fill themselves from context and explain their errors with the fix, on a desk or on a phone.
  • The same form engine asks for values in the middle of a flight (a Clearance (approval) with fields) and draws every wizard in the product.
  • Saved answers can live as files in the repository, read at the Sortie's commit, owned by the level they belong to; a Standing order says which of them may fill a Sortie bound for a protected Airfield.
  • A Flight plan can be offered as a job: a form, a Patrol, credentials by reference and a "may run" right, under the same Clearance, Standing orders and record as a Launch.

Where it sits

Inputs belong to layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer, where a pipeline is written. They lean on layer 1 for levels, permissions, variables and locks (the system; Levels, people and secrets) and write every answer to layer 2, the record (the record). Layer 4 runs the steps that receive the values. Layer 6, command, reads them when a Standing order (policy) or a Clearance is judged.

Builds on
Typed inputs in the pipeline file, the start form and branch picker of today, variables at levels with locks, the one expression language inside ${{ }} (Pipelines, values and expressions), and the Detachment (site agent) for private networks (Stations and where work runs).
Used by
Every way of starting a Sortie (what starts a Sortie), Clearances (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold), Flight plans (pipeline templates) used as job templates (Reuse that keeps growing), every wizard (screens) and every module that asks a person for something (module contract rule 4).
Layers
3 (authoring), with 1 (foundation) and 2 (record).

What you will be able to do

You open the storefront release form. Airfield (environment) is already staging, because that is where you launched last time. You choose api, and the version list fills with the ten newest images of storefront-api in the Depot (registry), each with its build time and whether it passed its Inspection (security scan). You pick 2.4.0 and press Start. You typed nothing.

You switch the Airfield to prod. Two fields appear: a change ticket, picked from your open work items, and a launch window, already set to the Airfield's change window of Tuesday 14:00 to 16:00 Central. The summary on the right now says "Protected Airfield: two Go answers from storefront-leads are needed" before you have started anything.

You pick 2.5.0-rc.1 for prod. The version field turns red at once and says, beside it: "This version has not flown in staging yet. Pick a version marked 'in staging', or launch it to staging first." The Start button stays available so you can read every problem, and the server would refuse the same thing in the same words from the command line.

You run launchway runs start storefront in a terminal. It asks the same questions in the same order, shows the same versions as a numbered menu, and accepts -i environment=staging to skip a question. An agent calling the agent endpoint gets the same schema, the same options filtered by its own narrow rights, and the same refusals.

Halfway through the Sortie, the prod Clearance card on your phone asks the approver two things before Go: the launch window and the share of traffic the Pathfinder (canary) takes first. Both answers become typed outputs that the Launch (deployment) step reads, and the record says who gave them.

The platform team adds a lookup named clusters that reads the list of edge-kiosk host groups from an inventory service on a private network. The kiosk-rollout pipeline offers that list as a choice. The call goes through the team's Detachment; the inventory service is never opened to the internet and its credential never leaves the Detachment.

How it works

One definition, every way in

An input definition is data in the pipeline file, under inputs:. No script runs in the browser. Everything that changes (options, defaults, visibility, whether a field is required, whether a value is allowed) is computed on the server from the definition and the answers so far. The web form, the command line, the API, the agent endpoint, Patrols, triggers and re-runs all call the same server check, so the browser and the server cannot disagree, and no way in can skip a rule.

A person sees fields. The command line sees prompts and flags. The API sees a schema, an options call and a validate call. A Patrol or a trigger supplies values without a person, so its values are checked exactly as a person's, and a value that fails is a recorded refusal, not a silent default.

The storefront release form

The Harbor Lights team launches the storefront Flight (codebase) (a Go service called api, a web front end called web, and a PostgreSQL database) through dev, staging and prod. This is its release form, today and as designed.

Available today

Five types (string, number, boolean, choice, list), with pattern, min, max, default, required and from (a variable). Options are a fixed list; options_from is refused. The version must be typed.

pipeline: storefront
inputs:
  component:   { type: choice, options: [api, web], default: api }
  environment: { type: choice, options: [dev, staging, prod], default: dev }
  version:     { type: string, pattern: "^[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+(-rc\\.[0-9]+)?$", required: true }
  migrate:     { type: boolean, default: true }
  region:      { type: string, from: region }      # a variable set at the Wing, possibly locked
Design: not built

Key names follow today's file and your design documents. The names available inside ${{ }} (inputs, chosen, me, environments, vars) are proposed.

pipeline: storefront
inputs:
  component:
    type: choice
    label: What to launch
    options:
      - { value: api, label: "Go service", description: "storefront-api, with database migrations" }
      - { value: web, label: "Web front end", description: "storefront-web, static assets" }
    default: api
  environment:
    type: environment                    # an Airfield picker: only Airfields you may launch to
    default: "${{ me.last.environment ?? 'dev' }}"
  version:
    type: image                          # picked from the Depot, newest first
    repository: "${{ 'harbor-lights/storefront-' + inputs.component }}"
    record: digest                       # the form shows the tag; the Sortie records the digest
    must_exist: true                     # checked again when the Sortie starts
  migrate:
    type: boolean
    label: Run database migrations first
    visible_if: "${{ inputs.component == 'api' }}"
    default: true
  ticket:
    type: choice
    label: Change ticket
    options_from: { source: work.items, with: { state: open, assigned: me } }
    search: true
    required_if: "${{ inputs.environment == 'prod' }}"
    visible_if: "${{ inputs.environment == 'prod' }}"
  window:
    type: window                         # a start and an end, in a time zone
    label: Launch between
    visible_if: "${{ inputs.environment == 'prod' }}"
    default: "${{ environments[inputs.environment].change_window }}"
  notify:
    type: group
    label: Tell
    default: "${{ me.squadron }}"
form:
  rules:
    - when: "${{ inputs.environment == 'prod' && 'staging' not in chosen.version.meta.flown }}"
      field: version
      message: "This version has not flown in staging yet. Pick a version marked 'in staging', or launch it to staging first."

Field kinds

Each kind says what it holds, how it is drawn, and how it is filled without typing. The machine names are the plain words (environment, runner, project), as for every pipeline key.
