Today's list type stays and is read as a multi-choice that allows typed values, so no existing pipeline changes. Every kind may carry label, description, help (a longer disclosure), default, required, visible_if, required_if, enabled_if and section.

Where options come from

An option is a value with a label, an optional description, an optional group heading, and optional facts (meta) that rules and the summary can read. A disabled option says why. There are four sources, and every one of them returns only what the person asking may see: an option the person may not see is absent, not grayed out.

SourceWrittenExamplesWhere it is evaluated
A fixed list Availableoptions:api, webThe pipeline file
Launchway's own objectsoptions_from: { source: ... }, or a kind with its own sourcegit.branches, git.tags, git.commits, git.pulls, depot.images, depot.tags, depot.packages, environments, targets, releases, projects, pipelines, people, groups, runners, runner_pools, variables, secrets (names only), files, work.itemsThe server, as the asker
A named lookup an operator definesoptions_from: { source: lookup.clusters }Host groups from an inventory service, cloud regions an account may use, tickets in an outside trackerThe server, or the Detachment when the system is on a private network
The outputs of an earlier Sortieoptions_from: { source: sorties, with: { pipeline: build, result: succeeded }, value: "${{ option.outputs.image }}" }The images the last five green builds produced; the plan a dry run wroteThe server, from the record

Shaping keys work on every source: filter (an expression over option), sort (newest, label or an expression), limit (50 by default, 500 at most), search, and group_by. A lookup is an object in the product, not in Git, because it holds a connection; the pipeline names it, and the triggers and forms that use it are listed on its page.

Fields that react to other answers

A field can appear, disappear, become required, become read-only, or narrow its options because of earlier answers. Each rule is one expression in the one language, inside ${{ }}, type-checked before the pipeline is saved. A field that reads another field depends on it; the server works out the order and refuses a cycle with the line numbers.

  • Appear and disappear. visible_if hides a field and drops its value; a hidden field is never sent and never required.
  • Required when. required_if makes a field required only in some cases: a ticket only for prod.
  • Narrowing. A source parameter may read an earlier answer: the image repository follows component; the target list follows the Airfield.
  • Search as you type. Long lists send the query to the source after a short pause, page by page, and keep keyboard order.
  • Freshness. Fetched lists show "as of 10:42" and a refresh button. Identical questions in flight share one request. A reply that arrives after a newer question is thrown away.
  • Slow or down. Each source has a time limit (5 seconds by default). A failed source affects only its own field: "Could not load versions: the Depot did not answer. Try again." Where the author allows typing (allow_custom: true), the field accepts a typed value checked against the same rules.

Defaults from context

A good default is a value nobody has to think about. Defaults may be fixed or an expression, and the form shows where each came from in a small gray line under the field.

Where the value comes fromWrittenShown as
The branch you are ondefault: "${{ run.branch }}""from the branch page you came from", or "from your checkout" on the command line
Your last answer for this pipelinedefault: "${{ me.last.environment }}""your last answer"; never for secret references or files
The Airfield's own settingsdefault: "${{ environments[inputs.environment].change_window }}""from the prod Airfield"
A variable at a level Availablefrom: region"from the Wing (organization)", with the lock and its reason when locked
Saved answers or a link(chosen by the person)"from the saved answers nightly-staging (repository, at this commit)" or "from the link you opened"

The order is fixed and shown on the form: a value the person gave, then a link or saved answers, then a locked variable (which nothing can override), then the default expression.

Checked as you type, and the same on the server

Every rule is one server function. The form calls it as you leave a field, and the start call runs it again in full, as does every other way in. Errors appear beside the field, in plain words, with the fix. A field is never cleared silently: a value that became invalid stays and is marked.

RuleWrittenThe message a person reads
Pattern with a messagepattern, message, or a named pattern"A kiosk name is three letters and four digits, such as SEA0042."
Rangemin, max, step, min_length, max_items"Pick at most 50 percent for the first Pathfinder share."
Required, or required whenrequired, required_if"A change ticket is needed for prod. Pick one of your open tickets."
Across fieldsform.rules"This version has not flown in staging yet. Pick a version marked 'in staging', or launch it to staging first."
Must exist nowmust_exist: true"2.4.0 was deleted from the Depot after you opened the form. Pick another version."
Uniqueunique: in-list or against earlier Sorties"Version 2.4.0 was already cut as a release. Pick 2.4.1."

Each refusal carries the input, the rule, the value and the fix (error and next, as every Launchway refusal does). A re-run is checked again with today's rules, and says what changed if it now fails.

What will run, before you start

Beside the form, the server draws a live summary: the pipeline and the commit, the resolved values (the digest behind a tag), which steps will run and which will be skipped by their when, the Airfields touched, which Clearances will be asked and of whom, any Hold (freeze) in the way, the Standing orders that will be judged, and an estimate of the wait for a Station from recent history. It is Preflight (checks) shown before the button, not after.

Reaching a private system safely

A named lookup is defined by an operator, not by the pipeline author: which connection, which paths, how the answer becomes options, how fresh, how long to wait, and who may use it. When the system is on a private network, the lookup runs in the team's Detachment, which connects outward to Launchway; nothing on the private network is opened.

On a self-hosted Base (installation) without a Detachment, the server makes the call itself through its outbound guard, which refuses private addresses unless an administrator allowed them. Lookups run in a small pool at lower priority than Sorties, so a busy form can never slow a build.

Saved answers and locks from above

Saved answers (the roadmap item calls them saved input sets) are a named group of answers with an owner: a person (only they see them) or a Squadron (its members see them, people with pipeline edit rights change them). "Nightly staging check" or "Kiosk wave 2". Choosing one fills the form; every value is still checked, and a value that no longer fits is shown as an error, not dropped. Saved answers never hold secret references or files. They are a convenience: nothing requires them, and two never stack on top of each other.

Locks are today's variable locks. A Wing (organization) that locks region to eu, with a reason, makes the field read-only everywhere: in the form, in all saved answers, on the command line and through the API. The field shows "Locked by the Wing: everything ships to the EU region" with the name of who set it.

Saved answers kept in the repository, owned by level

Answers a team relies on (the nightly check, the weekly restart, the second kiosk wave) should be reviewed like code and travel with the commit they were written for. So saved answers may also be files in the repository, beside the pipeline. They are read at the Sortie's own commit, so the answers and the inputs they fill always belong to the same version of the pipeline, and a change to them is a pull request.

Owned byKept inWho changes themSeen by
A Flight (codebase).launchway/answers/<name>.yaml in the repository, read at the Sortie's commitAnyone who can merge to the branch, under its review rulesEveryone who can start the pipeline
A Squadron or the WingThe level's settings, which are also kept as code where the level keeps its settings in GitPeople with pipeline edit rights at that levelEvery Flight beneath the level
A personThe productThat personThat person

The "Fill from" menu groups saved answers by owner and says where each comes from. One choice fills the form; they still never stack, and a lock from above still wins over all of them.

Design: not built

The file layout, its keys and the Standing order are sketches; names are not final.

# storefront/.launchway/answers/nightly-staging.yaml
answers: nightly-staging
pipeline: storefront
description: The nightly check of what is on main, in staging
values:
  component: api
  environment: staging
  migrate: true

Which saved answers may aim at a protected Airfield. A Standing order (policy) decides, judged at run start with the rest of the plan. The built-in default: a Sortie whose plan lands on a protected Airfield may be filled only from saved answers kept in the repository at a commit on the default branch (so they were reviewed) or at a level; personal saved answers fill a form for prod but cannot be the source of a start without a person confirming each value. A level may tighten this, for example to "only answers kept at the Squadron".

standing_orders:
  saved_answers_for_protected:
    allow_from: [repository_default_branch, level]    # not: personal, repository_other_branch
    mode: enforce

When the Patrol (schedule) of storefront starts the nightly check, it names nightly-staging; the Sortie records the file, its commit and the values it gave. When Dana points the same answers at prod by hand, the form says "Saved answers from the repository at main: allowed for prod by the Wing's Standing order", and the Clearance (approval) Ana gives is unchanged by where the values came from.

Inputs asked mid-flight: a Clearance with fields

A Clearance can ask the approver for typed values. The fields use the same kinds, sources and rules as a run form, appear on the decision card, and become the step's typed outputs when the answer is Go. Who gave each value, and when, is on the record.

Design: not built

Today an approval step has message, approvers and deployment; fields is a design.

  approve-prod:
    kind: approval
    needs: verify-staging
    message: "Launch storefront ${{ inputs.version }} to prod?"
    approvers: { groups: [storefront-leads], count: 2 }
    fields:
      window:   { type: window, label: "Launch between", default: "${{ environments.prod.change_window }}" }
      first:    { type: number, label: "First Pathfinder share", unit: percent, min: 1, max: 50, default: 10 }
      watch:    { type: duration, label: "Overwatch after the Launch", min: 15m, max: 4h, default: 1h }
  launch-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: approve-prod
    environment: prod
    version: "${{ inputs.version }}"
    window: "${{ steps.approve-prod.outputs.window }}"

With a quorum of two, the first Go answer fills the fields and the second approver sees them and confirms or sends back a No-go with a reason. A changed value after the first Go starts the count again.

The same forms in every wizard

Every wizard in the product (Connect a repository, Add an Airfield, Add a Station, Add a Standing order, Add a lookup) is a form of the same engine, with steps. A wizard step is a section with a title; the engine gives each wizard the fetched options, dependent fields, checks as you type, the plain messages and the "what will be created" summary that run forms get. So a field that is free text in a wizard today, such as an Airfield's target, becomes a picker by changing its definition, not by writing a new screen. A large run form may use the same steps: form.steps: [{ title, inputs }], with validation per step.

Flight plans as jobs, with a form

Operations teams run the same tasks again and again: restart a service on one host, rotate a certificate, re-index a search store. Each needs a form, sometimes a schedule, a credential, and a short list of people allowed to press the button, and each should be as safe and as recorded as a Launch (deployment). A job in Launchway is not a new object: it is a pipeline that is started by hand or by a Patrol and has a form, usually built from a Flight plan (pipeline template). The Jobs page of a Flight lists those pipelines with a Run button.

  • The form. The pipeline's inputs, drawn by the same engine: the host picked from the Airfield's targets, the Airfield from a list, a reason only where it is required.
  • A Patrol. A schedule in the pipeline's on, naming saved answers, so the unattended run is checked exactly like a person's.
  • Credentials by reference. A secret reference, picked in the secret browser, resolved on the Station; nobody who runs the job sees it, and the form never accepts a value.
  • Who may run it. A right given in the product, "may run this job", to a person or group, without the right to edit the pipeline or start other ones. It is a role binding like any other, shown in the Logbook (audit trail).
  • The same safety as a Launch. A job that touches a protected Airfield asks for the same Clearance; Standing orders are judged at run start; a Hold (freeze) stops it; every run is a Sortie on the record.
Design: not built

The Jobs page, the "may run this job" right and a Patrol naming saved answers are sketches. Hand-started Sorties with typed inputs, Patrols, secret references and approval steps exist today.

# billing/.launchway/jobs/restart-billing.yaml
pipeline: restart-billing
description: Restart the billing service on one host
on:
  schedule: { cron: "0 3 * * 1", timezone: America/Chicago, answers: weekly-staging }   # a Patrol; answers is the new key
inputs:
  environment: { type: choice, options_from: environments, default: staging }
  host:   { type: choice, options_from: { source: targets, with: { environment: "${{ inputs.environment }}" } } }
  reason: { type: string, min_length: 10, required_if: "${{ inputs.environment == 'prod' }}" }
steps:
  restart:
    image: harbor-lights/ops-tools:3
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}       # prod is protected: a Clearance is asked first
    env: { HOST: "${{ inputs.host }}" }
    secrets: { SSH_KEY: { store: vault, key: ops/billing, field: ssh_key } }
    run: ansible-playbook ops/restart-billing.yml --limit "$HOST"

The "back office" Squadron gives its on-call group the right to run restart-billing, and nothing else in billing. Priya, on call, opens the job on her phone, picks prod and the host billing-vm-2 from lists, gives a reason, and presses Run. The Sortie waits for Ana's Go, as any change to prod does, restarts one host, and the Logbook says who ran it, why, with which answers, and who cleared it.

On a phone, and with a keyboard or a screen reader

  • Phone. One column. Labels above fields. Pickers open as full-height sheets with search at the top and 44-pixel rows. The summary becomes a bar fixed to the bottom ("api 2.4.0 to staging · Start"), which opens the full summary when tapped.
  • Keyboard. Every picker follows the combobox and listbox patterns of WAI-ARIA: type to search, arrows to move, Enter to choose, Escape to close. Tab order is reading order. After a refused start, focus moves to the first wrong field.
  • Screen readers. Each field's help and error are tied to it. Loading and results are announced politely ("12 versions loaded, as of 10:42"); errors are announced assertively. A cleared value says why.
  • Never color alone. A problem is a red border, an icon and words. An option's verdict (Inspection passed, failed) is an icon and a word.

Today's pipelines keep working

Every key of today keeps its meaning. list reads as a multi-choice that allows typing; string stays free text; options_from stops being refused once a server supports it, behind a schema version, so an older server refuses a newer file instead of misreading it. Values still reach steps only as LAUNCHWAY_INPUT_<NAME> variables, and as typed values inside ${{ }}, never pasted into script text.

Built today

The start dialog reads the inputs of the pipeline at the chosen commit, keeps answers whose name and type still match when the commit changes, shows the variables in effect with their level and lock, checks each field when you leave it and again on the server, and moves focus to the first wrong field after a refusal. Re-runs reuse the recorded inputs.

The foundation it relies on

  • Levels and permissions. Every source filters by the asker's rights. Locks come from the existing variable chain. Saved sets belong to a person or a Squadron.
  • The record. A Sortie records each value, the label the person saw, the option's facts and when the list was fetched, so "which 2.4.0 did we launch" has one answer.
  • The expression language. Rules, defaults and source parameters are ${{ }} expressions, checked when the pipeline is validated, with the same names as everywhere else.
  • The Detachment. Private lookups run where the network and the credential already are.
  • Every way in is the same way in. The schema, options and validate calls exist in the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and the web, kept equal by the parity test; saved sets and lookups are Terraform resources.

Safety

When something fails

  • A source that is slow or down fails only its own field, after its time limit, and says how to go on.
  • Start is blocked only by a missing required value or a broken rule, never by a lookup that is still loading.
  • If the server restarts while you fill the form, your answers stay in the page and are checked again.
  • A Patrol or trigger whose values fail is a recorded refusal with the reason, never a Sortie with silent defaults.

Who may do what

  • Pipeline authors write inputs; operators with config.manage define lookups and approve each connection a lookup uses.
  • Anyone who may start a pipeline sees its form, with options filtered to their own rights; an agent sees options filtered to its token's rights.
  • A person saves personal sets; people with pipeline edit rights save sets for a Squadron.
  • Only the approvers of a Clearance fill its fields.

On by default

  • Server-side checking of every start, from every way in, including re-runs.
  • Options are plain text, escaped; no code from a source ever runs in the browser.
  • Inputs are visible to everyone who can see the Sortie, so the form says "do not put secrets here", and secrets are only references.
  • A pre-filled link only fills the form; it never starts a Sortie.
  • Sharing a pipeline with another Squadron lists every free-text input and refuses until each is restricted or explicitly allowed.

Shown in three states: empty with defaults; prod chosen, with the ticket and window revealed; and a refused version with the cross-field message.

  5. Jobs: a Flight's Jobs page (each job's name, description, last run, next Patrol, who may run it, and Run), the job's run form on a desk and on a phone, and the "may run this job" right in access settings, with people and groups picked, never typed.

Open question

Saved answers and "no input sets"

The ruling on fewer concepts says Launchway has "no ... input sets or layered overrides" to learn first. This chapter keeps saved answers (the running-text name for saved input sets) because you asked for them by name, but makes them optional, flat (they never stack), never required to run, and filled through the same checks. Whether to have them at all is still yours to confirm.

Saved answers in the repository

Keeping saved answers as files read at the Sortie's commit makes them reviewed and repeatable, but adds a folder to the repository. The default rule for protected Airfields (only answers from the default branch or a level) is this chapter's proposal. Confirm both, or keep saved answers in the product only.

The right to run one job

"May run this job" is a narrower right than today's roles per Flight. Confirm that a right scoped to one pipeline is wanted, rather than a role for the whole Flight.

Kinds or one choice type

This chapter gives common pickers their own kind (type: environment, type: image) so authors write less, and keeps choice with options_from for everything else. Your design wrote all of them as choice plus a source. Both cannot be offered for the same thing without breaking "one way to do each thing". Recommendation: kinds for Launchway's own objects, choice for fixed lists, lookups and earlier Sorties.

Key names

The model sheet sketched show_if; design wrote visible_if, required_if and enabled_if. This chapter uses the document's three, which read as a family. Choose one spelling before the first slice ships.

Free text in shared pipelines

A shared pipeline refuses to share until every free-text input is restricted or explicitly allowed. Keep that strict default, or warn only?

What starts a Sortie

Something happens; Launchway decides in the open whether it starts a Sortie (run), which pipeline at which commit, and with which values, and writes down why every time.

  • Triggers are declared with the pipeline, in Git, under on:, and filtered in the one expression language inside ${{ }}.
  • Every kind of event takes the same path: arrive, prove it is authentic, pass the filter, find the trusted declaration, become typed inputs, settle duplicates, wait its turn, start, and leave a record.
  • Only reviewed code can arm a trigger. A pull request cannot switch triggers on for itself, and forks and automation accounts run restricted.
  • Every decision is on the record with a sentence, can be tried before it happens and replayed after.
  • Pipelines can start each other and wait for a typed answer, and Launchway's own events go out to other systems in one open standard event format.
  • Every moment of a pull request's life can start a Sortie (run), including "ready for review", and a person with the right to write can start one by typing a command in a comment, with typed arguments and a reply that links to the Sortie.
  • The triggers page says, for every connected code host, whether events arrive by webhook or by polling, and how long a push took to become a Sortie.

Where it sits

Triggers are part of layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer: they are written in the pipeline file beside the steps they start. Every event and every decision is a row in layer 2, the record. Layer 1 supplies who may start what (Levels, people and secrets) and the sealed secrets of incoming endpoints. Layer 4 receives the Sortie from the Holding pattern (queue).

Builds on
Today's on: keys (push, pull_request, schedule, webhook), event sources, triggers on results, the event log, lanes, supersede and run limits, restricted runs for untrusted pull requests, and inputs and run forms, which turn event data into checked values.
Used by
Delivery (One way to launch, anywhere), the Depot (registry) (the Depot), code hosting (Code and review), the software graph (the software graph and Maintenance), insights from the record (Radar, insight and keeping it healthy), and outside systems through Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints (extension points).
Layers
3 (authoring) and 2 (record), with 1 (foundation) and 4 (execution).

What you will be able to do

A new harbor-lights/base-go image lands in the Depot (registry). Within a minute storefront rebuilds on it. The event page says: "Image base-go 1.24.3 pushed. Trigger depot: started Sortie #212 with base = sha256:4e1a…".

You add the label run-e2e to a pull request. Only then does the long browser test suite run, once, against the pull request's head. A colleague from outside the team opens a pull request from a fork that adds the same trigger to the pipeline file: nothing extra runs, and the event says why: "a pull request cannot arm a trigger for itself; the default branch does not ask for it".

payments finishes a Launch (deployment) to staging. storefront's contract tests start against it, with the payments version as a typed input, because payments allowed it and storefront asked for it in its pipeline file.

The nightly Patrol (schedule) of storefront did not run. You open its triggers page, see "Patrol 04:00 America/Chicago: skipped, Schedules are switched off for this Base (installation) since 22:10 by Sam", and switch them back on. It does not run twice for the missed night.

Your release Sortie needs a yes from payments's contract-check pipeline before it may launch to prod. A step starts that pipeline, waits, and reads its verdict output. No secret or log crosses between the two Flights (codebases).

Dana's pull request #482 ("Show the delivery date at checkout") is ready for a closer look. She types /launchway run e2e suite=checkout in a comment. Within seconds Launchway replies under her comment: "Started Sortie 418 of storefront/e2e at the head of #482 with suite = checkout", with the link. When the Sortie ends, the reply is updated with the result. A comment from someone who may not write to the repository gets a polite refusal that says why, and nothing runs.

The team's incident tool listens for Launchway events. Every Launch, Return to base (rollback) and Hold (freeze) arrives in the same open standard event format that the tool already reads for everything else, signed, with an identifier it can use to ignore repeats.

How it works

The path from "something happened" to "a Sortie started"

Every trigger kind, from a push to a message on a queue, takes the same nine stages. Each stage can end the journey, and every ending is a decision with a reason on the record. The guarantee, across any number of servers, is one start or one recorded reason, for every event and every trigger.

  1. The event arrives. A push seen by polling or announced by a code host, a pull request change, a Patrol firing, a signed call, a message, a result of another Sortie, a change in the Depot or an Airfield (environment). It is stored before anything else happens, with credential-like values removed and a size cap.
  2. Is it authentic? A signed call must match its signature within five minutes, once. An event from inside Launchway is authentic by construction. A code host's notice is only a hint: Launchway checks the repository itself, so a forged notice can at most cause a check.
  3. Does it pass the filter? The trigger's closed keys (branches, paths, moments) and its when expression decide.
  4. Which pipeline, at which commit, is trusted? The declaration that counts depends on the kind of event (see trust).
  5. Event data becomes typed inputs. Each input is an expression over the event, checked by the same rules as a person's answers.
  6. Duplicates and superseded Sorties. A dedupe key seen before is a duplicate. A newer event may replace an older one that has not started.
  7. Queueing and lanes. Run limits and lanes decide whether it starts now, waits, replaces the holder, or is skipped.
  8. The start. The Sortie and its "started" decision are written together.
  9. The record. The event page shows the payload, each trigger's decision and the Sortie it started.

Every trigger, in the pipeline file

Today four kinds are written in the pipeline file and two more (event sources and triggers on results) are created in the product. The design puts every declaration of "this pipeline starts when" into on:, so the triggers are reviewed, versioned and branched with the steps. What holds a secret or a permission stays in the product: an incoming endpoint and its sealed secret, a queue connection, and one Flight's permission for another to follow it. The pipeline names them; it never contains them.

Something happenedKeyTodayDesign
A push to a branchpush.branches, paths, paths_ignoreAvailableAdds when
A tagpush.tagsAvailableAdds when (for example only signed tags)
A pull request, through its whole lifepull_request.into, paths, momentsAvailable for opened and updatedmoments: opened, updated, merged, closed, labeled, reviewed
A releaserelease.momentsRelease events only send notificationspublished, promoted, returned
A Patrol (schedule) with a time zoneschedule[].cron, timezone, ref, inputsAvailableinputs as expressions; when

Event names keep the stored source words of today's event log (push, pull_request, schedule, webhook, event_source, manual, run_result, launch_result), and add release, depot, environment and together. A step's when: { event: ... } can test every one of them.

The storefront triggers

Available today

Every key here works today (steps left out). The trigger on platform-library's result exists too, but is created with launchway run-triggers create, not in the file.

pipeline: storefront
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"], paths: ["**", "!docs/**"] }
  pull_request: { into: [main] }
  schedule:
    - { cron: "0 4 * * MON-FRI", timezone: America/Chicago, inputs: { environment: staging } }
  webhook:
    name: hotfix-request
    inputs: { version: body.version, environment: body.environment }
inputs:
  environment: { type: choice, options: [dev, staging, prod], default: dev }
  version:     { type: string, default: latest }
lane: { name: storefront, per: [ref], when_busy: wait }
# steps: left out of this example
Design: not built

moments, when on triggers, depot, run_result in the file, dedupe and expressions in inputs are designs. Key names are not final. The names inside ${{ }} are proposed.

pipeline: storefront
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]
    paths: ["**", "!docs/**"]
  pull_request:
    into: [main]
    moments: [opened, updated, labeled]
    when: "${{ event.moment != 'labeled' || event.label == 'run-e2e' }}"
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 4 * * MON-FRI"
      timezone: America/Chicago
      inputs: { environment: staging, component: web }
  depot:
    image: harbor-lights/base-go
    tags: ["1.*"]
    when: "${{ event.signed }}"
    inputs: { base: "${{ event.digest }}" }
  run_result:
    project: platform-library
    pipeline: publish
    result: succeeded
    when: "${{ event.run.branch == 'main' }}"
    inputs: { library_version: "${{ event.outputs.publish.version }}" }
  webhook:
    name: hotfix-request
    when: "${{ event.body.severity in ['high', 'critical'] }}"
    dedupe: "${{ event.body.incident.id }}"
    inputs:
      version: "${{ event.body.version }}"
      environment: prod
lane: { name: storefront, per: [ref], when_busy: wait }
Design: not built

Further kinds, each a separate snippet of the same on: mapping.

on:
  launch_result:                   # payments reached staging: run the contract tests
    project: payments
    environment: staging
    result: deployed
    inputs: { payments_version: "${{ event.launch.version }}" }

  environment:                     # the prod Hold ended: launch what waited
    name: prod
    moments: [hold_ended]

  release:                         # a release was published: build the kiosk image
    moments: [published]
    inputs: { version: "${{ event.release.version }}" }

  event:                           # a message on the order bus (a queue source)
    source: orders-bus
    when: "${{ event.body.type == 'checkout.errors.rising' }}"

    inputs: { environment: prod }

  together:                        # both happened within six hours
    within: 6h
    events:
      api:  { run_result: { project: storefront, pipeline: build-api, result: succeeded } }
      web:  { run_result: { project: storefront, pipeline: build-web, result: succeeded } }
    inputs:
      api_image: "${{ events.api.outputs.image.digest }}"
      web_image: "${{ events.web.outputs.image.digest }}"

One filter language

Today there are two ways to filter: patterns on push and pull_request, and a small home-grown expression language on event sources and triggers on results, while webhook cannot filter at all. The design keeps the patterns, because a branch list reads best as a list, and adds one when on every trigger, written in the one expression language inside ${{ }}. It is the same language as step conditions, run form rules and input defaults. Inside it, event holds what happened: event.kind, event.moment, event.ref, event.sha, event.actor, event.labels, event.body, event.run, event.launch, event.outputs, event.digest. The expression is type-checked when the pipeline is validated, has no loops and no calls out, and an error in it is a recorded error decision, never a silent false. Existing event source filters keep working and are read as the same language.

A pull request through its whole life

Today a pull request starts a Sortie when it is opened or its head moves. moments names the others. Leaving it out means [opened, updated], so no existing file changes.

MomentWhat runsTypical use in storefront
opened, updated AvailableThe pipeline at the head commitTests on every change
labeledThe pipeline at the head commit; event.label names the labelThe long browser suite, only when run-e2e is added
reviewedThe pipeline at the head commit; event.review is approved, changes requested or commentedBuild a preview Airfield after the first approving review
mergedThe pipeline at the merge commit on the target branchClean up the preview Airfield; post release notes
closedThe pipeline on the default branch (the head may be gone)Clean up the preview Airfield without merging

A label or review counts only when the person who gave it may write to the repository, so a label is not a way for an outsider to start privileged work. On a connected code host, moments arrive as the host's notices (hints) and are checked against the host's own answer; a host that cannot report a moment says so on the triggers page.

The rest of a pull request's life. Teams also act on smaller moments. Each one below is a value of moments, carries its facts in event, and has its own trust rule. The "reported by" column says where the moment comes from: the built-in code host reports every one; a connected host reports what its notices or its interface can tell, and Launchway checks the host's answer before it believes the notice.

MomentWhat runs, and what event holdsTrust ruleReported byTypical use in storefront
ready_for_reviewThe pipeline at the head; event.pull_request.draft is now falseAs updated: forks and automation accounts run restrictedThe built-in host; most connected hostsRun the long browser suite once the author says it is ready, not on every draft push
converted_to_draftThe pipeline at the head; draft is now trueAs updatedThe built-in host; most connected hostsTear down the preview Airfield pr-482 to save room
reopenedThe pipeline at the headAs opened; a first-time outside author still needs a maintainer's allowanceEvery hostRebuild the preview Airfield
editedThe pipeline at the head; event.changed lists title, body or baseCounts only when the editor may write to the repository; a changed base re-runs as updatedEvery hostRe-check that the title names a work item (STORE-41)
unlabeledThe pipeline at the head; event.label names the label removedCounts only when the person may writeThe built-in host; most connected hostsStop the nightly re-run of the browser suite when run-e2e is removed
review_requestedThe pipeline at the head; event.reviewer is a person or a Squadron (team)Counts only when the requester may writeThe built-in host; most connected hostsPost the Debrief (test report) summary for the reviewer who was asked
assignedThe pipeline at the head; event.assigneeCounts only when the assigner may writeThe built-in host; most connected hostsLink the pull request to the assignee's work item
auto_merge_enabledThe pipeline at the head; event.merge_methodCounts only when the person may mergeThe built-in host; hosts with automatic mergeRun the checks the merge queue needs before it is reached, so the queue is not the first to find a failure
commentedOnly for a declared command; see commands in a commentChecked per command: the commenter's right, the command declared on the default branchThe built-in host; hosts whose notices or interface include comments/launchway run e2e suite=checkout

A moment a host cannot report is refused when the pipeline is checked for a Flight on that host, with the host and the moment named, rather than accepted and never fired. A draft pull request runs opened and updated as today; a team that wants drafts quiet writes when: "${{ !event.pull_request.draft }}" and listens for ready_for_review.

Commands in a pull request comment

Sometimes a person wants to start work on a pull request by hand without leaving it: run the long suite once, build a preview, retry one step. A comment command does that. It is a trigger like any other: declared in the pipeline file, judged by the rules on the default branch, turned into typed inputs, and recorded with its reason.

  • Grammar. A command is a line that starts with /launchway, then a verb, then name=value arguments. The verbs are run <command>, retry <step> (the latest Sortie of this pull request), cancel and help. Only the first command line of a comment counts; quoted text and code blocks are ignored, so quoting someone's command does not run it again.
  • Declared, typed arguments. Each command is declared under on.pull_request.commands, with the pipeline it runs and its arguments mapped to the pipeline's inputs. Arguments are checked by the same rules as a run form: a choice must be one of its options, a version must parse, a picker with options_from must name something that exists. A missing or wrong argument gets a reply with the usage and the allowed values, never a Sortie with a guess.
  • A permission check. The commenter must be able to write to the repository, and the command may narrow it further (allow: [pilot, controller]). The check uses Launchway's own record of the person, through the host's identity mapping; a host account Launchway cannot map gets a refusal that says so.
  • Forks. A command on a pull request from a fork starts a restricted Sortie (no secrets, no Launch (deployment), no cache writes) even when a maintainer types it. The fork's own author can never start one with a command. Allowing a fork's code to see secrets stays a separate, deliberate maintainer action, as today.
  • A reply with the link. Launchway answers in one reply under the comment: started, with the Sortie's link and the inputs it used; refused, with the reason and who could run it; or the list of commands from help. The reply is edited with the result when the Sortie ends. On a host that cannot reply, the result is in the pull request's one summary comment, as statuses are today.
  • Once only. A comment is judged once, by its identity on the host. Editing a comment does not run it again; a new comment does.
  • Typed help where you type. On the built-in code host the comment box suggests the declared commands and, for each argument, its allowed values, filled from the same sources as the run form. No other host gets this, because Launchway does not control their comment boxes; there help does the same job.
Design: not built

commands, allow and the /launchway grammar are designs. Key names are not final.

on:
  pull_request:
    into: [main]
    commands:
      e2e:
        pipeline: e2e
        allow: [pilot, controller]
        args:
          suite: { input: suite }            # input suite: { type: choice, options: [checkout, search, all] }
          environment: { input: environment, default: "pr-${{ event.pull_request.number }}" }
      preview:
        pipeline: preview
        allow: [pilot]

Patrols

A Patrol is a five-field schedule in a named time zone (America/Chicago, never "local"). When clocks go forward a missing time is skipped; when they go back a repeated time fires once. Each firing is claimed in the database, so it starts one Sortie however many servers run. A Patrol never fires for the past; after an outage it starts one Sortie for the latest missed time. Patrols are read only from the default branch, so a branch cannot schedule itself. All of this is available today. The design adds inputs as expressions (for example the week number), a when filter, and the next five firings shown on the triggers page with any daylight-saving change marked.

From the Depot, from releases and from Airfields

These events come from inside Launchway, so they are authentic by construction and carry facts, not a payload someone wrote. A depot trigger fires when a tag or version matching the pattern arrives, with the digest, signature state and Inspection (security scan) verdict in the event; it is proposed on the Depot side as "An event when something arrives in the Depot" (the Depot). When the Depot capability is served by a connected registry instead, its notices are hints and a periodic check is the source of truth, so a lost notice costs time, never a missed rebuild. A release trigger fires when a release is published, promoted or returned. An environment trigger fires when an Airfield's Hold starts or ends, when drift is found, or when its settings change.

From other Sorties and Launches

Triggers on results work today, with two sides of consent: the upstream Flight allows a downstream Flight to follow it (and, separately, to read its outputs), and the downstream Flight says what it waits for. Cycles are refused, history starts nothing, no secret, log or file crosses, and each result is judged once. The design moves the downstream half into the pipeline file as run_result and launch_result; the upstream allowance stays in the product, because it is a permission. Triggers created in the product today keep working, appear on the same triggers page, and offer "Move into the pipeline file", which opens a change with the equivalent lines.

Incoming webhooks, event sources, queues and buses

There are two incoming shapes, for two needs. A webhook belongs to one pipeline: its address ends in the trigger's name, its secret is named in the server's configuration, and today it maps body fields to inputs with a closed mapping. An event source belongs to a Flight and can feed many pipelines: it is created in the product with a sealed signing secret shown once, an optional JSON Schema, size and rate limits, debounce or batch windows and a dedupe key. In the design both filter and map the same way, both are signed, time-limited and single-use, and a pipeline subscribes to an event source with on.event.

Message queues and event buses are planned as event sources of their own kind. An operator names the connection, the topic or queue and the consumer group; the source reads through the Detachment (site agent) when the broker is on a private network; a message is acknowledged only after it has a start or a recorded reason; an ordering key keeps per-key order; and a message that cannot start goes to the list of starts that failed, with its reason, where a person can retry it. Pipelines subscribe exactly as they do to an HTTP source. A reply can be sent back on a named reply queue when the Sortie ends.

When several things have happened

together fires when every named event has happened within a window, and passes each of them to the inputs by name, not only the last. In storefront it starts the end-to-end suite only after both the api and the web builds of the same commit succeeded. An event that arrives with no partner inside the window is recorded as waiting until the window closes, then filtered with "no build-web result within 6 hours". A when on the whole can require the parts to agree (for example the same commit).

From event data to typed inputs

A trigger never hands the whole payload to a script. Each input is one expression over event, and the result is checked like a person's answer against the pipeline's input definition: its kind, its options, its pattern, whether the value must exist now. An input the trigger does not give takes its default. A value that fails is a refused decision with a message per input, never a Sortie with a guessed value. The mapping is checked against the inputs of the pipeline at the commit that will run when the pipeline is validated, so a renamed input breaks the build of the pipeline file, not a Sortie at three in the morning.

Duplicates, superseded Sorties, queueing and lanes

NeedHowToday
The same call sent twiceIdempotency-Key on a webhook; a dedupe key on an event source; in the design, dedupe on any trigger, an expressionAvailable for webhooks and event sources
A burst of eventsdebounce (start once after quiet) or batch (start once with all of them)Available on event sources
An old event arriving lateIn the design, order_by: an older event that arrives after a newer one is superseded, not runNot available
Runs that must take turnslane: { name, per, when_busy: wait|cancel|skip, queue: newest|all }Available
A newer push replacing an older Sortiesupersede: true (on by default for pull requests); a Sortie holding an open Launch is never supersededAvailable
A burst of automation pull requestsRun limits per Flight, per pipeline, per kind and for automation accounts; the default branch is never heldAvailable

Trust: who may arm a trigger

The rule behind every row: an event that the change itself did not cause is judged by the declarations on the default branch, which someone reviewed. A change can only arm what reviewed code already allows.

TriggerWhose declaration countsThe Sortie runs asRestricted when
pushThe pipeline at the pushed commitThe person or account that pushedLaunchway's own write-back commits never start a Sortie (decided; to be verified in the code); automation accounts follow their run limits
pull_requestBoth the default branch tip and the head must ask, for that momentThe authorA fork, an automation account, or a first-time outside author until a maintainer allows the run
scheduleThe default branch tipThe Patrol (patrol:<name>)Never
webhook, eventThe default branch tipThe source (source:<name>)A source marked untrusted by its owner
run_result, launch_result, togetherThe default branch tip, and the upstream's allowanceresult:<flight>#<number>When the upstream Sortie was restricted
depot, release, environmentThe default branch tipThe triggerWhen what arrived was pushed by a restricted Sortie
A personThe pipeline at the ref they choseThe person, with their own rightsNever beyond their rights; a draft never launches

Signed calls are time-limited (five minutes) and single-use; a bearer token is accepted where configured, and the page says plainly that a token can be replayed by anyone who sees one request. Every failed call gets the same answer whatever the reason, is recorded as unverified and counts toward the limit on failed attempts. Unverified events are kept separately and fewer of them, so a flood cannot push real events out of the record. In the design, a chain of triggers carries its chain: a cycle is refused when the pipeline is validated, and a chain longer than a Base limit stops with a recorded reason.

Every decision explained and replayable

The event log is available today: every received event, each trigger's decision (started, held, waiting, filtered, superseded, skipped, duplicate, refused, error) with a sentence, the Sortie it started, and Replay for a verified event. Three things are added.

The triggers page

For one pipeline, two lists: what starts it, and what it starts. Each trigger shows where it is declared (a file and line, or a product object), its last ten decisions as icons and words, and for Patrols the next firings. The same page exists for a Flight, a Squadron (team) and the Base, drawn as a graph of pipelines and the arrows between them. Planned as "A triggers page".

Try an event

Pick a past event, or a sample from a source, and see what each trigger of a changed pipeline would decide, with the inputs it would map, before you merge. Nothing starts. It is the trigger half of the Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it) proposed in Pipelines, values and expressions. New in this plan

Replay with today's rules

Replay today repeats the same ref and inputs. The design adds a choice: repeat as before, or judge the stored event against the current triggers and say what changed. An unverified event can be replayed only to see the decision. New in this plan

How events arrive, and how late

Today a connected code host's webhook starts a Sortie at once, and polling is both the fallback and the check: a Flight whose connection has had no delivery for five minutes is polled through the host's interface every minute, and a host with no webhooks at all is only polled. That works, but nobody can see which of the two is happening, or what it costs in time. The triggers page adds one panel per connected host.

ShownWhat it says, for Harbor Lights' code host connection
How events arriveOne of three states, as an icon and a word: Webhook (deliveries arriving, polling only as a check), Polling (no delivery for more than five minutes, polled every minute), Polling only (the host has no webhooks)
Delay from push to SortieThe median and the slowest of the last day, measured from the commit's push time on the host to the "started" decision on the record: "median 3 s, slowest 41 s (during 12 minutes of polling)"
Last deliveryWhen the last verified delivery arrived, how many were refused as unverified today, and how many were ignored as repeats
What to doWhen polling has lasted more than an hour, a sentence with the next step: "The host has not called Launchway since 09:12. Check the webhook on the repository; Poll now fetches at once."

The same figures are in the API and on the command line, and a long stretch of polling raises a notice in Comms (notifications), so a broken webhook is found in minutes, not when someone wonders why the builds are slow.

Events out, in one open standard event format

Launchway already sends signed notifications and repository webhooks in its own shapes. The design adds one format any event router understands: each record event is sent in the CloudEvents 1.0 format, an open standard event format. The id is the record's event id, so a receiver can ignore repeats by source and id; the type names what happened; data holds the same scrubbed facts the event page shows. It is signed with the same timestamped signature as today's notifications. Delivery uses today's notification channels with their delivery log and retries, a pull stream for systems that prefer to ask, and, once queue sources exist, the same queue connections in the other direction.

Design: not built

A Launch event as it would be sent. Type names are not final.

{
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "id": "evt_01JD7Q9K2W",
  "source": "https://launchway.example.com/flights/storefront",
  "type": "launchway.launch.finished",
  "subject": "prod/storefront-api",
  "time": "(the time it happened, RFC 3339)",
  "datacontenttype": "application/json",
  "traceparent": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01",
  "data": {
    "verdict": "deployed",
    "environment": "prod",
    "version": "2.4.0",
    "digest": "sha256:4f9c...a17",
    "sortie": 417,
    "url": "https://launchway.example.com/runs/417"
  }
}

Events out include Sorties queued, started and finished; Clearances (approvals) asked and answered; Launches started, finished and returned to base; Holds; Depot arrivals; releases; Switch (feature toggle) changes; and trigger decisions themselves. A subscriber sees only events of Flights its token may read.

Pipeline to pipeline: start another and wait for its answer

A trigger is fire-and-forget: the upstream does not know what it started. Sometimes a pipeline needs the answer. A step of kind pipeline starts another pipeline with typed inputs, waits without holding a Station (runner), and receives the outputs that pipeline declares. Everything is a step, so it takes needs, when, timeout and retry like any other.

Design: not built

No step can start another pipeline today; a team uses a trigger on results, or calls a webhook from a script. kind: pipeline and pipeline outputs are designs.

# storefront, the caller
steps:
  contracts:
    kind: pipeline
    needs: build
    project: payments
    pipeline: contract-check
    with:
      api_version: "${{ steps.build.outputs.version }}"
      consumer: storefront
    timeout: 30m
  launch-staging:
    kind: deploy
    needs: contracts
    when: "${{ steps.contracts.outputs.verdict == 'compatible' }}"
    environment: staging
    version: "${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}"

# payments, the pipeline that is called
pipeline: contract-check
inputs:
  api_version: { type: version, scheme: semver }
  consumer:    { type: string, options_from: flights }
outputs:
  verdict: "${{ steps.check.outputs.verdict }}"

The called Flight must allow the caller, as for triggers on results; the allowance is held in the product and shown on both triggers pages. The called Sortie appears inside the caller's step with its live state, and on its own Flight as "started by storefront Sortie #417, step contracts". A cycle (storefront calls payments calls storefront) is refused when either pipeline is validated.

Not a goal: a durable workflow engine at very large scale

Some platforms run code-first workflows in which each step is a durable call, at a scale of millions of steps for agents. Launchway does not try to be that engine. When a pipeline needs one, a step starts the workflow on the outside engine through a provider Hardpoint (Hardpoints), waits for its answer without holding a Station, and records the workflow's identity and its typed result, exactly as start-and-wait does for another pipeline. The workflow's own history stays in its engine; the Sortie links to it.

Built today

One start or one recorded reason per event and trigger, across servers; Patrols claimed per firing with daylight-saving rules and one catch-up; signed webhooks accepted once within five minutes with idempotency keys; event sources with sealed secrets, JSON Schema, filters, mapping, dedupe, debounce and batch; triggers on results with consent on both sides and cycle refusal; replay of verified events, recorded in the Logbook.

Documentation to reconcile

The triggers guide still says reporting a Sortie's outcome to a pull request is "not there yet", while the outside-host guide lists commit statuses as working. The software graph guide lists starting dependents after a push as not built, while the command line can create such triggers. Both should be corrected before this chapter is published.

The foundation it relies on

  • Git for declarations, the product for permissions and secrets. What starts a pipeline is written with the pipeline. Incoming endpoints, sealed secrets, queue connections and one Flight's allowance for another live in the product, where access is managed.
  • The record. An event and its decisions are rows; a start is written with its Sortie in one transaction.
  • The expression language. Filters, mappings and dedupe keys are ${{ }} expressions, checked when the pipeline is validated.
  • Inputs. Event data becomes values only through the input definition and its checks (inputs and run forms).
  • The Detachment. Brokers and systems on private networks are reached outward from the customer's side.
  • Every way in. The triggers page, try an event, replay and subscriptions exist in the web, the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and, for product-held objects, Terraform.

Safety

When something fails

  • An event accepted with a success answer is stored first; a crash afterwards cannot lose it.
  • A start that fails for a passing reason (the database is busy, a server is restarting) is retried with growing pauses, then kept in the list of starts that failed with the last error, where a person can retry it.
  • A code host's notice that never arrives costs latency: polling finds the push anyway.
  • When Patrols are switched off, firings are recorded as skipped, and switching them back on does not run a backlog.
  • A trigger whose filter has an error records error with the expression and the value; it never quietly evaluates to false.

Who may do what

  • Anyone who may change the pipeline file on the default branch may change its triggers, through review.
  • Operators of a Flight create event sources and see their secret once; rotating a secret ends the old one at once.
  • Only the upstream Flight's operators may allow another Flight to follow or call it, and to read its outputs.
  • Operators replay events; a replay is a manual start recorded in the Logbook with their name.
  • A trigger can never start what its source could not start by hand.

On by default

  • Pull requests from forks and automation accounts run restricted.
  • Webhooks and event sources require a signature or token; the same answer for every failure.
  • Size and rate limits per source; payloads scrubbed of credential-like values.
  • Pushes to the default branch are never held behind automation.
  • Launchway's own write-back commits never start a Sortie (decided; to be verified in the code).

Screens

Full descriptions are in the screens notes for this chapter and on the screens page.

  1. Triggers page for a pipeline: "What starts storefront" and "What storefront starts", each trigger with its declaration, last decisions and next firings; the same page for a Flight, a Squadron and the Base as a graph.
  2. Add a trigger, a wizard: pick the kind, fill each field with pickers (branch patterns with a preview, moment checkboxes, a Patrol builder with a time zone picker, Depot repository and tag pattern, upstream Flight and result), build the filter from chips, map inputs by clicking fields of a sample event, and finish by opening a reviewable change to the pipeline file.
  3. Event detail: the scrubbed payload, verified or not, each trigger's decision and sentence, the Sortie it started, Replay.
  4. Try an event: pick a past event or a sample and see each trigger's decision for the pipeline as it is, or as it would be after a change.
  5. Event source page, including a queue source: address or topic, secret rotation, schema, limits, subscribed pipelines, recent events.
  6. Starts that failed: the list with the last error and a Retry button.
  7. Patrol editor: frequency, days and time as chips, an IANA time zone picker, and the next five firings with daylight-saving changes marked.
  8. A called pipeline inside a step on the Sortie page, and Send events out: a subscription with the open standard event format as a format choice and a test delivery.
  9. Pull request moments in the Add a trigger wizard: every moment as a checkbox with its one-line meaning, and those the Flight's host cannot report shown unavailable with the reason.

Comment commands: the Add a command wizard (command name, pipeline picked from a list, arguments mapped to inputs by picking, roles allowed as checkboxes, a preview of the help reply), the reply as it appears on the pull request (started, refused, help), and on the built-in host the comment box suggesting commands and argument values.
