Open question

The command prefix

Comment commands start with /launchway. A shorter prefix is easier to type but more likely to collide with other bots on the same pull request. Confirm /launchway, or let a Wing (organization) choose its own from a short list.

Commands on forks

This chapter makes a command on a fork's pull request start only a restricted Sortie, even when a maintainer types it, so a comment can never hand secrets to outside code. The alternative is to let a Controller's command count as the maintainer's allowance. Recommendation: keep the two separate.

"Triggers defined in the product" and "pipelines in Git"

You asked for triggers defined in the product, showing which pipelines they call, and for pipelines kept in Git. This chapter reads both: the product is where you see, create and try triggers (its wizard writes a reviewable change to the pipeline file), while the declaration lives in Git and the secrets and permissions live in the product. Today event sources and triggers on results are held only in the product. Confirm the direction, or keep product-held triggers as a second way.

The word for pull request moments

The model sheet sketched a list key for pull request activity. This chapter calls it moments, uses the same key for releases and Airfields, and avoids a key name another tool made familiar. Key names are not final.

A delivery event vocabulary

The event format is the stable open standard. A shared vocabulary for delivery events (pipeline started, artifact published, service deployed) is being standardized alongside it but is not yet at a first stable version. Adopt that vocabulary for outgoing event types now, pinned to a version, or keep Launchway's own type names until it is stable?

Two incoming shapes

A pipeline's own webhook and a Flight's event source both receive signed calls. This chapter keeps both (one belongs to a pipeline, one feeds many) and makes them filter and map the same way. Alternatively, every incoming endpoint becomes an event source and on.webhook is read as a subscription to one. Choose before queue sources are built.

Bringing work in

Point Launchway at what you have and see it running here, with an honest account, construct by construct, of what came across.

  • Launchway reads the pipelines, templates, packaged steps, shared libraries, variables, triggers, approvals, deployments and policies of every major kind of build and delivery system, and writes as much of it as it can into its own model, even when the result is incomplete.
  • Every construct ends in one of three outcomes: converted exactly, converted with a stated difference, or needs a person, with the next step written out. Nothing is dropped silently and no behavior is invented.
  • The result is a proposal in a pull request, checked by the same checker as any pipeline. Your original files are never touched, and an unfinished import cannot launch anything.
  • You scan first, convert one pipeline, run it side by side with the old one, compare, and cut over one pipeline at a time.
  • Five source formats are built today. This chapter adds the rest, and uses the richer pipeline model (expressions, typed outputs, custom steps, Maneuvers, Flight plans, run forms, triggers, Launches) as real targets the importer lacked.
  • The repository itself comes first: moving it in, with its issues, pull requests, releases and wikis, is the optional first step of the same guided flow, and its verify report and mirror back sit beside the pipeline comparison.
  • Switches (feature toggles) come across too, with a dry run and an evaluation check against the old service, and a whole Flight or Base can move between self-hosted and hosted, in either direction, after a preview.

Where it sits

Import belongs to layer 3 of the map, the flight plan layer (authoring): its output is an ordinary pipeline file, library and configuration, written in the same words as anything a person writes. It reads through layer 1 (connections to code hosts, levels, the names of secrets), writes every finding and decision to layer 2 (the record), runs its side-by-side Sorties (runs) in layer 4, lands deployments in layer 5 and policies, approvals and freezes in layer 6. The Wingman (AI helper) in layer 7 may help finish what needs a person, when it is turned on.

Builds on
The one pipeline graph and the expression language in ${{ }} (Pipelines, values and expressions), tested custom steps (Code you can test), Maneuvers (step templates), Flight plans (pipeline templates) and libraries (Reuse that keeps growing), typed inputs and run forms (Inputs and run forms), triggers and Patrols (schedules) (what starts a Sortie), the one Launch (deployment) model and the Route (promotion path) (One way to launch, anywhere), Standing orders (policies), Clearances (approvals) and Holds (freezes) (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold).
Used by
Every team arriving from another system; the coverage chapter, which reads the importer's classification as evidence of what Launchway matches; the Wingman's import purpose (the Wingman and agents).
Layers
3 (authoring), with 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7.
Built today
An importer for five file formats, with the three-outcome report, a dry mode that keeps delivery off, the guide "Move your pipelines over", a web wizard, the command launchway import pipeline, the API call POST /api/v1/import/pipeline and the agent tool import_pipeline.

What you will be able to do

You connect Launchway to the code host where your Wing (organization) keeps its forty repositories and press Scan. Before anything is converted, you see every pipeline found, which kind of system it was written for, how many constructs it uses, which packaged steps appear and how often, which secrets it names, and how many of those pipelines would convert with nothing left for a person. Each pipeline has a size, small, medium or large, and the rule that gave it that size.

You pick the smallest pipeline and press Convert. A pull request appears that adds one pipeline file and nothing else. The report beside it lists 41 constructs: 27 converted exactly, 11 with a stated difference you read once, and 3 that need you, each with the file, the line, the reason and the next step. The checker has already passed the proposal, and the three unfinished places fail loudly if anyone runs them.

You merge it with delivery switched off. For a week every push runs in both systems. The comparison page pairs the old run with the Sortie for the same commit and shows, step by step, where they agree and where they do not: a test that failed only here, a build that took twice as long, an archive with one file missing.

A packaged step from outside has no equivalent in Launchway. The import wrote a custom step skeleton in your repository with a manifest made from the inputs the old pipeline passed it, a test that fails until it is written, and a note naming what the step must do. The Wingman, which your Wing has turned on for imports, proposes the code and the tests as a change you review. You accept it, the test passes, and the finding closes.

Your old deployment pipeline sent ten percent of traffic to a new version, checked error rates, then widened. The import turns it into a Launch with a Pathfinder (canary) and Overwatch (post-deploy watch), on a Route through staging and prod. The old freeze window becomes a Hold on prod, the old approval stage a Clearance, and of the two policies the old platform enforced, one matches a Standing order exactly and the other is kept, marked as needing a person.

Results have agreed for a week and no finding is open. You press Cut over. Launchway opens one change that turns delivery on, records the decision in the Logbook (audit trail), and offers a second change that removes the old files when you are ready. If something goes wrong, turning delivery off again is one line.

How it works

The principles of import

Generate as much as possible

An incomplete pipeline that runs most of the work is worth more than a refusal. The importer converts every construct it can, keeps going past the ones it cannot, and writes a skeleton where it cannot write the whole.

Never drop, never invent

Every construct the importer meets is classified and reported. A construct it does not understand stays visible in the proposal and the report. It never guesses a behavior the old file did not state.

Three outcomes, each with a next step

Converted exactly, converted with a stated difference, or needs a person. A construct that needs a person always says why and what to do; a test refuses a table entry without a next step.

Your files are never touched

The importer reads. It does not run, fetch or evaluate anything in the files, and never changes or deletes them. Removing the old files is a separate change a person opens at cut-over.

A proposal a person reviews

The result is a pull request, checked by the same checker and the same Standing orders as any pipeline change. An import authorizes nothing that a hand-written pipeline would not.

Unfinished means grounded

A converted pipeline that still needs a person cannot launch anything. Delivery starts switched off, unfinished places fail when run, and a Launch from a pipeline with open findings is refused.

The three outcomes

OutcomeWhat it meansWhat the proposal containsWhat you do
Converted exactlyLaunchway does the same thing.The converted construct.Nothing.
Converted with a differenceConverted, and the finding states the one way the behavior differs (a service reached at a different host name, a cache kept under Launchway's rules, a time limit that now applies per step).The converted construct and a comment naming the finding.Read it once and accept it, or change the line.
Needs a personNot converted, or converted only as a skeleton. The finding gives the reason and the next step.A step that prints NEEDS A PERSON and fails, or a custom step skeleton whose test fails until it is written, with the original kept beside it for reference.Finish it, by hand or by accepting a reviewed proposal from the Wingman.

The classification is data. Each source format has a table of every construct it knows, with its outcome, its plain note and its next step. The same table produces the findings, the guide's pages and the public quality numbers, so none of them can drift from what the importer does. A test checks that the outcomes of a file add up to every construct read.

What is imported, and where it lands

Launchway's model has one graph of typed steps, one expression language and one way to reuse, so many shapes from other systems land in fewer places here. The table lists every kind of thing teams keep in a build and delivery system.

Kind of thing in the old systemWhere it lands in LaunchwayHow it comes across
Pipeline files, with their jobs, stages and stepsOne pipeline, one graph of steps joined by needs (Pipelines, values and expressions)Stage order becomes dependencies; jobs become steps; commands carry over in one script per step.
Conditions and expressionsExpressions in ${{ }}, type-checked before the Sortie, and the closed when: tests where they fitTranslated where the meaning is exact; a stated difference where the old language converted types loosely; needs a person only for a function with no counterpart. Today most of these fall to "the job now always runs", because the pipeline file had no expression language to land in.
Variables and their scopesVariables at the right level: Base (installation), Wing, Squadron (team), Flight (codebase), pipeline or stepValues written in the file carry over at the level they were written; variables kept in the old system's settings become names to create, at the level the scan found them used.
Secret referencesSecret references bound to steps, resolved on the Station (runner)Names only. No value is ever read, copied or stored. The report lists every name to create. A value an old file pasted into script text moves into an env binding, and the finding says the result is safer than the original.
Values passed between jobsTyped outputs on steps, read as ${{ steps.name.outputs.key }}Exact where the old file declared the value; a stated difference where the type had to be inferred.
Matrices and fan-outfor_each, with exclusions and added entries; fan-out over a list an earlier step producedStatic lists convert exactly today. Lists made at run time land on fan-out over a step's output.
Services beside a job, caches and artifactsServices on the step, caches keyed by files, Cargo (artifacts) kept and fetched by nameMostly exact; host names, cache scope and retention are stated differences.
Reusable templates, packaged steps and shared librariesManeuvers, Flight plans, custom steps and a library, pinned by tag (Reuse that keeps growing)A whole reusable pipeline becomes a Flight plan; a reusable piece becomes a Maneuver; code that was inline past the limit, or written in a scripting language the step runner does not run, is lifted into a custom step with a manifest and a generated test skeleton (Code you can test).
Triggers and schedulesTriggers declared in the pipeline, filtered in the same expression language, and Patrols (What starts a Sortie)Pushes, pull requests, tags, paths and times convert exactly; other events land on the declared triggers for another Sortie, a Launch, a Depot (registry) push or an outside event.
Run forms and parametersTyped inputs with pickers (Inputs and run forms)Types, defaults, choices and patterns carry over; an input that listed environments, branches or images becomes a picker of Airfields (environments), branches or Depot images.
Environments, approvals and freezesAirfields, Clearances with Go and No-go, Holds (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold)Protection rules kept in the old system are read where an export holds them; otherwise the finding says they were not read and asks for a Clearance.
Deployment definitions and strategiesLaunch steps, a strategy (all at once, rolling, Pathfinder, two-fleet swap), Overwatch and a Route (One way to launch, anywhere)What is deployed and where becomes a Launch to an Airfield; the order of environments becomes a Route; checks after a deployment become Overwatch.
Policies written in an established open policy languageStanding orders where a catalog rule matches; otherwise kept as rules for the import pathA policy that means the same as a catalog rule is replaced by that rule, exactly. Any other policy is kept as a file and marked needs a person until custom rules can run (see open for you).
Machines and labels the old jobs asked forA container image on a Station chosen by Launchway, or a Station of that kind from a Ramp (runner pool)A stated difference; a Windows or macOS machine needs a Station of that kind.
History: past runs, logs, test results, old artifactsNot importedHistory stays in the old system. Launchway's record starts with the first Sortie. The report says so in its first line, so nobody looks for it.

Which source systems

The importer recognizes a format by the file's place and its contents, not by its name alone. A file in the wrong place can be named with --from. Formats are listed by the kind of system and the shape of its files, as the product's guide does.

Kind of systemIdentified byTodayWith this plan
Hosted workflow filesYAML files in a workflows folder of a code host's dot-directory, the same layout on a self-hosted forge (--from hosted-workflows)Built. 60 constructs: 18 exact, 20 with a difference, 22 need a personExpressions, job outputs, run-time matrices, more events; reusable workflow files and packaged-step metadata files read when they are supplied
Stage-based YAMLA .*-ci.yml file at the top of the repository (--from stages-yaml)Built. 44 constructs: 16, 12, 16Rule expressions, includes from other repositories when supplied, reusable components, child and generated pipelines
A self-hosted automation server: declarative pipeline filesA file with a pipeline { } block (--from groovy-declarative)Built. 38 constructs: 13, 10, 15Program conditions as expressions where the shape is recognized; tool installations mapped to images
A self-hosted automation server: scripted pipeline filesA file whose top is a node { } programDetected; the recognized stages are listed; not convertedStages, commands, parallel branches and common conditions read from the program without running it; everything else lifted into skeletons
A self-hosted automation server: shared librariesA repository with folders of global steps, classes and resourcesDetected where a pipeline uses one; not convertedConverted into a Launchway library: global steps to Maneuvers, logic to custom step skeletons with tests, pinned by the same tag
A self-hosted automation server: jobs kept only in its settingsExported job configuration files (XML) and the list of plug-ins and credentials (names only)Not readAn inventory of every job, folder, trigger and credential name, and conversion of jobs that have no pipeline file
Job-based hosted configurationconfig.yml in a dot-directory at the top of the repository (--from jobs-config)Built. 30 constructs: 13, 7, 10Parameters, shared packages read when supplied, matrix jobs, generated configuration
Task pipelinesA file named *-pipelines.yml at the top of the repository (--from tasks-pipelines)Built. 33 constructs: 13, 10, 10Step, job and stage templates and extending templates, variable groups from an export, environments with their checks, deployment strategies, named matrices
A commercial delivery platform's pipelines, templates and policiesExported YAML of pipelines, templates of every size, saved sets of run values, service and environment definitions, freeze windows, and policy filesNot readPipelines to pipelines, templates to Maneuvers and Flight plans, services and environments to Launches and Airfields, strategies to Launch strategies, approvals to Clearances, freezes to Holds, policies to Standing orders or kept rules
Agent-based pipelines with uploaded stepsA pipeline YAML file in a dot-directory, often with a script that uploads more steps while the build runsNot readCommand steps, waits, pause-for-input steps, plug-ins, concurrency limits, retries, matrices; uploaded steps to generated steps
Cluster-native tasks and workflowsKubernetes resources (YAML) describing tasks, pipelines, runs, workflows, workflow templates, scheduled workflows, event sources and sensorsNot readTasks to custom steps or Maneuvers, graphs to the step graph, shared volumes to the workspace, results to typed outputs, clean-up steps to steps that always run, schedules to Patrols, event sensors to declared triggers
Container-step pipelinesOne or more YAML files in a dot-directory, in which each step names a container imageNot readSteps, services, conditions, matrices; plug-in images to library steps or skeletons
Build-chain serversProject settings exported as XML, or kept as code in a typed programming language in a settings folderNot readBuild configurations to pipelines, chains of dependent builds to needs and Sortie triggers, shared configuration templates to Maneuvers, parameters to typed inputs; settings written as code read only from their exported form
Code-defined pipelinesA program that uses a pipeline toolkit in a general-purpose language, with the toolkit's module fileNot readWrapped whole as one custom step that runs on a Station, then split into steps by a person (see the hard cases)
GitOps controllers and deployment serversApplication definitions, sync and promotion settings; release processes and multi-stage delivery pipelines exported as YAML or JSONNot readLaunch steps, Airfields, a Route and Holds; existing applications adopted rather than redeployed
Built today

Five formats, 205 known constructs in all: 73 converted exactly, 59 with a stated difference, 73 that need a person, plus ten notes every import adds (a standard language job replaced by a built-in template, a job with no image, a secret read by name, a delivering step switched off, and others). The test files are written for Launchway from each format's public reference, not copied from real pipelines. The importer is on the main branch with its guide, wizard, command, API call and agent tool; the roadmap still lists "A converter and a move-over guide" as Planned (see status).

What the richer model changes

Most of today's "needs a person" findings are not hard. They were refused because Launchway had nowhere to put them. Each new part of the model gives the importer a target, and the finding moves to a better outcome without any change to the reader's honesty.

Construct (any format)TodayWith this planWhat makes it possible
A condition written as an expressionNeeds a person: the job now always runsExact, or a stated difference where types were looseExpressions for conditions
A condition on one command inside a jobNeeds a person: the command always runsA stated difference: the command becomes its own step with the conditionExpressions for conditions
A value one job passes to a later jobNeeds a personExact: a typed outputTyped outputs between steps
A matrix built at run time from dataNeeds a personA stated difference: fan-out over a list a step producedFan-out over a list a step produced (proposed in Pipelines, values and expressions)
Steps generated while the build runsNeeds a personA stated difference: generated steps, checked like written onesGenerated pipelines
A call to a reusable pipeline or template in another fileNeeds a personExact when that file is supplied: a Flight plan or Maneuver in a libraryShare and pin steps and templates
A packaged step from outsideNeeds a person, apart from a handful of known onesMapped to a built-in or library equivalent by a catalog, or a custom step skeletonCustom steps in your own language; the catalog proposed here
Runs that must not overlapNeeds a person: add a laneExact: a lane, written by the importerConditions, retries, lanes and re-runs (already available)
Events other than push, pull request and timeNeeds a personExact or a stated difference: a declared trigger on another Sortie, a Launch, a Depot push, a pull request label or an outside eventThe triggers in what starts a Sortie
A run input that listed environmentsA difference: written as plain textExact: an Airfield pickerTyped inputs with pickers
A deployment strategyNeeds a person: only the deploy steps carriedExact or a stated difference: a Launch with its strategy, Overwatch and Return to base (rollback)The one Launch model
A job on a Windows or macOS machineNeeds a personExact: a step on a Station of that kindWindows and macOS runners

The hard cases

Some constructs cannot be converted by reading alone. Each has one stated way through, and each way still ends in one of the three outcomes.

A pipeline written as a program

A scripted pipeline file, a build-chain server's settings written as code, and a code-defined pipeline are programs. The importer never runs them. It reads the shapes it can recognize without running anything (stages, shell commands, parallel branches, a branch test around a stage) and converts those. Everything else becomes a step that needs a person, with the original text kept beside it, line for line.

A code-defined pipeline whose toolkit runs its own containers has one more way: the program is wrapped whole as one custom step that runs on a Station, so it works on the first day (a stated difference: one step, one log, no graph). The team then splits it into steps at its own pace. Settings written as code on a build-chain server are read from their exported form, which the server writes for you, never by running the code.

Shared libraries

A shared library is imported on its own, from its repository, into a Launchway library with the same name and the same tags. Global steps whose bodies are glue become Maneuvers. Bodies with logic become custom step skeletons: a manifest made from the arguments the pipelines pass, the original code beside it for reference, and a generated test that fails until the step is written in a language the team picks. Pipelines that called the library are rewritten to use the new library at the same tag. Where the library's code plainly does what a built-in already does (copying files to hosts and restarting a service, for example), the finding suggests the built-in instead.

Dynamically generated pipelines

Some pipelines print more pipeline at run time: an uploaded list of steps, a generated child pipeline, a setup stage that writes the real configuration. The generator is lifted into a custom step that declares it generates steps. What it prints is still in the old format, so the step passes its output through the same importer at run time, and Launchway checks the result like any written step. If the generated text contains anything that needs a person, the Sortie stops before those steps run and shows the report. The finding is a stated difference, with the next step "change the generator to print Launchway steps", which removes the run-time conversion.

Conditions that call functions Launchway does not have

Function calls with an exact counterpart in the expression language are translated. Where the old language compared text and numbers loosely, or treated an empty text as false, the translation states the difference and writes the explicit test. A function with no counterpart (one that reads files, hashes them, or asks about any earlier job) becomes a small custom step that computes the value as a typed output; the condition then reads that output. The step is a skeleton with a test, so the finding is needs a person, but the shape is already right.

Third-party packaged steps

A catalog maps packaged steps from other systems, by name and version range, to a Launchway equivalent: a built-in step kind (an image build, a Launch, a cache), a Maneuver from the Hangar (the built-in library) or a step in a shared library. A mapped step converts exactly or with a stated difference, and the catalog entry says which. An unmapped step becomes a custom step skeleton: if the step's own metadata file is supplied, the manifest copies its declared inputs and outputs; otherwise the manifest is made from what the old pipeline passed it. The finding names what the step must do. The importer never downloads the packaged step.

The catalog is data in the product, with a test for every entry. Its size, and the share of packaged-step uses in the scanned Wing it covers, are shown in the inventory.

Things with no equivalent at all

A few constructs have no meaning in Launchway: a post-run action that fires only when the result changed from the previous run, a setting of the old server's own process, a step type only the old vendor runs. These stay visible as needs a person, with the original text and the plain reason. The coverage chapter reads the same list, so every construct with no equivalent is either answered by a planned item or recorded as a decision not to match it.

The guided flow: scan, convert one, compare, cut over

  1. Bring the repository (optional). Move the repository into Launchway's own code host, or connect the host where it stays. Either way is a full first step of this flow, described in the repository comes first.
  2. Scan. Through a connection to a code host (the same connections that move repositories in), or from an uploaded export of a server's settings, Launchway reads every pipeline file, template, library and settings export it can see, with read-only rights. It stores the report: counts, construct codes, files and lines. It does not store the files; they stay where they are.
  3. Inventory. One page answers the questions you ask before you commit: how many pipelines of which kind, which constructs appear and how often, which packaged steps are used and which of them the catalog maps, which secrets and variables are named, which pipelines would convert fully today, and a size for each pipeline with the rule that set it (small: no program code and at most five findings that need a person; medium: six to fifteen; large: more, or any program code). The size is an estimate and says so; it is checked against how long finished imports actually took.
  4. Convert one. You pick a pipeline. The proposal arrives as a pull request on a new branch that adds Launchway files and changes nothing else. Delivery steps are written switched off behind one input. The checker and the Flight's Standing orders judge it like any change.
  5. Side by side. After merging, both systems run on every push. Launchway pairs results by commit (below) and keeps the comparison open until you close it.
  6. Cut over. When results agree and no finding is open, Cut over opens one change that turns delivery on and records the decision. A second, separate change removes the old files when you choose. Pipelines move one by one; the inventory shows which have moved.

The repository comes first

Pipelines live in repositories, so a team that is moving everything starts with the repository. Launchway already does that part well, and the guided flow now begins with it rather than leaving it on a separate page.

Built today

Move your repositories in imports repositories, issues, pull requests, labels, milestones, releases and wikis from another Git host and keeps a mirror back while you switch. Full-ref import and a read-only issue archive brings every ref, including the source's pull request refs kept read-only, reports ref by ref in a verify step, and keeps another server's issues and comments as a read-only archive. Both are Available.

  • One flow, one page. The import page's first card is the repository: moved in, connected, or not yet chosen. Choosing "move in" runs the existing repository import from inside the flow; choosing "keep the host" connects it, and nothing about the repository changes.
  • The verify report gates the scan. The scan starts from the moved copy only when the verify step has passed ref by ref, so a pipeline is never converted from a half-copied repository. The inventory links to the verify report.
  • The mirror back keeps the old system running. While pipelines run side by side, pushes to the moved repository are mirrored to the old host, so the old pipelines keep running on every commit and the comparison has both sides. The comparison page shows the mirror's lag beside each commit; a commit the mirror has not delivered is "waiting for the mirror", never "no result".
  • Two cut-overs, in order. The pipeline cut-over turns delivery on in Launchway. The repository cut-over, a separate decision, stops the mirror back and marks the old repository read-only where the connection may. The page will not offer the repository cut-over while any of its pipelines still runs side by side, and says which.

Running side by side

Steps are paired by the import's own map from old jobs to new steps. For each pair the comparison shows the result, the time taken, the number of tests run, passed and failed (from the Debrief (test report) and any old report you upload), and the list of files kept as Cargo. A difference is one of four kinds: only here, only there, slower or faster beyond a margin, or different files. Each difference links to the import finding that most likely explains it. When the old system reported nothing for a commit, the comparison says "no result from the old system" and never counts it as agreement.

Today a dry import already writes delivery steps behind an enable_delivery input that is false by default, and the guide asks you to compare by hand. The comparison page, the pairing and the reading of old statuses are new in this plan.

The Wingman finishes what needs a person, when you let it

Where a Wing has turned on the Wingman's import purpose (it is off until a Commander (owner) turns it on), each finding that needs a person can carry a proposed completion: the custom step's code and its tests, a translated condition, a rewritten command, a suggested built-in in place of library code. A proposal is a reviewable change on the import's branch, labeled as written by the Wingman, checked by the same checker, and its tests must pass before it can be accepted. The finding closes only when a person accepts. The Wingman works with the asking person's rights or fewer, sees no secret value, and uses a local model first where one is configured. It never marks anything "converted exactly"; only the importer's table can.

Measuring import quality

  • A public table, generated. One page lists every format, every construct and its outcome, made by the same code that reports findings. The guide's tables are generated this way today; this plan adds one page across all formats with the totals and their history.
  • Tests from real pipelines. Today's test files are written for Launchway from each format's public reference. The plan adds a corpus taken from public repositories whose licenses allow it, with the origin and license kept beside each file. A format ships only with its corpus, and every "converted exactly" claim has a test file whose output is validated and run locally in the test suite.
  • A number that only goes up. The share of known constructs converted exactly is 73 of 205 today (36 percent), and 132 of 205 (64 percent) are converted exactly or with a stated difference. The plan adds the same share weighted by how often each construct appears in the corpus, which is what a team actually feels. Both are kept in a quality baseline that may only rise: a change that lowers either fails the build unless a reason is recorded.
  • Claims stay honest. A wrong "exact" is worse than an honest "needs a person". Moving a construct to a better outcome needs a test that proves it, and a reported mistake moves it back first and fixes it second.

Switches from another toggle service

Teams that used an outside feature-flag service bring their flags with them, and sometimes they must: a service can announce that it will retire its flag product. Launchway imports Switches (feature toggles) as it imports pipelines: read everything, convert what it can, say plainly what it could not, and prove the result before anyone relies on it. The model the flags land in is described in Switches.

In the old serviceWhere it landsHow it comes across
Flags with their kind and variationsSwitches of the same kind (on or off, a choice of values, a number, a structured value)Exact for on or off and choices; a stated difference where a value type is wider than Launchway's
EnvironmentsAirfields (environments), mapped by picking: production to prodExact once mapped; an unmapped environment is listed and its rules are not imported until it is
Targeting rules and percentage rolloutsSwitch rules in the same order, with the same percentages and the same bucketing attributeExact where the operators exist (equals, in a list, a version comparison, a percentage); needs a person for an operator Launchway lacks, with the rule kept as text
Segments of usersSegments with the same members or the same rulesExact; a segment synced from an outside list becomes a named source to connect
Prerequisites between flagsRules that read another SwitchExact; a cycle is refused and reported
Owners, tags, descriptions, stale markersThe same fields, owners mapped to people and Squadrons by pickingExact once mapped
History and evaluation countsNot importedSaid on the first line of the report; history stays in the old service
  1. Read. From the old service's export file, or through a read-only connection, Launchway reads every project, environment, flag, rule and segment, and stores the report, not the data, until you go on.
  2. Dry run with counts. One page shows how many flags, rules and segments convert exactly, with a difference, or need a person, per environment, with the same three outcomes as pipelines.
  3. Evaluation check. Before anything is switched, Launchway evaluates a sample of contexts (taken from the old service's own test contexts if it has them, or generated from the rules) against both the old service and the imported Switches, and lists every context where the answers differ. This is the side-by-side comparison, for flags.
  4. Import into the Airfields you pick, off by default in prod until you switch it, each change on the record.
  5. Switch the applications. Applications that read flags through an open standard flag interface move by changing the provider they are given; the report lists each application's way of reading flags and the change it needs.

The import page asks for the date the old service stops, picked from a calendar, and shows how many flags are still read from the old service as that date comes nearer, so a team is never caught by a retirement.

Moving a Flight or a whole Base between self-hosted and hosted

Launchway runs three ways: self-hosted, hosted, and hosted with your own Detachment (site agent) on your side. A team should be able to change its mind in either direction without starting again. The roadmap already plans this as Guided moves between the three and Secrets move without being exposed; this is how the move works, in the same spirit as an import: preview, mirror, verify, switch, and a way back.

PartHow it moves
Repositories, pull requests, issuesMirrored with every ref, then verified ref by ref, as a repository import is today
The record and the Logbook (audit trail)Copied whole, with its hash chain checked on arrival, so the history of every Sortie, Clearance (approval) and Launch is the same after the move and an auditor can tell it was not changed
Cargo, Depot images and cachesCargo and images by digest, verified; caches are not moved, because they only make things faster
SecretsOne of three ways, chosen in the preview: re-sealed to the destination's key, exported under a passphrase only you know, or re-entered and rotated. Never in the clear on the way.
StationsNever moved: keys stay on their machines. Each Ramp (runner pool) gets new join tokens at the destination; the preview lists every Station to enroll again, and a Station behind the Detachment is re-pointed by one command.
Connections and Hardpoints (extension points)Listed in the preview; each credential is re-entered or re-granted at the destination, because a credential made for one installation is not reused at another
Launches in flight, Holds, waiting ClearancesThe switch waits until no Launch is airborne for the Flights that move; Holds and waiting Clearances move as they are

Until the switch, the source keeps working, and a Return to base (rollback) runs there. After the switch it runs at the destination. Either way it is never blocked by the move. After the switch, the source stays read-only for a window you pick (30 days by default), and "Move back" in that window reverses the switch without copying again.

The worked example: Harbor Lights brings in three pipelines

The Harbor Lights team runs storefront (a Go service, a web front end and a PostgreSQL database, on a Kubernetes cluster) on hosted workflow files; a legacy billing service on two virtual machines behind a load balancer, built by a scripted pipeline on a self-hosted automation server with a shared library; and payments on a commercial delivery platform, with a stage template, a canary deployment, an approval, a freeze window and two policies. The numbers below are an illustration of the design, not output of the product.

Design: not built

The command launchway import scan, its flags and its output are a sketch. launchway import pipeline exists today.

launchway import scan --connection harbor-git --owner harbor-lights
Scanned 14 repositories: 3 pipelines, 1 shared library, 1 settings export.
History is not imported: past runs, logs and test results stay in the old systems.

PIPELINE    KIND                                       CONSTRUCTS  EXACT  DIFFERENCE  NEEDS A PERSON  SIZE
storefront  hosted workflow files                              41     27          11               3  small
billing     automation server, scripted, with library          33      9          12              12  large
payments    delivery platform pipeline and template            52     30          16               6  medium

Shared library platform-library (tag v4): 7 global steps, 4 become Maneuvers, 3 need a custom step.
Packaged steps used: 9 kinds, 23 uses. The catalog maps 6 kinds (19 uses).
Secrets to create (names only): 11.  Variables to create: 4.
Convert fully today: none.  Convert fully once the findings are finished: all three.

The old workflow tests on two Go versions with a database beside the tests, lints with a packaged step, works out a version in fourteen lines of inline script, builds an image only on main or on a pull request labeled release, runs a smoke check through a packaged step nobody maps, and deploys through a reusable workflow kept in another repository.

In the old fileOutcomeIn the proposal
Two Go versions as a matrixExactfor_each
A database container beside the testsDifferenceA service reached at localhost, not by its name
The packaged lint stepExactMapped by the catalog to a Hangar Maneuver
Fourteen lines of inline version scriptDifferenceLifted into the custom step steps/compute-version with a test skeleton; the code is the same, it now runs sandboxed with no network
"Build on main, or on a pull request labeled release"ExactAn expression in ${{ }}
The version passed to later jobsExactA typed output
The unmapped smoke-check stepNeeds a personA custom step skeleton named after it; its test fails until written
The reusable deploy workflow (supplied with the scan)ExactA Maneuver in platform-library
The environment's reviewers, kept in the old host's settingsNeeds a personA Clearance on prod, approvers to pick
A token the old system made for every runNeeds a personA named secret to create
Design: not built

The imported block, the names inside ${{ }}, options_from: environments and approvers are sketches. for_each, services, libraries, kind: image, kind: deploy and the enable_delivery input exist today.

pipeline: storefront
imported:                        # written by the importer; removed at cut-over
  from: hosted-workflows
  report: .launchway/import/storefront.json
  open: 3                        # findings that need a person; Launches are refused while open
libraries:
  platform-library: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.2.0 }
inputs:
  enable_delivery: { type: boolean, default: false }
  environment: { type: choice, options_from: environments, default: staging }
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request: { into: [main], moments: [opened, updated, labeled] }
containers:
  db: { image: postgres:17, service: true }
steps:
  test:
    for_each: { go: ["1.26", "1.27"] }
    image: { each: go, format: "golang:%s" }
    services: [db]               # difference: reached at localhost, not as "db"
    run: go test ./...
  lint:
    uses: launchway/go-lint      # was a packaged lint step; mapped by the catalog
  version:
    uses: ./steps/compute-version   # lifted from inline script; output tag: string
  image:
    kind: image
    needs: [test, lint, version]
    when: ${{ run.branch == "main" || "release" in event.pull_request.labels }}
    tags: [{ repository: harbor-lights/storefront, tag: "${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}" }]
  smoke:
    uses: ./steps/smoke-check    # NEEDS A PERSON: skeleton; its test fails until written
    needs: image
  approve:
    kind: approval
    needs: smoke
    approvers: []                # NEEDS A PERSON: pick the group that says Go
  launch:
    uses: platform-library/deploy-service
    needs: approve
    with: { environment: "${{ inputs.environment }}", image: "${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}" }
    when: ${{ inputs.enable_delivery }}

The old file is a program: a node block with five stages, a branch test written in code around the deploy stage, credentials bound for one block, a question that waits for the billing-leads group, a nightly schedule with a spread minute, and a call to the library's deployToVms global step. The library is scanned too.

Reading scripted pipelines and importing libraries are new. kind: approval, secrets, schedule and libraries exist today; approvers and the expression are sketches.

pipeline: billing
libraries:
  platform-library: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.0.0 }   # the same tag as before
inputs:
  enable_delivery: { type: boolean, default: false }
on:
  push: { branches: [main, "release/*"] }
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 2 * * *", timezone: America/Chicago }]   # a Patrol; the old minute was spread
steps:
  build:
    image: registry.example.test/billing-build:3
    run: make build
  test:
    needs: build
    run: make test
    reports: { tests: build/test-results/*.xml }
  approve:
    kind: approval
    needs: test
    when: ${{ run.branch == "main" }}
    approvers: [billing-leads]
  deploy:
    uses: platform-library/deploy-to-vms   # NEEDS A PERSON: skeleton lifted from deployToVms
    needs: approve
    with: { hosts: billing-vms }
    secrets: [billing-db-user, billing-db-password]
    when: ${{ inputs.enable_delivery }}

Importing from a delivery platform, options_from: images, strategy and the Route are sketches; the Route is a proposed word that needs your yes. kind: deploy, environment and version exist today.

pipeline: payments
libraries:
  platform-library: { repo: platform-library, version: v4.2.0 }
inputs:
  enable_delivery: { type: boolean, default: false }
  version: { type: string, options_from: images, repository: harbor-lights/payments }
steps:
  build:
    uses: platform-library/go-service-ci      # was the platform's stage template
  launch:
    kind: deploy
    needs: build
    route: payments                           # staging, then prod; Clearance and Hold on prod
    version: "${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}"
    strategy: { pathfinder: [10, 50, 100], watch: 15m, metric: error_rate }
    on_fail: rollback
    when: ${{ inputs.enable_delivery }}

All three run side by side for a week. storefront agrees on the first day once the test host name is changed to localhost. billing shows one difference, a test that fails only here because the old machine had a time zone set; the finding about machine labels pointed at it. payments agrees, and its open policy finding keeps it grounded until the team decides to accept the catalog rule alone. The team cuts over storefront first.

The foundation it relies on

  • One checker. A proposal passes launchway validate and the Flight's Standing orders, or it is not written. Today a proposal that does not validate is not saved.
  • One record. Scans, imports, findings, acceptances, Wingman proposals, comparisons and cut-overs are events with their reasons. The open-findings count on a Flight is read from the record, so the interface, the command line and the Standing order cannot disagree.
  • Every way in. The web wizard, the command line, the HTTP API and the agent endpoint do every import task; the interface parity test covers each new one, as it covers import pipeline today. Terraform has nothing to manage here and says so.
  • Connections, not copies. The scan reads through the same code host connections Launchway already uses, with read-only rights and the egress allow-list, and stores the report, not the files.
  • Safe with any file. The readers are pure functions from files to a model. They run nothing, fetch nothing and evaluate nothing, and limit size, depth and the expansion of references, so they are safe to give files nobody on the team wrote.

Safety

On by default
Dry import: delivery steps are off behind enable_delivery. Unfinished places fail when run. The Standing order "No Launch from an unfinished import" (proposed) refuses a Launch from a pipeline with open findings. The Wingman's import purpose is off.
When a file cannot be read
That file gets one finding with the reason (too large, too deep, not valid YAML, an unknown format) and the rest of the scan continues. A scan can be stopped and resumed; it never half-writes a proposal.
When a server or the database is lost
A scan in progress resumes from the last repository finished. A proposal is a branch in Git and survives on its own. The comparison is rebuilt from the record and the code host's statuses.
When the old system says nothing
The comparison shows "no result from the old system" and never counts it as agreement. Cut-over stays unavailable for a pipeline with fewer than a set number of compared commits, three by default.
Who may do what
A Commander or Controller (approver) of a Wing runs a Wing scan and sees its inventory; an Observer (viewer) sees inventories of Flights they can read. A Pilot (developer) imports into a Flight they can write. Cut-over is a change to the pipeline file, so the Flight's branch rules and Clearances apply. Accepting a finding "as is" needs the same right as merging, and the reason is recorded. The Wingman acts with the asking person's rights or fewer.
Secrets
Never read, copied or stored. The report holds names. A value an old file pasted into a script is moved out of the script into a binding, and the finding names the line so the old value can be rotated.
Return to base
Import never blocks it. Cut-over itself is undone by switching delivery off again, one line, recorded.

Screens

The full descriptions for the mock-up builders are in the screens notes for this chapter and on the screens page. In short:

  1. Scan and inventory. A wizard (where to scan, what to include, start) and the inventory page it fills: totals, a table of pipelines with kind, counts by outcome and size, the packaged steps used and their catalog coverage, the names to create. States: scanning with progress, finished, a file that could not be read, nothing found.
  2. The import report. One pipeline's findings grouped by outcome, each with file and line, the old text, the new text, the reason and the next step, beside the proposal. States: all exact, with differences to read, with findings open, every finding closed.
  3. Side-by-side comparison. Commits down the side, step pairs across, each pair agree or differ with the kind of difference and the finding it links to, and the Cut over button with what still stands in its way.
  4. A finding that needs a person. The finding, the skeleton or failing line, and, where the Wingman is on, its proposed completion as a diff with its tests and their result, with Accept, Change and Dismiss.
  5. Cut over. A dialog that shows what changes, the record entry and the optional second change to remove old files.
  6. Import quality. The public table of formats and constructs with the two numbers and their history.
  7. The repository step. The first card of the import page: move in or keep the host (radio cards), the repository picked from the connection's list, the verify report ref by ref, the mirror back's state and lag, and the repository cut-over with what still stands in its way.
  8. Import Switches. A wizard: source (export file or a read-only connection picked from a list), environments mapped to Airfields by picking, owners mapped by picking, the dry-run counts by outcome, the evaluation check's differing contexts, the retirement date from a calendar, then import.
  9. Move this Flight or Base. A preview page: direction (picked), what moves with sizes, the secrets choice (three radio cards), Stations to enroll again, connections to re-grant, the verify progress, Switch, and the Move back window.
