Open question

One home for import

This chapter puts every import item in one group in Milestone 2, because conditions, outputs, generated steps and custom steps are Milestone 2 work and most of the new importers need them. The other choice is Milestone 1, which is "now" and already holds the built importer; that would make Milestone 1 larger and slower to finish. Recommendation: Milestone 2, with the built converter shown there as Available.

"Run the files you already have" and the one-way ruling

The roadmap item says Launchway should "run the usual cases as they are, or convert them". A later delegated ruling chose a one-way importer and no compatibility layer. Both cannot hold in full. Recommendation: keep the ruling, and meet the item this way: when a Flight has only another system's files, Launchway converts them on the first push and runs the proposal with delivery off, so the usual cases run without anyone writing a file, and the team then merges the proposal. No second engine reads the old format at run time, except inside a lifted generator step until its generator is changed to print Launchway steps.

The status of the built importer

Five formats, the report, the wizard and the guide are on the main branch with tests, while "A converter and a move-over guide" is Planned. Confirm it meets the bar for Available, and that "Run old and new side by side" is In progress.

Policies with no catalog match

Which policy language runs beside the typed catalog is still open for you. Until it is decided, imported policies with no matching rule are kept as files and stay "needs a person", which keeps their pipelines grounded. Confirm this, or allow a person to accept them "as is" with a recorded reason so a team is not blocked by a rule Launchway cannot run yet.

Familiar function names in expressions

The expression language could accept function names that other formats use, as aliases, or the importer could translate every call. Recommendation: translate; no aliases, so there stays one way to write each thing.

Real-world test files

The quality corpus would hold pipeline files from public repositories, each with its license kept beside it, under the test data folder. Confirm which licenses are acceptable for a project under the AGPL with a contributor agreement.

Learning from what fails to convert

Counts of constructs that needed a person, across all installations, would show what to build next. Recommendation: off by default, opt-in per Base, construct codes and counts only, never file content.

When the Switch import can ship

The Switch import is its own item in the import group in Milestone 2, so it can be scheduled early for teams leaving another service. It needs Switches to land in, which are Milestone 3 work. Confirm that the import moves with Switches if they are not ready, rather than shipping an import with nowhere to put the flags.

The window to move back

After a move between self-hosted and hosted, the source is kept read-only for 30 days by default so you can move back without copying again. Confirm the default, or set another.

The word Route

This chapter uses Route for the ordered Airfields a release flies through, as the spine proposes. It needs your yes.

Fast pipelines and continuous deployment

Launchway treats speed as something the platform measures, explains and defends for every pipeline, so a change reaches production as fast as it safely can, and its Launch (deployment) goes out with no person in the way where the Standing orders (policies and repository standards) allow it.

  • Every Sortie (run) shows where its time went: waiting for a Station (runner), starting, fetching, building, testing and waiting on people, each measured from the record.
  • Only what a change can affect is built and tested. Launchway works the set out from the software graph and from what each step declares it reads, shows the reason for every step it runs, reuses or skips, and lets a person widen it.
  • Every pipeline has a speed budget. A slowdown is reported like a failing test and traced to the change that caused it.
  • Continuous deployment is a Route (proposed word: the ordered list of Airfields, or environments, a release flies through) advancing by itself, with Overwatch (watch after a Launch) and automatic Return to base (rollback) as the safety, and a Clearance (approval) only where a level above requires one.

Where it sits

This chapter spans three of the seven layers. It is written from the flight plan layer (authoring, layer 3), because speed is decided by what a pipeline declares. It works in flight operations (execution, layer 4), where Stations take steps and caches and reuse save time. It ends in Launch (delivery, layer 5), where continuous deployment is a Route that advances by itself. Every number comes from the record (layer 2), and every shortcut passes the Standing orders of Command (layer 6).

Builds on
Pipelines, values and expressions (typed steps, the checker and "explained before and after"); Code you can test (the Simulator, testing a pipeline without flying it; proposed word); Stations and where work runs (warmed images, scaling on steps waiting, the cache rule); The record; The software graph and Maintenance; One way to launch, anywhere (Routes); Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch.
Builds on it
Every way of branching (each pattern ends in the same fast path); Quality, reports and the Debrief (the speed check appears in the Debrief (test report)); Radar, insight and keeping it healthy (delivery measures over time).
Advantage claimed
Number 3 of What only Launchway does: the fastest safe path. It leans on number 1 (proven before it flies) and number 2 (stable releases by proof, not hope).

What you will be able to do

You are Dana, a developer on the Flight (codebase) storefront. You change two files in the web front end and open a pull request. The first result arrives in 1 minute 40 seconds. The Sortie page says: "Ran 4 steps, reused 3, skipped 2. api-build and api-test reused from Sortie 409: nothing they read changed. web-test ran: you changed web/src/cart.tsx." You press Why? on any line and see the files and graph links behind it.

Your pull request adds 41 end-to-end tests. The Debrief shows a failed speed check beside the test results: "This change makes the pull request Sortie 3 minutes 10 seconds slower, over its budget of 8 minutes. web-e2e went from 4m 10s to 7m 20s; the new tests in cart.spec.ts take 2m 55s." It offers to split web-e2e across three Stations and shows, from the Simulator, that the Sortie would take 6m 05s.

You are Dana, who also owns the checkout tests. One of them failed on the same commit and then passed. Launchway marks it flaky, proposes a quarantine as a pull request with you as owner and an end date in 30 days, and keeps running it. Two weeks later the same test fails with a different message. That failure is not excused: it is new, and the Sortie fails.

You merge a change to storefront at 10:02. It passes the merge queue, is built once, flies through dev and staging by itself, and reaches prod behind a Pathfinder (canary) at 10:40, with no person in the loop, because the Standing orders allow it for this kind of change. Overwatch watches it against the service's Envelope (the measured limits inside which it is healthy; proposed word). Had it left the Envelope, it would have returned to base by itself.

You are Sam, who looks after the platform. The Clearance on storefront production has said Go 118 times out of 118 in ninety days and added a median of 3 hours 10 minutes to each release. Launchway shows the evidence on one card and offers to replace it with Overwatch alone, as a change a person reviews. The Simulator replays the ninety days without the Clearance and shows the two Launches that were returned to base would still have been caught, by Overwatch, within four minutes.

You lead the Squadron (team) "shop". Its page shows lead time, how often it launches, how often a Launch fails and how fast it recovers, and where the waiting happens: 31 percent of the time from merge to production is spent waiting for review. Nothing on the page ranks a person.

How it works

Speed is something the platform manages

Most teams tune speed by hand: a cache key here, a parallel step there, and nobody notices when it slowly gets worse. Launchway turns speed into a property of the pipeline that it measures from the record, keeps within a budget and defends like a test. Three rules hold everywhere in this chapter.

  1. Faster, never different. The product's rule for caches is "a cache makes a build faster; it never changes what the build produces". This chapter applies the same rule to every saving: skipping a step, reusing its result, splitting tests and warming Stations. If a shortcut could change an answer, it is not taken.
  2. Every saving says why. A step that is reused, skipped or split says so, with the facts it was decided on, on the Sortie page, in the record and over every way in.
  3. A person can always widen it. The existing principle "the system works out the order; a person can always override" applies to what runs. Any Sortie can be started as "run everything", and any step can be forced to run, with the reason recorded.

Where the time goes in a Sortie

A Sortie's time falls into six parts. Each is already, or will be, a recorded fact, so the page that shows them is a reading of the record, not a guess.

PartWhat countsRecorded todayIn this plan
Waiting for a StationFrom a step being ready to a Station taking it, including time held by limits in the Holding pattern (queue)Available A waiting step says why, with a stable code (quota_full, no_runner, runners_busy and others); held Sorties show their place in lineThe waiting time is summed per Sortie and per pipeline, by cause
StartingMaking the pod or container, the sandbox and the services a step asks forBounded by a start timeout; not shown as its own figureNew in this plan Shown on every step (proposed in Stations and where work runs as "Image pull time on every step")
FetchingPulling the step's image, preparing the workspace, restoring caches, fetching Cargo (artifacts)Available Each cache restore states its size and seconds ("restored key 3f9c, 118 MiB, 4 s")Image pull and workspace time join the cache time as one figure
BuildingThe step's own work, for steps that are not testsAvailable Each step's time; a typical time from earlier SortiesUnchanged; the budget reads it
TestingThe own work of steps that report test results, and the time inside each testAvailable Each test's duration, the slowest tests and what they usually takeUsed to split tests and to explain a slowdown
Waiting on peopleClearances, holds by an operator, a lane held by a Sortie waiting for a decisionAvailable Waits for a Clearance are named and left out of time estimatesSummed per release, so the cost of each manual step is visible
Built today

The Sortie page already streams live, gives each step a typical time from earlier Sorties (the median, ignoring one freak run), shows "about 6 min left" along the longest path still to run, keeps time in the Holding pattern and time waiting for a Clearance apart, and ends with "took 8m 03s, 12% faster than usual". What is missing is the split into the six parts and the sums across Sorties.

Design: not built. The view that shows this is Where the time went: one bar per part along the critical path, the step that bounds the Sortie named in words ("web-e2e sets the length of this Sortie; everything else finished 2m 30s before it"), and the same numbers in a table under the bar. It is described in the screens notes.

The fastest safe path: only what a change can affect

Path filters already let a step run only when certain files change (when: { changed: [...] }), and when a change cannot be known (a first push, a force-push, more than 1000 files) the step runs. That is the right instinct, but the patterns are written by hand and drift from the code. Launchway can do better because it already knows two things a hand-written filter does not.

  • The software graph knows that web imports platform-library/ui, that the api image is built from api/ and the go.mod beside it, and that payments depends on a package storefront publishes. It already answers "what is affected if this changes" with the reason for each link.
  • Typed steps can declare what they read: paths, the outputs of steps they need, variables, secret references and the image they run in. A custom step already declares its inputs and outputs in a manifest; this plan adds the paths it reads.

From the two, Launchway works out the affected set for a change before the Sortie starts, and shows it in the same "will run, will not run, depends on" form the checker uses.

# Design: not built. A step declares what it reads. Key names are not final.
steps:
  api-test:
    image: golang:1.27
    reads:
      paths: [api/**, go.mod, go.sum]          # what this step's result depends on
      graph: true                             # also everything the graph says api/ depends on
      variables: [DATABASE_URL]               # a changed value is a changed input
    run: go test ./api/...
  web-test:
    image: node:24
    reads:
      paths: [web/**, package.json, package-lock.json]
      graph: true                             # brings in platform-library/ui at the pinned version
    run: ./scripts/web-test.sh

A step that declares nothing is treated as reading everything, so it runs on every change, exactly as today. Nothing becomes faster by accident; a step becomes faster when it says what it reads. The checker warns about a declaration that is clearly too narrow: a Go test step that does not read go.sum, a step that reads an output of a step it does not list.

The worked answer for Dana's pull request #478, as the Sortie page will show it (Design: not built):

StepVerdictWhy, in the product's words
api-buildReused from Sortie 409Nothing it reads changed: api/**, go.mod, go.sum, image golang@sha256:7b1e…
api-testReused from Sortie 409As above; the Debrief shows its 412 results marked "reused"
web-buildWill runYou changed web/src/cart.tsx and web/src/price.ts
web-testWill runAs above
web-e2eWill run, 2 of 6 groupsThe graph links price.ts to the checkout and cart pages only; the other four groups test pages that do not import it
inspectionWill runStanding orders always inspect a pull request; findings are judged against what the change introduces
migrate-checkWill not runNo file under api/migrations/ changed
Test selection from the record, as well as the graph

Inside one test step, the same question can be asked per test. When a test tool reports which files each test touched (most coverage tools can), Launchway keeps that map with the Debrief and runs first, or only, the tests whose files changed. Selection never decides alone on the default branch: there, a selected run is followed by the full set, and any test that the selection left out but that fails is reported as a selection miss, which tightens the map. On a pull request the default is "run the selected tests first, then the rest", so the first signal is fast and the final answer is complete. A team may choose "selected only" for pull requests; the Debrief then says plainly how many tests were left out and why.

Reusing results that cannot differ

A cache is a head start inside a step. Reuse goes further: when nothing a step reads has changed, its recorded result is used and the step does not run at all. Re-running from a chosen step already does a safe version of this: steps before it are "recorded in the new run with the outcome and outputs it had, marked as reused from the original". This plan applies the idea to every Sortie, keyed on what each step declares.

Part of the reuse keyWhy it is there
The step as written, after templates and libraries are expandedA changed script or a new library version is a different step
The image, resolved to its digestThe same rule as cache keys today: a tag can move, a digest cannot
The contents of every declared path, and the graph links it followsWhat the step reads
The outputs of the steps it needsUpstream results are inputs
Declared variables, and the versions of secret references (never values)A rotated secret or a changed variable is a changed input
The Station's operating system and architectureAs for caches

What is never reused: Launch, Return to base, Clearance and rollout steps; a step that reads something that moves (a branch head, a "latest" version, an advisory database) unless the moving thing is pinned and part of its key; and any step a Standing order marks as "always fresh". The Inspection (security scan) is reused only when the advisory data it used is the same version, so a new advisory is never missed because a result was old.

Reuse follows the trust scopes caches already use. A pull request may reuse what the default branch produced. The default branch never reuses what a pull request produced, because a pull request runs code anyone can write. A fork reuses nothing. A reused result points to the Sortie that produced it, so the evidence chain for a release still leads to the place the work was done.

Trust, then check: reused results are built again on a sample

A declaration can be wrong. So a small share of reused steps (one in twenty by default, and always on a Patrol (schedule) once a day) is run anyway, in the background, and the two results are compared: outcome, outputs, test results and, for builds, the digest. A difference is a finding against the step's declaration, shown to its owner with the paths that differed, and reuse for that step stops until the declaration is fixed. This is the roadmap's planned "Build twice and compare", applied to reuse.

Tests split across Stations by how long they take

Built today

Launchway keeps each test's typical duration. launchway tests split storefront --shards 4 --shard 2 prints a balanced share (longest tests first, each to the lightest shard; the same history gives the same split), used inside a for_each loop. A test with no history is given the average. The same split is in the API and the agent endpoint. It is documented, not yet a Maneuver (reusable step template) of the starter library.

The plan makes splitting a property of a test step rather than a script the team maintains.

# Design: not built. Key names are not final.
steps:
  web-e2e:
    image: node:24
    split:
      tests: { list: ./e2e/list-tests.sh, run: ./e2e/run-tests.sh --only-file "$LAUNCHWAY_SPLIT_FILE" }
      target: 3m            # aim for each share to take about this long
      max_shares: 8         # never more Stations than this
    reports:
      tests: test-results/results.json
  • How many shares. Launchway picks the number from the recorded durations, the target and the free Stations in the Ramp (runner pool): seven minutes of tests with a three-minute target and four free Stations gives three shares. With few free Stations it uses fewer and says so, rather than queueing shares behind each other.
  • Re-balanced from history. Every Sortie updates the durations, so the split follows the tests as they grow. New tests get the average and are spread across shares.
  • Handed out live where the tool allows. With the step kit, each share can ask the server for its next batch instead of taking a fixed list, so one slow test does not leave the other shares idle. A fixed split stays the default, because it is easier to reproduce.
  • One Debrief. The shares' results join into one Debrief, with the share shown on each result, as matrix members are today.

Flaky tests: found, quarantined, never hiding a real failure

Built today

A test is flaky when its results go against its own history with no change to explain it: the same commit both passed and failed it, or it failed on one commit between passing ones, at least twice. A pass after a retry is shown as "passed on retry: flaky", never as a plain pass. A repository lists quarantined tests in .launchway/quarantine.yml, each with an owner, an end date at most a year ahead and a reason; the file is read from the commit under test, so adding an entry is a reviewed change. A quarantined test still runs and is shown loudly; after its end date it excuses nothing. Launchway suggests entries and never writes the file.

Three additions close the ways a quarantine can hide a real failure.

  1. A quarantine excuses only its known failure. When a test is quarantined, Launchway records the shape of the failures that made it flaky: the message with numbers and addresses removed, and the top of the stack. A later failure with the same shape is excused; a failure with a new shape is a real failure and fails the step, with "this test is quarantined for lock timeouts; this failure is different: expected 3 items, got 2".
  2. A quarantine arrives as a pull request. From the Flaky tests page, Quarantine opens a pull request that adds the entry, with the owner picked from the code owners of the test's file and an end date picked from a short list (14, 30 or 90 days). Launchway still never writes the file without a review.
  3. Quarantine debt is visible. Each Squadron sees its quarantined tests, how long each has been there, which end soon, and which keep failing in the known way. An expired entry is listed as such and counts again at once.

Retries are treated the same way. A step's retry stays the step's own choice, but every retry that turned a failure into a pass is counted against the test or step that needed it, so "it passes on the second try" becomes visible instead of normal.

Warm before the Sortie needs it

Stations and where work runs proposes two things this chapter relies on: images warmed as soon as a Sortie is planned, by digest, and Ramps that grow when steps wait and shrink when idle. Three more come from the declared reads above.

  • Fetch only what a step reads. A step that declares its paths gets a workspace with those paths and what they need, not the whole repository, where the step's kind allows it. A large repository then costs each step only its part.
  • Caches sent ahead. The server knows which cache entries a step will restore before a Station takes it, so the Station can start fetching them while the image is pulled.
  • One build cache for the whole Base. Build tools that can ask a remote cache "has this exact thing been built?" ask Launchway's own, through the Station on their machine, so the first build of the morning makes every later one faster on every Station. It is designed in the hosted build cache, with the same trust scopes as caches today.
  • Capacity before the busy hour. The record shows when a Flight's Sorties arrive: the morning wave of pushes, the Patrols at 02:00. A Ramp can be asked to be at a given size a few minutes before, sized from the last four weeks, and to shrink afterwards. It is advice the Ramp's owner turns on; it never takes room from the platform.

Parallelism chosen from the graph

Steps that do not need each other already run side by side and are drawn that way. What teams lack is knowing where more parallelism would help. Launchway works out the critical path of each pipeline from recorded step times and answers one question: "what would make this pipeline faster?" The table below is a design of that answer, not built.

Suggestion for storefront, pull request SortiesSaving, from the SimulatorWhat it changes
Split web-e2e into 3 sharesabout 3m 40sOne split: block; three Stations instead of one
Declare what api-test readsabout 2m 10s on 70% of pull requestsOne reads: block
Let lint start without waiting for web-buildabout 50sRemoves one needs entry that nothing uses

Each saving is computed by the Simulator, which replays the changed pipeline against the recorded step times of the last fifty Sorties: it already knows which steps would run and in what order, and the record knows how long each took. Each suggestion opens as a change to the pipeline file that a person reviews; nothing is rewritten silently. The number of loop members that run at once (max_parallel) defaults to what the Ramp can take, so a matrix does not queue against itself. A fan-out of thousands of members, handed out in waves as Stations free up, is designed in Stations and where work runs.

A speed budget for every pipeline

A budget is the time a pipeline should take, per kind of Sortie. Launchway proposes one from the pipeline's own history (the 80th percentile of the last month, rounded up), and the team may change it. The roadmap's planned "First signal fast" (two minutes to the first result on a pull request) becomes one line of the budget.

# Design: not built. Key names are not final.
speed:
  pull_request: { first_signal: 2m, total: 8m }
  default_branch: { total: 12m }
  merge_to_prod: 60m          # lead time from merge to Mission complete in prod
  on_slowdown: advise         # advise (the default) or block, as a Standing order allows

A Sortie over budget gets a speed check, reported like a failing test: in the Debrief, on the pull request and in Comms (notifications). It says by how much, which steps grew, and which change made them grow.

Noise is handled honestly. A step needs at least five earlier Sorties of the same kind before a slowdown is called; a single slow Sortie on a busy Station is reported as "slower than usual, waiting for Station time was the cause", not as a regression; and where there is not enough history the check says "not enough data", never "passed". Waiting for a Station and waiting on people are reported apart from the pipeline's own time, so a busy Ramp is never blamed on a pull request.

A slowdown on the default branch that nobody caused on purpose opens as a finding for the Flight's owners, with the commit and the step. Because on_slowdown can be set by a level above, a Wing (organization) can make "no pull request may slow a protected pipeline by more than 20 percent" a Standing order with waivers, like any other rule.

Continuous deployment: merge to production with no person in the loop

Continuous deployment in Launchway is not a separate feature. It is a Route whose stops advance by themselves, with the safety that already exists on every Launch: Standing orders judged before each Launch, a Pathfinder, Overwatch against the Envelope, and automatic Return to base.

  1. Tested as it will land. The merge queue tests the merged result with the real pipeline before it lands (available today, serial; batches are proposed in Code and review). The affected set and reuse keep the queue short.
  2. Built once. The release is the digest the merge built. Every later Launch moves that digest; nothing is built again.
  3. Advances by itself. Each Route stop says how a release advances: by itself, on a Clearance, or by hand. Continuous deployment is "by itself" on every stop, as proposed in One way to launch, anywhere.
  4. Judged, not trusted. Before each Launch, Standing orders give one of four answers: allow, warn, require a Clearance or deny (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold). A rule can let low-risk changes flow and send risky ones to a person: "a change that touches api/migrations/ requires a Clearance in prod", "a change with a new high finding is denied", "a change whose tests reused more than half their results needs one fresh full Sortie first".
  5. Watched and brought back. The Launch uses a Pathfinder. Overwatch judges it against the Envelope learned from the service's own good Launches; leaving it means Return to base, by itself, with the reason on the record (Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch).
  6. A Clearance only where a level above requires it. A Wing may require a Clearance for payments in prod, with a lock; the Squadron cannot remove it. Everywhere else the team decides.
# Design: not built. The storefront Route under continuous deployment. Key names are not final.
route: storefront
releases: { from_branch: main }
stops:
  - airfield: dev
    advance: by_itself
  - airfield: staging
    advance: by_itself
    verified_when: { overwatch: pass, stay_at_least: 20m }
  - airfield: prod
    advance: by_itself                 # the Standing orders verdict can still ask for a Clearance
    strategy: pathfinder
    window: business-hours

Worked example. Dana's next change merges at 10:02. The merge queue Sortie takes 7 minutes (four steps reused). dev receives 2.4.1 at 10:11 and Overwatch passes at 10:16. staging receives it at 10:16 and stays 20 minutes. At 10:37 the Standing orders verdict for prod is "allow": tests passed with no new failures, 91 percent of changed lines covered, no new findings, no migration, inside the business-hours window, and the error budget of storefront is 74 percent unspent. The Pathfinder starts at 10:38, takes 5 percent of traffic for ten minutes, then all of it. Mission complete at 10:52: fifty minutes from merge to production, under the 60-minute budget, and nobody had to say Go. The same afternoon a change to payments follows the same path to staging and waits for Ana's Clearance, because the Wing requires one there.

The evidence that a manual step can go

Teams keep manual Clearances long after they stop catching anything, because nobody can show it is safe to remove them. The record can. For every Clearance on a Route, Launchway keeps a card with the facts (Design: not built).

Fact, over the chosen periodClearance before storefront in prod, last 90 days
Go and No-go118 Go, 0 No-go
Time it addedMedian 3h 10m per release; 61 releases waited overnight
Launches it cleared that later went wrong2 returned to base; both caught by Overwatch, in 3 and 4 minutes
Would the automatic checks have caught what people caught?Nothing to compare: no No-go in the period
Quality of the signal it relies onFlaky rate 0.4 percent; changed-line coverage 88 percent median; no quarantine past its end date
The Simulator, without this ClearanceAll 118 releases would have reached prod a median 3h 10m sooner; the 2 returns to base happen the same way
ReadinessReady to replace with Overwatch alone, by the Squadron's own criteria

The card never removes anything by itself. It offers the change to the Route or Standing order as a pull request, with the card attached. A Clearance a level above requires shows the same card, but only that level can act on it. When a No-go did happen, the card lists what the person saw and whether an automatic proof would have seen it too, so the team knows what to automate first.

Velocity, seen honestly

The release report already works out the four delivery measures from what Launchway records: how often a Flight launches, the lead time from commit to Airfield, the share of Launches that fail or return to base, and the time to restore. Nothing is guessed, and the report says plainly that the measures "are not a way to rank people". This plan keeps that stance and adds the measures that explain the four.

MeasureWorked out fromShown for
Lead time, launch frequency, failure rate, time to restoreLaunches and releases on the record (available today)Flight, Squadron, Wing; each Airfield
Where lead time goesTime in review, in the merge queue, in Sorties, waiting for Stations, between Route stops, waiting on ClearancesFlight and Squadron
Time to first signal, and Sortie time against budgetThe speed checks abovePipeline, Flight
Work done againRe-runs, retries that turned a failure into a pass, Sorties canceled by newer commitsPipeline, Flight
Flaky rate and quarantine debtThe DebriefFlight, Squadron
Time savedReused and skipped steps, at their typical timesPipeline, Flight

Every number opens on the Sorties, pull requests and Launches behind it. A person sees their own figures and their Squadron's; nobody sees a table of people. A Wing sees its Squadrons, each beside its own past, never as a league table.

The foundation it relies on

  • The record. Every time, every reuse verdict, every speed check and every Clearance is an event with its facts. Budgets and the Clearance card are readings of the record; they invent nothing.
  • Typed steps and the checker. Declared reads are part of a step's type and are checked before the Sortie starts, like its inputs and outputs.
  • The software graph. The affected set follows the graph's links, each with where it was found and how sure Launchway is. A link the graph only inferred widens the set; it never narrows it.
  • The Simulator. Savings, suggestions and "without this Clearance" are replays against recorded Sorties, not estimates from nowhere.
  • Standing orders. Every shortcut and every automatic advance passes the same judging points. There is no fast lane around them.

Safety

If this fails or is wrongWhat happens
A step's declared reads are too narrowThe sample check finds a difference, reports it to the step's owner and turns reuse off for that step. The default branch's daily full Sortie catches what the sample missed.
The graph is missing a linkSelection on the default branch is followed by the full test set, so a missed test fails there and is reported as a selection miss. A person can add the link with a reason.
The change cannot be knownEverything runs, as path filters do today.
The server dies while working out the setThe set and its reasons are written with the Sortie in one transaction; another server works it out again from the same facts and gets the same answer.
A Station dies during a shareThe share is handed out again, as any step is; its tests are not counted twice.
The database is lostNothing new is reused, judged or advanced. Launches already in Overwatch keep their automatic Return to base, which runs from the deploy Station's own record.
Overwatch cannot reach its signalsThe Launch does not advance and the Route stop says "not enough data"; it never counts as a pass.
Who mayIn this plan
Force a step to run, or start a Sortie as "run everything"Anyone who may start the Sortie; recorded with the reason
Change a pipeline's budgetWhoever may change the pipeline file; a level above can set a floor with a lock
Mark a step "always fresh"The pipeline's author, or a Standing order at any level
Turn a Route stop to "advances by itself"A Commander (owner) of the Flight, by a reviewed change; never past a Clearance a level above requires
Replace a Clearance after reading its cardThe level that set the Clearance, by a reviewed change
Return to baseOverwatch by itself, or an operator at any time; never blocked

On by default: steps with no declared reads run every time; reuse follows trust scopes (a pull request's results are never reused by the default branch); one reused step in twenty is checked by running it again; a speed check advises and never blocks unless a Standing order says so; continuous deployment is off until a Flight's Route says "by itself"; Return to base is never blocked.

Screens

The full list, with every field and state, is in the screens notes for this chapter. In short:

Where the time went

What ran and why

Make it faster

Flaky tests

Delivery measures

Open question

  1. May a release reuse test results? Reuse is safe by the rules above, and the evidence still points to the Sortie that ran the tests. Some auditors expect a release build to run every test fresh. Recommendation: allowed by default, with a Standing order "fresh tests for releases" offered in the payment-card and health-data packs. Open question
  2. Default speed budgets. Proposed from each pipeline's own history (80th percentile of the last month), plus two minutes to first signal on pull requests. Confirm, or set fixed defaults. Open question
  3. The sample rate for checking reused results. One in twenty, and a full Sortie of the default branch once a day. A higher rate costs Station time; a lower one trusts declarations more. Open question
  4. The default Route for a new Flight. Recommendation: dev and staging advance by themselves; prod advances on a Clearance until the Clearance card says it is ready, so continuous deployment is earned, not assumed. Open question
  5. Stopping a Sortie whose answer is known. When a required step has failed, other long steps could be stopped to save Station time, at the cost of a less complete Debrief. Recommendation: off by default, a pipeline choice. Open question
  6. Plain words. This chapter adds no aviation word. "Speed budget", "affected set" and "declared reads" are working names in plain English; confirm or choose others. Open question

Every way of branching

Launchway supports every major way teams branch and release, recognizes the one a repository already uses, offers the Flight plan (ready-made whole pipeline) and the Route (proposed word: the ordered list of Airfields, or environments, a release flies through) that fit it, and lets a team move to another pattern step by step without rewriting its pipelines.

  • Ten patterns are supported as equals, from trunk-based development to a branch per environment, forks, many projects in one repository and many repositories released together. None is forced.
  • A change that spans several repositories is one linked change: tested against each other's heads with one combined check, merged in dependency order through each repository's merge queue, and never left half-merged without a revert opened.
  • A pattern is data, not a pipeline. It gives each branch a role (trunk, change, integration, release, hotfix, environment), and pipelines say what to do for a role. Changing pattern changes the roles, not the pipeline file.
  • Launchway reads a repository's history, says which pattern it looks like and why, and offers the matching Flight plan, Route and branch rules as one change a person reviews. A team can correct it.
  • Moving between patterns is a plan of small reviewed steps, each replayed first in the Simulator (proposed word: testing a pipeline without flying it) against the team's own recent history.

Where it sits

This chapter is the flight plan layer (authoring, layer 3) of the seven layers, where triggers and pipelines are declared. It reaches into Launch (delivery, layer 5), because a pattern decides which branch's builds fly which Route, and into Command (layer 6), because each pattern is protected by branch rules and Standing orders (policies and repository standards). Recognition reads the record (layer 2) and the Git history.

Builds on
What starts a Sortie (push, pull request with into, tags, path filters); Reuse that keeps growing (Flight plans set by level); Code and review (branch rules, protected tags, the merge queue, forks); One way to launch, anywhere (releases, Routes and previews); The software graph and Maintenance (what depends on what, Formations (releases that go together)); Code you can test (the Simulator).
Builds on it
Fast pipelines and continuous deployment (every pattern ends in the same fast, safe path); Bringing work in (an imported repository is recognized on arrival); Quality, reports and the Debrief (release notes and reports follow the pattern's versions).
Advantage claimed
Number 4 of What only Launchway does: continuous deployment for the way you already branch.

What you will be able to do

You are Ana, on the Squadron (team) "back office". You import the billing repository. Before you finish the wizard, a card says: "This repository looks like a long-lived integration branch with release and hotfix branches. Sure: high. develop has existed for three years and receives 94 percent of pull requests; eleven release/* branches were merged into main and tagged; production Launches (deployments) always came from tags on main." You press Keep this pattern and review one change: the Flight plan, the Route and the branch rules that fit it.

You are Dana, on storefront. Your team works in short branches with pull requests into main and wants to go trunk-based. The Flight (codebase) page offers the move as four steps. The Simulator replays the last six weeks under the new pattern: "38 pull requests; 38 Sorties (runs) of the same pipeline; the median change would have reached prod 6 hours sooner; no step that ran would have been skipped." Your pipeline file does not change; only the pattern's roles do.

You are on the Squadron "kiosks". Three versions of kiosk-os run on image-based hosts in shops. You fix a receipt bug on main. Launchway finds the supported release branches that contain the bug and lack the fix, release/4.1 and release/4.2, and opens a carry-back pull request into each. One conflicts; it is marked for a person, with the lines.

An outside contributor opens a pull request from a fork of platform-library. It does not run until a maintainer approves it, then it runs restricted, with no secrets, no Launch and no preview. When a maintainer merges it and pushes the tag v3.1.0, the library is published to the Depot (registry) and the Flights that use it are offered the update.

A team arrives with env/staging and env/prod branches. Launchway supports them. It maps each branch to its Airfield (environment), and when env/prod receives a merge whose files are the same as what passed in staging, it launches the image already built and verified there instead of building again. When the files differ, it says which, before anything launches.

How it works

One idea: branches have roles

Every branching pattern answers the same few questions: where changes are made, where they come together, what is released, how a fix reaches what runs in production, and which builds go to which Airfield. Launchway names the answers as roles. A pattern is a small piece of data that says which branches play which role; pipelines, Routes, branch rules and release settings read the role, not the branch name.

RoleWhat it isTypical names
TrunkThe branch everything comes together on and releases are made frommain
ChangeA short-lived branch for one change, merged by pull requestfeature/*, fix/*, any other branch
IntegrationA long-lived branch where work collects before a releasedevelop
ReleaseA branch that stabilizes or maintains one line of versionsrelease/4.2
HotfixA branch for an urgent fix to what runs in productionhotfix/*
EnvironmentA branch whose contents are what one Airfield runsenv/staging, prod
ContributionA pull request from a fork, from outside the teamany branch of a fork

Roles answer your point that "the branch strategy probably helps dictate the type of pipelines that repo might need" without a separate machinery for many branches. A change-role branch runs the CI pipeline (and, if the team chooses, deploys its build to a preview Airfield). Trunk, release and hotfix roles run the release pipeline. Utility pipelines ignore roles.

# Design: not built. The pattern a Flight uses, kept in .launchway/branching.yaml
# or in the Flight's settings. Key names are not final.
branching:
  pattern: release-branches
  roles:
    trunk: main
    release: "release/*"
    hotfix: "hotfix/*"
    change: "*"                       # everything else
  versions:
    trunk: { scheme: calver, prerelease: true }
    release: { scheme: semver, line_from_branch: true }   # release/4.2 gives 4.2.x
  route:
    trunk: [dev]
    release: [staging, prod]
  carry_back: { fixes_on: trunk, to: release, while: supported }
# Design: not built. The pipeline reads roles, so it is the same under every pattern.
pipeline: kiosk-os
on:
  push: { branch_roles: [trunk, release, hotfix] }
  pull_request: { into_roles: [trunk, release] }
steps:
  image:
    kind: image
    # ...
  release:
    needs: image
    when: ${{ run.branch_role in ["release", "hotfix"] }}
    uses: platform-library/release-publish@v3

Today's triggers keep working: branches, tags and into are still valid and mean what they mean now. Roles are an addition a pipeline may use; a pipeline that names branches directly is still supported and is simply not portable across patterns. The expression above is written in the open-source expr language, as everywhere in Launchway.

What a pattern decides

For each pattern, Launchway sets the same six things from the roles: what starts a Sortie, previews, the merge queue, versions and release notes, the Route through Airfields, and the hotfix path. The table is the summary; each pattern has its own section below with a diagram.

PatternWhat starts SortiesPreviewsMerge queueVersions and notesRouteHotfix
Trunk-basedPull requests into the trunk; every mergeOptional per pull requestRecommendedDigest and date; tags optionalTrunk through every Airfield, by itselfFix forward on the trunk
Main with feature branches (default)Pull requests into main; every mergePer pull requestRecommended on busy repositoriesProposed from merged pull requestsmain to dev by itself, then by ruleA fix branch from main, first in the Holding pattern (queue)
Release branchesPull requests and merges on the trunk and each release branchPer pull request into the trunkOn the trunkOne version line per release branchTrunk to dev; release branches to staging and prodFix on the trunk, carried to supported release branches
Integration branchPull requests into the integration branch; release and hotfix branches; tags on mainPer pull request; an integration AirfieldOn the integration branchFrom the release branch name, tagged on mainIntegration to its Airfield; release to staging; tags on main to prodFrom main, carried back to the integration branch
Branch per environmentMerges into each environment branchPer pull request into the first oneOn each environment branchFrom the trunk's buildEach branch to its Airfield, in orderInto the first environment branch, merged onward
ForksPull requests from forks, after a maintainer's approval, restrictedOnly after a person says Go, never with secretsAs the base patternBy maintainersAs the base patternBy maintainers
Many projects in one repositoryPer component, from what the change affectsPer affected componentWhole repositoryPer component, tags such as web/v5.2.0Per componentPer component
Many repositories released togetherEach repository's own pattern; dependents checked before a library mergesPer pull request, with linked changes togetherPer repository; linked changes merge in orderEach its own; the Formation names the setOne Formation, in dependency orderPer repository; the Formation returns together
Tag-based releasesPull requests and merges on the trunk; protected version tagsNot usuallyOptionalThe tag is the versionNone: done means publishedA patch tag from the trunk or a release branch
Promotion by pull requestMerges on the trunk; promotion pull requests in the GitOps repositoryPer pull requestAs the base patternThe digest in each environment folderOne folder per Airfield on one branchRevert the promotion pull request

1. Trunk-based development with short-lived branches

Everyone integrates into one branch at least daily. Branches live hours, not weeks. Unfinished work is hidden behind a Switch (feature toggle), not kept on a branch. A very small team may commit straight to the trunk; Launchway offers that as an option with its prerequisites listed (fast tests, Switches, a merge queue), never as the default.

In Launchway this pattern is the shortest path of Fast pipelines and continuous deployment: the affected set keeps each pull request short, the merge queue tests what will land, and the Route advances by itself where Standing orders allow. Release tags are optional; the digest and the date identify what runs.

2. A main branch with feature branches and pull requests

The default for a new repository, as the roadmap's recommender already proposes: it is the simplest pattern that keeps main always releasable, works for one person and for a team, and every other pattern is this one plus one thing.

Every pull request gets a preview Airfield if the Flight asks for one (planned: "A preview environment for every pull request"). A hotfix is a normal pull request marked urgent from a list: it goes to the front of the Holding pattern and the merge queue, reuses every result that cannot differ, and still passes every Standing order. Nothing is skipped to be fast.

3. Release branches cut from main, with fixes carried back

For software where customers stay on older versions: mobile and desktop applications, on-premises products, and the kiosk-os image that runs on hosts in shops. All work lands on the trunk. When a release is prepared, a branch such as release/4.2 is cut. Fixes are made on the trunk first and carried to each release line that is still supported.

Built today

A release can be made from a maintenance branch with a version lower than the highest so far (--allow-lower), and its notes are written from the changes since the previous release of that line. Carrying a fix back is a pull request that someone makes by hand with git cherry-pick; the release guide says plainly that Launchway does not cherry-pick for you yet.

4. A long-lived integration branch with release and hotfix branches

Work collects on an integration branch (usually develop). A release branch is cut from it, stabilized, merged into main and tagged; production runs tags on main. Urgent fixes branch from main and are merged back into both. It suits scheduled, explicitly versioned releases. Launchway supports it as an equal, and the recommender says honestly that a simpler pattern fits continuous delivery better.

The two places this pattern usually breaks are both checked: a hotfix that reached main but not develop (the next release would undo it), and a release branch that drifted from develop. Both are findings with the commits named, offered as carry-back pull requests.

5. A branch per environment

Some teams keep a branch per Airfield and promote by merging one into the next. The usual risk is that each environment builds its own code, so what reaches production is not what was tested. Launchway supports the pattern and removes that risk where it can.

  • Built once, even here. When env/prod receives a merge, Launchway compares the files with the commit that passed in staging. If they are the same, it launches the digest already verified there. If they differ, it lists the files and, by default, asks for a Clearance (approval) before building anything new for prod.
  • Merges only in Route order. A branch rule lets env/prod accept merges only from env/staging, so a change cannot skip an Airfield.
  • Advice, never refusal. A finding explains the risk and offers a move to promotion by digest. Whether this advice may ever become a requirement is open for you, as it has been since the dependency-order design.

6. Forks with pull requests from outside contributors

Open-source and inner-source projects take pull requests from copies of the repository. The pattern sits on top of any other: maintainers keep their own pattern, and contributions arrive through the contribution role.

This is built on what exists: forks of hosted repositories (see the forks guide and Code and review), restricted Sorties for pull requests from forks and automation accounts (no secrets, no deploys, no cache written outside their own scope), and a pull request that cannot switch pull-request Sorties on for itself because the pipeline is read from the default branch. A preview for a fork's pull request is made only after a maintainer says Go, and never with secrets.

7. Many projects in one repository

One repository can hold several things that are built, versioned and released on their own: storefront holds api and web, and could hold a shared libs/ui. Each component keeps the repository's branching pattern; what differs is that a change runs only for the components it affects.

Tags carry the component (web/v5.2.0), release notes are written from the pull requests that touched that component, and code owners keep ownership by path. The affected set is the one described in Fast pipelines, so "which components does this change touch" has one answer everywhere.

8. Many repositories released together

Several repositories, each with its own pattern, sometimes have to go out together: a library and the applications that use it, or storefront and payments for a sale.

Formations exist today, with an order you write or the software graph's dependency order, all or nothing to begin with, and a report that says what happened. Checking dependents before a library merges, linked changes merged together, and one Go, one watch and one way back for a Formation are planned in Milestone 5.

A linked change: a design. Sometimes one piece of work needs a pull request in several repositories at once: a new field in platform-library, used by storefront and payments. A linked change is a named set of those pull requests that Launchway tracks, tests and merges as one.

  • Linking. Any pull request can be linked to others from a picker on its page (repositories and open pull requests from lists), from the command line, or by the agent endpoint. The link is shown on every member, with the others' states.
  • One combined check, against each other's heads. The library's head is built and published as a prerelease visible only to this linked change. Each dependent's Sortie resolves the library to that prerelease instead of its pinned version, through the same lockfile mechanism it uses every day, and says so on the Sortie. The linked change has one combined check that is green only when every member's checks are green against the others' current heads. A new push to any member re-runs the members that depend on it.
  • Merged in dependency order, through each repository's queue. The order comes from the software graph (or is written by hand). Each member enters its own repository's merge queue only when the one before it has merged, and its queue check runs against the real released version, not the prerelease. Branch rules and Standing orders apply to every member as if it merged alone.
  • All or none, honestly. Nothing merges until every member is approved and green. For repositories hosted in Launchway, the branch moves happen in one database transaction, so all land or none does. A member on an outside host cannot land in the same transaction, and the page says so plainly: there the order is kept, and if a later member still fails after an earlier one merged, Launchway stops, opens a revert pull request for each merged member as a draft, marks the linked change broken with the reason, and launches nothing from it.
  • Then flies as one. The releases a linked change produces can fly together as one Formation (releases that go together), with one Go and one way back.
  • On connected hosts too. Members may be on the built-in code host or on connected ones; the combined check is reported to each host as a status on its member.
Design: not built

Linking, the combined check, the prerelease for one linked change and the ordered merge are designs. Formations and the merge queue exist today. The existing roadmap item Linked changes across repositories (Milestone 5) delivers this.

9. Tag-based releases for libraries and tools

A library, command-line tool, chart or base image is published, not deployed. A protected version tag is the release.

Protected tags exist today (nobody may move or delete a v* tag by default), and so does a release made from a tag with notes from the merged pull requests. Maintenance (dependency updates) then offers the new version to the Flights that use it.

10. Promotion by pull request

For changes that need a reviewed record of every step to production: the application repository builds once, and promotion is a pull request in the GitOps repository that changes the digest in one folder per Airfield, on one branch. Argo CD (or the built-in deployer) applies what is merged.

The Route is the same object as in every other pattern; each stop's way of advancing is "open a pull request in the GitOps repository" instead of "launch". GitOps write-back exists today. Returning to base is reverting the promotion pull request, with the stable state recorded as for any Launch. This is the pattern payments uses at Harbor Lights.

Recognizing the pattern a repository already uses

Most teams do not start from nothing; they arrive with history. Launchway reads it and says what it sees, with the evidence, before it suggests anything.

SignalRead fromPoints to
How long branches live before they mergeBranch creation and merge timesHours: trunk-based; days: feature branches; months: integration or release
Where pull requests goEach pull request's targetMostly a non-default long-lived branch: integration branch
Branches cut from the trunk and tagged laterBranch names, ancestry and tagsRelease branches
Merges always in one direction between long-lived branches whose Launches go to one Airfield eachMerge history and the record of LaunchesA branch per environment
Fix branches from the release point merged into two placesAncestry of hotfix/* and their mergesIntegration branch with hotfixes
Version tags and no LaunchesTags and the recordTag-based releases
Pull requests from forksFork recordsForks, on top of the base pattern
Several components with their own build files and tagsThe software graph and tag prefixesMany projects in one repository
Folders per Airfield in a GitOps repository changed by pull requestsGitOps write-back historyPromotion by pull request

Design: not built. The card names the pattern in plain words, how sure Launchway is (high, medium, low, with the numbers behind it), the three strongest pieces of evidence, the branches it would give each role, and what it would set up. Correct it lets a person pick another pattern or change a role (for example "trunk is master, not main"); the correction and its reason are kept, and the card is never shown again for that repository unless its history changes shape. For a new repository with no history, the six plain questions of the planned recommender ask the same things directly: what it is, how often it releases, how many people work on it, whether old versions are supported, whether change must be reviewed for a regulator, and whether outsiders contribute.

Offered as one reviewed change

Accepting the card never changes the repository directly. Launchway prepares the pattern file, the Flight plan bound to the Flight, the Route, the branch rules and the protected tags as one change, shown line by line, that a Commander (owner) of the Flight approves. On a repository hosted elsewhere, branch rules are written through the code host's connection where it allows, and the card says plainly which rules that host cannot hold.

Moving from one pattern to another

A move is a plan of small steps, each a reviewed change that leaves the team able to work. Before each step, the Simulator replays the team's own recent pushes and pull requests under the new roles and shows what would have happened: which Sorties would have run, which Launches would have gone where, and how long changes would have taken, using recorded step times. Time spent in review and waiting on people is kept as it was recorded, and the replay says so.

Worked example: billing, owned by the Squadron "back office", moves from an integration branch to feature branches into main.

  1. Protect main and add the merge queue. Nothing else changes. Replay: no Sortie differs.
  2. Bring develop and main together. Launchway opens a pull request that merges develop into main on a trial branch first and runs the release pipeline on it. Replay: the trial Sortie's Debrief (test report) matches the last develop Sortie.
  3. Change the roles. main becomes the trunk; new pull requests target it; develop becomes read-only. The pipeline file does not change, because it reads roles. Replay over six weeks: 41 pull requests, the same 41 CI Sorties, and 23 releases to staging instead of 3.
  4. Turn the Route on from main. dev and staging advance by themselves; prod keeps its Clearance. Replay: median time from merge to staging falls from 9 days to 40 minutes.
  5. Archive develop. Only after a set number of releases from main, picked from a list.

Each step can be undone by the change that reverses it. The plan is kept with the Flight, shows which step it is on, and is recorded in the Logbook (audit trail). A level above may recommend a pattern for a kind of repository; whether it may require one, with a lock, is open for you. Either way, the move is offered, never forced.

Protecting each pattern

Branch rules exist today on hosted repositories: required approvals, required checks, up to date, resolved threads, no self-approval, owner approval, the latest push approved by someone else, stale approvals dismissed, checks by path, the merge queue and an audited administrator bypass. Protected tags exist too. A pattern sets them per role, so the right rules follow a branch from the moment it is created.

RoleRules the pattern sets
TrunkPull request required; required checks including the Inspection (security scan); one approval; no force push; merge queue where the pattern recommends it
IntegrationAs the trunk, without the merge queue unless asked
ReleasePull request required; only fixes accepted (below); no force push; deleted only after the line's support ends
HotfixPull request required; the same checks; first in line
EnvironmentMerges only from the branch before it on the Route; no direct pushes
Version tagsProtected: made by an administrator or the release Sortie, never moved or deleted

Two Standing orders come with the patterns that need them, judged at the merge point proposed in Standing orders, Clearance and Hold:

  • Fixes first on the trunk. A pull request into a release branch must carry commits already on the trunk, or be marked "this line only" with a reason picked from a list (the code no longer exists on the trunk, a fix specific to this version). This stops a fix from reaching an old version and being lost from the next one.
  • Nothing skips an Airfield. For environment branches and promotion by pull request, a change may enter an Airfield only if it passed the one before it.

Drift is advice. Findings tell a team when its practice drifts from its chosen pattern: a change branch that has lived longer than the pattern expects, a hotfix not carried back, a release branch still receiving fixes after its support ended, a version tag that moved on a host without protection, a branch whose role nothing triggers. Each finding has the evidence and a proposed fix. None blocks unless a level above makes it a rule.

Hotfixes, and fixes carried back

Every pattern has a hotfix path, and in every pattern it is the normal path, faster, never weaker: the change is marked urgent from a list, goes first in the Holding pattern and the merge queue, reuses every result that cannot differ, and passes every Standing order. A Hold (freeze) still applies unless the person has the right to an emergency change, which is recorded.

The harder part is making sure a fix reaches every place the bug lives. Launchway knows, from the software graph and the record, which release branches are supported, which versions run in which Airfield and on which hosts, and which of them contain the files the fix changes without the fix itself. For kiosk-os that is release/4.1 and release/4.2, running on 212 and 1,040 hosts. It opens a carry-back pull request into each, with the original pull request linked, marks any that conflict for a person with the lines, and tracks each line until a release containing the fix has launched. The tracker says plainly what it could not decide, for example a fix that rewrote a file the old line does not have.

Versions and release notes, by role

Built today

Each Flight chooses a version scheme (semantic versions by default, calendar versions, natural order, or order of creation). launchway release next proposes the next version from merged pull requests and commit prefixes, with the reason for each change, and a person confirms it. Notes are written from merged pull requests (or closed work items) grouped as breaking changes, security, features, fixes, dependencies and other changes. A published release never changes.

The plan sets the scheme per role: the trunk can publish prereleases or calendar versions; a release branch takes its version line from its name (release/4.2 gives 4.2.x); a component in a shared repository has its own tags; a tag-based release is the tag as written. Release notes for a release branch are written from the changes on that line since its last release, including what was carried back, and say "carried back from 4.3.0" beside each such entry.

The running example: how Harbor Lights branches

FlightSquadronPatternWhy, in the recognition card's words

The foundation it relies on

  • Git and the record. Recognition reads branches, merges, tags and forks from Git and Launches from the record. A role is stored with each Sortie, so "which role did this run under" has a permanent answer.
  • Typed triggers and the checker. Role-based triggers are checked like any other: a role that no branch matches, or a pipeline that no role triggers, is reported before the change lands.
  • Flight plans and levels. A pattern's Flight plan is set at a level and filled in below it, as Flight plans are today, with locks where a level requires them.
  • Routes and releases. Every pattern ends in the same release, built once and moved by digest.
  • The Simulator. Every move and every recognized pattern can be replayed against the team's own history before it is accepted.

Safety

If this fails or is wrongWhat happens
Recognition is wrongNothing has changed: the card proposes, a person decides. A correction is kept with its reason.
A branch matches no roleIt is a change branch by default, so it runs the CI pipeline and never launches beyond a preview.
A branch matches two rolesThe pattern file is refused with the line and the two roles, before it is saved.
A carry-back conflictsThe pull request is opened as a draft and marked for a person, with the lines; nothing is merged by itself.
An environment branch holds files that were never verified upstreamThe Launch asks for a Clearance by default and lists the files; a level may make it a denial.
A move is stopped half-wayEach step is a complete change on its own; the team works on at whichever step it reached, and the plan shows it.
The server or database is lostRoles are files in Git and settings in the database with history; nothing about branching is held only in memory. Sorties in flight keep the role they started with.
Who mayIn this plan
Accept or correct a recognized patternA Commander of the Flight, by a reviewed change
Start or continue a moveA Commander of the Flight; each step reviewed
Recommend a pattern for a kind of repositoryA Commander of the Wing (organization) or Squadron
Mark a pull request "this line only"Its author, with a reason from a list; judged by the Standing order
Mark a change urgentAnyone who may open the pull request; recorded; it changes order, never checks

On by default: recognition runs on import and when asked, and changes nothing; a new repository is offered main with feature branches; version tags are protected; fixes-first is on for release branches; drift findings advise and never block.
