Open question

  1. Branch roles. The idea and the role names (trunk, change, integration, release, hotfix, environment, contribution) are proposed here. They are plain words, not new aviation words. Accept, or choose others. Open question
  2. The default pattern for a new repository. The earlier design recommends main with feature branches, and for a library the same plus tag-based releases. Confirm. Open question
  3. May a level require a pattern? Recommendation: a level recommends, and may require only for a kind of repository it names, with a lock; a move is always offered as a plan, never forced. Open question
  4. Environment branches. Supported, with advice to move to promotion by digest. Confirm that the advice never becomes a requirement by default, as the earlier design proposed. Open question
  5. When branching moves in the roadmap. This chapter proposes moving the two existing branching items from Milestone 5 to Milestone 3, leaving only the graph-dependent patterns in Milestone 5. Open question
  6. Carry-back pull requests on by default? Recommendation: on for release branches, opened as drafts, so nobody is surprised by a merge. Open question
  7. A linked change that breaks half-way. When a member on an outside host fails after an earlier one has merged, this chapter opens revert pull requests for the merged members and launches nothing. The alternative is to leave the merged members and ask a person. Recommendation: open the reverts as drafts, so a person decides in one click either way. Open question

Launch · the shared model

One way to launch, anywhere

Every Launch (deployment), to any kind of place, is the same flight: one release, named by its digest, flies a Route through Airfields (environments), is cleared, launched with a strategy, judged by Overwatch (the watch after a Launch), and can always return to base.

  • What is launched is a release: built once, named by digest, never rebuilt on its way to production.
  • Where it goes is an Airfield made of one or more targets. How an Airfield is served is the Airfield's choice; the pipeline only names the Airfield.
  • How it gets there is a Route (proposed word): the ordered Airfields a release flies through, with what must be true at each stop. A stop can advance by itself once it is verified.
  • Return to base (rollback) is always possible, never blocked by a lock, a Hold (freeze) or a Clearance (approval), and is recorded as a Launch of its own.
  • Many at once, with the same rules: one release to many tenants in waves; several releases as one Formation (releases that go together) with one Clearance, one watch and one way back; and infrastructure stacks launched from a reviewed plan kept by digest.
  • Every failure reads the same on every kind of target: one list of causes, one sentence, its evidence and one next action.

Where it sits

This chapter is the core of layer 5 on the map, Launch (delivery). Every other Launch chapter is a case of it: Launching to Kubernetes, Launching to virtual machines and physical servers, Launching to image-based hosts and Launching to serverless. How traffic moves and how a Launch is judged is in Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch.

Builds on
The levels and permissions of layer 1 (the system); the one record of layer 2 (the record); steps and run forms of layer 3 (Pipelines, values and expressions; Inputs and run forms); Stations (runners) and Cargo (artifacts) of layer 4, with the Depot (registry) holding what was built by digest (the Depot).
Built on by
Layer 6, Command: Standing orders (policies) are judged at the Preflight (checks) of every Launch, Clearances and Holds stop it, and evidence packs read its record (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; the Logbook and evidence). Layer 7 modules: Switches (feature toggles) and Drills (chaos tests) reuse Overwatch (Switches).
Layers used
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

What you will be able to do

You are a Pilot (developer) on the storefront Flight (codebase). You merge a pull request. The image is built once. Release 2.4.0 lands in dev, passes Overwatch, moves to staging by itself, and waits there for one Go from a Controller (approver) before prod. You started one Sortie (run); the Route did the rest.

You open the Route board for storefront. It shows 2.4.0 verified in staging, 2.3.2 running in prod, and the reason 2.4.0 is not moving: "Waiting for one Clearance; the business-hours window opens at 09:00."

You are on call. Fifty minutes after 2.4.0 reached prod, checkout errors climb. A Hold for the weekend is in force and another Launch is mid-flight. You press Return to base, read one sentence saying what will change, give a reason, and prod is back on 2.3.2. Nothing stopped you, and the return is on the record as a Launch of its own.

You open a pull request on storefront. A short-lived Airfield named pr-482 appears with its own address on the pull request. It expires when the pull request merges, or after three days of no change.

An auditor asks who put digest sha256:4f9c…a17 into prod, and why it was allowed. One Launch record answers: who asked, when, on whose Clearance, which Standing orders passed, the strategy, the Overwatch verdict with its evidence, and that it was later returned to base.

You run the platform for Harbor Lights. You move staging from a GitOps controller to direct installs. No pipeline changes, because pipelines name the Airfield, never the machinery.

Harbor Lights also runs storefront for three partner shops. You launch 2.4.0 once. It reaches your own shop first, then one partner, then the other two, each with its own settings, and one partner that asked to approve its own changes gets its own Clearance card. The page shows one row per tenant and one verdict each.

You change the size of the storefront database in code. The pull request shows the infrastructure plan: one resource changed in place, nothing destroyed, about 38 dollars a month more. Ana gives Go on exactly that plan; the apply refuses to run anything else.

How it works

The nouns

Nine things, and every target uses all of them. Each has an aviation name and a plain word.

WordPlain wordWhat it isToday
ReleasereleaseAn immutable set of Cargo (artifacts) built from one commit, each named by digest: images, a chart or manifest set, a package, an operating-system image, a function package. Shown by version, decided by digest.Available as a release with a version, notes and assets; digests passed to the pipeline as digest and digests.
AirfieldenvironmentA policy boundary: who may launch there, which Standing orders apply, whether it is protected, which Holds and windows apply, which secrets it holds. Made of one or more targets.Available with one target each.
TargettargetOne real place a release runs: a cluster and its namespaces, a group of hosts, a fleet of image-based hosts, a function. Each target says how it is served.Available for a cluster through Argo CD. Others below.
Routepromotion pathThe ordered Airfields a release flies through, with what must be true to enter each stop and what makes it verified.New in this plan The word needs your yes.
LaunchdeploymentOne release into one Airfield, from Preflight to verdict, with one record.Available as a deploy step and its deployment record.
StrategystrategyHow the change spreads: all at once, rolling, Pathfinder (canary), or a two-fleet swap.Available through a rollout controller and over SSH; see Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch.
Preflight, Standing orderschecks, policiesRules judged before a Launch starts, with a verdict and reasons on the record.Available as policy gates "before deploying".
ClearanceapprovalA person (or a rule) saying Go or No-go, with who and why.Available
Overwatchwatch after a LaunchThe judgment of the new version against live traffic, health and earlier good Launches, with a verdict and its evidence.Available as a verify step. Planned as a watch that carries on after the last step.
Return to baserollbackGoing back to the last good release. Always possible, never blocked, and recorded as a Launch.Available by Git revert, also after success.

What is launched: a release, built once

A release is made once, by one Sortie, from one commit. Every artifact in it is stored in the Depot and named by its digest. A tag such as 2.4.0 is a name people read; the digest is what Launchway launches, compares and records. Moving a release from dev to prod moves the same digests. Nothing is built again on the way.

That rule holds for every kind of target. On Kubernetes the image reference is written with its digest. On an image-based host a tag is refused and only a digest is accepted, which is how Launchway works today. For a package on a virtual machine the digest is the checksum of the package file. For a function it is the digest of the package or image behind the function version.

Built today

A release has a version, notes and assets, and is immutable once published. Promotion starts the Flight's own pipeline at the release tag with the inputs release, version, airfield, sha, digest and digests, and refuses a pipeline that declares none of them rather than rebuilding. The deployment record, however, has no digest field: the digest is only there when a pipeline passes it as the version text, or inside the Git commit.

Proposal

Every Launch records one entry per artifact with its digest, and, separately, the digest Launchway reads back from each target. "What we launched" and "what is running" become two facts that can be compared, and drift becomes a finding with a cause. See proposed changes.

Where it goes: an Airfield and its targets

An Airfield is where a team's rules live. A target is where the software runs. The prod Airfield at Harbor Lights has four targets: the shop-cluster namespace for storefront, the two virtual machines of the billing pool, the kiosks fleet of image-based hosts, and the resize function. A Launch of storefront touches only its own target; the Airfield's rules apply to all four.

Delivery by choice: the pipeline names the Airfield, never the machinery

Each target says how it is served. The pipeline does not. This is 's "pipelines name the capability, never the product" applied to delivery, and 's "how a pipeline delivers is the user's choice" made per Airfield.

Kind of targetServed by (pick one per target)Today
KubernetesA GitOps controller (Argo CD first; others through an adapter), or direct: chart installs or plain manifests applied by a launch Station.Available GitOps with Argo CD. Planned Built-in Helm and Kubernetes deploys.
Virtual machines and physical serversA host fleet over SSH, an Ansible playbook, and later an agent on the host that pulls.Available Delivery to machines over SSH, run by a Station (see the caveat below).
Image-based hostsAn image fleet built on bootc: stage by digest, reboot in batches, admit.Available Image-based hosts, with the same caveat.
ServerlessA function platform: a cloud's function or container service, or Knative on Kubernetes.Planned

A team that does not want a GitOps controller does not need one. A team that has one keeps it. The pipeline is the same either way:

The deploy step names the Airfield and also the Argo CD application and the file it writes. This keeps working; no existing pipeline changes.

steps:
  deploy-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [image, approve-prod]
    environment: prod
    service: storefront
    version: { output: image.digest }
    argocd:
      application: storefront
      write_back:
        repo: gitops
        branch: main
        changes:
          - { file: apps/storefront/prod/values.yaml, image: harbor-lights/storefront, digest: { output: image.digest } }
      sync: { request: auto, windows: wait }
      health: application

Design: not built. The step names the Airfield, the service and the release. Everything about the machinery comes from the Airfield.

steps:
  launch:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [image]
    environment: ${{ inputs.airfield }}
    service: storefront
    release: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}   # a digest, recorded as a fact of its own

Design: not built. The prod Airfield as the platform team keeps it, on screen or as a file. Key names are not final.

airfield: prod
protected: true
targets:
  - name: shop-cluster
    kind: kubernetes
    served_by: gitops                 # gitops | direct
    namespaces: [storefront]
  - name: billing-pool
    kind: machines
    served_by: host-fleet
  - name: kiosks
    kind: image-hosts
    served_by: image-fleet
  - name: resize
    kind: functions
    served_by: function-platform
services:
  storefront: { target: shop-cluster, strategy: pathfinder }
  billing:    { target: billing-pool, strategy: rolling }
Built today

An Airfield is held in the database (launchway environments set) with a name, one target, the Flights allowed, queue: newest|all, protected, reviewers, a minimum number of Clearances and, for a repository Launchway hosts, how write-back reaches it (direct or by pull request). Part of the machinery already lives on the Airfield; the rest is still in the step.

Caveat

The roadmap marks delivery to machines over SSH and image-based hosts Available. The pipeline reference says the server refuses to schedule a fleet step inside a Sortie: a Station runs it with launchway fleet run, and the host inventory is a file. Until the server schedules it, a fleet Launch takes no Airfield lock, writes no deployment record and passes no Standing order gate. The chapter Launching to virtual machines and physical servers covers the fix.

How it gets there: a Route

A Route is the ordered list of Airfields a release flies through. Each stop says three things: what must be true to enter it, what makes it verified, and how the release advances from it: by itself, on a Clearance, or by hand.

A Route adds no second way to launch. When a stop advances, Launchway starts the Flight's own pipeline at the release tag with the airfield, release and digest inputs, exactly as a promotion does today. The Route only decides when, and writes why on the record.

# Design: not built. The storefront Route. Key names are not final.
route: storefront
releases: { from_branch: main }
stops:
  - airfield: dev
    advance: by_itself
    verified_when: { overwatch: pass, stay_at_least: 15m }
  - airfield: staging
    advance: by_itself
    verified_when: { overwatch: pass, stay_at_least: 2h, checks: [contract-tests] }
  - airfield: prod
    enter_when: { clearances: 1, window: business-hours }
    advance: by_hand                    # the last stop; nothing after it

Rules every Route keeps:

  • It never rebuilds, and never skips a stop.
  • A release that failed a stop does not move on. A release returned to base at a stop stays there until a newer one arrives or a person re-admits it with a reason.
  • A newer release that reaches a stop replaces an older one still waiting there, as queue: newest does for Launches today. A Route can say "every release, in turn" instead.
  • A stop may hold several Airfields, launched together or one after another (for example prod-east, then prod-west).
  • Enter conditions are Standing orders, Clearances, Holds and windows, judged the same way as everywhere else. A Route can add rules but never remove one a level above has set.
  • A Route never holds back a Return to base.
Proposal

Harbor Lights keeps dev and staging on one Base and prod on another, as you chose for your own installations. A Route stop can therefore be another installation. The Route sends the verified release and its evidence as an event; the other installation takes it, judges its own Preflight and Clearances, and reports its verdict back. No credential crosses the line.

One release to many tenants

New in this plan Some teams run one copy of their software for each customer. Each copy is a tenant: its own place to run, its own settings, often its own database, and sometimes its own rules about when it may change and who must agree. The usual answer elsewhere is a loop in a script, or one pipeline per customer. Launchway's answer comes from the model: the release, the Route and the Airfield stay the same, and tenants are a fan-out inside one stop, launched in waves, each tenant with its own Launch record.

A tenant hasWhat it meansHow it is filled
Name and placementWhere this tenant's copy runs: a namespace, a cluster, a group of hosts, a function, or a whole Airfield target of its own.Name checked as you type; placement picked from the Airfield's targets and the namespaces or host groups a Station reports.
SettingsValues that differ per tenant (theme, currency, limits) and references to its own secrets. They override the Airfield's values and use the same typed schema, so Preflight (checks) can say "the release adds delivery_cutoff; two tenants have no value for it" before anything moves.A form built from the Flight's declared settings; secrets picked from the store by reference, never typed.
WaveWhich wave of the fan-out it joins. Waves are ordered; the first is usually a tenant you run yourself.Picked from the Airfield's waves, or by label (ring=internal).
ClearanceNone beyond the Airfield's, or its own: named people (a customer's contact can hold a role that only sees that tenant and only says Go or No-go).People and groups picked from the Wing (organization).
Window and HoldIts own change window and its own Holds, on top of the Airfield's.Drawn on the week grid of the Hold calendar.
PinKeep this tenant on a version line, with a reason, until a person lifts the pin. A pinned tenant is skipped and listed, never silently left behind.A version line picked from the releases it may run; a reason picked or typed.
  • Waves advance on proof. The next wave starts only when every tenant in the wave before it has an Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) pass and has stayed the time the wave asks. A wave can also stop after a set number of failed tenants (one by default).
  • One lock per tenant. A slow tenant, or one waiting for its window, never holds up the others, and a Return to base for one tenant never waits for the rest.
  • A failure stays small. The failing tenant returns to base by itself. Tenants that already passed keep the new release until you choose, on one confirmation, between Return every tenant and Keep and fix forward.
  • Nobody is forgotten. A tenant waiting for its window, its own Go or a host that is away is shown as waiting, with the reason. The parent Launch stays open until every tenant is done, skipped with a reason, or pinned.
  • Judged against itself and its peers. Each tenant is compared with its own earlier good Launches, and also with the other tenants already on the new release, so a tenant that is worse than its peers is named even when its own numbers look ordinary.
  • One record, cut per tenant. One parent Launch and one child Launch per tenant, each with its settings digest, its Clearance and its verdict. A customer's auditor can be given a view of that tenant's records only.
# Design: not built. Tenants and waves on the prod Airfield. Key names are not final.
airfield: prod
tenants:
  - { name: harbor-lights,   wave: internal, placement: { target: shop-cluster, namespace: storefront } }
  - { name: pier-books,      wave: early,    placement: { target: shop-cluster, namespace: t-pier-books },
      values: { theme: pier } }
  - { name: dockside-gifts,  wave: rest,     placement: { target: shop-cluster, namespace: t-dockside-gifts } }
  - { name: lighthouse-cafe, wave: rest,     placement: { target: shop-cluster, namespace: t-lighthouse-cafe },
      clearance: { by: [lighthouse-cafe-contacts] }, window: tuesday-early }
waves:
  - { name: internal, then: { overwatch: pass, stay_at_least: 30m } }
  - { name: early,    then: { overwatch: pass, stay_at_least: 2h } }
  - { name: rest,     stop_after_failed: 1 }

Worked moment. Launch L-312 takes storefront 2.4.0 into prod. Its tenant view shows four rows: harbor-lights Mission complete after 30 minutes; pier-books Mission complete two hours later; dockside-gifts Airborne; lighthouse-cafe "Waiting for its contact's Go and its Tuesday window". The parent stays Airborne until the last row is done.

A Formation: one Clearance, one watch, one way back

A Formation (releases that go together) is several releases that must fly as one: a database change and the services that use it, or a provider and the consumer that needs its new field. Launchway already groups releases of several Flights, checks them all before any starts, and promotes them in the order you write or in dependency order Available in the product (see the proposed status change to "Releases across services"). This section designs the rest: one decision, one watch and one way back, with the database first. Planned One go or no-go, one watch, one way back; Database first, then the application.

  1. Order. Members are ordered from the software graph (storefront calls payments, so payments goes first) or in the order you write. A database change is always first and only ever its expand half; its contract half joins a later Formation, once the Route says nothing still needs the old shape (see databases that stay up).
  2. One Clearance. One card lists every member: its digest, what changes against what runs now, its Preflight verdict, and the order of the way back. One Go covers the set of digests; a change to any member voids it. The person who says Go may have written none of the members.
  3. One watch. Each member keeps its own Overwatch. The Formation adds a joint proof that only the set can fail, such as checkout success measured at the edge, or contract tests between members run after each member lands. The Formation passes only when every member and the joint proof pass.
  4. One way back. If any member or the joint proof fails, members already launched return to base in reverse order, each taking its own lock in that order. It is never blocked, as for any Return to base. A Hold covers the whole Formation going forward and none of it going back.
  5. One record. A Formation record links its members' Launch records, the one Clearance, the joint verdict and the return, so an auditor reads one story.

Worked moment. Release 2.4.0 shows the delivery date at checkout, and the date comes from payments 3.8.0, which needs change set 43 on the payments database. The three fly prod as the Formation checkout-dates. Ana reads one card and says Go once. Change set 43 is applied, payments 3.8.0 passes, storefront 2.4.0 passes, and the joint checkout proof passes. Had the joint proof failed, storefront would have returned to 2.3.2 and then payments to 3.7.4, with change set 43 left in place and named on the record as safe for both.

Each Launch uses a strategy

The strategy says how the change spreads inside one Airfield. There are four, and every target offers the ones it can honestly do. The detail, with how traffic moves and what is watched, is in Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch.

StrategyIn one lineKubernetesMachinesImage-based hostsServerless
All at onceReplace everything together. Short downtime unless something in front holds requests.yesyesyesyes
RollingReplace a few copies at a time, never below the floor of healthy copies.yesyes, in batchesyes, in reboot batchesnot meaningful
Pathfinder (canary)Send a small, growing share of traffic to the new version and compare it with the stable one.yesyes, a second host groupyes, a first batch of hostsyes, version weights
Two-fleet swapBring up a full new fleet beside the old, test it, switch traffic at once, keep the old one ready.yesyes, with a load balanceronly with spare hostsyes

Before it starts: Preflight, Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

  1. Preflight. The Standing orders that apply to the Airfield are judged: tests passed, no blocking findings, a parts list exists, every image pinned by digest, signed and scanned, the Clearances required, the refs allowed. A refusal says which rule and why, and nothing reaches Git or a target. Available
  2. Clearance. If the Airfield or the Route stop asks for it, a Controller says Go or No-go. The person who started the Sortie may not clear its Launch into a protected Airfield (a one-person Base may allow it by policy, with a note on the record). Available
  3. Holding for the lock. One Launch per service per Airfield at a time. A Launch that finds the lock held waits in the Holding pattern (queue). Available
  4. Judged again at the lock. Facts change while a Launch waits: a Hold may have started, a finding may have arrived. Preflight is judged again, quickly, the moment the lock is taken. New in this plan
To verify

The survey found freeze handling only on the release promotion path ("Check and promote"), and inferred that a plain deploy step is not stopped by a freeze. This plan proposes that a Hold is judged on every Launch forward and never on a Return to base or a Master switch (kill switch) to its safe value. The roadmap change for it is proposed in Standing orders, Clearance and Hold, which owns Holds.

While and after: Overwatch

Overwatch judges the new version from the first copy that takes traffic until a set time after the last step. It compares the new version with the stable one and with earlier good Launches, reads logs for new error patterns, and gives one of three verdicts: pass, fail, or not enough data. A fail returns to base by itself, which is on by default and can be tuned by the team. Not enough data is never a pass. The full design is in Overwatch.

Return to base: always possible

Going back must never depend on the thing that is broken. A Return to base is a Launch of an earlier good release, with its own record.

  • A Return to base is a Sortie of its own with one step. It reverts in Git, newest first, the commit of every Launch after the version you chose, all or nothing, and waits until the application is healthy.
  • It records a new deployment of the restored version, and the original Sortie gains a link "returned to base later by run #N".
  • By default it goes to the previous successful Launch; Roll back to… lists every earlier one still in effect.
  • On a protected Airfield it is an emergency action: no Clearance first, only a reason, and an approver reviews it afterwards.
  • If another Launch holds the lock, it is queued behind it, ahead of every other waiting Launch.
  • An Airfield may set emergency_rollback: require_approval, which puts a Clearance in front of it.
  • If later commits changed the same lines, the revert does not apply; nothing changes in Git and the Sortie fails with a sentence naming the files.
  • It never restores a database or configuration, and says so. It lists Switch changes made since, and offers to revert them.

Design: not built.

  • Past a lock. If a Launch holds the lock, the Return to base first stops that Launch's shift (its own return to the stable version), then takes the lock. It does not wait.
  • Past a Hold. A Hold never applies to a Return to base.
  • Past a Clearance. No Clearance comes first. On a protected Airfield it is reviewed afterwards, as today.
  • Two ways back. The default is the Git revert, because it keeps history. When a revert cannot apply, the confirmation offers the second way: a new Launch of the last good digest, written over the files, with the exact difference shown first. One of the two always works while a launch Station can reach the target.
  • Automatic too. When Overwatch fails a Launch, the same Return to base runs by itself, and the record says "started by Overwatch" with the evidence.

What it cannot do is stated plainly every time: a Return to base restores the release, not the data. A schema change is made safe in a different way, by changing it in an order that keeps both versions working; see databases that stay up.

The record of a Launch

Every Launch writes one record, built from events on the one record of layer 2. Nothing about a Launch is true that is not on it.

The lifecycle of a Launch

Every target walks the same states. Screens, the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and events all use the same words.

StateStatus shownWhat is true
Requested, PreflightHoldingNothing has changed anywhere yet.
Waiting for ClearanceWaiting for clearanceWho may say Go is listed. A Clearance can expire.

ShiftingAirborneTraffic or work is moving step by step; each step is judged. A person may pause.

One list of failure causes for every target

Today a failed Launch to Kubernetes opens with one sentence, its evidence and one recommended action Available Why did it fail to deploy. The plan makes that sentence read the same for a cluster, a fleet of hosts, an image-based fleet, a function and an infrastructure stack. Each kind of target maps its own errors to one short list of causes; an error it cannot place is shown as "the target refused the change" with the target's own words attached, never as a new cause made up on the spot. New in this plan

Cause (machine name)The sentence readsEvidence it carriesThe one next action
Refused before start (refused)"Preflight refused the Launch: the image is not signed."The rule, the fact it read, the level that set itFix the finding, or ask for a time-limited waiver
Not cleared (not_cleared)"Ana said No-go: release notes missing."Who, when, the reason, or the expiryAnswer the reason and ask again
Release not fetched (fetch_failed)"The host could not fetch the release from the Depot."The digest, the Depot's answer, the place that askedCheck the Depot's reach from that target
Target refused the change (target_refused)"The cluster refused the change: the quota for storefront is used up."The target's own error, the object, host or version it concernsThe action the target's error points to, named
Never became ready (not_ready)"billing-2 failed its health check twice after the install."A crashing copy's last words, a check's answers, a host's boot report, a function's start errorOpen the log at the first error
Proof failed (proof_failed)"Overwatch failed the Launch: checkout errors 1.4 percent against 0.2."The metric, the reference, the band, new log patternsCompare with the stable version; the return already ran
Not enough data (not_enough_data)"41 requests in 10 minutes; at least 200 needed."Counts against the minimum, the source that answeredWait, add test traffic, or a person decides
Target unreachable (unreachable)"The kiosk in the harbor shop has not reported for 40 minutes."Last contact, last known stateCheck the network or the host; the Launch waits as stated
Station lost (station_lost)"The launch Station stopped answering during step 2 of 4."Which Station, the last event it sentResume or return from another Station
Ran out of time (timed_out)"The sync did not finish within 30 minutes."Where it was when time ran outExtend the time, or find what it waited for
Changed outside a Launch (changed_outside)"prod runs a digest no Launch put there."Launched digest against observed digest, when it changedReturn to the launched release, or adopt the change with a reason
Could not return (return_incomplete)"billing-2 could not be returned and is out of rotation."What runs where, per copy or hostA person takes the named host or object in hand

The causes Kubernetes Launches name today fold into this list without loss: analysis failed becomes proof failed; sync failed and command failed become the target refused the change; rollout failed becomes never became ready or the target refused, by its evidence; timeout, refused and Station lost keep their meaning. The cause is a field on the Launch event, so Radar, the Debrief (test report), Comms (notifications) and the agent endpoint all count failures by the same names. Design: not built for every target other than Kubernetes.

Previews: a short-lived Airfield for every pull request

A preview is an Airfield like any other, made from a template Airfield the platform team names, with three extra rules: it has a time limit, a cost cap, and it disappears when its pull request merges or closes. Because it is an Airfield, a preview gets the same Launch, the same record and the same Overwatch. Its address is posted on the pull request.

  • Kubernetes: a namespace per pull request, installed directly (no GitOps commit for something that lives three days). See previews on Kubernetes.
  • Serverless: a function version with its own address and no share of live traffic.
  • Machines and image-based hosts: a throwaway virtual machine, as Launchway already uses to test a new operating-system image.
  • Forks: a pull request from a fork gets no secrets and no preview until a person says Go.
  • Data: a preview gets its own short-lived database, never production data unmasked.
Built today

Not yet possible: deploy steps do not run in pull request Sorties, and a deployment can only record an address. Three planned roadmap items cover previews; this plan joins them under one model without removing any.

Preview data: masked, capped and removed with the preview

A preview that tests a schema change needs a database, and a preview that shows a realistic shop needs realistic rows. Production rows never leave production unmasked. The template Airfield picks one of three sources, and the preview's database lives and dies with the preview. Planned Masked and preview databases (Milestone 10), widened by this plan from guidance to a design.

SourceWhat the preview getsWhen to pick it
Fixtures (the default)An empty database with the pull request's schema changes applied, then the fixture files kept in the repository.Most previews; every pull request from a fork, which never gets more.
Masked seedA copy restored from a masked seed: a snapshot made on a Patrol (schedule) inside production's network by a masking step on a Station there, with every column handled by a reviewed masking rule file. The seed is stored in the Depot by digest, encrypted, with the version of the masking rules it was made with.Previews that need realistic volume and shape.
Branch from the masked copyA branch, in seconds, from a long-lived masked copy, where the database service can branch by copying on write.Large data sets where restoring a seed is too slow.
  • Masked or refused. A seed is made only if every column of every table is covered by a rule (keep, fake, hash, blank or drop). A new column with no rule stops the next seed and opens a finding on the Flight; it is never copied as is. A Standing order (policy) "preview data comes only from a masked seed" checks the seed's masking record before the preview's Launch.
  • Capped. The template sets a size cap for the seed and for each preview database. A seed over the cap is cut by the rule file's sampling rules (for example "orders from the last 90 days, with the customers they need"); a preview database that reaches its cap stops taking writes and says so on the pull request, rather than growing the bill.
  • Tested as it will ship. The pull request's own schema changes run against the preview's database through the same database change step as in prod, so the preview proves the change set too.
  • Removed with the preview. When the pull request merges, closes or expires, the database and its storage are deleted, and the deletion is an event on the record. A preview's data never outlives the preview.

Spend against the cap, on the pull request. Every preview has a cost cap. The pull request shows one line, updated as the preview runs: "Preview pr-482: 1.90 dollars of 5.00 so far, expires in 2 days." The figure is an estimate from what the preview runs and for how long, replaced by the billed figure where a cost source is connected (see Radar, insight and keeping it healthy). At 80 percent of the cap the line turns to a warning; at the cap the preview scales to zero and wakes only when someone opens it or pushes, and its data is kept until it expires. Planned A preview environment for every pull request (cost cap); spend on the pull request New in this plan.

Worked moment. Dana opens pull request #482. Preview pr-482 restores the masked seed storefront-seed@sha256:2e7a…c90, made last night with masking rules version 14; it applies the pull request's change to the orders table; the shop answers at its preview address with masked customers and real order shapes. The pull request merges; the database is gone a minute later, and the record says so.

Four kinds of target, one model

Your words name five places software runs: image-based hosts, virtual machines, physical servers, Kubernetes and serverless. Virtual machines and physical servers are launched the same way, so they share a column. The last row is the honest one: where each kind does not fit the model, and what Launchway does about it.

FactKubernetesVirtual machines and physical serversImage-based hostsServerless
What is launchedImage digests, and a chart or manifest set at its digest or commitA package or file by checksum, or an image by digestAn operating-system image by digest (tags refused)A function package or image by digest, as an immutable version
Served byA GitOps controller, or direct installsA host fleet over SSH, a playbook, later an agentAn image fleet: stage, reboot, admitA function platform, in a cloud or on Kubernetes
A target isA cluster and its namespacesA group of hosts from the Airfield's inventoryA fleet of hostsOne function or service
How traffic movesCopies replaced; route weights through the Gateway API or a service meshHosts drained and admitted at a load balancer, in batchesHosts drained, rebooted into the new image, admittedWeights between versions
How health is knownReadiness, the controller's health, OverwatchA check you declare per host, plus OverwatchBooted digest equals launched digest, plus a check, plus OverwatchThe platform's metrics per version, plus Overwatch
Return to baseGit revert, or re-apply the previous setPrevious release kept on the host; switch back and restartBoot the previous imagePoint traffic at the previous version, in seconds
Where it does not fitA rollout controller can go back to stable without changing Git, so what runs and what Git says differ until the revert lands; Launchway records both and finishes the revert. A controller also changes live state with no Launch (self-heal, drift), so those are recorded as observations, not Launches.Pushing over SSH leaves no desired state on the host: a host that is off misses the Launch. It is shown as "waiting for this host" and launched when it returns. Health is only what you declare. Going back to an older package is not always clean.Activation is a reboot, so "staged" and "running" differ for a while. A host can update itself on a timer unless pinned by digest, which Launchway does. The verdict can arrive late, after the reboot. Data on the host's writable disk is never returned.There is no lock at the provider: someone can change the function from its console, which Launchway reports as drift. Queues, tables and buckets live outside the version. Early latency is distorted by cold starts, which Overwatch discounts.

Infrastructure stacks: a plan you clear, applied exactly

The databases, buckets, networks and address records a service needs are described in code and changed by an infrastructure tool (OpenTofu or Terraform). In Launchway such a description is an infrastructure stack, and a stack is one more kind of target in an Airfield. It carries no traffic, so it has no strategy and no Pathfinder (canary), but everything else in the model holds: a reviewed artifact kept by digest, a Clearance on exactly that artifact, one lock, one record, drift as a finding, and a way back.

PartHow Launchway does itStatus
A stack is an Airfield targetOne stack in code (for example infra/shop-data) becomes one instance per Airfield: shop-data in dev, in staging and in prod. Each instance has its own typed variables, its own state, its own lock and its own drift. This is what other tools call a workspace; here it is simply the stack's place in an Airfield, so Standing orders, Holds and Clearances that guard the Airfield guard the stack too.New in this plan Infrastructure stacks as Airfield targets
The plan is CargoThe plan step runs on a Station in the Airfield's Ramp (runner pool) with a short-lived cloud identity, and stores the plan file in the Depot, encrypted, by digest. Beside it go a readable difference with sensitive values shown as "changed, hidden", and typed plan facts: resources added, changed, replaced and destroyed by kind, anything that becomes reachable from the internet, and the estimated monthly cost before and after.Available A configuration change is a plan; New in this plan kept by digest, typed facts and cost
Standing orders on the planThe plan facts are facts like any other, judged at Preflight: "nothing destroyed in prod without a second Clearance", "no new public address". The rule catalog for plans belongs to Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; this chapter supplies the facts.New in this plan
The Clearance cardShows the difference grouped as destroyed, replaced, changed and added (destroyed first, loud), the plan facts, the Standing order verdicts and the estimated cost change, labeled as an estimate. Go is given on the plan's digest and the state version it was made from.New in this plan
The apply refuses a changed planThe apply fetches the plan by digest and runs exactly it. It refuses, with the reason, if the digest differs from the cleared one, if the state version moved since the plan was made, or if the commit or the inputs differ. A refused apply changes nothing; a new plan starts the review again.Available for the plan file; New in this plan the state-version and commit refusal
State, kept insideState is stored, versioned, encrypted and locked inside Launchway, with who, when and which Sortie made each version. The plan adds a masked difference between any two versions, and a choice per stack of where state is served from: built in (the default) or your own backend as a connection, one provider in charge, shown as "served by".Available State and locking built in; New in this plan State versions compared, secrets masked
Drift per stack and AirfieldA Patrol runs a refresh-only plan for every stack instance and shows what differs on the Airfield page as a finding with the resources named. Converge now is an ordinary stack Launch of the current commit, under the same Clearance as any change. Take into code opens a pull request that writes the change into the stack, for the team to review.Available Drift and converge now; New in this plan per Airfield and Take into code
Outputs that flow onA stack's outputs (a database address, a bucket name) become typed values that later steps and other targets read, and a source a fleet can take its hosts from.New in this plan
The way backReturn to base plans the stack at the last good commit and applies it. It is never held by a lock, a Hold or a Clearance; if that plan would destroy or replace a resource that holds data, the confirmation names each one and the person pressing must tick them, because a return restores the code, not the data.New in this plan
# Design: not built. A stack as a target of the prod Airfield. Key names are not final.
targets:
  - name: shop-data
    kind: stack
    served_by: opentofu            # or terraform
    source: infra/shop-data
    state: built-in                # or a connected backend
    variables: { db_size: large, region: us-central }
    drift: { patrol: every-6h }

Worked moment. Dana changes db_size for prod from medium to large. The plan step stores plan sha256:c3a8…51f: one database changed in place, nothing destroyed, about 38 dollars a month more. Standing orders pass. Ana opens the card, reads the difference and says Go. Before the apply runs, another cleared change to shop-data lands first and writes state version 32, so the apply refuses: "state moved from version 31 to 32 since this plan was made". A new plan, identical in effect, goes back to Ana. The second apply runs and records state version 33 and the new database outputs.

Worked example: storefront 2.4.0, from a commit to prod and back

  1. Built once. Dana merges pull request #482. Sortie 417 tests, builds and signs the image, Inspection (security scan) passes, and the Depot stores harbor-lights/storefront@sha256:4f9c…a17. Release 2.4.0 is cut as a candidate.
  2. dev. The Route launches it into dev with a rolling strategy. Preflight passes ("pinned by digest, signed, no new critical findings"). Overwatch passes after 15 minutes. Launch L-301 is Mission complete.
  3. staging. The Route advances by itself, same digest. Contract tests against payments pass; Overwatch passes after two hours. The release is published.
  4. prod, waiting. The stop asks for one Clearance and the business-hours window. Dana may not clear her own change. Ana reads the evidence and says Go.
  5. prod, airborne. Preflight is judged again as the lock is taken. Pathfinder sends 5, then 25, 50 and 100 percent of traffic, judged at each step. Overwatch watches for 30 minutes and passes. Launch L-312 is Mission complete, and the stable state of prod now names 2.4.0.
  6. Trouble later. Fifty minutes on, checkout errors climb for one card type. A Hold for the weekend has started, and a storefront Launch of 2.4.1 is waiting for the lock. Priya, on call, presses Return to base. The confirmation says: "prod goes from 2.4.0 back to 2.3.2; one Launch is reverted in Git; the database is not returned; the Switch delivery-date was turned on since, revert it too?" Priya ticks it and gives a reason.
  7. Back. Launch L-319 records the return: who, why, the Hold it passed through, and the Switch it turned back. The Route marks 2.4.0 "returned at prod" and will not send it again. Release 2.4.1, with the fix, flies the Route from dev.

The foundation it relies on

This is a foundation chapter, so instead of the module contract it names what it stands on and what it promises every module.

Levels and permissions

Airfields, Routes and Standing orders are set at a level (Base, Wing, Squadron, Flight) and flow down with locks. A Squadron (team) can require Pathfinder in prod; a Flight cannot loosen it.

The one record

Every Preflight verdict, Clearance, advance, step, verdict and return is an event with its reasons. The Launch record, the Logbook (audit trail) and the delivery measures are read from it.

The step contract

A Launch is a step on a Station, like every other step. A launch Station sits beside the target and holds its credentials; the server holds none.

The Depot

What is launched is what the Depot holds, by digest. Retention never deletes a digest that any Airfield still runs or could return to.

What it promises modules: one Launch record to read, one Overwatch to reuse (Switches use it for a Switch change; Drills use it as the stop condition), and rule 10 of the module contract: nothing a module does may block a Return to base.

Safety

What happens on failure

What is lostWhat happens
A Launchway serverAnother server takes the Sortie on. A Launch in progress is not repeated: every step a launch Station takes records the state it expected, and a repeated command is refused.
The databaseLaunch Stations keep shifting only to the end of the current step and hold there; they spool events and send them when the server is back. No step starts that the server has not recorded. An automatic Return to base that Overwatch already decided goes ahead.
A launch StationThe Launch stops where it is, the failure reads "runner lost", and the target keeps running what it ran. Return to base is offered as soon as another Station serves the target; the page says that one is missing.
The metrics sourceOverwatch says not enough data, never pass. The Launch pauses at its current step and asks; it does not move forward on silence.
A target, part wayThe record lists what is where, per copy or per host. A host that cannot be returned is taken out of traffic and marked; the Launch ends in "needs a person".
The code hostA release is already in the Depot by digest, so nothing needs the code host to launch it. Where an Airfield takes its desired state from the Depot, its controller keeps working and write-back to Git catches up later. See when the code host or Launchway is down.
Launchway itselfTargets keep running what they run. A break-glass Return to base on a launch Station can re-apply an earlier set the server recorded and signed, and the server records it as a Launch when it is back. No new release can be launched this way.
One tenant of manyIts own lock and its own Launch, so it fails, waits or returns alone; the parent Launch lists it.

Who may do what

ActionWho
See Airfields, Routes, Launch recordsObserver (viewer) and above on the Flight
Launch into an unprotected Airfield; advance a Route by handPilot (developer) with launch rights on that Airfield (today: the operator role)
Give a ClearanceController (approver) for that Airfield, never the person who started the Sortie, unless a one-person Base allows it by policy
Return to baseAnyone who may launch to the Airfield, with a reason; reviewed afterwards on a protected Airfield
Edit an Airfield, its targets or a RouteCommander (owner) of the level that holds it, or someone they grant it to

On by default

  • Digests, not tags, for everything launched; a signed image for protected Airfields.
  • One Launch per service per Airfield at a time.
  • Overwatch after every Launch into a protected Airfield, and automatic Return to base on a fail. A team may tune or turn these off; a level above may require them.
  • Separation of duties for Clearances.
  • Previews off until a platform team names a template Airfield.

Screens

Full descriptions are in the screens notes; the screens chapter draws them.

Route board

One row per release, one column per stop. Each cell shows the Launch state, the verdict, and why a release is not moving ("waiting for one Clearance"). Buttons: Advance, Clear, Return to base, each shown only where it works.

Route editor

A wizard: pick Airfields from a list in order, then per stop pick enter conditions (Clearances from a number field, windows from the calendar, checks from the Flight's steps) and the advance mode from three choices. A preview shows the release that would move next.

Airfield page

Targets with how each is served, what runs on each by version and digest, observed against launched, the lock holder, the Holding pattern, Holds, and history.

Airfield setup wizard, served by

Per target: the kind (four choices), how it is served (only the choices that kind supports, each probed live), the default strategy and the floor of healthy copies.

Return to base confirmation

The sentence of what will change, the target version picked from a list of good Launches, the Switch changes to revert as tick boxes, the way back (revert or re-launch), and a reason picked from common reasons or typed.

Preview list

Open previews with their pull request, address, age, expiry, cost so far and health; Extend and Tear down.

Tenants of an Airfield

One row per tenant: placement, wave, release it runs, pin, its own Clearance and window, and the state of its latest Launch. During a Launch the same rows show each tenant's progress and verdict, with Return this tenant and Return every tenant.

Formation Clearance card

Every member with its digest, difference and Preflight verdict; the order going forward and the order going back; the joint proof; one Go or No-go with a reason picked from common reasons.

Stack plan review

The Clearance card for an infrastructure plan: destroyed, replaced, changed and added resources, plan facts, Standing order verdicts and the estimated cost change, bound to the plan digest and state version.

Stack on the Airfield page

Per stack instance: state versions with who and which Sortie, a masked difference between two picked versions, the lock holder, drift findings with Converge now and Take into code, and outputs.

Preview data, in the template Airfield

Source picked from three cards (fixtures, masked seed, branch), seed Patrol from the schedule picker, size caps as numbers with units, the masking rule file picked from the repository, and the rule coverage shown as a meter.

Failure sentence

The top of every failed Launch: cause, one sentence, evidence, one next action, the same on every target.
