Open question

  1. Open question The word Route. Proposed in the spine for the ordered Airfields a release flies through. Without it, the plain word is "promotion path".
  2. Open question Tenants as a plain word. The plan adds no aviation word for a tenant. Recommendation: keep "tenant", and keep tenants inside an Airfield rather than one Airfield per customer, so the Route and the Standing orders stay one.
  3. Open question Returning an infrastructure stack. The plan lets a stack's Return to base run past a Hold and without a Clearance, like any return, but makes the person tick each resource that holds data before a plan that destroys or replaces it. Recommendation: keep it; the other way is to require a Clearance for any return that destroys.
  4. Open question Where masked seeds are made. Recommendation: only on a Station inside production's network, so unmasked rows never cross it; the seed leaves only after every column has a rule.
  5. Open question A Clearance before an emergency return. The spine says a Return to base is never blocked by a Clearance. The product today lets an installation or an Airfield set emergency_rollback: require_approval. Recommendation: keep review afterwards as the only control and retire the option, with a notice to anyone who set it. The other way is to keep it as an option only a level above may set, shown on the Airfield in red.
  6. Open question Where a Route lives. Recommendation: with the Flight's settings in the database (ruling: configuration in the database), editable on screen or as a file in the repository, each producing a reviewable change in the other.
  7. Open question Does Overwatch hold the lock? Recommendation: yes, so a second Launch cannot start before the first is judged, with "end the watch early" available to a Controller with a reason.
  8. Open question Routes across installations. Your own prod is a separate installation. Recommendation: a stop may be another installation that takes the release by event and judges it itself; confirm this is how you want prod to be told.

For the plan's editor: the roadmap marks "Promotion across environments" and "Releases across services" Planned while the promotion guide describes the matrix, promotion and Formations as built; "Formations: things that go together" (Milestone 5) is Planned for the same reason. "Rollout control inside a run" (Available) depends on "Argo CD in depth" (Planned).

Launch · Kubernetes

Launching to Kubernetes

A Launch (deployment) to a Kubernetes cluster works today through a GitOps controller; this chapter adds launching directly, several clusters in one Airfield (environment), a preview for every pull request, autoscalers in plain view, and cluster rules that leave no side door.

  • Today a Launch writes one commit, asks Argo CD to sync, watches the rollout and its health, verifies the result, and returns to base by reverting that commit. The server never holds a cluster credential.
  • Next, the same Launch without any GitOps controller: Launchway renders a chart or plain manifests on its Station (runner), applies them, prunes only what it owned, and keeps the previous set to return to.
  • An Airfield can hold several clusters; a pull request gets its own namespace; a Pathfinder (canary) works with or without a rollout controller.
  • The cluster keeps its desired state when the code host is down, a break-glass return works when Launchway is down, a two-fleet swap needs no rollout controller, and the GitOps controller can be hosted or yours, run under Launchway's roles with its sync windows on the Hold calendar.
  • Milestones 3, 8 and 11 already plan most of this. The chapter puts it in one order and proposes one home for each GitOps idea that is listed twice.

Where it sits

Layer 5, Launch, for the Kubernetes kind of target. It is a case of One way to launch, anywhere: same release by digest, same Route, same Launch lifecycle, same record. How traffic moves and how a Launch is judged is in Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch.

Builds on
Launch Stations (layer 4) that sit beside a cluster and hold its access; Cargo (artifacts) in the Depot (registry) by digest (the Depot); Standing orders (policies) judged at Preflight (checks) (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold); the record (the record).
Built on by
Previews used by the developer experience; the cluster and fleet views of Milestone 11; virtual machines on Kubernetes (Launching to virtual machines and physical servers); functions on Kubernetes (Launching to serverless).
Layers used
1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.

What you will be able to do

You merge to main. storefront 2.4.0 reaches prod on shop-cluster through Argo CD: one commit pins the image by digest, the rollout sends 5, 25, 50 and 100 percent of traffic, and the Launch page shows every pod, its logs and the weights as they move. This works today.

Your team has no GitOps controller and does not want one. You set staging to be served directly. The next Launch shows the difference against the live cluster, applies it, removes the one object the new chart no longer renders, and records the full set it applied so a Return to base (rollback) can put it back exactly.

Harbor Lights opens a second cluster in another region. You add it as a second target of prod. A Launch now goes to shop-east first and to shop-west only after shop-east passes, with one record and one Return to base for both.

You open pull request #482. A namespace pr-482 appears, the change is installed there, its address and health are on the pull request, and the namespace and its database are gone when you merge.

During a Launch the autoscaler adds six copies of the stable version. The Launch page says so on its timeline, and shows that the new version's share of traffic stayed at 25 percent because weights are set at the gateway, not by the number of copies.

Someone with cluster access tries to apply an unsigned image into the storefront namespace by hand. The cluster refuses it, because the Standing order "only images launched by Launchway" is also a rule in the cluster. The refusal is a finding on the Airfield page.

How it works

Through a GitOps controller: what works today

Today's path uses Argo CD and is Available. A launch Station runs beside the cluster. It talks to the cluster's own API with its own identity: no Argo CD token, no step container, no cluster command-line tool. What it may do is a closed set: read applications, rollouts and their analyses; set an application's sync operation and its refresh marker; and, where allowed, send rollout commands.

PartExactly what it does today
GateStanding orders "before deploying": tests, findings, parts list, images pinned by digest, signed and scanned, Clearances (approvals), allowed failures, refs. A failing rule stops the step before anything reaches Git or the cluster. Waivers are time-limited (30 days by default) and on the Logbook (audit trail).
LockOne lock per service per Airfield, held from opening the Launch until the deploy, any rollout steps, verification and a Return to base on the path between are done. queue: newest (the default) skips an older waiting Sortie (run) when a newer one arrives; queue: all goes in turn.
Write-backUp to 50 changes in one commit: an image with its tag, its digest or both, or a value at a YAML path. Comments and layout are kept. A push that finds the branch moved retries up to 12 times, never forces, and finds its own earlier commit by a Launchway-Deployment line. For a repository Launchway hosts, the Airfield chooses a direct commit (with a one-hour credential for one repository and one branch) or a pull request that a person or a rule merges.
Ordered syncA parent application and its values are written as two ordered commits, the values only once the cluster shows the new pin; parents sync before children.
SyncA refresh, then a sync request (auto, always or never), optionally limited to named resources and with pruning. The controller's sync windows are never overridden: the step waits or fails, as the step says. Objects left over are reported, never a failure.
Healthy meansThe synced revision includes the commit; the judged resources are Synced and Healthy; and the named rollout, if any, is Healthy with its stable set of pods on the new template. Missing or stale observations are never a pass.
RolloutsPromote, promote fully, abort and retry from a pipeline step, or from the Launch page; wait until healthy or until paused. On a protected Airfield the person who started the Sortie cannot promote or retry; anyone with the operator role can abort.
VerificationA verify step reads Prometheus and other metric, log and SQL stores through sources an operator names, or calls the service itself with a built-in HTTP or TCP health proof. It compares with the stable version and with the last passed verifications (three by default), clusters log lines and fails on a new error pattern, and says inconclusive when data is thin.
Return to baseA rollback step runs only if its Launch was made and a step it needs did not succeed. It reverts the Launch's commit, never forcing, and waits for healthy; it can abort the rollout first. After a success, a Return to base is a Sortie of its own (see Return to base).
Failure causesEach failure names one cause with evidence and a next step: analysis failed, rollout failed, sync failed, timeout, refused, Station lost, command failed. A crash-looping pod fails the step with its own last words; a stuck sync is named and ended.
Seeing itThe Launch page shows the live tree of every object the Launch owns, events, live manifests, logs of any pod with stable and Pathfinder side by side, the steps and weights intended and measured, every proof measurement, and controls that appear only where they work. Drift is read every 30 seconds for up to 100 services per target.
TimeThe whole step has a timeout, 30 minutes by default, between 1 minute and 24 hours. When Git already holds the change, nothing is committed but the step still syncs and verifies.
Not there yet

Each of these is a gap this chapter closes or places:

  • No Launch without Argo CD: no chart install, no manifest apply. The deploy Station never runs a script and changes nothing else in the cluster.
  • One cluster per Airfield target; a rollout on another target is refused.
  • No previews: deploy steps do not run in pull request Sorties.
  • The Launch record has no digest field; the digest is only in the version text or the commit.
  • No sync to a revision without a commit; no pause step for a rollout in the pipeline (the Launch page can pause one); no separate analysis step kind.
  • No gRPC health check in the built-in proof.

Launching directly, with no GitOps controller

Planned as "Built-in Helm and Kubernetes deploys" and "Delivery by choice". A target served directly is launched by the launch Station itself. You asked for direct chart installs and plain manifests "with pruning and recorded previous state". The design keeps every rule of the GitOps path: Standing orders first, one lock, one record, the same Overwatch and the same Return to base.

  • Rendered on the Station, never on the server. The server never holds cluster access or values with secrets in them.
  • Judged on what will be applied. Standing orders that read manifests (no privileged containers, resource limits set, images by digest) are judged on the rendered objects, not on the chart source.
  • Pruning that cannot surprise. Only objects that carry this service's ownership label and were in the previous rendered set are removed. Anything else is reported, never deleted.
  • Recorded previous state. The rendered set is stored as Cargo in the Depot, by digest. Return to base re-applies the previous set, then prunes what the bad set added. It never depends on the chart still being able to render old values.
  • Progressive without a GitOps controller. If the target has a rollout controller, the rendered set contains its rollout resource and Launchway drives it as it does today. If not, see the next section.
# Design: not built. The staging Airfield's target, served directly.
targets:
  - name: shop-cluster
    kind: kubernetes
    served_by: direct
    namespaces: [storefront-staging]
    services:
      storefront:
        source: { chart: harbor-lights/storefront, version: 3.1.0 }   # or { manifests: deploy/k8s, overlay: staging }
        values: { file: deploy/values-staging.yaml }
        prune: owned-only

A Pathfinder with or without a rollout controller

Argo Rollouts is the rollout controller Launchway drives today, and you asked that it can be driven through the cluster API without Argo CD. Where no rollout controller is installed, the plan offers two more ways, so progressive delivery never depends on one product:

What the cluster hasHow traffic is splitHow exactStatus
A rollout controllerThe controller's own steps, through a gateway or a service mesh where configuredExact with a gateway or mesh; by copies withoutAvailable (control); Planned Every rollout strategy
A gateway that speaks the Gateway APITwo workloads side by side; Launchway sets route weights step by stepExactPlanned Gateway API as the default path
NeitherTwo workloads behind one service; the share follows the number of copiesApproximate; moves when an autoscaler acts. The page shows measured beside intended.New in this plan

A two-fleet swap with no rollout controller

New in this plan A two-fleet swap brings up a whole new fleet beside the old one, tests it where no shopper can reach it, switches everyone at once, and keeps the old fleet warm so going back is one switch. Today Launchway does this only through a rollout controller. The plan does it with what every cluster already has: two workloads, a preview service and a switch of the main service's selector, or of a Gateway API route where there is a gateway.

  1. New fleet beside the old. The launch Station applies a second workload for the release, named for it (storefront-2-4-0) and labeled with the release digest, sized to the old fleet's current copies, not its minimum, so the switch never lands on a cold, small fleet.
  2. Preview service. A service that selects only the new fleet (storefront-preview) gives it an address inside the cluster. Test calls, contract tests and any checks the Route stop names run against it. No shopper reaches it.
  3. Optional Clearance. The plan can hold here for a Go with the test results on the card, holding no Station (see a Clearance between Pathfinder steps, which works the same way here).
  4. The switch. One change: the main service's selector moves from the old release label to the new one, or the Gateway API route's backend moves to the new fleet at 100 percent. Old copies leave the endpoints and finish the requests they hold; nothing restarts.
  5. Warm, then watched. Overwatch watches the new fleet at full traffic for its set time while the old fleet stays at its copies. A fail moves the selector back in seconds and the record says "started by Overwatch".
  6. Clean up. After the watch, the old workload is removed and the rendered set of the new one is the recorded state. Return to base after that is the ordinary re-apply of the previous rendered set.

The swap costs twice the copies while both fleets run; Launchway asks for the headroom before it starts and shows the cost in the plan. A team with a rollout controller keeps using it; this path is for every cluster that has none.

Worked moment. staging is served directly and has no rollout controller. storefront 2.4.0 comes up as storefront-2-4-0 with six copies beside the six of 2.3.2, answers 20 test calls and the contract tests against payments through storefront-preview, and the selector switches. Overwatch passes after two hours; the 2.3.2 workload is removed.

Many clusters and many targets in one Airfield

An Airfield is a set of rules; a cluster is a place. Harbor Lights' prod can hold shop-east and shop-west, each served by its own launch Station, under one set of Standing orders, one Clearance and one lock per service.

  • Waves are set on the Airfield: one cluster first, or a share of clusters, then the rest.
  • A service may span kinds. While billing moves from its two virtual machines to the cluster, prod can hold both targets for it. One Launch reaches both, each with its own mover; see Launching to virtual machines and physical servers.
  • Through a GitOps controller the write-back changes the file each cluster's application reads, in wave order, and waits for each cluster's sync and health before writing the next. One controller managing many clusters and one controller per cluster both work.
  • A cluster that cannot be reached stops the waves after it; clusters already done keep the new version until a person decides, and the page states which cluster runs what.

Previews per pull request, in their own namespace

A preview is a short-lived Airfield made from a template Airfield (see previews). On Kubernetes it is one namespace per pull request, served directly, because a preview that lives three days does not need a GitOps commit.

  • Limits come from the template: a time limit, a cost cap, a cap on how many previews one Flight (codebase) may have, and the namespace quota.
  • Secrets are the template Airfield's preview secrets, never prod's. A fork gets none until a person says Go.
  • Data is a short-lived database for the preview; planned in Milestone 10 as "Masked and preview databases".
  • Address is a name under the preview domain the template names; with Milestone 9 the DNS record is one the Launch owns and removes.

Autoscalers, and what the interface shows while they act

An autoscaler and a Launch both change how many copies run. Launchway never fights an autoscaler; it shows what it did and plans around it.

  • Today: the Launch page lists horizontal scalers and disruption budgets among the Launch's objects, and does not offer Scale while an autoscaler manages the count ("Scale is not offered: the autoscaler shop manages the replica count"). Available
  • On the Launch timeline: copies wanted and running for the stable and the new version, and each scaling event with its reason. New in this plan
  • Share of traffic: where weights are set at a gateway, scaling does not move the share, and the page says so. Where the share follows the number of copies, a scaling event changes it; the page shows the measured share and warns. New in this plan
  • Two-fleet swap: the new fleet is sized to the stable fleet's current copies, not its minimum, so the switch does not land on a cold, small fleet. New in this plan
  • Headroom: a Launch and a load test ask for headroom before they start instead of racing the scaler, and always put back what was there. Planned Scaling during a rollout and a test; Temporary capacity for tests.
  • Event-driven scaling of queue workers with KEDA: Overwatch reads backlog as a signal. Planned Queue and stream consumers.

Cluster rules from Standing orders: no side door

A Standing order judged only inside Launchway can be walked around by anyone with cluster access. The plan writes the same rules into the cluster, for the namespaces the Airfield owns.

  1. The prod Airfield's Standing orders include "only images launched by Launchway, signed, pinned by digest" and "no privileged containers".
  2. Launchway turns each rule it can into the cluster's built-in admission policy, or hands it to a policy engine the platform team connected. It proposes them as a change the platform team reviews; it never writes policy into a namespace the Airfield does not own.
  3. Every Launch carries a statement, signed by Launchway, of the release digest, the Airfield and the Launch. The admission rule checks it.
  4. An image applied by hand has no such statement and is refused. The refusal appears on the Airfield page as a finding with the object and the rule.
  5. A Return to base re-launches a digest that already has its statement, so the rule never blocks it.
  6. An emergency path exists for the platform team, and every use is in the Logbook.
Proposal

New roadmap item "Cluster admission rules from Standing orders" in Milestone 11, beside "Cost, policy and backup in context", which only reads policy results today.

One item, not two

The Standing orders, Clearance and Hold chapter proposes the same capability as "Cluster admission generated from Standing orders" in Milestone 3. The completeness check asks for one item: keep that one, owned by Standing orders, and read this chapter's proposal as the Kubernetes detail of it (rules only for namespaces the Airfield owns, a signed statement per Launch, Return to base never refused). The milestone pass merges the two; nothing in this section is narrowed.

When the code host or Launchway is down

Going back must never depend on the thing that is broken, and neither should a cluster's ability to keep its desired state. Today the GitOps controller reads its desired state from Git, so when the code host is down nothing new can be synced, and when Launchway is down nothing can be launched or returned through it. The plan removes both dependencies without adding a second way to launch. New in this plan

What is downWhat still worksHow
The code hostLaunches forward and back, through LaunchwayEvery Launch also publishes the desired state for its target (the rendered set, or the application's folder at the launched commit) to the Depot as a signed open-standard artifact, by digest, with a moving name per Airfield (storefront-desired:prod). An Airfield chooses where its controller reads from: Git (the default) or the Depot. With the Depot as the source, the controller keeps syncing while the code host is away, and the Git write-back is queued and written when the host returns; the record marks the commit "Git catching up" until then.
LaunchwayThe cluster runs what it ran; the controller keeps reconciling from the Depot or Git; a Return to base by break-glassEach launch Station keeps the last few desired sets the server recorded and signed for its targets. A Commander holds a break-glass key issued in advance. With it, launchway breakglass return on the Station re-applies an earlier signed set, and only such a set: it cannot launch anything the server never recorded. The Station writes a signed local journal of who, why and what changed.
Both come backThe record is whole againThe Station uploads its journal. The server records a Launch "made while Launchway was away", judges Standing orders against it after the fact (a violation is a finding, never a silent pass), and on a protected Airfield opens a Clearance afterwards, as for any emergency return.
# Design: not built. A break-glass return on the launch Station beside shop-cluster.
$ launchway breakglass return --target shop-cluster --service storefront --to 2.3.2 \
    --reason "checkout errors, Launchway unreachable"
Break-glass key: commander-sam (issued for this Station)
Earlier signed sets for storefront in prod: 2.4.0 (running), 2.3.2, 2.3.1
Will re-apply the 2.3.2 set signed by the server; 4 objects change; the database is not returned.
Applied. Journal entry written; it will be recorded when the server is back.

Worked moment. The code host is being upgraded for an hour. prod reads its desired state from the Depot, so Ana's Go on 2.4.0 goes ahead: the Depot artifact moves, the controller syncs, Overwatch passes, and the write-back commit appears in Git when the host is back, linked to Launch L-312.

The GitOps controller: hosted or yours, and run from Launchway

The GitOps controller is a capability slot with two equal choices, shown on the target as "served by", with one provider in charge of each target. Planned Hosted or your own Argo CD; Safe sync and control; Health checks set up from the interface.

Hosted by LaunchwayYours, connected
Who runs itLaunchway installs, upgrades and watches a controller for the Wing, with its version on the target page. On a self-run installation it is installed into a cluster you pick; on the hosted service it runs beside your Detachment (the small program on your side).You do, as today. Launchway reads it through the launch Station.
How clusters connectOutbound only: the launch Station in each cluster opens the connection; nothing reaches into the cluster from outside. The controller's access is limited to the namespaces of the Airfield's targets.As you set it up; Launchway needs only the Station's closed set of rights.
One provider in chargeA target is served by exactly one controller. Adding a second to the same namespaces is refused with the reason. Moving from one to the other is a wizard that adopts each application, shows a dry run with no change to live objects, and switches the target only when every application is adopted.

Controller work under Launchway's roles. Every application the controller manages, launched by Launchway or not, gets the same operations, each shown only where it will work, each with a sentence saying its consequence before you press it, and each on the Logbook (audit trail):

  • The tree: parent and child applications and every object under them, with sync state, health, history and the live manifest.
  • Sync with a preview: "Sync will change 3 objects and delete 1 in storefront; prod serves 2.4.0 now." Refresh, and stop a stuck sync.
  • Pause automatic sync during an incident, with a banner on the Airfield and a reminder to resume.
  • Resource actions: restart a workload, and the actions a resource kind declares; Scale is not offered while an autoscaler manages the count.
  • Custom health checks, written and tested against live resources before you save, then proposed to the controller's configuration as a change in Git.

Who may do each follows Launchway's roles, not the controller's own: Observer (viewer) sees the tree; the operator role syncs, refreshes and runs actions, with a reason on a protected Airfield; a Commander changes the controller's configuration. The controller's own interface can be left off entirely, so there is one place to grant access and one Logbook.

Controller sync windows on the Hold calendar

The controller's sync windows are respected today: a deploy step waits or fails as it says, and never overrides them Available. The plan makes them visible where every other time rule lives. The launch Station reads each controller's windows and sends them to the server, which draws them on the Hold (freeze) calendar beside Holds, Airfield windows, fleet reboot windows and tenants' windows, labeled with their source. A Launch whose sync would fall in a closed controller window says so before it starts: "Waits until 18:00: the controller's window for storefront is closed." New in this plan

Because one object should govern every target, the calendar offers Turn into a Hold on a controller window: it proposes the same times as a Hold or an Airfield window in Launchway and a change that removes the window from the controller's configuration, reviewed like any change. Nothing is moved without that review. The calendar itself belongs to Standing orders, Clearance and Hold.

Clusters and the fleet, with upgrade readiness

Planned Clusters and the fleet; Upgrade readiness; Fleet lifecycle and node upgrades (Milestone 11).

  1. Register a cluster. Install the launch Station in it with one command; it connects outward, proves its identity and reports the cluster's version, nodes, capacity, namespaces and quotas. Access starts read-only, and the page says what each higher level of access would add.
  2. The fleet view. One row per cluster: health, version, nodes, requested against allocatable CPU and memory, the Airfields and targets it serves, which controller serves it, its Station's last contact, and its upgrade readiness for the next version.
  3. Upgrade readiness, per application. Pick the version you plan to move a cluster to. Launchway checks every application's live objects and the rendered sets of releases still on their way along a Route against the interfaces that version removes, and lists what would break by application and owning Squadron (team). Each finding arrives as a proposal: a Maintenance (dependency update) pull request that moves the object to the supported interface.
  4. Judged before a Launch, too. A Standing order "no interfaces removed in the target cluster's version" is judged at Preflight, so a release that would break on the cluster it is about to reach stops there with the object named, instead of failing during the sync.

Worked moment. You plan to move shop-cluster up one version. Readiness lists one finding: the storefront chart renders a disruption budget with an interface that version removes, owned by Squadron "shop". The proposed pull request fixes the chart; release 2.4.1 carries it; readiness turns clean and the upgrade can be scheduled on the calendar.

Worked example: storefront on shop-cluster

This pipeline runs today. The prod Airfield is protected and needs one Clearance; Ana gives it.

pipeline: storefront
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
steps:
  image:
    kind: image
    context: .
    tags: [{ registry: depot, repository: harbor-lights/storefront, tag: { run: short_sha } }]
    sign: true
    scan: { fail_on: high, mode: enforce }
  approve-prod:
    kind: approval
    needs: image
    message: "Launch this digest into prod?"
  deploy-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: approve-prod
    environment: prod
    service: storefront
    version: { output: image.digest }
    rollout: { name: storefront, namespace: storefront, until: paused }
    argocd:
      application: storefront
      write_back:
        repo: gitops
        branch: main
        changes:
          - { file: apps/storefront/prod/values.yaml, image: harbor-lights/storefront, digest: { output: image.digest } }
      sync: { request: auto, windows: wait }
      health: application
  promote-prod:
    kind: rollout
    needs: deploy-prod
    deployment: deploy-prod
    action: promote-full
  verify-prod:
    kind: verify
    needs: promote-prod
    deployment: deploy-prod
    duration: 10m
    baseline: 3
    on_fail: rollback
    on_inconclusive: fail
    metrics:
      - name: healthy
        source: checks
        check: { url: http://storefront.storefront.svc:8080/healthz, status: [200], success: 0.99 }
  rollback-prod:
    kind: rollback
    deployment: deploy-prod
    needs: [verify-prod]
    abort_first: true

What happens: Preflight passes; the lock on storefront in prod is taken; one commit pins harbor-lights/storefront@sha256:4f9c…a17; Argo CD syncs; the rollout pauses at its first step; the pipeline promotes fully; the verify step calls /healthz for ten minutes and compares with the last three passed Launches; it passes and the lock is released.

Design: not built. The same Flight, after staging is switched to be served directly. The pipeline is unchanged except that it no longer names the machinery.

steps:
  launch:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [image]
    environment: ${{ inputs.airfield }}
    service: storefront
    release: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }}

The Launch page for staging opens on a plan: "3 objects change, 1 new (ConfigMap storefront-delivery-dates), 1 removed (Service storefront-legacy, owned by this service and no longer rendered)". It applies, waits for readiness, removes the one object, and stores the rendered set as harbor-lights/storefront-rendered@sha256:91d0…3be. A Return to base later re-applies the previous rendered set.

The order this chapter proposes

Milestones 3, 8 and 11 already hold almost all of this ground. The order below is by value and by what each piece needs; it is not a schedule.

  1. Now Finish what is nearly there: digests on every Launch record; "Fix actions with their consequence"; Preflight judged again at the lock.
  2. Next "Delivery by choice", then "Built-in Helm and Kubernetes deploys" (fourth in the build queue). Previews need direct installs, so "Preview environments" follows straight after, with the two Milestone 2 preview items.
  3. Next "Progressive delivery without the GitOps controller" and "A Pathfinder with no rollout controller", so Pathfinder works on any cluster; "Several clusters in one Airfield".
  4. Next Milestone 8's "Argo CD, first class": seeing and diagnosing first (tree, context, one sentence, items and logs), then control and creating (safe sync, create through Git, adopt). "Hosted or your own Argo CD" sits here.
  5. Next "Launch from the Depot when the code host is down" with direct Launches (both store sets in the Depot), then "A break-glass return when Launchway is down" and "A two-fleet swap with no rollout controller" beside the Pathfinder work.
  6. Later Milestone 11: clusters and the fleet, "Removed interfaces judged before a Launch", every workload kind, why is it not healthy, the scaling view and "Autoscalers in view during a Launch", then "Cluster admission rules from Standing orders", upgrade readiness and fleet lifecycle.

The overlap between Milestones 3 and 8 on GitOps depth

The same ideas are listed twice. Milestone 3 has "Argo CD in depth" (hierarchy views), "Applications and ApplicationSets from the interface", "Health checks set up from the interface", "A single pane of glass", "Everything deployed" and "Logs where you need them". Milestone 8's group "Argo CD, first class" has "See every application and its tree", "Create and change through Git", "A problem in one sentence" and "Every item and its logs". The delivery area page places the depth in Milestone 3; the build-order page places it in Milestone 8. Several Available items in Milestone 3 depend on "Argo CD in depth", which is Planned.

Proposal: one home for each idea

Milestone 3 owns launching through the controller: getting a release in and back out, and seeing what one Launch made. Milestone 8 owns the controller's applications as a whole: every application, launched by Launchway or not, its tree, its context, its diagnosis, and changing it through Git.

  • "Argo CD in depth" stays in Milestone 3, becomes In progress (Launchway reads applications, rollouts and analyses, and lists the applications a Station has seen), and its text points to Milestone 8 for the full tree.
  • "Applications and ApplicationSets from the interface" moves to Milestone 8 beside "Create and change through Git".
  • "Health checks set up from the interface" moves to Milestone 8.
  • "Everything deployed" and "Logs where you need them" stay in Milestone 3 and become In progress: the Launch page already does most of both for a Launch's own objects. Milestone 8's "Every item and its logs" extends them to every application.
  • No title is removed. Both pages then say the same thing.

The foundation it relies on

Launch Stations

One per cluster or per group of clusters, holding the only cluster access. The rights are listed per feature (read, sync, rollout commands, inspect, direct apply), each off until an administrator turns it on, and each shown in the Station's self-check.

Guarded monitoring reads

Overwatch reads metrics and logs only through the guarded query layer; a Station never gets a raw route to a store.

The Depot

Images, charts and rendered sets by digest, with retention that never deletes a digest an Airfield runs or could return to.

The record

Every command a Station sends is an event with the state it expected, so a repeated command after a lost connection is refused, not applied twice.

Safety

What happens on failure

FailureWhat happens
The launch Station is lost mid-LaunchThe step fails as "runner lost"; the cluster keeps what it has. Return to base is offered once another Station serves the target.
The GitOps controller is downThe commit is written; the step waits for sync until its timeout, then fails as "sync failed" with the controller's state. Git already names the new version, so the page says that the next sync will apply it unless a Return to base reverts it.
A direct apply half-appliedThe record lists each object applied. Return to base re-applies the previous rendered set, which is complete by itself.
A revert cannot applyToday the Return to base fails with the files named. Planned: the second way back, a new Launch of the earlier digest (see Return to base).
The old chart cannot read the new valuesToday the pin is not reverted, the step says which keys, and the Airfield is marked as needing a person; if the controller still cannot render, Launchway reverts its own revert. With direct Launches the previous rendered set avoids this entirely.
A cluster in a wave cannot be reachedLater waves stop; the page states which cluster runs which version.
The code host is downAn Airfield that reads its desired state from the Depot keeps launching; write-back is queued and marked "Git catching up". An Airfield that reads from Git waits, and says so.
Launchway is downThe cluster keeps running; a Commander's break-glass return can re-apply an earlier signed set from the Station, and is recorded and reviewed when the server is back.
A two-fleet swap fails after the switchThe selector or route moves back to the old fleet, which is still warm; the new fleet is kept at zero traffic for the investigation.

Who may do what

  • See the tree and manifests: Observer (viewer) of the Flight. Logs: the operator role on the Flight, from a binding that covers the Airfield.
  • Promote, abort, retry, pause, restart, scale: the operator role; on a protected Airfield the starter cannot promote or retry. Each needs a reason where it changes a live object, and each is on the Logbook.
  • Change how a target is served, or approve generated cluster rules: Commander (owner) of the level that holds the Airfield, or the platform team they name.
  • Sync, refresh, pause automatic sync or run a resource action on any controller application: the operator role on the Flight that owns it, with a reason on a protected Airfield. Change the controller's configuration or its sync windows: Commander.
  • Hold a break-glass key: a Commander, issued per Station in advance; every use is reviewed afterwards.

On by default

  • Inspection of a Launch is off until an administrator grants the Station the rights; direct apply is off until a target is set to be served directly.
  • Pruning only of owned objects; sync windows never overridden; force-pushes never.
  • Secrets shown by name, type and key names only; values redacted on the Station before anything leaves it.
  • Previews off until a template Airfield exists; forks never get secrets without a person's Go.

Open question

  1. Open question Pathfinder on Kubernetes without Argo Rollouts, in the first phase. The zero-downtime design recommends Argo Rollouts only in phase 1; a later delegated answer says Gateway API weights first, Argo Rollouts when present, and the ratio of copies as the baseline. This chapter follows the delegated answer. Recommendation: keep it, since makes the Argo family an integration, never a dependency.
  2. Open question The overlap between Milestones 3 and 8. Accept the split above (Milestone 3 launches, Milestone 8 sees and changes every application), or keep all GitOps depth in one milestone.
  3. Open question Generated cluster rules. Recommendation: proposed as a change the platform team merges, never applied by Launchway on its own, and only for namespaces the Airfield owns.
  4. Open question The Depot as the controller's source. Recommendation: Git stays the default; the Depot is a choice per Airfield, and prod uses it, so a code host outage never stops a Launch or a return. Git still receives every change, late if it must.
  5. Open question Break-glass keys. Recommendation: issued per Station to named Commanders, able only to re-apply sets the server already signed, and every use reviewed afterwards. The other way is no break-glass at all, which leaves a return impossible while Launchway is down.
  6. Open question Turning controller windows into Holds. Recommendation: offer it, never do it without a reviewed change, so the Hold calendar becomes the one place time rules live.
  7. Open question Previews served directly by default. The existing "Delivery by choice" item already says short-lived Airfields use direct installs; confirm that a team with a GitOps controller still gets previews without a commit per preview.

Launch

Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

You launch to a fleet of machines the way you launch to a cluster: one release by digest, one Route through your Airfields, hosts changed a few at a time behind the load balancer, and every touched host put back if anything goes wrong.

  • A fleet is a named set of hosts inside an Airfield (environment), held in the product: added by hand, picked from a hypervisor or cloud inventory, or enrolled by the host itself.
  • Each fleet chooses how hosts are reached: a launch Station (deploy runner) that reaches in over a secure shell with pinned host keys, or a small host agent that connects outward and pulls its work.
  • Zero downtime comes from the per-host sequence: drain, change, check, admit. Batches never cross the fleet's floor, stepped traffic can move to a second group, and a failure returns every touched host to its previous release.
  • Beyond releases: containers with the runtime as a plug point, configuration applies bound to their check run, procedures run on a fleet with a form and a Clearance, cloud machine images rolled through instance groups, Windows hosts, and a one-command start that keeps its record.
  • The per-host code is built and tested today, but the server refuses to schedule it inside a Sortie (run) and nothing writes the host list. This chapter proposes the status that evidence supports, and the work that makes it a real Launch.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 5 of the model, Launch (delivery), applied to machines. It uses the foundation (levels, permissions, secrets resolved on the Station), the record (every host step is an event), flight operations (Stations and Ramps (runner pools) do the work) and command (Standing orders (policies), Clearance (approval) and Hold (freeze) gate it). It adds no second model: a fleet is one kind of target behind the shared launch model described in One way to launch, anywhere.

Builds on
One way to launch, anywhere (a release by digest; a Route, the Airfields it flies through in order; a strategy; Overwatch, the watch after a Launch (deployment); Return to base (rollback), never blocked),Stations and where work runs; Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; the record.
Built on by
Launching to image-based hosts (the same fleet and the same per-host sequence, with a reboot), Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch (load balancers as the part that moves traffic), the software graph and Maintenance (machines and what runs on them).
Words
"Fleet" always means a set of target hosts. A set of Stations is a Ramp, never a fleet.

What you will be able to do

You merge a fix to the legacy billing service. The Sortie builds release 4.13, and the Route takes it to prod. Launchway drains billing-1 from the load balancer, installs 4.13, checks it twice, admits it, and only then does the same to billing-2. One host serves the whole time. The Launch page shows each host's step as it happens.

The health check on billing-2 fails after the install. Launchway stops, returns both hosts to 4.12 in the same drained, checked way, and the record says which check failed, on which host, with the answers it got.

You add a third virtual machine. Instead of typing an address and a key, you pick the hypervisor connection, tick billing-3 in the list it shows, and confirm the key fingerprint Launchway fetched. The host joins the fleet's stable group with the fleet's labels.

A server in a branch office sits behind a firewall that allows no inbound connection. You run one enrollment command on it. It appears as waiting; a Commander admits it; from then on it pulls its Launches and reports back, and if it is offline during a Launch it catches up when it returns.

You want more care for a risky release. You bring up two fresh machines as a new group, and the Launch moves 10, then 50, then 100 percent of traffic to them, judged by Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) at each step. The old group stays at zero for the way back.

You change a setting on the hosts with a configuration playbook. Launchway runs it in check mode first, shows what would change per host, waits for Clearance, then applies it in batches, with the same per-host results as a release.

How it works

A fleet, held in the product

A fleet lives inside one Airfield and belongs to the Flight (codebase) or Squadron (team) that launches to it. It is configuration in the database, like an Airfield, never a file passed on a command line. Every way in reads and writes the same fleet: the web interface, the HTTP API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform.

Part of a fleetWhat it holdsHow it is filled
Name and Airfieldbilling-vms in prodName checked as you type; Airfield picked from the list you may launch to
ReachPushed by a launch Station, or pulled by a host agentTwo cards; the choice explains what the network must allow
HostsName, address, pinned key or enrolled identity, groups, labels, the service address, the load balancer's name for the hostBy hand, from an inventory source, or by enrollment (below)
Groups and labelsstable and new groups; labels such as site=dc1, os=linuxPicked from labels already in use, or added with a key and value checked as you type
Load balancerWhich balancer drains and weights these hosts, through which admin addressPicked from connections; tested before saving
FloorHow many hosts must keep serving, at least one when there is a balancerA number with the fleet size beside it; zero only with "accept downtime" switched on
WindowsWhen hosts may change; a Hold still applies on topDays and hours picked on a week grid

Hosts get into a fleet three ways, and all three end in the same host record:

  1. By hand. You give a name and an address. Launchway fetches the host's public key from inside the network and shows its fingerprint for you to confirm. It never trusts a key on first use without that confirmation, and a host whose key later changes is refused.
  2. From an inventory source. You pick a connection to a hypervisor, a public cloud, the outputs of an infrastructure stack (Terraform or OpenTofu) or an inventory file in the repository, then tick the machines you want. The source is read by a Station on your side, so no platform credential reaches the server. A source can keep the fleet in step; additions and removals arrive as proposals you accept.
  3. By enrollment. You make a one-time code for the fleet and run one command on the host. The host gets its own identity and waits until someone with the right role admits it. On a protected Airfield, admitting a host needs Clearance, because a new host is new trust.

Two ways to reach a host

Each fleet picks one. Both run the same per-host sequence, write the same events and obey the same gates. The difference is only who opens the connection.

Push: launch Station over SSHPull: host agent
Best forData-center and cloud machines a Station can reachHosts behind firewalls, in shops and branch offices, or often offline
What runs on the hostNothing extra; commands arrive over SSHA small agent, proposed as the Station program in a host mode
TrustThe host's key is pinned; the Station's key comes from a secret store by reference; short-lived certificates per Sortie are plannedThe host's own enrolled identity; it accepts only the host actions on its allow-list
NetworkStation to host on the SSH portHost to server, outbound only; no inbound port
A host that is offMisses the Launch and is listed as behindTakes the release its Airfield wants now when it returns
AuditEvery command written to the record, one line eachEvery action and its result written to the record

The host agent is not a new kind of program. The proposal is that it is the Station program running in a host mode: same enrollment, same identity, same signed updates, same step contract, but it runs only on its own host and only the actions a fleet allows (install a release, restart a service, run a check, report status, go back). That keeps one program to secure and one way to update it. See the open question at the end.

What you can launch

A program with a service

A built file, from Cargo (artifact) by digest, installed beside the previous releases and run by the host's service manager. The switch is a link flip and a restart; the previous release stays on disk for the way back. Built in code

A package

An operating-system package from the Depot (registry), by version and checksum, with the previous version kept. Launchway says when a package's own scripts make the way back unclean. Planned

Containers on the host

A container image by digest, run as a service the host restarts. A moving tag is refused. The previous image stays on the host. Planned

A configuration run

An Ansible playbook as a step: check mode first, Clearance, then the apply, with results per host and "run again on the failed hosts". Chef later. Available for Ansible.

Containers on a host: the runtime is a plug point

Planned Containers on a host, by digest (proposed in this plan). Many teams run containers on plain virtual machines with no cluster. The design keeps the per-host sequence and adds three things: the container runtime is a plug point, health comes from the runtime itself as well as from the fleet's check, and both the switch and the way back are by digest.

  • The runtime is found, not assumed. When a host joins, the Station (or the host agent) probes which open-standard container runtime it has: one that runs as a background service, or one that runs each container directly under the host's service manager. The fleet page shows it; a Launch uses an adapter with the same five verbs for each (pull, start, stop, health, remove). A host with no runtime is refused with the reason.
  • Pulled before the drain. The new image is pulled by digest while the host still serves, so the time out of rotation is only the stop and start. A moving tag is refused.
  • Health from the runtime too. The container's own health check, declared in the image or in the fleet, must report healthy, and the fleet's check through the service address must pass the set number of times in a row, before the host is admitted. A container that restarts in a loop fails the host with its last log lines as the evidence.
  • Switch and return by digest. The old container is stopped, not removed, and its image stays on the host. Return to base starts the previous digest again with nothing to download. The host keeps the running digest and the one before it; older ones are removed by the fleet's retention, never one a Return to base may need.
  • Settings and secrets travel with the Launch. Environment values and secret references are part of the release's settings, resolved on the host when the container starts, and recorded by digest, so a return brings back the settings that went with the old image.

A configuration run applies what was checked

A playbook run starts with a check that shows what would change on each host; a person gives Go on that; then the apply runs Available Ansible; Results for every host. The tool itself does not force the apply to do what the check showed, and the roadmap says so honestly. The plan closes the gap from Launchway's side:

  1. Bound to the check. The check run records the commit, the playbook's digest, the inputs, the host list and the result digest. The Clearance is given on that check run.
  2. Refused if anything moved. The apply runs the same commit, the same playbook digest, the same inputs and the same hosts, and refuses, with the reason, if any of them changed since the check. A refused apply changes nothing; a new check starts the review again.
  3. Compared afterwards. After the apply, Launchway compares the tasks that changed on each host with the tasks the check said would change. A difference is a finding on the record ("billing-2: 1 task changed that the check did not show"), so a gap between check and apply is never silent.
  4. Run again on the failed hosts keeps the same binding: the hosts that failed, with the same commit and inputs, under the same Clearance while it is valid.

New in this plan A configuration apply bound to its check run.

The per-host sequence

Every change to every host goes through the same five moves. A host is never changed while the load balancer still sends it requests, and never admitted before its checks pass.

Zero downtime on machines

Machines have no scheduler to replace an instance for you, so Launchway carries the rules a scheduler would. Each is on by default, and a fleet owner can tune it within what the level above allows.

  • Batches. A rolling Launch changes a few hosts at a time (one by default), in an order you can see before it starts.
  • The floor. A fleet states how many hosts must keep serving. A Launch that would cross it is refused before it starts, with the numbers. A fleet without a load balancer must switch on "accept downtime", and its page says hosts drop requests while they change.
  • Drain first. The host is taken out of the balancer and given time to finish in-flight requests. Long-lived connections need longer drains; the roadmap item for them says plainly what cannot be made seamless.
  • Check before admit. The host's own health address must answer correctly a set number of times in a row. Test transactions to the host before any user reaches it are planned.
  • Proofs between batches. After each batch, Overwatch can compare the fleet's error rate and latency with how it normally behaves before the next host is touched.
  • Stepped traffic to a second group. With the Pathfinder (canary) strategy, a new group takes 10, 50, then 100 percent of traffic by load balancer weights, judged at each step. The old group stays at weight zero until Overwatch is done, so the way back is a weight change. A two-fleet swap moves all traffic at once after the new group passes its checks.
  • Return every touched host. On a failed check, Launchway stops and returns every host it changed in this Launch to its previous release, with the same drain and check. A host that cannot be returned is kept out of rotation (quarantined) and reported, never silently put back.

The same gates and record as every target

A fleet Launch is a step in a Sortie, so it gets everything a cluster Launch gets, with nothing private:

  • Route. The release flies dev, staging, prod by the same digest. Nothing is built again on the way. A fleet in staging and a fleet in prod are two stops on one Route.
  • Standing orders. Judged at the same point, before any host is touched: the Cargo is signed and scanned, the tests passed, no Hold is on, the window is open.
  • Clearance. A protected Airfield waits for a Go from someone other than the author.
  • The Airfield lock. One Launch per service per Airfield at a time; a second one waits in the Holding pattern (queue).
  • Overwatch. After the last batch, the fleet is watched against its baseline through the guarded query layer, and a worsening returns it to the stable state.
  • The record. The release digest, the hosts in each batch, each host's drain, install, check, admit or return, and the release each host now runs. The fleet page reads the same record.

Windows hosts come later. They use the host agent on the host and a Windows service in place of the service unit; the fleet, the sequence and the gates do not change.

Windows hosts, in more detail

Planned Windows hosts as Launch targets (proposed in this plan). The same per-host sequence (drain, change, check, admit, return every touched host) and the same record. What differs is how the host is reached and how a release is put in place.

PartOn a Windows host
ReachThe host agent (the default), connecting outward. Or pushed by a launch Station over the secure shell server the system ships with, with the host key pinned exactly as for any host. A Station never uses a stored administrator password; the step's identity is short-lived.
Putting a release in placeEach release goes into its own folder beside the earlier ones, because a running program's files are locked; the service's path points at a fixed link that is moved to the new folder while the service is stopped. The previous folder stays for the way back.
ServicesInstalled and switched through the system's service manager: stop, move the link, start, with the service's start mode and account recorded and restored on a return.
PackagesThe system's own installer packages and its package manager, from the Depot by version and checksum, with the previous version kept; Launchway says when an installer cannot be undone cleanly.
HealthThe fleet's check through the service address, plus the service reporting "running", plus new error entries in the system's event log since the start, grouped into patterns like any log.
Before it startsA host with a restart already pending from an update is reported and not changed, so a Launch never meets a surprise reboot halfway.

Procedures on a fleet

Most of what people do to machines is not a release: restart a service, rotate a key, clear a cache, collect diagnostics. Elsewhere these are runbooks: scripts people paste, or jobs with their own permissions. In Launchway a procedure is a Flight plan (ready-made whole pipeline) with typed inputs, run against a fleet or an Airfield with the same controls as a Launch. Planned Flight plans as job templates, with a form; New in this plan Procedures run on a fleet.

  • Declared, then allowed. A procedure says what it touches: changes: none for one that only reads (diagnostics), or changes: hosts, and whether a host must be drained first. A fleet lists the procedures it allows; nothing else appears in its menu.
  • A form, not a command line. The run form is built from the procedure's typed inputs: hosts picked from the fleet by name, group or label, options from lists, durations from a picker. The only free text is a reason.
  • The same gates. A procedure that changes hosts takes the service's Airfield lock, is judged by Standing orders, needs a Clearance on a protected Airfield when it says it is risky, runs in batches that never cross the floor, and drains a host when it says so.
  • Results per host. Each host's steps, output and result are on the record, with "run again on the failed hosts". A procedure can also run on a Patrol (schedule), for example a weekly log rotation.
  • Never in the way of a return. A Return to base takes the lock from a running procedure, which stops at the next host boundary and says where it stopped.

Worked moment. At 03:00 billing-2 stops answering its health check. Priya opens billing-vms, picks the procedure "Restart the billing service", ticks billing-2 and picks the reason "Not answering". The procedure says it changes hosts and drains first; prod is protected, but the procedure is marked low risk, so no Clearance is asked. The record shows billing-2 drained, restarted, checked twice and admitted, under Priya's name.

Cloud machine images, baked and rolled through instance groups

Planned Machine images with Packer; Packer builds as a first-class step; Cloud instance groups as fleets (proposed in this plan). A cloud machine image is the cloud's version of an image-based host: the whole machine, built once and launched by reference. It follows the image's flight from image-based hosts, and launches through an instance group.

  1. Bake. An image-builder step starts from a pinned base image, applies the same configuration playbook the team uses elsewhere, and produces a machine image in each region it is asked for. It runs on a Station with a short-lived cloud identity.
  2. Prove and seal. The image boots in a throwaway machine and must pass its checks; it is scanned and signed, and its contents list and provenance are stored in the Depot.
  3. A digest for something that has none. A cloud image's identifier is a name the cloud gives, not a content digest. Launchway records a digest over the image's contents list and disk manifest, and keeps the map from that digest to each region's identifier. The release names the digest; the Launch resolves the identifier per region, and the record holds both.
  4. Roll through the group. The Launch writes a new version of the group's machine template that names the image, then replaces machines in batches that Launchway drives one at a time: start new machines, wait until the load balancer counts them healthy, run the proof between batches, then remove old ones, never below the floor. A two-fleet swap instead brings up a second group with the new template behind the same balancer and moves weights.
  5. Scaling during a Launch. Machines the cloud starts while the Launch runs take the template the Airfield wants, and are counted in the current batch. The cloud's own replacement of unhealthy machines stays on underneath.
  6. The way back. Return to base puts back the previous template version and replaces the machines already changed. Retention keeps every image a return may need, in every region.

Worked moment. Suppose billing moves from its two virtual machines to a cloud instance group of four. Release 4.14 bakes billing-image@sha256:a61f…0d2, which maps to one image identifier in the team's region. The Launch replaces one machine at a time, with the proof billing-errors between batches; a scale-out at the third batch starts a fifth machine already on 4.14.

The smallest start: one command, and the record kept

Some teams only want to push a program to a few servers they own, with nothing to run. Launchway's smallest start is one command, and it is the same per-host sequence that runs inside a Sortie. In progress VM deploys (Station-run today); New in this plan Launch from one command, with the record kept.

# Design: not built. From a laptop or one server, with no Launchway server.
$ launchway launch billing --artifact ./bin/billing --host billing-1 --host billing-2 \
    --check /healthz --drain 45s
billing-1: host key SHA256:Qw3n…  Trust it? yes
billing-1: drained, installed, restarted, healthy twice, admitted
billing-2: drained, installed, restarted, healthy twice, admitted
Recorded in .launchway/record (signed). Run "launchway record send" when a server is set up.
  • Nothing to install first. The one program, a secure shell to the hosts, and a health address. Host keys are shown for you to confirm, then pinned; a changed key is refused.
  • Kept, not lost. Every Launch writes a signed local record. When a server exists, the record is sent and becomes ordinary Launch records with their history.
  • Grows without starting over. Once a server is set (even the single-server shape), the same command asks the server instead: it becomes a Sortie, the hosts become a fleet held in the product, and the lock, Standing orders and Clearance apply. Commands do not change.

Worked example: billing 4.13 to prod

The legacy billing service is its own Flight, billing, owned by the Squadron "back office". It runs as a program with a service on two virtual machines, billing-1 and billing-2, behind one open-source load balancer. staging has one machine and no balancer, so its fleet has "accept downtime" switched on and says so.

Design: not built

The step names a fleet instead of carrying an inventory. Hosts, keys, reach, the load balancer and the floor come from the fleet held in the product. Keys that exist today (strategy, max_unavailable, drain, check) keep their meaning.

steps:
  build: { uses: launchway/go-build }        # exists today: programs kept as the Cargo "bin"

  launch-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [build]
    environment: prod
    service: billing
    version: { input: version }               # 4.13, given when the release is promoted
    fleet:
      name: billing-vms                      # Design: not built. The fleet held in the product
      payload: { cargo: bin, file: bin/billing }   # Design: not built. Taken by digest
      strategy: rolling
      max_unavailable: 1
      drain: 45s
      check: { url: /healthz, status: [200], success: 2 }
      proof: billing-errors                   # Design: not built. A proof between batches
  1. The Sortie builds billing 4.13; the Cargo is stored by digest, scanned and signed.
  2. The Route reaches prod. Standing orders pass: signed, scanned, tests green, no Hold. Clearance: Ana gives a Go.
  3. Launchway takes the lock for billing in prod and checks the floor: two hosts, floor one, batch one. Allowed.
  4. billing-1: drained in 6 seconds, 4.13 installed, service restarted, health answered 200 twice, admitted.
  5. The proof billing-errors compares the fleet's error rate for two minutes: steady. billing-2 follows the same sequence.
  6. Overwatch watches the fleet for 30 minutes and records 4.13 as the stable state. The fleet page shows both hosts on 4.13 since 14:12, from this Sortie.

If billing-2 had failed its check, Launchway would have stopped, drained and returned billing-2, then billing-1, to 4.12, checked both, admitted both, and ended the Sortie as Returned to base with the failing answers in the record.

What exists in code today, and what it takes

Built today

The fleet package does the per-host sequence (drain, install, restart, check until it passes a set number of times in a row, admit) in batches of 1 to 100 that must leave a host serving behind a balancer; returns every touched host on a failed check and quarantines a host it cannot return; requires a pinned host key and never trusts one on first use; writes every command to an audit file, one line each; drives one open-source load balancer through its runtime admin socket; runs the Pathfinder as a second inventory group at 10, 50 and 100 percent by weights with a bake time and a watch, for the service-unit method; and holds a planner that chooses rolling or a second fleet from a probe of what the environment allows, or refuses naming what is missing. A Station runs it with launchway fleet probe and launchway fleet run and an inventory file. The Ansible step runs inside a Sortie today with pinned keys, check mode, Clearance and per-host results.

Not what the roadmap says

The roadmap marks "VM deploys" and "Delivery to machines over SSH" Available. The server refuses any Sortie with a fleet step ("this server does not schedule fleet deploy steps yet; a Station runs them with launchway fleet run"), and nothing outside the fleet package writes the host table, so there is no API, command or screen to define a fleet. Run from the command line, a fleet Launch has no Airfield lock, no deployment record, no Clearance and no Standing order. The status this evidence supports is In progress.

To make it a scheduled, recorded, gated part of a Sortie:

  1. Fleets held in the product. Wire the existing store to the API, command line, web, agent endpoint and Terraform, with a parity test; host changes on protected Airfields need Clearance.
  2. The server schedules the step. Remove the refusal; place the step on a launch Station in a Ramp that can reach the fleet; take the Airfield lock.
  3. The gates. Judge Standing orders and Clearance at the deploy point, before any host is touched, as for a cluster Launch.
  4. The record. Record the release by digest (today a deployment carries only a version) and turn the package's per-host events into record events; keep the release each host runs.
  5. Resume and return. Let a new Station resume or return a Launch whose Station was lost, from the record; make Return to base after success a forward Launch of the previous release.
  6. Overwatch and proofs. Run proofs between batches and the watch after the last one through the guarded query layer.
  7. Tests. Engine tests for scheduling and gates, and the existing real-machine tests run in the gate.

The contract, checked

RuleHow machines meet it
1. Same levels and permissionsA fleet belongs to a Flight or Squadron inside an Airfield; who may change it and who may launch to it are ordinary role bindings.
2. One recordFleet changes, host enrollment and every host step are events; the fleet page reads them.
3. Gates are Standing ordersJudged at the deploy point before any host is touched; the floor and "accept downtime" are Standing orders too, lockable from above.
4. Typed inputsFleets, hosts, labels and balancers are picked or fetched; the only typed text is a name or an address, checked as you type.
5. Steps on StationsThe launch Station runs the step; the host agent is the Station program in host mode.
6. One capability slotThe slot is "launch to machines". The built-in fleet Launch is the default; a configuration tool connection (Ansible, later Chef) is an equal choice. The fleet page says which one serves it.
7. Off until wantedNo fleet, no fleet screens: the Hosts menu appears when the first fleet is made.
8. Every way inWeb, API, command line, agent endpoint and Terraform resources for fleets, hosts and enrollment codes, kept equal by the parity test.
9. Loss and rolesSee Safety below.
10. Never blocks Return to baseGoing back is never held by Clearance, a Hold or a window; only the floor and the drain still apply, because they are what keep users served.

Safety

When this failsWhat happens
A host check failsStop; return every touched host; Sortie ends Returned to base with the answers.
A host cannot be returnedIt stays drained and out of rotation, marked quarantined, and Comms (notifications) tell the fleet's owners. The floor is recomputed without it.
A host key changedThe host is refused and nothing is sent to it. A person confirms the new key, and the change is recorded.
The load balancer does not answerBefore the Launch: refused. During it: no further host is drained; the hosts already changed are checked and the Launch pauses for a person.
The launch Station is lostThe lock stays held. The record says which hosts were touched; another Station in the Ramp resumes or returns, as the person on duty chooses.
The server or database is lostA pushing Station finishes the host in hand and stops at the next safe point. Pulling hosts keep the last release they were told and keep serving.
A pulling host is offlineIt is listed as behind; the Launch completes after its stated wait; the host catches up to what its Airfield wants when it returns.
Pilot (developer)
Launch to fleets in Airfields they may launch to; see hosts and results.
Controller (approver)
Give Clearance for Launches and for host changes on protected Airfields.
Commander (owner)
Create fleets, connect inventory sources and load balancers, make enrollment codes, admit and remove hosts, tune floors and windows within the locks above.
Observer (viewer)
See fleets and Launches.
On by default
Pinned keys, drain before change, a floor of one, a health check before admit, return on failure, Overwatch, audited commands.

Screens

Design: not built

None of these screens exists yet. Each is described field by field, with its states, in the screens notes for this chapter.

  • The fleet page. The hosts of one fleet as rows: name, group, labels, the release each runs and since when, last heard, and a state (Serving, Drained, Changing, Behind, Quarantined, Not answering). A band on top shows the fleet's release, its floor and its reach. Actions: Launch, Add hosts, Return to base.
  • The host page. One host: its release history, the record of every step on it, its key fingerprint or enrolled identity, its labels and groups, and the actions a person may take now.
  • Add hosts. A wizard with three cards (By hand, From an inventory source, Let hosts enroll), ending in a review list with fetched key fingerprints to confirm.
  • Make a fleet. Name, Airfield, reach (two cards), load balancer (picked and tested), floor, windows.
  • A rolling Launch, host by host. The launch line with a row per batch and a cell per host moving through drain, install, check, admit, the proof between batches, and Return to base always at hand.
  • A stepped Launch to a second group. Two groups with intended and measured weights, the proof at each step, and the old group held at zero.
  • Run a procedure. The procedures a fleet allows as a list; picking one opens its form (hosts by name, group or label; options from lists; a reason), shows whether it takes the lock and needs a Clearance, and then a host-by-host result grid with Run again on the failed hosts.
  • Configuration check and apply. The check result per host, the Clearance bound to it, and after the apply the comparison of what changed against what the check showed, with differences as findings.
  • Machine images. Each baked image with its digest, the identifier in each region, boot test, Inspection (security scan) and signature, and the instance groups that run it; an instance-group Launch shown as batches of machines with the proof between them.
  • Host runtime. On the host page, the container runtime found, the running and previous digests, and the container's own health beside the fleet's check.
