Open question

Decision needed

Status of two Available items. "VM deploys" and "Delivery to machines over SSH" are marked Available, but the server will not run them in a Sortie. This plan proposes In progress until a scheduled, recorded, gated Launch works. Do you agree to lower them?

Decision needed

One program or two. The plan proposes that the host agent is the Station program in a host mode, so there is one program to secure, sign and update. The alternative is a separate, smaller agent with less on the host. Which do you want?

Decision needed

New hosts on protected Airfields. The plan makes adding or admitting a host to a protected Airfield a change that needs Clearance, because a host is new trust. Is that the default you want, or only a Standing order a Wing (organization) can turn on?

Decision needed

Which inventory source and which cloud load balancer first. The existing answer is the open-source balancer already built, then one cloud balancer. The plan does not choose the cloud or the hypervisor; that is a choice of customers.

Decision needed

Low-risk procedures without a Clearance. The plan lets a procedure declare itself low risk, so a restart on a protected Airfield runs without a Go while still taking the lock and the floor. A Standing order can take that away per Airfield. Is low risk allowed by default, or must a level turn it on?

Decision needed

The one-command start. The plan keeps a signed local record that is sent to a server later. The alternative is to require a server for any Launch, which loses the smallest teams. Do you want the start without a server?

Decision needed

Where fleets live on the roadmap. The plan puts the fleet object and the scheduled step in Milestone 3, beside the code that exists, and the zero-downtime depth in Milestone 8. The alternative is to move all host work into Milestone 8.

Launch

Launching to image-based hosts

When the whole operating system is an image, a host is launched like an application: the image is built, scanned, signed and promoted by digest, each host boots into it in turn, and the image it came from stays on the disk as the way back.

  • The operating system is built in a pipeline as one image, tested by booting it in a throwaway virtual machine, scanned, signed and stored in the Depot (registry) by digest.
  • A Launch stages the new image on every host first, then reboots hosts in batches inside the fleet's window, checks each one after it boots, and admits it or boots it back into the previous image.
  • Launchway owns four things the host does not do safely alone: deciding when a host changes, recording which host booted which digest, keeping the host's own update timer from undoing a Return to base (rollback), and going back by itself when a host is unhealthy after a reboot.
  • The rollout code is built and tested with a real boot test, but the server does not schedule it and nothing records what each host booted. This chapter proposes the honest status and the missing pieces.

Where it sits

Layer 5 of the model, Launch (deployment), for one more kind of target. A release flies a Route (the Airfields (environments) it passes through, in order); Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) judges it; a Station (runner) or a host agent does the work. It reuses the fleet, the two ways to reach a host and the per-host sequence from Launching to virtual machines and physical servers, and the Depot and Inspection (security scan) from the Depot and Security and the supply chain. What it adds is the reboot: a change that is staged first and becomes real only when the host starts again.

Builds on
One way to launch, anywhere; Launching to virtual machines and physical servers; the Depot; the Logbook and evidence (signatures and attestations).
Built on by
The software graph and Maintenance (which host runs which image, and what it needs), Radar, insight and keeping it healthy (patch deadlines across a fleet).
Words
The existing roadmap calls these "image-based hosts" and its item builds on bootc, an open-source tool that boots a container image as the whole operating system. This chapter uses "image-based host" and "image" throughout.

An image-based host, from the ground up

On an ordinary server you install an operating system once and then change it piece by piece. Every server slowly becomes different. On an image-based host the whole operating system is one image, built from a recipe in Git like a container image. Every host that boots the same digest runs exactly the same system.

The system part

Programs and libraries come from the image and are read-only. Nobody changes them on the host; a change is a new image.

Host configuration

Settings that differ per host persist. When a new image boots, local changes are carried over and merged with the image's defaults.

Data

One data area is shared by every image on the host and is never rolled back. Content an image puts there is applied only at the first install.

An update has three moments. Stage: the host downloads the new image and prepares it beside the running one; nothing running changes. Reboot: the host starts into the new image; this is the only moment of change, and the host is unavailable while it restarts. Keep the way back: the image the host came from stays on the disk, so going back is one more reboot with nothing to download.

Two things the host does not do safely on its own, and Launchway must:

  • It may update itself. Hosts often ship with a timer that fetches a newer image and reboots on its own schedule. That would change hosts outside any Launch, and would re-apply a release you just sent back. When a host is pinned to an image by digest, its own update command has nothing to do; only a new instruction changes it.
  • It does not judge its own health. The host tool does not check, after a reboot, whether your service works and go back if it does not. That decision must come from outside, or from a guard placed on the host.

What you will be able to do

You change the kiosk image recipe to add a font and a security fix. The Sortie (run) builds kiosk-os 7, boots it in a throwaway virtual machine to prove it starts and its services come up, scans it, signs it and stores it in the Depot by digest. It is now a release like any other.

The Route sends image 7 to the two kiosks on the office rack in staging. Both download it during the day, reboot, pass their checks and report the new digest. Overwatch watches them for an hour. Ana gives Clearance for prod.

In prod, the twelve shop kiosks download image 7 during opening hours without changing. At 22:00, when the reboot window opens, Launchway reboots one kiosk per shop at a time, checks each one after it boots, and moves on. By morning the fleet page shows twelve kiosks booted on image 7, each with the time it booted.

One kiosk comes back from the reboot with its touch screen service failing. The guard on the kiosk sees the check fail and boots it back into image 6 before Launchway even hears from it. Launchway stops the Launch, returns the kiosks it already changed, and the record shows that this one went back by itself, and why.

A kiosk in the harbor shop was offline all week. When it comes back it asks what to run, gets the image its Airfield wants now, stages it, and waits for the next reboot window. If a Return to base happened in the meantime, it gets the returned image instead.

How it works

The image's flight, from commit to booted host

  1. Build. The image is built from its recipe on a Ramp (runner pool) whose Stations may run privileged builds, restricted to named repositories and never for pull requests from forks. Configuration that is the same on every host is baked in at build time, with Ansible where the team uses it.
  2. Boot test. The image boots in a throwaway virtual machine inside the Sortie. Its services must come up and its checks must pass. The result is a Preflight (checks) verdict with a Debrief (test report).
  3. Inspection, sign, attest. The image is scanned like any image. It is signed, and its parts list and provenance are stored beside it. Hosts are configured to refuse an unsigned image.
  4. Depot by digest. The image is stored once. Tags are for people; hosts are told the digest. A tag is refused as a Launch target because it can move.
  5. Route. The release flies staging, then prod, with Standing orders (policies) and Clearance (approval) at each stop, exactly as an application does.
  6. Launch. Stage everywhere, reboot in batches, check after boot, admit or go back (below).

A batch reboot, step by step

Staging is separated from rebooting. Staging is safe at any time, so it happens first on every host, while they keep serving. Rebooting is the change, so it happens in batches, inside the fleet's window, behind the drain, and never below the floor.

Two details make this safe:

  • Verdicts arrive late. A rebooting host cannot answer. Launchway waits for the host's report, up to a stated time. A host that does not report in time is treated as failed: the Launch stops, and the host is listed as "not answering" with its last known state.
  • The guard works offline. After the reboot, a small check on the host gives the new image a set time to prove itself. If the checks fail, or the host cannot reach anything it must reach, the guard boots the previous image on its own and reports that when it can. This is the health-check rollback the host lacks, and it works for a kiosk with no network.

What Launchway must own for this to be safe

When hosts change

Each host is pinned to a digest. Only a Launch changes the pin. Staging and rebooting are separate, and reboots happen only inside the fleet's window and outside any Hold (freeze). Going back is never held by a window.

Which host booted which digest

Each host reports three digests: booted, staged and previous. Launchway keeps the history and compares it with what the Airfield wants. A report is labeled "reported by the host"; attestation of what booted comes later.

The host's own timer

On enrollment Launchway checks whether the host would update itself and reports it as a finding. Launched hosts have the timer off and the digest pinned, so a Return to base is never undone by the host.

Going back by itself

The guard on the host boots the previous image when its checks fail after a reboot. Launchway stops the Launch, returns the hosts already changed, and records which return was made by the host.

Two images on a host, and the way back

Going back has limits, and Launchway states them before the Launch, not after:

  • Data does not go back. If the new image changed the format of data it keeps, the old image must still read it. The rule for application databases applies: expand first, contract later.
  • Host configuration changed since the update. The quick way back can revert configuration changed on the host after the update. Launchway lists host files changed by hand, and offers to reset them to the image or to carry them into the next image.
  • Content placed in the data area by a new image is ignored on existing hosts. Launchway's lint of the image recipe warns about it.

Applications that ride on the host

Most image-based hosts exist to run an application, usually as containers. There are three ways, and each is pinned by digest:

WayHow it changesUse it when
Baked into the imageOnly with a new image and a rebootThe application and the system are tested and shipped as one
Bound to the imagePulled while the image is staged, before the reboot; starts with the new imageThe application must be present from the first second after boot
Launched on its ownAs containers on the host, with the per-host sequence of machines and no rebootThe application changes much more often than the system

A moving tag is never allowed: an application on a moving tag would change without a Launch and without a record. The release of an image-based host lists the image digest and every application digest it carries. When the image and an application must change together, they fly as a Formation (releases that go together).

Edge fleets that are often offline

Kiosks, shop servers and devices in vehicles are reached by the host agent, which connects outward. Their Launches are built for absence:

  • A Launch states how long it waits for hosts that are away, then completes with them listed as behind.
  • A host that returns takes the image its Airfield wants now, after the same Standing orders, and stages it until its next reboot window. It never takes an image that was since returned.
  • Downloads can be limited to a window, too, for shops with slow links.
  • The host keeps its reports while offline and sends them when it can, so the record is complete, late but not lost.
  • The guard does not need the network, so a bad image never strands a kiosk on a broken screen.

The same model, gates and record

Nothing here is private to image-based hosts. The release is an artifact by digest. It flies a Route. Each Launch uses a strategy: rolling batches by default, or a Pathfinder (canary) that reboots one host per site first and watches it before the rest. Overwatch judges it. Return to base is a reboot into the image on the disk and is never blocked. Standing orders, Clearance, Hold and the Airfield lock apply at the same points as for any Launch, and the fleet page reads the same record.

First boot belongs to Launchway too, on the roadmap: a first-boot step gives a new host its name, network, keys and zone, and may run a configuration playbook once before the host takes traffic. Running a playbook on a host already serving traffic stays refused, because that is what brings drift back.

Cloud machine images take the same flight

A cloud machine image is built, boot-tested, scanned, signed and given a digest the same way, and then launched through a cloud instance group instead of a fleet of hosts that reboot. The bake step, the digest kept for an image the cloud names by identifier, and the roll through instance groups are designed in cloud machine images. Planned Machine images with Packer.

Reboot and download windows on the Hold calendar

A fleet's reboot and download windows are drawn on the Hold (freeze) calendar beside Holds, Airfield windows, tenants' windows and the GitOps controller's sync windows, each labeled with its source, so one view shows when anything may change. A staged image waiting for its window shows there as a planned change: "shop-kiosks: 12 hosts reboot into image 7 from 22:00". Going back is never held by a window. New in this plan, with controller sync windows.

Worked example: kiosk-os 7 to the shops

The Harbor Lights kiosks show the shop's catalog in four harbor shops. The image recipe is the kiosk-os Flight (codebase), owned by the Squadron (team) "kiosks". The kiosk application is bound to the image. Twelve kiosks in prod carry the label store; two on the office rack are staging. The fleet is reached by pull: the host agent is part of the image. The shops close at 21:00; the reboot window is 22:00 to 06:00. There is no load balancer: each kiosk serves the people in front of it, so the floor is one kiosk per shop, and the drain is the kiosk's own "back in a minute" screen.

Design: not built

An image Launch names the fleet and the image output. The batch is grouped by label so each shop keeps a kiosk. method: bootc, image and check exist today; the rest is the design.

steps:
  image:
    kind: image                                # exists today: build, scan, sign, push by digest
    context: kiosk
    tags: [harbor-lights/kiosk-os]
    sbom: true
    sign: true
    scan: true

  boot-test:                                   # Design: not built. Today only inside Launchway's own tests
    needs: [image]
    uses: launchway/boot-test
    with: { image: { output: image.image }, checks: [kiosk-ui, kiosk-agent] }

  launch:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [boot-test]
    environment: prod
    service: kiosk-os
    version: { input: version }
    fleet:
      name: shop-kiosks                        # Design: not built. Held in the product
      method: bootc
      image: { output: image.image }           # name@sha256:...; a tag is refused
      strategy: rolling
      batch: { by_label: store, per_value: 1 } # Design: not built. One kiosk per shop at a time
      window: after-hours                      # Design: not built. Named in the fleet
      check: { url: /healthz, status: [200], success: 2 }
  1. The Sortie builds image 7, boots it in a throwaway virtual machine (both checks pass), scans it (no blocking finding), signs it and stores kiosk-os@sha256:4be1….
  2. staging: both rack kiosks stage and reboot at once (their fleet allows it), report booted on 7, and pass an hour of Overwatch.
  3. prod: Standing orders pass, Ana gives Clearance. All twelve kiosks stage image 7 during the afternoon and keep running 6; the fleet page shows "staged 7" on each.
  4. 22:00: batch 1 is one kiosk in each of the four shops. Each shows its "back in a minute" screen, reboots, the guard passes, and the kiosk reports booted on 7. Batches 2 and 3 follow. By 23:10 all twelve are on 7.
  5. Overwatch reads kiosk errors and session counts the next morning against the baseline. Steady: image 7 becomes the stable state, and image 6 stays on every disk until image 8 replaces it.

If the kiosk in the harbor shop had failed its checks, its guard would have booted image 6 and reported. Launchway would stop the Launch, reboot the three other changed kiosks back into 6 (inside the window, but going back is never held by it), and end the Sortie as Returned to base with the failing check in the record.

What exists in code today, and what is missing

Built today

The fleet package has an image method: it takes an image by digest only and refuses a tag; reads the host's booted, staged and previous digests; switches the host to the digest, stages it, drains, reboots, checks and admits; and on a failed check returns the host to the image it came from with one more reboot and stops. It refuses to act on the machine its own Station runs on. A test boots a real image in a throwaway virtual machine. The report says plainly that a fleet of one drops requests while it reboots.

Not what the roadmap says

"Image-based hosts" is marked Available, and its text promises host setup at first boot. The server refuses to schedule the step, as for every fleet step; there is no host list or image catalog in the product; nothing keeps which host booted which digest; the host's own update timer is not handled; there is no guard on the host, so the only health-check return is the one a reachable Station makes; and first-boot setup is the planned item "First boot owned by Launchway". The status this evidence supports is In progress.

Missing, in order: the fleet held in the product and the server scheduling the step (shared with machines); the per-host digest report and its history; the timer check and the pin; the boot test as a pipeline step; the host agent baked into the image; the guard; reboot and download windows; then first boot, the image catalog and the stack designer already on the roadmap.

The contract, checked

RuleHow image-based hosts meet it
1. Same levels and permissionsAn image-based fleet is a fleet; the image is a Depot item of a Flight.
2. One recordBuild, boot test, signature, every stage, reboot, guard verdict and return are events; the per-host digest history is read from them.
3. Gates are Standing orders"Signed", "scanned", "boot test passed", "timer off" and the windows are Standing orders judged before a host is touched.
4. Typed inputsImages are picked from the Depot by name and shown by digest; windows are drawn on a week grid; labels are picked.
5. Steps on StationsBuild and boot test run on a privileged Ramp; the Launch runs on a launch Station or the host agent.
6. One capability slotPart of "launch to machines". The built-in image Launch is the default; a configuration tool can do first-boot work as a connection.
7. Off until wantedThe image method and the Machine images menu appear when the first image is built or the first image-based host enrolls.
8. Every way inSame as fleets, plus image items in the Depot through every way in.
9. Loss and rolesSee Safety below.
10. Never blocks Return to baseThe previous image is on every disk; going back needs no download, no window and no Clearance, and the guard can do it with no network at all.

Safety

When this failsWhat happens
The new image does not bootThe boot test should have caught it. If a host still fails, the boot loader or the guard falls back to the previous image; the host reports "returned by itself".
The host boots but checks failThe guard boots the previous image; Launchway stops the Launch and returns the hosts already changed.
The host does not report after a rebootTreated as failed after the stated time: the Launch stops, the host is "not answering" with its last known digests.
A host would update itselfFound at enrollment; a Standing order can refuse to launch to it until its timer is off.
A host booted a digest nobody launchedShown as "changed outside a Launch", with the digest; a finding is raised.
The server or database is lostHosts keep their pinned image and keep serving. A staged image waits; a host mid-reboot is judged by its guard.
The image is unsigned or a tagRefused before staging; hosts are configured to refuse an unsigned image too.
Pilot (developer)
Change the image recipe, run the build and boot test, launch to Airfields they may launch to.
Controller (approver)
Clearance for image Launches to protected Airfields.
Commander (owner)
Fleets, windows, enrollment, the privileged Ramp and who may use it.
On by default
Digest only, signed only, boot test before the Route, staging before reboot, one batch at a time, the guard, the timer check, Overwatch.

Screens

Design: not built

None of these screens exists yet. Each is described field by field, with its states, in the screens notes for this chapter.

  • The image-based fleet page. One row per host: booted digest (with release name), staged digest, previous digest, booted since, last heard, own-updates state, and a state (Up to date, Update waiting, Rebooting, Returned by itself, Behind, Changed by hand, Not answering). A band shows the image the Airfield wants and how many hosts run it.
  • Machine images. The catalog of images: name, digest, base, size, Inspection result, signature, boot test result, and where each runs.
  • Launch an image. A short wizard: pick the image, pick the fleet, see the plan (stage everywhere, batches by label, window), confirm.
  • A batch reboot in progress. Batches as rows and hosts as cells moving through staged, draining, rebooting, checking, admitted or returned, with the window's remaining time.
  • The host page. The two images on the disk as two cards, the way back as one button, boot history, and files changed by hand with "Reset to the image" or "Keep in the next image".

Open question

Decision needed

Lower "Image-based hosts" to In progress. The code and its boot test are real; the Launch, the record of booted digests and first-boot setup are not. Do you agree?

Decision needed

The default way to reach image-based hosts. The code reaches them over SSH today; an earlier delegated answer chose an agent baked into the image, outbound only, with an allow-list. The plan makes both a choice per fleet and proposes the baked-in agent as the default for image-based fleets. Do you agree?

Decision needed

Which way back. The quick way back reorders the boot entries and can revert host configuration changed since the update; switching back to the previous digest keeps that configuration but behaves like an update. The plan proposes the quick way by default, with the reverted files listed. Which do you want as the default?

Decision needed

Restarting without a full reboot. Some hosts can restart only the user space into a new image, which is much faster. The plan uses it only where the image says it is safe, and off by default. Is that the right default?

Decision needed

Bases beyond the first family. An earlier delegated answer labels other base distributions experimental and claims no support for them. The plan keeps that. Confirm or widen.

Launch

Launching to serverless

A serverless Launch makes a new version from a digest with no traffic, moves traffic to it by weights while Overwatch judges it, and goes back by moving the weights back, in seconds.

  • Functions and managed container services, on your own cluster or on a public cloud, are one kind of target with one model. The pipeline names the platform connection, not the product.
  • Every Launch creates an immutable version. A preview is a version with no traffic and its own address, so it costs almost nothing. Return to base (rollback) is one change of weights.
  • Serverless is different in honest ways: no hosts to drain, cold starts, platform limits, scale to zero, and state that lives outside the version. Each has a stated answer.
  • Edge functions are a third family with versions by digest, region-by-region steps and preview addresses. Durable business workflows are a stated non-goal: a step starts one on an outside engine and waits for its answer.
  • Nothing of this is built. The existing roadmap spreads it over Milestones 3, 8 and 11; this plan gathers it into one group in Milestone 8.

Where it sits

Layer 5, Launch (deployment), for platforms that run your code without hosts you manage. It is the same model as every other target: a release by digest flies a Route (the Airfields (environments) it passes through, in order), a strategy moves traffic, Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) judges it, and Return to base is never blocked. It relies on the foundation for short-lived identity per step, on the record, and on command for Standing orders (policies), Clearance (approval) and Hold (freeze).

Builds on
One way to launch, anywhere; Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch; Levels, people and secrets; the Depot (registry).
Built on by
Radar, insight and keeping it healthy (cost in context), the software graph and Maintenance (a function as a platform node and what it needs).

What you will be able to do

You merge a change to the image-resize function. The Sortie (run) builds its image and stores it by digest. In prod, Launchway creates version 42 from that digest with no traffic, warms it with 50 test requests, then moves 5, 25 and 100 percent of traffic to it, judging each step on at least 500 real requests. Twenty minutes later version 42 is the stable state.

At 25 percent, Overwatch sees errors on large images rise on version 42. Launchway moves all traffic back to version 41 in one change of weights. It takes three seconds; nothing is built or downloaded. The record says which proof failed and shows the requests it counted.

You open a pull request. Its preview is a version with no traffic and its own address, shown on the pull request with its check result. It costs nothing while nobody calls it, and it is removed when the pull request closes.

staging runs on your own cluster; prod runs on a public cloud. The pipeline does not change. Before the prod Launch, Launchway reads what that platform allows (only two versions may share traffic, weights in whole percent) and shows the plan it can really make there.

The Launch page shows that version 42 costs 12 percent more per million requests than version 41, because it uses more memory. A Standing order for prod asks for Clearance when cost per request rises by more than 10 percent, so the Launch waits for a Go with the numbers beside it.

No cloud key is stored anywhere in Launchway. The Launch step proves who it is with a short-lived token that names the Flight (codebase), the branch and the Airfield; the cloud was told once to trust exactly that.

How it works

One kind of target

A serverless platform is a connection on an Airfield, like a cluster or a fleet. It is either on your own cluster (the roadmap names Knative, with KEDA for event-driven scaling) or a public cloud's function or managed container service. Every one of them has the three things the model needs:

The model needsWhat every serverless platform has
An immutable version from a digestA version or revision, made from a container image or a code package, that never changes once made
A way to move trafficA named pointer or a route that splits requests between versions by weight
Signals to judge byRequests, errors, duration, cold starts and throttling per version, read through the guarded query layer

Two families are launched the same way. Functions run a handler per request or event. Managed container services run a container image that listens for requests and scale to zero when idle. Managed instance groups, which are cloud machines rather than serverless, are launched as fleets: see Launching to virtual machines and physical servers.

Edge functions: a third family

New in this plan Edge functions run small handlers in an edge provider's locations around the world, close to the people calling them. They fit the model: a bundle that can be named by digest, versions the platform keeps, a way to move traffic, and signals per version. They are launched as a third family beside functions and managed container services, with three differences stated plainly.

The model needsOn an edge platform
A version from a digestThe bundle is built once and stored in the Depot by digest. The platform gives each upload its own version identifier; the record keeps both, so "what we launched" and "what the edge runs" can be compared.
A way to move trafficWeights between two versions where the platform can split by percentage. Where it cannot, by location: one region first, then the rest, each a step judged by Overwatch. The probe says which, before the plan is offered.
A previewEach version's own preview address where the platform gives one, or a route on a preview host name the template Airfield names. A pull request's preview is that address, posted on the pull request.
SignalsRequests, errors and time spent per version and per region, read through the guarded query layer.
  • Spreading takes time. A new version reaches every location over seconds to minutes. Overwatch starts judging only when Launchway has read the active version back from a sample of regions, and the record shows when each answered.
  • Limits are tight. Bundle size, start time and time per request are probed and checked at Preflight (checks), so a bundle that is too large is refused before anything moves.
  • Data at the edge is outside the version. Key-value stores and settings kept at the edge do not go back with a Return to base (rollback); Launchway says so before the Launch, as for any state outside the version.

Worked moment. If Harbor Lights put a small edge function in front of the shop to show the delivery cut-off for the visitor's region, its Launch would upload bundle sha256:b5e2…44c as a new edge version, check its preview address, send it to one region, wait until three regions report it active, judge it, then send it everywhere; going back would point every region at the previous version.

Previews with their own address on every serverless family. Whatever the family, a pull request's preview is a version with no share of live traffic, a tag or alias named for the pull request (pr-482), and its own address on the pull request. It is removed when the pull request closes.

A serverless Launch, step by step

  1. Resolve and check. The image or package is taken by digest from the Depot; a tag is resolved before anything else. Standing orders run: signed, scanned, tests green, no Hold. A protected Airfield waits for Clearance.
  2. Probe the platform. Launchway reads what this platform allows: how many versions may share traffic, the smallest weight, how many versions it keeps, concurrency and quotas. A strategy it cannot make there is not offered.
  3. Create the version with no traffic. Settings and secret references that belong to the version are set now, so they travel with it and go back with it.
  4. Preview and warm. The version's own address answers test requests and the health check before any user reaches it; that also warms it.
  5. Move traffic by weights. In the steps the plan states. Each step waits for its time and its request count, then Overwatch judges it.
  6. Overwatch, then the stable state. After 100 percent, the watch goes on for the time the Airfield sets; then the new version becomes the stable state. The previous version is kept until the next one is stable.

How it maps to the shared model

StrategyOn a serverless target
All at onceStill a new version first, checked on its preview address; then 100 percent in one move. Overwatch and the way back are the same.
Pathfinder (canary)Weights in steps, judged by time and request count. The default for prod.
Two-fleet swapThe new version is tested on its preview address with test transactions, then traffic moves from 0 to 100 in one step, and the old version stays ready at 0.
RollingDoes not apply: there are no hosts to change a few at a time. The plan says so instead of offering it.

What is different, and where the model does not fit

DifferenceWhat it meansLaunchway's answer
No hosts to drainRequests already running finish on the version they started on; new ones follow the weightsNo drain step; the weight is the only lever. The record shows weights, not hosts.
Cold startsA new version's first requests are slow while it startsWarm before weight with test requests, or ready capacity where the platform has it, with its cost shown. Cold-start time is shown on its own and not mixed into the version's latency.
Platform limitsSome split only between two versions, round weights, keep a limited number of versions, or limit deploys per minuteProbe first; plan inside the limits; say plainly what cannot be done there. Keep the stable and previous versions from the platform's own cleanup.
Scale to zeroA quiet function has no traffic and therefore no signalSteps wait for a request count as well as a time; test transactions can supply requests; too little data is "not enough data", never a pass.
State outside the versionTables, queues and stored files are not part of the version and do not go backLaunchway says so before the Launch. Data changes follow the expand-then-contract rule of the database work.
Events, not requestsA function started by a queue, a schedule or an event may not be splittable by weightMove a share of the event source where the platform allows; otherwise all at once with Overwatch on failures, retries and the age of waiting events. The plan says which.
Shared limitsOld and new versions may share one concurrency or quota budgetShown in the plan; a step that would starve the stable version is refused.

Cost beside the Launch

On a serverless platform a slower or larger version is also a more expensive one, so cost belongs on the Launch page. During each step Launchway works out the cost per million requests of the old and new versions from measured duration, memory and request counts, and the cost of the Launch's previews. It is labeled as an estimate; where a cost connection is set up, the billed figure replaces it later. A Standing order can ask for Clearance when the rise passes a set share. This is the same cost that insights shows across services; the Launch page shows the part that this change causes.

Short-lived identity, never a stored key

A step that launches to a public cloud gets a short-lived token from Launchway that states who it is: the Base, the Flight, the branch, the Airfield and the Sortie. The cloud is told once to trust tokens with exactly those claims, and grants a role for the length of the step. No cloud key is stored in Launchway, in a variable or in a secret. On your own cluster, the launch Station uses its own workload identity, limited to the namespaces of its Airfield. On the hosted service the exchange happens on your side, through your Detachment (the small program on your side), so the service never holds a credential to your cloud.

Worked example: image-resize

The Harbor Lights shop resizes product photos with a function in the image-resize Flight, owned by the Squadron (team) "shop". It is packaged as a container image. dev and staging run it on the team's own cluster; prod runs it on a public cloud's function service. The platform connections are set on each Airfield, so the pipeline names none of them.

Design: not built

The serverless block does not exist. The image step, { output: … }, { input: … } and the check shape exist today.

steps:
  image:
    kind: image                       # exists today: build, scan, sign, push by digest
    context: functions/image-resize
    tags: [harbor-lights/image-resize]
    sign: true
    scan: true

  launch:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [image]
    environment: { input: airfield }  # dev, staging or prod along the Route
    service: image-resize
    version: { input: version }
    serverless:                       # Design: not built
      image: { output: image.image }  # by digest
      strategy: pathfinder
      steps: [5, 25, 100]
      bake: 5m
      min_requests: 500               # each step waits for this many requests too
      warm: { requests: 50 }
      check: { url: /healthz, status: [200], success: 2 }
      cost: { show: true }
  1. The Sortie builds the image, scans and signs it, and stores image-resize@sha256:7d0c….
  2. staging (own cluster): a new revision with no traffic, warmed, then 5, 25, 100 percent. Steady for 30 minutes of Overwatch.
  3. prod (public cloud): the probe finds two versions may share traffic and weights are whole percent. Standing orders pass; the cost check shows +12 percent, so Clearance is asked with that number beside it; Ana gives a Go.
  4. Version 42 is made with no traffic, answers its preview checks and 50 warming requests, then takes 5 percent. After 5 minutes and 500 requests: pass. 25 percent: errors on large images rise.
  5. Return to base: weights 100 and 0. The Sortie ends Returned to base; version 42 is kept for the investigation; the timeline shows the weights, the proof and the requests it counted.

Durable workflows: not a goal, and how a step uses one

Some teams run long, durable business workflows written as code, with many steps that survive restarts and run at very large scale on a dedicated engine. Launchway does not try to be that engine, and says so: a pipeline is for changing software, and its guarantees (one record, a Station per step, Clearances) are the wrong shape for millions of business processes a day. This is a stated non-goal, not a gap left open.

What Launchway does instead, and does well, is the two places a delivery pipeline meets such an engine:

  1. A step that starts a workflow and waits. A ready-made step starts a workflow on an outside engine through a connection, with typed inputs, and waits without holding a Station: the server keeps the wait and takes the answer from the engine's callback through the events-in Hardpoint (extension point), or by asking it at intervals. The workflow's identifier, its state changes and its typed result are on the record; canceling the Sortie cancels the workflow unless the step says otherwise; a time limit ends the wait with "timed out" and the workflow's last state. It is the same shape as starting another pipeline and waiting for its answer. New in this plan Wait for a workflow on an outside engine.
  2. Launching the workers safely. The engine's workers are ordinary software and launch as any target does. Because a workflow started on one version of the code may still be running when the next version lands, the old workers are kept serving the workflows they started until those finish or a stated time passes, exactly as functions keep versions while they may be needed. The Launch page shows how many workflows are still running on the old version.
# Design: not built. A step that starts a workflow on an outside engine and waits.
  reindex-catalog:
    uses: launchway/await-workflow
    with:
      connection: workflow-engine          # picked from the Airfield's connections
      workflow: catalog-reindex
      inputs: { release: ${{ steps.image.outputs.digest }} }
      wait: { at_most: 2h }

The existing roadmap has five planned serverless items in three milestones and no owner. The plan gives them one group, Serverless, one kind of target, in Milestone 8, which already owns the model of the part that moves traffic and names "a function alias" as one of them. Nothing is dropped or narrowed.

The contract, checked

RuleHow serverless meets it
1. Same levels and permissionsA platform connection belongs to an Airfield; launching to it is an ordinary role binding.
2. One recordVersions, weights, proofs, costs and returns are events.
3. Gates are Standing ordersSigned, scanned, Hold, cost rise and platform limits are judged at the deploy point.
4. Typed inputsPlatforms are picked from connections; weights are picked from what the probe allows; nothing is typed but a number.
5. Steps on StationsThe launch Station calls the platform with the step's short-lived identity.
6. One capability slot"Launch to serverless". The built-in Launch drives the platform directly; where a team already runs its own deployment controller on the cluster, it can serve the slot as a connection.
7. Off until wantedThe Functions screens appear when the first platform connection is made.
8. Every way inPlatform connections, Launches and weights through web, API, command line, agent endpoint and Terraform.
9. Loss and rolesSee Safety below.
10. Never blocks Return to baseWeights back is never held by Clearance, a Hold or cost; the previous version is protected from cleanup.

Safety

When this failsWhat happens
A proof failsWeights back to the stable version; the new version is kept with no traffic for the investigation.
The platform does not answerThe platform keeps serving at the current weights. The Launch pauses; a Return to base is retried until it lands, and the page says so.
The launch Station is lost mid-LaunchWeights stay where they were. Another Station resumes or returns from the record.
The server is lost mid-LaunchProposed: a launch Station that loses the server during a weighted step moves the weights back to stable after a stated time, because going back is never gated. On by default; see Open question.
The step's token expiresA new token is issued for a resumed step; a return always gets one.
Someone changed weights outside LaunchwayShown as drift on the function's page with the actual weights; the Launch does not continue over it.
Pilot (developer)
Launch to Airfields they may launch to; make previews.
Controller (approver)
Clearance, including over a cost rise.
Commander (owner)
Platform connections and the cloud trust set-up; defaults for steps, warming and request counts.
On by default
Digest only, no traffic until checked, warming, request counts per step, Overwatch, protected previous version, cost shown.

Screens

Design: not built

None of these screens exists yet. Each is described field by field, with its states, in the screens notes for this chapter.

  • Connect a serverless platform. A wizard: where it runs (your cluster or a public cloud), the trust set-up with the exact claims to paste into the cloud, a test, and the probe's findings.
  • The function page. Versions as rows with digest, created by, weights now, requests, errors, cold starts and cost per million; the stable and previous versions marked; previews listed.
  • A serverless Launch in progress. Intended against measured weights, the step's time and request count, each proof's verdict, cold starts shown apart, cost beside it, and Return to base at hand.
  • Return to base. A dialog that says "all traffic to version 41, about 3 seconds, nothing rebuilt".
  • An edge Launch in progress. The regions as rows: the version each reports active, when it answered, its requests and errors per version, the step it belongs to, and Return to base at hand.
  • A step waiting for an outside workflow. Inside the Sortie: the engine connection, the workflow's identifier and state changes as they arrive, the time left to wait, the typed result when it comes, and Cancel with its consequence ("the workflow is canceled too").

Open question

Decision needed

Milestone 8 owns serverless. The plan moves three items into one new Milestone 8 group. The alternative is Milestone 11, which holds the scaling view. Milestone 8 is proposed because it owns the part that moves traffic for every target.

Decision needed

Going back when the server is lost. The plan proposes that a launch Station that loses the server in the middle of a weighted step moves the weights back to stable after a stated time, on by default. It follows the rule that going back is never gated, but it is an action taken without the server's say. Do you want it on by default?

Decision needed

Edge functions now or later. The plan adds them as a third family in the same Milestone 8 group, after functions and managed container services. The other way is to state them out of scope until a customer asks. Which do you want?

Decision needed

Durable workflows as a non-goal. The plan states that Launchway is not a durable workflow engine and offers a step that waits for one. Confirm the non-goal.

Decision needed

Which public cloud first. The plan does not choose; the earlier answer was one cloud first. That is a choice of customers.

Decision needed

Function frameworks on your own cluster. The existing item says they come later, after revisions on the cluster. The plan keeps that order.

Launch · traffic

Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Zero downtime is a property Launchway proves on every Launch (deployment), not a hope: new copies serve only once ready, old ones stop only once drained, healthy copies never drop below the floor, and a Launch that fails its checks returns to base by itself.

  • Five strategies, each saying how traffic moves and what is watched: all at once, rolling, Pathfinder (canary) with stepped weights, a two-fleet swap, and shadow traffic where the target supports it.
  • Radar (monitoring) shows requests, errors and latency from the edge to the workload, per version, during and after a Launch, from sources the team already has.
  • Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) compares the new version with the stable one and with earlier good Launches, reads logs for new error patterns, and gives a verdict with its evidence: pass, fail, or not enough data.
  • Overwatch can be pinned to a past Launch, held to the service's Envelope, and told to fail fast on a hard limit; every verdict can be replayed from the record. A Pathfinder can go to a subset of clients first, with a verdict per subset, and can stop for a Clearance between steps without holding a Station.
  • Databases stay up because schema changes are launched like code, in an order that keeps both versions working. Switches (feature toggles) release without a Launch, under the same Overwatch. Drills (chaos tests) prove the claims.

Where it sits

Layer 5, Launch, and the edge of layer 7. It fills in two nouns of the shared model: the strategy and Overwatch. It applies to every target: Launching to Kubernetes, Launching to virtual machines and physical servers, Launching to image-based hosts and Launching to serverless.

Builds on
The Launch lifecycle and the record (lifecycle, the record); guarded reads of monitoring data; Standing orders (policies) for the floor and the defaults (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold).
Built on by
Routes, which advance only on a pass; Switches; Drills; the evidence for an auditor (the Logbook and evidence); the reliability and insight views (Radar, insight and keeping it healthy).
Layers used
2, 4, 5, 6 and 7.

What you will be able to do

You launch storefront 2.4.0 into prod with a Pathfinder. The Launch page shows "5 percent intended, 4.8 percent measured", and Radar draws the new version's errors and latency beside the stable version's, from the edge to the pods, as the share grows to 25, 50 and 100 percent.

Twelve minutes into the step at 25 percent, the new version's checkout latency is 40 percent above the stable version's, and a log pattern never seen before appears. Overwatch fails the Launch, sends all traffic back to 2.3.2, and writes one sentence with the charts and the sample log lines. You did nothing.

At 2 in the morning a Launch into dev gets almost no traffic. Overwatch says "not enough data: 41 requests in 10 minutes, at least 200 needed", waits one more window, and then holds the Route at dev instead of calling it a pass.

You add a delivery_date column. Launchway launches the change in two halves: the column is added first, both versions keep working, and the old column is removed weeks later, only when no Airfield on the Route still runs a version that reads it.

You turn the Switch delivery-date on for 10 percent of shoppers. Errors rise among them. Overwatch turns the Switch back off and tells you which Switch it was and why.

Before you let the Route advance into prod by itself, you run the zero-downtime Drill in a rehearsal Airfield: a Launch under steady load while one copy is removed and a dependency is slowed. It passes only if no request failed above the baseline.

How it works

Zero downtime: four rules the platform checks

1. Ready before traffic

A new copy gets no user traffic until its readiness check passes. On a protected Airfield it must also answer test calls through a preview path first.

2. Drained before stopped

An old copy is taken out of the load balancer or the service endpoints, finishes the requests it holds, and only then stops. The drain time covers the longest normal request.

3. Never below the floor

Each service has a floor of healthy, serving copies. Every strategy plans its batches from it, adding copies first when it must.

4. Back by itself

A Launch that fails its checks returns to base without anyone pressing a button. On by default; the team can tune it; a level above can require it.

Each rule is checked three times.

  1. Before the Launch, by Preflight (checks): a readiness check exists and differs from the liveness check; the shutdown grace is longer than the drain time; there are at least two copies, or the plan adds a second before removing the first; the plan never goes below the floor. A plan that cannot keep the rules is refused with the reason, or allowed with a plain warning where the Airfield permits downtime. Planned Rollout readiness scan.
  2. During the Launch, by measuring: healthy serving copies at every moment, and failed requests compared with the same minutes before the Launch.
  3. After the Launch, on the record, as one sentence: "Zero-downtime proof: fewest healthy copies 6 (floor 4); failed requests during the shift 0.03 percent against 0.03 percent the hour before." When a source is missing it says "not measured", never "zero". New in this plan

Rule 0 sits under all four: both versions must work at the same time, because during any strategy except all at once they serve side by side. Launchway checks what it can (contract tests, the backward-compatibility lint for schema changes) and says plainly what it cannot.

What it will not do

Launchway cannot make a change that is not backward compatible safe, and a rollout alone cannot give a whole system full nines. A service with one copy cannot be replaced without a gap unless a second copy is added first; Preflight says so. Connections that stay open for hours are drained up to a limit and then closed, and clients must reconnect. A job that must run exactly once is handed over with a short, controlled pause, not an overlap. DNS caches keep old answers, so a cutover by DNS is never instant.

The strategies in detail

How traffic moves. A few copies at a time are replaced. Each new copy joins once ready; each old copy leaves once drained. Traffic follows the copies, so the new version's share grows with each batch.

What is watched. Readiness of each new copy; healthy copies against the floor; errors and latency of the whole service after each batch; for hosts, a check that passes several times in a row (two by default today) before a host is admitted.

Where. Kubernetes replaces pods a few at a time (Available for a plain Deployment). Machines roll in batches with draining at a load balancer (Available over SSH, Station-run, one open-source load balancer). Image-based hosts stage the image, drain, reboot, check and admit (Available, Station-run).

Its limit. The new version is never compared with the old one at the same moment, so a slow regression is judged against the baseline only.

How traffic moves. The new version runs beside the stable one and gets a small share of traffic that grows in steps, with a judgment at each step. The share is set at a gateway or mesh where there is one (exact), or by the ratio of copies where there is not (approximate).

What is watched. The new version against the stable version in the same minutes, and both against earlier good Launches; new log patterns in the new version only; the intended share against the measured share.

MinutesIntended shareMeasured shareNew version errorsStable version errorsVerdict
0 to 20 percent0 percenttest calls: 20 of 20 answered0.20 percentready
2 to 125 percent4.8 percent0.21 percent0.20 percentpass
12 to 2225 percent24.6 percent0.19 percent0.20 percentpass
22 to 3250 percent50.3 percent0.22 percent0.21 percentpass
32 to 62100 percent100 percent0.20 percentbaseline 0.20 percentpass

Where. Kubernetes through a rollout controller (Available control and the rollout panel; Planned Every rollout strategy), or with no rollout controller (New in this plan). Machines: a second host group that gets 10, 50 and 100 percent by default at the load balancer (Available, Station-run, one install method only). Serverless: weights between function versions (Planned). By client type, through the Gateway API or a mesh (Planned Weighted canaries and traffic control).

How traffic moves. A full new fleet comes up beside the old one, sized to the old fleet's current copies. It is tested through a preview path while users stay on the old fleet. Then all traffic switches at once. The old fleet stays warm for a set time, so going back is one switch, and is then scaled down.

What is watched. Test calls and their answers through the preview path before the switch; then the same Overwatch as a Pathfinder at 100 percent, against the baseline, with the old fleet still there.

Where. Kubernetes through a rollout controller (Available: the Launch page shows "preview up, tests, switch, old kept, scale down"). Machines behind a load balancer (Planned Hosts and pools; Test transactions to a not-yet-live host). Image-based hosts only with spare hosts. Serverless by moving all weight to the new version (Planned).

With no rollout controller. On a cluster with none, the swap is two workloads, a preview service and one switch of the main service's selector or of a Gateway API route; see a two-fleet swap with no rollout controller (New in this plan).

Its cost. Twice the capacity for the length of the swap; Launchway asks for the headroom first (Planned Temporary capacity for tests).

How traffic moves. Users are served only by the stable version. A copy of some live requests is also sent to the new version, and its answers are thrown away.

What is watched. The new version's errors and latency on real requests, against the stable version's answers to the same requests.

Where and when. Only where the gateway or mesh can copy requests, and only for requests that are safe to repeat: reads by default. A write path is opted in only with a sandbox behind it, because a copied payment is still a payment. Off by default; the share copied is capped; the copy stops by itself if the stable version's latency rises. New in this plan as a strategy; Milestone 9 already plans sending "a mirror of traffic" to a new version.

How traffic moves. Every old copy stops and every new copy starts together. There is a gap unless something in front holds requests while the new copies become ready.

What is watched. Readiness, then Overwatch against the baseline.

When it is allowed. Previews, dev, and Airfields that say downtime is acceptable (today a fleet step must say allow_no_traffic: true). A Standing order can forbid it in protected Airfields, and the plan proposes that it does so by default.

Seeing traffic: Radar

Radar answers one question during and after a Launch: is the new version serving people as well as the old one did, at every step from the edge to the workload?

  • Three numbers per version: requests, errors and latency (median and the slow tail), for the stable and the new version separately.
  • From the edge to the workload: edge provider, DNS, gateway or load balancer, service, copies. A step whose numbers come from no source is drawn dotted and given no number, because making one up would be worse than leaving it out.
  • From sources the team already has: a metrics store such as Prometheus, the gateway, the mesh, the load balancer, an edge provider, each a signal source with a test. Launchway reads them through the guarded query layer: only the server reads a monitoring store, read-only, under its own permission, with the selector pinned on the server, every query on the Logbook, and values redacted.
  • Per version, honestly: where requests are not labeled with the version that served them, Radar says "per-version numbers not available" and proposes the label as a change the team accepts or declines.
  • During and after: the Launch's steps, Switch changes and scaling events are marked on the same time axis, and the view stays open through Overwatch and after it.
  • Never the contents: addresses, names, ports, protocols, counts and timings only.
Built today

The Launch page shows the share of traffic intended and measured, and requests, errors and latency for the stable and the new version, drawn from the verify step's metrics and the rollout analyses' queries, not from a metrics source of its own. The guarded query layer is in progress. The traffic map, the request path and signal sources are planned (Milestones 3 and 9).

Signal sources, in order

Radar and Overwatch read only through the guarded query layer, and every source joins the same way: a connection with a test that runs a known query against it when it is saved and on a Patrol (schedule), a contract test in Launchway's own suite that replays recorded answers, and a "served by" line on every chart that names the source and links to the query. A team connects what it already has, one source at a time. The order below is the order of value, not a schedule. Planned Signal sources; Guarded queries for monitoring data In progress.

OrderKind of sourceWhat Overwatch and Radar get from itStatus
0The built-in health proofAnswers from the service itself over HTTP or TCP, with no store neededAvailable
1Metrics stores that speak the Prometheus query languageRequests, errors and latency per version; the first Pathfinder (canary) proofsAvailable in the verify step
2Log storesLog lines for pattern comparison; error counts where no metric existsAvailable one log store
3SQL and analytics stores, and plain HTTP sourcesBusiness signals: orders placed, checkout successAvailable two analytics stores, SQL, HTTP
4Load balancers in front of host poolsPer-host and per-group requests and errors during a fleet LaunchIn progress the open-source balancer the fleet code drives
5Gateways that speak the Gateway APIPer-route and per-version requests, errors and latency; per-subset numbersPlanned Milestone 9
6Service meshesPer-version and per-subset numbers between services, with no change to the applicationPlanned Milestone 9
7Tracing stores using the open standard for tracesWhere time went in the new version; new slow pathsPlanned
8Serverless and edge platforms' own metricsPer-version requests, errors, duration, cold starts, throttling, per regionPlanned Milestone 8
9Edge providers and DNSThe first hop of the request pathPlanned Milestone 9
10Commercial monitoring services, through a connection adapterThe same signals from wherever a team already keeps themPlanned, one adapter at a time

Error tracking as a source kind is designed in Radar, insight and keeping it healthy. A source that is missing is never filled in: its step on the request path is drawn dotted and its proofs say "not measured".

Overwatch: the verdict and what follows

Overwatch starts when the first new copy takes traffic and ends a set time after the last step. It is the verify step that exists today, carried on past the last step, and joined to the Route.

PartHow it worksStatus
Comparison with the stable versionEach interval, each metric of the new version against the stable version in the same interval.Available
Baselines from earlier good LaunchesThe last passed verifications of the same service in the same Airfield (three by default, up to ten). A pass a person marked by hand is never added to the baseline.Available
SensitivityLow, medium or high: fails beyond 4.5, 3 or 2 standard deviations and at least 25, 10 or 5 percent of the reference; a metric fails after two failing intervals in a row by default.Available
Log pattern changesLog lines are grouped into patterns by a standard clustering method and compared with what earlier passed Launches saw; a new error pattern, or a known one at an unusual frequency, fails.Available
Not enough dataAn interval needs a minimum number of readings and a metric a minimum number of intervals; a check that could not run is inconclusive, never a silent pass. Today the step chooses fail, pass or pause.Available; the default below is New in this plan
The verdict with its evidenceOne sentence ("error rate 0.042 against the stable version's 0.003, 6.1 standard deviations above"), the charts with the bands, the failing points, and the log patterns with sample lines, new ones first. Every interval is an event, so any server reaches the same verdict.Available
An optional modelOff by default. It may turn a pass into not enough data or a fail, never a fail into a pass. Policy may require a person for production.Available as explanation; Planned AI analysis as an optional rollback gate
After the last stepThe watch carries on for a set time and can return to the last stable state by itself.Planned The watch; Automatic return to stable
Cause outside the releaseWhen the stable version is just as bad, a failing dependency is named and no pointless return is made.Planned
Extend, end or overrideEach with a reason on the record; in production by someone other than the person who started the release.Planned

What happens on each verdict.

  • Pass at a step: the next step starts. Pass at the end: the Airfield's stable state now names this release (its version, settings, secret versions, Switches and routes), and the Route may advance.
  • Fail: if a Switch changed during the Launch, it is turned back first; then the Launch returns to base by itself, and the record says "started by Overwatch" with the evidence. On by default; a team may change it to "pause and ask" per Airfield; a level above may lock it on.
  • Not enough data: wait one more window; if still thin, pause the Launch at its current step and ask the people who may clear it. In a protected Airfield it never advances a Route by itself. New in this plan as the default.

Pinned baselines and fail-fast verdicts

New in this plan Overwatch compares with the last good Launches by default. Two more controls make the verdict faster and harder to fool, and every choice is written into the verdict so it can be worked out again from the record.

ControlWhat it doesHow it is set
Rolling baseline (the default)The last passed Launches of the same service in the same Airfield, three by default. A pass a person marked by hand never joins it.A number from 1 to 10.
Pinned baselineOne past Launch you choose stands as the reference, for example when the recent ones all ran in a bad week. The pin carries a reason and lasts until it is lifted or for a set number of Launches, and every verdict made against it names it.Picked from a list of passed Launches of this service and Airfield, each shown with its version, when it landed and its verdict; reason picked or typed.
The service's EnvelopeThe Envelope (proposed word: a service's flight envelope, its measured healthy limits, learned from its good Launches and bounded by its reliability targets). Leaving it fails the step whatever the baseline says.Read from the service's reliability targets and learned limits; shown, not typed.
Fail-fast limitA hard line for one metric (errors above 2 percent, slow tail above 1.5 seconds) that ends the step on the first interval that crosses it, without waiting for a second interval or the end of the window, and returns to base at once.A metric picked from the source's list, a comparison and a number with its unit.
Required signalA signal that must be present. If its source does not answer, the step fails at once instead of pausing for "not enough data". Off by default; useful where silence itself is a fault.A switch per metric.

Every verdict can be worked out again. The verdict records the baseline kind and the Launches it used (or the pinned one), each limit and its value, the query text and source, and a digest of the data each interval read. Replay this verdict recomputes it from the record alone and must reach the same answer; an auditor can run it.

Worked moment. The last three prod Launches of storefront landed during a slow payment provider week, so Priya pins the baseline to Launch L-298 (2.3.2) with the reason "recent baselines include the provider incident", for the next five Launches. 2.4.0 is also given a fail-fast limit of 2 percent checkout errors. It passes; its verdict names L-298 and the limit.

Routing a subset of clients, with a verdict per subset

A Pathfinder can start with who rather than how many: your own staff first, then one client type, then one region, then a share of everyone. Each subset is a match at the gateway or mesh, and Overwatch judges each subset on its own. Planned Routing by client attributes; Weighted canaries and traffic control (Milestone 3); Route a subset of clients or requests; Per-subset proofs (Milestone 9).

  • Matches, picked not typed. A subset is a header, a cookie, a client type, a region or a list of accounts or tenants, picked from what the gateway or mesh reports it can match. Launchway shows a preview of the rule and an estimate of how much traffic it catches before it is applied.
  • Sticky by default. A client in a subset stays on one version for the step, so a shopper does not flip between versions mid-checkout.
  • A verdict per subset. Each subset is compared with the same kind of clients on the stable version over the same minutes, using the subset's own route numbers from the gateway or mesh. Where requests cannot be told apart, the verdict says "per-subset numbers not available" and the step falls back to the whole-service comparison, never to a pass.
  • One fail, everyone back. The same code serves every subset, so a fail in any subset returns the whole Launch, with the failing subset named in the sentence.
  • Exposure in one number. The page shows how many people see the new version right now, combining the subset rules, the weights and any Switch (feature toggle).
  • Next to a running rollout. Subset rules are judged before weights, and Launchway owns both, so the two never fight over the same route.

Worked moment. 2.4.0 goes first to Harbor Lights staff, matched by their sign-in cookie, for 20 minutes; then to the mobile app, matched by its client header; then by weight. Each subset passes on its own numbers. Had the mobile verdict read "checkout errors 0.9 percent against 0.2 for mobile clients on 2.3.2" while web clients looked normal, everyone would have gone back to 2.3.2 and the sentence would have named the mobile subset.

A Clearance between Pathfinder steps

A Clearance (approval) is a step that can sit anywhere in a pipeline today Available, and a rollout can be paused and promoted from the Launch page. The plan lets a Pathfinder plan place a Clearance between two of its steps, so a person decides with the step's evidence in front of them, while nothing waits on a machine. New in this plan

  • No Station held. The weights stay at the gateway or platform; the server keeps the Launch's state; the launch Station is free for other work and any Station that serves the target continues after the Go.
  • Still watched. Overwatch keeps judging the held step. A fail while the card waits returns to base at once; the card closes with "returned while waiting". A Clearance never stands between a Launch and its return.
  • The evidence on the card. The step's verdict, its charts against the stable version and the baseline, the verdict for each subset, new log patterns, exposure in one number, and the next step's plan.
  • Who and how long. A Controller (approver) for the Airfield, not the person who started the Launch. The card can expire; on expiry the plan says what happens: return to base (the default) or stay and ask again.
# Design: not built. A Pathfinder plan with a Clearance after the 25 percent step.
strategy: pathfinder
steps:
  - { weight: 5,  for: 10m }
  - { weight: 25, for: 10m }
  - { clearance: { by: controllers, expires: 4h, on_expiry: return } }
  - { weight: 50, for: 10m }
  - { weight: 100, watch: 30m }

Databases that stay up

A Return to base restores the release, not the data. So a schema change is made safe before it ships: it is launched like code, in an order in which both versions always work, and each half has its own way back.

  1. Checked before it runs. What the change will run, what it will lock and for how long, how large the table is, and whether it removes something a running version still uses. A long rewrite is flagged with an online method proposed. Planned Preflight and clearance; Lock and size estimates; Backward-compatibility lint.
  2. Applied by a standard tool. Liquibase first, others behind the same interface, with a backup taken first by the database operator's own mechanism. Planned A database change step with Liquibase; Backup before change.
  3. Expand, then launch, then contract. In a Formation (releases that go together), the database goes first and the contract step later. Planned Database first, then the application.
  4. Contract only when nothing needs the old shape. Launchway knows from the Route and the Launch records which versions run in which Airfield, so the contract change waits by itself until the last old version has left every Airfield on the Route. New in this plan
  5. The same change set everywhere. Its checksum is carried through every Airfield; a Clearance is void if the file changes. Planned Promotion through environments.
  6. The way back, honestly. An expand step returns with the application. A contract step has no Return to base: the way back is to roll forward, a compensating change, or a restore, and a restore is always a person's decision.

Switches: releasing without a Launch

A Switch changes who sees a feature without launching anything. Harbor Lights launches 2.4.0 with the delivery-date Switch off, so the new code runs for everyone but shows nothing new. Then the team turns the Switch on for 10 percent of shoppers.

  • The same Overwatch. A Switch change opens a watch with the same verdict and evidence as a Launch. The comparison is shoppers with the Switch on against shoppers with it off, where the application reports the Switch in its metrics; otherwise before against after. New in this plan
  • Back by itself. On a fail the Switch is turned back. In progress Kill switches and automatic toggle-back.
  • Never held. A Master switch (kill switch) to its safe value, and any revert, is never held for a Clearance. In progress
  • Exposure in one number. During a Pathfinder at 25 percent with the Switch at 10 percent, 2.5 percent of shoppers see the feature; Launchway always shows that product. Planned Routing by client attributes.
  • On one timeline. Switch changes sit beside Launches on the Airfield's timeline, and a Return to base lists them and offers to turn them back. Available A toggle service in the model.

Drills that prove the claims

A claim of zero downtime is only as good as the last time it was tested. A Drill is a controlled, authorized experiment that injects a fault, checks that the steady state holds, and always restores everything, even if Launchway itself fails.

  • The zero-downtime Drill. A Launch into a rehearsal Airfield under steady load while one copy is removed, a dependency is slowed and a node is drained. It passes only if no request failed above the baseline and the floor held. A Route stop can require a recent pass. New in this plan
  • A seeded bad release must be stopped and returned within the time the plan states, and a seeded good one promoted. Planned as the Milestone 8 measure of done.
  • Safety rules for every Drill: off until switched on, allowed only where declared, bounded in what it reaches, cleared by someone other than the starter, and a fault is never left on. Planned Chaos authorization and safety.

Worked example: storefront 2.4.0 in prod

  1. Preflight. The rollout readiness scan finds a readiness check, a shutdown grace of 45 seconds against a drain of 30, six copies, and a floor of four set by the Squadron (team) "shop". The plan is a Pathfinder at 5, 25, 50 and 100 percent through the gateway.
  2. Ready first. Two new copies start. They take no shopper traffic until they answer 20 test calls through the preview path.
  3. Stepped weights. Each step lasts ten minutes. Radar shows both versions side by side from the edge to the pods. Each step passes.
  4. Overwatch. At 100 percent the watch runs for 30 minutes against the baseline of the last three good Launches, and passes. The record says: "Zero-downtime proof: fewest healthy copies 6 (floor 4); failed requests during the shift 0.03 percent against 0.03 percent the hour before."
  5. The Switch. The next morning the team turns delivery-date on for 10 percent. Errors among those shoppers rise to 1.4 percent against 0.2 percent for the rest. Overwatch fails the change and turns the Switch off within two minutes. The release itself stays.
  6. The schema. The delivery_date column arrived a week earlier as change set 41. The contract step, change set 42, waits on the Route board with the reason "staging still runs 2.4.0".

The foundation it relies on

This chapter is part of the Launch layer, not a module, but Switches and Drills inside it are modules and meet the module contract: the same levels and permissions; decisions on the one record; gates as Standing orders; changes through typed forms; work as steps on Stations; one provider in charge (the built-in Switch service, or a connected one through OpenFeature); off until wanted (Drills, shadow traffic); equal from the web, the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform; and none of them blocks a Return to base.

Guarded monitoring reads

Every Radar chart and every Overwatch interval comes through the guarded query layer. No Station, step or pod gets a raw route to a metrics or log store.

The record

Every interval's data and every verdict is an event, so the verdict is the same on any server and can be shown to an auditor.

The stable state

Version, settings, secret versions, Switches and routes known to work, per Airfield: what a fail returns to.

Safety

What happens on failure

FailureWhat happens
The metrics source is downNot enough data. The Launch pauses at its step; it never advances on silence. A Return to base still works.
A Launchway server is lost mid-stepAnother server re-derives the verdict from the events. The gateway keeps its last weights, so traffic does not jump.
The launch Station is lost mid-stepWeights stay where they were. The page says the share is held and that Return to base needs a Station; one is started or another takes over.
The Switch service is downApplications keep their last known values (planned: Toggles keep working when Launchway is down), so an outage never flips a feature.
A Drill's controller failsEvery injected fault has its own expiry and ends by itself.

Who may do what

  • See Radar and verdicts: Observer (viewer) of the Flight, with the monitoring permission granted separately.
  • Pause, promote, end or extend Overwatch, mark a verdict: the operator role on the Flight; in production the person who started the Launch may not mark it passed or end its watch early.
  • Change a floor, a strategy default or the not-enough-data rule: Commander (owner) of the level; a level above can lock it.
  • Turn a Switch toward its safe value: anyone allowed to change the Switch, never held. Away from it: through policy and, in protected Airfields, a Clearance.
  • Start a Drill: as declared for that Airfield, cleared by someone other than the starter.

On by default

  • Readiness before traffic; draining before stopping; the floor in protected Airfields; automatic Return to base on a fail; Overwatch after every Launch into a protected Airfield.
  • Not enough data is never a pass.
  • Off by default: shadow traffic, the optional model, Drills, automatic compensation for data.

Screens

Launch page: Traffic and Overwatch

Intended against measured share per step, both versions' requests, errors and latency, the zero-downtime proof, and the verdict panel with charts, bands and log patterns.

Radar, per version

The request path from the edge to the pods for one service, each step with its source or drawn dotted, the stable and new version as two lines, Launch steps and Switch changes marked.

Overwatch verdict

One sentence, the evidence, what happens next and when, and Extend, End or Override with a reason.

Strategy picker

In the delivery plan assistant: the strategies the target supports, the floor, the steps and their lengths from a list, and a picture of the plan.

Schema change review

The change set, its half (expand or contract), what it locks and for how long, what running versions use, and for a contract step which Airfields still block it.

Switch change watch

Shoppers with and without the Switch, the verdict, and the automatic turn-back.

Signal sources

One row per connected source with its kind, its last test result, the charts and proofs that read it, and Connect a source as a wizard: kind from the table's list, connection picked, a known query run as the test.

Baseline and limits

In the delivery plan: rolling or pinned baseline (pinned Launch picked from passed Launches), the Envelope shown read-only, fail-fast limits as metric, comparison and number, required signals as switches; on a verdict, Replay this verdict.

Subset step editor

Match kind picked from what the gateway or mesh supports, values picked from what it has seen, a preview of the rule and the share of traffic it catches, stickiness, and the subset's own verdict during the Launch.

Clearance between steps

The card shown while a Pathfinder holds: the step's evidence, per-subset verdicts, exposure, the next step's plan, time to expiry and what expiry does, Go and No-go with a reason.
