Open question

  1. Open question How long Overwatch watches by default. The zero-downtime design recommends 30 minutes for production-class Airfields and 10 elsewhere, with automatic return on, and a release counted stable after 10 minutes of passed proofs. Not yet answered.
  2. Open question The first way to split traffic on Kubernetes. The zero-downtime design says a rollout controller only in phase 1; a later delegated answer says Gateway API weights first. See Launching to Kubernetes.
  3. Open question All at once in protected Airfields. Recommendation: forbidden by a default Standing order that a team can relax only with a level's consent, since it cannot be zero downtime.
  4. Open question Shadow traffic for writes. Recommendation: reads only, unless the team declares a sandbox behind the write path; never on by default.
  5. Open question Required signals. Recommendation: off by default and offered for prod, since a missing source failing a Launch at once can surprise a team that expects a pause.
  6. Open question What an expired Clearance between steps does. Recommendation: return to base, because a Launch left half-way for hours is a risk of its own.
  7. Open question Not enough data at night. Recommendation: wait one window, then pause and ask; in a protected Airfield never advance a Route on it. The alternative is a synthetic load step that makes data, which costs capacity.

Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Before a change merges, a Sortie (run) starts, an image is pushed or a Launch (deployment) leaves the ground, Launchway judges it against the same Standing orders (policies and repository standards), asks the right people for Clearance (approval), and refuses to launch during a Hold (freeze), while Return to base (rollback) always stays open.

  • Standing orders are typed rules judged at fixed points on the path to production. Every path passes through them; there is no side door.
  • Every verdict is one of four answers (allow, warn, require a Clearance, deny), recorded as an event with its reasons and readable by a person.
  • Rules are set at the Base, Wing, Squadron or Flight. A level above can lock a rule; a level below can only add or tighten.
  • A Clearance records who said Go and what they were shown. A Hold stops every Launch in its scope. Return to base is never blocked.
  • Rules can also ask outside services through checks run on a Station, read infrastructure plans and their cost, be attached by the owner of a Ramp or a connection, and impose scheduled checks on every Flight below: wider sight, never a side door.

Where it sits

This chapter is layer 6 of the seven layers: Command. It answers three questions for every change on its way to production: what must be true, who must say Go, and when nothing may launch.

Builds on
The levels, permissions and locks of Levels, people and secrets (Base (installation), Wing (organization), Squadron (unit), Flight (project)); the one event record of the record, where every verdict is written; the typed inputs and the expression language of the flight plan layer; digests of Cargo (artifacts) and the Depot (registry) from flight operations; and Airfields (environments) from One way to launch, anywhere.
Builds on it
Every module's gates (rule 3 of the module contract: "its gates are Standing orders judged at the common points; no private policy"); security and the supply chain, whose Inspection (security scan) findings and signatures are facts these rules judge; and the Logbook and evidence, which reads the verdicts and Clearances back as evidence.
Words on this page
Standing orders cover both the rules in this chapter and the repository standards of the Inspection. Today the product shows them on two screens; one area is proposed below.

What you will be able to do

You are Sam, who looks after the platform for the Harbor Lights team. You want every image that reaches prod to be signed and built by Launchway. You write the rule once at the Wing and press Try it on last month. The answer comes from the record: it would have blocked 2 of 41 Launches, both a hand-built hotfix image of storefront. You fix the hotfix path, watch the rule in report mode for a week, then switch it to enforce.

You are Dana, a developer on storefront. Your pull request edits the pipeline file and drops the shared security Maneuver (reusable step template). The pull request says, before anyone reviews it: "this change removes the required Maneuver platform-library/inspect; it needs a Clearance from a Controller (approver) of the Squadron to merge". Nobody has to notice it by eye.

You start a Hold on prod for every Flight from Friday evening to Monday morning. On Saturday a pipeline's deploy step to prod stops at the Hold with its reason, and so does a Switch (feature toggle) change. Builds, tests and Launches to staging carry on. When checkout breaks on Saturday night, Return to base goes at once, and the Logbook (audit trail) says why.

You are Ana, who clears releases. A Clearance card on your phone shows the digest, what changes compared with what runs in prod, the tests, the Inspection verdict and every Standing order judged so far. It asks you to pick the change ticket from a list and a risk level. Dana started the Sortie, so Dana cannot say Go. You can.

A finding blocks your Launch and you know it cannot be exploited. You ask for a waiver: you pick the rule from the verdict, the scope, the kind ("not affected"), an end date within the allowed limit and the work item that tracks the fix. A Controller grants it; it is on the record and it ends by itself.

How it works

The path to production, and every point where it is judged

A change travels one path. Each point on it is a place where the server stops, gathers the facts from the record, and judges the Standing orders that apply. The same rules, the same verdict format and the same waivers serve every point. Three points are built today; five are proposed so that no path to production goes around them.

PointWhen it is judgedWhat a deny doesStatus
MergeA pull request is merged or added to the merge queue into a protected branch, on any way in (web, API, command line, agent endpoint, auto-merge)The pull request cannot land; the one sentence that says why is shown on every screenNew in this plan Branch rules already judge here; Standing orders join them
Setting changeA secret's version, a variable, a Switch or a traffic route is about to change in an AirfieldThe change is not applied; a Clearance may be asked for insteadNew in this plan
Trigger savedA trigger is declared or changed beside a pipeline, or created in the product: what may start a Sortie, under which identity, with which filtersThe trigger is not switched on; a pull request that adds it shows the verdict before it mergesNew in this plan
Connection savedA connection, a secret store or a token is created or changed: what it reaches, and which Flights, Airfields and Ramps (Station pools) may use itThe connection or token is not saved; the screen names the rule and what would satisfy itNew in this plan
Sortie startA Sortie is created, re-run or resumedEach step fails as it would start, saying why; nothing reaches a Station (runner)Available
Image pushAn image step that would push is about to be handed to a StationThe step fails before any Station sees itAvailable
Before LaunchA deploy step is about to take its Airfield's lock; a rollout is about to promote, promote fully or retryThe step fails before anything reaches the cluster, the hosts or GitAvailable
Cluster admissionThe cluster is asked to run a workload, whoever askedThe cluster refuses the workload; Launchway shows the refusal on the LaunchNew in this plan Generated from the same rules

The typed catalog, as built

Today a Standing order is a name, a scope, a mode and rules taken from a fixed catalog. Each rule is a typed setting with a fixed meaning, judged at exactly one point, and checked with its file and line when it is read. A test in the code keeps the catalog and its reference page in step.

RuleWhat it checksJudged at
library_versionsEvery shared library the Sortie uses resolved to a tag or a full commit, never a branchSortie start
required_templatesA step uses each listed template of each listed library, at an allowed version that is a tag or a commitSortie start
step_imagesEvery step and container image is pinned by digest, comes from allowed repositories, or bothSortie start
max_timeoutNo step's timeout is longer than the limit; waits for a Clearance are not countedSortie start
forbid_secretsA Sortie of the listed events (for example pull requests and drafts) has no step that asks for a secretSortie start
testsThe steps before the deploy step reported at least the minimum number of test results, none failedBefore Launch
findingsThose steps reported findings, none worse than allowed overall or per tool, and every required scanner reported; no report is never "no findings"Before Launch
sbomA step before the deploy step made a list of contents of at least the minimum sizeBefore Launch
deployed_imagesEvery image the Launch writes is pinned by digest, built by this Sortie, signed and scanned, as askedBefore Launch
approvalsAt least the minimum number of people other than the starter gave Clearance before the deploy stepBefore Launch
allowed_failuresAt most the allowed number of earlier steps failed and were allowed to (none by default)Before Launch
refsThe Sortie is of a branch or tag that matches the patternsBefore Launch
image_pushAn image step that pushes scans in enforce mode, signs, makes a list of contents and a record of how it was built, and pushes only to allowed DepotsImage push

A fourteenth name, source, appears only in failures: when a Standing order source kept in Git cannot be loaded, every Sortie of the Flights it covers is refused at every point, naming the source and the reason, and that refusal cannot be waived. A short outage of the repository does not refuse anything; the version loaded before stays in use until it is older than its stated limit.

Built today

Two modes: enforce stops the step or the Sortie; report judges, records and shows the same result as a warning and never changes an outcome. Each decision is stored in the same database transaction as the step it lets through, so a decision and its effect are stored together or not at all. Each decision is a policy.evaluated event with the rules as judged (their source and version), the facts, the waivers considered and the time, so it can be reproduced from the record alone. Return to base steps and Aborts (emergency rollbacks) are never judged.

Honest limits today

Rules judge what steps report: a step that writes a false test report satisfies a test rule as far as the report goes, which is why shared scanning and testing steps are required through required_templates. A Sortie started by a push records the commit's author as its starter, which anyone can set in Git. A person with direct access to the cluster, the GitOps repository or the Depot can change what runs without Launchway, and Argo CD can sync a commit Launchway did not make. The proposed merge, setting-change and admission points close most of these doors.

A verdict reads like this. The format is today's; the names are the running example's.

deploy-prod failed. blocked by Standing order prod-evidence (enforce), rule tests:
no step before deploy-prod reported test results; needs at least 1 test result
from the steps before deploy-prod, none failed. Grant a waiver or change what was
found, then resume the Sortie (or re-run it from deploy-prod)

Rules the catalog gains

The catalog grows where a need recurs, one typed rule at a time, each with a fixed meaning, one or two judging points and a reference row kept in step by the same test. These are the rules this plan adds. Each reads facts that are already on the record or that a step writes there; none makes a network call while judging, so every verdict can still be judged again from the record alone.

RuleWhat it checksJudged atStatus
outside_checksThe named outside checks answered pass, and their answers are no older than allowedBefore Launch, setting changeNew in this plan
infrastructure_planAn infrastructure plan's typed facts: what it destroys or replaces, by kind; what becomes reachable from the internet; its estimated monthly cost changeBefore Launch (the apply step)New in this plan
database_changeThe statement facts Preflight (checks) records for a database change: drops, table rewrites, estimated lock time, rows touchedBefore LaunchNew in this plan
connectionsWhich Flights, Airfields and Ramps a connection or secret store may serve; for example "a production store is reachable only from production Ramps"Connection saved, Sortie startNew in this plan
secret_releaseEvery store has a release rule at least as strict as the level's: for example "never to a restricted Sortie or a debug session"Connection savedNew in this plan
triggersWhat a trigger's identity may reach: for example "a Patrol (schedule) never launches to prod"Trigger saved, Sortie startNew in this plan
token_lifetimeThe longest life of a new token for each kind (a person's, a service account's), and whether a source-address limit is requiredConnection saved (a token is made)New in this plan
scheduled_checksA Patrol required from a level above last passed no longer ago than the limit (for example a full Inspection of the default branch within 48 hours)Before LaunchNew in this plan
added_stepsThe steps a level adds to every Sortie in scope are present, pinned and unalteredSortie startNew in this plan

The facts these rules read follow the same honesty rule as the rest of the catalog: a fact that is not recorded never passes a rule. A plan with no cost estimate does not pass a cost limit; it answers "cannot tell", and the rule's answer applies.

Four answers

Every rule at every point gives one of four answers. Two exist under other names today; one is new.

AnswerWhat happensToday
AllowThe change goes on. The verdict is still recorded, with the facts that passed.Available a rule that passes
WarnThe change goes on with a visible warning on the Sortie, the pull request or the Launch.Available a rule in report mode
Require a ClearanceThe change pauses and a Clearance is added at that point, with the rule's reason on the card. Low-risk changes flow; risky ones go to a person automatically.New in this plan
DenyThe change stops, with what was found and what would satisfy the rule.Available a rule in enforce mode

A rule's answer is set with the rule, not by the person who meets it. Report mode stays as the way to introduce a rule: a new rule in report mode gives "warn" where it would otherwise give its answer.

How a verdict is reached and recorded

Judging is a pure function: the rules in force, the facts on the record and the waivers in force give the verdict. Nothing else is read, so any server reaches the same verdict, and the verdict can be judged again later from the record alone.

When several rules answer at one point, the strictest answer wins: deny over require a Clearance over warn over allow. The verdict lists every rule, not only the one that decided, so a person sees everything that must change in one reading.

One choke point, no side doors

The principle is "every path to production passes the same checks". Today three points hold it for Sorties and Launches that Launchway makes. Five additions close the remaining doors, each reusing the same judge.

One way, not two. Branch rules already exist on repositories Launchway hosts: required approvals and from whom, required checks, up to date, resolved threads, no self-approval, owner approval, latest push approved by someone else, dismissing stale approvals, checks by path, the merge queue, and an audited administrator bypass. They are judged by the server on every way in.

The proposal makes those branch rules the merge point's rules in the catalog, instead of building a second mechanism beside them. The Merge rules tab keeps its place and its words; behind it, each rule is a Standing order at the merge point, so a Wing can require "no self-approval on every protected main" once, with a lock, and the pull request shows one verdict that includes the Inspection result and any other merge rule. The administrator bypass becomes a waiver of the merge verdict, with the same reason and record it has today.

For a repository on a connected Git host, Launchway cannot stop the host's merge button. It reports the merge verdict as a required status (the roadmap's "Pull-request status everywhere"), and the host enforces it. The screen says so plainly.

A secret's version, a variable, a Switch or a traffic route can change what production does without a new build. The proposal judges each such change at a setting-change point with the same rules: for example "a Switch change in prod requires a Clearance" or "a variable locked at the Wing cannot be changed below it". The change is then applied as a rollout with a way back, as One way to launch, anywhere describes.

Moving a Master switch (kill switch) to its safe value is never judged, never held for a Clearance and never stopped by a Hold. This matches what is built today for Switches.

A GitOps controller can sync a commit Launchway did not make, and a person with cluster access can apply a manifest by hand. Neither passes a Launchway point. The proposal generates a cluster admission policy from the Base's Standing orders (for example "only images signed by this Base's key, from these Depots, may run in namespaces of prod") and commits it to the Base's own GitOps repository. The cluster enforces it with its own standard admission mechanism; no policy engine runs inside Launchway's server.

For targets without a cluster (virtual machines, image-based hosts, serverless functions) the deploy Station or the Detachment (the small program on the customer's side) verifies the same facts before it switches traffic. The supply chain describes what is verified.

Sortie start already judges the pipeline at the commit, however the commit arrived, and a pull request from a fork or an automation account runs the default branch's pipeline, so a pull request cannot rewrite its own checks. The merge point adds the earlier answer: a change to a pipeline file, a library pin or a Standing orders file is judged on the pull request, before it lands, with the verdict it would get at Sortie start.

A trigger decides what may start a Sortie and under which identity; a connection or a secret store decides what a step may reach. Either can open a way to production without any pipeline change being judged. The proposal adds a save point that judges each one when it is saved, on every way in, with facts any rule can read:

  • Trigger facts: its kind (push, pull request, Patrol, outside event, another pipeline's result), its source, the identity it runs as, the branches and Airfields it can reach.
  • Connection and store facts: its kind, the level that owns it, the Flights, Airfields and Ramps allowed to use it, the keys a store serves and its release rule.
  • Token facts: its kind, its life, its role, its Flights and whether it is limited to source addresses.

The same facts are judged again at Sortie start, as "this Sortie resolves a reference through store vault-prod on Ramp shared", so a connection saved before a rule existed is still caught the first time it is used. Example rules: "a store marked production is reachable only from Ramps marked production", "no Patrol launches to prod", "service-account tokens live at most 30 days and name source addresses".

Trying a rule before enforcing it

Every verdict on the record holds the facts it was judged on. A new rule can therefore be judged against the past without running anything: Launchway takes every recorded decision at that point in the chosen scope and period, applies the new rule to the facts stored with it, and lists what would have changed.

You press Try it on last month. The answer: "41 Launches to prod judged. This rule would have denied 2 and required a Clearance for 0. For 3 Launches the record does not hold the fact this rule needs (they ran before signatures were recorded), so it cannot tell." Each Launch in the list opens on its own verdict.

The replay is honest about its limits. A rule that needs a fact the record never held answers "cannot tell" for that decision, never "would pass". A rule that reads the time is replayed with the time stored in the verdict. Report mode remains the second step: it judges new changes live without stopping them.

Built today

Report mode is built, and the reference advises starting every new rule in it. There is no test command and no replay yet.

The Wingman drafts a rule; a person saves it

Writing a good rule is the hard part of governance. The Wingman (helper and AI helper) can turn a sentence into a draft, but it never saves one: it fills the same Add a Standing order wizard a person would, runs the replay on the record, and stops at the last step for a Commander (owner) of the level to read and save.

  • Catalog first. The draft uses a catalog rule when one fits. If your sentence needs something the catalog cannot say, the draft says so plainly ("the catalog has no rule for the day of the week") and, only if custom rules are chosen (option 2), offers a condition in the expression language that is type-checked like any other.
  • Proved before it is saved. Every draft runs Try it on last month before the save button is offered, and starts in report mode.
  • Explain this rule. Every rule, drafted or not, has a plain-words explanation on its page: what it checks, at which point, who meets it, and the last Launches it stopped, read from the record.
  • Never the last word. An agent cannot save or change a Standing order on its own, whatever its autonomy level; the Logbook (audit trail) records the draft, the sentence it came from and the person who saved it.
# Design: not built.
launchway orders draft --wing harbor-lights "Launches of payments to prod need two Controllers"
draft: payments-prod-two (point: launch, rule: approvals.min 2, scope: flight payments, airfield prod)
replay, last 30 days: 18 judged, 4 would require a second Go, 0 cannot tell
not saved: a Commander of Wing harbor-lights must review it (launchway orders save payments-prod-two)

Waivers

A waiver lets one rule pass for a stated scope until a stated end. Today a waiver names the Flight, the rule and, optionally, one Sortie, one Airfield or one finding by its fingerprint. A reason and an end within the limit (30 days by default) are required. Waivers are written to the Logbook when granted and revoked, are shown wherever the verdict they changed is shown, and end by themselves: a decision made after the end does not count them, even in a Sortie that started before. The role needed to grant one is set per installation (administrator by default). On a protected Airfield the starter of a Sortie cannot waive its Launch rule.

The plan keeps that model and joins it with the Inspection's accepted risks, so there is one exception model for rules and findings (the roadmap's "Exceptions with an owner and an expiry"). Each waiver gains a kind picked from a list (accepted risk, false positive, not affected, fix scheduled), an owner, and a link to the work item that tracks it. A rule locked at a level states who may waive it at that level, and nobody below can widen that.

Inheritance down the levels, with locks

Standing orders follow the same four levels as variables and the Inspection settings. A rule set at a level applies to everything below it. Rules add up as they go down: a lower level can add rules and tighten a parameter, never remove a rule from above or loosen it. A level can lock a rule; a locked rule cannot be tightened in a way that changes its answer below, waived below the level that locked it, or switched to report mode.

Built today

Locks exist for variables and for the Inspection settings (a lock wins and the page says so: "locked by your Wing"). Standing orders themselves are scoped by Flight patterns in the server's configuration or in a source kept in Git at a pinned tag, with a projects list per source. They do not yet inherit down the levels.

Where Standing orders live is the same answer as for repository standards today: edited in the web interface or kept as files in a repository the level owns, in either place, kept in step, with every change reviewed and recorded. A change to a Standing order is itself always a change a person reviews; an agent cannot make one land on its own.

# Design: not built. A Standing order kept in the Wing's repository.
# Key names are not final.
standing_orders:
  - name: prod-needs-signed-images
    point: launch
    scope: { airfields: [prod] }
    rules:
      deployed_images: { digest: true, built_by_run: true, signed: true, scanned: true }
    answer: deny
    mode: report              # watch it first; enforce later
    lock: true                # nothing below may loosen or waive it
    waivable_by: wing         # only a Wing Commander may grant a waiver

Rules a resource owns

Today a protected Airfield (environment) owns its protections: its min_approvals applies to every Clearance that guards a Launch there, whatever the pipeline says. The plan gives the same power to every shared resource a pipeline can use. A Standing order's scope can name an Airfield, a Ramp, a connection (a cloud account, a cluster, a change system), a secret store or a repository. The Commander of that resource attaches rules to it; every Sortie that uses it meets them; and the pipeline's author cannot remove them, because they are not in the pipeline.

Before attaching a rule, you see Who uses this: every Flight and pipeline whose Sorties used the resource in the period, read from the record, and the replay of the new rule against them. The verdict panel names the source of each rule ("attached by Ramp prod-deploy, owned by Squadron shop"), so a Pilot (developer) who meets it knows whom to ask. Waivers of a resource's rule are granted only by its owner or a level above.

# Design: not built. Rules a Ramp owns.
standing_orders:
  - name: prod-deploy-ramp
    scope: { ramps: [prod-deploy] }
    point: sortie_start
    rules:
      refs: { patterns: [main] }
    answer: deny
    lock: true
  - name: prod-deploy-ramp-alerts
    scope: { ramps: [prod-deploy] }
    point: launch
    rules:
      outside_checks: { require: [no-open-alerts], fresh_for: 10m }
    answer: deny

Scheduled checks required from a level above

Some checks must happen whether or not anyone pushes: a full Inspection of a repository nobody has touched for weeks, a weekly Maintenance (dependency updates) pass, a monthly Drill (chaos test). A Standing order of the kind patrols adds a Patrol (schedule) to every Flight in its scope. The level that sets it locks it: a Flight cannot remove it or run it less often, only add its own.

  • What runs. A pinned Maneuver (reusable step template) or Flight plan (ready-made pipeline): the full Inspection, Maintenance, a Drill against staging, an outside check, or a level's own pinned steps. Its Sorties are marked "added by Standing order nightly-inspection (Wing)".
  • As whom. The Patrol's own identity, patrol:nightly-inspection, with the grants the level gives it (trigger identities), on the Ramp the order names, with no secret unless a store's release rule allows Patrol Sorties.
  • What it proves. Each run's result is on the record. A run that did not happen (a Ramp was empty, the Flight was archived) is listed as missed, never as passed. The scheduled_checks rule turns freshness into a Launch fact.
  • Where you see it. The level's coverage view: every Flight in scope, its last run, its result and its missed runs, exportable as evidence.

Nobody has pushed to kiosk-os for three weeks. The Wing's nightly Patrol inspects it anyway and finds a new critical advisory in a library the image carries. Maintenance opens the fix as a pull request. When the kiosks' next Launch is planned, its verdict already says "nightly Inspection passed 6 hours ago", because the fix merged and the Patrol ran again.

# Design: not built.
standing_orders:
  - name: nightly-inspection
    kind: patrols
    scope: { wing: harbor-lights }
    patrol:
      every: "0 2 * * *"         # 02:00 in the Wing's time zone
      branch: default
      run: platform-library/full-inspection@v3.2.0
      ramp: shared
    lock: true

Instructions for the AI, kept like Standing orders

The Wingman and every agent at a level read the same plain-language instructions: "write release notes in American English", "never propose a change to the payments schema without a work item", "explain findings for a developer who is new to security". They are kept at the Base, Wing, Squadron or Flight, add up downward like Standing orders, and can be locked from above. Only a Commander of the level, or a custom role that holds the action to edit them, may change them; every change is a reviewed, recorded difference, and every AI answer records which version of the instructions it was given.

What instructions cannot do

Instructions shape what the AI writes; they never grant a right. Whatever an agent is told, its token, its autonomy level and the Standing orders still decide what it may do, and an instruction that asks for something a rule forbids is shown as a conflict on the level's page. The Wingman and agents describes how each purpose reads them.

One Standing orders area

You ruled that "standards and policies" are both Standing orders. In the product today the screen called Standing orders holds the Inspection's repository standards, and the rules of this chapter are on a separate screen called Policy (under Settings, Rules). One word names two screens.

Proposal

One area named Standing orders with two parts: Rules (this chapter's catalog, by point) and Inspection (which checks run and what blocks). An Inspection check set to block becomes a rule at the merge and Sortie-start points, so its verdict appears in the same verdict list as every other rule, with the same waivers. Nothing is removed from either screen; they are joined.

Beyond the typed catalog

The catalog answers most needs and nobody can write a wrong rule in it. Some needs it cannot express: a rule that depends on the day of the week, on a combination of facts, or on a fact the product's authors did not foresee. How Launchway answers those is open for you. Three options:

OptionWhat you can sayWhat it costsFit with "one way to do each thing"
1. The typed catalog aloneOnly the rules the catalog offers; it grows when a need recurs (a time-window rule, a merge rule, a license rule on the list of contents)Each new need waits for a releaseBest: one form only
2. Custom rules in the one expression languageAny condition over the recorded facts, written in the same ${{ }} expressions people already write in pipelines, type-checked before useThe judge must expose a documented, versioned set of facts per pointGood: the language people already know, the same points, verdicts and waivers
3. Rules in an established open policy languageRules a team already keeps for other systems, accepted as an import or judged through a connection at the same pointsA second language with a different style; a connection to run itAcceptable as a connection, as an equal choice for teams that already have one
Recommendation, for you to decide

Keep the typed catalog as the first way and grow it when a need recurs. Add custom rules in the one expression language for what the catalog cannot say, judged at the same points, giving the same four answers and taking the same waivers. Keep the roadmap's planned "Policy rules in an open language" as a connection for teams that already write rules in an open policy language, so their rules are judged at the same points and shown in the same verdict. Whatever is chosen, the documents that recommend otherwise are marked as superseded.

# Design: not built. A custom rule in the expression language (option 2).
standing_orders:
  - name: weekend-launches-need-two
    point: launch
    scope: { airfields: [prod] }
    when: ${{ launch.time.weekday in ["Sat", "Sun"] && launch.clearances.count < 2 }}
    answer: clearance
    reason: Weekend Launches to prod need a second pair of eyes.

Clearance

A Clearance is a step that pauses a Sortie until people decide Go or No-go. It runs nothing on a Station.

Built today

An approval step takes a message (static text), a timeout, and approvers (groups or users and a count from 1 to 5, distinct people). No-go, or no decision before the timeout, fails the step and skips what follows; resuming asks again. With sign-in on, the starter of a Sortie may say No-go but not Go, unless approvals.allow_self is set. A protected Airfield's min_approvals raises the count for a Clearance that guards a Launch there. A release has its own Clearance per Airfield, which its publisher may not give. Every pending Clearance appears on the Waiting for a decision page and as a decision card that reads on a phone; Go and No-go work from the web, the API, the command line and the agent endpoint, and each decision is kept with the Sortie: who, when and their comment. A Clearance cannot yet ask the approver for any values, and the card cannot show the version or the digest.

The plan adds five things.

  1. It shows what it clears. The card shows the digest, what changes compared with what runs in the Airfield now, the tests, the Inspection verdict, every Standing order verdict so far and the Hold calendar.
  2. It asks for typed fields. A Clearance can collect fields through the same typed input forms as a run form: a change ticket picked from a connected change system, a risk level picked from a list, a window picked from the calendar. The values become the step's outputs and are on the record.
  3. Separation of duties goes further. Today the starter cannot clear their own Sortie. The plan adds the commit author and the person who published the release, and "nobody clears a rule that applies to them" (the roadmap's "Separation of duties").
  4. Counts from distinct groups. "One from shop-controllers and one from security", not only a count of people.
  5. Timeouts with a stated outcome. A timeout fails the step by default; a reminder through Comms (notifications) goes before it does.
# Design: not built. A Clearance that asks for typed fields.
steps:
  clear-prod:
    kind: approval
    needs: launch-staging
    message: Launch storefront to prod?
    approvers: { groups: [shop-controllers], count: 1 }
    timeout: 8h
    fields:
      change_ticket: { type: choice, options_from: connection.changes.open }
      risk:          { type: choice, options: [low, medium, high] }
  launch-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: clear-prod
    environment: prod
    version: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
    note: ${{ steps.clear-prod.outputs.change_ticket }}

Agents follow the same rules as people: the author of a change never clears its own work. Where a Standing order allows it, an independent reviewing agent with a different identity may clear listed kinds of change, and a share of its decisions is sampled by a person (the roadmap's "An independent reviewing agent").

Open question

You said, after being told someone else must approve your own Sortie: "I should be able to approve." The design response, which you have not confirmed, is that a one-person Base may let the starter clear by a Standing order, with a plain note on the record, while larger teams keep separation of duties (the roadmap's "You can approve what you started, if policy allows"). This chapter does not decide it. Either way the record says plainly when a starter cleared their own work and which Standing order allowed it.

Outside checks: asking a service before a Launch

Some answers live outside Launchway: is an alert open for this service, is the change ticket approved, is it inside business hours on the company calendar, does the team's own script say yes. A rule cannot ask, because judging is a pure function that never calls the network; that is what makes every verdict repeatable. So the asking is a step, and the rule reads its recorded answer.

An outside check is a step of the kind check. It runs on a Station (runner) in your network, with your credentials resolved there, asks one service or runs one program, and returns a typed answer:

AnswerMeaningWhat happens next
passThe condition holds nowRecorded; valid for fresh_for
waitNot yet, or the service could not be reachedAsked again after every, until timeout; between asks the step holds no Station, like a Clearance
failThe condition does not hold, or the timeout passedThe step fails with the service's reason; a timeout is never a pass

Each answer is one check.answered event with typed fields (an alert count, a ticket number and its window, the end of business hours), a short reason, the target asked (never a secret), a digest of the response and the Station that asked. A Standing order then requires it with outside_checks; if the pipeline does not contain the check, the server adds it, marked "added by Standing order", exactly as it adds the Inspection. Attached to an Airfield or a Ramp, it cannot be dropped by a pipeline's author.

Check kindWhat it asksTyped fields
alertsThe monitoring connection Radar (monitoring) already uses: open alerts for this service and Airfield at or above a severitycount, worst severity, names
change_ticketThe connected change system: the ticket picked on the Clearance is approved and its window covers nowticket, state, window start and end
calendarAn outside business-hours or holiday calendar. A calendar kept in Launchway needs no check: the judge reads it as a recorded fact.inside hours, next opening
httpAny address, with a credential reference; the response is judged by an expression you write once and testthe fields the expression extracts
scriptA custom step: a tested program with a manifest that prints a typed answerdeclared in its manifest
 
# Design: not built. An outside check that a Standing order on prod requires.
steps:
  no-open-alerts:
    kind: check
    uses: alerts
    with: { service: storefront, airfield: prod, severity_at_least: warning }
    every: 2m
    timeout: 1h
    fresh_for: 10m
  launch-prod:
    kind: deploy
    needs: [clear-prod, no-open-alerts]
    environment: prod
    version: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

Freshness. When the before-Launch point is reached, the judge reads the latest answer. An answer older than fresh_for is asked again before the Launch takes its Airfield's lock, so a pass from an hour ago never clears a Launch now.

Tested like code. A check is a step under the one step contract, so it has stand-in answers in the Simulator, its expression has tests, and replaying a rule on last month works, because every answer is on the record. A check that never ran answers "cannot tell", never "pass".

Before storefront 2.4.0 goes to prod, the check no-open-alerts finds one warning open on checkout latency and answers wait. Six minutes later the alert has cleared and it answers pass. The check change-approved reads CHG-88: approved, window 14:00 to 16:00, inside it. Ana's Go and both answers sit side by side on the verdict, and Priya, on call, sees from the record why the Launch waited six minutes.

Go now, launch at a set time

A Controller (approver) often decides before the best moment to launch. A Go can therefore carry when, picked on the Clearance card: now (the default), at a time picked from the calendar, or in the next window of the Airfield. The Sortie then waits in the state "Cleared, waiting for its time", holding no Station, and the calendar shows it as a planned Launch with who cleared it.

  • Judged at the time, not at the Go. When the time comes, the before-Launch point judges again: a Hold begun since, a window, outside checks, findings that arrived. A Go is bound to the digest; if anything it cleared has changed, it is void.
  • Lapse. If a Hold covers the time, the Sortie waits for the Hold to end; past the Airfield's lapse_after grace, the Go lapses and the card asks again.
  • Superseded, with a reason. When a newer Sortie of the same Flight reaches the same Clearance for the same Airfield (and the same lane, where lanes are used), older Sorties waiting there, cleared or not, are closed as superseded: the server records "superseded by Sortie 417", the older Sortie ends Scrubbed, and whoever gave or was asked for the older Go is told. The Airfield's supersede setting is newer by default, or none. Return to base is never superseded.

Sortie 412, with an older build of storefront, has been waiting for Clearance since the morning. Sortie 417, carrying 2.4.0 (sha256:4f9c…a17), reaches clear-prod at 11:05, and 412 closes as superseded. Ana reads 417's card at 11:20 and gives Go "in the next window", 14:00. At 14:00 the before-Launch point judges again, finds no Hold, fresh outside checks and the same digest, and the Launch starts.

Infrastructure plans and their cost

Today "A configuration change is a plan" is built: people give Go on the reviewed plan, and Launchway applies exactly what was reviewed, with state kept and locked inside the product. The plan adds two things: Standing orders read the plan, and the Clearance card shows what the plan will cost.

  • Plan facts. The plan step reads the tool's machine-readable plan on the Station and records typed facts: resources to create, change, replace and destroy, by kind; the names of what would be destroyed; what would become reachable from the internet (an open inbound rule, a public bucket, a public address); whether every module is pinned.
  • Cost. The estimated monthly cost before and after, with its currency, comes from the cost capability: a connected cost source that estimates from a plan, or an estimate step run on the Station. One provider is in charge and the card says "served by". No estimate is a missing fact, and a cost rule answers "cannot tell", never pass.
  • Database changes too. The database_change rule reads what Preflight records for a schema change (drops, table rewrites, estimated lock time, rows touched), so a destructive statement can require a Clearance like a destroyed resource.
# Design: not built.
standing_orders:
  - name: prod-infra-guard
    point: launch
    scope: { airfields: [prod] }
    rules:
      infrastructure_plan:
        deny_destroy_kinds: [database, storage_bucket, dns_zone]
        clearance_if_public: true
        clearance_if_monthly_increase_over: { amount: 100, currency: USD }
    answer: deny          # each limit gives its own answer, the strictest wins

For 2.4.0, the stack storefront-infra in prod adds a read replica for the checkout queries. The plan creates one database replica and changes one network rule; nothing is destroyed or made public; the connected estimate is about 140 USD a month more. The rule requires a Clearance above 100 USD, so Ana's card shows the plan difference grouped by kind, the cost before and after, and the reason. She says Go; the apply runs exactly the plan with that digest. The schema change that adds the nullable column delivery_date has no drop, no rewrite and a lock estimate under a second, so database_change allows it.

Hold

A Hold is a time when nothing launches in its scope. Work up to it carries on: builds, tests, Inspections and Launches outside its scope are not affected.

Built today

A Hold covers one Flight or all, and one Airfield or all, until an end, with a reason. It is a line of the release checklist, judged when a release is promoted, beside change windows (allowed days and hours in a time zone). An administrator of the Flight may override a Hold, a window or a soak time with a reason, kept with the promotion and recorded in the Logbook. A Hold of one Flight needs the administrator role on it; a Hold of every Flight needs it everywhere. When a Hold begins, notification rules that name it are told. A calendar shows Holds and planned promotions.

Unverified

Reading the code (not running it) found Hold handling only in the release and promotion path. A plain deploy step in a pipeline appears not to be stopped by a Hold, so a person could ship around a Hold by running a pipeline instead of promoting. This must be confirmed before it is relied on either way.

The plan makes a Hold a Standing order judged at the before-Launch and setting-change points, so it covers every Launch in its scope, not only promotions:

  • What it stops: deploy steps, promotions, a rollout moving forward, and, by choice when the Hold is begun, Switch changes, configuration and secret rollouts, and database changes.
  • Scope: a level (Base, Wing, Squadron or Flight), a set of Airfields, and the kinds of change above. One-off or recurring (every month's last two days), in a time zone.
  • Who may begin and lift it: a Commander (owner) of the level it covers. Lifting early takes a reason and is recorded. A Hold begun at a level cannot be lifted below it.
  • Emergencies: a change that must go during a Hold goes as an emergency change: it requires a Clearance, the record marks it, and it is reviewed afterwards (the roadmap's "Standard, normal and emergency changes").
  • Never stopped: Return to base, Abort, and a Master switch moved to its safe value.
  • One calendar for every target: Holds, change windows, planned promotions, Gos timed for later, and the sync windows of a GitOps controller, which the deploy Station reads from the controller. Launchway respects those sync windows and never overrides them; the calendar shows them so one view answers "can anything launch here now?" for every kind of target.

Return to base is never blocked

The rule: stop, return and roll back always work, and are never blocked by a Standing order, a lock, a Hold or a Clearance. Moving toward the safe state is immediate and recorded; moving away from it passes every gate. Today's policy judge already never judges Return to base steps and Aborts, and a Master switch moved to its safe value is never held for a Clearance.

One place the product contradicts the rule

On a protected Airfield, a Return to base after a successful Launch is an emergency action: by default it goes at once with a reason, and an approver reviews it afterwards. But an installation or an Airfield can set emergency_rollback: require_approval, which puts a Clearance in front of the Return to base. That setting lets a Clearance block the way back. Options for you: (a) remove the setting, keeping the review afterwards; (b) keep it, and state plainly that it breaks the rule; (c) keep it only for Airfields that are not production. Recommendation: (a), because review afterwards already gives separation of duties without delaying the way back.

Verdicts across a level

One verdict explains one change. A platform team and an auditor need the other view: across every Flight of a Wing or a Squadron, which rules deny, which warn, which send changes to a person, and which exceptions are holding things open. Because every verdict and waiver is already an event with its facts, the report is a reading of the record, not a second data store.

Part of the reportWhat it shows
By ruleFor the period: allowed, warned, Clearance required and denied, per rule, with the level it comes from and the trend
By FlightEach Flight's denials and warnings, its waivers in force, and the rules it meets only by waiver
ExceptionsWaivers in force, ending within 14 days, ended, and renewed more than twice, with owner, kind and work item
Ready to enforceRules still in report mode, with what they would have stopped this period
GapsFlights with no verdict at a point where one is expected, for example a repository on a connected host whose merges are not reported back

The report filters by level, Airfield, point, rule and answer, all picked; exports as a table, as JSON and inside the signed evidence of the period; and an auditor with a read-only grant can open it for the scope of the grant. Its score-like summary feeds the posture view; it is a view, never a gate by itself.

Worked example: storefront 2.4.0, from a commit to prod and back

Dana adds the delivery date at checkout in storefront (work item STORE-41) and opens pull request #482, "Show the delivery date at checkout", into main. These are the verdicts on the record, in order. Rows marked new are this plan's proposals.

PointRules judgedAnswer
Merge (new)Branch rules: one approval by someone other than the author (Ana approves), ci/test and storefront/inspection passed, branch up to date. Wing rule: a change to the pipeline file needs a Squadron Controller (not triggered: the file did not change).Allow
Sortie startlibrary_versions: platform-library pinned at a tag. step_images: every image pinned by digest. max_timeout: within 2 hours.Allow
Image pushimage_push: scanned in enforce mode at high, signed with the Station's key, list of contents and build record made, pushed only to the Base's Depot.Allow
Before Launch to stagingtests: 412 results, none failed. findings: worst is medium. deployed_images: digest, built by this Sortie, signed, scanned.Allow
Before Launch to prodEverything above, plus Hold (new on every Launch: none in force), Wing rule "Clearance by one other person for prod". Dana's merge started Sortie 417, which built digest sha256:4f9c…a17; Ana clears it and picks change ticket CHG-88 and risk "low". New: the Ramp's outside check no-open-alerts answers wait, then pass; change-approved passes; the plan of storefront-infra needs a Clearance for its cost; Ana's Go is timed for the 14:00 window.Require a Clearance, then allow
Cluster admission (new)The generated admission policy checks the image is signed by the Base's key and comes from the Depot.Allow
Return to baseOverwatch (watch after a Launch) sees errors rise at the 10% Pathfinder (canary) step and returns to 2.3.2. Not judged by any rule; recorded with the reason and the measurements.Never judged

The same before-Launch point judges the two virtual machines of billing, the image-based kiosk hosts and the image-resizing function: one set of rules, one verdict format, whatever the target.

The foundation it relies on, and what it asks of every module

Command is not a module; every module relies on it. It relies in turn on four things below it.

  • The record. Facts come only from events on the record: step summaries, Clearances, digests, signatures, Inspection results. A fact that is not recorded never passes a rule.
  • Levels, permissions and locks. Who may write, lock, waive and clear is the same permission model as everything else; there are no private roles.
  • Typed inputs. Waiver requests, Clearance fields and Hold forms are typed input forms, filled by picking.
  • One expression language. If custom rules are chosen, they use it; nothing else.

It asks every module for three things: put each of its decisions through one of the judging points (a module never has a private gate); write each decision to the record with its facts; and never put a judging point in front of Return to base.

Safety

If this failsWhat happens
A server dies mid-decisionThe verdict and the step it allows are one database transaction: both are stored, or neither is, and another server judges again from the same inputs.
The database is lostNothing new is judged, so nothing new launches. Changes already in Git stay there. The deploy engine's own history remains the emergency way back.
A Station is lostVerdicts do not depend on Stations. The step is handed out again and judged again before it starts.
A Standing order source kept in Git cannot be loadedFails closed: every Sortie of the Flights it covers is refused at every point, naming the source. A short outage is ridden through with the version loaded before.
A fact is missingThe rule does not pass. Missing evidence is never taken for good evidence.
Who mayTodayIn this plan
Write or change a Standing orderWhoever controls the server's configuration or tags the source repositoryA Commander of the level, by a reviewed change
Lock a Standing orderNot available for rulesA Commander of the level that sets it
Grant a waiverThe role set per installation (administrator by default); never the starter on a protected AirfieldAs today, at or above the level that locked the rule
Give ClearanceOperator role, narrowed by the step's approvers; never the starter by defaultA Controller (approver) named by the step or the rule; never the author, starter or publisher
Begin or lift a HoldAdministrator of the Flight, or of every FlightA Commander of the level it covers
Return to baseOperator role; on a protected Airfield with a reason, reviewed afterwardsUnchanged, and never blocked
Attach a rule to a Ramp, connection, store or AirfieldNot availableA Commander of the level that owns the resource
Require an outside check, or a Patrol, from a levelNot availableA Commander of that level; the check itself is a pinned step anyone can read
Save a Standing order the Wingman draftedNot availableA Commander of the level; never an agent
Edit the instructions for the AINot availableA Commander of the level, or a custom role holding that action
Give a Go timed for laterNot availableWhoever may give the Go now
If this failsWhat happens
The service an outside check asks is downThe check answers wait and asks again until its timeout, then fails. A Launch that requires it waits; Return to base never does.
The server restarts while a Go waits for its timeThe timed Go is on the record; at the time, any server judges the Launch as usual.
A Patrol cannot run (no Station, the Ramp is empty)It is recorded as missed, never as passed; a rule that needs it fresh answers as it was set.
No cost estimate can be madeThe cost fact is missing; a cost rule answers "cannot tell" and does not pass.

On by default: the starter cannot clear their own Sortie once sign-in is on; Standing order sources fail closed; Return to base and Aborts are never judged; a new rule is offered in report mode first. Controller is a role word that arrives with custom roles (the roadmap's "Directory groups and custom roles"); until then the operator and administrator roles carry these permissions.

Screens

The full list, with every field and state, is in the screens notes for this chapter. In short:

Standing orders area
Rules and Inspection side by side; each rule with its level, point, answer, mode, lock and its verdicts over the last weeks as a small chart; filters picked from lists.
Add a Standing order (wizard)
Pick the level, the point, a rule from the catalog, its typed parameters, the scope from lists of Airfields, branches and events, the answer and the mode; ends on "Try it on last month".
Try this rule
The replay: counts by answer, the list of changes that would have been stopped, and "cannot tell" with the missing fact.
Verdict panel
On a pull request, a Sortie and a Launch: every rule, what was found, what would satisfy it, links to the evidence, and the waiver that passed it.
Request a waiver
Rule and scope picked from the verdict, kind from a list, end date capped by the rule, work item picked; one short reason field is the only typing.
Clearance card
What, who, digest, the change from what runs, evidence and risk, the typed fields, Go and No-go; readable on a phone.
Hold calendar and Begin a Hold
Holds, windows and planned Launches on one calendar; the wizard picks level, Airfields, kinds of change, start, end or recurrence and time zone.
Levels view for Standing orders
The inheritance diagram for one Flight and Airfield: which rule comes from which level, what is locked, what a level tried to loosen.
Add an outside check (wizard) and Check answers
Pick the kind (alerts, change ticket, calendar, address, script), the connection, the typed parameters, how often to ask, the timeout and the freshness; try it once on a Station. On a Sortie, each answer in order with its fields, reason and age.
Clearance card: when to launch
Go now, at a time picked from the calendar, or in the next window; superseded Sorties shown with the newer one that replaced them.
Clearance card: infrastructure plan
The plan difference grouped by kind, what is destroyed or made public, the cost before and after with "served by", and the rule that asked.
Rules this resource attaches
On a Ramp, connection, store or Airfield page: its rules, Who uses this, and Try it.
Required Patrols and coverage
At a level: each imposed Patrol, and for every Flight in scope its last run, result and missed runs.
Draft with the Wingman
A sentence box that fills the Add a Standing order wizard, the replay, the plain-words explanation, and Save for a Commander only.
Instructions for the AI
At a level: the instructions in force, inherited and locked lines, the version history as differences.
Verdicts across a level
The report by rule, by Flight, exceptions, rules ready to enforce and gaps; export; readable by an auditor grant.
