Open question

  1. The policy language beyond the typed catalog. Catalog only; catalog plus custom rules in the one expression language; or rules in an established open policy language by import or connection. Recommendation above: the catalog first, custom rules in the one expression language, and the planned open-language connection kept as an equal choice. Open question
  2. The setting that lets a Clearance block Return to base (emergency_rollback: require_approval): remove it, keep it, or keep it outside production. Recommendation: remove it. Open question
  3. Clearing your own Sortie in a one-person Base: the design response is unconfirmed. Open question
  4. Whether a Hold also stops Switch, configuration and secret changes by default, or only when the person beginning it says so. This chapter makes it a choice on each Hold. Open question
  5. Whether some waivers need a second person, for example in production. Payment-card change control favors it; favors a one-person Base working alone. Open question
  6. Where Standing orders live. A later ruling puts policies in the database with an export to Git; what is built reads them from configuration or from Git. This chapter proposes both, kept in step, as repository standards already are. Confirm. Open question
  7. Which judging point comes first. Suggested order: a Hold on every Launch (small, closes a real gap), then cluster admission, then the merge point, then the setting-change point. Open question
  8. One Standing orders area. Joining the two screens under the ruled word needs your yes. Open question
  9. Superseding waiting Sorties. supersede: newer on every Airfield by default (proposed), or only on Airfields marked protected. Open question
  10. Where cost estimates come from. Proposed: a connected cost source or an estimate step run on the Station, one in charge, and no built-in price data. A built-in estimator would need price lists kept current. Open question
  11. Instructions for the AI. This chapter keeps them as a level setting with locks, like Standing orders; the Wingman chapter describes how they are read. Confirm that they live here and that a lock from above may forbid a lower level from adding its own. Open question
  12. Who may write the outside checks a Standing order requires. Proposed: any Pilot may write a check; only a Commander of the level or resource may require one, pinned. Open question

Security and the supply chain

Secure by default is the topmost constraint: every change is inspected, every image carries a list of what it holds and a signed record of how it was built, every Launch (deployment) verifies both before anything runs, and no secret value ever reaches the server.

  • The Inspection (security scan) runs on every Sortie (run) with nothing to install, and blocks only what a change introduces.
  • Only what was built and cleared can run: the signature, the build record and the list of contents are verified at Launch, on every kind of target.
  • Secrets are resolved on the Station (runner), never seen by the server; short-lived identities replace stored keys.
  • Every part holds the least it needs. Where the sandbox is weaker today, this page says so plainly.
  • The running application is tested too: dynamic, API and fuzz testing against a preview Airfield feed the same findings list; provenance rises to a level the build cannot forge; and a posture view scores every level against the published top risks of build and delivery systems.

Where it sits

This chapter spans three of the seven layers. Secrets, encryption at rest and the wall between Bases (installations) belong to the foundation. Signing, lists of contents and the Depot (registry) belong to flight operations. Verification at Launch belongs to Launch. All of it is judged through Standing orders (policies and repository standards) at the points described in Standing orders, Clearance and Hold, and all of it is read back as evidence in the Logbook and evidence.

Builds on
Stations and Ramps (runner pools) from Stations and where work runs; the Depot and Cargo (artifacts) from the Depot; Hardpoints (extension points) from Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints; libraries and pinning from Reuse that keeps growing.
Builds on it
Every Launch target in the Launch chapters; Maintenance (dependency updates) and the software graph in the software graph and Maintenance; the hosted service's promise that it never holds a customer's secrets.

What you will be able to do

You are Dana, a developer on storefront. You bump a library and push. The Inspection finds a new high-severity vulnerability that has a fixed version and blocks the merge; the finding offers the fix, and Maintenance opens it as a pull request. An old medium finding on main is shown as existing and does not block you.

An outside contributor opens a pull request from a fork. It runs the pipeline from main, with no secrets, no Launch, no cache write and no Depot push. Ana reads the change and chooses Run with secrets; that decision is on the record with Ana's name.

Someone builds a kiosk image on a laptop and pushes it to the Depot by hand. The Launch to the edge kiosks refuses it: no signature from the Base's key, and no build record from a Sortie. The kiosks keep running the image they had.

The Launch to the two billing virtual machines needs to reach them over secure shell. Instead of a stored key, the step receives a certificate valid for fifteen minutes and only for those two hosts. A leaked log shows nothing that can be reused.

A new advisory is published for a library inside storefront and the image-resizing function. Without anyone pushing a commit, Launchway says which running versions are affected, in which Airfields (environments), opens one fix per repository, and tracks each until the fixed version is seen running.

An assessor asks: "Can the server read our payment-processor key?" You open the secrets map and answer with the record: the key lives in your secret store, is read by the Station in your network just before the step, is masked in every log, and the server holds only its name.

How it works

Secure by default

Every protection starts on. A team may tune or turn off a protection for its own Flight (project), with a reason on the record, unless a level above locked it. Each new capability states its access, its blast radius and its default before it is built.

DefaultStatus
Sign-in required from the first moment; a one-time setup code; a second factor required for administratorsAvailable
The Helm chart starts with default-deny network policies, restricted pods and no public exposureAvailable
Stored secrets sealed under a root key held outside the databaseAvailable
The Inspection on for every repository; secrets and new fixable high or critical vulnerabilities blockAvailable
Pull requests from forks and automation accounts run restrictedAvailable
Standing order sources fail closedAvailable
The starter of a Sortie cannot give its Clearance (approval)Available
Signatures, build records and lists of contents verified at every LaunchPlanned
Every Station proves its own identity; no shared tokenNew in this plan
Every executor enforces the same sandbox for custom stepsNew in this plan

The Inspection

Every Sortie gains an Inspection with no change to the repository: one step per check that fits what the repository holds, run in parallel, then a verdict step. The steps are added by the server, marked on the Sortie's graph as added by Standing orders, and run in the tool's own image pinned by digest. They never see the Flight's secrets, so they run unchanged for a pull request from a fork.

What is inspectedThe checkDefaultStatus
CodeSecurity rules for Go and Python code; reachable vulnerabilities for Go (does your code call the vulnerable function?)AdviseAvailable More languages planned
SecretsCredentials in the history: every commit the first time, then the commits since the last SortieBlockAvailable
DependenciesKnown vulnerabilities in locked dependencies, matched against open advisory dataBlock high and critical with a fixAvailable
LicensesDenied, not allowed and unidentifiable licenses; a deny list by open license identifierAdviseAvailable
Infrastructure filesMisconfiguration in Terraform, Helm charts, manifests and Dockerfiles; Kubernetes practice (limits, probes, security context); unsafe pipeline files (images not pinned, secrets in plain text, downloads piped into a shell); shell mistakesAdviseAvailable
ImagesThe image step scans every image it builds today. The Inspection's own image check is not available yet.Block at the level the Standing order setsIn progress Image step today; Inspection check planned
ContentsA list of contents (an open bill-of-materials format) kept with every SortieAlways madeAvailable
The running applicationDynamic scanning, API testing and fuzzing against a preview Airfield or staging (below)Advise; block new high and criticalNew in this plan
What runs in productionFindings from the team's own runtime protection tool, tied to the running digest (below)Shown; a rule may act on themNew in this plan

Where findings go. Every check reports into one findings model: what, where, how serious, the fix, the fingerprint that follows it across Sorties, and its standing (new, existing, accepted, false positive). The Sortie's Security tab starts with the Inspection's verdict; the Flight's page shows open findings over time, oldest first, with the mean time to fix; exports are available in the open static-analysis results format, as CSV and as JSON. A tool that Launchway does not run can report into the same list.

How findings gate. A pull request is blocked only by what it introduces; the default branch's findings are its baseline and never block you. A check that did not run is never taken for a clean result. The verdict step is a required check of a branch rule, and with one Standing orders area it becomes a rule at the merge point. Before a Launch, the findings rule judges the same results against the Airfield's limit.

Only free and openly licensed tools are in the default set, each pinned. Tools a team already pays for come in through adapters into the same list and gates (the roadmap's "Adapters for the tools teams already pay for").

Code checks for every major language

Today the built-in code rules cover Go and Python, and only Go has reachability (does your code call the vulnerable function?). The plan brings security rules for code to the ten most used languages, each run by an openly licensed rule engine in its own pinned image, reporting into the same findings model, with the same new-only gate. Reachability follows wherever the language's advisory data names the affected function.

LanguageSecurity rules for codeReachable vulnerabilitiesOrder
GoAvailableAvailableBuilt
PythonAvailablePlannedNext
JavaScript and TypeScriptPlannedPlannedNow
Java and KotlinPlannedPlannedNow
C#PlannedPlannedNext
C and C++PlannedNot offered: advisory data rarely names functionsNext
PHPPlannedPlannedLater
RubyPlannedPlannedLater
RustPlannedPlannedLater
SwiftPlannedNot offered at firstLater

Shell, Dockerfiles, Terraform, Helm charts and manifests are already covered by the infrastructure-file checks above. Advise is the default for code rules in every language; a level may set them to block, and only what a change introduces blocks.

Steps a level adds to every Sortie

The server already adds the Inspection's steps to every Sortie, marked on the graph as added by Standing orders. The plan makes that the one mechanism for anything a level must run everywhere: a Standing order of the kind added_steps names a pinned Maneuver and where it goes (at the start, after every image step, before every deploy step, or at the end). The Inspection becomes simply the Base's built-in set of added steps.

  • Cannot be dropped. A Flight cannot remove, skip or reorder an added step; the added_steps rule checks at Sortie start that each one is present, pinned and unaltered.
  • Visible. On the Sortie's graph each is marked "added by Standing order license-report (Wing)", with a link to the order.
  • Contained. It runs in the sandbox like any custom step, sees no secret unless it declares one and the store's release rule allows it, and its reports feed the same findings, tests and verdicts.

Today required_templates can only require that a pipeline uses a template, so the pipeline's author must add it. Added steps remove that burden and the chance to forget.

# Design: not built.
standing_orders:
  - name: license-report
    kind: added_steps
    scope: { wing: harbor-lights }
    add:
      - uses: platform-library/license-report@v1.4.0
        place: after_image_steps
    lock: true

Testing the running application

Some weaknesses only show when the application runs: a route that leaks an error page, an API that accepts what it should refuse, a parser that crashes on odd input. The plan tests the running application with three pinned steps against a preview Airfield, the one each pull request gets, or against staging, and reports into the one findings list.

StepWhat it doesWhat it needs
Dynamic scanCrawls the running application, passively and then actively, with a test account given by secret reference; rate-limited and time-boxedA preview or staging address; a test account
API testReads the service's API description from the repository and sends boundary, malformed and unauthorized requests to each operationAn API description in an open format
FuzzRuns the code's own fuzz targets on a Station for a time budget; the corpus is kept as Cargo (artifacts), so each Sortie starts where the last one stopped; a crash becomes a finding with its inputFuzz targets in the code; no Airfield
  • One model. Findings carry a fingerprint (rule, route or function, parameter), so a finding follows across Sorties; the baseline is the last scan of the default branch; the same waivers and the same findings rule apply.
  • Never against production. An Airfield is scannable only when marked so; the Base locks prod as not scannable. Scan traffic carries a marker, so Radar (monitoring) and Overwatch (watch after a Launch) leave it out of their measurements and no alert fires.
  • Built in or connected. Openly licensed engines in pinned images are the default; an engine a team already pays for reports through the adapters.
Today

Launchway's own repository is fuzzed and scanned in its release program ("Security scans as a program"). The product does not yet offer dynamic, API or fuzz testing as checks for your Flights.

Pull request #482 adds a route that returns the delivery date. In the preview Airfield pr-482, the API test sends a negative day offset and gets a server error: a new medium finding, shown on the pull request, not blocking. The fuzz step finds that the date parser panics on a malformed time zone: a new high finding with the crashing input attached, which blocks the merge. Dana adds the input to the tests, fixes the parser, and the next Sortie clears both.

Findings from what runs in production

Protecting a running application from attacks is a deep specialty, so Launchway connects to the tool a team already runs rather than building a second one. The tool posts its findings through the events-in Hardpoint in an open results format. Launchway ties each finding to the digest that was serving at that moment, read from the Launch record, and to its owner through the software graph, and puts it in the same findings list marked "seen in production".

  • The same weakness found earlier by the Inspection is raised in priority: it is no longer theoretical.
  • A rule can refuse a new digest that still carries a component a runtime finding names, so a fix is never blocked and a known-attacked version is never launched again.
  • Nothing about it can block Return to base.

The supply chain, from commit to verified Launch

Three records travel with every image: a list of contents (what is inside), a signed build record (which commit, which pipeline, which Station, which inputs made it) and a signature. The goal is one sentence: only what was built by your Sorties and cleared by your people can run.

Built today

Commits and tags can be signed and verified, and the verdict is shown. The image step builds rootless, scans with a scanner pinned by digest, makes a list of contents and a build record in the open supply-chain provenance format (SLSA version 1), and signs with the Station's own key; the Depot stores the signatures and records beside the image and shows them. The image_push and deployed_images rules can require all of it. Launchway's own releases are built reproducibly with a list of contents, and signing and provenance are in their release workflow.

Not built yet

A deploy step does not verify a signature against a key: the rules check what the record says the image step did. Keyless signing is designed, not built. A branch rule cannot yet ask for signed commits. Promotion by digest is planned.

The plan verifies all three records at the before-Launch point, against the Base's trust policy: which keys may sign, which Depots may serve, which build records are acceptable (built by a Sortie of this Base, from a protected branch, by a pipeline pinned to these libraries). Then each target checks again where it runs:

TargetWhere the second check happensStatus
Kubernetes (storefront)A standard cluster admission policy generated from the Base's Standing orders refuses an unsigned image, whoever applied itNew in this plan
Virtual machines (billing)The deploy Station verifies the package or image digest and signature before it drains the first machineNew in this plan
Image-based hosts (edge kiosks)Each host verifies the signed image before it stages it for the next boot; a host that cannot verify keeps its imageNew in this plan
Serverless (image resizing)The deploy Station verifies before it moves the alias or revisionNew in this plan
 
# Design: not built. A Base's trust policy, kept with its Standing orders.
trust:
  signers:
    - key: base://harbor-lights/signing        # the Base's own key, held by Stations
  depots: [depot://harbor-lights/**]
  build_records:
    built_by: this-base
    branches: [main, "release/*"]
    libraries_pinned: tag
  verify_at: [launch, admission]

Provenance the build cannot forge

Today's build record meets level two of the open provenance format: it is signed, but by the Station's own key, so a Station taken over could sign a record of a build that never happened. The highest level asks for more: the record must come from the build platform, not from the build, and runs must be isolated from each other. Launchway's model already has the pieces: the server observes every Sortie event, and Stations only ever hold their own work.

  1. Written from what the server saw. The record names the commit, the pipeline at its digest, every library pin and step image digest, the Sortie's inputs, the Station's proven identity and the output digest, all taken from events on the record, not from a file the build wrote.
  2. Signed where the build cannot reach. A signer role of the one program holds the signing key under the key hierarchy, or in an outside key service; it can be scaled and secured apart. No build Station ever holds it.
  3. Isolated runs. Level-three builds run on Ramps marked isolated: each Station takes one Sortie and is destroyed, runs the one sandbox profile, and never writes to a cache an untrusted Sortie can read.
  4. Attached and verified. The record travels with the image in the Depot, by digest. The trust policy can require build_level: 3 for prod; the before-Launch point and the cluster's admission policy verify it.
  5. Reproduced, as an option. A Standing order can ask a second isolated Station to rebuild and compare digests. "Reproduced by a second Station" then becomes a recorded fact a rule can require.
Honest limit

The output digest is still reported by the Station that built it; level three trusts the platform's isolation, not the build. The rebuild-and-compare option is what closes that gap for teams that need it.

Generated steps, signed by the Station that made them

A step can print more steps (the roadmap's "Generated pipelines"). Generated steps already pass the same parser, locked libraries, inline-code limits and Standing orders as written ones. The plan adds proof of where they came from:

  • The Station that ran the generating step signs the generated text with its own key, bound to the Sortie, the step, the attempt and the digest of the text.
  • The server checks the signature against that Station's enrolled key and its lease, and refuses text that is unsigned, altered, signed by another Station or for another step.
  • Before parsing, the Inspection's secret rules run over the text; a value that looks like a credential is refused, so no secret travels inside a step definition.
  • The graph marks each generated step "generated by step plan-tests, signed by Station build-03", and the record keeps the digest.

Shared pieces, pinned and locked

A pipeline is only as safe as what it borrows. Libraries, Maneuvers (reusable step templates), Flight plans (ready-made pipelines) and custom steps are taken by tag or commit, and a pinned piece never changes under a pipeline. Today the library_versions rule refuses a branch, required_templates requires the shared security Maneuver, step_images requires images by digest, and update notices for custom steps call out when a new version asks for more permissions. A Sortie records the library commits it used, and a re-run uses the same ones even if a tag has moved. A lock file for everything taken from libraries is proposed in Reuse that keeps growing.

Third-party code never runs inside the server

The server runs no code a user, a library or an outside system brings. Custom steps run on Stations, in a sandbox. Outside systems connect through Hardpoints that run outside the product. A pipeline can name only libraries the server lists; it can never give the server an address to fetch. An optional model explains a failure but never runs inside the server's process with access to secrets.

Secrets: where each one lives and travels

A pipeline holds only references. The server, the interface and the record hold only references. The value is looked up by the Station, inside the network that owns the secret, just before the step runs, and is replaced by *** in logs and outputs.

SecretLivesTravels toNever
A pipeline's secretYour secret store: an environment variable or a mounted file on the Station, or a store such as Vault or OpenBaoThe Station, then the step, in memoryThe server, the database, the record, a log
The Station's own credentialOn the Station: an Ed25519 key made at enrollment, rotated every 30 daysSigned assertions for 15-minute access tokensThe server holds only the public half
Launchway's own keys (sign-in, webhook secrets, host keys)Sealed in the database under the root keyThe server, in memoryIn the clear on disk or in a backup
Sessions and API tokensStored only as one-way hashesThe callerRecoverable from the database, even with every key
The root keyOutside the database: a key file, an environment variable, a passphrase or a vault's transit serviceThe server at startIn the database it protects

Every store takes allow-lists of Flights and keys, checked on the Station. A secret that does not exist or may not be read fails the step, naming the store and the key. On Kubernetes a step's environment is held in memory inside the Sortie's pod, where the Sortie's other containers could read it; the plan closes that (below).

Short-lived identity instead of stored keys

Each Sortie and each step can prove who it is with a short-lived token in the open OpenID Connect format, carrying the Base, Wing (organization), Flight, branch, Airfield and step. A cloud, a secret store, the Depot or a host trusts the token once, by rule, and then issues a credential that lasts only as long as the step. No long-lived cloud or host key is stored anywhere.

What the step reachesWhat it getsRoadmap item
A cloudA token for the step's durationCloud sign-in per step Planned
A secret store or a databaseA credential issued for the Sortie and revoked after itWorkload identity and dynamic credentials Planned
Object storageA temporary keyShort-lived storage credentials Planned
Hosts over secure shellA certificate for these hosts, for minutesShort-lived access to hosts Planned
Package clients and the DepotA short-lived pull or push credentialNative endpoints for package clients Planned

Least privilege for every part

PartHoldsNever holds
Server and databaseThe record, masked logs, findings without code snippets, lists of contents, hashes of sessions and tokens, mirrors of Flights and librariesSecret values, Depot or cluster credentials of Stations, sessions or tokens in the clear
Build StationIts own key, its secret store credentials, Depot credentials, its signing key, the workspace of the Sorties it runsCluster credentials for Launches
Deploy StationIts Ramp's token, a Git credential limited to the listed files, a cluster identity limited to sync, refresh and rollout controlScripts: it never runs one; nothing on pods or secrets
A stepOnly the secrets and network it declared, for its own durationThe Station's key, other steps' secrets
The Detachment (the small program on your side; hosted service, planned)Your secrets, your clusters, your traffic, on your sideAnything the hosted side can read
An agentExactly the rights of the token it holds, under an autonomy level set by a Standing orderThe right to clear its own work

The sandbox for custom steps, and the hardening still owed

A custom step declares the network hosts, the workspace paths and the secrets it needs. The Station gives it those and nothing else. Today that promise holds fully on one kind of executor and partly on the others. This is the plain state, from reading the code and the reference.

ExecutorWhat is enforced todayWhat is still owed
Container (a container engine on the machine)No network unless hosts are listed; a read-only root filesystem; a read-only workspace except the listed paths; all capabilities dropped; no new privileges; only the named secretsThe host list is recorded, shown and audited, but not enforced by name: a step that may reach the network may reach any host
KubernetesNon-root user, no capabilities, the runtime's default system-call filter, so the namespace can enforce the restricted pod standard; no egress from the chart's network policy unless hosts are set; pods removed when the step ends and leaked ones reapedThe workspace write list is recorded, not enforced; the host list is not enforced by name; the Sortie's other containers in the pod can read the step's environment, secrets included
HostRefuses custom steps unless allow_unsandboxed_steps is setEnforces nothing for ordinary steps; the auto executor falls back to the host on a machine with no container engine
Other limits today

A Station enrolled on the shared token has no identity of its own: the server cannot tell such Stations apart, and anyone with the token can take that Ramp's work, so require_identity should be set on every Ramp. A Station trusts the server it connects to. Git credentials written into a repository address travel with the Sortie. API tokens keep the groups of the last sign-in until revoked. Any signed-in viewer can list the Stations. There is not yet a wall between Wings inside one installation; the wall between Bases is in progress.

The plan owes four things, each a Standing order that is on by default and locked at the Base for shared Ramps:

  1. One sandbox profile on every executor. The same declared hosts, paths and secrets are enforced on containers and Kubernetes alike; a step's secrets are mounted only into its own container.
  2. No silent fall-back to the host. A shared Ramp refuses the host executor; auto never falls back to it on a shared Station.
  3. Identity required. Every Ramp requires each Station to prove its own key; the shared token is retired.
  4. Builds reach what they need, and every refusal shows. A default allow-set by category (package registries, Git hosts, image registries), enforced by name through an egress guard, with each refused connection shown on the Sortie with its destination, and each Sortie's traffic visible.

On the hosted service each step runs in its own isolated machine with no route to anything but the internet (the roadmap's "Sandboxed hosted runners"); the same profile is offered to any self-hosted installation.

Pull requests from forks

A pull request from a fork, or from an automation account, runs in a restricted mode until a maintainer has read it: the pipeline comes from the default branch, no step reads a secret, Launch and Return to base (rollback) steps are skipped, the cache is read but never written, and image steps build and scan but never push. A first-time contributor's pull request also waits for a person with write access to approve running it. Run with secrets lifts the restriction for the steps that have not started, and is recorded like a Go. An administrator can lift the restriction for automation accounts; nothing lifts it for a fork.

Encryption at rest, and Launchway's own vault

A root key held outside the database protects a small hierarchy of keys. A copy of the database, a backup or a volume snapshot alone reveals no secret Launchway stores.

Protected nowNot yet encrypted by Launchway
The keys every server shares; the shared Station token; Git host keys; webhook secrets and addresses; addresses with a password in them are refused; sessions and tokens stored only as hashesCargo, test reports, logs and run records, build caches, hosted Git packs, Depot images, the Logbook (audit trail). Until the next slice, encrypt the database volume and the Cargo store as well; launchway doctor encryption says plainly what is and is not covered.

The root key comes from a key file (the default, made once), an environment variable, a passphrase-unsealed store, or a vault's transit service; cloud key services, hardware modules and platform chips follow behind the same interface. Rotation without downtime, stream encryption of files, logs and caches, and keys a customer holds on the hosted service are planned.

Launchway's own vault is planned: a team with no secret store keeps its secrets in Launchway, with Standing orders and a Logbook, and every built-in stays optional, with popular stores behind the same interface and a published parity matrix.

Open question

The roadmap item "A built-in secret store" says values are "sealed by the same key hierarchy", which is the server's. The plan's foundation says "secrets are resolved on the Station, never seen by the server". Both cannot hold if the server can unseal the vault. Options: (a) values sealed to the Stations' (or the Detachment's) keys, so the server stores only ciphertext it cannot open, with the server's key hierarchy as a second layer at rest; (b) values sealed by the server's hierarchy and handed to Stations on request. Recommendation: (a), because it keeps the one promise people rely on: the server never sees a value.

Maintenance and automated patching

Maintenance finds outdated and vulnerable dependencies and proposes updates as ordinary pull requests, with no outside update robot. Security fixes come first and are never held back; other versions wait a few days after release; lock files are rebuilt in an isolated container with no secrets and no route to your network, and checked before the pull request opens. Launchway never edits code silently.

Planned on top: base images rebuilt when their base changes; stored lists of contents rechecked when an advisory is published, so affected repositories and running versions are named without a push; a campaign that opens one fix per affected repository and tracks it until the fixed version is seen running, with deadlines and evidence; and automated patching, off by default and turned on per zone, where updates pass tests and change management and roll out through the normal Launch with Overwatch (watch after a Launch).

Hardened base images

Most of what an image holds comes from its base. Rebuilding when the base changes is planned; which bases a team starts from is not yet decided. Under the rule of one provider in charge per capability, "base images" is a capability slot with two equal choices:

ChoiceWhat it givesWhat it costs
Built inA small set of minimal base images for the built-in language starters, rebuilt every day from upstream packages, each with its list of contents and a level-three build record, signed by the Base and served from the DepotA daily build and the care of a small set
ConnectedAn outside catalog of hardened images as the provider of the slot; Launchway pins them by digest, inspects them like any image and rebuilds yours when they changeA connection and, often, a subscription
Recommendation, for you to decide

Both, with one in charge per Squadron: the built-in set for the starters, because a solo developer needs a safe base on the first day, and a connection as an equal choice for teams that already have a catalog. "Served by" shows which one a Squadron uses.

A posture view against published top risks

Every protection on this page is a setting or a fact on the record. The posture view reads them and scores each level, from the Base down to each Flight, against a published list of the top ten security risks of build and delivery systems, and each repository against a published repository-security benchmark. Each control reads one recorded fact; each failing control shows the one step that fixes it.

Risk in the published listControls read from the record
1. A change can reach production without enough reviewBranch rules on protected branches, the merge verdict, a Clearance on production Airfields, no self-approval
2. Weak identity and access managementSecond factor for Commanders, accounts unused for 90 days, tokens past the level's lifetime, service-account tokens without address limits
3. Abuse of the dependency chainLock files present, Maintenance on, new packages quarantined in the Depot, package sources pinned to the Depot
4. Poisoned pipeline executionForks restricted, pull requests run the default branch's pipeline, no secrets for pull-request Sorties, pipeline-file changes need a Controller
5. Too much access for pipelinesSteps declare secrets and hosts, the sandbox enforced on each executor, production Ramps apart, short-lived identities instead of stored keys
6. Poor credential hygieneNo open secret findings, no cloud keys stored as variables, a release rule on every store, rotation age
7. Insecure system configurationThe doctor's checks: encryption at rest, sign-in, network policies, no host executor on shared Ramps, Station identity required
8. Ungoverned outside servicesEvery connection with its scope and last use, unused connections, signed Hardpoint deliveries
9. Weak integrity of what was builtImages signed, provenance level, verification at Launch on, promotion by digest
10. Too little logging and visibilityThe Logbook chain whole, a stream configured, retention at or above the floor, reads recorded
Needs a check against the published text

The risks above are paraphrased in plain words from memory of the published list of top ten security risks for CI/CD systems; their order, names and identifiers must be checked against the current published version, and which repository-security benchmark to score against is still to be chosen.

The score is the share of controls that pass, per risk and per level, with a trend; it is a view, never a gate by itself (the roadmap's "A standards home and a posture view"). Any single control can still be required by a Standing order and locked. The same facts feed the verdicts across a level and the control checks of the evidence.

The independent audit and the penetration test

The roadmap plans a specialist firm to audit the server, sign-in, the Station protocol, encryption and the chart's defaults, with a published summary; and independent penetration testing with a response runbook and a public summary of findings. Both follow encryption at rest and the vault. The hosted service's first public opening requires an independent penetration test, and its fully hosted stage a second one. The plan adds the Standing orders judge, supply-chain verification and the Detachment to the audit's scope.

A validated cryptographic build (planned) is a separate build variant of the server, the Stations and the Detachment that uses only a cryptographic module validated under the published FIPS 140-3 standard. The claim is made for that variant only, and the variant says which it is wherever it reports its version; the default build never claims it.

Honest wording

Launchway is not certified against any standard today, and claims only what is true that day. It provides controls and evidence. The certification path is written down in an honest order: practices first (a public security badge, a scorecard, signed builds with provenance), then an independent audit, then an attestation of the hosted service.

Worked example: storefront 2.4.0 through the supply chain

  1. Dana's commit for pull request #482 is signed with her secure shell key; the commit page shows it as verified.
  2. Sortie 417's Inspection runs eleven checks; none finds anything new. The list of contents for the Go service and the web front end is kept with the Sortie.
  3. The image step builds storefront rootless, scans it (worst finding: medium, existing), writes the list of contents and the build record, signs with the Station's key and pushes to the Base's Depot by digest sha256:4f9c…a17.
  4. The Launch to prod reaches the cluster with a short-lived identity limited to the storefront application. The database password is read by the deploy Station from the secret store, never by the server.
  5. Before Launch, the trust policy is checked: signer, Depot, build record from main, libraries pinned by tag. Then the cluster's admission policy checks the signature again.
  6. The same release's resizing function and the kiosk image follow the same path; each target verifies before it switches.

The foundation it relies on

  • The record holds every signature, build record, list of contents, finding and identity decision, so verification and evidence read the same facts.
  • Standing orders are the only place where a security gate lives; this chapter adds facts and rules, never a private gate.
  • Levels and locks let a Base lock a protection for every Flight below it.
  • Stations that only call out keep secrets, signing keys and cluster credentials on your side.

Inspection and Maintenance are modules and meet the module contract: they use the same permissions, write to the one record, gate only through Standing orders, run as steps on Stations, are served by the built-in tools or by an adapter with "served by" shown, can be turned off with a reason (they are on by default, by ruling), and are equal on every way in. Neither ever blocks Return to base.

Safety

If this failsWhat happens
A scanner cannot run or its advisory data cannot be reachedThe verdict says which check did not finish; it is never a clean result. Today an incomplete Inspection passes by default (gate.incomplete: pass); see the open items.
A secret store is unreachableThe Station asks again for 30 seconds, then hands the step back to run later. The server is not involved.
The root key is missing or wrongThe server refuses to start rather than run unsealed, says which key it expected, and a recovery command exists for a damaged key file.
A signing key is lost or leakedThe Base's trust policy removes it; images it signed fail verification at the next Launch; running workloads are not touched, and Return to base to an image signed by a trusted key stays open.
A Station is compromisedIt holds only its own Ramp's work and stores, by allow-list. Revoking its key stops it at once. At level three it cannot sign a build record at all, and a generated step it signs is bound to its own lease.
A test of the running application cannot reach the previewThe step reports that it did not finish; the verdict says so, and a missing scan is never a clean one.
The signer role is downLevel-three images wait for their record; nothing launches without one where a rule requires it. Return to base to an image already verified stays open.

Who may do what. A Commander (owner) of a level sets its trust policy, its Inspection settings and its locks; turning the Inspection off at a level takes a reason and is recorded, and the Security pages show a reminder while it is off. A Controller (approver) may accept a risk on a finding; anyone with the operator role may end an acceptance early. Only a maintainer may choose Run with secrets. Only an installation administrator may change the root key. A Commander of a level sets the steps it adds and marks its Airfields scannable; the Base keeps prod not scannable by a lock.

Screens

Inspection findings
The Sortie's Security tab and the Flight's list: verdict first, checks and whether each ran, findings split into new, existing and accepted; filters picked from lists.
Finding detail and Accept the risk
What, where, why, the fix, first seen; accept with a kind, an end date and a work item picked, and one short reason.
Supply chain of a release
One line from commit to each Airfield: signature, list of contents, build record and each verification, with its verdict and where it happened.
Trust policy
A Base's signers, Depots and accepted build records, edited by picking keys, Depots and branches from lists.
Secrets map
Each store, its allow-lists, which Flights and steps asked for which reference, and where the value was read; never a value.
Station hardening
Each Ramp and Station: executor, identity, and each sandbox promise marked enforced, recorded only, or not enforced.
Security overview
The doctor's checklist in the interface: encryption, sign-in, network, Stations, with the one step to fix each gap.
Advisory campaign
From an advisory: affected repositories and running versions, each fix pull request, its owner and its deadline.
Posture view
For a level: the score per risk of the published list and its trend; each control passed or failed with the fact it read and the one step that fixes it; repositories scored against the benchmark; drill down to a Flight.
Test the running application (wizard)
Pick the Airfield (only scannable ones are offered), the steps (dynamic scan, API test, fuzz), the test account's secret reference, the API description file from the repository, the time budget; the result lands in the findings list.
Added steps
At a level: each step it adds, where it goes, its pinned version and the Flights it reaches; on a Sortie, the marker on each added step.
Code checks by language
Each language found in the Flight, its rule engine and version, advise or block, and reachability where offered.
Build record detail
On an image: provenance level, who signed it (Station or the Base's signer), the observed facts, the isolated Ramp, and "reproduced by a second Station" when present.
Base images
The base-image slot: served by the built-in set or a connection, each base with its digest, age, findings and the images built on it.

Open question

  1. How the built-in vault seals values. Sealed to Stations' keys (recommended) or by the server's key hierarchy. Open question
  2. An Inspection that did not finish. Today it passes by default. Recommendation: fail merges into protected branches and Launches to production, pass elsewhere. Open question
  3. Keyless signing. Whether it may rely on a public transparency log, or only on records the Base keeps. Recommendation: the Base's own key by default, keyless as a choice. Open question
  4. Retiring the shared Station token. Requiring identity on every Ramp breaks Stations that have not enrolled. Confirm the default and the notice. Open question
  5. The default allow-set for builds: which categories are allowed out of the box. Open question
  6. Hardened base images. Built in, connected, or both with one in charge per Squadron. Recommendation: both. Open question
  7. Which rule engines and rule sets ship for code checks in each language. Some community rule sets carry licenses that need counsel before they are shipped in a product with a commercial license. Open question
  8. Which repository-security benchmark the posture view scores against, beside the published top-ten list of CI/CD risks. Open question
  9. Where the level-three signer runs: a role of the one program (recommended, simplest to install) or only a separate signer with an outside key service. Open question

The Logbook and evidence

Everything Launchway does is on one record; the Logbook (audit trail) and every evidence pack are readings of that record, produced as a by-product of normal work and never assembled by hand.

  • The Logbook records every change, refusal, sign-in and decision, with who, when, from where and why.
  • For any release, one evidence pack shows what was built from which commit, what the tests and the Inspection (security scan) said, which Standing orders (policies and repository standards) were judged and how, who cleared it, where it launched, what Overwatch found and whether it made a Return to base (rollback).
  • Evidence is mapped to the controls of PCI DSS and HIPAA. Launchway provides controls and evidence; it is not certified, and it never says it is.
  • Separation of duties works for a team of any size, and the record says plainly when a team of one cleared its own work.
  • Every setting change is kept as a before-and-after difference, and control checks that each read one recorded fact are mapped to more published frameworks, with every clause number marked until it is checked against the published text.

Where it sits

This chapter reads the record (layer 2) on behalf of Command (layer 6). It adds no new source of truth: the Logbook, the Flight recorder (run log), the Debrief (test report), change records and evidence packs are all readings of one append-only event record, as the seven layers describe.

Builds on
The record; the verdicts and Clearances (approvals) of Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; the signatures, build records and lists of contents of security and the supply chain; the levels and roles of Levels, people and secrets.
Builds on it
Change records for outside change-management systems; delivery metrics in Radar, insight and keeping it healthy; the hosted service's promise that everything the vendor does shows in your Logbook.

What you will be able to do

Your assessor asks for proof that every change to prod in the period was reviewed, tested, scanned and cleared. You open Evidence, pick the Flight (project) storefront, the Airfield (environment) prod and the period, and export 37 evidence packs and one summary. Nobody fills in a spreadsheet.

Your security team streams the Logbook to the system it already uses to watch logs. One night a delivery arrives with a sequence number missing; the receiving side raises it, and Verify the Logbook shows the chain is whole on Launchway's side and the gap was in transit.

You lead the shop Squadron (unit). You read the Logbook of your Squadron's Flights, and nothing from the payments Squadron, without being an administrator of the whole Base (installation).

Every Launch (deployment) to prod opens a change record in the change-management system your company uses. The approval given there comes back to Launchway as a Clearance, with the approver's name, and the record closes itself when Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) ends.

You give an outside auditor read-only access to the Harbor Lights Wing (organization) for two weeks. They see the evidence, export it and verify the chain. They cannot change anything, and every page they open is in the Logbook.

How it works

One record, many readings

What is recorded

Built today

The Logbook records every call that changes something (starting, canceling, resuming and re-running Sorties (runs), saving pipelines, giving Go or No-go, making and revoking tokens, Launch commands, Cargo (artifact) deletions), allowed or refused, plus every refused token, every webhook call, every waiver granted or revoked, every merge past a branch rule, every override of a Hold (freeze) or window, and every sign-in, failed sign-in and sign-out. Each entry has the time, who, their address, the action, the Flight, the target, the outcome and a short detail. Pipeline text, secrets, tokens and session ids are never written to it. Launchway only adds to it. The same entries also go to standard output as JSON lines with a request id, for any log collector.

Beside the Logbook, each Sortie has its own append-only event log: the Sortie created, each step's attempts and what each was given (with secrets by reference only), each Standing order verdict with its facts, each Clearance with who and when, each Launch and its result. Every event carries a schema version. A release record holds the images, build records and Clearances of what was actually launched.

Not recorded yetPlanned
Reads: who opened which evidence, which Logbook page, which secret reference a Station (runner) resolvedReads recorded where they matter (below); every monitoring query is already ruled to be recorded
Before-and-after differences of every setting changeSettings changes recorded with what changed, as a difference: designed below
Everything the vendor of the hosted service does to a Base"Everything the vendor does shows in your Logbook"

Setting changes recorded as a difference

Today the Logbook says that a setting changed, by whom and from where; it does not say what the setting was before. The plan records every setting change as a typed difference, for every kind of setting, in the same event that the setting-change point judged:

  • Every kind. Variables and their locks, role bindings and custom roles, Standing orders and waivers, Airfield protections and change windows, connections and secret stores with their release rules, Ramps and their accept lists, Switch rules, trust policies, retention floors, the instructions for the AI, and Launchway's own server settings.
  • Field by field. Each changed field with its old and new value and its type; lists show what was added and removed, not two whole lists.
  • Secrets by reference. A secret's value never appears. Its change is recorded as "version 6 to version 7 of payments/gateway", with who rotated it.
  • Wherever the change came from. A change made on screen, through the API, the command line, the agent endpoint or Terraform carries the same difference; a change that arrived as a merged file in the level's settings repository links to its commit.
  • Put back. "Put this value back" makes a new change that passes the same judging points; nothing is rewritten in place.
# Design: not built. One setting change, as written to the Logbook stream.
{ "event": "setting.changed", "seq": 18431, "time": "14:02:11Z",
  "actor": "sam", "via": "web", "address": "10.20.0.14",
  "object": { "kind": "airfield", "flight": "storefront", "name": "prod" },
  "verdict": "policy.evaluated#18430",
  "changes": [
    { "field": "protection.min_approvals", "before": 1, "after": 2 },
    { "field": "windows", "added": ["Tue 14:00-16:00 America/Chicago"], "removed": [] },
    { "field": "secrets.db_password", "before": "ref v6", "after": "ref v7" } ] }

The Logbook shows the difference beside each entry, filtered by kind of object; the timeline of what changed before a problem reads the same events; and the export carries before and after so an outside log system can answer "who changed the production approvals, and from what" without Launchway.

Who can read what, at each level

Built today

Administrators read the Logbook on its page (Settings, Logbook) or through the API, filtered by person, Flight, action and time. Anyone who can see a Sortie can see its events, its verdicts and its Clearances.

The plan opens the Logbook level by level, on the same permissions as everything else, and puts the most sensitive streams behind a higher permission, as the ruling on monitoring data requires.

Retention and export

Built today

The Logbook is kept until someone removes old rows from its table. How long Sortie events are kept is not documented. The Logbook can be read page by page through the API. Retention rules exist for Depot (registry) images, and an image an Airfield runs is never deleted.

The plan gives each kind of record a retention with a floor:

  • A floor set at the Base. A Base sets the shortest time each kind is kept: Logbook entries, Sortie events with their verdicts and Clearances, waivers, evidence packs, Flight recorders, Cargo. A level below may keep longer, never shorter.
  • Verdicts live as long as the Logbook. A verdict, the Clearance that answered it and the waiver that passed it are evidence; they are never cleaned up before the Logbook entries that point to them.
  • Legal hold overrides cleanup. A hold on a Flight or a release stops every deletion that would touch it, and is itself on the record.
  • Deletion is proved. What is deleted is listed in the Logbook with a count and a digest, never silently.

PCI DSS asks for at least twelve months of audit history, with the last three immediately available. The default floor is open for you.

Tamper evidence

Today the Logbook is append-only by design but not tamper-evident: a person with write access to the database could change a row and nothing would show it. The plan chains the entries.

  1. Each entry carries a hash of the entry before it, so an edit or a deletion breaks the chain at that point.
  2. At regular intervals the Base signs a checkpoint of the chain's head with its own key.
  3. A checkpoint can be exported for safekeeping, stored in storage the customer owns, or timestamped by a timestamp authority the Base chooses (the open timestamp protocol, RFC 3161).
  4. Verify the Logbook walks the chain from any checkpoint and names the first entry that does not match, if any. It works on an export, offline.
# Design: not built.
launchway logbook verify --from checkpoint:812 --export ./logbook-export.jsonl
chain whole: 18,422 entries from checkpoint 812 to 829, signatures valid (key harbor-lights/signing)

Streaming to an outside system

The Logbook can be sent, as it is written, to a log or security-monitoring system the team already runs. Delivery uses the "events out" Hardpoint (extension point): each delivery is signed, numbered in sequence so a receiver can see a gap, retried until it is accepted, and shown in a delivery log, as notifications are today. A team that only collects standard output already gets every entry as a JSON line.

Evidence packs

For any release, an evidence pack is one document that answers an assessor's questions in order. It is produced from the record when it is asked for, so it costs nobody any work, and it is signed by the Base so it can be checked after it leaves Launchway. It comes as a page to read, a printable document and a machine-readable file.

SectionWhat it showsWhere it comes from
WhatFlight, version, image digests, the commit, its author and whether its signature verifiedThe release and the commit
ReviewThe pull request, its reviewers, the merge verdict, any merge past a branch rule and its reasonPull request events
BuildThe Sortie, the Station, the pipeline at its commit, library pins, the build record, the list of contents, the signatureSortie events and the Depot
TestsThe Debrief summary: totals, failures, flaky tests, coverage of the changeStep summaries
InspectionFindings new, existing and accepted, with each acceptance's reason, owner and endThe Inspection verdict
Standing ordersEvery verdict at every point: rule, answer, facts, waiverspolicy.evaluated events
ClearancesWho said Go or No-go, when, what they were shown, the typed fields they gaveClearance events
LaunchesEach Airfield in order, the strategy, start and end, any Hold or window overrideLaunch events
OverwatchThe proofs, their measurements against the baseline, the verdictVerification events
Return to baseIf it happened: when, why, who, and what ran afterLaunch events
IntegrityThe Logbook checkpoint that covers the pack, and the Base's signature over the packThe chain
Built today

A release already carries its images, build records and Clearances. Each Sortie's verdicts can be read through the API (GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/policy). There is no single evidence document yet, and no period report.

# Design: not built. The machine-readable form of one pack, shortened.
evidence:
  release: storefront 2.4.0
  digest: sha256:4f9c...a17
  work_item: STORE-41
  commit: { sha: 9d2e71a, author: dana, signature: verified }
  review: { pull_request: 482, approved_by: [ana], merge_verdict: allow }
  build: { sortie: 417, station: build-03, provenance: slsa-v1, contents: 214 components, signed_by: harbor-lights/signing }
  tests: { total: 412, failed: 0 }
  inspection: { new: 0, existing: 3, accepted: 1 }
  standing_orders: [ { point: launch, airfield: prod, rule: approvals, answer: clearance } ]
  clearances: [ { by: ana, decision: go, fields: { change_ticket: CHG-88, risk: low } } ]
  launches: [ { airfield: staging, result: complete }, { airfield: prod, result: returned_to_base } ]
  overwatch: { verdict: failed, reason: error rate above baseline at 10 percent }
  integrity: { logbook_checkpoint: 829, pack_signature: valid }

Mapping evidence to published frameworks

Your requirements and the roadmap name two frameworks: PCI DSS and HIPAA. The compliance pack lists each control area, the controls Launchway provides for it, and the evidence that shows those controls ran. Every page carries the label: Evidence support. Not a certification or attestation. What Launchway helps with and what remains the customer's own work is in the roadmap's responsibility matrix.

Control areaPCI DSSHIPAA Security RuleControls and evidence Launchway provides
Change controlRequirement 6.5—Reviewed merges, tests, Clearances with typed fields, a way back for every Launch; evidence packs and change records
Separate duties and environmentsRequirement 6.5—Separate Airfields; the starter, author and publisher cannot clear; the separation-of-duties report
Software inventory and vulnerabilitiesRequirement 6.3—Lists of contents per release; Inspection findings; Maintenance pull requests; patch deadlines
Secure developmentRequirement 6.2—The Inspection on every change; required shared scanning steps
Access by needRequirement 7164.312(a)(1)Roles per level; who can do what, and why
Identify and authenticateRequirement 8164.312(d)Sign-in with a second factor; expiring tokens; Station identity
Audit logs and reviewRequirement 10164.312(b)The Logbook, its chain, its retention floor and its stream
IntegrityRequirement 10164.312(c)(1)Signatures, digests and the Logbook chain
Protect stored keys and dataRequirement 3164.312(a)(2)(iv)Encryption at rest under a root key held outside the database
TransmissionRequirement 4164.312(e)(1)Encrypted transport; refusal of unencrypted database connections (planned)
Unverified

The requirement and section numbers above are written from memory of the published texts and must be checked against the current published versions before this mapping is shipped. The mapping itself is a proposal.

Control checks, and more published frameworks

A mapping says which controls answer which clause; an assessor then asks whether each control actually ran, every day of the period. The plan answers that with control checks: each one reads one recorded fact, for one scope and one period, and passes or fails with links to the events it read. Nobody fills them in, and they cannot drift from what happened, because they are computed from the record.

Beside PCI DSS and HIPAA, the plan proposes mappings for three widely used published frameworks: the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (common criteria), ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, and NIST SP 800-53 as a government baseline, with the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218) for the build controls. The first control checks:

Control checkFact it readsSOC 2ISO/IEC 27001 Annex ANIST SP 800-53
Every change to a protected branch was reviewed by someone other than its authorMerge verdictsCC8.1A.8.32CM-3
Every production Launch had a Clearance from someone other than its starter and authorClearance eventsCC8.1A.5.3AC-5, CM-3
Every production Launch was judged by the Standing orders in enforce modepolicy.evaluated eventsCC8.1A.8.32CM-4
Every release has tests, an Inspection and a list of contentsStep summaries, Inspection verdictsCC7.1A.8.29SA-11
New high and critical vulnerabilities were fixed within the level's deadlineFindings and their fixesCC7.1A.8.8RA-5, SI-2
Every production image was signed and its build record verified at LaunchVerification eventsCC8.1A.8.32SI-7
Every person with Commander rights used a second factorSign-in eventsCC6.1A.8.5IA-2(1)
No token outlived the level's maximum; unused access was removedToken and binding eventsCC6.2A.5.18AC-2
Roles were granted per level, and every change to them is recorded as a differenceSetting-change eventsCC6.3A.5.15AC-6
The Logbook chain was whole and its checkpoints signedThe chainCC7.2A.8.15AU-9
Stored secrets and keys were sealed under a root key held apartThe doctor's encryption check, recorded dailyCC6.1A.8.24SC-28
Every waiver had an owner, a reason and an end, and none outlived itWaiver eventsCC3.4A.5.36CA-7
Needs a check against the published text

Every criterion, control and clause number in this table is written from memory of the published frameworks and has not been checked. Each must be checked against the current published version before the mapping ships, and the pack shows "not yet checked" beside any reference that has not been. The SSDF practice references for the build controls are left out until they are checked.

  • Honest words. Every page keeps the label "Evidence support. Not a certification or attestation." A passing control check says a control ran; it never says an organization meets a framework.
  • Per period and per scope. Each check runs for a Base, Wing, Squadron or Flight and a period; a failure lists the events that failed it, and an exception (a waiver, a self-clearance in a one-person Base) is shown, never hidden.
  • One list, many frameworks. A control check is written once and cited by every framework that needs it; adding a framework adds a mapping, not new evidence.
  • Open to every edition. Control checks and every mapping are part of the product for everyone, not a higher tier.

Who is assessed matters. A self-hosted installation is the customer's own system, so the customer's assessor examines it; Launchway's job is to make that easy with secure defaults, controls that can be shown to be on, and evidence that can be exported. A certificate or attestation of Launchway itself matters only for the hosted service, and the roadmap orders it after the service has run.

Separation of duties in a team of any size

TeamRules that applyWhat the record says
One person (a freelancer's Base)Two people are not possible. Whether the starter may clear their own Sortie is open for you. Overwatch and Return to base stay on, so a bad Launch still comes back by itself."Cleared by the starter, allowed by Standing order solo-base", on the Sortie, in the evidence pack and in the separation-of-duties report
A small team (Harbor Lights)The starter cannot clear (today). The author of a change is never its only approver; the publisher of a release cannot clear it (today, for release Clearance).Each Clearance names the person and why they were allowed to give it
A larger or regulated teamCounts from distinct groups; nobody clears a rule that applies to them; a change to a Standing order is cleared by someone other than its author; a waiver in production may need a second person (open for you).The separation-of-duties report for the period lists every exception
AgentsAn agent never clears its own work. Where a Standing order allows, an independent reviewing agent with a different identity may clear listed kinds of change, and a share is sampled by a person.The agent, its autonomy level and the sampling decision

Change records, built in or in your own system

Every Launch to an Airfield marked for change control becomes a change record with its evidence, without anyone filling in a form. A repeatable low-risk change is a standard change approved by a rule; a normal change goes to the right people with the evidence; an emergency change acts first and is reviewed after. Risk is computed from facts and shown with its reasoning.

The built-in change records work with no other system. A team that already runs a change-management system connects it instead, as an equal choice: the roadmap's existing connections to ServiceNow and Jira Service Management, and others through the same interface. One provider is in charge per Base: the record is opened there, and the approval given there comes back as a Clearance with the approver's identity. If the outside system cannot be reached, the Launch waits with that reason; Return to base never waits for it.

What an auditor can see and do

An auditor is an Observer (viewer) with the evidence permission: no new role. A Commander (owner) grants it for a scope (a Base, a Wing, a Squadron or a Flight) and for a stated time, after which it ends by itself.

Can

  • Read the Logbook, verdicts, Clearances, waivers, findings and lists of contents of the scope
  • Open, export and verify evidence packs and the Logbook chain
  • Read the separation-of-duties report, the compliance pack and its control checks, and the verdicts across the levels of the scope

Cannot

  • Change, start, clear or waive anything
  • See a secret value (none is stored)
  • See source code, unless also given read access to the repository
  • See anything outside the scope or after the grant ends

Is recorded

  • The grant, who gave it and why
  • Every page opened and every export, in the Logbook of the scope

Worked example: the evidence for storefront 2.4.0

Sam is asked, weeks later, why storefront 2.4.0 (sha256:4f9c…a17, built by Sortie 417 from pull request #482) returned to base. Sam opens the release and its evidence pack. In one page: Dana's signed commit and work item STORE-41; Ana's review and Clearance with change ticket CHG-88 and risk "low"; 412 tests passed; no new findings, one accepted with its end date; every Standing order verdict at the merge, Sortie start, image push and both Launches; the Launch to staging and then prod with a Pathfinder (canary) at 10 percent; Overwatch's measurement of the error rate against the baseline; the automatic Return to base to 2.3.2 with its reason; and the Logbook checkpoint that covers all of it. The change record in the connected change system was closed with the same facts. Nobody assembled anything.

The foundation it relies on

  • One append-only record. Nothing is true that is not on it; every reading on this page is computed from it.
  • Events that carry their reasons. Verdicts, Clearances and Launch decisions record their facts, so they can be read back and judged again.
  • The Base's key. It signs Logbook checkpoints and evidence packs.
  • Levels and permissions. Who reads what is the same model as who does what.

Change records are a module of their own and meet the module contract: built in by default, a connection to an outside system as an equal choice with "served by" shown, off until wanted, equal on every way in, and never in front of Return to base.

Safety

If this failsWhat happens
A server dies while writingAn action and its Logbook entry are written together; there is no action without its entry.
The database is lostThe record is restored from backup; the last exported checkpoint shows exactly how far the restored chain reaches and what is missing.
The outside log system is downDeliveries wait and retry in order; nothing is dropped; the delivery log shows the backlog.
Someone edits the database by handThe chain breaks at that entry and verification names it.
A Station is lostIts Sortie events up to the loss are on the record; the lost attempt is recorded as lost.

Who may do what. A Commander (owner) of the Base sets retention floors, legal holds, streaming destinations and auditor grants. A Commander of a level reads that level's Logbook. Reading sign-ins, tokens, monitoring queries and vendor actions needs the security permission. Nobody can edit or delete an entry, and cleanup under a retention rule is itself an entry. On by default: every action and refusal is recorded; secrets and pipeline text are never recorded.

Screens

Logbook
A list filtered by level, person, action, outcome and time, all picked; the chain's state at the top; each entry opens its detail and links to its target.
Evidence pack
One page per release in the order of the sections above, each with its source, and a header with the pack's signature and checkpoint.
Export evidence (wizard)
Pick the scope, the Airfields, the period, the framework mapping and the format; preview the count; export.
Compliance pack
A framework picked from a list, its control areas, and for each the controls and their evidence, with the label "Evidence support. Not a certification or attestation."
Retention and legal hold
Each kind of record with its floor and current size; a legal hold added by picking a scope.
Streaming destinations
A wizard to add a destination, test it and see its delivery log.
Grant auditor access
Pick a person, a scope and an end date; one short reason.
Setting change difference
In the Logbook: each setting change with its fields before and after, secrets as version references, the verdict that let it through, the commit if it came from a file, and Put this value back.
Control checks
For a scope and a period: each control check passed or failed, the events it read, the frameworks that cite it, and "not yet checked" beside any clause reference still unverified.
Separation-of-duties report
For a period: every Clearance, self-clearance, merge past a rule, Hold override and waiver, with who and why.
