Open question

  1. The default retention floor for the Logbook and for verdicts. PCI DSS asks for twelve months with three immediately available. Open question
  2. Self-clearance in a one-person Base, which decides the first row of the separation-of-duties table. Open question
  3. Frameworks beyond PCI DSS and HIPAA. The design workspace discusses others for the hosted service; none is on the roadmap. Whether to add mappings for more published frameworks, and in which order. This chapter now designs control checks and proposes SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST SP 800-53 (with the SSDF for build controls) as the next three, in that order; the choice and the order stay yours, and the hosted service's own assessments remain a separate, unanswered decision. Open question
  4. Clause references. Every criterion and clause number in the control-check table must be checked against the published texts before the mapping ships; until then the pack marks them "not yet checked". Open question
  5. Where checkpoints are anchored by default: only signed by the Base, or also timestamped by an outside authority. The recorded delegated decision is "signed checkpoints by default; timestamping optional". Confirm. Open question

Code and review

Keep your code in Launchway or on the code host you already use, and every change is reviewed, checked and merged under the same rules, the same Clearance (approval) and the same record as the Launch (deployment) that follows it.

  • Two equal choices for where code lives: the built-in Git host, or a connection to an outside code host. One of them is in charge of a Flight (codebase), never both.
  • A pull request shows the Sortie (run), the tests, the findings and one plain sentence saying what still stops the merge.
  • Branch rules, code owners, required approvals and suggested changes are built; the merge queue tests the real merged result, one change at a time today and several at once next.
  • Review joins the rest of the flight: merging becomes a point where Standing orders (policies) are judged, and every decision lands in the same Logbook (audit trail).
  • Planned around the code: batches sized from the branch's recent failure rate, large files with locks and quotas shared with the Depot (registry), static pages with a preview per pull request, a wiki and documents with live status beside the code, linked changes across repositories, and an optional workspace in the browser, built in or connected.

Where it sits

Code and review is the first leg of every flight in the story: a change is proposed, checked and cleared before anything is built for an Airfield (environment). It is a module of layer 7 (mission support) that leans on almost every other layer.

Builds on
The foundation: levels and permissions, the database and the blob store that hold repositories (the system; Levels, people and secrets). The record: every push, review and merge is an event (the record). Flight operations: a pull request starts a Sortie on a Station (runner) (What starts a Sortie, Stations and where work runs).
Command
Branch rules today, and Standing orders judged at merge as proposed below (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; Security and the supply chain).
Builds on it
The Depot (registry) receives what the merged commit builds (the Depot); releases are cut from tags (One way to launch, anywhere); Maintenance (dependency updates) and patching arrive as pull requests (the software graph and Maintenance); work items link to the changes that answer them (Work, from idea to running software).
Capability slot
Code host: served by the built-in Git host or by one connection to an outside code host.

What you will be able to do

You push fix/cart-rounding to storefront and open a pull request from the push itself. The page draws the Sortie on its launch line, the Debrief (test report) and the Inspection (security scan) arrive as they finish, and one sentence says: "needs 1 more approval; ci has not passed".

A reviewer from the group that owns /web/ suggests a one-line change. You apply it in one click; it becomes a commit, the earlier approval is dismissed because the code moved, and the checks run again by themselves.

You add the approved pull request to the merge queue. The queue brings it up to date with main, runs the real pipeline on exactly what will land and merges it. If someone else's change ahead of yours breaks it, yours is taken out with the reason and you are told.

The payments code stays on the outside code host the team already pays for. Launchway runs the pipeline, writes a status and one summary comment on the pull request there, and the host's own branch protection refuses the merge while the Sortie fails.

An outside contributor opens a pull request from a fork. It waits until someone with write access approves the first run, then runs restricted: the pipeline file of the default branch, no secrets, no Launch, nothing pushed to the Depot.

Each pull request on storefront gets its own short-lived Airfield with an address on the pull request, torn down when it closes. Planned

You open pull request #482, "Show the delivery date at checkout". Besides the shop on the preview Airfield pr-482, the help pages that explain the new date are published at their own preview address, and the wiki page for checkout shows, live, that prod still runs 2.3.2. Planned

You lock the large checkout banner file before you edit it. Anyone else's push that changes it is refused with your name, and your pull request shows the lock until you release it. Planned

The merge queue on main tests four entries at once because few changes have failed lately, and says so in one sentence; after a failure it halves the batch by itself. Planned

You open a workspace in the browser from pull request #482, with the branch checked out and the Flight's development secrets only, and nothing to install. Your team may serve workspaces from the built-in launcher or from the workspace service it already runs. Planned

How it works

One provider in charge of a Flight's code

A Flight (codebase) reads its code from exactly one place. Either Launchway hosts the repository, or a connection to an outside code host serves it: a narrow service-account token, stored as a reference to a secret, through which Sorties check out, report, tag and write back. Both are equal choices. Everything after checkout (triggers, Sorties, Clearances (approvals), releases, the record) is the same, because the built-in host is one provider under the same contract as the others.

The two can coexist only in a named role: a push mirror kept alongside for one stated purpose (a public copy, a safety copy), or an import that is migrating and ends. The guide already refuses to attach a Flight to an outside repository when its code is hosted here.

What a team needsHosted in LaunchwayAlongside an outside code host
A Sortie on push, tag and pull requestAvailable with no webhook round tripIn progress by webhook, or polling where the host cannot call Launchway
A failing Sortie blocks the mergeAvailable as a required check in branch rulesIn progress as a status the host's protection marks required; a summary comment where the host has no statuses
Review, code owners, required approvalsAvailableDone by the host; Launchway reads the host's branch protection and refuses a direct write that would bypass it
Merge queueAvailable (serial)The host's own, where it has one; Launchway's statuses gate it
Cut a releaseAvailableIn progress tag and release made on the host through the connection
What it cannot doNothing hidden: features that are off are not shownA connection cannot create repositories, merge, review or change branch protection; the Code host page says so, host by host, from a generated matrix
Built today

Nine outside host kinds have connections on the main branch, each declaring for every feature whether the host does it, Launchway emulates it, or it cannot be done, with what to do instead. Each kind is labeled experimental until it passes the conformance suite against the live service. The roadmap item Every Git host, equally is therefore In progress.

A change, from branch to merged

The built-in host moves a branch and records the checks the change waits for in one database step, so a change never looks mergeable before its checks exist. A push opens a pull request (git push -o pr.create) or prints the address to open one. Every revision of the head is kept, so a review belongs to the revision it read.

Whether a change may merge is worked out by the server once, as a list of actions with the plain reason each is or is not available. The web page, the API, the command line, the agent endpoint, auto-merge and the queue all read the same answer, so no screen offers a button that would be refused.

Review in depth

Comments and suggestions

Comments on a line or a range stay attached as the code moves and are marked outdated when the lines themselves change. A suggested change applies as a commit; several apply as one, all or none, and two that touch the same lines are refused, naming both reviewers.

Verdicts

Comment, approve or request changes, tied to a revision. New commits dismiss approvals when the repository says so (on by default). A request for changes stays until it is dismissed with a reason.

Code owners

.launchway/owners is read from the target branch, never from the pull request, so a change cannot give itself an owner. Owners are people and groups; owners are asked to review by themselves, in turns or by fewest open requests.

Branch rules

Required approvals with the lowest role allowed, required checks (also by path), up to date, resolved threads, no self-approval, owner approval, latest push approved by someone else, verified commits only, and an administrator bypass that records what it waived.

Built today

All four cards are on the main branch and documented. Two guides disagree on two points: the pull-request guide still lists forks and signed-commit rules as missing, while the forks guide and the verified-commits guide document both as working (require_verified_push). The newer guides are right; the stale list should be corrected.

Conflicts resolved in the browser

When a pull request cannot merge cleanly, the server already returns each conflict as data (the file, the two sides and the common ancestor), and the API, the agent endpoint and launchway pr can submit the commit that resolves it. The web page is next: for each file you choose ours, theirs or edit; edit opens both sides beside the result, already filled in, and the commit message is filled in too. A file too large or binary to edit on the page is offered as ours or theirs only, with the reason.

The resolving commit is a new commit like any other, with no special path. The required checks run again on it, approvals given before it are dismissed where the repository dismisses stale approvals (the default), and the merge answer is worked out again. A resolution cannot quietly carry an earlier approval past a change of code. In progress: API, agent and command line built; the page is planned.

The merge queue: today and next

Today the queue is serial. It takes the entry at the front, merges main into it (a push, so the branch's own checks run on exactly what will land), waits for the required checks and merges. An entry that fails, conflicts, loses an approval or gets new commits is taken out with the reason, the person who queued it is told, and the next one goes on. The Holding pattern (queue) is visible on each change.

Next, the queue tests several entries at once, each stacked on the ones ahead, in parallel Sorties. When all pass, all land in order. When one fails, the queue splits the batch to find which entry caused it, takes that one out and lands the rest. A busy repository then merges at the speed of its slowest Sortie, not of the sum of them.

How big a batch is, and lanes that keep failures apart

A fixed batch size is wrong most of the time: too big on a bad day, when nearly every batch fails and has to be split, and too small on a good day, when Stations sit idle. The queue sizes each batch from the branch's own recent history instead.

  1. Start from the failure rate. The share of the last 50 entries on the branch that failed sets the starting size: the largest batch that would land whole at least two times in three.
  2. Follow the day. After a batch lands whole, the next one may be one bigger; after a batch fails, the next one is half the size. The size never goes below one or above the ceiling and the most Sorties per batch that the protected branch sets.
  3. Do not split for a known flaky test. When the only failure is in a test already marked flaky (see Fast pipelines and continuous deployment), that test runs once more before the batch is split, so one unreliable test does not throw out good changes.
  4. Say why. The Holding pattern (queue) page shows the size in use and one sentence: "Batch of 4: 4 of the last 50 entries failed (8 percent); a batch of 4 lands whole about 72 percent of the time."

Lanes. Most changes in a busy repository cannot affect each other: a change to the web front end and a change to a database migration reach different components. The software graph already knows which components each file reaches. With lanes, entries whose reach does not meet wait in separate lanes of the same queue and are tested in parallel, so a failure holds only its own lane. Entries whose reach meets share a lane and its order. Every Sortie still tests the merged result, and every landing is still one compare and swap. A file the graph cannot place puts its entry in every lane, so a gap in the graph makes the queue slower, never unsafe. This is advantage 3 of the plan, the fastest safe path, applied to merging.

# Design: not built. Merge queue settings on a protected branch, chosen on the Merge rules page.
merge_queue:
  batch: { size: follow_failures, ceiling: 8, most_sorties: 8 }
  flaky_retry: once
  lanes: from_graph

How review connects to everything else

Review is not a separate product with its own users, rules and log. It uses the same pieces as a Launch (deployment).

PieceIn reviewIn a LaunchStatus
PermissionsThe Flight's roles decide who may push, review and mergeThe same roles, plus the Airfield's reviewersAvailable
Standing ordersBranch rules today; proposed: merging into a protected branch becomes a fixed point where Standing orders are judgedJudged at Sortie start, before a Launch and before an image pushNew in this plan
ClearanceA review approval is recorded with the fields of a Clearance: who, which role, which revision, under which ruleA Clearance with Go or No-goNew in this plan
The recordpull.create, pull.review, pull.merge and the rest in the LogbookLaunch, verdict and Return to base (rollback) eventsAvailable
EvidenceThe release lists the merged pull requests and who approved themThe release lists who cleared each AirfieldAvailable in part

With the merge point in place, one Standing order such as "nothing with a new blocking finding reaches main or prod" is written once and judged at both points, and the status Launchway posts to an outside host carries the same verdict.

# Design: not built. A Standing order judged at the merge point and before a Launch.
standing_orders:
  no-new-blockers:
    at: [merge, launch]
    into: [main]
    airfields: [prod]
    rule: findings
    block: new_blocking

Forks and their trust rules

A fork is your own hosted copy that remembers its parent, root and fork point. It is never more visible than its parent, never sees commits the parent received after the fork unless you sync, and shares stored packs so it costs almost nothing. A pull request from a fork lives in the target: only the head commit and what it needs are copied in.

  1. A first-time contributor's pull request does not run until someone with write access approves it, for that head only.
  2. Once approved it runs restricted: the default branch's pipeline file, no secrets, no Launch, no cache written outside its scope, nothing pushed to the Depot.
  3. Run with secrets is a separate decision on the Sortie, recorded with who made it.
  4. Maintainers may update the fork's branch only when the author allowed it.

The same restricted mode applies to pull requests from forks on an outside host and to automation accounts such as the Maintenance updater.

Results of a Sortie on the pull request, and previews

The pull request page shows the latest Sortie on its launch line, the required checks, the plain reason a change cannot merge, and the Debrief. On an outside host the same result arrives as a status per Sortie and per failed step, and one summary comment updated in place with step counts, test totals and findings. Next: findings and test failures drawn as notes on the lines they concern, so what you read on the line is what blocks the merge.

A preview gives each pull request its own short-lived Airfield with an address, a cost cap and an expiry, posted on the pull request and torn down on close. It reuses the Launch model; there is no second kind of deployment.

# Design: not built. A preview Airfield for every pull request.
steps:
  preview:
    kind: deploy
    preview: true
    needs: [build]
    version: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

Mirrors and releases cut from the code

A pull mirror brings a repository in on a schedule so a team can move at its own pace; a push mirror sends every change to another host as a safety or public copy. Status, last error and lag show on the Tower (home) and raise an alert. Next, a single release branch can be mirrored only after its required checks pass.

Cutting a release reads the merged pull requests since the last one, proposes the next version, makes an annotated tag (refused by protected tags if it would move one), attaches the Cargo (artifacts) and image digests of the Sortie at that commit, and publishes. A push mirror can also publish the release on the outside host, and a connected Flight's release is made on its host. Promotion of the release is in One way to launch, anywhere.

Planned batches, as Queued changes tested together, the failing one found by splitting (Milestone 1, New in this plan); lanes, as Merge queue lanes from what a change affects (Milestone 5, New in this plan).

Linked changes across repositories

Some changes only make sense together: a function added to platform-library and the code in storefront that calls it. A linked change is a named set of pull requests, one per repository, tracked on one page. It is built from the plan's own pieces: the software graph gives the order, the merge queue lands each member, and a Formation (releases that go together) flies the releases.

  • One combined check. Each member is built against the heads of the other members, not against what is on main, so storefront is tested with the library change it needs.
  • All or none. No member merges until every member has passed and been approved under its own repository's rules. For repositories hosted in Launchway the branches move in one database transaction, so either all land or none does; this is possible because every hosted repository keeps its branch heads in the same database. For a member on an outside host the order is kept, and the page says plainly that the landing there cannot be atomic.
  • Each repository keeps its own rules. Owners, required checks and the queue of each repository apply as if the member were alone. The deeper design for many repositories released together is in every way of branching.

Planned Linked changes across repositories, Milestone 5.

Large files: locks, quotas and cleanup

Design files, video, game assets and test data do not belong in Git history. Large files keep a small pointer in the history and the content outside it, through the common Git large-file protocol, so the clients people already use work unchanged. What Launchway adds is that large files are not a separate system: they use the same blob store, quota model and cleanup as the Depot.

Stored once, by digest

Each file is kept by its SHA-256 in the blob store the Depot uses. The same file in two branches, a fork or a release costs once. Uploads are checked against the digest before they are accepted, and a broken upload leaves nothing behind.

Locks that are enforced

Patterns in .launchway/lockable on the default branch mark files that are read-only until locked. A push that changes a file someone else has locked is refused with who holds it. A pull request that changes a locked file shows the lock on the file and cannot merge until the lock is released or its holder approves. Locks are listed on the repository, taken and released from the file page as well as from the client, and an administrator may break one with a reason, recorded in the Logbook.

Quotas shared with the Depot

Large files count in the one quota model that also covers the Depot, Cargo (artifacts) and logs (Repository quotas and size limits). The repository page shows usage by kind, a warning comes before the limit, and a push over quota is refused with what to do.

Cleanup with a preview

An object that no branch, tag, release, open pull request or fork still points to is removed by the Depot's mark and sweep after a grace period. The preview lists what would go and why. A Sortie fetches only the large files the paths of its steps need, and the Station keeps them in its cache by digest.

Planned Large files and Repository quotas and size limits, Milestone 1.

Static pages, with a preview for every pull request

A team often wants a site from its repository: help pages, a design system, a report. Static pages are published by a step, stored in the Depot by digest and served by Launchway with the repository's access rules. Because a site is stored by digest, serving it is a Launch in miniature: a branch points at a digest, a new version is a change of that pointer, and Return to base (rollback) moves the pointer back at once.

# Design: not built. The storefront help pages published as static pages.
steps:
  site:
    run: npm run build-help
  pages:
    kind: pages
    needs: [site]
    from: help/dist
    serve_from: main
    preview: true
  • Same access as the code. A private repository's site needs sign-in and shows only to people who may read the repository; a public one is public.
  • A preview per pull request. The preview reuses the preview Airfield of the pull request (pr-482) and its expiry. It is removed when the pull request closes, and the address is posted on the pull request.
  • Your own domain. A domain is picked from the ones the Wing has verified, and certificates are obtained and renewed automatically through the open ACME protocol.
  • Kept as long as it is served. Retention never removes a digest that a branch or an open pull request serves.

Planned Static pages, Milestone 1, with A preview address for every pull request, Milestone 2.

The wiki and documents beside the code

Documentation goes stale when it lives somewhere else. In Launchway it lives beside the code in two forms, and both are plain Git.

FormWhere it livesWho may edit
The wikiA repository beside the code (storefront.wiki) with history, shown as pages with a sidebarAnyone who may push to the code, edited on the page as commits; a level can require a pull request for chosen pages
Documents in the repositoryA documents folder in the code repository itself, shown with a table of contents and changed through ordinary pull requestsThe repository's own branch rules and owners

Live status in a page. A page can hold live blocks: the version an Airfield runs, the last Sortie of a pipeline, a Launch, a Switch's state, an open work item. Blocks are typed and inserted from pickers in the editor, never typed by hand; each is drawn with the reader's permissions, so a reader who may not see prod sees "not available to you", never the value.

# Design: not built. Live blocks as a page stores them; the editor inserts them from pickers.
[[status: airfield storefront prod]]
[[status: pipeline storefront ci main]]
[[status: work STORE-41]]

Wiki pages and documents are covered by code search (see the graph), can be published as static pages, and the catalog of services reads each service's overview page. The table of what work items offer is in Work, from idea to running software.

Planned A wiki per repository, Milestone 1.

A workspace in the browser, built in or connected

A ready workspace in the browser helps a new person, a quick fix from a phone, or a reviewer who wants to run a pull request. Your normal editor stays as it is; this is optional and off by default.

The test for building it in. The plan builds a capability in when at least two of three hold: it is on every pipeline's path; a solo developer needs it on day one; the commercial products are costly and the commonly used part is tractable. A workspace is on no pipeline's path, and a solo developer starts with the editor on the laptop. The editor itself is a deep specialty, and deep specialties are connected well, not replaced. So Launchway does not write an editor. What it does own is the part that is already its model: starting a container on a Station, the permissions, the secrets and the record.

Provider in charge of "Workspace"What runsWhat Launchway does
Built-in launcherA long-lived step on a Station of the Flight's Ramp (runner pool), from the repository's workspace definition, with an open-source browser editor in it, made available, not copiedStarts and stops it, gives it the branch, the allowed secrets and its own address, stops it when idle and keeps uncommitted changes on a work branch
A connectionThe workspace service the team already runsSends the repository, branch and allowed secret references; shows the address and state the service reports; records who opened what
  • The same rules as a Sortie. A workspace from a fork's pull request runs restricted: no secrets, nothing pushed to the Depot. Otherwise it gets only the secrets the Flight marks for development, never production ones.
  • Laptop first. The workspace definition (.launchway/workspace.yaml, or an existing open workspace definition the repository already carries) opens on a laptop as well, so the browser is a convenience, not a second way to build.
  • Off until wanted. A level turns it on (A development environment in the browser, optional); until then the Open workspace action is not shown.

Planned A development environment in the browser, optional (Milestone 2) and A development environment in the browser (Milestone 14).

Worked moment: pull request #482 with the new pieces

  1. Dana takes a lock on web/assets/checkout-banner.psd and opens pull request #482, "Show the delivery date at checkout", for work item STORE-41. The banner is stored once by digest; the Files tab shows "locked by Dana".
  2. The new date needs DeliveryEstimate from platform-library. Dana links #482 and the library's pull request as the linked change delivery-date; the combined check builds storefront against the library's head.
  3. The help pages are built in the same Sortie and published at the preview address of pr-482; the checkout page of the wiki shows, live, that prod runs 2.3.2.
  4. A reviewer opens a workspace from #482 to try a date format, served by the built-in launcher; it gets the development secrets only and stops after an idle hour.
  5. Both members pass and are approved. Each repository's queue tests its member on the merged result, storefront's in a batch of four; when both are ready, the two branch moves are made in dependency order inside one transaction, because both repositories are hosted here. Dana releases the lock.
  6. Sortie 417 on main builds storefront 2.4.0, digest sha256:4f9c…a17, and publishes the help pages; the preview address of pr-482 is removed.

Worked example: Harbor Lights changes checkout

  1. Dana pushes fix/cart-rounding to storefront, hosted in Launchway, with -o pr.create. Pull request 214 opens; the Logbook records pull.create with the source git push.
  2. .launchway/owners on main says /web/ belongs to @group:storefront-web and /db/ to @group:data. The change touches both, so both groups are asked.
  3. Sortie 389 runs ci: tests pass, the Inspection finds nothing new. The rule on main asks for one approval, owner approval and ci; the page says "needs approval from an owner of /db/".
  4. Ana, in @group:storefront-web, approves. Sam, in @group:data, suggests renaming a column in a migration. Dana applies the suggestion as a commit; Ana's approval is dismissed because new commits arrived, and Sortie 390 runs.
  5. Ana and Sam both approve revision 3. Dana chooses Add to the merge queue. Another change is ahead; 214 waits second, and its place shows on the page.
  6. The queue merges main into 214, Sortie 391 passes on that exact result, and the server merges with compare and swap. Sortie 392 on main builds the image and pushes it to the Depot by digest.
  7. Meanwhile payments, served by a connection to the team's outside code host, gets status ci and one summary comment on its own pull request; the host's protection keeps it from merging until that status is green.

Which is right

The Git hosting area page says serving over HTTPS is in progress and that SSH and review are planned. The roadmap data and the guides say Git hosting, SSH, pull requests, review, code owners and the merge queue are Available. The guides are right; the area page is stale. Five more items are understated by the roadmap against the guides: Forks and templates, Resolve conflicts in the browser, Repository trash, Create, rename, archive and set visibility and Templates for changes and work. The proposals below move each to In progress, with what is still missing.

The module contract check

Contract pointHow Code and review meets itStatus

10. Never blocks Return to baseA Return to base launches a recorded earlier digest; it needs no merge and no review. Where a Launch writes back to a GitOps repository, the write-back of a Return must pass protected branches as a recorded bypass of kind "return", never wait in a merge queue. A large-file lock or a linked change never holds a Return to base, which moves no files; a static site returns by moving its pointer back.New in this plan

Safety

A server dies mid-push
A push is acknowledged only when it is durable in the database and the blob store; servers keep only caches they can rebuild. The proof is a test that stops servers mid-push (Safe storage and failover for repositories, Planned).
A merge races a push
The merge and the move of the branch are one compare-and-swap; on a race it is made again on the new tip, up to five times, then fails cleanly and says so.
The database fails over
Branch heads and history live in the database with atomic updates; a failover never loses an acknowledged push (Database failover and no lost push, In progress).
A Station dies during a check
The Sortie's step is retried or fails with its reason; the pull request shows "has not passed" and never a stale green.
An outside host is unreachable
The Flight is polled when deliveries stop; a pull request whose author cannot be checked waits, and the decision says so, instead of running unchecked.
A large-file upload breaks
Content is accepted only when its SHA-256 matches; a broken upload leaves nothing, and a commit whose pointer names content that never arrived is refused.
A site fails to publish
The branch keeps pointing at the digest it served; nothing half-published is ever served.
A workspace's Station dies
Uncommitted changes are pushed to the work branch every few minutes and on idle stop; the workspace can be opened again from that branch.
Who may do what
viewer reads and comments; operator pushes, reviews, queues and merges within the rules; admin sets rules, protected tags and fork settings and may bypass a rule with a reason. Nobody may push to refs/pull/. Planned: anyone who may push may lock; only an admin may break someone else's lock, with a reason; publishing a site to a domain needs admin.
On by default
Dismiss stale approvals, protected tags that nobody may move, restricted fork runs, first-time contributors held, forks off for private repositories, the merge answer computed once. Planned: locks enforced at push and merge, batch size that follows failures, sites and workspaces off until a level turns them on.

Screens

Full field lists are in the screens notes for this chapter; the mock-up views draw them (screens).

Pull request

Launch line of the change, the gate box with the one sentence, tabs for conversation, commits and files, the queue place, and the results of the latest Sortie. Actions come from the server's list.

Open a pull request (wizard)

Pick the branch with the changes and the target from lists of branches with their last result; the description starts from the template; reviewers are pre-filled from owners.

Merge rules

Per protected branch or pattern: each rule as a switch or a number with its plain meaning, checks picked from the pipeline's steps, and a preview of what it would change on open pull requests.

Merge queue

The Holding pattern of a branch: entries in order, the Sortie testing each, batches next, and every exit with its reason.

Code host (served by)

Which provider serves the Flight, the host's feature matrix, the webhook setup and the last delivery, and the guided move between providers.

Fork and contributor runs

Make a fork from a picker of owners you may write to, see ahead and behind, sync; approve a first-time contributor's run on the Sortie.

Resolve conflicts

Each conflicting file with ours, theirs or edit; both sides beside the result; the message filled in; a note that checks run again and stale approvals are dismissed.

Large files and locks

Usage against the shared quota by kind, the lockable patterns, every lock with its holder and age, lock and release from the file page, break a lock with a reason.

Static pages

The site's address, the branch it serves from, the digest served and the ones before with one Return to base action, previews per pull request, and the domain picked from verified ones.

Wiki and documents

Pages with history, edit as a commit, live blocks inserted from pickers, and the documents folder of the code with its table of contents.

Linked change

The members, the order from the graph, the combined check, each member's approvals and queue place, and whether the landing will be atomic.

Workspaces

Open workspace from a branch or pull request, the provider in charge, running workspaces with their idle timer, and the turn-on wizard for a level.

Proposed roadmap changes

New items and changes to existing ones, in the roadmap's item shape. Each names the requirement or ruling it serves. The same list is kept for the editor in the proposals notes.

Open question

Decision needed

Merge as a Standing orders point. Branch rules are the repository's own gates; Standing orders are a level's. Should a level's Standing orders also be judged at merge (proposed), and when both say something, does the stricter win? Recommendation: yes, and the stricter wins, shown in one sentence.

Decision needed

A review approval recorded as a Clearance. The proposal keeps the word "approve" on the review screen and records the decision with a Clearance's fields. The alternative is to call it a Clearance on the screen too. Recommendation: keep "approve" for review; Clearance stays the word for Airfields and releases.

Decision needed

Return to base through a protected GitOps branch. Should the write-back of a Return to base pass protected branches as a recorded bypass of kind "return" by default? Recommendation: yes; a level may require a second person after the fact, never before.

Decision needed

Built-in workspaces at all. The build-or-connect test says connect the editor. Should Launchway offer the built-in launcher (an open-source editor made available on a Station) beside the connection, or the connection only? Recommendation: both, the launcher off by default, because it is only the step contract on a Station and needs no editor of its own.

Decision needed

How strict a lock is. Recommendation: a lock refuses others' pushes and holds the merge, and its holder's approval lets the merge through; an administrator may break it with a reason.

Decision needed

Batch size by itself. Recommendation: batches follow the failure rate by default once batches are built, with a fixed size as a choice on the Merge rules page.

Decision needed

Squadrons as reviewers. Owners are people and groups today. Should a Squadron be usable as an owner, meaning "the people with a role in this Squadron"? Recommendation: yes, resolved to people at the time of the review.

The Depot

The Depot (registry) is one place for everything a build produces and everything it consumes, kept by digest, judged on the way in and on the way out, and promoted from Airfield (environment) to Airfield without ever being built again.

  • Images, charts, other OCI content and Cargo (artifacts) from Sorties (runs) are stored today, in the same database and blob store as everything else; packages in every major format and a pull-through cache of outside registries are next.
  • Everything is known by its digest. A release records digests, and promotion launches the same digest; nothing is rebuilt between Airfields (environments).
  • Inspection (security scan), signatures and contents lists sit beside what they describe, and Standing orders (policies) judge a push and a Launch (deployment).
  • An outside registry is an equal choice. One provider is in charge per Squadron (team), and pipelines name the capability, never the product.
  • Planned: every format with your own, cached and one-address repositories; one table of every kind it holds, each inspected on arrival and again when advisories appear; search by name, digest, file, component, advisory, license and user; infrastructure state kept with locks, versions and recorded reads; permissions per package that read the same for every format; replication that carries signatures and attestations; retention that also keeps what a published release or a running host needs; and a view of who uses which version.

Where it sits

The Depot is the hand-off between building and launching. In the story it is the hold where Cargo waits, sealed and labeled, until a flight takes it to an Airfield.

Layers
Layer 4, flight operations: what a Sortie (run) built, by digest. It feeds layer 5, Launch, which takes a digest as the release (One way to launch, anywhere), and it is checked by layer 6, command, at the image push and before a Launch (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold).
Builds on
The blob store and database of the foundation (the system); the roles of the Flight (codebase) (Levels, people and secrets); credentials made per Sortie on the Station (runner) (Stations and where work runs).
Builds on it
The software graph keys its facts by digest (the software graph and Maintenance); release promotion and Return to base (rollback) launch recorded digests; Maintenance (dependency updates) reads versions from it; triggers start Sorties when something arrives (What starts a Sortie).
Capability slot
Depot: served by the built-in Depot or by one outside registry or artifact repository.

What you will be able to do

Your storefront Sortie builds an image and pushes it with no password: the step gets a credential made for that Sortie, which can push only to its own Flight and stops working when the Sortie ends. The image arrives with its contents list, its scan result and its signature beside it.

You promote storefront 2.4.0 from staging to prod. The Launch uses the digest the release recorded; nothing is built again, so what was tested is exactly what flies.

Retention clears out a month of untagged test images, and the preview shows two digests it will not touch: the one prod runs and the one a Return to base would go back to.

platform-library publishes a new Go module version to the Depot. The arrival is an event; the Flights that depend on it start, providers first, and the library page shows who fetched which version. Planned

The public package registry is down for an hour. Your builds keep going, because the Depot's pull-through cache serves every pinned version it already holds, and says plainly which moving versions it could not check. Planned

Your security group already runs an outside artifact repository. You keep it in charge for the payments Squadron; the pipelines do not change, the Standing orders still judge each push, and the Depot page says who serves it.

Someone publishes a package called platform-library on the public registry, hoping your builds will pick it up. They do not: the name is published in your own repository, so the Depot's one address never looks it up outside. Planned

You open the platform-library page and see that payments still pins a version with an advisory while storefront is current. One button asks Maintenance for the update pull request. Planned

Your disaster-recovery registry receives storefront 2.4.0 with its signature, contents list and provenance, and the copy is checked at the far end before the rule calls it done. Planned

Every kind of thing the Depot holds

One table says what the Depot holds, how each kind is found, whether Inspection (security scan) reads it, and what is built. The Depot is an OCI registry: it speaks the open OCI distribution protocol, and it will claim conformance only after the standard's own conformance tests pass (they have not been run yet; see the status).

Contents lists, signatures, provenance and other attestationsOCI referrers of the digest they describe, listed with the open referrers callNot scanned themselves; they are what Inspection reads. Signatures are verifiedAvailable stored; In progress verification on pull and Launch
ReportsScan results as referrers of their digest; test reports and the Sortie report as Cargo of the SortieNot scanned: they are results, kept beside what they describeAvailable
Infrastructure stateStack instance (stack and Airfield) and version numberNo vulnerability scan; its values are never shown as raw text, and plans made from it are judged by Standing ordersAvailable State and locking built in; Planned as a Depot kind
Stored plans of infrastructure stacksDigest, encrypted, with the state version and commit they were made fromJudged by Standing orders on their plan facts, not scannedNew in this plan (see infrastructure stacks)

Packages in every format: your own, cached, and one address

Each package format (Go modules, npm, Python, Maven and Gradle, NuGet, Rust crates, RubyGems, a classic Helm index, Debian and RPM, infrastructure modules and providers, generic files) gets the same three kinds of repository. Each speaks the format's native protocol, so the package tool needs only an address (Native endpoints for package clients).

KindWhat it holdsWhat makes it safe
Your ownPackages your Sorties and people publishA published version can never be overwritten; publishing is one step with a credential made for the Sortie
CachedA copy of one outside source, fetched once and keptInspected on arrival like any push; a pinned version is reused, a moving name is looked up again and the Sortie says how old its answer was
One addressReads your own repositories first, then the cached ones, in a fixed order you setA name published in your own repository is never resolved from a cached one, so a public package cannot take the place of yours
  • Versions are immutable. Version-based formats have no tags to move: a version, once published, is fixed. A bad version can be withdrawn: it stays fetchable by an exact pin or a lock file, so nothing that already depends on it breaks, but it is no longer chosen for a version range, and its page says why it was withdrawn.
  • Retention by version. Rules keep the newest N versions and versions matching patterns. A version a default branch's lock file still names (read from the software graph), or that a published release carries, is never removed.
  • Infrastructure modules behave like libraries. Modules and providers are published and fetched through the open module registry protocol, pinned by version and checksum where they are used. A new version raises a notice on the module page and on each Flight that uses it, and Maintenance (dependency updates) offers the update as a pull request, exactly as for a pipeline library.

Planned More package formats and Native endpoints for package clients, Milestone 4; infrastructure modules as Infrastructure modules pinned and updated like libraries, Milestone 4, New in this plan.

Permissions per package, the same for every format

Today a repository in the Depot follows the roles of its Flight: viewer pulls, operator pushes, admin deletes. That is too coarse for a shared library that many may read and only two people may publish. The design adds role bindings at each level, written once and read the same way for an image, a Go module and a Debian package.

  • A binding names a person, a group or a Squadron, a role (viewer, operator, admin) and a scope: a level, a Depot repository, or a package name pattern.
  • Levels narrow, never widen. A binding set nearer can narrow what a level above allowed; it cannot widen what a level locked. The verb list is the same for every format: read, publish, withdraw, delete, set rules.
  • Protected packages. A name pattern marked protected refuses overwrite and delete for everyone, including administrators; only withdrawal is possible. Protected tag patterns for images are the same rule.
  • Sorties publish only their own. A Sortie's credential carries the publish right only for the packages its Flight owns, whatever the person who started it may do.
# Design: not built. Bindings on the platform-library package, set by Squadron "shop".
depot_access:
  - package: "harborlights/platform-library*"
    bind:
      - { who: "squadron:shop", role: operator }
      - { who: "wing:harbor-lights", role: viewer }
    protected: true

Planned Per-package permissions for every format, Milestone 4, New in this plan. Today: Per-project packages and permissions, Available, by Flight roles only.

Everything by digest

A digest is the fingerprint of the content: change one byte and it changes. A tag is only a name that points at a digest, and tags that match a protected pattern (v*) can never be moved or deleted once pushed; a pattern set at a wider level cannot be removed nearer. A release records the digests its Sortie built, the pipeline's deploy step receives them as inputs, and the matrix of releases shows which digest runs in each Airfield. That is why a promotion moves no bytes and builds nothing.

The same rule governs the cache. A pinned version or a digest is fixed: the Depot reuses it. A moving name (latest, a version range, a branch) is looked up again, and the Sortie says what it used and how old it was. A cache is a head start, never the answer.

Promotion by digest across Airfields

Today promotion happens on the release: Check and promote starts the Flight's own pipeline at the release's tag with the release's digests as inputs, checks the Airfield's checklist and Clearance (approval) first, and refuses to run a pipeline that cannot be told what to launch. A pipeline that would rebuild is refused with a sentence, not run.

Next, the Depot records the promotion itself: the digest is marked as promoted to the next stop of the release's route (a proposed word, see One way to launch, anywhere), with who cleared it and which proofs passed, in the same record. A digest that has not passed the stop before cannot be launched at the next one, whichever way the Launch is asked for.

Inspection and Standing orders on the way in and out

An image step builds, scans, writes a contents list and provenance, signs and pushes. The image_push Standing order is judged before the step is handed to a Station: it can require a scan at a severity, a signature by the Station's own key, a contents list, provenance, and that the push goes only to named Depots. The deployed_images Standing order is judged before a Launch and refuses an unscanned or unsigned image. Every decision is a policy.evaluated event with its reasons.

What is planned is the rest of the doors: a push by a person or an outside tool, and a copy fetched by the cache, judged the same way, with a quarantine state. A quarantined item is kept but cannot be fetched by a Sortie or launched until it passes, or until an exception with an owner, a reason and an expiry is granted.

Asking for an exception is a Clearance (approval), not a setting. The request names the item, the finding that held it, the reason and the expiry asked for; it waits for Go from someone with the right role who is not the person who asked; and the decision is on the record beside the item. When the exception expires the item is quarantined again, and anything that still uses it is told. A Return to base never waits for an exception: it launches a digest that already ran.

# Built today: a level's Standing order on image pushes (names are the machine names).
policies:
  supply-chain:
    image_push: { scan: high, sign: runner, sbom: true, provenance: true, registries: [launchway] }

Inspection of everything stored, and again when advisories appear

Scanning only at build time leaves a gap: what was clean last month may be known vulnerable today. The Depot closes it with two moments of Inspection for every kind in the table above that has contents to read.

  1. On arrival. Whatever the route in (a Sortie, a person, the cache, replication), the item is inspected before it can be pulled by a Sortie or launched, and the result is attached beside its digest as a referrer. Kinds with no known format are marked "not inspected" with the reason, so nobody reads silence as a pass.
  2. When a new advisory appears. Stored contents lists are matched again with no rebuild (Stored parts lists rechecked against new advisories, Continuous scanning of what runs). Each affected digest gets a new result beside it, and the software graph says where it runs.
  3. Standing orders decide. The verdict is judged at the common points: whether a Sortie may pull it, whether it may be launched, whether it is quarantined. A newly affected item already running is never stopped by the Depot; Maintenance and the patching loop take it from there (the graph). A Return to base is never judged.

Planned on arrival for every kind: Inspection of everything that arrives, however it arrives (New in this plan); again on new advisories: Stored parts lists rechecked against new advisories (Milestone 12).

Signatures and contents lists beside what they describe

Signatures, provenance and contents-list attestations an image step writes are stored next to the image, and the scan result and each platform's contents list are attached as OCI referrers, so GET /v2/NAME/referrers/DIGEST lists them with the open protocol any client understands. The image page shows signed or not, contents list, the scan summary and the Sortie and commit that built it. Next: verifying signatures when an image is pulled and launched, and the same referrers for every package kind.

Retention, cleanup and quotas

  • Retention rules per Base (installation), Flight or repository: keep the newest N tagged, keep tags matching patterns, delete untagged older than D days. An exact preview comes first. An image an Airfield runs is never deleted, by retention or by hand.
  • Garbage collection is mark and sweep with a grace period, re-checked at each delete, so a push in progress is never collected; one server collects at a time.
  • Quotas: 20 GiB per Flight by default; a layer counts once however many images use it; a push over quota is refused with what to do.
  • Proposed: retention also keeps the digests of each Airfield's recent stable states, so a Return to base always finds its digest.
  • Proposed: the protected set also holds every digest a published release references, and every digest a running host, function or cluster reports through the software graph, including hosts Launchway only observes. It is worked out just before each sweep, and the preview gives the reason for each digest kept.

Replication and arrival events

Replication copies chosen repositories to and from other registries on a rule, for a disaster-recovery copy or a customer-facing mirror. A copy is the whole item, not only its image: its signatures, contents lists, provenance and scan results travel with it as OCI referrers, and the signature is checked at the far end before the copy is called done. A rule names the repositories and tag patterns, the direction, and either a schedule or "on arrival". The Depot page shows each rule with its lag, its last copy and its last error, and a rule that falls behind raises an alert. Arrival events make the Depot a trigger: a pipeline declares the repository and tag pattern it cares about beside its other triggers, and a new base image or library version starts it.

# Design: not built. A Sortie started when a new base image arrives in the Depot.
on:
  image: { repository: platform/base-go, tags: ["1.*"] }
steps:
  publish:
    kind: publish
    package: { type: go, module: example.com/harborlights/platform }
    version: ${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}

Who uses which version

A library page answers three questions at once, because the Depot and the software graph hold the three facts: the version each Flight's lock file names on its default branch, the version its last Sortie fetched, and the version that runs in each Airfield. The view lists the Flights that are behind first: a version with an advisory, then a major version behind, then the rest. Each row has one action, Ask for the update, which makes Maintenance open the pull request on that Flight; the row then shows the pull request and its state.

FlightLock file namesLast Sortie fetchedRuns in prodAction
payments1.10.4 (advisory)1.10.41.10.4Ask for the update
storefront1.12.01.12.01.11.2Current; prod is behind until 2.4.0 launches

Design, not built: the table above shows the view with example values.

Planned Who uses which version, Milestone 4.

Search across the Depot

Today the Depot area has a search over names in its folders. The design makes the Depot answer the questions people actually ask, from one search box, the do bar, the HTTP API and the command line (launchway depot search, proposed), with the same answers everywhere.

You ask byExampleAnswered from
Name, version or tagstorefront 2.4.0Repository, package and tag records
Digest, or the start of onesha256:4f9cManifests and checksums of every kind
A file inside a package or an image layer/etc/ssl/openssl.cnfThe file list Inspection records when it unpacks an item
A component at a versionWhich images contain platform-library 1.10.4Stored contents lists
An advisory identifierEvery item with that advisory, and where each runsInspection results and the software graph
A licenseEvery package or image that carries a given licenseContents lists
Who uses itFlights and Airfields that fetched or run an itemFetch records and the graph (who uses which version)
  • Filtered by what you may read. Rights are checked when you search. An item you may not pull is not listed or counted, exactly as if it did not exist; infrastructure state is searched by stack name and resource address only, never by value.
  • No second system. Names, digests, contents lists, licenses and findings are already records in the database; file lists are written once on arrival by the Inspection step. Nothing is indexed by a separate search service.
  • Filters are picked from lists: kind, level, repository, format, "runs in" an Airfield, has a finding of a severity, signed or not.

Planned Search across everything the Depot holds, Milestone 4, New in this plan.

Infrastructure state, kept safely

Infrastructure state is the most sensitive thing the Depot keeps: it maps code to real resources and can hold secrets. How stacks are planned, cleared and applied is in One way to launch, anywhere (infrastructure stacks); this section is only the storage side.

PartHow it worksStatus
A state store with lockingThe infrastructure tools reach it over their standard HTTP backend. One lock per stack instance (stack and Airfield); a lock records who took it and which Sortie. Only an admin may break a lock, with a reason, and never while an apply is running.Available
Every version keptEach write is a new sealed version with who, when and which Sortie; the last 50 are kept today. Planned: retention by the Depot's rules, never removing a version a cleared plan was made from.Available; retention rules Planned
EncryptedState is encrypted before it is stored and decrypted only for the Sortie that needs it, with run-scoped credentials. Planned: under the key hierarchy of Encrypt stored files, logs and caches.Available; key hierarchy Planned
Reads are permissioned and recordedThe API, the command line and the agent endpoint never show a value. Planned: a masked difference between any two versions for people with operator; reading raw state is a separate right, given per stack, and every raw read is an event in the Logbook with who and why.Available no values shown; Planned masked difference (State you can read safely) and the raw-read right
Recovery of an earlier versionChoose a version from the history; the restore writes it as a new version, under the stack's lock, so history is never rewritten. In a protected Airfield the restore is a Clearance. The next plan then shows what the restored state means for the real resources.Available Return to base of a version; Planned the Clearance in protected Airfields
One Depot kindState versions appear in the Depot with quotas, search by stack and resource address, and "served by" when a stack keeps its state in your own backend instead.Planned Infrastructure state as a kind the Depot holds, New in this plan

An outside registry as an equal choice

Pushing to any OCI registry works today and stays first class: an image step names a registry connection, and the connection holds the credential. The proposal makes the Depot a capability slot like the others: a Squadron is served by the built-in Depot or by one outside registry or artifact repository, and pipelines say registry: depot. An outside one can also stand in a named role: in front (a cache the team already runs), alongside for one stated purpose (a customer-facing copy), or migrating with a visible end. Its extra features show in place, marked as coming from it.

Worked example: one release of Harbor Lights

  1. Sortie 417 of storefront runs on main at commit 8b63ca7. Its image step pushes storefront/web with digest sha256:4f9c…a17 for two platforms, a contents list for each, a scan with no high findings and a signature by the Station's key. The image_push Standing order passes and is on the Sortie's record.
  2. The same Sortie keeps the resizing function's package as Cargo (resize.zip, SHA-256 recorded) for the serverless target, and the kiosk team's Sortie pushes an operating-system image for the image-based hosts as OCI content.
  3. Dana cuts storefront 2.4.0. The release records the digest and the Cargo; it is fixed once published.
  4. Promotion to dev and staging launches 4f9c by digest. prod is protected: the checklist shows the Clearance waiting; Ana says Go; the deployed_images Standing order confirms the image is scanned and signed; the Launch flies.
  5. Retention runs at night. Its preview keeps 4f9c (runs in prod) and, with the proposal, 9a07 (2.3.2, the last stable state before it).
  6. Later, with packages: platform-library publishes its Go module 1.12.0 to the Depot. The arrival event starts storefront and payments, providers first; the legacy billing service on its two virtual machines receives its next build as a Debian package from the same Depot.

Which is right

Three sources disagree. The registry area page says the Depot is In progress and lists what is not built. The roadmap data marks seven items Available. The guide shows the first slice working and says what is not. The guide is right, and both other sources need a correction: the area page understates (seven items are on the main branch), and two Available items overstate. A built-in OCI registry claims to pass the OCI conformance suite, which the guide says has not been run; The Depot: one area for everything stored lists a proxy cache, replication and packages, which the guide calls later slices. The proposals reword both to what is built; nothing is dropped, because each missing part has its own item.

The module contract check

Contract pointHow the Depot meets itStatus
1. Same levels and permissionsA repository belongs to the Flight named by its first path part; viewer pulls, operator pushes, admin deletes and sets rules; a token limited to Flights is limited here too. Per-package access inside a Flight is planned as role bindings at each level, the same for every format (permissions per package).Available
2. Decisions on the one recordPushes by Sortie, deletes, policy changes, retention and collection are in the Logbook (registry.*); push verdicts are on the Sortie. Planned: every Inspection result on arrival and on a new advisory, every raw read of infrastructure state and every state restore are events too.Available
3. Gates are Standing ordersimage_push and deployed_images are judged at the common points; pushes from outside a Sortie and cached copies join them, and an exception for a quarantined item is a Clearance answered by someone other than the person who asked.In progress
4. Typed input formsRetention rules, quotas and tag patterns are typed fields with a preview; repositories, tags and digests are picked, never typed. Bindings pick people, groups and roles from lists; replication rules pick repositories and far registries from connections.Planned in the web
5. Runs as steps on StationsBuilds, scans, signing and publishing are steps on Stations; retention and collection are server housekeeping with a preview, not steps.Available
6. One capability slot, served bySlot "Depot": built-in or one outside registry per Squadron, with the in-front, alongside and migrating roles.New in this plan
7. Off until wantedregistry.enabled: false turns the store off, but it is on by default wherever sign-in and a Cargo store exist, and the Depot area still shows when the store is off. This differs from the contract; see the open decision.Open question
8. Every way inWeb, API, command line (launchway registry) and agent tools are equal for reading and deleting; Depot rules are not yet in Terraform or Base settings.In progress
9. Loss of a server, the database or a StationSee Safety below.Available
10. Never blocks Return to baseA Return to base launches a recorded digest and is never judged by Standing orders; retention never deletes what runs, and the proposal keeps stable-state digests too.In progress

Safety

A server dies mid-upload
Any server can take the next chunk of an upload another began. Content is not an image until its manifest is pushed, so a broken push leaves nothing anyone can pull, and blobs no manifest needs are collected after the grace period.
The database fails over
Manifests, tags and rules are in the database; blobs are in the Cargo store (the database by default on PostgreSQL, or a directory or S3-compatible storage). Nothing lives only on one server.
A Station dies during a push
The Sortie's credential expires with the Sortie and the step fails with its reason; without a manifest, nothing half-pushed can be pulled.
Collection under load
Mark and sweep with a grace period and a re-check before each delete; one server collects at a time.
Who may do what
Nothing is anonymous: with sign-in off the Depot answers 503 rather than be open. A repository you may not pull answers exactly like one that does not exist. Pull-request and draft Sorties never push.
At rest
Launchway does not encrypt Depot blobs itself in this release: encrypt the volume, the database or the bucket. Per-object encryption is the next slice.
On by default
Private by default, per-Sortie credentials, immutable tag patterns where set, retention that never deletes what runs, a scan and contents list on every image step.

Screens

Full field lists are in the screens notes for this chapter (screens).

Depot home

One area with folders by Wing, Squadron and Flight, a search, and tabs by kind: Images, Charts, Packages, Files, Cached. Each tab says why it is empty.

Item page

For any digest: where it runs now, tags, platforms, contents, findings with fixes, signature, provenance, the Sortie and commit that built it, and its promotions.

Retention and quotas (wizard)

Rules picked as typed values with an exact preview of what goes and what is kept, and why.

Promote by digest

The route of a release, the checks and Clearance at the next stop, and one action that launches the same digest.

Connect an outside registry (wizard)

Pick the kind, give the address and a secret reference, test, choose its role, and see "served by" change.

Quarantine

Items held by Inspection, the finding that held each, and the action to grant an exception with an owner and an expiry.

Package repositories (wizard)

Pick a format, then your own, cached (pick the outside source from connections) or one address (order the members); retention by version and name protection shown before saving.

Access

Bindings by level for a repository or package pattern, who set and locked each, protected patterns, and "who can publish this?" answered for any person.

Replication rules

Each rule with direction, scope, schedule, lag, last copy and last error; a test copy; evidence carried with each item.

Library usage

Each Flight with the version its lock file names, its last Sortie fetched and each Airfield runs, behind first, with Ask for the update.

Depot search

One box with a mode picked from a list (name, digest, file, component, advisory, license, used by) and filter chips; results by kind with digest, where it runs and the latest Inspection result.

Infrastructure state

Per stack instance: the lock and its holder, every version with who and which Sortie, the masked difference between two picked versions, restore as a new version, and the raw-read right with its record.

Exception request (Clearance)

The held item, the finding, the reason and expiry picked from allowed lengths, and the Go or No-go of someone other than the requester.
