Open question

Decision needed

Is the Depot on by default? The contract says a module is off until wanted, and nothing switched off appears in menus. The Depot is on by default wherever sign-in and a Cargo store exist, and its area shows even when the store is off. Recommendation: treat the Depot like Cargo, part of every pipeline's path and on by default, and hide the area only when both the store is off and no outside registry is connected.

Decision needed

Order of package formats. names every major format. A recorded recommendation orders them OCI, Go, npm, then Maven and Gradle, Python, NuGet, Rust crates, RubyGems, with Debian and RPM later. Recommendation: that order, with generic files and Terraform modules beside Go and npm, because releases and infrastructure already need them.

Decision needed

How many stable states retention keeps. Recommendation: the last three per Airfield by default, with a floor a level can lock.

Decision needed

The outside registry you run today. The ruling on the built-in registry keeps it in place and first class, with any move "staged" and decided by you after a soak. This chapter keeps that: it is served by a connection until you decide otherwise.

Decision needed

Who may read raw infrastructure state. Recommendation: nobody by default; the right is given per stack to named people, expires, and every read is recorded with a reason.

Decision needed

Name protection on by default. Recommendation: yes; a name published in your own repository is never resolved from a cached one, and turning that off for one name needs a Clearance.

Decision needed

Can an administrator delete a protected package? Recommendation: no; withdrawal only, and a legal or security removal goes through a Clearance from two people, recorded.

Decision needed

Replication of unsigned items. Recommendation: a rule copies only signed items by default, and says so on the rule page.

Switches

Switches (feature toggles) are a second way to release: the code launches dark, a Switch turns it on for some people with a reason and, where it matters, a Clearance (approval), and Overwatch (the watch after a deployment) turns it back by itself if things get worse.

  • A built-in Switch service is on the main branch: typed Switches per Airfield (environment), rules, segments, sticky percentages, a reason on every change, a Clearance (approval) in a protected Airfield, history and revert.
  • A Master switch (kill switch) turned to its safe value never waits for anyone, and neither does any revert.
  • Applications evaluate Switches locally through small client libraries that follow the OpenFeature standard, so an outage never flips a feature and nothing about your users leaves the application.
  • Next: a Switch change as a pipeline step, rollouts in steps with proofs, Overwatch turning a Switch back by itself, stale Switches retired by a pull request, and an outside flag service as an equal choice.
  • Planned beyond that: experiments with variants, outcome metrics and a verdict from the same statistics as Overwatch, with a clear end; every place the code reads a Switch recorded in the software graph; and an import of Switches from another flag service with nothing dropped silently.

Where it sits

In the story, a Launch (deployment) brings the aircraft to the Airfield; a Switch decides who boards. Switches are a module of layer 7 that works inside layer 5: the last stable state of an Airfield is its version and its Switch values.

Builds on
Levels and their overrides and locks, as for variables (Levels, people and secrets); the record (the record); Clearance and Standing orders (policies) (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold); the Airfield timeline and Return to base (rollback) (One way to launch, anywhere).
Builds on it
Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) and automatic return to stable (Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch); experiments and the traffic view; the Wingman (helper), which reads Switches through the agent endpoint (the Wingman and agents).
Capability slot
Switches: served by the built-in Switch service or by one outside feature-flag service, read through OpenFeature either way.

What you will be able to do

You launch storefront 2.5.0 to prod with the new checkout behind checkout-v2, which is off. Nothing changes for customers. You turn it on for staff with a rule on the e-mail attribute and the reason "staff try-out".

You raise checkout-v2 to 5 percent in prod. Because prod is protected, the change waits until someone else says Go; until then the Switch serves what it served. Raising it later to 25 percent keeps everyone who already had it.

Errors rise ten minutes after the change. Overwatch, watching the same signals it watches after a Launch, turns checkout-v2 back to its value before the change and tells you which Switch it was and why. In progress

At night the card processor fails. The person on call turns the Master switch payments-fallback to its safe value. It takes effect at once, with no Clearance, and the Logbook (audit trail) records who and why.

A Switch has served "on" to everyone for a month. Its page says so, and Launchway opens a pull request that removes the check from the code, for the team to review like any other. Planned

Your company already pays for a feature-flag service. The payments Squadron (team) keeps it in charge; Clearances, the record and Overwatch work the same, and the Switches page says who serves them. Planned

Pull request #482 adds the delivery date at checkout. You do not know whether a countdown helps, so storefront 2.4.0 ships with an experiment of three variants. Nine days later the experiment ends by itself with a verdict you can read in one sentence, and the winner is kept. Planned

You try to delete checkout-v2. Launchway refuses and lists the two places in storefront that still read it, with a link to the pull request that would remove them. Planned

How it works

The model

A Switch belongs to a Flight (codebase), or is shared from a Squadron, a Wing (organization) or the Base (installation), with the same rule as variables: the nearer level overrides, a lock keeps it from being overridden.

PartWhat it is
Key and typeA key such as checkout-v2, and a type: true-or-false, text, number or a structured value. Every value served has that type.
KindRelease, Master switch (with a safe value), experiment, operational or permission. The kind decides the safeguards and how staleness is judged.
State per AirfieldOn or off, prerequisites, rules in order, and what everyone else gets. A Switch starts off in every Airfield.
LifecycleAn owner, an expected removal date, the change that made it, notes on when it may be finished with.

Targeting rules as typed settings

A rule is a list of conditions, each a typed test on one attribute of the context: is, is one of, starts with, ends with, contains, is present, is in a segment, a version comparison by semantic versioning, or a number comparison. A segment is a named, reusable set of rules. A rule serves one value or a percentage. There is no code in a rule, and no free text but the values you compare against; the forms offer attributes the applications have reported and segments that exist.

Percentages are sticky. Each key is hashed with the Switch's own salt into one of ten thousand buckets, the same way on every server and in every client, so raising 5 percent to 25 keeps the first 5 percent, and two Switches never put the same people first.

# Built today: the Switches file for storefront (machine names stay "toggles").
toggles:
  checkout-v2:
    type: boolean
    default: false
    owner: team-storefront
    environments:
      prod:
        on: true
        off_value: false
        rules:
          - id: staff
            clauses: [{attribute: email, op: suffix, values: ["@example.com"]}]
            serve: {value: true}
        fallthrough:
          rollout: {buckets: [{value: true, weight: 500}, {value: false, weight: 9500}]}   # 5 percent

How an application evaluates a Switch

Applications hold a key for one Airfield of one Flight. A server key downloads the rules and evaluates locally; it is a secret. A client key, for a web page or a phone app, never sees a rule: it asks for the values of the Switches marked visible to clients, for a context it sends. A client-visible value is public, so a Switch that guards something dangerous must not be client-visible.

Client libraries for Go and TypeScript, for servers and browsers, and OpenFeature providers for Go and TypeScript are built and tested against the same vectors as the server. They are in the repository and not yet published to package registries. Java, Python and .NET are next. Any application can also read Switches with no Launchway library, through the documented HTTP protocol.

Safeguards, on by default

SafeguardDefaultWhat it does
A reasonOn everywhereEvery change carries a sentence saying why.
A ClearanceOn in a protected AirfieldThe change waits until someone other than the person who asked says Go; the Airfield's reviewers decide who. A waiting change has not happened.
A watchOff todayMarks the Airfield as watched after a change. Proposed: on by default, and acting through Overwatch.
Never heldAlwaysA Master switch to its safe value and any revert are never held for a Clearance. They still need a reason and are recorded.

A team can turn a safeguard down at its level with a reason, recorded in the Switch's history and the Logbook. A level above can lock it; that is the only way a team loses the choice.

A Switch change on the record, and as a step

Every change records who, when, why, how (web page, command line, agent tool, API, pipeline, file, schedule, Return to base), the value before and after, and the Clearances. A change can be scheduled; the servers make it once, and the safeguards apply when it runs. Every change in an Airfield sits on its timeline beside its Launches, and the Return to base page lists the Switch changes made since the version it would restore, offering to revert them too.

Today a pipeline changes a Switch with a step that runs the command line, and the safeguards apply as to anyone. Next, the change is a step of its own kind, judged by Standing orders and watched by Overwatch like a Launch.

# Built today: a step that opens checkout-v2 to 10 percent after verification.
  open-to-ten-percent:
    needs: [verify]
    image: your-registry/launchway-cli
    secrets: [LAUNCHWAY_TOKEN]
    run: launchway toggles set storefront checkout-v2 prod --percent 10 --reason "after verify"
# Design: not built. The same change as a Switch step, with steps and proofs.
  open-checkout:
    kind: switch
    needs: [verify]
    switch: checkout-v2
    airfield: prod
    plan: [{ percent: 5 }, { percent: 25 }, { percent: 100 }]
    between: proofs

A release by Switch, watched by Overwatch

Overwatch judges a Launch against live traffic and metrics: verification after a Launch is built, and the longer watch after the last step is planned in Milestone 8. A Switch change is judged by the same signals, over the same baseline, with the same "starting the return" decision. When the signals worsen after a Switch change, Overwatch returns the Switch to its value before the change, says why, and records the decision; a cause outside the change, such as a failing dependency, does not trigger a pointless return. Today the change is shown as recent and a person reverts it.

Experiments: which variant is better, and by how much

A release by Switch asks "is it safe?". An experiment asks "is it better?". Both are answered by the same parts: the same sticky buckets decide who gets what, the same guarded query layer reads the numbers, and the same statistics component in the server that gives Overwatch its verdict gives the experiment its verdict. There is no second analytics product to set up.

PartHow it works
VariantsA Switch of the experiment kind has two or more typed variants, one of them the control. People are assigned by the Switch's sticky buckets in the split you set, so a person keeps their variant for the whole experiment, and targeting rules can limit who takes part.
Outcome metricsPicked from the measures your Squadron has defined in the guarded query layer (checkout completed, basket value, time to first result). The client library adds the variant to the measures the application already emits, through the OpenFeature hook, so counts are kept per variant and nothing about a person leaves the application. Exposure counts are the ones the libraries already send once a minute.
Sample and powerBefore you start, the form shows how many people each variant needs to detect the smallest effect you care about, and about how long that takes at current traffic.
The verdictA test that stays valid when it is looked at every interval, so watching the numbers does not make a lucky result look real. The verdict states the effect, its interval, the confidence and the sample: "date: checkout completion +1.6 points (0.7 to 2.5), 95 percent confidence, 39,410 people per variant".
A check on the splitIf the people counted per variant drift from the split you set, the verdict is marked untrustworthy with the reason, because a broken assignment makes every number wrong.
GuardsErrors and latency are watched by Overwatch the whole time, as after any Switch change. If a guard worsens, the experiment stops and every person is returned to the control, never held for a Clearance.
A clear endEvery experiment ends: when the sample is reached, at its time limit, or when a guard stops it. The result is then one of "better", "worse", "no difference detected, and the smallest effect this could have detected" or "stopped". The winner is kept for everyone, the Switch becomes a release Switch, and it is due for retirement.
# Design: not built. An experiment on the delivery date at checkout.
toggles:
  checkout-delivery-date:
    kind: experiment
    type: string
    variants: [none, date, date_and_countdown]
    control: none
    experiment:
      airfield: prod
      split: [34, 33, 33]
      outcome: checkout_completed_share
      guards: [error_rate, latency_p95]
      smallest_effect: 1%
      confidence: 95
      end: { sample: reached, at_most: 21d }

Where an outside flag service is in charge and has its own statistics, its results appear in place, marked as coming from it, and the guards, the Clearance and the record stay Launchway's.

  1. Worked moment. Dana defines checkout-delivery-date with three variants and the outcome "checkout completed". The form says each variant needs about 38,000 people to see a one-point change, about nine days at current traffic.
  2. storefront 2.4.0 is already in prod with the Switch on control. Starting the experiment in prod waits for a Clearance; Ana gives Go.
  3. On day three the split check passes and the guards are steady. Priya, on call, sees the experiment on the prod timeline beside the Launch.
  4. On day nine the sample is reached. The verdict: date is better by 1.6 points (0.7 to 2.5); date_and_countdown shows no difference detected. date is kept for everyone, the Switch becomes a release Switch, and maintenance-agent later proposes the pull request that retires it.

Planned Experiments with toggles, Milestone 3.

Stale Switches found and retired

A Switch that has served one value to everyone in every Airfield for 30 days, has not been evaluated for 30 days by any application that reports, or is past its expected removal date is mentioned on its page and in the list. Nothing is changed by it. Next, Launchway finds where the code reads the Switch and proposes a pull request that removes the check and keeps the branch that won; after it merges, deleting the Switch is offered, and a deletion can be reverted.

Where the code reads a Switch

Finding the reads is a scan step on a Station, run on every push to the default branch and on every pull request. Launchway has an advantage here: it ships the client libraries, so the scan knows their exact call shapes and those of the OpenFeature interface, and it uses the code index where one exists (code navigation). Each read becomes an edge in the software graph, "component reads Switch", with the commit, file and line, so the reads are on the record like any other fact.

  • Typos caught early. A pull request that reads checkout-v3 when only checkout-v2 exists is warned on the line, before the code silently gets the default.
  • Stale reads shown in the code. When a Switch is stale, every line that reads it is marked in the code browser with the Switch's state and a link to the retiring pull request.
  • A read the scan cannot be sure of (a key built at run time) is listed as "possible", never hidden, and never counted as proof that no code reads the Switch.

Planned Where the code reads each Switch, Milestone 3, New in this plan.

An outside flag service as an equal choice

OpenFeature is the seam. An application written against OpenFeature reads either the built-in service or an outside one by changing its provider, not its code. For a Squadron served by an outside service, Launchway keeps what is the same for every provider: the reason, the Clearance in protected Airfields, the record, the Airfield timeline, Overwatch and the automatic return. Changes made in Launchway are sent to the outside service; changes made there arrive as events and are recorded. The outside service's extra features, such as statistics for experiments, appear in place, marked as coming from it. An import copies Switches, rules and segments from another service with a dry run.

Bringing Switches in from another flag service

A team leaving another flag service needs its flags across before that service goes away, without a weekend of copying. The import follows the rule of bringing work in: generate as much as possible, drop nothing silently, and mark what a person must finish.

  1. Connect, read-only. A connection with a read-only key lists the other service's flags, rules, segments and environments.
  2. Map, in a dry run. Each environment is matched to an Airfield from a picker; each flag becomes a Switch with a kind and a type; each rule becomes typed conditions; each segment becomes a segment. The dry run shows counts one for one ("212 flags: 205 mapped, 7 need you") and lists what cannot be mapped (an operator with no equal, a rule that calls the other service's own data) with what to do instead.
  3. Apply. The Switches are created with "imported from" on each, and the import is one event on the record.
  4. Move applications one Airfield at a time. Because both services are read through OpenFeature, an application changes its provider, not its code. Both can answer side by side, and a comparison shows any context where they would give different values, until you cut over.

Planned Import Switches from another flag service, Milestone 2, New in this plan.

One home for Switches: resolving the overlap

Switch items sit in two milestones today: in Milestone 3, spread over four groups ("Runtime configuration", "Watch and protect", "Change and insight", "Built-in platform services"), and in Milestone 8 in "Levers: toggles, configuration and secrets". Both milestones are Next. The proposal gives the Switch service one group, "Switches", in Milestone 3, where the service already is, and leaves in Milestone 8 only what depends on the watch after a Launch.

Worked example: Switches across Harbor Lights

  1. storefront's Go service on the Kubernetes cluster reads Switches with a server key and the Go client, keeping a snapshot file on its volume. Its web front end uses a client key and sees only checkout-v2, which is marked visible to clients.
  2. The legacy billing service on its two virtual machines has no library. It reads invoice-pdf-v2 through the HTTP protocol with a server key kept in its secret store.
  3. The kiosks on the image-based hosts often lose their network. They read kiosk-new-menu from the snapshot file baked into their image and refreshed when online, so a lost link never flips the menu.
  4. The image-resizing function fetches the rules when it starts cold and evaluates locally; resize-avif is on for 10 percent of uploads.
  5. Dana raises checkout-v2 to 5 percent in prod with the reason "first public slice". Ana gives the Clearance. The change appears on the prod timeline beside the 2.5.0 Launch.
  6. Error rates rise. Today the timeline shows the change as recent and Dana reverts it with one action. With the planned item, Overwatch reverts it by itself and the Logbook names the signal.

Safety

Launchway is down
Applications keep evaluating with the last rules they hold; after a restart they read the snapshot file; with neither, every Switch answers the default the code gives, and the client says "not ready".
A server dies
Any server answers; a scheduled change is made once, never twice; streams resume from the last event.
The database is lost
Applications keep the last rules; no Switch flips. Changes cannot be made until it is back.
A Station dies
Only a pipeline's Switch step is affected; it fails with its reason and changes nothing half-way.
An experiment's numbers stop arriving
The interval is "not enough data", never counted; the experiment waits, and at its time limit ends as "no verdict" with the reason. Guards keep running on what Overwatch can read.
Privacy
Local evaluation sends nothing about the context. Remote evaluation sends the context over TLS to your own server, which does not store, log or audit it. What is stored is a count per Switch, Airfield, day, value and reason.
Keys
A server key is shown once and stored as a hash; rotation overlaps for a day; revoking is immediate. Toggles are not a security boundary, and a client-visible value is public.
On by default
A reason on every change, a Clearance in protected Airfields, never-held reverts and Master switches. Proposed: the watch on by default and acting through Overwatch.

Screens

Full field lists are in the screens notes for this chapter (screens).

Switches list

Every Switch of a Flight or level by Airfield, with share served, kind, owner, staleness, and a turn-off action where allowed.

Switch page

State per Airfield, the rule builder, "try a context", history with revert, waiting Clearances, evaluation counts and where the code reads it.

Change a Switch (dialog)

New state or percentage, the reason, what it will do in one sentence, whether it will wait for a Clearance, and an optional time.

Make a Switch (wizard)

Key, type, kind, owner, removal date and starting state, with a safe value for a Master switch.

Keys and safeguards

SDK keys per Airfield, safeguards per level with who set and locked each, scheduled changes.

Switches served by

Built in or an outside flag service, the connection test, the import with a dry run.

Start an experiment (wizard)

Variants and control, split, outcome and guards picked from defined measures, smallest effect and confidence from lists, the sample and time it needs, and the end.

Experiment page

The verdict sentence, the effect and interval per variant, the split check, guards from Overwatch, the progress toward the sample, and the end.

Where the code reads it

On the Switch page: every read by repository, file and line, possible reads marked, and the retiring pull request.

Import Switches (wizard)

Connection, environment-to-Airfield mapping, the dry run with counts and what needs you, apply, then the side-by-side comparison per Airfield.

Open question

Decision needed

One home for Switches. Accept the move of the Switch service's items into one Milestone 3 group, "Switches", with Milestone 8 keeping only what needs the watch? Recommendation: yes.

Decision needed

The word in titles. Roadmap titles say "toggle", while the words rule says Switch in text a person reads. Renaming the titles changes their addresses. Recommendation: rename them once, with the groups, and keep the old anchors as redirects if the generator allows.

Decision needed

The watch after a Switch change on by default. puts toggle revert among the safeguards that are on by default; the built watch is off and only marks the Airfield. Recommendation: on by default once Overwatch can act on it, tunable by the team and lockable from above.

Decision needed

Experiment defaults. Recommendation: 95 percent confidence, a test that stays valid when looked at every interval, guards on errors and latency always on, and a time limit of 21 days unless the team chooses another.

Decision needed

License of the client libraries. A recorded recommendation asks to confirm a permissive license for the client libraries beside the server's license, after counsel. Still open.

The software graph and Maintenance

One graph from code to hardware tells you what runs where, what a change or a vulnerability reaches and in what order to build, and Maintenance (dependency updates) turns what it finds into ordinary pull requests that fly the same path to a verified Launch (deployment).

  • The graph is built from facts Launchway already records: Git, pipelines, the results of Sorties (runs) and what each Launch delivered. It lives in the same database, with no extra service to run.
  • Every link says where it came from, how sure Launchway is and when it held, and you can correct it with a reason.
  • Built today: what is deployed where, what a change reaches, which deployments run a vulnerable version, build order with corrections, and starting dependents when you ask.
  • Maintenance proposes updates as pull requests, security fixes first, grouped and limited. Next: patching from a new advisory to a verified Launch in every affected Airfield (environment), off by default and turned on per zone.
  • Planned: code search across every repository you may read, inside the one server with no search cluster, including the code that runs in each Airfield; and definitions, references and callers from an index step, across repositories, for people and for the Wingman alike.

Where it sits

In the story the graph is the flight map: where every aircraft came from, what it carries and where it is now. It is a layer 7 module that reads almost only from layer 2, the record, and from Git.

Builds on
Hosted repositories and connected ones (Code and review); image steps and their contents lists (Pipelines, values and expressions); the Depot (registry) and its digests (the Depot); Launches to every kind of target (One way to launch, anywhere).
Builds on it
Build and release order and Formations (releases that go together); triggers on results (What starts a Sortie); Inspection (security scan) findings and patching (Security and the supply chain); the Wingman (helper), which answers from the graph instead of reading files (the Wingman and agents); insights (Radar, insight and keeping it healthy).
Capability slots
Software graph: the core is always built in, by ruling; outside scanners, inventories and contents lists feed it as connections. Maintenance: served by the built-in updater or by an outside update tool whose pull requests are judged the same way.

What you will be able to do

An advisory names a version of an image library. You ask the graph which deployments run it and get two: storefront in prod and the image-resizing function, each with the digest, the Airfield and the owner.

Before you change platform-library, you open "What it affects": payments and storefront depend on it, through which package, and which of their digests run where.

A merge to platform-library builds it first; payments and storefront start when it ends well, providers before consumers, because each Flight (codebase) asked for it and the library allowed it.

On Monday Maintenance opens one pull request with the minor and patch updates of storefront's npm packages. A security fix for a Go module arrives on Wednesday on its own pull request, at once, outside the schedule.

You turn automated patching on for the edge zone. A fixed base image arrives; the kiosk image is rebuilt, launched to the image-based hosts through the usual route and Clearance (approval), and the finding closes only when Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) has seen the fixed version healthy. Planned

Your auditor asks whether every production host was patched within your own deadline. The answer is a query with evidence, not a spreadsheet. Planned

You search for DeliveryEstimate across the Wing and filter to "runs in prod". Nothing comes back from storefront, because prod still runs 2.3.2; without the filter you see the new lines from pull request #482 on main. Repositories you may not read are not even counted. Planned

Reviewing the platform-library half of the linked change for pull request #482, you see that the changed function has eleven callers in two other repositories, and that three of them run in prod. One click takes you to each, at the version its lock file names. Planned

How it works

Nodes and edges

A node is a thing; an edge is a relation between two things. Repositories in one Base (installation) find each other with no configuration: a Go module path, an npm package name or a Python distribution name is the same node whoever mentions it, so a dependency in one repository meets the package another publishes.

SourceReadsGivesStatus
ManifestsGo, npm and Python manifests and lock files, owners filesPackages, components, dependencies with constraint and resolved version, ownersAvailable
ContainersContainer build files and the pipeline's image stepsBase images by stage, what each pipeline builds and for which platformsAvailable
Requirements.launchway/requirements.yaml, the pipeline, build files, Kubernetes manifestsWhat each component needs, declared or inferred with evidenceAvailable
SortiesResults of image stepsBuilt images by digest and platform, the commit, the contents listAvailable
DeploymentsWhat is launched nowDeployments and the digests each runsAvailable
Code index and Switch scanThe index step's output per commit; the scan of Switch readsSymbols, definitions, references and calls; "reads Switch" edges with file and linePlanned: see below and Switches
Inventory, Depot, infrastructure, clustersMachines, platforms, Depot contents, infrastructure state, cluster workloadsMachines, platforms, what hosts what, what configures whatPlanned: the typed adapters exist and are tested with fixtures

Every edge says who asserted it, at which commit or time, and how sure: declared (a person wrote it), extracted (read from a file or a result) or inferred (worked out, and said so). An edge is closed, never deleted, so you can ask "as of this commit". A declared fact always wins; an inferred one that differs is shown as advice and never applied.

Every question is asked as you: a node you may not read is not listed, followed or counted, and answers exactly as one that does not exist. Every walk is bounded by depth, nodes and time, and a cut-short answer says truncated and which limit.

Code search across every repository you may read

Search inside one repository is built today: it reads the repository at the commit you are looking at, with bounds on time and size, and keeps no index. Across a whole Wing that approach is too slow, so cross-repository search adds an index, but keeps the promise of one program and a database: there is no search cluster to run.

  • Built by a step. The index step runs on a Station under the one step contract, never inside the server. It builds a compact index of short character sequences for each repository and commit, stored in the blob store with its record in the database. Outside-host repositories are indexed through the same connection a Sortie uses to check them out.
  • What is indexed. The default branch, release tags, and the commit each Airfield runs. That last one is Launchway's own: the graph knows which commit runs where, so you can search the code that runs in prod, not only the code on main.
  • Never wrong about a line. The index only narrows the candidates; every hit is confirmed against the file at the indexed commit before it is shown, so a result never shows text that is not there.
  • What you can ask. Exact text, regular expressions, file names and symbols, filtered by Squadron, repository, language, path and kind (code, pipeline, template, step, wiki page or document), and "runs in" an Airfield. Pipeline files, templates and steps are results of their own kind, with the Flight that uses them.
  • Rights at query time. Your rights are checked when you search, not when the index was built, so a permission removed this minute applies this minute. A repository you may not read is never opened, listed or counted.
  • Fresh, and honest about it. Each result names the commit it came from. A repository pushed since its last index is searched live with the bounded search that exists today, and its results are marked; when a bound is reached the page says "partial results" and why.
  • Every way in. The same search is a web page, an HTTP route, a command (launchway search, proposed) and an agent tool, with the same results.

Planned Code search across repositories, Milestone 5. Today: Search inside a repository, Available, one repository at a time with no index.

Definitions, references and calls

Search finds text; navigation knows what a name means. An indexer step per language reads a commit and writes an open, language-neutral code index: every symbol, where it is defined, where it is referenced, and what calls what. The index is kept as Cargo (artifacts) keyed by repository and commit, so it is fetched, retained and permissioned like everything else the Depot holds. Indexers for Go, TypeScript and JavaScript, Python, Java and C# are the proposed first set, matching the client libraries' order; until a language has one, answers come from search and are marked approximate.

  • Across repositories, at the right version. A symbol that comes from another repository's package is tied to the graph's package node, so going to the definition from storefront opens platform-library at the version storefront's lock file names, not at the library's latest commit.
  • In the code browser. Go to definition, find references and callers, on any line of any indexed commit, with the access of the person reading.
  • On the pull request. Definitions and references on the diff, and a box that lists, for each changed function, its callers in other repositories and which of them run in each Airfield. That turns "what does this change reach" from a guess into a list before the merge (Dependents checked before a change merges).
  • For the Wingman and agents. The agent endpoint offers the same answers as tools: search, definition, references and callers. Each answer cites repository, commit and line, so an agent reads a few exact lines instead of whole repositories (Code knowledge for AI, with fewer tokens).

Planned Code intelligence and Code knowledge for AI, with fewer tokens, Milestone 5.

Build and release order, open to correction

Two things make one repository depend on another: it depends on a package the other publishes, or its container build starts from an image the other's pipeline builds. The order comes out in levels that can be built together. It is worked out from the code and never hidden: each link shows where it was found, and every correction carries a reason, is audited, survives a rebuild of the graph and can be taken away.

Maintenance: proposed updates as pull requests

Maintenance finds the dependencies a repository uses, finds those that are out of date or carry a known vulnerability, and proposes each update as an ordinary pull request. Nothing changes behind your back: the pipeline judges it like any other change, a person reviews it, and the branch rules and merge queue apply.

Security first

A known vulnerability with a published fix is proposed at once, on its own pull request, with the advisory and the lowest fixed version. It is not held back by the wait or the limit on open pull requests.

A wait for new releases

Other versions are proposed after they have been public for three days, because a version a minute old may be withdrawn or tampered with.

Grouped and limited

Minor and patch updates of one ecosystem and folder share a pull request; a major update is always its own. At most three update pull requests are open at a time.

Kept current, never repeated

One pull request per dependency or group, rebuilt in place when a newer version appears; closed with a note when no longer needed. Closing with "ignore this version" is remembered.

The server never runs a package manager. The updater runs as a step on a Station (runner), edits the manifest, and lets the ecosystem's own tool write the lock file inside a container with no secrets and only the registries the Base allows; it takes back only the files meant to change. Its pull requests come from an automation account and so run restricted, like a fork's.

# Built today: Maintenance on a Patrol (schedule), as a step on a Station.
pipeline: dependency-updates
on:
  schedule: "0 6 * * 1"
steps:
  updates:
    image: your-registry/launchway-cli
    run: launchway updates run -R harbor-lights/storefront

Covered today: Go modules, npm, Python manifests, container base images and image references, and workflow files a repository still carries. Coming: Maven and Gradle, Rust crates, .NET, Helm chart dependencies, Terraform providers, and the lock files of pnpm and other JavaScript package managers, which are listed as "found, not updated" until then so nobody thinks they are covered.

From a vulnerability to a patched Launch

Patching is not a separate machine. It is the graph, Maintenance and the ordinary flight joined end to end, and every step is a decision on the record.

  1. Find. Stored contents lists are matched again whenever an advisory appears, with no new commit. Built: matching on request. Planned: matching on arrival.
  2. Weigh. Findings are ordered by severity, by whether the vulnerability is known to be exploited, by the likelihood of exploitation and by whether it is reachable; signals from public lists are on by default where their terms allow.
  3. Propose. Maintenance opens one pull request per affected repository; a base image change also rebuilds the images built from it.
  4. Judge. The same pipeline, Standing orders (policies), review and merge queue as any change. Automatic merging stays off unless a level allows named kinds.
  5. Launch. The fixed digest flies the release's route; production may require a person; a Hold (freeze) stops the Launch, never a Return to base (rollback).
  6. Verify and close. Overwatch watches; the graph sees the fixed digest delivered; the finding closes in that Airfield, and the time it was open counts toward the deadline evidence.

Automated patching is off by default and turned on per zone with a guided Standing order. Once scanning is on, dependency and base-image updates open pull requests by themselves; merging and promotion stay with policy.

# Design: not built. Automated patching turned on for one zone.
standing_orders:
  patch-edge:
    zone: edge
    patching:
      open: [security, base_image]
      merge_by_itself: [patch]
      airfields_without_a_person: [dev, staging]
      deadline: { critical: 7d, high: 30d }

Worked example: an advisory reaches Harbor Lights

  1. An advisory names versions below 3.2.2 of an npm image-transform package. launchway graph reach package:npm:image-transform answers: storefront's web front end in prod (digest 4f9c…a17, version 3.2.1, exact) and the image-resizing function (serverless, version 3.1.0, exact), both owned by @group:storefront-web.
  2. Maintenance opens two security pull requests at once, one per folder, each moving to 3.2.2 with the advisory in the description. The lock files are written by npm inside a container with no secrets.
  3. The pipeline runs, the Inspection shows the finding gone, Ana approves, and the merge queue lands both. Sortie 402 builds digest b71e… and the new function package.
  4. Dana cuts 2.4.1. It is promoted to dev and staging by digest; prod waits for Ana's Clearance and then launches. Overwatch watches the same signals as for any Launch.
  5. The graph records b71e delivered to prod. With the planned item, the finding closes in prod with the time it was open, and the function's finding closes when its new version is live.
  6. The two virtual machines of billing do not use the package. The graph says so, with the path it checked, instead of leaving the question open.

Available today, in progress, planned

Milestone 5 is Later, although several of its items are on the main branch. Milestones 3, 12 and 13 are Next; Milestone 4 and Beyond are Later.

Which is right

The software-graph area page says the graph and patching are planned in Milestone 5. The roadmap data marks One graph from code to hardware Available and What is deployed where In progress, and the graph and release guides document more: link provenance with corrections, start-dependents through triggers, Formations ordered by the graph, vulnerability reach on request, and owner edges. The guides are right. Five items are moved to In progress in the proposals; patching itself stays Planned.

Inconsistency

Hosted review reads owners from .launchway/owners; the graph reads owners from a root owners file in another format. One owners source should serve both; the proposal for Who owns what names it.

The module contract check

Contract pointHow the graph and Maintenance meet itStatus
1. Same levels and permissionsEvery question is asked as you, with the access of the pages it reads; Maintenance settings are by level with locks. Code search and navigation check your rights when you ask, never when the index was built.Available
2. Decisions on the one recordThe graph is built from the record and Git; overrides are audited; Maintenance pull requests and their outcomes are events. Patching verdicts join them.In progress
3. Gates are Standing ordersThe graph gates nothing on its own. Patching is a Standing order per zone; its pull requests and Launches meet the same gates as any change.Planned
4. Typed input formsFocus nodes, kinds, depths and overrides are picked; Maintenance settings have no web form yet, and the page never offers a button that would not work.In progress
5. Runs as steps on StationsMaintenance runs as a step on a Station. The graph's sources read Git and results inside the server; a code indexer for symbols will be a step. Planned: the search index and the code index are both built by steps on Stations; the server only narrows, confirms and answers.Available
6. One capability slot, served by"Software graph": built in by ruling, with connected sources and an export. "Maintenance": built in, or an outside update tool as an equal choice.New in this plan
7. Off until wantedMaintenance is on for new repositories (security and grouped routine updates), which the standards ruling asks for; automated patching is off by default. The graph is on whenever the server runs; see the open decision.Open question
8. Every way inEvery graph question is equal across the API, launchway graph and agent tools; the web has the five graph views. Planned: code search and navigation in the web, the API, the command line and the agent endpoint alike. Maintenance settings are not in the web or Terraform yet.In progress
9. Loss of a server, the database or a StationSee Safety below.Available
10. Never blocks Return to baseA Return to base never consults the graph. A patch Launch returns like any other; a Hold stops the patch, never the return.Available

Safety

The graph is lost or stale
It is rebuilt from Git, results and Launches (launchway graph rebuild), and people's corrections are kept. Nothing in a Launch depends on it; a Formation asked to follow the graph's order refuses with a sentence and an explicit order still works.
An index is lost or behind
Search falls back to the bounded live search for that repository and says so; the index step rebuilds it from Git. Navigation without an index answers from search and marks the answer approximate.
A server dies
The graph is in the shared database; any server answers. Pushes are read at once, new results and Launches within about thirty seconds.
A Station dies during Maintenance
The update step fails and the next scheduled run tries again; it never opens a pull request with files it did not mean to change.
An outside source is down
Version and advisory lookups go through the Base's network rules with an hour of caching; an offline mirror of advisories works; an answer that lacks data says so.
Who may do what
Anyone reads what they may already read; a search or a reference never reveals a repository you may not read, even by a count. Overrides need the Flight's operator role and a reason. Turning patching on for a zone needs the level's administrator; production may require a person.
On by default
Security updates and grouped routine updates for new repositories, the three-day wait, the limit on open pull requests. Off by default: automated patching and automatic merging.

Screens

Full field lists are in the screens notes for this chapter (screens).

Graph explorer

A focus picked from search, its neighbors as a table with a picture one button away, filters by kind, and the path between two things.

What it affects

From a package, image, repository or machine: every deployment reached, why, by owner and Airfield.

Build order

Levels, cycles with their path, and corrections with their reasons; add a correction from the row.

Dependencies and Maintenance

Each dependency, the version in use and the one proposed, vulnerabilities, the open pull request, and settings by level.

Turn on patching (wizard)

Zone, kinds, deadlines, which Airfields need a person, a preview of what would open now.

Advisory campaign

One advisory, every affected repository and Airfield, the pull request, its state, owner and deadline, until the fix is seen running.

Code search

One search box with mode (text, regular expression, file name, symbol) and filters picked from lists (Squadron, repository, language, path, kind, runs in), results grouped by repository with the commit and freshness of each.

Code navigation

In the file view and on the pull request: go to definition, references and callers in a side panel, across repositories, with "approximate" marked and "runs in" shown for each caller.

Open question

Decision needed

Is the graph a switch? The contract says off until wanted; the graph is on whenever the server runs, because Formations, impact answers and other modules read it. Recommendation: the graph always collects, and its menus appear once a Base has more than one Flight or a first Launch.

Decision needed

Default patch deadlines. Recommendation: none by default; the wizard proposes 7 days for critical and 30 for high, and the team accepts or changes them.

Decision needed

Exploit signals from public lists. A recorded decision turns them on by default "if terms permit"; the terms still need counsel. Until then they stay off and the screen says why.

Decision needed

What is indexed by default. Recommendation: the default branch, release tags and the commit each Airfield runs; other branches on request, so the index stays small.

Decision needed

Which languages get an indexer first. Recommendation: Go, TypeScript and JavaScript, Python, Java and C#, in that order, the same order as the client libraries.

Decision needed

One owners file. Choose one source for owners, read by review and by the graph. Recommendation: .launchway/owners, with the other format read when it is the only one present.

Mission support · module

Work, from idea to running software

Every change starts as a reason, and Launchway keeps the reason, the code and the running software on one line, so "where is my fix?" always has a one-click answer.

  • Work items, boards, sprints, a roadmap and optional time tracking are built in and available today. They are one set of items drawn several ways, not several tools.
  • An item is tied to its branch, pull request, Sortie (run), release and Launch (deployment). The item says where the fix is running, read from real Launches, never from what someone typed.
  • People and agents work the same items under the same rules. Only a person finishes work, approves a pull request through review, or plans a sprint.
  • An outside work tracker is an equal choice: one provider is in charge per Squadron (team), and Launchway still links code and delivery to whichever one it is.
  • People's own testing joins the same line: manual test runs (designed in the Debrief chapter) arrive as inbox assignments, failures become bugs, and the item's launch line shows what was tested by hand on which build. Requirements from an outside requirements tool are traced to the tests, releases and Airfields that prove them, and the evidence is written back.

Where it sits

Layer
Mission support (layer 7). It reads and writes the record (layer 2) and links to flight operations (layer 4) and Launch (layer 5).
Builds on
The levels and permissions of the foundation; hosted Git or a connected Git host for references in commits and pull requests; the record of Sorties and Launches for delivery status; the inbox shared with every way in.
Built on it
Agents that take work (The Wingman and agents), release notes and promotion (One way to launch, anywhere), flow and delivery measures (Radar, insight and keeping it healthy), and evidence for change records (the Logbook and evidence).
Capability slot
work-tracking: built in by default, or an outside tracker. One provider in charge per Squadron.

What you will be able to do

You open story STORE-41, "Show the delivery date at checkout". Under the title you see its launch line: the branch, the pull request with its checks, the Sortie that built it, release 2.4.0, and one sentence: "Merged, on dev since 14:02, on staging since 15:10, not yet on prod." You choose the staging station and its health and verification open underneath. Available today as the delivery status on the item; New in this plan as the full launch line drawn on the item.

You plan Sprint 14 for the storefront Flight (codebase). You drag six items into it, or move them with the keyboard. The sprint warns that it holds 34 points against a capacity of 30. It changes nothing for you: you take one item out. When you start the sprint, Launchway keeps what you committed to, so later estimate changes never rewrite how the sprint went. Available

You label task STORE-44, "Document the delivery-date field in the API guide", with agent:docs. The registered agent maintenance-agent claims it on a lease, opens a pull request and hands the item over for review. The item appears in your inbox under "Agent review". You read the change, approve it and merge. The item moves to Done because a person merged it. Available

Your Wing (organization) already runs an outside tracker that the whole company uses. Your Commander (owner) sets it as the provider in charge of work for the "shop" Squadron. Branch names and commit messages that name its tickets still link, and Launchway writes the delivery status back to each ticket. The built-in Work pages disappear from the menu for that Squadron. New in this plan, building on Planned Import and sync from other trackers.

A scan of a repository you just imported finds 212 problems. You do not get 212 tickets. You get five grouped proposals, held for a person, which you accept, edit or decline. Available as proposals from analysis; Planned A first look on import.

Release 2.4.0 is on staging. You start the checkout test plan against it; Launchway pins the run to digest sha256:4f9c…a17 and puts four cases in Priya's inbox and four in yours. One case fails on a phone: you choose Fail and "File a bug", already linked to the case and the build. The Debrief for 2.4.0 now shows 412 automated tests and 8 manual cases, one failed. New in this plan

Your auditor asks which requirements 2.4.0 delivered. STORE-41 satisfies REQ-118 in your requirements tool. The evidence pack shows REQ-118 linked to pull request #482, three tests that name it, all passed, and the release running on prod; your requirements tool shows the same, written back. New in this plan

You need to know why the team chose one PostgreSQL database per Airfield (environment). You search decision:accepted and open STORE-12: the question, the three options, the recommendation, the answer, who gave it and when. Planned on the roadmap as Decision records; the product guide already documents them (see the note below).

How it works

One set of items, drawn several ways

Work lives in the same database as Sorties, Launches and Clearances (approvals). An item belongs to one scope: a Flight, or a level above it (a Squadron, the Wing or the Base). Each scope has a short prefix, so STORE-41 names exactly one item anywhere it is written.

An item has a type: issue, bug, story, task, epic or decision. Every state of the workflow belongs to a category (to do, doing, review, done, canceled), and boards, charts and roll-ups read the category, not the name. A level may define its own workflow of 2 to 20 states; a nearer level replaces the farther one's as a whole.

ViewWhat it isStatus
List and saved viewsThe items, filtered by one query language (state:in_progress type:bug assignee:me); a query can be saved as a private or shared view.Available
BoardA column per state, in backlog order, with swimlanes by assignee, epic or priority. A work-in-progress limit warns and never locks. Every move works by drag, by keyboard through a "Move to" menu, and by command, API and agent tool.Available
BacklogOne order per scope. Moving one item changes one number, so two people reordering at once never overwrite each other.Available
SprintsA goal, dates and a capacity per person. Starting a sprint records the commitment. Completing it records what was done and carries the rest over with its history.Available
Milestones and roadmapMilestones at any level; a roadmap of epics, milestones and sprints drawn as bars on a time line and always also as a table.Available
ChartsBurndown, velocity, cumulative flow, lead time and cycle time, computed on request from each item's history, each with a table of numbers beside it.Available
TimeEstimates in points or hours, start and due dates, a personal timer, entries by hand, a report per person and item, and a spreadsheet export. Off until a Flight turns it on.In progress (see the note)
Status to check

The product guide (tracking-work.md) documents decision records with accept, supersede and export, and personal timers. The roadmap still lists "Decision records" as Planned and says timers are missing from "Optional time tracking and due dates". This chapter keeps the roadmap's statuses. The editor should check the main branch and, if both are merged, tested and documented, move them to Available.

The launch line of one change

Nobody copies a link by hand. Writing an item's name in a branch name, a commit message or a pull request ties them together. A closing word (fixes STORE-41) also moves the item: to In review when the pull request opens, to Done when a person merges it. Which words close is a setting of the level.

Once the pull request has merged, the item shows its delivery status. Launchway asks, for each Airfield, whether a successful Launch there ran the merge commit or a descendant of it. If one did, the fix is running there, since the earliest such Launch. A Return to base (rollback) to an older commit stops it counting. Nothing is guessed: with no Airfield configured, the item says so.

Today the item shows the delivery status as a sentence and a line per Airfield. This plan draws the same facts as the launch line itself on the item page, the same component the Tower (home) and the pull request page already use. One item that carries several pull requests shows one line per change.

Work shared between people and agents

An agent is software that takes work from the same items, does it, and hands it back to a person. It has its own identity and token, may touch only the Flights and types of work it was registered for, and holds an item only on a lease. The server enforces the rules whatever program holds the token, and each rule has a test that fails if it is lost.

Rule the server enforcesEffect
Only a person finishes workAn agent moves work only to In progress, In review or Ready. Done and Won't do are a person's.
An agent changes only what it holdsOn a live lease, in the Flights it was registered for. Planning fields (assignees, priority, estimate, sprint, dates, confidentiality) are a person's; an agent says what it wants in a comment.
Agents never planThey do not reorder the backlog or start or complete a sprint.
Nothing hidden is offeredA confidential or blocked item is never offered to an agent and cannot be claimed.
An agent's merge never finishes workThe item waits in review for a person.
Master switchesSwitching one agent off takes back everything it holds at once. A level's Master switch (kill switch) stops every agent there and below.

How far an agent's pull request may go without a person (the autonomy policy, levels 0 to 4, the always-a-person list and the pause after reverts) is set per level and explained in The Wingman and agents.

The inbox

Your inbox is one list of what concerns you, newest first: assignments, mentions, comments and moves on items you watch, an item that is no longer blocked, an agent that handed work over or gave it back, reviews asked of you, approvals waiting for you and failed Sorties of yours. You are never told of what you did yourself. You mark entries read or done, one at a time or all at once, and the unread count shows in the top bar and on the Tower. E-mail follows your choices per kind and carries only names and links for repositories that are not public. Agents have no inbox: they hear through their list of work. How people are told is part of Comms (notifications), described in Every way in.

An outside tracker as an equal choice

Ticketing is a deep specialty, and many Wings already pay for a tracker the whole company uses. says such specialties are connected well, not replaced. Work tracking is therefore one capability slot with two providers: the built-in tracker, and a connection to an outside tracker. For each Squadron exactly one is in charge, and the Work area says which: "Work for storefront is served by the built-in tracker" or "... by your outside tracker".

What happensBuilt-in tracker in chargeOutside tracker in charge
Where items are created and plannedIn LaunchwayIn the outside tracker; the built-in Work pages are hidden for that Squadron
References in branches, commits, pull requestsRead and linkedRead and linked the same way, by the outside tracker's keys
Delivery statusShown on the itemWritten back to the outside ticket as a comment or a field, and shown on the pull request and the release
Release notesFrom finished itemsFrom the linked outside tickets that the release carries
AgentsClaim built-in itemsClaim through the same holding pattern, which reads the outside tracker's ready list; the same rules apply
While switchingBoth may run at once only in the named role "migrating", with a visible end: a dry run reports counts first, then items sync in both directions until the cut-over.

The connection passes the same conformance suite as the built-in tracker, and its limits are stated in the wizard. Pipelines and Standing orders name the capability (work-tracking), never the product.

Manual test runs, tied to what was built

Some checks are done by people: a walk through checkout on a phone, an accessibility pass with a screen reader, a regulated sign-off. The design of manual test runs is in Quality, reports and the Debrief: test cases live in the repository as a small reviewed file, a run is created for one build's digest, people record pass, fail, blocked or skipped by picking, the results are a manual suite in the Debrief (test report), the release report and the evidence pack, and a manual_tests step and Standing order (policy) can wait for or require a passed run. This chapter adds what Work brings to it.

  • Assignments arrive in the inbox. Each person's cases for a run are one inbox entry, "8 checkout cases on 2.4.0 in staging", and leave it when recorded. Agents are never assigned a case and never record a result; an agent may draft new cases from an item's acceptance criteria as a pull request.
  • A failure becomes work. A failed case files a bug with one click, linked to the case, the run, the digest and the work item the release carries.
  • The launch line shows it. On the item, the station for an Airfield shows "tested by hand: 7 passed, 1 failed" for the digest that runs there.
  • Only what changed is run again. When staging moves on to a new digest, the old run's results stay with the old one, and Work offers a new run of only the cases whose components changed between the two digests, worked out from the software graph.
  • Cases verify requirements. A case can name the requirements or acceptance criteria it verifies, so its result counts in the trace below.

Requirements from an outside tool, traced to evidence

Formal requirements management (versions, baselines, sign-off of the requirement text) is a deep specialty, so it is connected, and the connection is designed. The built-in default is lighter: acceptance criteria on work items, which every item already has. A Wing that uses a requirements tool makes it the provider in charge of requirements, and Launchway does what the tool cannot: it proves, with evidence from the record, which requirements are built, tested and running where.

DirectionWhat is exchanged
From the toolEach requirement's key, title, version or baseline, status and parent, read live through the connection so the "Satisfies" picker on an item lists real requirements. Launchway never edits a requirement's text.
To the toolFor each requirement: the linked work items, the pull requests and releases that carried them, the tests that verify it (automated tests that name its key in their report, and linked manual test cases) with each one's latest result per release, and the Airfields where that release runs. Written as links and one status: "verified in 2.4.0, running on prod", or "not verified: 1 test failed".
  • Links are picked, not typed. An item's "Satisfies" field and a test case's "Verifies" field are pickers fed by the connection; an automated test names the key in its report, and the Debrief reads it.
  • A changed requirement is flagged. When the tool raises a requirement's version, everything linked to the old version shows "requirement changed since it was verified" until it is verified again.
  • A trace in the evidence pack. For every requirement in scope: items, changes, tests, results, the release by digest and where it runs, with gaps named: no test, a failing test, not released.
  • Nothing waits on the tool. A Standing order such as "every requirement linked to this release is verified" reads Launchway's own record, so it is judged even when the tool is down; only the write-back waits and is retried.

These are business requirements. The software graph's own "requirement" nodes (what a component needs: an architecture, memory, a port) are a different thing and keep their name in that chapter.

Worked example: Harbor Lights ships the delivery date

  1. Plan. Sam, the Commander (owner) of the Harbor Lights Wing, keeps epic STORE-30, "Faster checkout", on the storefront roadmap. Under it, story STORE-41 has three acceptance criteria and an estimate of 5 points. Sprint 14 starts with 30 points committed.
  2. Code. Dana, a Pilot (developer), starts a branch from the item. The branch is named STORE-41-delivery-date, so every push links. In progress: starting the branch from the item in one step is the missing part of "Confidential items and links to the code".
  3. Review. Dana's pull request #482, "Show the delivery date at checkout", says "fixes STORE-41". Opening it moves the story to In review. Checks and Standing orders (policies) run. The pull request shows its own launch line.
  4. Delegate. Dana also files task STORE-44 to document the new field and labels it agent:docs. The agent maintenance-agent claims it, opens a second pull request and requests review. Ana reviews and merges it.
  5. Merge and launch. Dana's pull request merges. The story moves to Done because a person merged it. Sortie 417 builds release 2.4.0 (digest sha256:4f9c…a17), which flies to dev and staging; the item reads "Merged, on dev since 14:02, on staging since 15:10, not yet on prod."
  6. Test by hand. On staging, Dana and Priya run the checkout test plan against 2.4.0; seven cases pass and one gift-order case fails, so a bug is filed against the digest. The Debrief and the release report show it.
  7. Clear and watch. Ana, a Controller (approver), gives Go for prod, replacing 2.3.2. Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) sees checkout errors double and starts a Return to base. The item now reads "Merged, on dev since 14:02, on staging since 15:10, not on prod: returned to base at 16:52." The release notes for 2.4.0 list STORE-41 and STORE-44.
  8. Learn. Dana reopens the story with a comment that links the Overwatch verdict. The sprint's burndown shows the story as done and reopened; the lead time chart counts it only when it finishes for good.

Built in, connected, or both

Your test for building in house: at least two of "on every pipeline's path", "needed by a solo developer on day one", and "the commercial product is costly and the commonly used 80 percent is tractable". Deep specialties are connected well, not replaced.

CapabilityAnswerWhy, by your test
Items, boards, backlog, sprints, milestones, roadmap, chartsBoth, built-in in charge by defaultEvery change carries a reason (on the path); a solo developer needs a list on day one; the common 80 percent is tractable and outside trackers are costly per seat. The connection serves Wings that already have one.
Links from code to work, delivery status, release notesBuilt in, alwaysIt is the delivery evidence chain, which is never outsourced. It works with either provider in charge.
Decision recordsBuilt inSmall, tied to the code, and exportable to the repository as files.
Agents working itemsBuilt inAI first class is ruled in house. Outside agents connect through the same published points.
Time trackingBuilt in, off by defaultSmall and tractable. Billing and payroll stay outside; the spreadsheet export feeds them.
Help-desk intake (requests by e-mail or form)ConnectedA deep specialty. A help desk posts a signed event through a Hardpoint (extension point); it becomes a proposal a person accepts.
Formal requirements managementConnected, with a designed connection; acceptance criteria on items are the built-in defaultNone of the three tests holds. The requirements tool is in charge of requirements; Launchway links them, proves them from the record and writes the evidence back (above).
Manual test cases and runsBoth, built-in in charge by defaultResults must be tied to the digest that was tested, which only Launchway knows; the common part (cases, runs, results) is small and tractable. A test-management service can be connected instead. Designed in the Debrief chapter; Work adds assignments, bugs and the launch line (above).
Large test-management suites (parameterized suites, lab devices, exploratory sessions)ConnectedA deep specialty; its results arrive as test results against the digest.
Wiki and notesBothA Git-backed wiki per repository is planned; a notes vault can stay in step through the planned Obsidian sync.
Portfolio budgets, objectives and key results, customer recordsLeft outNot delivery. Teams that need them keep their own tools.

What this module deliberately does not try to be

  • Not a second copy of the truth. A board, a backlog, a sprint and a chart are views of the same items. Nothing is stored twice.
  • Not a judge of people. Charts are for the team. There is no ranking of people anywhere, and velocity is never a target.
  • Not a lock. Work-in-progress limits and capacity advice warn and never refuse. A person decides.
  • Not a help desk, a requirements suite, a portfolio planner or a customer database. Those connect through Hardpoints.
  • Not a timesheet or billing system. Time is optional and exports to the tool that bills.
  • Not a place where an agent decides. Agents propose and hand over; people finish, plan and approve.

Contract pointHow work tracking meets itToday

This plan adds "Production changes traced to a work item" as a typed Standing order, judged at the before-Launch point with every other rule, so work brings no private policy.New in this plan

This plan makes the new-item form, issue forms and sprint planning the same typed forms used for Sorties: assignees, sprints, labels and parents are picked from lists.In progress in part

Agent work runs in the agent's own sandbox under the step contract (see the Wingman and agents).Planned for the first look

Work settings (workflows, agents, autonomy policy, close rules) become Terraform resources with the provider; items themselves are data, not configuration, and are listed in the parity table as an exemption with that reason.Available; Terraform Planned

Safety

When something fails

  • A server is lost. Another server answers; items, boards and the inbox are in the shared database. A save in flight either landed or is refused with a conflict and retried by the person.
  • The database is lost. Work is restored with everything else from the database's backups and point-in-time recovery; the history of each item comes back with it, so charts are recomputed, not lost.
  • A Station or an agent's sandbox is lost. The agent stops heartbeating, its lease runs out, the item returns to Ready, its owner is told, and the history says why. The branch stays where it is for a person or the agent to continue.
  • The outside tracker is down. References are queued and written back when it returns; nothing on the path to a Launch waits for it. The served-by screen says the connection is not answering.

ActionWho

Write test cases, start a manual run, assign casesPilot of the scope
Record a manual resultThe person the case is assigned to; never an agent
Connect a requirements or test-management toolCommander of the Wing (requirements) or of the Squadron (manual tests)

On by default

Only a person finishes work. Agents are offered nothing confidential or blocked. The autonomy policy is level 1: a person approves and merges. Mail carries only names and links for anything not public. Limits and capacity advice warn and never refuse. Work tracking itself, time tracking and agents stay off until someone turns them on.

Screens

Each screen is described for the mock-up builders in the Screens chapter and in the screen notes for this chapter. Every field is a picker or a typed control; free text is only for titles, descriptions and comments.

Work home for a Flight

The served-by line, the active sprint with its burndown, what is blocked, what agents hold, and a short list "Ready next". Tabs: Items, Board, Backlog, Sprints, Roadmap, Charts, Milestones, Settings.

The item page with its launch line

Title, type, state and key; the launch line per change underneath; criteria with evidence; links; history. The right column holds planning fields, each a picker.

New item

A typed form: type as cards, scope from a list, parent and sprint from searchable pickers, labels as chips, custom fields by their type.

Board and backlog

Columns by state with limits, swimlanes, the "Move to" menu, and a backlog with "Move" choices and sprint placement.

Sprint plan and close

A two-step wizard: choose items with the capacity meter, then start. Closing asks where each unfinished item goes, as choices, never typing.

The inbox

One list with filters by state, source and kind, and "Mark read" and "Done" on each entry.

Choose who serves work

A wizard: built-in or an outside tracker, test the connection, map states and people on five real items, dry run, then the named "migrating" role with its end.

Manual test work

The run screens are the Debrief chapter's. Work adds the inbox entry per person and run, "File a bug" on a failed case, the "tested by hand" mark on the item's launch line, and "Run again only what changed".

Requirements and their trace

Connect a requirements tool; the "Satisfies" picker on an item; a trace view per requirement from items to tests, release and Airfields, with gaps named.

Give this to an agent

A dialog from any item: pick a registered agent or a pool label; shows the agent's class, budget left and the autonomy level in force, with where it comes from.

Proposed roadmap changes

Five new items. Nothing existing is removed or narrowed. The same JSON is in the proposals file for this chapter.
