Mission support · module

The Wingman and agents

AI helps wherever you turn it on: it explains with the evidence, proposes changes you review, and does real work under its own name, but it never sends what you have not allowed and never overrules a check.

  • Off until wanted. Every AI purpose is off until an administrator of the Base (installation) turns it on. With every purpose off, no model is ever called, and no AI button is shown.
  • The statistics decide; a model may only make a verdict stricter. A model can turn a pass into "inconclusive" or a fail, or start a Return to base (rollback). It can never turn a fail into a pass, approve, or finish work.
  • The Wingman (helper) sits beside every screen. It already explains the page and the next step without AI; with AI on it explains failures, proposes fixes as pull requests, writes pipelines and custom steps with their tests, fills forms for you to submit, and answers "what is deployed where".
  • Launchway's own AI follows instructions set by level, drafts Standing orders (policies) that only a Commander saves, and may call outside agent tools only under allow, ask or refuse rules, with no secret ever passed.
  • Agents use the agent endpoint with exactly the rights of their token, work items on a lease, and are on the record under their own identity. A sandbox with a short-lived identity and a spend limit, a model gateway with local models, and autonomy levels with a Clearance (approval) where a person must decide are planned.

Where it sits

Layer
Mission support (layer 7), reaching into every other layer: it reads the record (2), writes flight plans as proposals (3), runs on Stations (runners) like any step (4), may make a verdict of Overwatch (the watch after a Launch, or deployment) stricter (5), and is bound by Standing orders (policies) and Clearances (6).
Builds on
The agent endpoint and the parity table of every way in; work items and leases from Work, from idea to running software; the software graph from the software graph and Maintenance; verification from One way to launch, anywhere.
Built on it
Agent-written changes, AI help on the Tower (home) and in the editor, assisted triage in Radar, insight and keeping it healthy.
Capability slots
model-gateway (the built-in gateway, or an outside gateway as the provider in charge); agents (agents Launchway runs in its sandbox, or your own agents through the endpoint). Model providers themselves are always connections: hosted ones, or local models on your machines.

What you will be able to do

A Sortie (run) of storefront fails at the tests. The page shows what went wrong from the structured results first: the failing test, its message, the line. You choose Explain. A local model reads the redacted log tail and the failed tests and says, in three sentences, that the new delivery-date field is empty for gift orders, citing the test and the line. Available for a failed step; Planned for a failed Launch (AI help with failures).

Under the explanation you choose Propose a fix. A task is filed and given to an agent. It works in a sandbox with a token that ends with its lease and a spend limit of two dollars, runs the checker and the tests, and opens a pull request labeled as AI-written, with evidence for each criterion. You review and merge. In progress Assign a story to an agent (the sandbox is missing); Planned AI-proposed fixes.

You ask the Wingman, from the Launches page, "what is running on prod for storefront, and does it contain the vulnerable image library?" It answers from the software graph with your permissions, links the release, the digest and the finding, and says which facts it could not see. New in this plan, on Planned Code knowledge for AI, with fewer tokens.

You start a Sortie of the payments release pipeline. The Wingman fills the run form from your last run and the release you are looking at: version, Airfield (environment), change ticket. Each value it chose is marked "proposed by the Wingman". You change one and press Start yourself. New in this plan

Your Commander (owner) turns on AI for one purpose only, "explain failures", allows only local models for the payments Flight (codebase) because it holds card data, and sets a monthly limit of fifty dollars. Nothing else changes. Planned AI off until a purpose is turned on; A protected path for regulated data; Spending limits.

You ask the Wingman for a rule: "production Launches of payments need two Clearances from back office". It fills the Standing order wizard from the catalog, tries the rule on the last 30 days ("would have asked for a second Clearance on 3 Launches"), and waits for you, the Commander, to save it. New in this plan

Explain, on a failed Launch, asks to call your error tracker's tool for the new error group. The tool is allowed for that purpose, so the explanation quotes the stack and marks it as coming from outside. Another tool, never approved, is refused, and the refusal is on the record. New in this plan

You type one command in your terminal. It configures your agent tool to use Launchway with a viewer token that expires, and prints what the tool may now do. Planned One-step setup for agent tools; the Connect an agent page that makes the token and shows the configuration is Available.

How it works

Five rules that do not bend

  1. Off until a purpose is turned on. Purposes are named jobs: explain failures, review changes, write pipelines, agent work, the Wingman's answers. Each is off until an administrator turns it on for a level. Today nothing is sent unless an operator has configured a model, and every AI feature says so when none is.
  2. Nothing leaves that a team has not allowed. Each purpose sends a listed set of fields, cut to size, with every secret the Station knows masked first. A regulated Flight reaches only models whose data terms you recorded. A local model keeps everything on your machines.
  3. A model may only make a verdict stricter. In a verification with decide: model-assisted a model may turn a pass into inconclusive or a fail, never a fail into a pass, and its reasoning is recorded with the verdict. Plain threshold checks stay the default.
  4. A model's answer is untrusted text. In an AI step it can set outputs and a Cargo (artifact), never run anything. Logs and commit messages are written by people and programs and may contain text that reads like instructions; what limits the harm is what an answer is allowed to do.
  5. A person decides what matters. Agents never approve through review, never finish work, never change their own limits, and never touch the always-a-person list. Everything AI produced is labeled.

Instructions for the AI, set by level

Every team has conventions a model should follow: "write tests with the standard testing package", "never propose a change to payments without a reviewer from back office", "answer in plain American English". Launchway keeps them as instructions at each level (Base, Wing, Squadron, Flight), in plain language, and sends them with every purpose and every agent it runs.

  • Combined down the levels. Lines are joined from the Base down to the Flight. A level above can lock a line, so no level below can remove or contradict it; a level below adds its own.
  • Edited only by a Commander (owner) of that level, and versioned on the record: every change is an event with the old and new text, shown in the Logbook (audit trail) as a difference. Before saving, "Try it" shows an answer to a recorded example with the old and the new instructions side by side.
  • They shape answers, never rights. Instructions come after the five rules above and cannot change them: they cannot turn a purpose on, widen the data a purpose may send, raise autonomy or loosen a Standing order (policy). A line that tries is refused when it is saved, with the reason and where the setting really lives.
  • Shown where they act. Each answer and each agent transcript records which versions of the instructions it was given ("3 from the Wing, 1 from storefront") with a link to them. Where a line conflicts with a Standing order, the instructions page shows the conflict, and the Standing order wins.
  • One source for every assistant. The same lines are written into the instruction files that editor assistants read (Instruction files kept current), so a rule set once reaches the Wingman, Launchway's agents and the assistants in your editor alike.
# Design: not built. Instructions for the AI at one level.
kind: ai-instructions
scope: wing:harbor-lights
lines:
  - text: Write Go tests with the standard testing package and table-driven cases.
  - text: Never propose a change to payments without a reviewer from back office.
    locked: true               # no level below may remove or contradict it

The Wingman in every screen

The Wingman is the column at the right of every page. Today it works without any model: it says where you are, what you can do here, and where to read more in Flight school (learning). That stays true with AI off. With the Wingman's purpose turned on, the same column gains a question box and five jobs.

JobWhat it doesWhat it never doesStatus

Write a pipeline or a custom stepDrafts a pipeline from a sketch or a description, or a custom step as a real program with its manifest and its tests, checks it with the checker and the Simulator, and proposes it in Git.Put logic in YAML beyond the inline limit; apply anything unseen.Planned; a write_pipeline prompt is Available on the agent endpoint
Fill a formProposes values for a run form, a wizard or a new item, each marked as proposed, using the same typed fields.Press the final button. You submit.New in this plan

The Wingman is exactly as powerful as the person using it and no more: it acts through the same API with that person's rights, and everything it changes is recorded as "by Dana, with the Wingman".

# Design: not built. A purpose switched on for one Wing, in the typed configuration.
kind: ai-purpose
name: explain-failures
scope: wing:harbor-lights
enabled: true
models: [local]                # names from the gateway, never endpoints or keys
data: [step-log-tail, failed-tests, findings]
monthly_limit_usd: 50

The Wingman drafts a Standing order

Writing a rule is easier from a sentence than from a blank form, and safer when you can see what it would have done. A Commander types "Production Launches of payments need two Clearances from back office" in the Wingman column on the Standing orders page.

  1. It fills the wizard. The Wingman opens Add a Standing order and fills it from the typed catalog: the rule, the scope (payments, Airfield prod), the point where it is judged (before a Launch), the answer (Clearance required, two people, from the Squadron "back office"). When no catalog rule fits it proposes a custom condition in the one expression language. Each value is marked "proposed by the Wingman".
  2. It tries the rule on the record first. It runs the proposed rule against the last 30 days (Try a rule against the record): "would have asked for a second Clearance on 3 Launches and denied none". Each case opens.
  3. It explains what is already there. Every Standing order in force at that level, in plain words, and how the new one meets them: a duplicate, a stricter version of a rule from above, or a conflict.
  4. A person saves it, in report mode first. Only a Commander can save. A Standing order is on the always-a-person list, so no agent or autonomy level can save one. Every draft starts in report mode, so it is judged and shown before it blocks anything, and the record keeps the sentence, the draft and who saved it.

An agent fixing a failed Sortie, end to end

Every arrow is on the record. The agent's own log shows its claims, heartbeats, tool calls and hand-over; the item carries its transcript as an attachment; the Logbook (audit trail) has each changing call as "via agent endpoint, token maintenance-agent, tool open_pull_request".

The agent endpoint, and getting connected

Every server serves the agent endpoint at /mcp, speaking the open Model Context Protocol. There is nothing else to deploy. An agent with nothing but a token can learn how to write a valid pipeline, check it, start Sorties, watch them, read why they failed, list approvals and steer a rollout, each tool calling the same HTTP API with the token's rights. Tool descriptions, a pipeline reference, worked examples and two prompts (diagnose a failed Sortie, write a pipeline) are served by the endpoint itself.

  • Same capability as every other way in. The parity table ties every API route to its tool and command, and the build fails when one falls behind (see the parity test).
  • Untrusted text is marked. Logs, commit messages, findings and file contents are returned only in fields named untrusted, never in instructions or tool descriptions.
  • People are not crowded out. Each token may make 120 requests a minute with 4 at once; each server answers at most 32 agent requests at once.
  • Sign-in. A Launchway token, or the access token of your sign-in provider when the endpoint is set up as its resource server.

Today the Connect an agent page makes a token and shows the configuration with this server's address filled in, and launchway mcp forwards an agent tool that starts its servers as commands. The planned one-step setup writes that configuration into the agent tool for you.

# Design: not built. One-step setup for agent tools.
launchway agent-tool setup
Found 2 agent tools on this machine. Which one?  [1] (picked from a list)
Token: viewer on storefront and payments, expires in 30 days
This tool may now: read Sorties, logs, tests, findings, Launches; check a pipeline.
It may not: start Sorties, decide approvals, change settings.
Written: the tool's configuration file (a backup of the old one was kept)

A place where an agent can do real work

An agent that writes code needs somewhere to run the code. Today the agent brings its own machine; Launchway controls what its token can do, not where it runs. The plan adds a sandboxed Station for agents, built on the same isolation profile as the hosted service's sandboxed Stations.

PropertyDesign
IdentityA token minted for one lease on one item, limited to that item's Flight and the agent's tools, ending when the lease ends or the agent is switched off.
SecretsNone. The sandbox reads no secret store. Steps that need secrets run in the ordinary pipeline after review.
SpendModel calls go through the gateway, which counts them, so the limit is enforced, not only reported. A claim is refused when the budget is spent; work in progress is never cut part-way.
NetworkOnly what builds reasonably need, by category, with every refusal shown on the agent's page with its destination.
WorkspaceA clone of the Flight at the item's branch, and the same step images and caches as its pipeline, so a test that passes here passes there.
RecordA transcript of plan, model turns, tool calls, diffs and masked output, attached to the item.
StopThe agent's off switch, the level's Master switch (kill switch), and a person's take-over all end the lease at once.

Tools that let an agent test what it wrote

An agent should prove its change before a person reads it. Two tools make that cheap. The checker (validate_pipeline, the server's own validator, with line numbers) is Available. The Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it: given an event and stand-in results for each step, it shows which steps would run, in what order, with which values, and why others are skipped) is New in this plan and is described in Code you can test. Exposed as a tool, it lets an agent show "with this change, a push to main still runs the image build and skips the docs check" as evidence on its pull request.

Levels of autonomy, and where a person must decide

LevelWhat an agent's change may do without a personStatus
0. Propose onlyNothing. The agent comments and hands back.Available
1. A person approves and mergesNothing. The default everywhere.Available
2. Auto-merge listed changesMerge when every required check passed, the change is only in the listed paths and types, within 10 files and 200 lines, and autonomy is not paused. Needs a recorded reason.Available
3. Launch to non-productionLaunch the merged change to Airfields not marked production, through the same Preflight (checks), Standing orders and Overwatch as anyone.In progress: stored, held to level 2
4. Launch to productionAsk for the production Launch. A person still gives the Clearance (Go) for production; an agent never answers a Clearance.In progress: stored, held to level 2

Whatever the level, these always need a person: pipeline files, everything under .launchway/, owners files, quarantine files, a change that deletes a test or adds a skipped one. Autonomy pauses by itself when three of a Flight's recent agent changes were reverted within fourteen days, until a person clears the pause with a reason. A level cannot loosen what a level above switched off.

Proposal

Today the autonomy policy is a work setting. This plan expresses it as Standing orders judged at the common points (before merge, before Launch), so an agent's change meets exactly the gates a person's change meets, plus the checks below, and nothing else decides.

Checks for AI-written changes

A pull request opened by an agent, or with commits marked as AI-assisted, passes every ordinary check and these, as typed Standing orders. Each reports by default; a level can make one block.

  • Code changed means tests changed or added, or a written reason from a person.
  • No new outside dependency, widened permission or new network destination without a person.
  • The change stays within the item's scope: listed paths, sizes, and the Flights the agent may touch.
  • Every acceptance criterion has evidence: a test, a Simulator run, a screenshot from a preview Airfield.
  • Where a level allows an independent reviewing agent, its review counts only if it never held the work and, if asked, runs on a different model; a share of such merges is sampled by a person.

The model gateway, and what leaves the installation

Every model call, from a step, the Wingman, Explain or an agent in the sandbox, goes through one gateway. Pipelines and screens name a model or a purpose, never a provider, so moving to another provider needs no pipeline change.

PurposeWhat may be sentWhat is never sent
AI stepIts instructions, prompt and declared inputs, each cut to its size limitAnything the step did not declare; any secret the Station knows
Verification helpThe service, the Airfield, each metric's means and spread and why it passed or failed, up to 20 log templates per query with one redacted sample lineThe queries, the sources' addresses, credentials
Explain a failed stepThe last log lines, failed test names and messages, findings, redactedThe workspace, other steps' logs
Wingman answersFacts you may see, chosen from the record and the graph, with their sourcesAnything outside your permissions
Agent in the sandboxWhat the agent sends, through the gateway's limits and loggingSecrets (the sandbox has none)

Today models are configured once by name in the server's configuration (or the Add an AI model wizard), with limits per model and per Flight, and a Station marked for AI makes the call with keys from its own secret stores, so a key never enters a step's container. The gateway adds provider switching and fallbacks, local and self-hosted models served like any other, usage by model, Flight and purpose with cost, limits in money, context compression that never drops file paths, line numbers or error codes and marks each omission, routing by difficulty with plain tools before any model, and a reserve of capacity for interactive work.

Outside agent tools, called through the gateway

Other systems offer tools for models over the open agent protocol: a team's documentation search, its error tracker, its ticket system. Launchway's own AI can use them, under Launchway's rules, the same way outside agents use Launchway's endpoint under its rules.

RuleHow it works
Registered as a connectionA Commander registers an outside tool server at a level: its address, which Stations may reach it, and a reference to its credential, which is opened only on that Station. The server never sees the credential.
Allow, ask or refuse, per tool and levelEvery tool it lists starts at "ask". A Commander can allow or refuse each one per level and per purpose, with the same three answers as the per-tool rules for Launchway's own endpoint. "Ask" sends a decision card to the person using the Wingman, or to an agent's owner.
Pinned descriptionsThe tool list and each description are pinned when they are approved. If the server changes a tool or its description, that tool is refused until a Commander looks at the difference and approves it again, so a changed description cannot quietly change what a model is told.
Nothing secret goes outArguments pass the purpose's data rules: listed fields only, secrets masked. A call whose arguments contain a value the Station knows as a secret is refused. No Launchway token is ever passed to an outside tool.
Answers are untrusted textA result is returned only in an untrusted field. It can be quoted and cited; it can never approve, change a setting, or call another tool that the rules do not allow.
On the record and on the budgetEach call is in the Logbook with the purpose, tool, connection, who asked, the rule's answer, how long it took and its cost, and counts against the purpose's spend limit.

Explain, on a failed Launch of 2.4.0, may call the error tracker's tool for the new error group (allowed for the purpose "explain failures") and cite the stack it returns. An agent fixing the bug asks to search the team's documentation; the rule is "ask", Dana allows it once, and the transcript shows the call.

Worked example: Harbor Lights turns AI on, carefully

  1. Sam, the Commander (owner) of the Wing, runs the Add an AI model wizard twice: a local model on the team's GPU server, and a hosted model with a key held in the secret store. Sam records the hosted provider's data terms.
  2. Sam turns on two purposes for the Wing (organization): "explain failures" (local only) and "agent work" (local, then hosted as a fallback), with a monthly limit of fifty dollars and two dollars per item. payments is marked regulated, so only the local model may see anything from it.
  3. Sam registers the agent maintenance-agent for storefront only: tasks and bugs, class medium, one item at a time, autonomy level 1, and adds two instruction lines for the Wing, one of them locked. The Logbook records each setting with Sam's name.
  4. Sortie 212 fails. Dana asks for an explanation and a fix. The agent works in the sandbox, uses the checker and the Simulator, and opens a pull request that changes the gift-order code and adds a test. The AI-change checks pass. Ana reviews and merges.
  5. At month end the usage page shows forty-one requests, the cost of each purpose, and "cost per merged change: 0.38 dollars"; the same numbers appear in Insights beside the delivery measures (Radar and insight).
  6. Sam asks the Wingman to draft "no agent change to payments merges without a reviewer from back office". It fills the Standing order wizard, shows that the rule would have touched no change last month, and Sam saves it.

Built in, connected, or both

You ruled AI first class, to be built in house. Models themselves are always outside Launchway's code: a hosted provider, or a local model server on your machines.

CapabilityAnswerWhy
The Wingman, purposes, data rules, limitsBuilt inOn every screen's path and needed on day one; ruled in house.
Model gatewayBoth, built-in in charge by defaultRuled built in . An outside gateway a Wing already runs can be the provider in charge instead.
ModelsConnectedHosted providers through adapters; local and self-hosted models served on your own machines.
AgentsBothAgents Launchway runs in its sandbox, and your own agents through the same endpoint at a lower autonomy ceiling, with their own credential and a small budget.
Code completion and chat in the editorConnectedEditor assistants exist; Launchway feeds them facts through the agent endpoint and instruction files.
Evaluating your own AI applicationsConnectedRun your evaluation tool as a step and gate on its report like any test.
End-to-end tests written in natural languageConnectedA deep specialty. The team's tool runs as a step against a preview Airfield, and its report is read by the Debrief (test report) like any other test report, with the same gates.
Outside agent tools for Launchway's own AIConnected, under built-in rulesThe tools are other systems'; whether, when and with what data they are called is Launchway's, through the gateway.
Instructions for the AI by levelBuilt inSmall, on every AI call's path, and the same model of levels and locks as every other setting.
Guardrails for your applications' model trafficLeft outA different product for a different buyer.

The module contract check

Contract pointHow the Wingman and agents meet itToday
1. Same levels and permissionsAgents are registered at a level with scoped tokens; the Wingman uses the person's own rights. No AI feature has users or roles of its own.Available
2. One recordEvery changing call through the endpoint is in the Logbook with token, tool and client; an AI step records tokens and cost; verdict reasoning is kept with the verdict. The gateway adds one usage entry per call (purpose, model, Flight, tokens, cost, who).Available in part
3. Gates are Standing ordersModel-assisted verdicts only tighten the common verification gate. The autonomy policy and the AI-change checks become typed Standing orders at the common points. The Wingman may draft a Standing order but never save one; instructions for the AI shape answers and can never loosen a rule.New in this plan
4. Typed input formsModels, purposes, budgets and agents are set through typed wizards (Add an AI model exists). Forms the Wingman fills are the same typed forms, with each value marked.Available in part
5. Runs as stepsAn AI step is a step on a Station marked for AI. The sandbox for agents is a Station under the step contract. One exception today: Explain is a server call; with the gateway it passes the same purpose, data and budget rules.Available; sandbox Planned
6. One capability slot, served bymodel-gateway and agents, each with "served by" on the AI settings page.New in this plan
7. Off until wantedEvery purpose is off; with none on, no model is called and no AI button appears. The agent endpoint is on by default because it gives no right a token does not already have; it can be turned off.Available (no model configured means none called)
8. Every way inModels are listed by API, command (launchway models) and tool; every endpoint tool has its route and command. Models, purposes, budgets, agents and the autonomy policy become Terraform resources.Available; Terraform Planned
9. Failure and who may do whatSee Safety.Available in part
10. Never blocks Return to baseA model can start a Return to base where a verification allows it, never delay or block one. With every model down, Return to base works exactly as before.Available

Safety

When something fails

  • A model or provider is down. The gateway uses the fallback you named; with none, the feature says "not available now" and everything else works. A verification falls back to the statistics alone.
  • A budget runs out. Calls stop or warn before the limit is passed, with the reason. An agent's next claim is refused; work in progress is not cut part-way.
  • A server is lost. The endpoint keeps no sessions, so any server answers the next request. The gateway runs in every server role that needs it.
  • The database is lost. Usage and the Logbook are restored with the record; budgets are recomputed from the restored ledger before any new call is allowed.
  • The sandbox or Station is lost. The lease runs out, the item returns to Ready, the owner is told, the branch stays.
  • An agent goes wrong. Reverts pause autonomy by themselves; the off switch, the Master switch and take-over act at once.

Who may do what

ActionWho
Add a model, turn a purpose on, set limits, mark a Flight regulatedCommander at the Base or Wing; a level below can only narrow
Register, rotate, switch off an agentCommander of the scope or the agent's owner; never an operator, never an agent
Raise autonomy above level 1A maintainer of the level, with a written reason on the record
Clear an autonomy pauseA maintainer of the Flight, with a reason
Approve a pull request, give a Clearance, finish workPeople only
Ask the Wingman, use ExplainAnyone who may see the page, where the purpose is on
Edit or lock instructions for the AICommander of that level
Register an outside tool server, set its tools' rules, re-approve a changed toolCommander at the Base, Wing or Squadron; a level below can only narrow
Answer "ask" for an outside tool callThe person using the Wingman, or the agent's owner
Save a Standing order the Wingman draftedA Commander only, as for any Standing order

On by default

No purpose is on. Autonomy is level 1. The always-a-person list cannot be shortened. Agents are offered nothing confidential or blocked. Pull-request Sorties get no model unless the Flight allows secrets on pull requests. Untrusted text is marked as such. New agent-tool tokens are viewer tokens that expire.

Mission support · module

Radar, insight and keeping it healthy

The signals you already collect, read through connections and shown beside the change that caused them, together with the measures, targets, costs, Drills, services and incidents that keep software healthy, in one place instead of eleven.

  • Today these pieces are scattered: observability has no owning milestone, cost, chaos testing, reliability targets and the service catalog are almost all planned, and nothing covers on-call. This chapter gives each one a home, and says for each whether it is built in, connected, or both with one in charge.
  • Radar (monitoring) reads metrics, logs and traces from the stores a team already runs, through a guarded, audited query layer. It does not replace an observability backend; it adds what only Launchway knows: which change, which Launch (deployment), which Clearance (approval).
  • Insights come from the record: the four delivery measures (available today), Sortie (run) success and duration, flaky tests, slow steps, time in the Holding pattern (queue), and planned, the cost of a Sortie.
  • A reliability target leaves an error budget. Overwatch (the watch after a Launch) and Standing orders (policies) use it, so a team that has spent its budget slows down by rule, and Return to base (rollback) is never held back.
  • Deep specialties are connected, and each connection is designed: your error tracker's new error groups become an Overwatch proof with the line, pull request and work item behind them; panels from your dashboard tool sit on Launchway's pages with your permissions; cloud cost brings its budgets and anomalies; cloud-rule findings join the one findings list. AI usage and spend, and what AI work delivered, are insights like any other.

Where it sits

Layer
Mission support (layer 7). It reads the record (layer 2) and the outcomes of flight operations (layer 4) and Launch (layer 5), and gives Command (layer 6) the numbers its Standing orders judge.
Builds on
Verification and its signal sources (One way to launch, anywhere); guarded queries for monitoring data; the software graph (the software graph and Maintenance); work items for lead time from request (Work, from idea to running software); Hardpoints (extension points) for events in and out (Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints).
Built on it
Overwatch and automatic Return to base, error-budget Standing orders, the catalog of services, and the Wingman's answers to "is it healthy?" (the Wingman and agents).
Capability slots
signals (always connected), dashboards, reliability-targets, cost, drills, catalog, incidents. Each shows "served by".

Every number opens the Sorties and Launches behind it. Available

How it works

One home, seven slots

Insight is one area of the product, Radar, with one page per question. Each question is served by one capability slot. Your test decides what is built in: at least two of "on every pipeline's path", "needed by a solo developer on day one", and "the commercial product is costly and the commonly used 80 percent is tractable". Deep specialties (application monitoring, paging, cloud billing) are connected well, not replaced.

QuestionSlotAnswerWhy, by your test
What do my metrics, logs and traces say?signalsConnectedStoring telemetry is a deep specialty and none of the tests holds. Launchway reads stores through guarded queries and never ships a second observability server.
What changed when it broke?none: always onBuilt inOnly Launchway knows the change, the Launch and the Clearance; it is on every Launch's path.
How is delivery going?none: always onBuilt inComputed from the record; on every pipeline's path; useful to a solo developer; costly elsewhere.
Which errors did this change bring?signals (an error tracker)Connected, judged built inGrouping and storing errors is a deep specialty. Only Launchway knows which Launch, digest, pull request and work item an error group belongs to, and it judges that per Launch (below).
Where else do people look at charts?dashboardsBoth, built-in pages in chargeLaunchway's own pages show its own facts. Every other chart stays in the dashboard tool a team runs; Launchway links to it, can pin its panels on its own pages (below), and exports its own metrics so that tool can show them.
Is the service meeting its target?reliability-targetsBoth, built-in in chargeOn every Launch's path once used by Overwatch; the common 80 percent is tractable. Targets import and export in an open format; an outside reliability tool can be in charge and Launchway reads its budget.
What does it cost?costBoth: own meters built in, cloud cost connectedStation time, Depot (registry) storage and model spend are Launchway's own facts. Cloud price books and cluster allocation are endless to rebuild; they are connected.
Does it survive what the plan claims?drillsBoth, built-in in chargeSimple faults (stop a replica, stop a machine, add delay on a connection) are built-in steps; deeper fault engines run as steps and feed the same verdict.
What services exist and who owns them?catalogBuilt in, with a feed outThe catalog is a view of the software graph, which is never outsourced. An outside portal can show it through a feed.
Who is paged, and what is the incident?incidentsConnected, with the record attachedSchedules, escalation, phone delivery and status pages are a deep specialty. Launchway adds the Launch, the timeline and the record to each incident.
Are our cloud resources within our rules?none: findings onlyConnected, findings onlyRules over cloud resources (untagged, public, idle, oversized) are a deep specialty with rule engines of their own, and none of the three tests holds. A cloud-rules tool posts its findings through the events-in Hardpoint; the software graph links each resource to its Flight and Airfield; the findings join the one findings list with owners, waivers and expiry. Launchway runs no second rule engine for cloud resources.
What does AI work cost, and what did it deliver?none: always on with the gatewayBuilt inEvery model call already passes the gateway and every change is on the record, so the numbers are Launchway's own facts (below).

Signals in, views out

The query layer follows . Only the server reads monitoring stores; Stations (runners) and steps never get a route. Reads are read-only, behind their own permission, with a second, higher permission for sensitive streams. A person's question is never passed through raw: the server pins the selector to the services that person may see. Every query is in the Logbook (audit trail), results are redacted, and credentials come from the secret store. The controls are built before any log store is connected.

Every chart names its source and links to the query in the tool it came from. A connection that is not observed shows no number at all, because a made-up number is worse than a gap.

Built today

Verification reads metric and log stores, Prometheus among them, and can call the service it just launched with no monitoring set up. The servers, Stations and the launch Station expose their own metrics in the standard text format, with labels from small closed sets (never a repository, a branch, a person or a Sortie id), and can send traces to a collector over OTLP, the open telemetry protocol, with the Sortie page linking to the trace. The Insights pages and launchway insights give Sortie success rate, median and 95th percentile duration, time in the Holding pattern, the slowest and flakiest steps, test totals and the four delivery measures.

Errors from your error tracker, judged per Launch

An error tracker groups crashes and exceptions from running code and keeps their stacks. That is a deep specialty, so Launchway does not build one: it connects the tracker you have as a kind of signal source, with one tracker in charge per Squadron (team), shown as "Errors served by your error tracker". What it adds is what the tracker cannot know: which Launch, digest, pull request and work item each new error group belongs to, and a verdict on every Launch.

DirectionWhat is exchangedWhat is never exchanged
Launchway to the trackerAt each Launch, a release marker: the Flight, the version, the digest, the commit and the Airfield, and for a Pathfinder which copies run which versionSecrets, logs, anything about people
The tracker to LaunchwayFor the Launch's window and both versions: each error group's identifier and title, first seen, count per version, how many sessions it touched as a number, the top stack frames (file, line, function), and a link backError payloads, variable values, user details: they stay in the tracker
  • A proof for Overwatch. "No new error group in the new version with more than a set number of events that the stable version does not have", and "known groups not worse than in the stable version". A group can be marked as a crash class that starts a Return to base by itself. When the tracker does not answer, the proof says "not enough data", never pass.
  • From a frame to a change. The top frame's file and line, read at the release's commit, open the code view at that line, the last change to it, its pull request, its work item and the Squadron that owns it. The tracker shows a stack; Launchway shows who changed that line, why, and which Launch carried it.
  • Into the incident and the timeline. A new error group is a symptom on the timeline and is added to the incident in your on-call tool, beside the Launch.
# Design: not built. An error tracker as a signal source, as typed configuration.
kind: signal-source
name: harbor-errors
type: error-tracker          # picked from the list of source kinds
scope: squadron:shop
release_marker: on           # send a marker at every Launch
proof:
  new_groups_max: 0          # events above the floor below
  event_floor: 25
  crash_classes: [panic, out-of-memory]   # picked from the tracker's own list

Panels from your dashboard tool

Teams already have dashboards. A Flight, Airfield or Launch page can pin a named panel from a connected dashboard tool, so the chart people trust sits beside the change. Launchway reads the panel's definition (its query and its data source) through the connection, runs the query through the guarded query layer with the viewer's own monitoring permission and with the selectors pinned to the services the viewer may see, and draws it with Launch, Switch and Clearance markers on top. Every panel says where it came from and opens in the dashboard tool.

  • A panel whose query the guarded layer cannot read or pin (a store that is not a connected signal source, or a query it cannot narrow) is shown as a link card with the reason, never as an unfiltered picture.
  • Panels are never required: a page without them works, and when the dashboard tool does not answer the card says so.
  • Pinning a panel for everyone at a level needs the right to arrange that level's pages; pinning for yourself needs nothing.

One timeline of changes and symptoms

The roadmap has two timeline items, A timeline of changes and symptoms (Milestone 3) and One timeline of what changed (Milestone 8). In this plan they are one component, a reader of the record: Launches, Switch flips, setting and secret changes, Clearances, scaling, and the symptoms that came in (alerts, new error groups, a target burning its budget), in order, with "what changed since it last worked". The Milestone 3 item builds it and owns it; the Milestone 8 item adds the kinds that land with it. It is drawn once and shown on the Launch page, on Radar home, on the Reliability page and in the record.

Measures are for teams. An individual sees only their own numbers, and nothing ranks people. A period with no Launches shows zero; a measure with no data says "none". Every chart is also a table, and every page exports as one self-contained HTML file.

Status to check

The command-line reference documents slowest and flakiest steps on the Insights pages, while the roadmap item "Pipeline history and flaky tests" still lists duration charts and the slowest steps across Sorties as missing. The editor should check the main branch before either text changes.

What AI work costs, and what it delivered

Every model call passes the model gateway (the Wingman chapter), which writes one usage entry per call: purpose, model, Flight, agent or person, tokens and cost. Every change an agent opens is on the record with its fate. Insights read both, so AI is measured the way delivery is: by what it cost and what reached production.

MeasureHow it is worked out
Spend and useModel spend and calls by purpose, model, Flight, Squadron and agent, against each limit, with local and hosted models apart
What agents deliveredChanges opened by agents, merged, reverted within fourteen days, and returned to base after a Launch; time from claim to merge
Cost per merged changeSpend on agent work over the changes that merged and stayed merged
Help that was usedExplanations and proposed fixes asked for, and how many proposed fixes became merged changes

The same rules as every measure apply: agents may be compared with each other, people never are; a person sees only their own use; every number opens the calls and changes behind it. Spend limits themselves are set in the Wingman chapter; Insights only reads them.

Reliability targets and the budget they leave

A reliability target says what "healthy enough" means for one service, in one sentence a person can check: "99.9 percent of checkout requests succeed, over 28 days." It names a signal from a connected source, so it is only as good as that signal, and it says so. The error budget is what the target still allows: 0.1 percent of requests may fail. The Reliability page ranks services by budget left, with Launches, setting changes, Switches (feature toggles) and scaling marked on the same time line.

Overwatch uses the target's signal as one of its proofs: a Launch that burns budget many times faster than normal starts a Return to base. A proof says "not enough data" rather than pass when the signal is too thin. Targets import and export in an open format, so a team that already defines them elsewhere does not write them twice.

# Design: not built. A reliability target, as typed configuration.
kind: reliability-target
service: storefront
airfield: prod
objective: 99.9            # percent
window: 28d
good: checkout_requests_ok        # picked from the source's metric list
total: checkout_requests_total
source: harbor-metrics            # a connected signal source, by name
budget_rule: hold-below-10        # a Standing order from the typed catalog

Cost in context

Cost is shown where a decision is made, not on a separate finance page. The Launch page and the release show what the Flight costs in that Airfield and how it moved since the last release. The Sortie page shows what the Sortie cost. The Squadron page adds Station time, Depot storage and model spend. The source of each number is named: "from your cost tool" or "measured by Launchway".

  • Built in: Launchway's own meters: Station time per Ramp, storage, model spend through the gateway, and the real resource use of the server and each Station for capacity planning.
  • Connected: the cluster's cost allocation and the cloud bill, through a cost source connection (a tool the platform team runs, or a billing export in an open format). Cost by service uses the software graph to map resources to Flights and Airfields.
  • Budgets and anomalies, read where they live. When the connected cost source keeps budgets and finds anomalies, the cost card shows them with the source named: "prod is 6 percent over this month's budget", "spend on prod rose 40 percent on Tuesday", with a marker for the Launch of that day beside it. Launchway does not compute cloud anomalies itself; for its own meters it gives one plain notice when a Sortie, Ramp or agent costs far more than its usual.
  • Never: rebuilding cloud price books, or spending money on your behalf. Right-sizing is a proposal a person accepts.

Drills that prove the plan

A Drill is a step, so it adds no new concept: it is planned, cleared, run on a Station, judged by proofs and recorded. Each Drill injects one fault, checks that steady state holds, and restores everything. Breaching a proof aborts it. A fault is never left on: it expires by itself even if Launchway fails.

The plan for a service can state what it survives: "loses one replica", "loses one of two machines", "the payments API is slow for a minute". Each claim is proved by a Drill on a Patrol, and a claim that fails becomes a finding on the scorecard and in the findings list. Drills are off until switched on, allowed only on Airfields declared for them, bounded in what they can reach, and cleared by someone other than the person who started them; production may need a lock from a level above.

A proof a Standing order can require. A survival claim's last Drill result is a fact on the record, so a Standing order can read it before a production Launch: "every survival claim of billing proved within the last 14 days". A claim with no recent proof, or a failed one, holds the Launch with the reason and who can clear it. As with every rule here, a Return to base is never held.

# Design: not built. A Drill step proving one claim about billing.
steps:
  lose-one-machine:
    uses: launchway/drill
    with:
      airfield: staging
      fault: stop-machine            # from the built-in fault catalog
      target: billing-vm-2           # picked from the inventory
      hold_for: 5m
      proof: billing-errors-under-1-percent
      restore: always

The catalog of services

The catalog is not a second database that people keep up to date. It is a view of what Launchway already knows: every service with its owning Squadron, its Airfields and the version on each, its health from Radar, its dependencies from the software graph (with where each link came from), its documents (README, wiki pages, runbooks), its Standing orders verdicts as a scorecard, its cost and its last Launch. Self-service actions ("create a new service", "add a preview Airfield") are Flight plans with forms, offered from the catalog. A feed lets an outside portal show the same facts; Launchway stays the source of truth for delivery.

Incidents and on-call

Paging, schedules, escalation and status pages stay in the tools teams already use. Launchway does three things well. It takes alerts in through a signed events Hardpoint and links each to the nearest change: the Launch, the setting change or the Switch flip just before it. It adds the Launch, the timeline of what changed and the record to the incident in the outside tool, and keeps them up to date as Overwatch acts. And it computes time to restore from its own record. Where no tool is connected, the Launch page itself is the incident's home.

Worked example: the delivery-date release, seen from Radar

  1. Before. storefront in prod has 98 percent of its error budget left. The Standing order allows the Launch.
  2. Launch. Release 2.4.0 (digest sha256:4f9c…a17, built by Sortie 417) goes out as a Pathfinder (canary) at 16:40, replacing 2.3.2. The metrics chart on the Launch page shows the marker, and the error tracker receives the release marker.
  3. Signal. At 16:44 the error tracker reports a new error group in 2.4.0 only, its top frame on a line pull request #482 changed. At 16:47 checkout errors double for the new version. The team's alerting tool pages Priya, who is on call; its incident already carries the Launch link, the new error group and the timeline.
  4. Overwatch. The burn rate is fourteen times normal. Overwatch starts a Return to base at 16:52 and says why. The incident is updated with the decision.
  5. After. The budget left falls to 41 percent. Insights count one failed Launch and a time to restore of 12 minutes. The cost card is unchanged. The Wingman, asked "what happened?", answers from the same record and cites it.
  6. Next week. The Drill on billing runs as usual; the scorecard stays green. The catalog entry for storefront shows the incident and the fix that followed.

The module contract check

Contract pointHow Radar and insight meet itToday
1. Same levels and permissionsInsights show only Flights you may read. Monitoring data is its own permission, with a higher one for sensitive streams. The catalog is filtered by what you may see. Cost has a permission of its own at the Wing.Available for insights; In progress for monitoring data
2. One recordEvery measure is computed from the record. Every monitoring query, Drill, target change and budget verdict is on it, and the Logbook records each query.Available for measures
3. Gates are Standing ordersThe error-budget rule, the performance gate, Drill authorization and "survival claims proved recently" are typed Standing orders judged at the common points. New error groups are an Overwatch proof, not a private gate.Planned
4. Typed input formsA target picks its signal from the source's own metric list; a Drill picks its fault from a catalog and its target from the inventory; periods and Airfields are pickers.Planned
5. Runs as stepsDrills, load tests and outside chaos tools are steps on Stations. Monitoring queries are deliberately not steps: by only the server reads monitoring stores, through the guarded layer, and a launch Station verifying a Launch uses the same layer.Available for verification
6. One capability slot, served bySeven slots, each with "served by" on Radar's settings page. An error tracker is a kind of signal source, one in charge per Squadron; dashboard panels belong to the dashboards slot; cloud-rule findings arrive through the events Hardpoint into the findings list, with no slot of their own.New in this plan
7. Off until wantedRadar's pages appear when a source is connected; targets, cost, Drills, the catalog and incident connections are switches. Safeguards that use them (Overwatch) follow : on by default, tunable by the team.Available for the menus
8. Every way inlaunchway insights and the release report exist with their API routes and tools. Sources, targets, cost sources, Drills and incident connections become API objects, commands, tools and Terraform resources.Available in part
9. Failure and who may do whatSee Safety.
10. Never blocks Return to baseA spent budget holds advance, never a Return to base. A Drill that breaches its proof restores at once. A missing signal never holds a Return.Available for verification

Safety

When something fails

  • A signal source is down. Charts show the gap, labeled. A proof says "not enough data", never pass; what Overwatch then does is set per Airfield (hold the next step, or ask a person).
  • A server is lost. Another answers; measures are computed from the shared database on request.
  • The database is lost. The record, targets and Drill history come back from backups; measures are recomputed, not restored from copies.
  • A Station is lost during a Drill. The fault expires by itself; restoring the previous values does not depend on the Station or on Launchway.
  • The on-call or cost tool is down. Updates are queued and sent when it returns. Nothing on the path to a Launch waits for them.

Who may do what

ActionWho
See insights and delivery measuresObserver (viewer) of the Flight; individuals see only their own numbers
Read monitoring dataThose granted the monitoring permission; sensitive streams need the higher one
Connect a source, a cost tool, an on-call toolCommander (owner) of the Wing or Base
Set a reliability targetCommander of the Flight; a level above may lock a minimum
Start a DrillA Pilot (developer) where Drills are allowed, cleared by another person; production only under a lock from above
Clear a budget Hold (freeze)A Controller (approver) other than the change's author, with a reason

On by default

Monitoring data is never passed through raw. Queries are audited. Drills are off and cannot reach production. Nothing ranks people. Charts never rely on color alone and always have a table. Overwatch is on with plain threshold checks.
