Quality, reports and the Debrief

The Debrief (test report) becomes the one place where everything known about a change's quality comes together, judged by the same Standing orders (policies and repository standards) as everything else, and written out as one self-contained report for every Sortie (run) and every release that people want to open, share and hand to an auditor.

  • Tests in every common format, coverage with a floor and a view of changed lines, flaky-test history, performance, code quality, Inspection (security scan) findings, licenses and accessibility, each from a built-in default or a connected tool, with one in charge.
  • Quality gates are Standing orders: "no new failures", "coverage of changed lines", "no new severe findings", with waivers that have an owner and an end.
  • Each report is one file: it works offline, reads well on a phone, is accessible, can be attached to a pull request, and can prove it was not edited.
  • The release report and the auditor's evidence pack are the same facts from the record in two views.
  • Any step, even a plain script, can write a summary and typed notes on lines of code; people can record manual test runs against the exact build they tested; and evaluation scores of AI features are read like test results and can gate a Launch.

Where it sits

This is a module of Mission support, layer 7 of the seven layers. It reads results that steps produce in flight operations (layer 4), writes every result and verdict to the record (layer 2), puts its gates through Command (layer 6), and follows a release through Launch (delivery, layer 5) to say how it behaved.

Builds on
The Debrief and test reports that exist today; Standing orders, Clearance and Hold (the judging points, answers and waivers); Security and the supply chain (the Inspection, signatures, lists of contents); Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch (how a Launch (deployment) behaved); Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints (one provider in charge per capability).
Builds on it
The Logbook and evidence (the evidence pack reads the same facts); Fast pipelines and continuous deployment (speed checks and flaky tests appear here); Radar, insight and keeping it healthy (quality trends beside delivery measures).
Advantage claimed
Number 6 of What only Launchway does: reports worth opening. It supports number 5, audit-ready as a by-product.

What you will be able to do

You are Dana, a developer on the Flight (codebase) storefront. Your pull request's Debrief opens on one sentence: "Ready to merge: no new test failures, 91 percent of changed lines covered, no new severe findings; 2 pieces of advice." Below it, every kind of result has a line: tests, coverage, code quality, security, licenses, accessibility, performance and speed. The two pieces of advice are on the lines of your diff: a function in price.ts grew too complex, and a button lost contrast.

You are Dana. A test that is quarantined fails with a new message. The Debrief lists it under New failures, not under Quarantined, with the known failure shape beside the new one, so nobody mistakes it for the old flakiness.

You are a product manager. Release 2.4.0 of storefront reached prod this afternoon. You open its report on your phone on the train: what changed, in plain titles from the pull requests and work items; what was tested and what passed; how it compares with 2.3.2, which it replaced; who said Go and what they were shown; when it reached each Airfield (environment); and how it behaved there for the first hour under Overwatch (watch after a Launch). It is one page, with no sign-in needed once it is on your phone.

You are Sam, who looks after the platform. An auditor asks for evidence that every production change in the last quarter was reviewed, tested, scanned and approved by someone other than its author. You give them access to the auditor's read-only view, and the release reports they open there are the same documents your team reads. For one release they ask "is this the original?". The report says it can be checked: launchway report verify storefront-2.4.0.html answers "unedited, signed by the Harbor Lights Base (installation), made from 214 recorded events".

You lead the Squadron (team) "shop". The trends page shows, per Flight and per Airfield, pass rate, flaky rate, coverage, open findings and how fast they are fixed, accessibility issues, and how releases behaved after launch, each chart with a table. Coverage of changed lines has stayed above 85 percent for three months; flaky rate rose last month, and the page names the four tests behind it.

How it works

What exists today

Built today

Launchway reads test results in thirteen formats, from the common XML format of unit-test tools to the JSON formats of browser and behavior-driven test tools, each checked against the real tool's output, and coverage in the six common formats. A step's results are read whether it passed or failed. The Debrief puts them in the order a person needs: a summary, a comparison with the last good run of the default branch, failures with expected against actual, the Sortie where a failure began and whether the default branch fails too, flaky and quarantined tests, the slowest tests, suites, a grid by browser or version, coverage and the trend. It exports as one HTML file with no script or network use, light and dark; as a PDF; as JSON; and in the common XML test-result format. Coverage of a change is worked out from line data and advises below a floor (80 percent by default). Tools' own HTML reports are kept and served in a sandbox that cannot act as the viewer. The release report works out the four delivery measures and exports one self-contained HTML page. Security, license and quality findings arrive through the Inspection and through SARIF files any step can report.

What is missing is one place that brings all of it together for a change, gates that judge all of it the same way, and a report that covers a whole release from commit to behavior in production.

What flows into the Debrief

KindWhat the Debrief holdsBuilt-in defaultConnected insteadToday
TestsEvery result with its suite, time, output, attachments, retries and historyReaders for thirteen formatsA test-management service receives the same results and may keep historyAvailable
CoverageLines, branches, functions; per file; changed lines; against the default branchReaders for six formatsA coverage service may be in charge of history and the floorAvailable
Flaky-test historyEach test's flaky score, known failure shapes, quarantine owner and endWorked out from the recordNone neededAvailable; failure shapes are planned
PerformancePercentiles, throughput, errors and saturation, against the last releaseA built-in constant-rate load StationOpen-source load tools run as separate containersPlanned (Milestone 8)
Code qualityComplexity, duplication and style findings, and measures per file over timeThe linters and analyzers of each language profile, run as visible stepsA code-analysis service through an adapterAvailable in part: lint advice and SARIF findings. Measures: Planned
Inspection findingsSecrets, vulnerable dependencies, insecure code, images, manifests; new, existing, acceptedStanding orders' checks, on by defaultA security product through an adapterAvailable
LicensesEach dependency's license against the allow and deny listsThe license check of Standing ordersA license service through an adapterAvailable
AccessibilityIssues by page and by success criterion of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, new and existingAn open-source accessibility engine run against a preview Airfield or built pagesAn accessibility service through an adapterPlanned
Summaries and notesA short summary from any step, and typed notes on files and linesThe step contract's results file, offered to every stepNone neededAvailable for custom steps; every step New in this plan
Manual testsTest cases run by people against one build's digest, with pass, fail, blocked or skippedTest cases kept in the repository and runs assigned in LaunchwayA test-management service through a HardpointNew in this plan
EvaluationsScores of AI features against a set of cases, per metric, against the last releaseA reader for one open, documented report formatThe team's evaluation tool, run as a stepNew in this plan

One in charge. Each kind is a capability slot. A Flight's settings show "served by" for each, as every module does. If a team connects a code-analysis service, the built-in analyzers for that kind stop being the source of verdicts; their findings can still be shown as advice, marked as such. Two tools never both decide the same gate by accident.

Facts, not files. Every kind is read into typed results on the record, in the same transaction as the step that produced it, as test results are today. A number in the Debrief always opens on its source: the step, the file it came from, the tool and its version. A file that is not what it claims is shown as such, with the reason, and never fails the step by itself.

New, existing, fixed, for every kind. The Inspection already blocks only what a change introduces, against the default branch as the baseline. The plan applies the same three states to every kind: a test failure, a quality finding, a license problem or an accessibility issue is new, existing or fixed. An old backlog never stops a change; a new problem always shows.

Coverage with a floor and a view of changed lines

Coverage of a whole project moves slowly and says little about one change. What matters for a pull request is whether the lines it adds or changes are tested. Launchway already works this out from line data and lists the uncovered lines. The plan puts that list on the diff itself, line by line, and makes "coverage of changed lines" a gate a level can set.

  • The diff view. On the pull request's files, each changed line is marked covered, not covered or not counted (a comment, a blank line), so the reviewer sees where the tests are.
  • The floor. A Flight's floor for changed lines (80 percent by default today, advice only) becomes a Standing order rule, so a Wing (organization) can set it for every Flight and a Flight can raise it. A drop in overall coverage beyond a set amount can be a second rule.
  • Honest limits. A change with no coverable lines passes and says why. A coverage report that cannot be read is "cannot tell", never a pass.

Quality gates as Standing orders

Today a step can fail on its own coverage threshold (fail_under), and Standing orders can require test results and judge findings before a Launch. The plan moves every quality gate into the typed catalog of Standing orders, so a gate is set once at a level, locked if needed, judged at the merge point and before each Launch, recorded with its facts, and waived the same way as any rule. A step's own fail_under keeps working.

RuleWhat it checksJudged atToday
testsAt least the minimum number of results; none failedBefore LaunchAvailable
tests, with fail_on: newOn a pull request, no failure that is new against the default branch; on the default branch and for a release, any failure countsMerge, before LaunchNew in this plan
changed_line_coverageChanged lines covered at least to the floor; optionally, overall coverage does not fall by more than a set amountMergeNew in this plan
findingsNo finding worse than allowed, overall or per tool; every required scanner reportedBefore LaunchAvailable
findings, with kinds and new_onlyThe same for quality, license and accessibility findings, judged on what the change introducesMerge, before LaunchNew in this plan
quarantineNo quarantine past its end date; at most a set number of quarantined tests in the FlightMergeNew in this plan
performanceThe release is within its baseline, with repeats and noise handled; "not enough data" never passesBefore LaunchNew in this plan, joining the planned "Performance gates in preflight"
manual_testsA named manual test plan was run against this release's digest and has no failed or blocked caseBefore LaunchNew in this plan
evaluationsEach named metric of an AI evaluation is at or above its floor for this Airfield, and has not fallen beyond a set amount against the last release; "not enough cases" never passesMerge, before LaunchNew in this plan
 
# Design: not built. Quality gates for every Flight of the Wing. Key names are not final.
standing_orders:
  - name: quality-floor
    point: merge
    scope: { branches: [main, "release/*"] }
    rules:
      tests: { fail_on: new }
      changed_line_coverage: { lines: 80, overall_drop_at_most: 2 }
      findings: { new_only: true, kinds: [security, license], fail_on: high }
      quarantine: { expired: deny, at_most: 10 }
    answer: deny
    mode: report              # watch it for two weeks first
    lock: true

Waivers work as they do for every Standing order: the rule and scope picked from the verdict, a kind picked from a list (accepted risk, false positive, not affected, fix scheduled), an owner, an end date within the limit, and a work item that tracks the fix. A waiver ends by itself and is shown wherever the verdict it changed is shown. A gate is never judged on a Return to base (rollback).

Summaries and notes from any step

Today a custom step can write a summary line (Markdown, shown on the step's page through a sanitizing renderer) and annotation lines (a file, a line, a level and a message) to the results file the step contract gives it. A plain script step cannot: its only voice is its log. This plan gives every step the same voice, through the same file, so a team does not have to wrap a script in a custom step to say one sentence on the Sortie page.

  • One file, made by the Station. Every step gets LAUNCHWAY_STEP_RESULTS, the path of a file the Station made for this attempt. Nothing is read from what a step prints, as the contract already requires, so a log line that looks like a note is just a log line.
  • A summary. At most 64 KiB of Markdown per step, rendered without script, without remote images and without raw HTML. It appears at the top of the step on the Sortie page, in the Debrief, in the Sortie report file, and, shortened, in the pull request's summary comment on a connected host.
  • Typed notes. Each note has a file, a line or a range, a level (note, warning, error), a title and a message, and optionally a kind (test, quality, security, performance) so it joins the right line of the Debrief. Notes are drawn on the pull request's diff where the line is part of it, and listed by file where it is not. At most 1,000 notes per step; the rest are counted, never silently dropped.
  • New, existing, fixed. A note is matched with the same note on the default branch by its file, its title and the text around its line, so a note that was already there is marked existing and does not shout on every pull request.
  • Never a result by itself. A note marked error does not fail the step; the step's exit code does. A Standing order may count notes of a kind, like any finding.
Design: not built

The results file for plain script steps, and the helper command, are designs; for custom steps the file and the summary and annotation lines exist today.

steps:
  bundle-size:
    image: node:22
    run: |
      npm run build
      launchway note --file web/src/cart.tsx --line 88 --level warning \
        --title "Bundle grew" --message "cart chunk is 41 KiB larger than on main"
      launchway summary "Bundle: 412 KiB (+41 KiB against main)"

Manual test runs

Not every check is automated. Before a large release, someone walks through checkout on a real phone; a regulated team must show that a person tested what was launched. Launchway records that work like any other test result, tied to the exact build that was tested.

  • Test cases live in the repository. A manual test plan is a small file under .launchway/manual-tests/: cases with steps and the expected result, each with an identifier. Changing a case is a reviewed change, like changing a test. A team that keeps its cases in a test-management service connects it through a Hardpoint (extension point) instead, as an equal choice, and results flow the same way.
  • A run is tied to a digest. A manual run is created for one build: a Sortie's image digest, or the preview Airfield where it runs, such as pr-482. Cases are assigned to people or to a Squadron by picking. Each person records pass, fail, blocked or skipped for each case, with an optional short note and attachments such as screenshots. Nothing else is typed.
  • Results are test results. A finished run appears in the Debrief as the suite manual: checkout, with who ran each case and when, and in the release report and the evidence pack. A failed case can open a work item with one click, linked to STORE-41.
  • A pipeline can wait for it. A step of kind manual_tests creates the run, waits without holding a Station (runner), and passes when the run passes. The manual_tests Standing order can require a passed run against the digest before a Launch (deployment) to prod.
  • A new build means a new run. A run counts only for the digest it was made against. When the digest changes, the page offers to copy the run's assignments to the new build and says which cases touch the files that changed.
Design: not built

Manual test plans, runs and the manual_tests step and rule are designs. Key names are not final.

# .launchway/manual-tests/checkout.yaml
plan: checkout
cases:
  - id: CHK-1
    title: Delivery date shows at checkout
    steps: [Add a product to the cart, Open checkout, Pick standard delivery]
    expect: The delivery date shows under the delivery choice
  - id: CHK-2
    title: Delivery date updates when the address changes
    steps: [Open checkout, Change the postal code]
    expect: The date updates within two seconds

AI evaluation results as a gate

A team that ships an AI feature tests its behavior with an evaluation: a set of cases, the model's answers, and scores per metric such as accuracy, groundedness or refusal rate. The team's own evaluation tool does the work; Launchway reads its report the way it reads test results, so the scores sit in the Debrief beside everything else and can be judged by a Standing order.

  • A step like any other. The evaluation tool runs as a step on a Station, in its pinned image, with the model credentials it needs as secret references. Launchway publishes one documented report format (cases, metrics, scores, the model and data versions) and a reader for it; tools that write another format convert with a small custom step.
  • In the Debrief. Each metric with its score, its floor and the last release's score; the cases that got worse first; the model and data versions used. A case that fails is shown like a failed test, with the expected and the actual answer.
  • A gate per Airfield. The evaluations Standing order sets a floor per metric and per Airfield (a looser floor in staging, a strict one in prod) and a largest allowed fall against the last release. Too few cases to judge is "not enough data", never a pass. Waivers work as for every rule.
  • On the record. Scores are facts on the record, so the release report shows them, trends show them per Flight over time, and an auditor can see what the AI feature was tested against before it launched.
Design: not built

The report format, the reader and the evaluations rule are designs. Key names are not final.

standing_orders:
  - name: assistant-quality
    point: before_launch
    scope: { environments: [prod] }
    rules:
      evaluations: { report: assistant-evals, metrics: { accuracy: 0.90, groundedness: 0.95 }, fall_at_most: 0.02 }
    answer: deny

The report itself

Every Sortie and every release gets one report, made from the record and designed to be opened by someone who was not there. The Sortie report is the Debrief written out whole; the release report follows a release from its commits to how it behaved in production.

Design: not built. The release report of storefront 2.4.0, part by part:

PartWhat it shows, for storefront 2.4.0
Verdict"Release 2.4.0 of storefront runs in prod since 14:08. Overwatch passed. No new test failures, no new severe findings." Digest sha256:4f9c…a17
What changed14 pull requests grouped as features, fixes, security and dependencies, with their work items, against 2.3.2 (what prod ran before)
What was testedSortie 417 at the release commit: 1,284 tests in 6 steps, 412 reused from Sortie 409 with the link; 3 quarantined tests that failed in their known way; performance run in staging
Passed and failedEvery kind with its counts; every failure with expected against actual and a small screenshot where the test attached one
Compared with 2.3.2Tests +38; coverage 82.4 percent (+0.6); changed lines 91 percent; findings 0 new, 2 fixed; checkout p95 182 ms against 176 ms (within noise); accessibility 1 fixed
Who cleared itAna gave Clearance (approval), saying Go at 14:05; the card showed the digest, the change from 2.3.2, the tests, the Inspection verdict and every Standing order so far. Dana wrote the change, so Dana could not clear it
Where it launchedIts Route (proposed word: the ordered Airfields a release flies through): dev 10:11, staging 10:16 (stayed 2 hours), prod 14:08 behind a Pathfinder (canary): 5 percent for ten minutes, then all
How it behavedFirst hour in prod: error rate 0.12 percent against 0.15 percent before; latency inside the Envelope (proposed word: the measured limits inside which the service is healthy); no Return to base
Supply chainSigned; list of contents with 312 components; how it was built; every Standing order verdict with its rule and the facts
Proof of originThe 214 events the report was made from, their hashes, and the Base's signature

The report is designed to be used, not filed.

  • One file that works offline. Styles, small images and fonts are inside the file. It loads nothing and runs no script, as the Debrief's HTML export does today. Sections fold with the page's own markup, so a phone reader sees the verdict first and opens what they need.
  • Reads well on a phone. One column below tablet width; tables become stacked rows with their headings; every chart is a simple bar or line with its table under it.
  • Accessible. Real headings, tables with headers, text for every image, colors that pass contrast in light and dark, and nothing that relies on color alone. The HTML is the accessible form; the PDF export is not tagged today, and the plan proposes tagging it.
  • Attached where people already look. A pull request gets a short summary and the file; on a connected code host the summary is part of the status Launchway reports. A release's page offers the file, a share link with an end date picked from a list, and the PDF.
  • Branded, never misleading. An installation's name and logo appear as today, and the report always says it was made by Launchway from the record, with the time.
Reports that prove they are unedited

A report is often passed around as a file, and a file can be edited. Each report carries, inside it, the list of record events it was made from with their hashes, and a signature by the Base, with the same key that signs evidence packs. launchway report verify checks a file offline against the Base's published key and says "unedited" or exactly what does not match; with access to the Base it also checks that the events are still on the record. An auditor can therefore accept a report from the team without taking the team's word for it. A report that cannot be signed (no key set up) says so on its first line.

Compared with the last good one

Every number means more beside the one before it. Today the Debrief compares a Sortie with the last successful run of the default branch, and the Coverage tab compares with the previous run and the default branch. The plan extends the comparison to every kind and to releases: a release is compared with what it replaces in each Airfield, which may differ (2.4.0 replaced 2.3.2 in prod but 2.3.3 in staging). The report shows each difference as "new", "fixed" or "changed by", never only a total.

Trends and metrics across time

Trends are readings of the record over time, per Flight, per Squadron and per Airfield. They are for seeing direction, not for ranking: nothing is shown per person except to that person.

TrendPer FlightPer SquadronPer Airfield
Pass rate, failures that reached the default branchYesYesFor tests run against it
Flaky rate and quarantine debtYesYesNo
Coverage, and coverage of changed linesYesYesNo
Code quality measures and hotspotsYes, by fileYesNo
Open findings, new and fixed, time to fixYesYesFor what runs there
Accessibility issuesYesYesFor previews and pages checked there
Performance per releaseYesNoYes
How releases behaved: Overwatch passes, Returns to baseYesYesYes

Every chart has its table, says which Sorties and Launches it is made from, and opens on them. The roadmap's planned posture score stays "a view, never a gate by itself"; trends never decide anything, Standing orders do.

Helping a team pass an audit

An audit asks the same questions every time: was the change reviewed, tested, scanned, approved by someone other than its author, deployed as built, watched, and undone when needed. Because the release report is made from the record, its answers are the evidence. The Logbook and evidence maps the same facts to the controls of published frameworks in an evidence pack; this chapter makes sure the two are never two different stories.

An auditor asksWhere the release report answersWhat is on the record
Was every change reviewed?What changed: each pull request with its approvalsReview and merge events, with the branch rules that judged them
Was it tested, and did the tests pass?What was tested; passed and failedStep results and test results in the same transaction
Were security scans run, and findings handled?Passed and failed: Inspection; waivers with owners and endsInspection verdicts, findings, waivers
Who approved production, and could they approve their own change?Who cleared itClearance events and the separation-of-duties verdict
Is what runs what was built and tested?Supply chain: digest, signature, list of contentsImage and Launch events by digest
Was it watched, and undone if it went wrong?How it behavedOverwatch verdicts, Returns to base
Is this report genuine?Proof of originThe events and their hashes; the Base's signature

An auditor gets the Observer (viewer) role on the levels in scope, or a time-limited auditor's view, and opens the same reports. Launchway is not certified against any standard; it provides controls and evidence, and says so on every evidence pack.

The module contract check

Rule of the contractHow this module meets it
1. Same levels and permissionsA Debrief or report is visible to whoever may see its Sortie or release. Squadron and Wing trends follow the levels. A restricted pull request sees history only for its own branch and the default branch, as today. No private roles.
2. Decisions on the one recordResults are stored with the step's event in one transaction, as test results are today. Gate verdicts, waivers and quarantines are events. A report is made from events and lists them.
3. Gates are Standing ordersEvery quality gate is a catalog rule judged at the merge point or before a Launch. A step's own fail_under keeps working as the step's check, not as a second policy system.
4. Typed input formsWaivers, quarantines, share links and report settings are typed forms: owners and work items picked, end dates from lists, one short reason the only typing.
5. Steps on StationsAnalyzers, accessibility checks and load tests run as visible steps on Stations (runners), in their tools' pinned images. The server only reads the files steps report.
6. One capability slot each, with "served by"Tests, coverage, code quality, security, licenses, performance and accessibility are each a slot with a built-in default and a connection as an equal choice, one in charge.
7. Off until wantedA kind appears only when a step reports it; tabs with nothing to show stay hidden, as today. The Inspection is the exception you ruled: on by default, opt out.
8. Every way inTests, coverage and reports are in the web interface, the HTTP API, the command line and the agent endpoint today. Report export, verification, share links and gate rules join them, with Terraform resources for rules and report settings.
9. Loss of a server, the database or a StationA Station keeps a step's results while the server is away and sends them when it returns. Another server can make the same report from the same events. If the database is lost, no new report is made; files already shared stay readable and verifiable offline.
10. Never blocks Return to baseNo quality gate is judged on a Return to base. A report of a Launch that returned to base says so at the top.

Safety

If this fails or is wrongWhat happens
A report file cannot be readThe kind shows "not a report", with the reason; the step's outcome is unchanged; a gate that needs that kind says "cannot tell" and does not pass.
A tool reports nothing"No report" is never "no findings". A required kind that is missing fails its gate, naming the step.
A report writes false resultsResults are only as true as the step that wrote them, which is why shared test and scanning steps can be required by a Standing order. The report names the step and the tool behind every number.
A tool's own HTML report holds hostile scriptIt is served in the sandbox that exists today, under a link that names one report and expires, on a separate origin where set. Launchway's own reports carry no script at all.
A shared report is editedVerification fails and says which part differs.
A share link leaksIt shows one report until its end date, can be revoked, and every opening is recorded in the Logbook (audit trail).
Who mayIn this plan
Read a Debrief or a reportWhoever may see the Sortie or release
Make a share linkA Pilot (operator) of the Flight; the end date from a list capped by the level
Set or lock a quality gateA Commander (owner) of the level, by a reviewed change
Waive a gateAs for every Standing order: at or above the level that locked it, never the change's author on a protected Airfield
Quarantine a testAnyone who may open a pull request; the quarantine is a reviewed change
Set up the report signing keyAn administrator of the Base

On by default: the Inspection on every Sortie; new, existing and fixed for every kind; coverage of changed lines advised at 80 percent; reports with no script; signing as soon as a key exists; share links that end; quality gates offered in report mode first.

Screens

The full list, with every field and state, is in the screens notes for this chapter. In short:

The Debrief, overview
The verdict sentence, one line per kind with new, existing and fixed, the gate verdicts, and the comparison with the last good run.
Coverage on the diff
The pull request's changed lines marked covered or not, with the changed-line figure and the floor.
Code quality and accessibility tabs
Findings by file or page with new, existing and fixed, measures over time, and "served by".
Release report, desktop and phone
The ten parts of the anatomy above, each folding to its evidence, light and dark, as one file.
Share and export
File, PDF, share link with an end date from a list, attach to the pull request; who opened it.
Verify a report
Drop a file and see "unedited" or what differs, and the events it was made from.
Quality trends
Per Flight, Squadron and Airfield, each chart with its table and its Sorties.
Quality gates
The rules in force for a Flight, where each comes from, and recent verdicts; part of the Standing orders area.
Step summary and notes
The summary at the top of a step, notes on the diff with level and kind, and notes listed by file where the line is not in the diff.
Manual test run
A wizard to start a run (plan and digest or preview Airfield picked from lists, cases assigned by picking people or a Squadron), and the tester's page: one case at a time with pass, fail, blocked or skipped, a short note and attachments.
Evaluations
A tab of the Debrief: each metric with score, floor and the last release's score, the cases that got worse, and the model and data versions.

Proposed roadmap changes

Each change is in the roadmap's item shape. The same list is kept as data beside this plan for the roadmap's editor. Three more items, Summaries and notes from any step, Manual test runs recorded in the Debrief and AI evaluation results as a gate, are in plan-notes/proposals/fixes-flightplan-b.json.

Open question

  1. Built-in tools for code quality and accessibility. Which open-source analyzers and which accessibility engine to ship, each in its own container, after the same license review the Inspection's tools had. Open question
  2. Coverage of changed lines: advice or gate by default? Today it advises at 80 percent. Recommendation: keep advice by default and offer the gate in report mode. Open question
  3. The key that signs reports. Launchway has no signing key for Git objects today. The Logbook and evidence proposes that the Base signs evidence packs. Recommendation: reports use the same Base key, kept like other root keys, with its public half published on the Base. Open question
  4. Share links for people without an account. Recommendation: allowed, with an end date from a list (7 days by default, 90 at most), revocable and recorded; a level can turn them off. Open question
  5. New-only failures on pull requests. Judging only new failures on a pull request lets a team merge while the default branch is broken for another reason. Recommendation: allow it, because the default branch and every release still count every failure. Open question
  6. Where manual test cases live. Recommendation: in the repository, so a case is reviewed like a test, with a test-management service as an equal connected choice. The alternative is to keep them as work items. Open question
  7. The evaluation report format. Launchway would publish one documented format for AI evaluation reports and read it. If an open standard for evaluation reports settles, adopt it instead. Open question

Mission support · around every layer

Every way in

Whether you click, call, type, ask an agent or write Terraform, you reach the same operation with the same rights, the same checks and the same record, and a test fails the build the day one way falls behind.

  • The Tower (home) tells you what needs you; every task has a wizard with the plain form beside it; the do bar finds any page and starts any task.
  • One operation, five ways in: the web interface, the HTTP API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform. A parity test already ties every API route to its agent tool and its command. This plan extends it to the web interface and, when the provider exists, to Terraform.
  • Editor plug-ins, one-step setup for agent tools and the phone bring Launchway to where you already are. Accessibility is checked on every change and becomes a release gate.
  • Comms (notifications), Flight school (learning) inside the product, words shown with their plain meaning, errors that say what to do next, and never a button that does not work.
  • A description of the HTTP API that tools can read, generated from the route table and kept true by the parity test; settings that can live in Git, each change on screen or in Git a reviewed change in the other; and the ways in deliberately not added, with the reason.

Where it sits

Layer
Around all seven layers. The spine says it in one line: every way in is the same way in.
Builds on
The server's route table and its checks (Levels, people and secrets); the actions list the server computes for each resource; the record and the Logbook (audit trail) (the record); typed inputs (Inputs and run forms); the words system.
Built on it
Every screen and wizard of every chapter (Screens), the Wingman (helper) (the Wingman and agents), and the inbox of Work, from idea to running software.
Capability slots
None of its own for the ways in: they are not optional providers, they are the product. Comms has destinations (inbox, e-mail, chat channels, webhooks), several at once, each with its delivery log.

What you will be able to do

You sign in. The Tower says "2 things need you": a failed Sortie (run) on main with "See what went wrong", and a Clearance (approval) waiting for you with "Review". A failure that is already being retried is not listed; it shows under "Running now" as "Retrying". When nothing needs you, the page is calm. Available

You press the slash key and type "turn off". The do bar offers "Turn a Switch off..." and opens the guided change, already scoped to the Flight (codebase) you were on. In progress A do bar for every task: pages, Sorties and repositories are found today; a guided action for every task is missing.

You add the staging Airfield (environment) with the wizard. Its last step shows exactly what will be created, and beside it the same thing as a command, an API call, an agent tool call and a Terraform resource, so you can put it in a script or in Git next time. Available as the wizard with a copyable configuration; New in this plan as the four other ways in shown side by side.

You write a script against the API. Your tool reads Launchway's published API description, generates a client, and tells you that starting a Sortie needs a token with the Pilot role and is written to the Logbook as run.start. When the next release changes an answer, the published list of changes says so. New in this plan

Your Squadron keeps its Airfield settings in Git. You change the staging queue on screen; Launchway opens a pull request with your change and a check showing the difference and the Standing order verdicts. Ana approves and merges it, and the screen shows it live with a link to the pull request. New in this plan, on Planned Launchway’s own settings as code, both ways.

In your editor you start a Sortie, read why a step failed with the failing line underlined in your file, and approve a change, without opening a browser. Planned Editor plug-ins; An editor extension.

On your phone, a notice says the storefront Launch (deployment) to prod waits for your Clearance. The decision card shows what changes, who started it, the risk, the evidence and what happens next. You press Go. If something goes wrong later, Return to base (rollback) is one button on the same phone. Available Decision cards that read on a phone; New in this plan one-tap Clearances with notices on the phone.

You hover the word "Sortie" and read "In plain words: run." You open Flight school from the top bar and read the guide for the release you are running, with an offline search, and press "Try it in the editor" under an example. Available

How it works

One operation, five ways in

Every operation is one route on the server. The web interface, the command line, the agent endpoint and, when it exists, the Terraform provider are clients of that route, with the caller's own token or session. So a permission, a Standing order (policy), a Hold (freeze) or a validation problem is decided once, in one place, and comes back to every client in the same words.

Here is one operation, adding the staging Airfield for storefront, in all five.

Add an Airfield wizard (Available): name and target, who may launch there, protection and queue, launch Stations (runners), check and create. Each step is checked against the server as you answer, nothing is created until you confirm, and Cancel leaves nothing behind. The plain form for the same object is one tab away in Configuration.

PUT /api/v1/config/environments/staging
{ "spec": { "projects": ["storefront"], "protected": false, "target": "..." },
  "comment": "Second Airfield for storefront" }

The configuration API (Available). Sending the same body twice changes nothing the second time. A wrong body answers 400 with every problem listed. The spec is shortened here; its fields are those of the configuration reference.

launchway config set environments staging -f staging.yaml --comment "Second Airfield for storefront"

The command line (Available), a call of the same route, with --json for scripts.

tool: put_config
arguments: { "kind": "environments", "name": "staging", "spec": { ... } }

The agent endpoint (Available), listed only to tokens that may change configuration, and recorded in the Logbook as made through the agent endpoint with the token's name.

# Design: not built. The provider is planned.
resource "launchway_environment" "staging" {
  name     = "staging"
  projects = ["storefront"]
  target   = "..."
}

The Terraform resource name is already reserved in the configuration reference (Planned Terraform provider). An object written by Terraform is marked as managed by it, and a change from another way in must carry the version it read, so neither silently overwrites the other.

The parity test, today and extended

Today a table in the code holds one row per operation: the route, its agent tool, its command, its Terraform resource, and a status: equal, gap (something one interface lacks today) or exempt (not an operation for people or agents, such as the Station protocol, with a written reason). The build runs these checks:

  1. Every route has a row, and every row a route. The test reads the server's own route list.
  2. Every named tool exists. The test opens a real agent-endpoint session, lists its tools, and requires each named tool to exist and each tool to be in a row.
  3. Every named command exists. The command's first word must be a real command and the rest must appear in its help.
  4. Gaps only shrink. The number of gaps is fixed in the code and may only go down; the build fails if it rises, and also if it falls without the number being lowered, so progress is locked in.
  5. The reference page is current. The published interface parity page is generated from the table and must match it.

Two things are not checked yet: Terraform is a column, not a test, because no provider exists; and the web interface is not in the table at all. This plan adds both.

ExtensionHow it worksStatus

A published description of the HTTP API, kept true by the parity test

Tools that call an API need a description they can read: to generate a client, to check a request before sending it, to show a developer what is there. Launchway generates one from the same source the server routes from, so it cannot fall behind.

  • Generated, never written by hand. Each release, the build turns the route table and the request and answer types into a description in the OpenAPI format, an open standard that many tools read.
  • More than shapes. Each route also says who may call it (its access class), what it writes to the Logbook (audit trail), and its other ways in: the command, the agent tool, the Terraform resource and the screen from the parity table. A tool reading the description knows the rights it needs before it calls.
  • Kept true. The parity test gains two checks: every route is in the description and every entry is a route; and the existing API tests run through a checker that compares each real request and answer with the description, so a field that changes in the code and not in the description fails the build. Examples in the description are run in the build too.
  • Published with what changed. Every server serves the description for its own version (Design: not built; for example GET /api/v1/description), the reference carries it for each release, and a list of what was added, changed and deprecated since the last release is published beside it. A documented field is never removed without a deprecation first, as the record's stages already promise for older answers.
  • One source for the agent endpoint. The agent endpoint's tool inputs are generated from the same types, so a tool and its route cannot disagree.
Built today

No description is published yet. The HTTP API reference page is checked by a test against the server's route table: every route appears exactly once, with its access class and its audit action. The generator builds on that table.

Settings on screen and in Git, each a reviewed change in the other

Settings live in the database, with a history for every object, and a whole-installation export to Git exists today (launchway config export, import and apply, all or none, each change carrying the version it read). The round trip makes Git a reviewed way in for settings, for the levels that want it, without a second source of truth.

  • Per level, by kind. A level names its settings repository and which kinds of object live there. The parity table gains a column per object kind: kept in Git, kept as a reference only (a secret is only ever its reference), or not kept, with the reason (tokens, sessions).
  • From Git. A pull request that changes settings files gets a check before merge: the difference from the live settings and the Standing order verdicts at the setting-change point. A merge is applied through the same route as config apply, all or none, and the result, or the refusal with its reasons, is posted back on the pull request.
  • From the screen. The level chooses one of two modes. "Git leads": a change on screen becomes a pull request with the person as author, and the object shows "waiting for review" until it merges. "Screen leads, Git follows": the change is live at once and the commit follows it.
  • Conflicts. Every change carries the version it read. A merge based on an older version than the live one is refused with the three-way difference on the pull request; there is never a last writer who wins silently.
  • Drift. A change made outside Git (a break-glass, for example) shows as drift on the object and on the level, with "Open a pull request to match" or "Put it back".

Ways in that are not added, and why

"One way in" cuts both ways: every way in is equal, and no second way is added to do the same thing. Two are recorded as exemptions in the parity table, each with its reason.

Not addedWhyWhat you use instead
A second API style with graph queriesIt would double the routes the parity test, the permission checks and the Logbook must cover, for answers the HTTP API can already give.The software graph's own routes for graph questions; and, to save round trips, the HTTP API lets a caller pick the fields and the related objects an answer carries (Design: not built), checked by the same parity test.
Pipelines and Sorties as objects in your cluster's APIPipelines live in Git with the code; a cluster-object way in would be a sixth way in with its own permission model (cluster roles) for the parity test and the Logbook to mirror.Settings through the settings repository above, which a GitOps controller applies like any other repository, or through the Terraform provider; Sorties started by the command line, the API or a trigger.

The Tower, the do bar and a wizard for every task

The Tower answers one question: what should I look at? It lists what needs you, with why it is here and what to do; what is running now; your Flights by Squadron (team); and what finished lately. A failure counts only while it still needs someone, by one rule shared with the Sortie list, the command line (launchway attention) and the agent tool attention. You can set an entry aside or snooze it; that is a personal preference, written to the Logbook as one. Panels are yours to arrange, including one that takes you back to where you left off.

Every task is a wizard of a few short screens. Each says what it is for, explains each option in a sentence, checks answers against the server as you type, creates nothing until the last screen, and shows exactly what it will create. The plain form for the same object is always beside it. Every wizard registers itself with the do bar, so any task can be started by name from anywhere.

RuleWhat it means on screen
Never a button that does not workThe server computes, once per resource, which actions exist, whether each is available now, why not, and who can. The web interface, the command line and the agent endpoint all read it. A control is shown working only when the action would work; otherwise it is absent or shown unavailable with the reason and what would make it available.
Full control, with warningsA permitted but risky action is not blocked. It shows the consequence in a sentence and a suggestion, asks for confirmation or a reason, then does it.
Errors say what to do nextEvery refusal names the problem, where it is, and the next step. The API, command line and agent endpoint share a written quality bar, tested: errors that say what to do, help for every command, a description for every tool.
Words with their plain meaningAn aviation word is shown once with a dotted underline; hover, focus or tap shows "In plain words: run." and its meaning. In tables the plain word sits beside it. A Base can switch to the plain word set or rename any word; addresses, commands and pipeline keys never change.
Every view has an addressAny page, filter and tab can be bookmarked and shared.
Nothing switched off is shownA new installation is small; sections appear as capabilities are turned on.

Comms: telling people

Comms has two halves. For people: one inbox with every notice that concerns you, e-mail by your choice per kind, watch levels per repository and Flight, quiet hours, a daily digest, and mute links that need no sign-in. Mail carries less than the inbox: for anything not public, only names and links. For other systems: rules that send a signed webhook or a chat message when a Sortie, a Clearance or a Launch changes, with a delivery log and retries. Both are Available. Planned: notices for every remaining kind of event as their features land, notices on the phone, and deciding a Clearance from a chat message.

Where you already are: editor, terminal, agent tool, phone

  • The terminal. One binary is the server, the Station, local runs and the API client. launchway init writes a first pipeline, launchway validate checks one offline with libraries expanded, launchway run runs it on your machine, and every command answers in JSON for scripts. Planned: signing in through the browser; and, proposed in Inputs and run forms as "One input check for every way in", a command line that asks with the same fetched choices as the form when a value is missing.
  • The editor. A published schema gives completion and inline errors today. Planned: plug-ins for the common editors from one signed package, showing Sorties, findings and decisions and starting Sorties, under the same permissions; and a language server generated from the same parser the server uses. This plan has the language server offer the checker and the Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it) inline: beside a trigger or a condition you see "a push to main runs build and test, skips docs", with the reason for each skip, before you commit.
  • Agent tools. The agent endpoint and the Connect an agent page exist; one-step setup is planned (see the Wingman chapter).
  • The phone. The interface already works at phone width with a bottom tab bar, and decision cards read in seconds. This plan adds an installable phone app built from the same interface, with notices and one-tap Clearances, Return to base and Abort.

Accessibility as a release gate

The web interface is built to WCAG 2.2 level AA. On every change, the build checks the contrast of every color pair in both themes, scans every component and routed page, and refuses a state shown by color alone. A real-browser run checks 26 pages at desktop and phone width in light and dark, reflow at 320 pixels, focus rings, and ten keyboard-only journeys. Baselines may only shrink. A person checks with a screen reader before a release, but the results are not yet written down for each release. This plan makes that check a recorded release gate: a release is not published until its accessibility record is complete, and the conformance statement is generated from it. The API, the command line and the agent endpoint keep their own quality bar.

The newcomer's first hour

The Harbor Lights team has a Kubernetes cluster and the storefront repository on a hosted code host. You are setting Launchway up for them for the first time.

  1. Install. launchway install asks the same few questions for a laptop, a server or Kubernetes, shows the cluster it will change and asks by name, then prints the address and a one-time setup code. Available
  2. Sign in. You enter the setup code and become the first administrator with a second factor. Available
  3. In-processing (first-run setup). The setup guide walks seven steps you may skip and return to: how people sign in, encryption and the root key, a Station, Git hosting, bringing in repositories, a first pipeline, finish. You name the Wing (organization) and choose aviation or plain words. Available
  4. First pipeline. storefront has no pipeline file. Launchway looks at what it holds (a Go service and a web front end) and proposes a pipeline, shown in full before anything runs. You save it as a pull request. Available
  5. First Sortie. It runs on the server's own Station; the launch line turns green; the Debrief (test report) shows the tests. Available
  6. First Airfield and Launch. The Add an Airfield wizard creates dev. The first Launch goes through a GitOps controller you connect; Available. Launching straight to the cluster with no controller is Planned (Delivery by choice), so the one-hour path without a controller waits for it.
  7. Next. The Tower shows "Your next step: add staging", with a progress bar of the essentials, and the Wingman column links the Flight school page on the launch line. Inviting a teammate with one link is Planned (A guided first project).

The plan turns this hour into a test with a clock, like the planned "first green build in ten minutes": a scripted newcomer goes from install to a first Launch on a throwaway cluster, and the build fails if it takes longer or needs a step that is not a wizard.

The contract check

This chapter is not an optional module; it is how every module is reached. It still meets the ten points, because a way in that broke one would break it for every module.

Contract pointHow every way in meets itToday
1. Same levels and permissionsEvery way in carries the caller's token or session and goes through the same checks. No client has a right the API lacks. The agent endpoint refuses browser session cookies.Available
2. One recordEvery change is in the record and the Logbook with how it came: screen, API, command line, agent endpoint, Git or Terraform.Available
3. Gates are Standing ordersNo way in bypasses a Standing order, a Hold or a Clearance: they are judged at the route, so a Terraform apply meets the same refusal as a button.Available
4. Typed input formsWizards and run forms use typed inputs; the API validates the same types; the command line will ask with the same fetched choices (Inputs and run forms).Available in part
5. Runs as stepsWays in run nothing themselves. Local runs use the same step images and the step contract.Available
6. Served byComms destinations are several at once by design, each with its delivery log; the inbox is built in, chat and webhooks are connections.Available
7. Off until wantedSections appear when there is something to show. Mail is off until an administrator sets a mail server. Editor plug-ins and the phone app are optional. The agent endpoint is on because it grants nothing a token does not already have, and can be turned off.In progress
8. Every way inThe parity test, extended to the web, to Terraform, to the published API description and to which settings may live in Git; the two ways in not added are recorded exemptions with their reasons.Available for three of five
9. Failure and who may do whatSee Safety.Available
10. Never blocks Return to baseReturn to base and Abort are equal in every way in and on the phone, and can never be listed as a gap.New in this plan as a test

Safety

When something fails

  • A server is lost. The API and the agent endpoint keep no sessions, so any server answers the next request; the web interface reconnects its live stream; a Sortie start carries an idempotency key, so a retried command does not start two.
  • The database is lost. Every way in answers with the same plain message and the doctor command's advice; nothing is accepted that cannot be recorded.
  • The web interface is broken. The command line, the API and the agent endpoint still work, including Return to base.
  • Mail or a chat channel is down. The inbox is not held; messages wait in a bounded outbox and are retried; the delivery log says so.

Who may do what

Exactly what the caller's role allows, wherever they come in. Tokens are scoped to Flights and roles and can expire; agent tool tokens start as viewer tokens. Arranging the Tower for everyone needs the right to arrange at that level; arranging your own needs nothing. Choosing the word set is an administrator's; reading in either set is everyone's.

On by default

Sign-in from the first moment. Status always an icon plus a word. Accessibility checks on every change. Mail that carries only names and links for anything not public. Risky actions that ask first, in plain words. An address for every view.

Screens

The Tower

Needs you, running now, by category, recently finished, where you left off, your next step; arranged for you or for everyone.

The do bar

Opened with the slash key: pages, objects and every task by name, each task opening its wizard with what you were looking at filled in.

The wizard frame

Stepper, one question per screen, live checks, "Check and create", and a panel "The same, another way" with the four other ways in.

Why not?

From any unavailable control: the permission or rule it needs, where it is set, each grant considered, and who can fix it.

Flight school

Paths by role, the release you run, offline search, "Try it in the editor", diagrams with their text.

Words

Choose the set, rename a word, preview the navigation and a decision card.

Comms settings

Per kind: inbox only, inbox and e-mail, or off; watch levels; quiet hours; digest; channels with their delivery logs.

API description and what changed

The description for this server's version, by area, with each route's rights, Logbook action and other ways in; a list of what changed since the last release; a download.

Settings in Git

Choose the repository and the kinds kept there from pickers, the mode (Git leads, or screen leads), and the drift list with "Open a pull request to match" and "Put it back".

The phone

Tower, inbox, decision card, Launch with Return to base and Abort, at 390 pixels with a bottom tab bar.

Proposed roadmap changes

Six new items. The command line that asks like a form is proposed once, in Inputs and run forms. Nothing existing is removed or narrowed. The same JSON is in the proposals file for this chapter.

Open question

Decision needed

Two ways in not added. This plan records a graph-query API and cluster objects for pipelines and Sorties as exemptions. Confirm, or ask for a thin set of cluster objects for Airfields and Ramps only?

Decision needed

Settings in Git, the default mode. When a level turns the settings repository on, should "Git leads" (screen changes become pull requests) be the default, as this plan suggests for production Airfields, or "screen leads, Git follows"?

Decision needed

Two editor items. "An editor extension" (Milestone 2) and "Editor plug-ins" (Milestone 14) describe the same work. Keep both and link them (this plan's default), or merge them into one item in one milestone?

Decision needed

A phone app, or the phone width only. The proposal is an installable app built from the web interface, not a separate native app. Is that enough for "a phone app with one-tap approvals"?

Decision needed

Web parity in Milestone 1. Adding the web column to the parity test lands in Milestone 1, which is marked Now. Accept it there, or schedule it with the first item of Milestone 2?

Launchway platform plan

All screens

Every screen this plan names, in one index: what each is for, whether it has been drawn yet, which chapter designs it, and whether it exists today.

  • 373 screens in 8 areas. 175 are drawn as mock-ups; 198 are specified in a chapter but not yet drawn.
  • The mock-up pages hold 194 drawn screens; some screens in the index are drawn in several states, so one row can link to more than one drawing.
  • Every screen is a design unless its status says otherwise. A drawing shows how a screen will look; it does not mean the screen is built.
  • Every screen follows the same rules, listed first, so a new screen can be checked against them before it is drawn.

The rules every screen follows

These come from the chapters on every way in and on inputs and run forms, and the frame is drawn in the anatomy of the frame.

Picked, not typed

Free text is the last resort. Wherever a value can be offered, it is picked from a list fetched from the place it lives (branches, versions in the Depot, Airfields, people, secrets by reference), and checked as you type and again on the server. Where free text remains, it has an example, a live check and a plain message.

Inputs and run forms · Inputs and run forms

Every refusal explains itself

A refusal names the problem, where it is, and the next step. A button that cannot be used now is never silently missing or dead: it says why not and who can.

An action that says why it is unavailable · Why was this refused?

The aviation word with its plain word

An aviation word is shown once with its plain meaning on hover, focus or tap; in tables the plain word sits beside it. Status is always an icon and a word, never color alone.

An aviation word and its plain meaning

Light, dark and phone

Every screen works in a light and a dark theme and at phone width, with a keyboard and with a screen reader. Decisions such as Go or No-go can be made from a phone.

One frame in light, dark and phone · Inputs and run forms

A wizard for every task, the plain form beside it

Each task is a few short screens that say what they are for, check answers as you go, create nothing until the last step and show exactly what will be created. The do bar starts any task by name.

A wizard in three steps · The do bar

Every view has an address; nothing switched off is shown

Any page, filter and tab can be bookmarked and shared. A new installation is small; sections appear as capabilities are turned on.

What happens next

The 198 screens not yet drawn are handed to a second round of mock-up builders, grouped by the page they belong on, each with a pointer to the place in the plan that specifies its regions, fields and states. As they are drawn, this index links to them.

Screens: the frame and the foundation

The frame every Launchway screen lives in, and the foundation screens inside it: the Tower, the do bar and wizards, levels and access, Stations, capabilities and connections, the record, and the health of the system itself.

  • One frame for everything: a top bar with a route of areas, a left column for the area, breadcrumbs, the page, and a guide rail for the Wingman.
  • Every task has a wizard made of pickers; free text is only for names and reasons, and says why.
  • An action you cannot take is shown unavailable with the reason beside it, never as a button that does nothing.
  • Each screen below is a design; the chip says whether it exists today, is in progress or is planned.

The frame and the Tower

The anatomy of the frame

Every screen sits in the same five regions. Notice that the left column belongs to the area you are in, and the guide rail is the Wingman, never page content.

Available Chapter: Every way in

One frame in light, dark and phone

The same Tower in three forms. Notice that on a phone the route becomes a bottom tab bar and the left column, where there is one, becomes a strip of pills.

Available Chapter: Every way in

The Tower

Home answers what needs you now, then what is on its way. Notice that each row says why it needs you and offers one recommended action, and that the launch line shows exactly where each change stands.

Available Chapter: Every way in

Go or No-go on a phone

A decision card carries what, who, risk and evidence, then two big buttons. Notice that No-go will ask for a reason and that Return to base stays available after a Go.

Screens: writing pipelines

These mock-ups show how pipelines are written, tested, reused, started and brought in from other systems, drawn in the product’s own look.

  • The editor checks as you type and explains the plan before a Sortie starts.
  • Tested code and the Simulator prove a pipeline without a Station.
  • The catalog, update notices and triggers page make reuse and starts visible.
  • Importing shows three outcomes per construct and compares old and new side by side.

The pipeline editor and checker

Writing a pipeline is checked as you type, explained before it flies, and explained again afterward.

The pipeline editor with live checking

Write the pipeline and see at once whether it is valid. A problem is marked on its line and explained with the fix beside it; the plan below stays gray until the error is gone. Planned Read the chapter

The plan preview

Before saving, choose an event and see what the pipeline would do. Each step is labeled will run, will not run (with the reason) or depends on a named value that is known only in flight. Planned Read the chapter

The reference picker

Put a value into a field without typing its name. Only names that are valid at this field can be chosen, each with its type and moment, and a gray name says why it cannot. Planned Read the chapter

Why was this skipped

Open any step that did not run and read the reason: the condition as written, each name with the value it had and where that value came from, and the decision recorded at the time. Planned Read the chapter

Where did this value come from

For any value a step received, follow the chain back to the step, input or level that produced it, with the time of each hop. Planned Read the chapter

Event filter translation

Move one event source from the old filter language to the one expression language. Old and new run side by side on recent calls before anything switches. Planned Read the chapter

Re-run plan

Before re-running from a step or only what failed, see what runs again, what is reused and which decisions are made again from the values recorded the first time. Planned Read the chapter

Tested code and the Simulator

Logic lives in tested code. The Simulator proves a pipeline with stand-in results and replays changes against history.

Move inline code into a custom step

When an inline block is over the limit, the editor offers to turn it into a tested custom step. Inputs and outputs are proposed from what the block reads and writes. Planned Read the chapter

Start a custom step from nothing, from the web, as the command line does. The kit shows exactly what will be written before anything is saved. Planned Read the chapter

Everything about one step: what it takes and gives, what it may reach, and the tests and coverage for each version. In progress Read the chapter

The Simulator

Choose an event, give each step a stand-in result, and see which steps would run, which are skipped and why, and what would launch, all marked not performed. Planned Read the chapter

Save a simulation as a test

Keep what the Simulator showed as a test that runs on every change, with the assertions you choose. Planned Read the chapter

Replay report

Before merging a change to a pipeline, see which of the last Sorties it would have run differently, and the value that decided each. Planned Read the chapter

Debrief: pipeline code

A section of the Debrief for the code a pipeline runs: step tests, contract checks, Simulator tests and condition coverage, with failures spelled out. Planned Read the chapter

Standing order: code in pipelines

Set the inline-code limits and the tested-shared-code rule at a level, with inherited values and who locked them shown beside each control. Planned Read the chapter

Screens: inputs and run forms

What the forms of the plan look like: the page that starts a Sortie, every kind of field, the wizard that defines an option source, saved answers, a Clearance that asks for values, and the explanation of a refused value.

  • Every field says how it is filled without typing: a choice, a picker with search, a switch, a slider or a calendar. Free text appears once, last, with an example and a live check.
  • The page that starts a Sortie shows, beside the form, what will run. It reacts to answers, says what is wrong in plain words and offers the fix.
  • The same form engine draws the phone page, the Clearance card, the wizards and the pipeline author's preview.
  • These are designs, not built. The chapter explains each idea: Inputs and run forms.

Start a Sortie

Start a Sortie: defaults from context

A page with an address, replacing today’s dialog. Airfield is already staging because that was Dana’s last answer, the version list is open with the newest images from the Depot, and the summary on the right says what it needs. Notice the machine name beside each label and that region is locked, not editable.

The form is never replaced by a blank page. A broken pipeline file shows its problems with line numbers, a source that is down only affects its own field, a version deleted meanwhile is reported by the server in the same words as the live check, and a person who cannot start it is told who can.
