Screens: launching

What it will look like to launch an application with Launchway, wherever it runs: one Route board, one Launch page, one way back, with the same screens for Kubernetes, virtual and physical machines, image-based hosts and serverless functions.

  • Every screen is drawn in the product's own look, with the Harbor Lights team: storefront on a Kubernetes cluster, billing on two virtual machines, kiosk-os on image-based hosts, and the image-resize function.
  • All of these are designs. Each one carries its status, and a link to the chapter it illustrates.
  • Three screens appear in the dark theme and three on a phone, because people launch and clear from both.
  • A Launch is watched the same way everywhere: strategy, progress, traffic by version, and the Overwatch verdict with its evidence.

The shared model

These screens are the same whatever the target: the Route, the Airfield, the way back, the Clearance and the preview.

Route board

The first page of Launches for a Flight: every release, every Airfield, and why each one is or is not moving. Notice that each cell says what holds it, in one sentence, and that the detail below spells out who may give the missing Clearance.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Route editor

Make or change a Route without writing a file. Each stop gets conditions that are picked, not typed; a locked switch shows which level above requires it. The right side always previews what the Route would do to the release that is waiting now.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Airfield page

What runs in prod, by digest, and how each target is served. Notice the drift banner (the digest on the cluster is not the one Launchway last sent), that the rule list shows its level and a lock, and that the history links each Launch to who cleared it.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Airfield setup: served by

Add a target and choose how it is served, without touching the pipeline. Each option is tested live against the chosen Station, so an option that cannot work says why and what would fix it.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Return to base

The confirmation says in one sentence what will change: the Airfield, the two releases, what is reverted and what is not. The earlier good releases are listed with what choosing each would undo, and anything it passes through is stated, not asked.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Preview list

Every short-lived Airfield made for a pull request, with its address, expiry and cost against its cap. Notice the fork pull request that waits for a person to say Go before anything is created, and the one scaled to zero with a Wake button.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Launch record

The auditor's and on-call view of one Launch: who asked, every digest, who cleared it and in what words, the rules checked, the traffic measured and the verdict. It is the same record every kind of target writes.

Planned Chapter: One way to launch, anywhere

Clearance to launch

The page a Controller sees when a Launch needs a Go. Everything needed to decide is above the buttons: what will happen, what was checked, who has already said Go. On the phone the same decision fits one screen.

Planned Chapter: Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Kubernetes

Launching to a cluster, with a GitOps controller or directly. These screens extend the rollout page that exists today.

Launch page

Everything you need to watch and steer one Launch: the strategy as a line you can read, the share of traffic each version has, and the Overwatch verdict with its evidence beside it. It extends today's rollout page and keeps its tabs.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

A Launch watched from a phone

The same Launch, as a short vertical line: where it is, how traffic is split, what Overwatch thinks, and the two buttons you might need. Return to base is never more than one tap away.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Launch across several clusters

The same Launch page with a strip of clusters in wave order. Each cluster has its own state, and a cluster chip filters every tab to that cluster. Notice what starts wave 3 and what happens to the earlier waves if wave 2 fails.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Direct Launch plan

For a direct Launch, shows exactly what will change before anything does: objects grouped as changed, new and to be removed, with the field difference one click away. The last group shows what is never deleted.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Kubernetes target setup: services

One step of adding a cluster target: where each service's chart or manifests come from. Every field is a picker fed by the Depot or the repository, so a path cannot be mistyped.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

One preview

Everything about one pull request's preview: its address, namespace, database, cost against its cap and each Launch into it. Extending and tearing down are one click each.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Cluster rules review

Admission rules generated from the Airfield's Standing orders, shown as text and as a difference against what the cluster has now. Approving opens a pull request; nothing is applied silently. Rules the cluster cannot express are labeled as checked only in Launchway.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Admission refusals

A short list of what the cluster turned away and why: the object, the rule and who or what applied it. A refusal that involved a Launch links to it, and an emergency use stands out.

Planned Chapter: Launching to Kubernetes

Virtual machines and physical servers

Fleets of machines in the Airfield, reached over SSH or by a host agent, launched host by host with zero downtime.

Hosts: the fleets list

Every fleet you may see, with whether it is healthy and current. A fleet is a named set of machines in one Airfield. Notice that the state column is an icon and a word, and that a Launch in progress shows its own meter.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

The fleet page

One fleet, its hosts and the release each runs. The band says where the fleet stands in one glance; the buttons say what you can do.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

The host page

One host's history and the actions possible right now. Here a host's key changed, so Launchway stops and shows the old and new fingerprints side by side. The only free text in the flow is the reason, and on prod a Clearance would also be asked for.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

Make a fleet

A wizard in five steps. This is "Reach": Pushed or Pulled, then picking the Ramp and the secret by name from what the store lists. Nothing here asks you to paste a key.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

Add hosts

Three ways to add machines: by hand, from an inventory source, or let hosts enroll with a code. This shows by hand, after fetching keys: one fingerprint waits for Confirm, and one host did not answer, with the reason.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

A rolling Launch, host by host

Watch and control a fleet Launch. Each host moves through Drain, Install, Restart, Check and Admit while the other keeps serving. The load balancer panel shows who is in rotation, so you can see that no request is lost.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

A Pathfinder Launch on machines, with weights over time

A stepped Launch to a second group of hosts: two groups, a share for each, steps with timers and a proof at each step. The chart shows the intended weights as steps and the measured weights as a dotted line.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

Return to base on machines

The same confirmation as everywhere, with the one sentence that matters for machines: how the hosts come back, one at a time, with the floor kept. Shown here in the dark theme.

Planned Chapter: Launching to virtual machines and physical servers

Image-based hosts

Hosts that boot a whole operating system image and keep the previous one as the way back. Here, the kiosks in the Harbor Lights shops.

The image-based fleet page

Which image every host booted, which is staged, and which is the way back. Digests are shown short with the release name beside them. Notice the host that returned itself to kiosk-os 6 and says why, and the one that was offline and is simply behind.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

Machine images

The catalog of operating system images in the Depot: digest, Inspection result, signature, boot test and where each runs. An unsigned image cannot launch to prod, and the row says which Standing order stops it.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

Launch an image

A wizard that turns choosing an image into a plan you can read: stage first, then reboot in batches inside the window, with checks after boot. The right side shows the plan as a line and says how much of the window it uses.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

A batch reboot in progress

Watch kiosks reboot into the new image, one store at a time. Each kiosk moves through Drain, Reboot, Booted, Guard checks and Admitted. Notice the offline kiosk that is called out instead of hidden, and the line that says going back is never held by the window.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

An image-based host

The booted image and the way back, side by side. One button goes back to kiosk-os 6 and says what it does in one sentence. Files someone changed by hand are listed so they can be reset or kept in the next image.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

Fleet windows

When the fleet may download and when it may reboot, drawn as a week you can see at a glance. A Standing order can lock the window, and the screen says which one.

Planned Chapter: Launching to image-based hosts

Serverless

Functions on a platform of your own or a public cloud, launched by shifting weights between versions.

Connect a serverless platform

A wizard in five steps; this is the test. It signs in with a short-lived token, reads what the platform allows, and says what Launchway will do because of it. A permission it could not read is a warning, not a silent gap.

Planned Chapter: Launching to serverless

Functions list

Every function and the weights its versions have now, with errors and cost per million calls beside them. A drifted function says what changed and when.

Planned Chapter: Launching to serverless

The function page

One function: which version has what share, how each behaves, and what it costs. Cold starts are shown apart from latency so they are not hidden in an average. When weights drift, the page offers the two honest choices and says Launches wait.

Planned Chapter: Launching to serverless

A serverless Launch

A Launch into a function, step by step: warm the new version, then shift weights with a proof at each step. The chart shows the weights over time, and under it is the instant way back.

Planned Chapter: Launching to serverless

Return to base for a function

The same confirmation, with the serverless promise in its first sentence: the whole way back is a weight change that takes about 3 seconds.

Planned Chapter: Launching to serverless

Traffic and Overwatch

How traffic moves during a Launch, how each version serves it, and what Overwatch decides.

The Launch page: traffic and Overwatch tab

How traffic moved during a Launch, how each version served it, and whether the limits held. The three charts share one time axis with the Launch steps marked, so a change in any line can be read against the step that caused it. A zero-downtime card sits beside the share of traffic.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Radar: one service, per version

The request path drawn from left to right, with requests, errors and latency at each step for each version. A step Radar cannot see is drawn dotted and says what granting a source would add. Shown here in the dark theme.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Overwatch: fail

The verdict first, in one sentence, then what happens next, then the evidence: the new version leaving the stable version's band, and the log patterns that are new. The actions are all here, each with who may use them.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Overwatch: pass and not enough data

Two more results, on a phone. A pass says what held and what happens to the evidence; a watch with too little traffic says so, and waits instead of guessing.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Strategy picker

Choose how a service's Launches spread in an Airfield, without writing a plan file. Strategies the target cannot do are shown unavailable with the reason, and the steps are picked from short lists with a preview as a line.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Schema change in steps

A database change reviewed before it runs and followed along the Route. The expand step is already applied everywhere; the contract step waits, and says which Airfield blocks it and why. A Go is void if the file changes afterwards.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Switch change watch

Turning a Switch on or widening it gets the same verdict as a Launch: users with it on are compared with users with it off. The red button is always there.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Zero-downtime Drill

Run the ready-made drill in a rehearsal Airfield and read it live: load, failed requests, healthy copies against the floor. Stop now is always available and ends every fault.

Planned Chapter: Traffic, zero downtime and Overwatch

Screens: Standing orders, security and evidence

Twenty designs for the governance screens: the rules that judge a change, the people who clear it, the Hold that stops it, the proof it was built safely, and the Logbook and evidence an auditor reads.

  • Every screen follows the chapters on Standing orders, Clearance and Hold; Security and the supply chain and The Logbook and evidence.
  • Words, names and numbers are the running example: the Harbor Lights team, the storefront Flight and the Airfields dev, staging and prod.
  • A secret is only ever a name. Evidence screens say evidence for and supports, never certified.
  • Some frames are dark and some are phones, to show the same screen in each setting.

Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

From the page of rules to the card that asks for Go, and the calendar that says when nothing may launch.

Standing orders area

One place for every rule that judges a change. Notice the three questions each row answers: where it comes from, where it is judged and whether it only reports or really stops.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Add a Standing order

The wizard writes the rule without a file. Notice the rule is picked from a catalog, its numbers are validated against a range and the hint uses a fact from your own Flights.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

A verdict, read by a person

Every rule says in words what it found and what would satisfy it. Notice that the sentence on top is the answer to read first, and that a waived rule shows who waived it and until when.

In progress Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Try this rule

A new rule is replayed on the last 30 days before anyone enforces it. Notice the two denials are named, and that three changes are honestly marked cannot tell because the fact was not recorded then.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Request a waiver

An exception with an owner, a kind and an end date. Notice that the reason is the only typed field; the rest is picked and the end date is capped by the rule.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

The path to production

Six judging points, always the same ones. Notice where the change is now and what each point has already said.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Inheritance down the levels

Rules flow from the Base to the Flight. Notice the lock on the Base's rules and the shop's attempt to loosen one, shown as ignored with the reason.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Clearance card, on a desk

The decision in a few seconds. Notice what, who and why come first, the evidence is one line of chips, and the typed fields are picked from lists, never free text.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Hold calendar

See and set when nothing may launch. Notice the Hold band reaches across the days it covers, the panel names the scope and who may lift it, and Return to base stays open.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Return to base during a Hold

The way back is always open. Notice the green line that says nothing judges it, and that the reason is picked from a list.

Planned Standing orders, Clearance and Hold

Security and the supply chain

What was found, what was built and signed, and where a secret lives without ever being shown.

Inspection findings for a change

The verdict comes first, then the proof. Notice new findings are separated from old ones, that only the new one blocks, and that an unfinished check is never shown as clean.

In progress Security and the supply chain

The supply chain of one release

One line from commit to every target. Notice each link has its record, the second check happens where the thing runs, and the failure names its reason.

Planned Security and the supply chain

Trust policy

Which images may run. Notice the key that expires soon, and the report mode that counts what it would have refused.

Planned Security and the supply chain

Secrets screen

A reference is picked from a list of names. Notice every row says Never shown, and the store with no allow-list is flagged rather than hidden.

Planned Security and the supply chain

Station hardening

Each promise is Enforced, Recorded only or Not enforced. Notice the one red row and the step that fixes it.

Planned Security and the supply chain

The Logbook and evidence

The record, the pack made from it, and the views an auditor is given.

The Logbook

Every action is one row; one row opens in full. Notice the chain state on top, the path each request came by, and the hash and checkpoint that make an entry provable.

In progress The Logbook and evidence

Evidence pack for release 2.4.0

The page an assessor asks for, made from the record. Notice each section is a sentence plus a link to the event it came from, and that the one waiver is shown rather than buried.

Planned The Logbook and evidence

Evidence mapped to a framework

Controls and evidence, in honest words. Notice the label at the top, a control that is off with who turned it off, and a row that is simply your own work.

Planned The Logbook and evidence

The auditor's read-only view

What an outside auditor sees: evidence and nothing to change. Notice the access dates, the absence of buttons and that their reading is itself logged.

Export evidence

Screens: modules

What the module screens of Launchway are meant to look like, drawn in the product’s own interface, for code and review, the Depot, Switches, the software graph, work tracking, the Wingman and Radar.

  • Every screen belongs to one module and says what serves it: the built-in default or a connection.
  • Each shows a thing that is new in the plan: the merge queue, a digest promoted across Airfields, a Switch watched after a change, a vulnerability followed to a patched Launch.
  • Status chips match the chapters, so a screen that is only a design says Planned.
  • Some frames are dark and some are phone-sized, to show the same screens in other settings.

Code and review

A pull request with its Sortie results, preview and place in the queue

The change’s launch line, the results of its Sortie, a preview address and its place in the merge queue all sit on one page. Notice that the one thing it is waiting for is written as a sentence.

Planned Chapter: Code and review

The merge queue

Where each queued change stands and why, with the batch being tested together. Notice that a failed batch is split rather than holding everything up.

Planned Chapter: Code and review

The same pull request on a phone

The launch line turns vertical and the actions become full-width buttons, so someone on call can see where a change stands.

Planned Chapter: Code and review

Screens: speed, branching and reports

What it will look like to ship fast, branch the way you already work, and open a report you actually want to share: where the time went, how a branching pattern is recognized and changed, and one report for every Sortie and every release.

  • Every screen is drawn in the product's own look with the Harbor Lights team: the storefront Flight, the billing and kiosk-os Flights, and the Airfields dev, staging and prod.
  • All of these are designs. Each carries its status and a link to the chapter it illustrates.
  • The release report is the centerpiece: one file that shows what changed, what was tested, who cleared it, where it launched and how it behaved.
  • Several screens are shown in the dark theme, and the release report also on a phone.

Milestones

The fifteen existing milestones stay as they are, in name, number and timing; this chapter shows, milestone by milestone, what the plan adds to each, what it changes and moves, which statuses it asks you to correct, and what “done” then means.

  • The roadmap holds 616 items today. This plan proposes 307 new ones, changes 127, moves 19 between groups or milestones, and asks for 26 status corrections, for 923 items in all. Nothing is removed and no value is narrowed.
  • 15 new groups give a home to themes that were spread or missing: run forms, triggers, the record, testing pipelines, import, speed, branching, Standing orders (policies and repository standards), Switches (feature toggles), serverless, Station (runner) hardening, insight and the phone. One group with no items left is retired.
  • 7 new area pages are proposed, so each new theme has a page that explains it in depth.
  • Every status correction, every move out of the Now milestone and every item that rests on an open question is marked for you. The roadmap rule stands: Available means merged, tested and documented, and order is by value, not by date.

Words on this page

The roadmap uses the product’s own words, each shown here once with its plain word: Base (installation), Wing (organization), Squadron (team), Flight (codebase), Sortie (run), Ramp (runner pool), Patrol (schedule), Airfield (environment), Launch (deployment), Pathfinder (canary), Overwatch (watch after a Launch), Return to base (rollback), Clearance (approval) with Go and No-go, Hold (freeze), Abort (emergency stop), Preflight (checks), Inspection (security scan), Maintenance (dependency updates), Drill (chaos test), Cargo (artifact), Depot (registry), Master switch (kill switch), Formation (releases that go together), Flight plan (ready-made whole pipeline), Maneuver (reusable step template), Hangar (the built-in library), Detachment (the small program on the customer’s side), Hardpoints (extension points), Logbook (audit trail), Debrief (test report), Tower (home), Radar (monitoring), Wingman (helper and AI helper); roles Commander, Controller, Pilot and Observer. Three words are proposed by this plan and need your yes: Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it), Route (the ordered Airfields a release flies through) and Envelope (a service’s measured healthy limits).

What this chapter is

The reconciliation of every roadmap proposal made by the chapters of this plan with the roadmap as it stands. The full change list, with every item in the roadmap’s own shape, is plan-notes/roadmap-changes.json; this page is its readable form. Nothing here is applied to the product’s roadmap until the owner says so.

Decision needed

Milestone 2 grows from 69 to 190 items, more than any other milestone, because most of the authoring layer lands in it. This plan does not split it; a concrete split is proposed in Should Milestone 2 be split? for you to decide.

Should Milestone 2 be split?

Milestone 2 holds 190 items after this plan, in 14 groups. One milestone of that size cannot be “done” in any useful sense: its six done-means lines would wait on the slowest of 190 items. A split along the lines the order of work already builds would let each part finish and be declared done on its own. Nothing is moved by this proposal; every item keeps its title, group and status, and the groups are only regrouped under three numbers.

2BBring everything with you, and start it any wayBring work in from any system; Move off a self-hosted automation server; What starts a Sortie38Stage 3Import and triggers both translate other systems into Launchway’s model and share the trust rules and the filter language.

AllMilestone 2 today14 groups190
  • If you split it: the three parts keep the number 2 with a letter (2A, 2B, 2C), so no other milestone is renumbered and every address of an item stays the same; each part gets its own promise and done means, drawn from today’s six lines and the lines this plan adds.
  • If you keep it whole: nothing changes; the order of work still builds it in stages 2, 3 and 7, and the milestone is done only when all three are.
  • Other ways to cut it are possible, for example moving import into its own milestone and leaving the rest; the proposal above follows the stages because that is how the work will actually finish.

Open question Not decided here.

How the milestones build on each other

Solid arrows are the dependencies the roadmap already records (each milestone’s “builds on”). Dotted arrows are dependencies this plan adds: items in the later milestone now need items in the earlier one.

One dependency runs against the roadmap’s timing: Milestone 2’s “Only what a change can affect is built and tested” needs “One dependency graph, with where each link came from” from Milestone 5, which is marked Later. That item is already In progress by the guides’ evidence (see the status corrections), so the dependency is real but not blocked. Milestones 9, 10 and 11 are drawn as one box to keep the picture readable; each keeps its own number and page.

Status corrections

26 items carry a status the chapters’ evidence does not support. 5 are marked Available but are not yet usable as the roadmap promises; 3 are marked Planned but are documented as built; the rest are marked Planned but are partly built. Each is listed under its milestone below with the evidence. None changes until you confirm it, because the roadmap’s rule is that Available means merged, tested and documented.

  • Machine and image-based host delivery (VM deploys, Delivery to machines over SSH, Image-based hosts): built and tested in code, but the server refuses to schedule a fleet step inside a Sortie, so it runs only from a Station’s command line, outside the Airfield lock, the record, Clearance and Standing orders. Proposed: In progress until a scheduled, recorded and gated Sortie can run it. The top-level available entry “Delivery to machines” follows.
  • The Depot (A built-in OCI registry, The Depot: one area for everything stored): the values promise a conformance pass, a proxy cache and replication that the registry guide says are not done. The chapter proposed narrowing the values; this list keeps the values whole and proposes In progress instead.
  • Built but marked Planned: Tokens and scoped access; A converter and a move-over guide; Re-run only what failed are documented as built (proposed Available); 18 more items in code review, import, delivery, Switches and the software graph are documented as partly built (proposed In progress).

One new item is proposed as Available: “Launchway’s own metrics and traces, exported”, which the chapter found built and documented but on no roadmap item. It too waits for your confirmation.

Duplicates resolved

Where two chapters proposed the same thing, it is proposed once and every sentence of both is kept.

  • Build network that allows what builds need and shows what it refused (Stations and where work runs): Duplicate of the security chapter's "Builds reach what they need, and every refused connection shows"; merged into that item (Milestone 12, Hardening every Station), keeping every sentence of both.
  • Return to base never waits for a Station (Stations and where work runs): Merged into "Return to base that nothing can block" (Milestone 8); its Ramp-room and no-pickup-wait rules are in that item's value and detail.
  • Return to base never waits for a Clearance (Standing orders, Clearance and Hold): Merged into "Return to base that nothing can block". Its Clearance half stands only if you remove the require_approval setting, so the merged item states that part as a decision still to be made (see owner_dependent).
  • Cluster admission rules from Standing orders (Launching to Kubernetes): Duplicate of "Cluster admission generated from Standing orders"; merged into it in the new Milestone 3 group Standing orders: one choke point, no side doors, with the per-namespace, signed-statement and emergency-path detail kept.
  • Clearances that ask for values (Inputs and run forms): Duplicate of "Clearances that show what they clear and ask for typed fields"; merged, keeping the quorum and record rules.
  • A merge judged by the same Standing orders as a Launch (Code and review): Duplicate of "Standing orders judged when a change merges"; merged into it in Milestone 3, with the required-merge evidence and the Clearance-shaped review approval kept. A Milestone 1 placement was proposed; the merge point joins the one choke-point group so Standing orders have one home.
  • One sandbox profile on every executor (Security and the supply chain): Same work as finishing the existing In progress item "Steps run in a sandbox"; carried as a change to that item (its sentences added to the detail) rather than a second item.
  • Canonical shared items: A lockfile for everything a pipeline borrows, Checks a shared step or template must pass, and Built-in steps on the one step contract were each proposed by two chapters (Capabilities, connections and Hardpoints and Reuse that keeps growing) and appear once, with both details joined. The changes two chapters made to Update notices for shared libraries, Expressions for conditions, the two tamper-evident audit items, Retention, legal hold and encryption at rest, A built-in secret store and Preview environments are each combined into one detail.

Changes to the roadmap’s frame

  • Vision: sentence 1 becomes “Launchway launches applications into the future: one place to host your code, build it, test it, scan it and launch it to wherever it runs …”; sentences 2 and 3 stay word for word, so the vision is still three sentences.
  • Principles: six are added (one expression language, written one way; logic is tested code and YAML holds only glue; one launch model for every place software runs; pick, do not type; built in by default, a connection is an equal choice; original answers, no other product named). All seventeen existing principles stay word for word; whether to reword “Everything optional, with built-in defaults” is open for the owner.
  • Who Launchway is for: a fifth card, the larger company, after the four that come first, as the roadmap’s own note already intends.
  • Where Launchway stands today: three “not there yet” lines (one launch model for every kind of target, run forms that offer choices, one expression language). The first is rewritten from its chapter’s draft so it agrees with the status corrections above.
  • The build queue: not changed here. The order of work sets out where each of its eight items sits and lists every difference as a decision for you.

What does not change

  • No milestone is renamed, renumbered or retimed; Now, Next and Later stay as they are.
  • No item is removed and no value is narrowed; where a chapter proposed a narrower value, the value is kept and the status corrected instead.
  • No existing title changes, so every address on the roadmap keeps working.
  • Existing items keep their area pages; only new items use the new ones.

Done means:

  • A repository can be created, cloned, pushed to, reviewed and merged in Launchway, and a deliberate failure of a server during a push never loses an acknowledged push.
  • A written acceptance suite for hosting passes, including importing from another host.
  • A pull request on a connected host receives a status from Launchway and cannot be merged when the Sortie fails.
  • Every pipeline feature in the milestone has a reference page and a worked example.
  • Every setting introduced has a command, an API call, an agent tool and a Terraform resource, checked by a test.
  • A new user can complete setup from Home without editing a file.
  • New in this plan A run form offers real branches, tags, Depot images and Airfields, and one server check applies the same input rules to every way in, proven by the parity test, which now has a web column.
  • New in this plan Every status correction proposed for this milestone has been confirmed or refused by you, so the page says only what is true.
  • New in this plan Every installation, from a laptop to a cluster, takes scheduled backups and passes a restore drill, and the HTTP API is published as a description tools can read.

Milestone 2: Deeper pipeline power, and a way off self-hosted automation servers

Next Pipeline power

Promise
Pipelines can be as dynamic as real code needs, and a team running an automation server can move its jobs without losing what it relies on.

Done means:

  • A custom step in at least three languages runs from a published contract and is unit-tested outside Launchway.
  • A generated pipeline is checked against the same schema and policy as a written one.
  • Expressions are checked before a Sortie and have no loops or side effects.
  • The designer and the text editor produce identical files for identical pipelines.
  • The gap analysis lists every gap with a test, and each gap is closed or recorded as a decision.
  • Stations on virtual machines update under policy without manual work.
  • New in this plan A pipeline can be flown in the Simulator and a pipeline change replayed against past Sorties before it merges; every condition says before a Sortie whether it will run and afterwards why it did not.
  • New in this plan Every trigger kind is declared with the pipeline and has its trust rules before it ships, and every saved event filter has been translated and run side by side before its source switches.
  • New in this plan An import of each supported format produces a pipeline and a findings list on the record, and a pipeline with open findings cannot launch.
  • New in this plan Every Sortie shows where its time went, and a pipeline over its speed budget is reported like a failing test.
  • New in this plan Every kind of decision in the event catalog carries its reasons, checked by a test in the build, and one Debrief report per Sortie is a single file with no script.

Done means:

  • An application, a virtual machine and an image-based host can each be deployed, verified and returned to base from the interface.
  • A failed deployment shows a diagnosis, its evidence and the full resource tree with logs.
  • Pathfinder weights by client type work on the gateway and on a mesh, and the map shows them.
  • State for infrastructure code is stored, locked and recoverable inside Launchway.
  • Toggles, settings and secrets resolve per zone with one clear rule.
  • Every lever change goes through preview, policy and audit, with an undo.
  • New in this plan Standing orders are judged when a change merges, when a Sortie starts, before a Launch, before an image push and when a setting changes, and no deploy step goes around a Hold.
  • New in this plan A fleet Launch to machines and to image-based hosts runs inside a Sortie, scheduled by the server, under the Airfield lock, Standing orders, Clearance and Overwatch, and records which host booted which digest.
  • New in this plan A branching pattern is recognized from a repository’s history, and a move to another pattern is replayed in the Simulator before it is offered.

Done means:

  • The same plan runs a progressive rollout on Kubernetes, with every Argo Rollouts strategy covered and shown.
  • A seeded bad release is stopped and returned within the time the plan states, and a seeded good one is promoted, in the rehearsal Airfield and in the automated tests.
  • After the last step, the watch returns to the last stable state when signals worsen, and a Return to base after a success works from the interface, the API, the agent endpoint and the command line.
  • A toggle that causes errors is switched back automatically, and a configuration or secret change can be rolled and returned by a plan.
  • Every Argo CD application and its tree are visible, with a plain-language diagnosis for the common failures.
  • No control is offered that cannot work, and every control says what it will do and who may press it.
  • New in this plan Every Launch records whether it kept its zero-downtime promise, against a floor of healthy copies and the failed-request baseline.
  • New in this plan A Return to base is never held by a lock, a Hold, a limit or a busy Station, proven by tests that try each.
  • New in this plan A serverless Launch creates a version by digest and returns by moving weights back; an image-based host boots back by itself on a failed check, even offline.
  • New in this plan Continuous deployment to production happens only where every Standing order allows it, and each remaining Clearance shows the evidence for keeping it.
  • New in this plan A Return to base can be started by the break-glass path while Launchway itself is down, in a rehearsed test.

The order of work

Launchway is built in nine stages, each standing on a foundation that is finished, tested and true before the next stage starts, beginning with the safety of what already exists and ending with the hosted service opened to strangers.

  • Stage 1 makes the ground solid: upgrades that cannot half-apply, the same sandbox on every Station (runner) and executor, tests over the code that runs untrusted steps and signs people in, signatures checked at every Launch (deployment), the one record, and a roadmap whose status is true.
  • Then the language layer (typed outputs, one expression language, tested custom steps, the Simulator and run forms), then triggers and import, then one launch model for every kind of target, then traffic and zero downtime, governance, speed and quality, the modules, and last the hosted service’s wall and sign-up.
  • Every stage ends with exit criteria a person can check: tests that pass, a measured result, a document. A stage that has not met them does not hand its work on.
  • The existing eight-item build queue is reconciled item by item. Where this order differs from it, the difference is listed as a decision for you, not made here.

Words on this page

Each product word is shown once with its plain word: Base (installation), Wing (organization), Squadron (team), Flight (codebase), Sortie (run), Ramp (runner pool), Airfield (environment), Pathfinder (canary), Overwatch (watch after a Launch), Return to base (rollback), Clearance (approval) with Go and No-go, Hold (freeze), Abort (emergency stop), Master switch (kill switch), Standing orders (policies and repository standards), Inspection (security scan), Depot (registry), Switch (feature toggle), Formation (releases that go together), Flight plan (ready-made whole pipeline), Hangar (the built-in library), Detachment (the small program on the customer’s side), Logbook (audit trail), Debrief (test report), Drill (chaos test), Wingman (helper and AI helper), Patrol (schedule). Three words are proposed and need your yes: Simulator (testing a pipeline without flying it), Route (the ordered Airfields a release flies through) and Envelope (a service’s measured healthy limits).

Where the order starts from

The roadmap already says how it is built. Its principles set the bar every stage below is held to:

  • High availability and security are part of done. “A feature says what happens when a server, the database or a Station dies, and who may do what, before it merges.”
  • Honest status. “An item is available only when it is merged, tested and documented. Order is by value and is not a schedule.”
  • Security first. “Everything Launchway holds is encrypted at rest, every part runs with least privilege, and the secure choice is the default.”
  • Boring upgrades. “One binary and a database, additive migrations, an older binary running on a newer schema, and Return to base by image.”

And it has a build queue, “after what is already in flight, in this order”:

  1. The wall between Bases, then sign-up.
  2. The upgrade gate and network detection.
  3. Works alongside a hosted code host.
  4. Delivery by choice.
  5. The Depot as one area.
  6. Editor plug-ins and one-step setup for agent tools.
  7. Agents that deliver, natively.
  8. Windows and macOS runners.

The chapters of this plan found that several things the queue takes for granted are not finished: machine and image-based host delivery is built in code but not scheduled by the server (Launching to virtual machines and physical servers, Launching to image-based hosts); the declared host and write lists of a custom step are not enforced on Kubernetes and the host executor enforces nothing (Stations and where work runs, Security and the supply chain); signatures are stored but never verified at Launch; the upgrade gate is still being finished (The system); events live in four streams with no common shape (The record); and 26 items on the roadmap carry a status their own guides contradict (Milestones). The order below therefore starts underneath the queue.

Decision needed

This order is a proposal. You decide the order: “we decide together”, and you decide. Every place it departs from the existing queue is listed in Reconciled with the build queue.

The stages and how they depend on each other

What can proceed in parallel

  • Inside stage 1, five tracks share no code and run at once: the upgrade gate; Station and executor hardening; signatures and digests at Launch; the event catalog; and making the roadmap’s status true.
  • After stage 1, stage 2 (authoring) and the first half of stage 4 run side by side: built-in chart and manifest deploys and the server scheduling fleet steps need only stage 1’s record, digests and verification. Routes, which carry conditions at each stop, wait for stage 2’s expression language.
  • Stage 6 needs the record (stage 1) and the expression language (stage 2), not the targets; the merge point and the evidence packs can be built beside stages 4 and 5.
  • Stage 5 follows stage 4 one target at a time: Kubernetes first, then fleets, image-based hosts and serverless, each as its target becomes a scheduled Launch.
  • Stage 8’s modules are independent of each other once their own dependencies are met, and are the natural place for work in parallel by more than one team.
  • Nothing in stage 9 starts its outward-facing part before stages 1 and 6 are done; its inward work (tests of the wall) can run as its own track earlier if you keep the wall first in the queue.

The nine stages

Each stage lists its goal, what is built (by the roadmap’s exact titles, with new items marked), what is deliberately not built yet, the exit criteria, the risks it retires, and the chapters that design it.

Stage 1. A solid, secure foundation

Now Goal: what Launchway already does is safe to run, safe to upgrade and safe to return, and the roadmap says only what is true.

Built
Upgrades that cannot half-apply: The upgrade gate In progress, with the release gate run against a real GitOps controller and a second network plugin; An upgrade preview New in this plan; Install and upgrade never need hand-made network fixes Planned (the queue’s network detection).
Hardening owed on every Station and executor: Steps run in a sandbox In progress, finished as one sandbox profile on every executor; Every Station proves who it is New in this plan; Builds reach what they need, and every refused connection shows New in this plan; Builds never take room from the platform New in this plan; Access, blast radius and default stated before a capability ships New in this plan.
Tests over the code that runs untrusted steps and signs people in: a coverage floor on the packages that run steps, hold secrets and sign people in, enforced by the build’s quality gates, plus escape tests on each executor. This is engineering work under the existing Available item Quality gates, not a new roadmap item.
Signature checks at Launch: Signing and verification In progress, finished for Kubernetes first; Provenance and contents verified before every Launch New in this plan, Kubernetes first; Digests on every Launch record New in this plan.
The one record, first stage: One common event format and one catalog for every event New in this plan; A decision without reasons fails the build New in this plan.
Status made true: the 26 status corrections in Milestones confirmed or refused; the area pages that disagree with the roadmap data (the cross-check found eighteen such places) corrected; the top-level available list matched to the items.
Added by the coverage review: Scheduled backups with a restore drill, on any installation; A published support window between the server and its Stations New in this plan; and Build provenance, level two now and three next Planned, extended.
Not built yet
No new authoring features, no new kind of target, no new trigger kind, no new module, no second Base turned on, no sign-up. Existing behavior only gets safer.
Exit criteria
  1. An upgrade and a Return to base by image pass in the release gate against a real GitOps controller and on a second network plugin; a test stops the upgrade at every migration step and the installation is left on the old version or the new one, never between.
  2. Escape tests run in the build on each executor (containers, Kubernetes, and the host executor, which shared Ramps refuse): a custom step reaches only the hosts it declared, writes only the paths it declared, and sees only its own secrets; every refused connection appears on the Sortie.
  3. No Ramp accepts the shared join token by default; an existing installation is warned and given a guided move to a key per Station.
  4. The coverage floor on the step-running, secret and sign-in packages is met and the build fails below it.
  5. In a test on Kubernetes, an unsigned image, an image signed by the wrong key and an image with no build record are each refused at Launch, and every Launch record carries the digest of what it launched.
  6. The event catalog is published, and the build fails when a decision kind lacks its reasons.
  7. Every roadmap status matches the code and its guide; the roadmap build passes with the corrected data.
  8. A measured week of production that counts as “solid, stable production” (proposed: no lost step, no platform restart caused by a build, one restore rehearsed, one upgrade and one Return to base performed).
  9. The threat model and the trust-model page are updated for the sandbox profile, Station identity and verification at Launch.
  10. A restore drill passes on a laptop, a single server and a cluster installation, from a scheduled backup, and a Station outside the published support window is refused with a plain message.
Risks retired
A half-applied upgrade; a build escaping its sandbox or reading another step’s secrets; a Station pretending to be another; an image nobody built reaching production; a busy day of builds starving the servers or the database; a roadmap that claims what the code does not do; a decision nobody can explain.
Chapters
The system, Stations and where work runs, Security and the supply chain, The record, One way to launch, anywhere, The Depot, Milestones.
Decision needed

Three exit criteria rest on open questions: the coverage floor numbers (the code-health audit proposed 70 percent for new packages and 80 percent for the security packages, unanswered); the definition of “solid, stable production” as a measured week (proposed in the order document of the design repository, unanswered); and the default allow-set for builds by category (recommended yes, unanswered). Until you answer, stage 1 uses the proposals and says so.

  1. One corpus of expressions gives identical verdicts in the editor, in launchway validate and on the server, in a test.

  7. Each feature has a reference page and a worked example.

What a first working slice looks like

The smallest end-to-end path through the running example, using only what exists today plus stage 1 and the first run form of stage 2. It follows a release of storefront, owned by the Squadron “shop” of the Wing “Harbor Lights”, from a commit to prod and back.

  1. Mia pushes a fix to main of storefront. The push trigger (available today) starts a Sortie; the start is an event in the catalog with its reason.
  2. The steps run on a Station that proved who it is with its own key, inside the one sandbox profile: the build step reaches the Go module proxy and the Depot, and a refused call to an unknown address is shown on the Sortie (stage 1).
  3. The image is built rootless, scanned, signed and pushed to the Depot with its build record and parts list (available today). The step’s typed output is the image digest.
  4. Mia opens the run form of the release pipeline. It offers the images the last green builds made and the Airfields she may launch to; she picks, she does not type (stage 2, first run form).
  5. Standing orders are judged before the Launch (available today). The Launch to staging goes through the GitOps path (available today); before anything is applied, the signature and build record of the digest are verified against the Base’s trust policy (stage 1). The Launch record carries the digest.
  6. Verification after the deploy reads the metrics and passes (available today). Sam, a Controller, gives Go on the decision card on his phone (available today); Mia, who started the Sortie, cannot clear its production Launch.
  7. The Launch to prod rolls out with a Pathfinder at 10 percent. Overwatch sees checkout errors above the baseline and returns to base by itself (available today), with the evidence on the record.
  8. Every step above is an event with its reasons, so “what happened to this release” is one thread, and the roadmap shows the status each piece really has.
Built today

Steps 1, 3, 5 (the GitOps Launch and Standing orders), 6 and 7 use items the roadmap lists as Available. The slice needs stage 1 for the hardened Station, verification at Launch and the event catalog, and stage 2 only for the run form. That makes it the first proof that the foundation holds, not a new feature.

Launchway platform plan

Coverage: nothing lost

For each of 369 capabilities that teams rely on in build and delivery tools, this page says whether this plan designs Launchway’s answer, whether that answer is better, equal or behind, where it is designed, which roadmap item carries it, and whether it exists yet.

  • 369 capabilities in 30 themes were checked strictly against the chapters: a mention is not coverage; only a design counts.
  • Before the fixes: 251 designed, 97 partly, 21 not at all; 69 behind. After the fixes written into the chapters: 366 designed, 3 partly, 0 not at all; 6 behind.
  • Designed is not built. After the fixes 86 capabilities are available today, 30 in progress and 250 planned.
  • 8 rows are still short, listed honestly below; 5 of them are deliberate choices to connect rather than build.

What was checked, and how

The list of capabilities was drawn from what teams rely on across the major build and delivery tools, written in plain words and grouped into 30 themes. No capability is tied to one product, and none of their names appear here: each row describes what a team needs, not how someone else provides it.

Each row was then checked against the chapters of this plan with one strict rule: a mention is not coverage. A capability counts as designed only when a chapter says how it works: the objects, the behavior, what is recorded, and what happens on failure. A table row that names it, a scenario that assumes it, or a roadmap title without a design counts as “partly” at best.

Designed
Yes: a chapter designs it. Partly: some of it is designed, or it is only named. No: no chapter answers it.
Level
Better: Launchway’s answer does more, or does it more safely, than what teams rely on today. Matches: it does the same job. Behind: it does less, or nothing yet.
Status
The roadmap’s three states: Available (merged, tested, documented), In progress, Planned. A row with no roadmap item at all says Not on the roadmap. When part of a capability exists and the rest is planned, the row takes the less advanced state and says “part available”.

The first check found gaps. Writers then added designs to the chapters and proposed roadmap items for them. Each fix was accepted here only after its design was found under a heading in a chapter, and the row now links to that heading. 133 rows were closed by a fix found in a chapter, and 2 more by a decision a chapter now records. Where a fix was proposed but no design could be found, the row keeps its first verdict (5 rows).

Three rules turn a found fix into a new verdict. Designed becomes yes. A level of “behind” becomes “matches”, never “better”, because a design on paper has not yet proved more. Status becomes the least advanced of the old status and the status of the items the fix added, so a capability that was available and gained planned work reads “Planned (part available)”.

Not yet checked twice

The after-fix verdicts rest on finding each fix’s design under its heading, not on a second strict reading of every design. A second pass by a fresh reader would make the numbers firmer.

The story: The principles

Designed is not the same as built. Of the rows now designed, most are planned; the theme tables show each one’s status, and the Milestones page shows where each item sits.

Deliberate non-goals: connected, not built

Launchway’s rule for building in house: a capability is built when it sits on every pipeline’s path, when a solo developer needs it on day one, or when the common part is small enough to do well and the alternatives are costly. Deep specialties are connected well instead of replaced: the connection is designed, its results land on the one record, and one provider is in charge of each capability. These are the choices the chapters make, with their reasons.

Not builtWhat Launchway does insteadWhyChapter
A durable workflow engine for code-first business workflows at very large scaleA step starts a workflow on an outside engine and waits for its answer without holding a Station.A pipeline is for changing software; its guarantees (one record, one step contract, Return to base) are not those of a business workflow engine.Serverless: Durable workflows: not a goal, and how a step uses one
What starts a Sortie: Pipeline to pipeline: start another and wait for its answer
A second API style with graph queriesThe software graph’s own routes, and an HTTP API that lets a caller pick the fields and related objects an answer carries (a design, not built).It would double the routes the parity test, the permission checks and the Logbook must cover, for answers the HTTP API can already give.Every way in: Ways in we do not add, and why
Pipelines and Sorties as objects in your cluster’s APISettings through a settings repository that a GitOps controller applies, or through the infrastructure-as-code provider; Sorties started by the command line, the API or a trigger.Pipelines live in Git with the code; a cluster-object way in would be a sixth way in with its own permission model.Every way in: Ways in we do not add, and why
An error trackerConnects the tracker you have as a signal source, one in charge per Squadron (team); new error groups become an Overwatch proof tied to the Launch, digest and pull request.Grouping crashes and keeping their stacks is a deep specialty.Radar, insight and keeping it healthy: Errors from your error tracker, judged per Launch
Rules over cloud resourcesFindings from a cloud-rules tool arrive through the events-in Hardpoint (extension point) into the one findings list, linked to owners by the software graph.A deep specialty with rule engines of its own; none of the tests for building in house holds.Radar, insight and keeping it healthy: One home, seven slots
Protection of a running application from attacksThe team’s tool posts findings; each is tied to the digest serving at that moment and its owner, and can refuse a new digest that still carries the named component.A deep specialty; a second product would not be better than the one a team runs.Security and the supply chain: Findings from what runs in production
Models, and code completion and chat in the editorHosted providers through adapters, or local models on your machines; editor assistants are fed facts through the agent endpoint and instruction files.Models are always outside Launchway’s code; editor assistants already exist.The Wingman and agents: Built in, connected, or both
End-to-end tests written in natural language, and evaluation tools for your own AI applicationsThe team’s tool runs as a step against a preview Airfield; its report is read by the Debrief (test report) and gated like any test.A deep specialty; the gate and the report are what Launchway adds.The Wingman and agents: Built in, connected, or both
Quality, reports and the Debrief: AI evaluation results as a gate
Guardrails for your applications’ model trafficLeft out.A different product for a different buyer.The Wingman and agents: Built in, connected, or both

A non-goal is still a choice you can revisit. Each is recorded in its chapter with the connection that replaces it, so a team moving to Launchway knows on day one what it keeps outside.
